They looked at the pictures in the gardening books and Dickon knew all the flowers by their country names and knew exactly which ones were already growing in the secret garden.

“I couldna’ say that there name,” he said, pointing to one under which was written “Aquilegia,” “but us calls that a columbine, an’ that there one it’s a snapdragon and they both grow wild in hedges, but these is garden ones an’ they’re bigger an’ grander. There’s some big clumps o’ columbine in th’ garden. They’ll look like a bed o’ blue an’ white butterflies flutterin’ when they’re out.”

But they were obliged to wait more than a week because first there came some very windy days and then Colin was threatened with a cold, which two things happening one after the other would no doubt have thrown him into a rage but that there was so much careful and mysterious planning to do and almost every day Dickon came in, if only for a few minutes, to talk about what was happening on the moor and in the lanes and hedges and on the borders of streams. The things he had to tell about otters’ and badgers’ and water-rats’ houses, not to mention birds’ nests and field-mice and their burrows, were enough to make you almost tremble with excitement when you heard all the intimate details from an animal charmer and realized with what thrilling eagerness and anxiety the whole busy underworld was working.
“They’re same as us,” said Dickon, “only they have to build their homes every year. An’ it keeps ’em so busy they fair scuffle to get ’em done.”

The most absorbing thing, however, was the preparations to be made before Colin could be transported with sufficient secrecy to the garden. No one must see the chair-carriage and Dickon and Mary after they turned a certain corner of the shrubbery and entered upon the walk outside the ivied walls. As each day passed, Colin had become more and more fixed in his feeling that the mystery surrounding the garden was one of its greatest charms. Nothing must spoil that. No one must ever suspect that they had a secret. People must think that he was simply going out with Mary and Dickon because he liked them and did not object to their looking at him. They had long and quite delightful talks about their route. They would go up this path and down that one and cross the other and go round among the fountain flower-beds as if they were looking at the “bedding-out plants” the head gardener, Mr. Roach, had been having arranged. That would seem such a rational thing to do that no one would think it at all mysterious. They would turn into the shrubbery walks and lose themselves until they came to the long walls. It was almost as serious and elaborately thought out as the plans of march made by great generals in time of war.

Rumors of the new and curious things which were occurring in the invalid’s apartments had of course filtered through the servants’ hall into the stable yards and out among the gardeners, but notwithstanding this, Mr. Roach was startled one day when he received orders from Master Colin’s room to the effect that he must report himself in the apartment no outsider had ever seen, as the invalid himself desired to speak to him.
“Well, well,” he said to himself as he hurriedly changed his coat, “what’s to do now? His Royal Highness that wasn’t to be looked at calling up a man he’s never set eyes on.”

Mr. Roach was not without curiosity. He had never caught even a glimpse of the boy and had heard a dozen exaggerated stories about his uncanny looks and ways and his insane tempers. The thing he had heard oftenest was that he might die at any moment and there had been numerous fanciful descriptions of a humped back and helpless limbs, given by people who had never seen him.
“Things are changing in this house, Mr. Roach,” said Mrs. Medlock, as she led him up the back staircase to the corridor on to which opened the hitherto mysterious chamber.
paragraphsZh: 当他说话的时候，烟灰庄严地从开着的窗户里飞进飞出，叽叽喳喳地谈论着风景，而坚果和贝壳则在外面的大树上游览，在树干上跑来跑去，探索树枝。船长蜷缩在迪肯身边，而迪肯则偏爱坐在壁炉边的地毯上。
他们查看了园艺书籍中的图片，迪肯知道所有花朵的国名，并且确切地知道秘密花园中已经种植了哪些花朵。
“我说不出那个名字，”他指着下面写着“耧斗菜”的一株说，“但我们管它叫耧斗菜，那儿有一种是金鱼草，它们都在树篱里野生生长，但这些是花园里的，它们更大更宏伟。花园里有一些大丛的耧斗菜。它们看起来就像一张蓝色和白色的床。蝴蝶飞出来的时候就会翩翩起舞。”

但他们不得不等待一个多星期，因为首先是风很大的日子，然后科林受到了感冒的威胁，这两件事接二连三地发生无疑会让他勃然大怒，但有那么多仔细而神秘的计划要做，迪肯几乎每天都会进来，哪怕只有几分钟，谈论荒野、小巷、树篱和溪流边缘发生的事情。他所讲述的关于水獭、獾和水鼠的房子的事情，更不用说鸟巢、田鼠和它们的洞穴了，当你从一个动物魔术师那里听到所有亲密的细节时，足以让你兴奋得几乎颤抖，并意识到整个忙碌的地下世界是多么令人兴奋和焦虑。
“他们和我们一样，”迪肯说，“只是他们每年都必须建造自己的家园。这让他们非常忙碌，他们不得不扭打着完成任务。”

然而，最吸引人的事情是在将科林充分保密地运送到花园之前要做的准备工作。当马车、迪肯和玛丽转过灌木丛的某个角落，进入常春藤墙外的步道后，任何人都不得看到他们。随着时间一天天过去，科林越来越坚信花园周围的神秘是它最大的魅力之一。任何事情都不能破坏这一点。任何人都不能怀疑他们有秘密。人们肯定认为他只是和玛丽和迪肯出去，因为他喜欢他们，并且不反对他们看他。他们就他们的路线进行了长时间而愉快的交谈。他们会沿着这条路走上那条路，穿过另一条路，在喷泉花坛中转来转去，就好像他们在看首席园丁罗奇先生布置的“花坛植物”一样。这似乎是一件非常理性的事情，没有人会认为它很神秘。他们会拐进灌木丛中的小道，然后迷失方向，直到来到长长的墙边。它几乎和战争时期伟大将军制定的行军计划一样严肃和深思熟虑。
关于病人公寓里发生的新奇事情的谣言当然已经从仆人大厅传到了马厩院子里，传到了园丁们中间，但尽管如此，有一天，当罗奇先生收到科林大师房间的命令时，他还是吃了一惊，大意是他必须在没有外人见过的公寓里报告自己，因为病人本人想和他说话。
“好了好了，”他一边自言自语，一边忙着换外套，“现在怎么办？太子殿下这可不是什么好看的，竟然把一个素不相识的人叫来了。”
罗奇先生并非没有好奇心。他从未见过这个男孩，甚至听过十几个关于他怪异的外表、行为方式和疯狂脾气的夸张故事。他最常听到的就是他随时可能死去，还有无数来自从未见过他的人对他驼背和无助的四肢的奇特描述。
“罗奇先生，这所房子里的情况正在发生变化，”梅德洛克夫人一边说，一边领着他走上后楼梯，来到走廊，走廊上打开了迄今为止神秘的房间。

title: The Secret Garden · 选段 2
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: He was a tall boy and a handsome one. He was glowing with life and his running had sent splendid color leaping to his face. He threw the thick hair back from his forehead and lifted a pair of strange gray eyes—eyes full of boyish laughter and rimmed with black lashes like a fringe. It was the eyes which made Mr. Craven gasp for breath.

This was not what Colin had expected—this was not what he had planned. He had never thought of such a meeting. And yet to come dashing out—winning a race—perhaps it was even better. He drew himself up to his very tallest. Mary, who had been running with him and had dashed through the door too, believed that he managed to make himself look taller than he had ever looked before—inches taller.

“Yes,” hurried on Colin. “It was the garden that did it—and Mary and Dickon and the creatures—and the Magic. No one knows. We kept it to tell you when you came. I’m well, I can beat Mary in a race. I’m going to be an athlete.”
He said it all so like a healthy boy—his face flushed, his words tumbling over each other in his eagerness—that Mr. Craven’s soul shook with unbelieving joy.
“Aren’t you glad, Father?” he ended. “Aren’t you glad? I’m going to live forever and ever and ever!”
Mr. Craven put his hands on both the boy’s shoulders and held him still. He knew he dared not even try to speak for a moment.

The place was a wilderness of autumn gold and purple and violet blue and flaming scarlet and on every side were sheaves of late lilies standing together—lilies which were white or white and ruby. He remembered well when the first of them had been planted that just at this season of the year their late glories should reveal themselves. Late roses climbed and hung and clustered and the sunshine deepening the hue of the yellowing trees made one feel that one, stood in an embowered temple of gold. The newcomer stood silent just as the children had done when they came into its grayness. He looked round and round.

It was the strangest thing he had ever heard, Archibald Craven thought, as it was poured forth in headlong boy fashion. Mystery and Magic and wild creatures, the weird midnight meeting—the coming of the spring—the passion of insulted pride which had dragged the young Rajah to his feet to defy old Ben Weatherstaff to his face. The odd companionship, the play acting, the great secret so carefully kept. The listener laughed until tears came into his eyes and sometimes tears came into his eyes when he was not laughing. The Athlete, the Lecturer, the Scientific Discoverer was a laughable, lovable, healthy young human thing.

“Now,” he said at the end of the story, “it need not be a secret any more. I dare say it will frighten them nearly into fits when they see me—but I am never going to get into the chair again. I shall walk back with you, Father—to the house.”

Ben Weatherstaff’s duties rarely took him away from the gardens, but on this occasion he made an excuse to carry some vegetables to the kitchen and being invited into the servants’ hall by Mrs. Medlock to drink a glass of beer he was on the spot—as he had hoped to be—when the most dramatic event Misselthwaite Manor had seen during the present generation actually took place.
paragraphsZh: 他是一个高高的男孩，而且很英俊。他焕发着生命的光彩，他的奔跑让他的脸庞焕发出绚丽的色彩。他把额前浓密的头发甩到脑后，抬起一双奇怪的灰色眼睛——眼睛里充满了孩子气的笑意，周围长着像刘海一样的黑色睫毛。正是那双眼睛让克雷文先生喘不过气来。
这不是科林所预料的——这不是他所计划的。他从来没有想过会有这样的会面。但如果能冲出来——赢得一场比赛——也许那就更好了。他挺直了身子，站到了最高的高度。玛丽一直和他一起跑，也冲进了门，她相信他成功地让自己看起来比以前更高了——高了几英寸。
“是的。”科林急忙说道。 “是花园——以及玛丽、迪肯和生物——还有魔法，做到了这一点。没有人知道。我们保留它是为了在你来的时候告诉你。我很好，我可以在比赛中击败玛丽。我要成为一名运动员。”
他说这一切时就像一个健康的男孩一样——他的脸涨红了，他的话语在他的热切中翻滚——克雷文先生的灵魂因难以置信的喜悦而颤抖。
“你不高兴吗，神父？”他结束了。 “你不高兴吗？我会永远活下去！”
克雷文先生把手放在男孩的肩膀上，让他保持不动。他知道他一刻都不敢说话。
这里是一片秋日金色、紫色、紫蓝色和火红色的旷野，四周都是一束束晚百合花，这些百合花是白色的，或者是白色和红宝石色的。他清楚地记得第一棵树是什么时候种植的，每年的这个季节，它们迟来的辉煌就会显现出来。迟来的玫瑰攀爬、悬挂、聚集，阳光加深了泛黄树木的色调，让人感觉那一朵玫瑰矗立在一座金碧辉煌的寺庙里。新来的人静静地站着，就像孩子们进入灰色世界时一样。他环顾四周。
这是他听过的最奇怪的事情，阿奇博尔德·克雷文想，因为它是以男孩的方式轻率地倾诉出来的。神秘、魔法、野生动物，奇怪的午夜聚会——春天的到来——被侮辱的骄傲的激情，把年轻的拉贾拖了起来，当面反抗老本·威瑟斯塔夫。奇怪的陪伴，戏剧性的表演，以及如此小心保守的伟大秘密。听者笑得泪流满面，有时不笑时也会流泪。运动员、讲师、科学发现者是一个可笑、可爱、健康的年轻人。
“现在，”他在故事的结尾说道，“这不再是秘密了。我敢说，当他们看到我时，他们会吓得几乎要发疯——但我再也不会坐在椅子上了。我会和你一起走回去，父亲——回到房子里。”
本·韦瑟斯塔夫的职责很少让他离开花园，但这一次，他借口搬了一些蔬菜到厨房，并被梅德洛克夫人邀请到仆人大厅喝了一杯啤酒，他当场——正如他所希望的——当米瑟斯韦特庄园当代最戏剧性的事件真正发生时。

title: The Secret Garden · 选段 3
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: And he went through the garden to the villa and ordered Pitcher to prepare for his return to England.

In a few days he was in Yorkshire again, and on his long railroad journey he found himself thinking of his boy as he had never thought in all the ten years past. During those years he had only wished to forget him. Now, though he did not intend to think about him, memories of him constantly drifted into his mind. He remembered the black days when he had raved like a madman because the child was alive and the mother was dead. He had refused to see it, and when he had gone to look at it at last it had been, such a weak wretched thing that everyone had been sure it would die in a few days. But to the surprise of those who took care of it the days passed and it lived and then everyone believed it would be a deformed and crippled creature.

He had not meant to be a bad father, but he had not felt like a father at all. He had supplied doctors and nurses and luxuries, but he had shrunk from the mere thought of the boy and had buried himself in his own misery. The first time after a year’s absence he returned to Misselthwaite and the small miserable looking thing languidly and indifferently lifted to his face the great gray eyes with black lashes round them, so like and yet so horribly unlike the happy eyes he had adored, he could not bear the sight of them and turned away pale as death. After that he scarcely ever saw him except when he was asleep, and all he knew of him was that he was a confirmed invalid, with a vicious, hysterical, half-insane temper. He could only be kept from furies dangerous to himself by being given his own way in every detail.

All this was not an uplifting thing to recall, but as the train whirled him through mountain passes and golden plains the man who was “coming alive” began to think in a new way and he thought long and steadily and deeply.
“Perhaps I have been all wrong for ten years,” he said to himself. “Ten years is a long time. It may be too late to do anything—quite too late. What have I been thinking of!”

Of course this was the wrong Magic—to begin by saying “too late.” Even Colin could have told him that. But he knew nothing of Magic—either black or white. This he had yet to learn. He wondered if Susan Sowerby had taken courage and written to him only because the motherly creature had realized that the boy was much worse—was fatally ill. If he had not been under the spell of the curious calmness which had taken possession of him he would have been more wretched than ever. But the calm had brought a sort of courage and hope with it. Instead of giving way to thoughts of the worst he actually found he was trying to believe in better things.
“Could it be possible that she sees that I may be able to do him good and control him?” he thought. “I will go and see her on my way to Misselthwaite.”

But when on his way across the moor he stopped the carriage at the cottage, seven or eight children who were playing about gathered in a group and bobbing seven or eight friendly and polite curtsies told him that their mother had gone to the other side of the moor early in the morning to help a woman who had a new baby. “Our Dickon,” they volunteered, was over at the Manor working in one of the gardens where he went several days each week.

Mr. Craven looked over the collection of sturdy little bodies and round red-cheeked faces, each one grinning in its own particular way, and he awoke to the fact that they were a healthy likable lot. He smiled at their friendly grins and took a golden sovereign from his pocket and gave it to “our ’Lizabeth Ellen” who was the oldest.
Then amid grins and chuckles and bobbing of curtsies he drove away, leaving ecstasy and nudging elbows and little jumps of joy behind.
paragraphsZh: 然后他穿过花园来到别墅，命令皮彻为返回英格兰做准备。

几天后，他又回到了约克郡，在漫长的铁路旅途中，他发现自己在想念他的儿子，这是他过去十年里从未想到过的。那些年，他只想忘记他。现在，虽然他不想去想他，但关于他的记忆却不断地涌入他的脑海。他记得那些黑暗的日子，他像个疯子一样胡言乱语，因为孩子还活着，而母亲却死了。他拒绝去看它，当他最后去看它时，它已经是一个如此虚弱、可怜的东西，以至于每个人都确信它几天后就会死去。但令那些照顾它的人惊讶的是，日子一天天过去了，它活了下来，然后每个人都相信它会是一个畸形且残废的生物。

他并不是想成为一个坏父亲，但他根本不觉得自己像个父亲。他提供了医生、护士和奢侈品，但他一想到这个男孩就退缩，把自己埋在自己的痛苦之中。阔别一年后，他第一次回到米瑟斯韦特，那只看上去可怜兮兮的小东西，懒洋洋地、漠不关心地把那双灰色的大眼睛举到脸上，周围长着黑色的睫毛，与他所喜爱的那双幸福的眼睛如此相似，却又如此可怕，他无法忍受看到它们，脸色苍白得像死人一样。从那以后，除了他睡着的时候，他几乎再也没有见过他，他只知道他是一个确诊的病人，脾气恶毒、歇斯底里、半疯狂。只有在每一个细节上都按照自己的方式行事，才能避免对自己造成危险的愤怒。
回忆起这一切并不是一件令人振奋的事情，但当火车带着他穿过山口和金色平原时，这个“活过来”的人开始以一种新的方式思考，他思考了很久、稳定而深刻。
“也许十年来我都错了，”他对自己说。 “十年是一段很长的时间。现在做任何事情可能都太晚了——太晚了。我到底在想什么！”
当然，这是错误的魔法——一开始就说“太晚了”。甚至科林也可以告诉他这一点。但他对魔法一无所知——无论是黑魔法还是白魔法。这是他还没有学到的。他想知道苏珊·索尔比是否鼓起勇气给他写信，只是因为这个母性生物意识到这个男孩的情况要糟糕得多——得了致命的病。如果他没有被那种奇怪的平静所吸引，他会比以前更加可怜。但平静也带来了某种勇气和希望。他实际上发现自己并没有屈服于最坏的想法，而是试图相信更好的事情。
“难道她看出我可以为他做好事，控制他？”他想。 “我会在去米瑟斯韦特的路上去看她。”
但在穿越荒原的途中，他把马车停在小屋前，七八个正在玩耍的孩子聚集在一起，友好而礼貌地行了七八个屈膝礼，告诉他，他们的母亲一早就去了荒原的另一边，去帮助一个刚刚生了孩子的妇女。他们自告奋勇说，“我们的迪肯”正在庄园的一个花园里工作，他每周都会去那里几天。
克雷文先生看着这群健壮的小身躯和红润的圆脸，每个人都以自己独特的方式微笑，他意识到他们是一群健康可爱的人。他对他们友好的笑容微笑着，从口袋里掏出一枚金币，交给了“我们的‘伊丽莎白·艾伦’”，她是最年长的。
然后，在咧嘴笑、咯咯笑和屈膝礼中，他开车离开了，留下狂喜、轻推肘部和喜悦的小跳跃。

title: Treasure Island
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: The excitement of these last manoeuvres had somewhat interfered with the watch I had kept hitherto, sharply enough, upon the coxswain. Even then I was still so much interested, waiting for the ship to touch, that I had quite forgot the peril that hung over my head and stood craning over the starboard bulwarks and watching the ripples spreading wide before the bows. I might have fallen without a struggle for my life had not a sudden disquietude seized upon me and made me turn my head. Perhaps I had heard a creak or seen his shadow moving with the tail of my eye; perhaps it was an instinct like a cat’s; but, sure enough, when I looked round, there was Hands, already half-way towards me, with the dirk in his right hand.

We must both have cried out aloud when our eyes met, but while mine was the shrill cry of terror, his was a roar of fury like a charging bully’s. At the same instant, he threw himself forward and I leapt sideways towards the bows. As I did so, I let go of the tiller, which sprang sharp to leeward, and I think this saved my life, for it struck Hands across the chest and stopped him, for the moment, dead.

Before he could recover, I was safe out of the corner where he had me trapped, with all the deck to dodge about. Just forward of the main-mast I stopped, drew a pistol from my pocket, took a cool aim, though he had already turned and was once more coming directly after me, and drew the trigger. The hammer fell, but there followed neither flash nor sound; the priming was useless with sea-water. I cursed myself for my neglect. Why had not I, long before, reprimed and reloaded my only weapons? Then I should not have been as now, a mere fleeing sheep before this butcher.

Wounded as he was, it was wonderful how fast he could move, his grizzled hair tumbling over his face, and his face itself as red as a red ensign with his haste and fury. I had no time to try my other pistol, nor indeed much inclination, for I was sure it would be useless. One thing I saw plainly: I must not simply retreat before him, or he would speedily hold me boxed into the bows, as a moment since he had so nearly boxed me in the stern. Once so caught, and nine or ten inches of the blood-stained dirk would be my last experience on this side of eternity. I placed my palms against the main-mast, which was of a goodish bigness, and waited, every nerve upon the stretch.

Seeing that I meant to dodge, he also paused; and a moment or two passed in feints on his part and corresponding movements upon mine. It was such a game as I had often played at home about the rocks of Black Hill Cove, but never before, you may be sure, with such a wildly beating heart as now. Still, as I say, it was a boy’s game, and I thought I could hold my own at it against an elderly seaman with a wounded thigh. Indeed my courage had begun to rise so high that I allowed myself a few darting thoughts on what would be the end of the affair, and while I saw certainly that I could spin it out for long, I saw no hope of any ultimate escape.

Well, while things stood thus, suddenly the HISPANIOLA struck, staggered, ground for an instant in the sand, and then, swift as a blow, canted over to the port side till the deck stood at an angle of forty-five degrees and about a puncheon of water splashed into the scupper holes and lay, in a pool, between the deck and bulwark.

We were both of us capsized in a second, and both of us rolled, almost together, into the scuppers, the dead red-cap, with his arms still spread out, tumbling stiffly after us. So near were we, indeed, that my head came against the coxswain’s foot with a crack that made my teeth rattle. Blow and all, I was the first afoot again, for Hands had got involved with the dead body. The sudden canting of the ship had made the deck no place for running on; I had to find some new way of escape, and that upon the instant, for my foe was almost touching me. Quick as thought, I sprang into the mizzen shrouds, rattled up hand over hand, and did not draw a breath till I was seated on the cross-trees.

I had been saved by being prompt; the dirk had struck not half a foot below me as I pursued my upward flight; and there stood Israel Hands with his mouth open and his face upturned to mine, a perfect statue of surprise and disappointment.

Now that I had a moment to myself, I lost no time in changing the priming of my pistol, and then, having one ready for service, and to make assurance doubly sure, I proceeded to draw the load of the other and recharge it afresh from the beginning.

My new employment struck Hands all of a heap; he began to see the dice going against him, and after an obvious hesitation, he also hauled himself heavily into the shrouds, and with the dirk in his teeth, began slowly and painfully to mount. It cost him no end of time and groans to haul his wounded leg behind him, and I had quietly finished my arrangements before he was much more than a third of the way up. Then, with a pistol in either hand, I addressed him.
paragraphsZh: 最后这些演习的兴奋在某种程度上干扰了我迄今为止对船长的观察，足够敏锐。即使在那时，我仍然非常感兴趣，等待着船触碰，我完全忘记了悬在我头上的危险，站在右舷舷墙上，看着涟漪在船头前蔓延开来。如果不是突如其来的不安袭来，让我转过头来，我可能会不费吹灰之力就倒下。也许我听到了吱吱声，或者看到他的影子随着我的眼尾移动；也许这是一种像猫一样的本能；但是，果然，当我环顾四周时，汉兹已经朝我走来了，右手拿着匕首。
当我们四目相对时，我们一定都大声叫了起来，但我的是恐怖的尖叫声，他的是像冲锋的恶霸一样的愤怒咆哮。与此同时，他向前扑去，我则向船头侧身跳去。当我这样做时，我松开了舵柄，舵柄猛地向下风方向弹起，我认为这救了我的命，因为它击中了汉兹的胸部，暂时阻止了他的死亡。
在他恢复过来之前，我已经安全地脱离了他困住我的角落，所有甲板都需要躲避。就在主桅杆前，我停了下来，从口袋里掏出一把手枪，冷静地瞄准，尽管他已经转身，再次直接追上我，并扣动了扳机。锤子落下，但没有发出闪光，也没有发出声音。启动对于海水来说是没有用的。我为自己的疏忽而咒骂自己。为什么我没有在很久之前就重新装填我仅有的武器？那时我就​​不会像现在一样，在这个屠夫面前只是一只逃亡的羊了。

尽管他受了伤，但他的移动速度却是惊人的，他的花白头发披散在他的脸上，他的脸因他的匆忙和愤怒而红得像一面红色的少尉。我没有时间尝试我的另一把手枪，实际上也没有太大的兴趣，因为我确信它毫无用处。我清楚地看到一件事：我不能在他面前简单地撤退，否则他会很快把我打到船头，自从他差点把我打到船尾后，这一刻就发生了。一旦被抓住，九或十英寸的沾满血迹的匕首将是我在永恒这一边的最后经历。我把手掌放在主桅上，主桅相当大，等待着，每一根神经都绷紧了。

见我有闪避的意思，他也顿了顿；一两分钟过去了，他做出了佯攻，我也做出了相应的动作。这是我在家里经常玩的关于黑山湾岩石的游戏，但你可以肯定，以前从来没有像现在这样心跳得如此剧烈。尽管如此，正如我所说，这是一个男孩的游戏，我认为我可以在面对一位大腿受伤的年老海员时坚持下去。事实上，我的勇气已经开始变得如此之高，以至于我允许自己对这件事的结局进行一些飞快的思考，虽然我确信我可以把它拖很久，但我看不到任何最终逃脱的希望。
好吧，就在事情就这样发生的时候，伊斯帕尼奥拉号突然发生了撞击，摇摇晃晃，在沙子里瞬间搁浅，然后，像打击一样迅速地向左舷倾斜，直到甲板呈四十五度角，大约一拳的水溅入排水孔，并躺在甲板和舷墙之间的水池中。

我们俩都在一秒钟内翻了，我们俩几乎一起滚进了排水孔，那个死去的红帽子，他的双臂仍然张开，在我们身后僵硬地翻滚。事实上，我们离得如此之近，以至于我的头撞到了船长的脚上，发出一声脆响，让我的牙齿格格作响。不管怎样，我又第一个站起来了，因为汉兹已经和尸体纠缠在一起了。船突然倾斜，甲板上没有可供奔跑的地方。我必须找到一些新的逃生方式，而且是立即的，因为我的敌人几乎就要碰到我了。我像想的那样快地跳进了后桅索，一手一手地嘎嘎作响，直到坐在横树上才喘了一口气。
我因及时而得救；当我向上飞行时，短刀已经击中了我下方不到半英尺的地方。以色列之手站在那里，张着嘴，仰着脸看着我，一尊完美的惊讶和失望的雕像。
现在我有了自己的时间，我不失时机地更换手枪的底火，然后，在准备好一支手枪供使用时，为了确保双重确定，我开始拉动另一支手枪的子弹并从头开始重新充电。
我的新工作让双手大吃一惊；他开始看到骰子对他不利，在明显的犹豫之后，他也重重地把自己拖进裹尸布，用牙齿咬住短刀，开始缓慢而痛苦地上升。他花了没完没了的时间和呻吟才把受伤的腿拖到身后，而在他爬上三分之一多的路程之前，我已经悄悄地完成了我的安排。然后，我双手各握一把手枪，对他讲话。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 2
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: In one way, indeed, he bade fair to ruin us, for he kept on staying week after week, and at last month after month, so that all the money had been long exhausted, and still my father never plucked up the heart to insist on having more. If ever he mentioned it, the captain blew through his nose so loudly that you might say he roared, and stared my poor father out of the room. I have seen him wringing his hands after such a rebuff, and I am sure the annoyance and the terror he lived in must have greatly hastened his early and unhappy death.

All the time he lived with us the captain made no change whatever in his dress but to buy some stockings from a hawker. One of the cocks of his hat having fallen down, he let it hang from that day forth, though it was a great annoyance when it blew. I remember the appearance of his coat, which he patched himself upstairs in his room, and which, before the end, was nothing but patches. He never wrote or received a letter, and he never spoke with any but the neighbours, and with these, for the most part, only when drunk on rum. The great sea-chest none of us had ever seen open.

He was only once crossed, and that was towards the end, when my poor father was far gone in a decline that took him off. Dr. Livesey came late one afternoon to see the patient, took a bit of dinner from my mother, and went into the parlour to smoke a pipe until his horse should come down from the hamlet, for we had no stabling at the old Benbow. I followed him in, and I remember observing the contrast the neat, bright doctor, with his powder as white as snow and his bright, black eyes and pleasant manners, made with the coltish country folk, and above all, with that filthy, heavy, bleared scarecrow of a pirate of ours, sitting, far gone in rum, with his arms on the table. Suddenly he--the captain, that is--began to pipe up his eternal song:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum! Drink and the devil had done for the rest-- Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

At first I had supposed “the dead man’s chest” to be that identical big box of his upstairs in the front room, and the thought had been mingled in my nightmares with that of the one-legged seafaring man. But by this time we had all long ceased to pay any particular notice to the song; it was new, that night, to nobody but Dr. Livesey, and on him I observed it did not produce an agreeable effect, for he looked up for a moment quite angrily before he went on with his talk to old Taylor, the gardener, on a new cure for the rheumatics. In the meantime, the captain gradually brightened up at his own music, and at last flapped his hand upon the table before him in a way we all knew to mean silence. The voices stopped at once, all but Dr. Livesey’s; he went on as before speaking clear and kind and drawing briskly at his pipe between every word or two. The captain glared at him for a while, flapped his hand again, glared still harder, and at last broke out with a villainous, low oath, “Silence, there, between decks!”
The old fellow’s fury was awful. He sprang to his feet, drew and opened a sailor’s clasp-knife, and balancing it open on the palm of his hand, threatened to pin the doctor to the wall.

The doctor never so much as moved. He spoke to him as before, over his shoulder and in the same tone of voice, rather high, so that all the room might hear, but perfectly calm and steady: “If you do not put that knife this instant in your pocket, I promise, upon my honour, you shall hang at the next assizes.”
Then followed a battle of looks between them, but the captain soon knuckled under, put up his weapon, and resumed his seat, grumbling like a beaten dog.

“And now, sir,” continued the doctor, “since I now know there’s such a fellow in my district, you may count I’ll have an eye upon you day and night. I’m not a doctor only; I’m a magistrate; and if I catch a breath of complaint against you, if it’s only for a piece of incivility like tonight’s, I’ll take effectual means to have you hunted down and routed out of this. Let that suffice.”
paragraphsZh: 从某种意义上说，他的确是要毁了我们，因为他一周又一周，最后一月又一个月地待着，以致所有的钱都早已用完，而我父亲却始终没有鼓起勇气坚持要更多。如果他提到这件事，船长就会大声地用鼻子擤鼻涕，你可以说他在咆哮，然后盯着我可怜的父亲走出房间。我见过他在遭到如此拒绝后绞尽脑汁，我确信他所生活的烦恼和恐惧一定极大地加速了他早日不幸的死亡。

船长和我们住在一起的时候，他的衣服没有任何改变，只是从小贩那里买了一些袜子。他的帽子的一个公鸡掉下来了，从那天起他就让它挂着，尽管风吹起来很烦人。我记得他外套的样子，是他在楼上自己的房间里亲自修补的，而在结束之前，那件外套只不过是补丁而已。他从未写过或收到过一封信，除了邻居之外，他从不与任何人交谈，而且大多数情况下，只有在喝醉了朗姆酒的情况下才与他们交谈。我们从来没有见过这个巨大的海底宝箱打开过。

他只被跨越过一次，那是在快要结束的时候，当时我可怜的父亲在衰弱中走得很远，导致他离开了。一天下午，利夫西医生来见病人，从我母亲那里拿了一点晚餐，然后走进客厅抽烟斗，直到他的马从小村庄下来，因为我们在老本博没有马厩。我跟着他进去，我记得我看到了一个鲜明的对比，那个整洁、聪明的医生，他的粉末像雪一样白，他的眼睛又亮又黑，举止愉快，就像一群粗鲁的乡下人，最重要的是，他和我们那个肮脏、沉重、模糊的海盗稻草人坐在一起，喝了很多朗姆酒，双臂放在桌子上。突然，他——也就是船长——开始唱起他那永恒的歌：
“死者胸口上有十五个人——哟嗬嗬，还有一瓶朗姆酒！喝了酒，魔鬼已经完成了剩下的——哟嗬嗬，还有一瓶朗姆酒！”

起初，我以为“死者的箱子”就是他楼上前室那个一模一样的大盒子，这个想法在我的噩梦中与那个单腿航海者的噩梦混在一起。但到了这个时候，我们早已不再对这首歌给予任何特别的关注；那天晚上，除了利夫西医生之外，对任何人来说，这都是新的，我观察到这对他来说并没有产生令人满意的效果，因为他相当愤怒地抬起头看了一会儿，然后继续与老园丁泰勒谈论治疗风湿病的新方法。与此同时，船长在自己的音乐中逐渐变得高兴起来，最后他用手拍了一下面前的桌子，我们都知道这意味着安静。除了利弗西博士之外，所有的声音都立刻停止了。他继续像以前一样清晰而友善地说话，每说一个或两个字，他就轻快地吸着烟斗。船长瞪了他一会儿，又拍了拍手，瞪得更厉害，最后恶狠狠地低声咒骂道：“甲板之间，安静！”
老家伙的怒火可厉害了。他跳了起来，拔出一把水手折刀，打开，放在手掌上保持平衡，威胁要把医生按在墙上。
医生根本没有动过。他像以前一样越过肩膀，用同样的语气对他说话，声音相当高，以便整个房间都能听到，但非常平静和稳定：“如果你不立即把那把刀放进口袋里，我保证，以我的名誉担保，你将在下次巡回审判中被绞死。”
然后他们之间发生了一场眼神交锋，但船长很快就屈服了，拿起武器，回到座位上，像一只被打败的狗一样咕哝着。
“现在，先生，”医生继续说道，“既然我现在知道我所在的地区有这样一个人，你可以认为我会日夜监视着你。我不仅仅是一名医生；我还是一名地方法官；如果我对你有一丝抱怨，如果只是为了像今晚这样的不文明行为，我会采取有效的手段来追捕你并赶走你。让那件事发生吧。”够了。”

title: Treasure Island · 选段 3
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: From the side of the hill, which was here steep and stony, a spout of gravel was dislodged and fell rattling and bounding through the trees. My eyes turned instinctively in that direction, and I saw a figure leap with great rapidity behind the trunk of a pine. What it was, whether bear or man or monkey, I could in no wise tell. It seemed dark and shaggy; more I knew not. But the terror of this new apparition brought me to a stand.

I was now, it seemed, cut off upon both sides; behind me the murderers, before me this lurking nondescript. And immediately I began to prefer the dangers that I knew to those I knew not. Silver himself appeared less terrible in contrast with this creature of the woods, and I turned on my heel, and looking sharply behind me over my shoulder, began to retrace my steps in the direction of the boats.

Instantly the figure reappeared, and making a wide circuit, began to head me off. I was tired, at any rate; but had I been as fresh as when I rose, I could see it was in vain for me to contend in speed with such an adversary. From trunk to trunk the creature flitted like a deer, running manlike on two legs, but unlike any man that I had ever seen, stooping almost double as it ran. Yet a man it was, I could no longer be in doubt about that.

I began to recall what I had heard of cannibals. I was within an ace of calling for help. But the mere fact that he was a man, however wild, had somewhat reassured me, and my fear of Silver began to revive in proportion. I stood still, therefore, and cast about for some method of escape; and as I was so thinking, the recollection of my pistol flashed into my mind. As soon as I remembered I was not defenceless, courage glowed again in my heart and I set my face resolutely for this man of the island and walked briskly towards him.

He was concealed by this time behind another tree trunk; but he must have been watching me closely, for as soon as I began to move in his direction he reappeared and took a step to meet me. Then he hesitated, drew back, came forward again, and at last, to my wonder and confusion, threw himself on his knees and held out his clasped hands in supplication.
“Ben Gunn,” he answered, and his voice sounded hoarse and awkward, like a rusty lock. “I’m poor Ben Gunn, I am; and I haven’t spoke with a Christian these three years.”

I could now see that he was a white man like myself and that his features were even pleasing. His skin, wherever it was exposed, was burnt by the sun; even his lips were black, and his fair eyes looked quite startling in so dark a face. Of all the beggar-men that I had seen or fancied, he was the chief for raggedness. He was clothed with tatters of old ship’s canvas and old sea-cloth, and this extraordinary patchwork was all held together by a system of the most various and incongruous fastenings, brass buttons, bits of stick, and loops of tarry gaskin. About his waist he wore an old brass-buckled leather belt, which was the one thing solid in his whole accoutrement.

I had heard the word, and I knew it stood for a horrible kind of punishment common enough among the buccaneers, in which the offender is put ashore with a little powder and shot and left behind on some desolate and distant island.

“Marooned three years agone,” he continued, “and lived on goats since then, and berries, and oysters. Wherever a man is, says I, a man can do for himself. But, mate, my heart is sore for Christian diet. You mightn’t happen to have a piece of cheese about you, now? No? Well, many’s the long night I’ve dreamed of cheese--toasted, mostly--and woke up again, and here I were.”

All this time he had been feeling the stuff of my jacket, smoothing my hands, looking at my boots, and generally, in the intervals of his speech, showing a childish pleasure in the presence of a fellow creature. But at my last words he perked up into a kind of startled slyness.
paragraphsZh: 从陡峭多石的山坡上，一股砾石被喷出，嘎嘎作响地从树林里蹦蹦跳跳地掉下来。我的目光本能地转向那个方向，只见松树树干后面有一个人影飞快地跳跃着。那是什么，是熊、人还是猴子，我根本无法分辨。它看起来又黑又蓬乱。更多我不知道。但这个新幽灵的恐怖让我陷入了困境。
我现在似乎被两边切断了；我身后是凶手，我面前是潜伏着的不伦不类的人。我立刻开始喜欢我所知道的危险，而不是那些我不知道的危险。与森林里的这个生物相比，西尔弗本人显得不那么可怕了，我转过身来，回头锐利地望着身后，开始朝船的方向折返。
立刻那个人影又出现了，绕了一大圈，开始挡住我的去路。无论如何，我很累了。但如果我像站起来时一样精力充沛，我就会发现，我在速度上与这样的对手抗衡是徒劳的。这个生物像鹿一样从一个树干飞到另一个树干，像人一样用两条腿奔跑，但与我见过的任何人都不一样，它在奔跑时几乎弯腰。但他毕竟是一个男人，对此我不能再怀疑了。
我开始回想起我听说过的食人者。我差点就呼救了。但光是他是一个男人，无论多么狂野，就多少让我放心了，我对西尔弗的恐惧开始相应地复苏。因此，我一动不动地站着，四处寻找逃跑的方法。正当我这么想着时，我的脑海里突然闪现出手枪的记忆。当我想起自己并非手无寸铁时，我的心中又燃起了勇气，我毅然决然地向这个岛上的男人迈着轻快的步伐向他走去。
此时他已经隐藏在另一棵树干后面；但他肯定一直在密切地注视着我，因为当我开始朝他的方向移动时，他又出现了，并向我迈出了一步。然后他犹豫了一下，后退了一步，又向前走来，最后，令我惊奇和困惑的是，他跪倒在地，伸出紧握的双手恳求。
“本·冈恩，”他回答道，他的声音听起来沙哑而尴尬，就像一把生锈的锁。 “我是可怜的本·冈恩，我是的；这三年我没有和基督徒说过话。”

我现在可以看出他是一个像我一样的白人，而且他的相貌甚至令人愉悦。他的皮肤，凡是暴露在外的地方，都被阳光晒伤了。甚至他的嘴唇也是黑色的，而他那双白皙的眼睛在如此黝黑的脸上显得相当惊人。在我见过或想象中的所有乞丐中，他是最衣衫褴褛的。他穿着旧船帆布和旧海布的破烂衣服，这件非凡的拼凑物全部由各种各样且不协调的紧固件、黄铜纽扣、木棍碎片和柏油垫片环组成的系统固定在一起。他的腰间系着一条旧的黄铜扣皮带，这是他整套装备中唯一坚固的东西。
我听说过这个词，我知道它代表了海盗中常见的一种可怕的惩罚，罪犯被用少量火药和子弹打上岸，然后留在某个荒凉而遥远的岛屿上。
“三年前被困，”他继续说道，“从那时起就以山羊、浆果和牡蛎为生。我说，无论一个人在哪里，一个人都可以为自己做事。但是，伙计，我的心因基督教饮食而感到痛苦。现在你可能不会碰巧有一块奶酪了？不是吗？好吧，很多个漫长的夜晚我都梦见奶酪——大部分是烤的——然后又醒来，而我就在这里。”
一直以来，他一直摸着我夹克的材质，抚平我的手，看着我的靴子，而且一般来说，在他讲话的间隙，在同伴面前表现出一种孩子气的快乐。但在我说完最后一句话时，他的脸上露出了一种惊讶的狡黠的神情。

title: The Jungle
author: Upton Sinclair
paragraphs: The “Appeal” was a “propaganda” paper. It had a manner all its own—it was full of ginger and spice, of Western slang and hustle: It collected news of the doings of the “plutes,” and served it up for the benefit of the “American working-mule.” It would have columns of the deadly parallel—the million dollars’ worth of diamonds, or the fancy pet-poodle establishment of a society dame, beside the fate of Mrs. Murphy of San Francisco, who had starved to death on the streets, or of John Robinson, just out of the hospital, who had hanged himself in New York because he could not find work. It collected the stories of graft and misery from the daily press, and made a little pungent paragraphs out of them. “Three banks of Bungtown, South Dakota, failed, and more savings of the workers swallowed up!” “The mayor of Sandy Creek, Oklahoma, has skipped with a hundred thousand dollars. That’s the kind of rulers the old partyites give you!” “The president of the Florida Flying Machine Company is in jail for bigamy. He was a prominent opponent of Socialism, which he said would break up the home!” The “Appeal” had what it called its “Army,” about thirty thousand of the faithful, who did things for it; and it was always exhorting the “Army” to keep its dander up, and occasionally encouraging it with a prize competition, for anything from a gold watch to a private yacht or an eighty-acre farm. Its office helpers were all known to the “Army” by quaint titles—“Inky Ike,” “the Bald-headed Man,” “the Redheaded Girl,” “the Bulldog,” “the Office Goat,” and “the One Hoss.”

But sometimes, again, the “Appeal” would be desperately serious. It sent a correspondent to Colorado, and printed pages describing the overthrow of American institutions in that state. In a certain city of the country it had over forty of its “Army” in the headquarters of the Telegraph Trust, and no message of importance to Socialists ever went through that a copy of it did not go to the “Appeal.” It would print great broadsides during the campaign; one copy that came to Jurgis was a manifesto addressed to striking workingmen, of which nearly a million copies had been distributed in the industrial centers, wherever the employers’ associations had been carrying out their “open shop” program. “You have lost the strike!” it was headed. “And now what are you going to do about it?” It was what is called an “incendiary” appeal—it was written by a man into whose soul the iron had entered. When this edition appeared, twenty thousand copies were sent to the stockyards district; and they were taken out and stowed away in the rear of a little cigar store, and every evening, and on Sundays, the members of the Packingtown locals would get armfuls and distribute them on the streets and in the houses. The people of Packingtown had lost their strike, if ever a people had, and so they read these papers gladly, and twenty thousand were hardly enough to go round. Jurgis had resolved not to go near his old home again, but when he heard of this it was too much for him, and every night for a week he would get on the car and ride out to the stockyards, and help to undo his work of the previous year, when he had sent Mike Scully’s ten-pin setter to the city Board of Aldermen.

It was quite marvelous to see what a difference twelve months had made in Packingtown—the eyes of the people were getting opened! The Socialists were literally sweeping everything before them that election, and Scully and the Cook County machine were at their wits’ end for an “issue.” At the very close of the campaign they bethought themselves of the fact that the strike had been broken by Negroes, and so they sent for a South Carolina fire-eater, the “pitchfork senator,” as he was called, a man who took off his coat when he talked to workingmen, and damned and swore like a Hessian. This meeting they advertised extensively, and the Socialists advertised it too—with the result that about a thousand of them were on hand that evening. The “pitchfork senator” stood their fusillade of questions for about an hour, and then went home in disgust, and the balance of the meeting was a strictly party affair. Jurgis, who had insisted upon coming, had the time of his life that night; he danced about and waved his arms in his excitement—and at the very climax he broke loose from his friends, and got out into the aisle, and proceeded to make a speech himself! The senator had been denying that the Democratic party was corrupt; it was always the Republicans who bought the votes, he said—and here was Jurgis shouting furiously, “It’s a lie! It’s a lie!” After which he went on to tell them how he knew it—that he knew it because he had bought them himself! And he would have told the “pitchfork senator” all his experiences, had not Harry Adams and a friend grabbed him about the neck and shoved him into a seat.
paragraphsZh: “呼吁书”是一份“宣传”文件。它有自己的风格——充满了生姜和香料，充满了西方俚语和喧嚣：它收集“富豪”的行为新闻，并为“美国劳动骡子”的利益提供服务。它会有致命的平行专栏——价值数百万美元的钻石，或者上流社会贵妇的豪华宠物贵宾犬店，旁边是饿死在街头的旧金山墨菲夫人的命运，或者是刚出院的约翰·罗宾逊，因为找不到工作在纽约上吊自杀。它从每日新闻中收集了有关贪污和苦难的故事，并从中制作了一些辛辣的段落。 “南达科他州邦敦的三家银行倒闭了，工人的更多积蓄被吞噬了！” “俄克拉荷马州桑迪克里克市的市长已经跳过了十万美元。这就是老党派给你的那种统治者！” “佛罗里达飞行器公司的总裁因重婚而入狱。他是社会主义的著名反对者，他说社会主义会拆散家庭！” “上诉”拥有所谓的“军队”，约有三万名信徒，为它做事。它总是劝告“军队”保持斗志，偶尔还通过有奖竞赛来鼓励他们，从金表到私人游艇，再到八十英亩的农场。它的办公室助手都被“军队”以古怪的头衔所熟知——“墨色艾克”、“秃头男人”、“红发女孩”、“斗牛犬”、“办公室山羊”和“一匹马”。

但有时，“上诉”又会非常严肃。它派出一名记者前往科罗拉多州，并印刷了描述推翻该州美国机构的页面。在该国的某个城市，电报信托公司的总部里有超过四十支“军队”，对社会主义者来说，从来没有一条重要的消息表明它的副本没有送到“上诉机构”。它会在竞选期间印出大量的大字报；尤吉斯收到的一份宣言是写给罢工工人的宣言，其中近一百万份已在工业中心分发，那里的雇主协会一直在实施“开放工厂”计划。 “你已经失败了！”它正在前进。 “那么现在你打算怎么办呢？”这就是所谓的“煽动性”呼吁——它是由一个被铁打入灵魂的人写的。当这个版本出版时，两万本被送到了牲畜饲养场地区；他们被拿出来藏在一家小雪茄店的后面，每天晚上和周日，包装镇当地人都会抱起一大堆雪茄，分发到街上和家里。帕金敦的人民已经失去了罢工，如果有一个民族曾经失败过的话，所以他们很高兴地阅读这些报纸，两万人还不足以分发。尤吉斯决定不再靠近他的老家，但当他听说这件事时，这对他来说实在是太难以忍受了，一周以来，他每天晚上都会骑上车去牲口场，帮助完成去年的工作，当时他把迈克·斯卡利的十瓶二传手送到了市市政委员会。

看到帕金敦十二个月的变化真是太奇妙了——人们的眼睛都睁开了！那次选举中，社会主义者几乎横扫了他们面前的一切，而斯卡利和库克县机器却因为一个“问题”而束手无策。在竞选活动即将结束时，他们意识到罢工已被黑人破坏了，因此他们派了一位南卡罗来纳州的食火者，他被称为“干草叉参议员”，这个人在与工人交谈时脱下外套，像黑森人一样咒骂和咒骂。他们为这次会议做了广泛的宣传，社会党也为这次会议做了宣传——结果当晚约有一千人参加。这位“干草叉参议员”在他们一连串的问题上待了大约一个小时，然后厌恶地回家了，会议的其余部分完全是党内事务。尤吉斯坚持要来，那天晚上他度过了一生中最美好的时光。他兴奋地手舞足蹈，挥舞着手臂——在高潮的时候，他挣脱了朋友们的束缚，走到了过道上，开始自己发表演讲！这位参议员一直否认民主党腐败。他说，总是共和党人收买了选票——而尤吉斯却愤怒地大喊：“这是谎言！这是谎言！”然后他继续告诉他们他是怎么知道的——他知道是因为他自己买了它们！如果不是哈里·亚当斯和一个朋友抓住他的脖子，把他推到座位上，他就会告诉这位“干草叉参议员”他的所有经历。

title: The Jungle · 选段 2
author: Upton Sinclair
paragraphs: After this there is beer for every one, the musicians included, and the revelers take a long breath and prepare for the great event of the evening, which is the acziavimas. The acziavimas is a ceremony which, once begun, will continue for three or four hours, and it involves one uninterrupted dance. The guests form a great ring, locking hands, and, when the music starts up, begin to move around in a circle. In the center stands the bride, and, one by one, the men step into the enclosure and dance with her. Each dances for several minutes—as long as he pleases; it is a very merry proceeding, with laughter and singing, and when the guest has finished, he finds himself face to face with Teta Elzbieta, who holds the hat. Into it he drops a sum of money—a dollar, or perhaps five dollars, according to his power, and his estimate of the value of the privilege. The guests are expected to pay for this entertainment; if they be proper guests, they will see that there is a neat sum left over for the bride and bridegroom to start life upon.

Most fearful they are to contemplate, the expenses of this entertainment. They will certainly be over two hundred dollars and maybe three hundred; and three hundred dollars is more than the year’s income of many a person in this room. There are able-bodied men here who work from early morning until late at night, in ice-cold cellars with a quarter of an inch of water on the floor—men who for six or seven months in the year never see the sunlight from Sunday afternoon till the next Sunday morning—and who cannot earn three hundred dollars in a year. There are little children here, scarce in their teens, who can hardly see the top of the work benches—whose parents have lied to get them their places—and who do not make the half of three hundred dollars a year, and perhaps not even the third of it. And then to spend such a sum, all in a single day of your life, at a wedding feast! (For obviously it is the same thing, whether you spend it at once for your own wedding, or in a long time, at the weddings of all your friends.)

It is very imprudent, it is tragic—but, ah, it is so beautiful! Bit by bit these poor people have given up everything else; but to this they cling with all the power of their souls—they cannot give up the veselija! To do that would mean, not merely to be defeated, but to acknowledge defeat—and the difference between these two things is what keeps the world going. The veselija has come down to them from a far-off time; and the meaning of it was that one might dwell within the cave and gaze upon shadows, provided only that once in his lifetime he could break his chains, and feel his wings, and behold the sun; provided that once in his lifetime he might testify to the fact that life, with all its cares and its terrors, is no such great thing after all, but merely a bubble upon the surface of a river, a thing that one may toss about and play with as a juggler tosses his golden balls, a thing that one may quaff, like a goblet of rare red wine. Thus having known himself for the master of things, a man could go back to his toil and live upon the memory all his days.

Endlessly the dancers swung round and round—when they were dizzy they swung the other way. Hour after hour this had continued—the darkness had fallen and the room was dim from the light of two smoky oil lamps. The musicians had spent all their fine frenzy by now, and played only one tune, wearily, ploddingly. There were twenty bars or so of it, and when they came to the end they began again. Once every ten minutes or so they would fail to begin again, but instead would sink back exhausted; a circumstance which invariably brought on a painful and terrifying scene, that made the fat policeman stir uneasily in his sleeping place behind the door.

It was all Marija Berczynskas. Marija was one of those hungry souls who cling with desperation to the skirts of the retreating muse. All day long she had been in a state of wonderful exaltation; and now it was leaving—and she would not let it go. Her soul cried out in the words of Faust, “Stay, thou art fair!” Whether it was by beer, or by shouting, or by music, or by motion, she meant that it should not go. And she would go back to the chase of it—and no sooner be fairly started than her chariot would be thrown off the track, so to speak, by the stupidity of those thrice accursed musicians. Each time, Marija would emit a howl and fly at them, shaking her fists in their faces, stamping upon the floor, purple and incoherent with rage. In vain the frightened Tamoszius would attempt to speak, to plead the limitations of the flesh; in vain would the puffing and breathless ponas Jokubas insist, in vain would Teta Elzbieta implore. “Szalin!” Marija would scream. “Palauk! isz kelio! What are you paid for, children of hell?” And so, in sheer terror, the orchestra would strike up again, and Marija would return to her place and take up her task.
paragraphsZh: 此后，包括音乐家在内的每个人都喝了啤酒，狂欢者们长长地吸了一口气，为当晚的盛事——acziavimas 做准备。 acziavimas 是一种仪式，一旦开始，就会持续三到四个小时，其中包括不间断的舞蹈。客人们手拉手围成一个大圈，当音乐响起时，他们开始围成一圈。新娘站在中间，男人们一一步入围场，与她共舞。每人跳几分钟——只要他愿意；这是一个非常愉快的过程，有笑声和歌声，当客人结束时，他发现自己面对着拿着帽子的 Teta Elzbieta。他在里面投入了一笔钱——一美元，或者五美元，这取决于他的权力和他对特权价值的估计。客人需要为这种娱乐活动付费；如果他们是适当的客人，他们会看到有一笔可观的钱留给新娘和新郎开始生活。

他们最害怕的是这种娱乐活动的费用。它们肯定会超过两百美元，也许三百美元；三百美元比这个房间里许多人一年的收入还多。这里有一些身体健全的人，他们从早到深夜，在冰冷的地窖里工作，地板上只有四分之一英寸的水——这些人一年中有六七个月从周日下午到下周日早上都见不到阳光——一年也挣不到三百美元。这里有很少的十几岁的孩子，他们几乎看不到工作台的顶部——他们的父母撒谎让他们得到自己的位置——他们一年赚不到三百美元的一半，甚至可能连三分之一都赚不到。然后就在你生命中的一天之内，在一场婚宴上花费了这么多钱！ （显然，无论你是在自己的婚礼上一次性花掉，还是在所有朋友的婚礼上花很长时间，这都是一回事。）

很不谨慎，很悲惨——但是，啊，它是如此美丽！这些可怜的人一点一点地放弃了其他一切；但他们用全部灵魂的力量坚持这一点——他们不能放弃veselija！做到这一点不仅意味着被击败，还意味着承认失败——而这两件事之间的区别正是世界继续前进的动力。 veselija 是从遥远的时代就降临到他们身上的。它的意义在于，一个人可以住在山洞里，凝视阴影，只要他一生中能够挣脱锁链，感受他的翅膀，看到太阳。假如他有生之年能有一次证明这样一个事实：生活，连同其所有的忧虑和恐惧，毕竟不是那么伟大的事情，而只是河面上的一个泡沫，一个可以像杂耍者抛​​掷金球一样被人们抛来抛去的东西，一个可以让人痛饮的东西，就像一杯稀有的红酒一样。因此，当一个人认识到自己是事物的主宰之后，他就可以回到自己的辛劳中，并在他的一生中依靠记忆而生活。
舞者们不停地转来转去——当他们头晕的时候，他们就转向相反的方向。这样的情况一小时又一小时地持续着——夜幕降临，房间里两盏冒着烟的油灯显得昏暗。音乐家们现在已经耗尽了所有的狂热，只演奏了一首曲子，疲倦而缓慢。大概有二十个小节，唱完后又开始了。每隔十分钟左右，他们就会无法再开始，而是精疲力竭地倒下去；这种情况无一例外地会带来痛苦而恐怖的场面，让门后睡觉的胖警察不安地不安起来。

都是 Marija Berczynskas 干的。玛丽娅是那些饥肠辘辘的灵魂之一，她绝望地紧紧抓住正在离去的缪斯女神的裙子。她一整天都处于一种极其兴奋的状态。现在它要离开了——她不会放开它。她的灵魂用浮士德的话呼喊：“留下来，你是公平的！”无论是通过啤酒，还是通过喊叫，还是通过音乐，还是通过动作，她的意思是它不应该消失。她会回去追逐它——而且一旦开始，她的战车就会偏离轨道，可以这么说，因为那些三次被诅咒的音乐家的愚蠢。每一次，玛丽娅都会发出一声嚎叫，飞向他们，在他们面前挥动拳头，跺脚，脸色发紫，气得语无伦次。受到惊吓的塔莫修斯试图说话，为肉体的局限性辩护，但徒劳无功。气喘吁吁、气喘吁吁的波纳斯·乔库巴斯坚持是徒劳的，泰塔·埃尔兹别塔恳求也是徒劳的。 “沙林！”玛丽亚会尖叫。 “Palauk！isz kelio！你们得到什么报酬，地狱之子？”因此，在纯粹的恐惧中，管弦乐队将再次演奏，而玛丽娅将返回她的位置并承担她的任务。

title: The Jungle · 选段 3
author: Upton Sinclair
paragraphs: Jurgis went home, carrying these new tidings to the family council. It was a most cruel thing; here in this district was his home, such as it was, the place he was used to and the friends he knew—and now every possibility of employment in it was closed to him. There was nothing in Packingtown but packing houses; and so it was the same thing as evicting him from his home.

He and the two women spent all day and half the night discussing it. It would be convenient, downtown, to the children’s place of work; but then Marija was on the road to recovery, and had hopes of getting a job in the yards; and though she did not see her old-time lover once a month, because of the misery of their state, yet she could not make up her mind to go away and give him up forever. Then, too, Elzbieta had heard something about a chance to scrub floors in Durham’s offices and was waiting every day for word. In the end it was decided that Jurgis should go downtown to strike out for himself, and they would decide after he got a job. As there was no one from whom he could borrow there, and he dared not beg for fear of being arrested, it was arranged that every day he should meet one of the children and be given fifteen cents of their earnings, upon which he could keep going. Then all day he was to pace the streets with hundreds and thousands of other homeless wretches inquiring at stores, warehouses, and factories for a chance; and at night he was to crawl into some doorway or underneath a truck, and hide there until midnight, when he might get into one of the station houses, and spread a newspaper upon the floor, and lie down in the midst of a throng of “bums” and beggars, reeking with alcohol and tobacco, and filthy with vermin and disease.

So for two weeks more Jurgis fought with the demon of despair. Once he got a chance to load a truck for half a day, and again he carried an old woman’s valise and was given a quarter. This let him into a lodging-house on several nights when he might otherwise have frozen to death; and it also gave him a chance now and then to buy a newspaper in the morning and hunt up jobs while his rivals were watching and waiting for a paper to be thrown away. This, however, was really not the advantage it seemed, for the newspaper advertisements were a cause of much loss of precious time and of many weary journeys. A full half of these were “fakes,” put in by the endless variety of establishments which preyed upon the helpless ignorance of the unemployed. If Jurgis lost only his time, it was because he had nothing else to lose; whenever a smooth-tongued agent would tell him of the wonderful positions he had on hand, he could only shake his head sorrowfully and say that he had not the necessary dollar to deposit; when it was explained to him what “big money” he and all his family could make by coloring photographs, he could only promise to come in again when he had two dollars to invest in the outfit.

In the end Jurgis got a chance through an accidental meeting with an old-time acquaintance of his union days. He met this man on his way to work in the giant factories of the Harvester Trust; and his friend told him to come along and he would speak a good word for him to his boss, whom he knew well. So Jurgis trudged four or five miles, and passed through a waiting throng of unemployed at the gate under the escort of his friend. His knees nearly gave way beneath him when the foreman, after looking him over and questioning him, told him that he could find an opening for him.

How much this accident meant to Jurgis he realized only by stages; for he found that the harvester works were the sort of place to which philanthropists and reformers pointed with pride. It had some thought for its employees; its workshops were big and roomy, it provided a restaurant where the workmen could buy good food at cost, it had even a reading room, and decent places where its girl-hands could rest; also the work was free from many of the elements of filth and repulsiveness that prevailed at the stockyards. Day after day Jurgis discovered these things—things never expected nor dreamed of by him—until this new place came to seem a kind of a heaven to him.
paragraphsZh: 尤吉斯回家了，把这些新消息带到了家庭委员会。这是一件极其残酷的事。这个地区是他的家，是他习惯的地方，也是他认识的朋友——而现在，这里的一切就业机会都对他关闭了。帕金镇除了包装厂什么也没有。因此，这与将他逐出家门是一样的。

他和两个女人讨论了一天半夜。去市中心、孩子们工作的地方会很方便；但后来玛丽亚开始康复，并希望在院子里找到一份工作。尽管由于他们的处境悲惨，她每个月都见不到她的旧情人一次，但她却无法下定决心离开并永远放弃他。然后，埃尔兹别塔也听说了在达勒姆办公室擦地板的机会，每天都在等待消息。最后决定让尤吉斯去市中心闯出一片天，等他找到工作后再决定。由于那里没有人可以向他借钱，他也不敢乞讨，怕被抓，所以安排他每天去见一个孩子，并给他十五美分的收入，让他继续生活。然后一整天，他都要和成百上千的无家可归的可怜虫一起在街上踱步，到商店、仓库和工厂寻找机会。晚上，他要爬进某个门口或一辆卡车底下，一直藏到午夜，然后他才能进入其中一间车站房，在地板上铺上一张报纸，躺在一群“流浪汉”和乞丐中间，浑身散发着酒精和烟草的臭味，浑身沾满了害虫和疾病。

于是，尤吉斯又与绝望的恶魔战斗了两周。有一次，他有机会装半天的卡车，然后他又搬运了一位老妇人的手提箱，并得到了25美分的奖励。这让他在旅馆住了好几个晚上，否则他可能会被冻死。这也让他时不时地有机会在早上买一份报纸并寻找工作，而他的竞争对手则在一旁观望并等待报纸被扔掉。然而，这实际上并不是表面上看起来的优势，因为报纸广告会导致人们浪费大量宝贵的时间和许多疲惫的旅程。其中整整一半都是“假货”，是无数机构利用失业者无助的无知而投放的。如果尤吉斯只失去了时间，那是因为他没有什么可失去的；每当有油嘴滑舌的经纪人告诉他手头有什么好职位时，他只能悲伤地摇头说自己没有足够的钱存入；当有人向他解释他和他的家人通过给照片上色可以赚多少钱时，他只能答应等他有两美元投资这套衣服时才会再来。
最终，尤吉斯通过一次偶然的机会遇见了他工会时期的老熟人。他在去收割机信托公司的大型工厂工作的路上遇到了这个人；他的朋友叫他过来，他会在他认识的老板面前替他说几句好话。于是尤吉斯跋涉了四五英里，在朋友的护送下穿过了门口等候的失业人群。当工头检查了他并询问了他之后，告诉他可以为他找到一个空缺时，他的膝盖几乎要垮了。

这次事故对尤吉斯来说意味着什么，他只是逐步意识到；因为他发现收割机工厂是慈善家和改革者引以为豪的地方。它为员工着想；它的车间又大又宽敞，它提供了一个餐厅，工人们可以用成本价买到好吃的食物，它甚至还有一个阅览室，还有像样的地方可以让女孩们的手休息。而且，这项工作没有堆料场中普遍存在的许多肮脏和令人厌恶的因素。日复一日，尤吉斯发现了这些事情——他从未预料到或梦想过的事情——直到这个新地方对他来说就像是天堂。

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
paragraphs: Yet he was afraid. Sometimes when he was down at his great house in Nottinghamshire, entertaining the fashionable young men of his own rank who were his chief companions, and astounding the county by the wanton luxury and gorgeous splendour of his mode of life, he would suddenly leave his guests and rush back to town to see that the door had not been tampered with and that the picture was still there. What if it should be stolen? The mere thought made him cold with horror. Surely the world would know his secret then. Perhaps the world already suspected it.

For, while he fascinated many, there were not a few who distrusted him. He was very nearly blackballed at a West End club of which his birth and social position fully entitled him to become a member, and it was said that on one occasion, when he was brought by a friend into the smoking-room of the Churchill, the Duke of Berwick and another gentleman got up in a marked manner and went out. Curious stories became current about him after he had passed his twenty-fifth year. It was rumoured that he had been seen brawling with foreign sailors in a low den in the distant parts of Whitechapel, and that he consorted with thieves and coiners and knew the mysteries of their trade. His extraordinary absences became notorious, and, when he used to reappear again in society, men would whisper to each other in corners, or pass him with a sneer, or look at him with cold searching eyes, as though they were determined to discover his secret.

Of such insolences and attempted slights he, of course, took no notice, and in the opinion of most people his frank debonair manner, his charming boyish smile, and the infinite grace of that wonderful youth that seemed never to leave him, were in themselves a sufficient answer to the calumnies, for so they termed them, that were circulated about him. It was remarked, however, that some of those who had been most intimate with him appeared, after a time, to shun him. Women who had wildly adored him, and for his sake had braved all social censure and set convention at defiance, were seen to grow pallid with shame or horror if Dorian Gray entered the room.

Yet these whispered scandals only increased in the eyes of many his strange and dangerous charm. His great wealth was a certain element of security. Society—civilized society, at least—is never very ready to believe anything to the detriment of those who are both rich and fascinating. It feels instinctively that manners are of more importance than morals, and, in its opinion, the highest respectability is of much less value than the possession of a good chef. And, after all, it is a very poor consolation to be told that the man who has given one a bad dinner, or poor wine, is irreproachable in his private life. Even the cardinal virtues cannot atone for half-cold entrées, as Lord Henry remarked once, in a discussion on the subject, and there is possibly a good deal to be said for his view. For the canons of good society are, or should be, the same as the canons of art. Form is absolutely essential to it. It should have the dignity of a ceremony, as well as its unreality, and should combine the insincere character of a romantic play with the wit and beauty that make such plays delightful to us. Is insincerity such a terrible thing? I think not. It is merely a method by which we can multiply our personalities.

Yet one had ancestors in literature as well as in one’s own race, nearer perhaps in type and temperament, many of them, and certainly with an influence of which one was more absolutely conscious. There were times when it appeared to Dorian Gray that the whole of history was merely the record of his own life, not as he had lived it in act and circumstance, but as his imagination had created it for him, as it had been in his brain and in his passions. He felt that he had known them all, those strange terrible figures that had passed across the stage of the world and made sin so marvellous and evil so full of subtlety. It seemed to him that in some mysterious way their lives had been his own.

The hero of the wonderful novel that had so influenced his life had himself known this curious fancy. In the seventh chapter he tells how, crowned with laurel, lest lightning might strike him, he had sat, as Tiberius, in a garden at Capri, reading the shameful books of Elephantis, while dwarfs and peacocks strutted round him and the flute-player mocked the swinger of the censer; and, as Caligula, had caroused with the green-shirted jockeys in their stables and supped in an ivory manger with a jewel-frontleted horse; and, as Domitian, had wandered through a corridor lined with marble mirrors, looking round with haggard eyes for the reflection of the dagger that was to end his days, and sick with that ennui, that terrible tædium vitæ, that comes on those to whom life denies nothing; and had peered through a clear emerald at the red shambles of the circus and then, in a litter of pearl and purple drawn by silver-shod mules, been carried through the Street of Pomegranates to a House of Gold and heard men cry on Nero Caesar as he passed by; and, as Elagabalus, had painted his face with colours, and plied the distaff among the women, and brought the Moon from Carthage and given her in mystic marriage to the Sun.
paragraphsZh: 但他还是害怕。有时，当他在诺丁汉郡的大宅里，招待他的主要同伴、与他同阶层的时尚年轻人，并以其肆意的奢华和华丽的生活方式震惊整个郡时，他会突然离开他的客人，冲回城里，看看门没有被动过，那幅画还在那里。如果它被偷了怎么办？光是这个念头就让他惊恐得浑身发冷。那时全世界肯定都会知道他的秘密。也许全世界都已经怀疑了。

因为，虽然他让很多人着迷，但也有不少人不信任他。他在伦敦西区的一家俱乐部差点被拒绝，而他的出身和社会地位完全有资格成为该俱乐部的会员。据说，有一次，当他被一位朋友带进丘吉尔酒店的吸烟室时，伯威克公爵和另一位绅士明显地起身走了出去。在他过了二十五岁之后，关于他的奇怪故事开始流传。有传言说，有人看到他在怀特查佩尔偏远地区的一个低矮巢穴中与外国水手争吵，而且他与小偷和钱币制造者交往，了解他们交易的奥秘。他的异常缺席变得臭名昭著，当他再次出现在社会上时，人们会在角落里窃窃私语，或者冷笑着经过他，或者用冷漠的目光看着他，仿佛他们决心要发现他的秘密。
对于这种无礼和企图的轻蔑，他当然没有在意，在大多数人看来，他坦率的温文尔雅的举止，他迷人的孩子气的微笑，以及那个似乎永远不会离开他的美好青春的无限优雅，本身就足以回答那些关于他的诽谤，因为他们如此称呼这些诽谤。然而，有人指出，一些与他最亲密的人在一段时间后似乎回避了他。如果道林·格雷走进房间，那些曾经疯狂崇拜他、为了他而勇敢地面对所有社会谴责、挑战传统的女人们会因为羞愧或恐惧而脸色苍白。

然而，在许多人眼中，他奇怪而危险的魅力只会让这些低声传出的丑闻愈演愈烈。他的巨额财富是某种安全感的一部分。社会——至少是文明社会——永远不会轻易相信任何有损于那些既富有又迷人的人的事情。它本能地感觉礼仪比道德更重要，而且在它看来，最高的尊重远不如拥有一个好厨师来得有价值。而且，毕竟，如果有人告诉你，一个给别人提供了一顿糟糕的晚餐或糟糕的酒的人在他的私生活中是无可指责的，这也是一种非常可怜的安慰。即使是基本的美德也无法弥补半冷的主菜，正如亨利勋爵在一次有关该主题的讨论中曾经说过的那样，他的观点可能有很多值得说的。因为美好社会的准则与艺术的准则是相同的，或者应该是相同的。形式对其来说绝对重要。它既应该具有仪式的尊严，又应该具有非现实性，并且应该将浪漫戏剧的不真诚特征与使此类戏剧令人愉悦的智慧和美丽结合起来。不真诚有这么可怕吗？我认为不是。它只是我们增强个性的一种方法。

然而，一个人在文学上以及在自己的种族中都有祖先，他们中的许多人也许在类型和气质上更接近，而且肯定具有人们更绝对意识到的影响。有时，道林·格雷觉得整个历史只不过是他自己生活的记录，不是他在行动和环境中经历过的，而是他的想象力为他创造的，就像它存在于他的大脑和激情中一样。他觉得自己认识他们所有人，那些奇怪而可怕的人物曾经穿过世界的舞台，使罪恶变得如此奇妙，使邪恶变得如此微妙。在他看来，从某种神秘的角度来说，他们的生活就是他自己的。

这本精彩小说对他的生活产生了如此大的影响，主人公自己也知道这种奇怪的幻想。在第七章中，他讲述了如何戴着月桂冠，以免闪电击中他，像提比略一样，坐在卡普里岛的一个花园里，阅读《大象》的可耻书籍，而矮人和孔雀在他周围昂首阔步，吹笛子的人嘲笑香炉的摇摆器；作为卡里古拉，他曾在马厩里与绿衫骑师一起狂欢，并在象牙马槽里与一匹镶着宝石的马共进晚餐。像图密善一样，他漫步在一条布满大理石镜子的走廊里，用憔悴的眼睛环顾四周，寻找那把即将结束他生命的匕首的倒影，并厌倦了那种厌倦，那种可怕的生活，这种感觉发生在那些生活不拒绝任何东西的人身上；透过清澈的祖母绿，凝视着马戏团的红色废墟，然后，穿着珍珠色和紫色的轿子，被银鞋骡子拉着，穿过石榴街，来到金屋，听到人们在尼禄·凯撒经过时哭泣。他以埃拉加巴卢斯的身份在自己的脸上涂上色彩，并在妇女中穿梭，从迦太基带来了月亮，并以神秘的方式将她嫁给了太阳。

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray · 选段 2
author: Oscar Wilde
paragraphs: “I hate the way you talk about your married life, Harry,” said Basil Hallward, strolling towards the door that led into the garden. “I believe that you are really a very good husband, but that you are thoroughly ashamed of your own virtues. You are an extraordinary fellow. You never say a moral thing, and you never do a wrong thing. Your cynicism is simply a pose.”

“Being natural is simply a pose, and the most irritating pose I know,” cried Lord Henry, laughing; and the two young men went out into the garden together and ensconced themselves on a long bamboo seat that stood in the shade of a tall laurel bush. The sunlight slipped over the polished leaves. In the grass, white daisies were tremulous.
After a pause, Lord Henry pulled out his watch. “I am afraid I must be going, Basil,” he murmured, “and before I go, I insist on your answering a question I put to you some time ago.”
“Well, I will tell you what it is. I want you to explain to me why you won’t exhibit Dorian Gray’s picture. I want the real reason.”
“No, you did not. You said it was because there was too much of yourself in it. Now, that is childish.”

“Harry,” said Basil Hallward, looking him straight in the face, “every portrait that is painted with feeling is a portrait of the artist, not of the sitter. The sitter is merely the accident, the occasion. It is not he who is revealed by the painter; it is rather the painter who, on the coloured canvas, reveals himself. The reason I will not exhibit this picture is that I am afraid that I have shown in it the secret of my own soul.”
“Oh, there is really very little to tell, Harry,” answered the painter; “and I am afraid you will hardly understand it. Perhaps you will hardly believe it.”

Lord Henry smiled, and leaning down, plucked a pink-petalled daisy from the grass and examined it. “I am quite sure I shall understand it,” he replied, gazing intently at the little golden, white-feathered disk, “and as for believing things, I can believe anything, provided that it is quite incredible.”

The wind shook some blossoms from the trees, and the heavy lilac-blooms, with their clustering stars, moved to and fro in the languid air. A grasshopper began to chirrup by the wall, and like a blue thread a long thin dragon-fly floated past on its brown gauze wings. Lord Henry felt as if he could hear Basil Hallward’s heart beating, and wondered what was coming.

“The story is simply this,” said the painter after some time. “Two months ago I went to a crush at Lady Brandon’s. You know we poor artists have to show ourselves in society from time to time, just to remind the public that we are not savages. With an evening coat and a white tie, as you told me once, anybody, even a stock-broker, can gain a reputation for being civilized. Well, after I had been in the room about ten minutes, talking to huge overdressed dowagers and tedious academicians, I suddenly became conscious that some one was looking at me. I turned half-way round and saw Dorian Gray for the first time. When our eyes met, I felt that I was growing pale. A curious sensation of terror came over me. I knew that I had come face to face with some one whose mere personality was so fascinating that, if I allowed it to do so, it would absorb my whole nature, my whole soul, my very art itself. I did not want any external influence in my life. You know yourself, Harry, how independent I am by nature. I have always been my own master; had at least always been so, till I met Dorian Gray. Then—but I don’t know how to explain it to you. Something seemed to tell me that I was on the verge of a terrible crisis in my life. I had a strange feeling that fate had in store for me exquisite joys and exquisite sorrows. I grew afraid and turned to quit the room. It was not conscience that made me do so: it was a sort of cowardice. I take no credit to myself for trying to escape.”
paragraphsZh: “我讨厌你谈论婚姻生活的方式，哈利，”巴兹尔·霍尔沃德一边说，一边向通向花园的门走去。 “我相信你确实是一个很好的丈夫，但你对自己的美德感到羞耻。你是一个了不起的人。你从不说道德的话，也从不做错事。你的愤世嫉俗只是一种姿态。”
“自然只是一种姿势，也是我所知道的最令人恼火的姿势，”亨利勋爵笑着喊道；两个年轻人一起走进花园，坐在高高的月桂树荫下的一张长竹椅上。阳光洒在光滑的树叶上。草丛里，白色的雏菊在颤抖。
停顿了一下，亨利勋爵拿出了手表。 “恐怕我必须走了，巴兹尔，”他低声说道，“在我走之前，我坚持要求你回答我之前向你提出的一个问题。”
“好吧，我会告诉你那是什么。我希望你向我解释一下为什么你不展示道林·格雷的照片。我想要真正的原因。”
“不，你没有。你说这是因为里面有太多你自己。现在，那太幼稚了。”
“哈利，”巴兹尔·霍华德直视着他的脸说道，“每一幅充满情感的肖像画都是艺术家的肖像，而不是画中人的肖像。画中人只是偶然，是场合。画家所揭示的不是他自己，而是画家在彩色画布上揭示了他自己。我不会展示这幅画的原因是我担心我在其中展示了我自己灵魂的秘密。”
“哦，真的没什么可说的，哈利，”画家回答道； “恐怕你很难理解。也许你很难相信。”
亨利勋爵微笑着，俯下身子，从草地上摘下一朵粉红色花瓣的雏菊，审视着它。 “我确信我会理解它，”他回答道，专注地凝视着那个金色的、白色羽毛的小圆盘，“至于相信什么，我可以相信任何事情，只要它是相当令人难以置信的。”
风吹落了树上的一些花朵，沉重的丁香花和簇拥的星星在慵懒的空气中来回移动。一只蚱蜢开始在墙边叽叽喳喳地叫着，一只又长又细的蜻蜓像一根蓝色的线一样，用棕色的纱翅飘过。亨利勋爵感觉自己仿佛能听到巴兹尔·霍华德的心跳声，不知道接下来会发生什么。

“故事就是这样。”过了一会儿，画家说道。 “两个月前，我去布兰登夫人家暗恋过。你知道，我们这些可怜的艺术家必须时不时地在社会上展示自己，只是为了提醒公众，我们不是野蛮人。正如你曾经告诉我的那样，穿着晚礼服和白色领带，任何人，甚至是股票经纪人，都可以赢得文明的声誉。好吧，在我在房间里呆了大约十分钟，与衣冠楚楚的贵妇和乏味的院士交谈后，我突然意识到，有些当我第一次看到道林·格雷时，我感到一种奇怪的恐惧感笼罩着我，我知道我面对的是一个如此迷人的人，如果我允许它这样做，它就会吸收我的整个本性，我的整个灵魂，我的艺术本身，我不希望任何外部影响。我的主人；至少一直都是这样，直到我遇到了道林·格雷——但我不知道如何向你解释，我有一种奇怪的感觉，命运为我准备了美妙的欢乐和悲伤，我转身离开了房间，这不是我试图逃脱的原因。

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray · 选段 3
author: Oscar Wilde
paragraphs: Was it really true that one could never change? He felt a wild longing for the unstained purity of his boyhood—his rose-white boyhood, as Lord Henry had once called it. He knew that he had tarnished himself, filled his mind with corruption and given horror to his fancy; that he had been an evil influence to others, and had experienced a terrible joy in being so; and that of the lives that had crossed his own, it had been the fairest and the most full of promise that he had brought to shame. But was it all irretrievable? Was there no hope for him?

Ah! in what a monstrous moment of pride and passion he had prayed that the portrait should bear the burden of his days, and he keep the unsullied splendour of eternal youth! All his failure had been due to that. Better for him that each sin of his life had brought its sure swift penalty along with it. There was purification in punishment. Not “Forgive us our sins” but “Smite us for our iniquities” should be the prayer of man to a most just God.

The curiously carved mirror that Lord Henry had given to him, so many years ago now, was standing on the table, and the white-limbed Cupids laughed round it as of old. He took it up, as he had done on that night of horror when he had first noted the change in the fatal picture, and with wild, tear-dimmed eyes looked into its polished shield. Once, some one who had terribly loved him had written to him a mad letter, ending with these idolatrous words: “The world is changed because you are made of ivory and gold. The curves of your lips rewrite history.” The phrases came back to his memory, and he repeated them over and over to himself. Then he loathed his own beauty, and flinging the mirror on the floor, crushed it into silver splinters beneath his heel. It was his beauty that had ruined him, his beauty and the youth that he had prayed for. But for those two things, his life might have been free from stain. His beauty had been to him but a mask, his youth but a mockery. What was youth at best? A green, an unripe time, a time of shallow moods, and sickly thoughts. Why had he worn its livery? Youth had spoiled him.

It was better not to think of the past. Nothing could alter that. It was of himself, and of his own future, that he had to think. James Vane was hidden in a nameless grave in Selby churchyard. Alan Campbell had shot himself one night in his laboratory, but had not revealed the secret that he had been forced to know. The excitement, such as it was, over Basil Hallward’s disappearance would soon pass away. It was already waning. He was perfectly safe there. Nor, indeed, was it the death of Basil Hallward that weighed most upon his mind. It was the living death of his own soul that troubled him. Basil had painted the portrait that had marred his life. He could not forgive him that. It was the portrait that had done everything. Basil had said things to him that were unbearable, and that he had yet borne with patience. The murder had been simply the madness of a moment. As for Alan Campbell, his suicide had been his own act. He had chosen to do it. It was nothing to him.

A new life! That was what he wanted. That was what he was waiting for. Surely he had begun it already. He had spared one innocent thing, at any rate. He would never again tempt innocence. He would be good.

As he thought of Hetty Merton, he began to wonder if the portrait in the locked room had changed. Surely it was not still so horrible as it had been? Perhaps if his life became pure, he would be able to expel every sign of evil passion from the face. Perhaps the signs of evil had already gone away. He would go and look.
paragraphsZh: 人真的永远无法改变吗？他对自己童年时期的纯洁无瑕感到一种疯狂的渴望——亨利勋爵曾这样称呼他的“玫瑰白的童年”。他知道自己玷污了自己，让自己的思想充满了腐败，让自己的幻想变得恐怖。他对别人产生了邪恶的影响，并因此而体验到了可怕的快乐；在他的一生中，他所带来的耻辱是最美好、最充满希望的。但这一切就已经无法挽回了吗？他就没有希望了吗？
啊！在一个充满骄傲和激情的可怕时刻，他祈祷这幅肖像能够承担他一生的重担，让他保持永恒青春的无玷光彩！他所有的失败都是因为这个。对他来说更好的是，他一生中犯下的每一个罪都必然会带来迅速的惩罚。惩罚中有净化作用。人向最公正的上帝祈祷，不应该是“宽恕我们的罪”，而应该是“惩罚我们的罪孽”。

亨利勋爵多年前送给他的那面雕刻奇特的镜子就放在桌子上，白肢丘比特像以前一样围着镜子大笑。他拿起它，就像在那个恐怖的夜晚，当他第一次注意到致命图片的变化时所做的那样，用狂野的、泪水模糊的眼睛看着它抛光的防护罩。有一次，一个非常爱他的人给他写了一封疯狂的信，最后以这些偶像崇拜的话语结束：“世界因为你是象牙和黄金而改变。你嘴唇的曲线改写了历史。”这些短语又回到了他的记忆中，他一遍又一遍地对自己重复着它们。然后他厌恶自己的美貌，把镜子扔到地板上，用脚后跟把它踩成银色的碎片。是他的美貌毁了他，毁了他的美貌，毁了他祈求的青春。如果没有这两件事，他的生活也许就不会沾染污点了。他的美貌对他来说不过是一张面具，他的青春对他来说不过是一种嘲弄。最好的青春是什么？一段青涩的时光，一段未成熟的时光，一段情绪浅薄的时光，一段病态的思想。他为什么穿着它的制服？青春把他宠坏了。

过去的事情最好不要想。没有什么可以改变这一点。他必须考虑的是他自己，以及他自己的未来。詹姆斯·韦恩被藏在塞尔比墓地的一个无名坟墓中。一天晚上，艾伦·坎贝尔在实验室开枪自杀，但没有透露他被迫知道的秘密。巴兹尔·霍华德失踪带来的兴奋很快就会过去。它已经减弱了。他在那里非常安全。事实上，最让他心神沉重的也不是巴兹尔·霍尔沃德的死。困扰他的是他自己灵魂的生死存亡。巴兹尔画的这幅肖像毁了他的生活。他无法原谅他。正是这幅肖像完成了一切。巴兹尔对他说了一些难以忍受的话，但他还是耐心地忍受了。这起谋杀案只是一时的疯狂而已。至于艾伦·坎贝尔，他的自杀是他自己的行为。他选择这么做。这对他来说不算什么。
新生活！这就是他想要的。这就是他所等待的。他肯定已经开始了。无论如何，他饶恕了一件无辜的事情。他再也不会诱惑无辜者了。他会很好的。
当他想到海蒂·默顿时，他开始怀疑锁着的房间里的肖像是否发生了变化。肯定还没有以前那么可怕吧？或许，如果他的生活变得纯洁，他就能从脸上除去一切邪恶的激情。也许邪恶的迹象已经消失了。他会去看看。

title: Walden
author: Henry David Thoreau
paragraphs: When a man is warmed by the several modes which I have described, what does he want next? Surely not more warmth of the same kind, as more and richer food, larger and more splendid houses, finer and more abundant clothing, more numerous incessant and hotter fires, and the like. When he has obtained those things which are necessary to life, there is another alternative than to obtain the superfluities; and that is, to adventure on life now, his vacation from humbler toil having commenced. The soil, it appears, is suited to the seed, for it has sent its radicle downward, and it may now send its shoot upward also with confidence. Why has man rooted himself thus firmly in the earth, but that he may rise in the same proportion into the heavens above?—for the nobler plants are valued for the fruit they bear at last in the air and light, far from the ground, and are not treated like the humbler esculents, which, though they may be biennials, are cultivated only till they have perfected their root, and often cut down at top for this purpose, so that most would not know them in their flowering season.

I do not mean to prescribe rules to strong and valiant natures, who will mind their own affairs whether in heaven or hell, and perchance build more magnificently and spend more lavishly than the richest, without ever impoverishing themselves, not knowing how they live,—if, indeed, there are any such, as has been dreamed; nor to those who find their encouragement and inspiration in precisely the present condition of things, and cherish it with the fondness and enthusiasm of lovers,—and, to some extent, I reckon myself in this number; I do not speak to those who are well employed, in whatever circumstances, and they know whether they are well employed or not;—but mainly to the mass of men who are discontented, and idly complaining of the hardness of their lot or of the times, when they might improve them. There are some who complain most energetically and inconsolably of any, because they are, as they say, doing their duty. I also have in my mind that seemingly wealthy, but most terribly impoverished class of all, who have accumulated dross, but know not how to use it, or get rid of it, and thus have forged their own golden or silver fetters.

If I should attempt to tell how I have desired to spend my life in years past, it would probably surprise those of my readers who are somewhat acquainted with its actual history; it would certainly astonish those who know nothing about it. I will only hint at some of the enterprises which I have cherished.

In any weather, at any hour of the day or night, I have been anxious to improve the nick of time, and notch it on my stick too; to stand on the meeting of two eternities, the past and future, which is precisely the present moment; to toe that line. You will pardon some obscurities, for there are more secrets in my trade than in most men’s, and yet not voluntarily kept, but inseparable from its very nature. I would gladly tell all that I know about it, and never paint “No Admittance” on my gate.

I long ago lost a hound, a bay horse, and a turtle-dove, and am still on their trail. Many are the travellers I have spoken concerning them, describing their tracks and what calls they answered to. I have met one or two who had heard the hound, and the tramp of the horse, and even seen the dove disappear behind a cloud, and they seemed as anxious to recover them as if they had lost them themselves.

To anticipate, not the sunrise and the dawn merely, but, if possible, Nature herself! How many mornings, summer and winter, before yet any neighbor was stirring about his business, have I been about mine! No doubt, many of my townsmen have met me returning from this enterprise, farmers starting for Boston in the twilight, or woodchoppers going to their work. It is true, I never assisted the sun materially in his rising, but, doubt not, it was of the last importance only to be present at it.

So many autumn, ay, and winter days, spent outside the town, trying to hear what was in the wind, to hear and carry it express! I well-nigh sunk all my capital in it, and lost my own breath into the bargain, running in the face of it. If it had concerned either of the political parties, depend upon it, it would have appeared in the Gazette with the earliest intelligence. At other times watching from the observatory of some cliff or tree, to telegraph any new arrival; or waiting at evening on the hill-tops for the sky to fall, that I might catch something, though I never caught much, and that, manna-wise, would dissolve again in the sun.

For a long time I was reporter to a journal, of no very wide circulation, whose editor has never yet seen fit to print the bulk of my contributions, and, as is too common with writers, I got only my labor for my pains. However, in this case my pains were their own reward.

For many years I was self-appointed inspector of snow storms and rain storms, and did my duty faithfully; surveyor, if not of highways, then of forest paths and all across-lot routes, keeping them open, and ravines bridged and passable at all seasons, where the public heel had testified to their utility.
paragraphsZh: 当一个人被我所描述的几种模式所温暖时，他接下来想要什么？当然，同类的温暖并不是更多、更丰富的食物、更大、更华丽的房屋、更精美、更丰富的衣服、更多、更不间断、更热的火等等。当他获得了生活所必需的东西时，除了获得多余的东西之外，还有另一种选择。也就是说，现在他要开始冒险生活了，他已经开始摆脱卑微的劳作了。看来，土壤适合种子，因为它已经将其胚根向下延伸，现在它也可以自信地向上延伸它的芽。为什么人类如此牢固地扎根于大地，却能以同样的比例升入天上呢？因为高贵的植物因其最终在远离地面的空气和阳光中结出的果实而受到重视，而不像低等的营养植物那样受到对待，后者虽然可能是二年生植物，但只栽培到根部完善为止，并且经常为此目的从顶部被砍掉，因此大多数人在开花季节不会认识它们。

我并不是要给坚强勇敢的人制定规则，他们会关心自己的事情，无论是在天堂还是地狱，也许比最富有的人建造得更宏伟，花钱更奢侈，却从不让自己陷入贫困，不知道自己如何生活——如果确实存在这样的人，正如人们所梦想的那样；也不适合那些在现状中找到鼓励和灵感，并以恋人的喜爱和热情来珍惜它的人——在某种程度上，我认为自己属于这一数字；我不是对那些在任何情况下都工作良好的人说话，他们知道自己是否工作良好；而是主要对那些不满的人说话，他们漫不经心地抱怨自己的命运或时代的艰难，而实际上他们可以改善它们。有些人抱怨得最激烈，也最无法安慰，因为正如他们所说，他们正在履行自己的职责。我心里也有一个看似富有，实则极其贫困的阶层，他们积累了糟粕，却不知如何利用、如何摆脱，从而铸就了自己的金银枷锁。
如果我试图讲述过去几年我希望如何度过自己的一生，可能会让那些稍微熟悉其真实历史的读者感到惊讶；这肯定会让那些对此一无所知的人感到惊讶。我只简单介绍一下我所珍视的一些企业。
无论天气如何，无论白天还是夜晚，我都渴望改善时间，并把它刻在我的手杖上；站在过去和未来两个永恒的交汇处，而这正是当下；遵守这条线。请原谅一些晦涩难懂的地方，因为我的行业比大多数人的行业有更多的秘密，但不是自愿保守的，而是与其本质密不可分的。我很乐意告诉大家我所知道的一切，并且永远不会在我的大门上画“禁止入内”。
我很久以前就失去了一只猎犬、一匹枣马和一只斑鸠，现在仍在追寻它们的踪迹。我曾与许多旅行者谈过他们的事，描述了他们的踪迹以及他们回应的呼唤。我遇到过一两个人，他们听到了猎犬的声音和马蹄声，甚至看到鸽子消失在云层后面，他们似乎急于找回它们，就像他们自己丢失了它们一样。
不仅仅要预见日出和黎明，如果可能的话，还要预见大自然本身！多少个早晨，无论夏天还是冬天，在邻居们开始忙他的事之前，我已经开始忙我的事了！毫无疑问，我的许多同胞都见过我从这个企业回来，在暮色中出发前往波士顿的农民，或者去工作的伐木工。确实，我从未在太阳升起的过程中为太阳提供过物质上的帮助，但是，毫无疑问，只有在太阳升起时在场才是最重要的。
这么多的秋天，哎呀，还有冬天，在城外度过，试图听到风中的声音，听到并表达它！我几乎把所有的资本都投入其中，并在这笔交易中失去了呼吸，面对它。如果它涉及任何一个政党，相信它，它就会以最早的情报出现在公报上。其他时候，我们会从悬崖或树上的观景台进行观察，以通报是否有新的到来。或者晚上在山顶等待天空落下，这样我就可以抓到一些东西，尽管我抓到的东西不多，而且，就甘露而言，它会在阳光下再次溶解。
很长一段时间里，我是一家发行量不大的期刊的记者，该期刊的编辑从未认为适合印刷我的大部分稿件，而且，就像作家中很常见的那样，我只得到了我的劳动成果。然而，在这种情况下，我的痛苦是他们自己的回报。
多年来，我自封为暴雪、暴雨巡查员，忠实履行职责；测量员，如果不是高速公路，那么是森林小路和所有跨地块路线的测量员，保持它们开放，并且在所有季节都架起桥梁和通行的峡谷，公众的脚后跟已经证明了它们的效用。

title: Walden · 选段 2
author: Henry David Thoreau
paragraphs: It is said that Mirabeau took to highway robbery “to ascertain what degree of resolution was necessary in order to place one’s self in formal opposition to the most sacred laws of society.” He declared that “a soldier who fights in the ranks does not require half so much courage as a foot-pad,”—“that honor and religion have never stood in the way of a well-considered and a firm resolve.” This was manly, as the world goes; and yet it was idle, if not desperate. A saner man would have found himself often enough “in formal opposition” to what are deemed “the most sacred laws of society,” through obedience to yet more sacred laws, and so have tested his resolution without going out of his way. It is not for a man to put himself in such an attitude to society, but to maintain himself in whatever attitude he find himself through obedience to the laws of his being, which will never be one of opposition to a just government, if he should chance to meet with such.

I left the woods for as good a reason as I went there. Perhaps it seemed to me that I had several more lives to live, and could not spare any more time for that one. It is remarkable how easily and insensibly we fall into a particular route, and make a beaten track for ourselves. I had not lived there a week before my feet wore a path from my door to the pond-side; and though it is five or six years since I trod it, it is still quite distinct. It is true, I fear that others may have fallen into it, and so helped to keep it open. The surface of the earth is soft and impressible by the feet of men; and so with the paths which the mind travels. How worn and dusty, then, must be the highways of the world, how deep the ruts of tradition and conformity! I did not wish to take a cabin passage, but rather to go before the mast and on the deck of the world, for there I could best see the moonlight amid the mountains. I do not wish to go below now.

I learned this, at least, by my experiment; that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours. He will put some things behind, will pass an invisible boundary; new, universal, and more liberal laws will begin to establish themselves around and within him; or the old laws be expanded, and interpreted in his favor in a more liberal sense, and he will live with the license of a higher order of beings. In proportion as he simplifies his life, the laws of the universe will appear less complex, and solitude will not be solitude, nor poverty poverty, nor weakness weakness. If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them.

It is a ridiculous demand which England and America make, that you shall speak so that they can understand you. Neither men nor toad-stools grow so. As if that were important, and there were not enough to understand you without them. As if Nature could support but one order of understandings, could not sustain birds as well as quadrupeds, flying as well as creeping things, and hush and who, which Bright can understand, were the best English. As if there were safety in stupidity alone. I fear chiefly lest my expression may not be extra-vagant enough, may not wander far enough beyond the narrow limits of my daily experience, so as to be adequate to the truth of which I have been convinced. Extra vagance! it depends on how you are yarded. The migrating buffalo, which seeks new pastures in another latitude, is not extravagant like the cow which kicks over the pail, leaps the cow-yard fence, and runs after her calf, in milking time. I desire to speak somewhere without bounds; like a man in a waking moment, to men in their waking moments; for I am convinced that I cannot exaggerate enough even to lay the foundation of a true expression. Who that has heard a strain of music feared then lest he should speak extravagantly any more forever? In view of the future or possible, we should live quite laxly and undefined in front, our outlines dim and misty on that side; as our shadows reveal an insensible perspiration toward the sun. The volatile truth of our words should continually betray the inadequacy of the residual statement. Their truth is instantly translated; its literal monument alone remains. The words which express our faith and piety are not definite; yet they are significant and fragrant like frankincense to superior natures.

Why level downward to our dullest perception always, and praise that as common sense? The commonest sense is the sense of men asleep, which they express by snoring. Sometimes we are inclined to class those who are once-and-a-half-witted with the half-witted, because we appreciate only a third part of their wit. Some would find fault with the morning-red, if they ever got up early enough. “They pretend,” as I hear, “that the verses of Kabir have four different senses; illusion, spirit, intellect, and the exoteric doctrine of the Vedas;” but in this part of the world it is considered a ground for complaint if a man’s writings admit of more than one interpretation. While England endeavors to cure the potato-rot, will not any endeavor to cure the brain-rot, which prevails so much more widely and fatally?
paragraphsZh: 据说，米拉波进行公路抢劫是为了“确定需要采取何种程度的决心才能正式反对社会最神圣的法律”。他宣称，“一名在队伍中作战的士兵所需要的勇气不及脚垫的一半”——“荣誉和宗教从来不会妨碍深思熟虑和坚定的决心。”就世界而言，这是有男子气概的；但它即使不是绝望，也是闲着的。一个理智的人会发现自己经常通过服从更神圣的法律来“正式反对”被认为是“社会最神圣的法律”，因此在不走偏路的情况下检验了自己的决心。一个人不应以这样的态度对待社会，而是要通过服从他的存在法则来维持他所发现的任何态度，如果他有机会遇到公正的政府，这永远不会反对公正的政府。
