The remedy for this inconveniency is to divide the legislature into different branches; and to render them, by different modes of election and different principles of action, as little connected with each other as the nature of their common functions and their common dependence on the society will admit. It may even be necessary to guard against dangerous encroachments by still further precautions. As the weight of the legislative authority requires that it should be thus divided, the weakness of the executive may require, on the other hand, that it should be fortified. An absolute negative on the legislature appears, at first view, to be the natural defense with which the executive magistrate should be armed. But perhaps it would be neither altogether safe nor alone sufficient. On ordinary occasions it might not be exerted with the requisite firmness, and on extraordinary occasions it might be perfidiously abused. May not this defect of an absolute negative be supplied by some qualified connection between this weaker department and the weaker branch of the stronger department, by which the latter may be led to support the constitutional rights of the former, without being too much detached from the rights of its own department?
paragraphsZh: 那么，我们最终应该采取什么权宜之计，才能在实践中维持宪法规定的几个部门之间必要的权力划分呢？唯一可以给出的答案是，由于发现所有这些外部规定都是不充分的，因此必须通过设计政府的内部结构来弥补缺陷，以便政府的几个组成部分可以通过它们的相互关系，成为使彼此保持在适当位置的手段。在不打算对这一重要思想进行全面阐述的情况下，我将冒昧地提出一些一般性的观察，这或许可以使我们对这一思想有更清晰的认识，并使我们能够对大会所规划的政府的原则和结构形成更正确的判断。

为了为政府不同权力的单独和明确行使奠定适当的基础（在某种程度上，这对于维护自由至关重要，每个部门都应该有自己的意愿；因此，其组成应使每一方的成员在任命其他方的成员时拥有尽可能少的代理权。如果严格遵守这一原则，就要求所有最高行政机关、立法机关和司法机关的任命都应来自同一个权力源泉——人民，通过彼此没有任何沟通的渠道。也许这样一个建立多个部门的计划在实践中不会像想象中那样困难。然而，执行过程中会遇到一些困难，并产生一些额外费用。因此，必须承认与原则的一些偏差。特别是在司法部门的组成中，严格坚持以下原则可能是不合适的：第一，由于成员必须具备特殊的资格，因此首先应该考虑选择最能保证这些资格的选择方式；其次，因为该部门任命的长期任期必须很快消除对授予他们的权力的所有依赖感。
同样明显的是，每个部门的成员在其办公室附属的薪酬方面应尽可能少地依赖其他部门的成员。如果行政法官或法官在这方面不独立于立法机关，那么他们在其他方面的独立性就只是名义上的。

但是，防止多个权力逐渐集中在同一部门的巨大保障在于，向管理每个部门的人提供必要的宪法手段和个人动机，以抵制其他部门的侵犯。与所有其他情况一样，在这种情况下，防御措施必须与攻击的危险相称。必须用野心来对抗野心。人的利益必须与地方的宪法权利联系起来。这可能是对人性的反思，这样的设备对于控制政府的滥用行为是必要的。但政府本身不就是对人性最伟大的反思吗？如果人是天使，就不需要政府了。如果天使要统治人类，那么对政府的外部或内部控制就不再是必要的了。建立一个人治人的政府，最大的困难在于：首先必须使政府能够控制被统治者；其次，迫使它自我控制。毫无疑问，对人民的依赖是对政府的首要控制；但经验告诉人类必须采取辅助预防措施。
这种通过对立和竞争的利益来弥补更好动机缺陷的政策，可以追溯到整个人类事务体系，无论是私人事务还是公共事务。我们在所有从属权力分配中都看到了这一点，其一贯的目标是划分和安排多个办公室，使每个办公室都可以相互制衡——每个人的私人利益都可以成为公共权利的哨兵。这些审慎的发明对于国家最高​​权力的分配来说是必不可少的。

但不可能赋予每个部门同等的自卫权。在共和政府中，立法权必然占主导地位。解决这种不便的办法是将立法机关划分为不同的分支；并通过不同的选举方式和不同的行动原则，使他们在其共同职能的性质和对社会的共同依赖所允许的范围内尽量减少彼此之间的联系。甚至可能有必要采取进一步的预防措施来防止危险的侵犯。由于立法权的分量要求如此划分，而行政权的弱点可能要求在另一方面加强它。乍一看，对立法机关的绝对否定似乎是行政法官应该武装起来的自然防御。但也许它既不完全安全，也不足够。在一般情况下，它可能不会得到必要的坚定执行，而在特殊情况下，它可能会被背信弃义地滥用。这种绝对否定的缺陷难道不能通过这个较弱的部门和较强部门的较弱部门之间的某种限定联系来弥补吗？通过这种联系，后者可能会支持前者的宪法权利，而不会过多地脱离自己部门的权利？

title: Smoke Bellew
author: Jack London
paragraphs: Smoke woke up.  A draught, that possessed all the rigidity of an icicle, was boring into the front of his shoulder as he lay on his side facing the wall.  When he had been tied into the bunk there had been no such draught, and now the outside air, driving into the heated atmosphere of the cabin with the pressure of fifty below zero, was sufficient advertizement that some one from without had pulled away the moss-chinking between the logs.  He squirmed as far as his bonds would permit, then craned his neck forward until his lips just managed to reach the crack.
"Breck," came the answer.  "Be careful you don't make a noise.  I'm going to pass a knife in to you."

"No good," Smoke said.  "I couldn't use it.  My hands are tied behind me and made fast to the leg of the bunk.  Besides, you couldn't get a knife through that crack.  But something must be done.  Those fellows are of a temper to hang me, and, of course, you know I didn't kill that man."

"It wasn't necessary to mention it, Smoke.  And if you did you had your reasons.  Which isn't the point at all.  I want to get you out of this. It's a tough bunch of men here.  You've seen them. They're shut off from the world, and they make and enforce their own law--by miner's meeting, you know.  They handled two men already--both grub-thieves. One they hiked from camp without an ounce of grub and no matches.  He made about forty miles and lasted a couple of days before he froze stiff.  Two weeks ago they hiked the second man.  They gave him his choice:  no grub, or ten lashes for each day's ration.  He stood for forty lashes before he fainted.  And now they've got you, and every last one is convinced you killed Kinade."
"The man who killed Kinade, shot at me, too.  His bullet broke the skin on my shoulder.  Get them to delay the trial till some one goes up and searches the bank where the murderer hid."

"No use.  They take the evidence of Harding and the five Frenchmen with him.  Besides, they haven't had a hanging yet, and they're keen for it. You see, things have been pretty monotonous.  They haven't located anything big, and they got tired of hunting for Surprise Lake.  They did some stampeding the first part of the winter, but they've got over that now.  Scurvy is beginning to show up amongst them, too, and they're just ripe for excitement."
"And it looks like I'll furnish it," was Smoke's comment.  "Say, Breck, how did you ever fall in with such a God-forsaken bunch?"

"After I got the claims at Squaw Creek opened up and some men to working, I came up here by way of the Stewart, hunting for Two Cabins. They'd beaten me to it, so I've been higher up the Stewart. Just got back yesterday out of grub."
"Nothing much.  But I think I've got a hydraulic proposition that'll work big when the country's opened up.  It's that, or a gold-dredger."
He was very much aware of the snores of the sleepers as he pursued the idea that had flashed into his mind.

"Good.  You've got to get into the brown canvas pack that's patched with moosehide.  You'll find a few pounds of lumpy gold.  You've never seen gold like it in the country, nor has anybody else. Here's what you've got to do.  Listen."

A quarter of an hour later, fully instructed and complaining that his toes were freezing, Breck went away.  Smoke, his own nose and one cheek frosted by proximity to the chink, rubbed them against the blankets for half an hour before the blaze and bite of the returning blood assured him of the safety of his flesh.
paragraphsZh: 烟醒了。 当他面朝墙壁侧躺时，一股像冰柱一样坚硬的气流正钻进他的肩膀前面。 当他被绑在铺位上时，没有这样的气流，而现在外面的空气，以零下五十度的压力进入机舱的炎热气氛，这足以证明有人从外面来了，把原木之间的苔藓缝隙吹走了。 他在束缚允许的范围内蠕动，然后向前伸长脖子，直到嘴唇刚好够到裂缝。
“布雷克，”回答道。 “小心别出声，我要把刀递给你。”
“不好，”斯莫克说。 “我不能使用它。我的双手被绑在身后，牢牢地固定在床铺的腿上。此外，你无法从那个裂缝中拿刀。但必须采取一些措施。那些家伙有脾气要绞死我，当然，你知道我没有杀那个人。”
“没必要提这件事，斯莫克。如果你提了，你也有你的理由。这根本不是重点。我想让你摆脱这一切。这里有一群强硬的人。你见过他们。他们与世隔绝，他们制定并执行自己的法律——通过矿工会议，你知道。他们已经处理了两个人——都是窃贼。其中一个是他们从营地徒步走出来的，没有带任何人。他走了大约四十英里，坚持了几天，然后他就僵住了。两周前，他们给了他一个选择：不给他食物，或者每天给他鞭打十下，然后他就昏倒了。”
“杀死Kinade的人也向我开枪。他的子弹打碎了我肩膀上的皮肤。让他们推迟审判，直到有人上去搜查凶手藏身的银行。”
“没用。他们拿走了哈丁和五个法国人的证据。此外，他们还没有绞死，他们很想绞死。你看，事情很单调。他们没有找到任何大东西，他们厌倦了寻找惊喜湖。他们在冬天的前半段时间发生了一些踩踏事件，但现在已经过去了。坏血病也开始出现在他们中间，他们刚刚成熟为了兴奋。”
“看来我会提供它，”斯莫克评论道。 “说吧，布雷克，你怎么会跟这么一群被上帝遗弃的人混在一起呢？”
“在我得到斯阔溪的矿区开放并且一些人开始工作后，我经由斯图尔特来到这里，寻找两间小屋。他们比我先一步，所以我已经在斯图尔特更高的地方了。昨天刚从食物中回来。”
“没什么。但我想我有一个液压方案，当国家开放时它会发挥很大作用。就是这样，或者是一艘淘金船。”
当他追寻脑海中闪现的想法时，他非常清楚睡眠者的鼾声。
“好。你必须进入那个用驼鹿皮修补的棕色帆布包。你会发现几磅块状黄金。你在这个国家从来没有见过这样的黄金，其他人也没有见过。这就是你要做的。听着。”
一刻钟后，布雷克在得到充分指示并抱怨他的脚趾冻僵后离开了。 烟雾、他自己的鼻子和一侧脸颊因靠近缝隙而结霜，在毯子上摩擦了半个小时，然后火焰和回流的血液的叮咬确保了他肉体的安全。

title: Smoke Bellew · 选段 2
author: Jack London
paragraphs: "I have just seen a copy of the Billow," Gillet wrote from Paris. "Of course O'Hara will succeed with it.  But he's missing some plays." (Here followed details in the improvement of the budding society weekly.)  "Go down and see him.  Let him think they're your own suggestions.  Don't let him know they're from me.  If he does, he'll make me Paris correspondent, which I can't afford, because I'm getting real money for my stuff from the big magazines.  Above all, don't forget to make him fire that dub who's doing the musical and art criticism.  Another thing, San Francisco has always had a literature of her own.  But she hasn't any now.  Tell him to kick around and get some gink to turn out a live serial, and to put into it the real romance and glamour and colour of San Francisco."

And down to the office of the Billow went Kit Bellew faithfully to instruct.  O'Hara listened.  O'Hara debated.  O'Hara agreed.  O'Hara fired the dub who wrote criticism.  Further, O'Hara had a way with him--the very way that was feared by Gillet in distant Paris.  When O'Hara wanted anything, no friend could deny him.  He was sweetly and compellingly irresistible.  Before Kit Bellew could escape from the office he had become an associate editor, had agreed to write weekly columns of criticism till some decent pen was found, and had pledged himself to write a weekly instalment of ten thousand words on the San Francisco serial--and all this without pay.  The Billow wasn't paying yet, O'Hara explained; and just as convincingly had he exposited that there was only one man in San Francisco capable of writing the serial, and that man Kit Bellew.

And thereat had begun his servitude to O'Hara and the insatiable columns of the Billow.  Week after week he held down an office chair, stood off creditors, wrangled with printers, and turned out twenty-five thousand words of all sorts weekly.  Nor did his labours lighten.  The Billow was ambitious.  It went in for illustration. The processes were expensive.  It never had any money to pay Kit Bellew, and by the same token it was unable to pay for any additions to the office staff.

"Thank God for good fellows then," O'Hara cried, with tears in his eyes as he gripped Kit's hand.  "You're all that's saved me, Kit. But for you I'd have gone bust.  Just a little longer, old man, and things will be easier."

A little later he thought he saw his way out.  Watching his chance, in O'Hara's presence, he fell over a chair.  A few minutes afterwards he bumped into the corner of the desk, and, with fumbling fingers, capsized a paste pot.
For several days he continued to fall over and bump into the office furniture.  But O'Hara's heart was not softened.

"I tell you what, Kit," he said one day, "you've got to see an oculist. There's Doctor Hassdapple.  He's a crackerjack.  And it won't cost you anything.  We can get it for advertizing.  I'll see him myself."
"There's nothing the matter with your eyes," was the doctor's verdict, after a lengthy examination.  "In fact, your eyes are magnificent--a pair in a million."
The result of this was that O'Hara sympathized and talked glowingly of the time when the Billow would be on its feet.

Luckily for Kit Bellew, he had his own income.  Small it was, compared with some, yet it was large enough to enable him to belong to several clubs and maintain a studio in the Latin Quarter.  In point of fact, since his associate editorship, his expenses had decreased prodigiously.  He had no time to spend money.  He never saw the studio any more, nor entertained the local Bohemians with his famous chafing-dish suppers.  Yet he was always broke, for the Billow, in perennial distress, absorbed his cash as well as his brains.  There were the illustrators who periodically refused to illustrate, the printers who periodically refused to print, and the office boy who frequently refused to officiate.  At such times O'Hara looked at Kit, and Kit did the rest.
paragraphsZh: “我刚刚看到了《巨浪》的副本，”吉列在巴黎写道。 “奥哈拉当然会成功。但他错过了一些比赛。” （这里是关于改善新兴社会周刊的详细信息。）“下去见他。让他认为这些建议是你自己的建议。不要让他知道这些建议是我提出的。如果他这样做了，他会让我成为巴黎记者，我负担不起，因为我从大杂志上得到真正的钱来购买我的东西。最重要的是，别忘了让他解雇那个正在做音乐和艺术评论的配音。另一件事，旧金山一直有文学但她现在没有了，请他四处走动，制作一部现场连续剧，并将旧金山真正的浪漫、魅力和色彩融入其中。”

基特·贝卢 (Kit Bellew) 前往巨浪办公室忠实地进行指导。 奥哈拉听着。 奥哈拉进行了辩论。 奥哈拉同意了。 奥哈拉解雇了撰写批评文章的人。 此外，奥哈拉对他有一套办法——正是远在巴黎的吉列所害怕的方式。 当奥哈拉想要什么时，没有朋友可以拒绝他。 他很可爱，令人无法抗拒。 在基特·贝卢逃离办公室之前，他已经成为一名副编辑，同意每周撰写批评专栏，直到找到合适的笔为止，并承诺自己每周为旧金山连载写一万字的文章——而这一切都是免费的。 奥哈拉解释说，巨浪尚未付款；他同样令人信服地指出，旧金山只有一个人有能力写这部连续剧，那就是基特·贝卢。
从那时起，他开始为奥哈拉和巨浪的贪得无厌的柱子服务。 一周又一周，他稳住办公椅，与债权人保持距离，与打印机争吵，每周打印出两万五千个字。 他的工作也没有减轻。 巨浪雄心勃勃。 它用于说明。这些过程非常昂贵。 它从来没有钱支付基特·贝卢的工资，同样，它也无法支付办公室工作人员的任何新增费用。
“感谢上帝赐予了我们这些好人，”奥哈拉抓住基特的手，泪流满面地喊道。 “是你救了我，基特。要不是你，我早就破产了。再等一会儿，老伙计，事情就会容易多了。”
过了一会儿，他认为自己找到了出路。 当着奥哈拉的面，他看到了自己的机会，从一张椅子上摔倒了。 几分钟后，他撞到了桌子的一角，手指摸索着，打翻了一个糊锅。
连续几天，他不断摔倒并撞到办公家具上。 但奥哈拉的心并没有软化。
“我告诉你，基特，”有一天他说，“你必须去看眼科医生。哈斯达普尔医生是个医生。他是个天才。而且这不会花你任何钱。我们可以拿来做广告。我会亲自去见他。”
经过长时间的检查，医生的结论是“你的眼睛没有任何问题”。 “事实上，你的眼睛非常漂亮——百万分之一。”
这样做的结果是，奥哈拉对巨浪将要站稳脚跟的时刻表示同情并热情洋溢地谈论着。

对于 Kit Bellew 来说幸运的是，他有自己的收入。 与一些人相比，它很小，但它足够大，使他能够加入几个俱乐部，并在拉丁区拥有一个工作室。 事实上，自从担任副主编以来，他的开支已经大幅减少。 他没有时间花钱。 他再也没有去过工作室，也没有用他著名的火锅晚餐招待当地的波西米亚人。 然而他总是身无分文，因为长期处于困境的巨浪吸收了他的现金和大脑。 有些插画家定期拒绝插画，有些印刷工定期拒绝打印，还有勤杂工经常拒绝主持工作。 在这种时候，奥哈拉看着基特，其余的事情都由基特来做。

title: Smoke Bellew · 选段 3
author: Jack London
paragraphs: "Huh!  I can hike along on the stumps an' wear the heels off your moccasins.  Though it ain't no use.  I've ben figgerin'.  Creek claims is five hundred feet.  Call 'em ten to the mile.  They's a thousand stampeders ahead of us, an' that creek ain't no hundred miles long. Somebody's goin' to get left, an' it makes a noise like you an' me."

Smoke laughed, and let out another link.  The whole aspect of the adventure had changed.  Through his brain was running a phrase of the mad philosopher--"the transvaluation of  values."  In truth, he was less interested in staking a fortune than in beating Shorty. After all, he concluded, it wasn't the reward of the game but the playing of it that counted.  Mind, and muscle, and stamina, and soul, were challenged in a contest with this Shorty, a man who had never opened the books, and who did not know grand opera from rag-time, nor an epic from a chilblain.

"Shorty, I've got you skinned to death.  I've reconstructed every cell in my body since I hit the beach at Dyea.  My flesh is as stringy as whipcords, and as bitter and mean as the bite of a rattlesnake.  A few months ago I'd have patted myself on the back to write such words, but I couldn't have written them.  I had to live them first, and now that I'm living them there's no need to write them.  I'm the real, bitter, stinging goods, and no scrub of a mountaineer can put anything over on me without getting it back compound.  Now, you go ahead and set pace for half an hour.  Do your worst, and when you're all in I'll go ahead and give you half an hour of the real worst."
"Huh!" Shorty sneered genially.  "An' him not dry behind the ears yet. Get outa the way an' let your father show you some goin'."

Half-hour by half-hour they alternated in setting pace.  Nor did they talk much.  Their exertions kept them warm, though their breath froze on their faces from lips to chin.  So intense was the cold that they almost continually rubbed their noses and cheeks with their mittens.  A few minutes cessation from this allowed the flesh to grow numb, and then most vigorous rubbing was required to produce the burning prickle of returning circulation.

Often they thought they had reached the lead, but always they overtook more stampeders who had started before them.  Occasionally, groups of men attempted to swing in behind to their pace, but invariably they were discouraged after a mile or two, and disappeared in the darkness to the rear.

"We've been out on trail all winter," was Shorty's comment.  "An' them geezers, soft from laying around their cabins, has the nerve to think they can keep our stride.  Now, if they was real sour-doughs it'd be different.  If there's one thing a sour-dough can do it's sure walk."
Once, Smoke lighted a match and glanced at his watch.  He never repeated it, for so quick was the bite of the frost on his bared hands, that half an hour passed before they were again comfortable.
"Three hundred and thirty-eight," Shorty corrected.  "I ben keepin' count.  Get outa the way, stranger.  Let somebody stampede that knows how to stampede."

The latter was addressed to a man, evidently exhausted, who could no more than stumble along, and who blocked the trail.  This, and one other, were the only played-out men they encountered, for they were very near to the head of the stampede.  Nor did they learn till afterwards the horrors of that night.  Exhausted men sat down to rest by the way, and failed to get up.  Seven were frozen to death, while scores of amputations of toes, feet, and fingers were performed in the Dawson hospitals on the survivors.  For of all nights for a stampede, the one to Squaw Creek occurred on the coldest night of the year. Before morning, the spirit thermometers at Dawson registered seventy degrees below zero.  The men composing the stampede, with few exceptions, were new-comers in the country who did not know the way of the cold.
paragraphsZh: “哈！我可以在树桩上徒步旅行，把你的莫卡辛鞋的鞋跟磨掉。尽管这没有用。我一直在想。小溪声称有五百英尺。称他们为十英里。他们在我们前面有一千个踩踏者，而那条小溪没有一百英里长。有人要离开，它发出像你一样的噪音和'我。”
烟笑了一声，又放出了一个链接。 冒险的整个方面都改变了。 他的脑子里流淌着疯狂哲学家的一句话——“价值的重估”。 事实上，他对击败矮子更感兴趣，而不是赌上一大笔钱。毕竟，他总结道，重要的不是游戏的奖励，而是玩游戏的过程。 头脑、肌肉、体力和灵魂都在与这个矮子的较量中受到了挑战，这个矮子从来没有翻过书，不知道大型歌剧和拉格泰姆音乐，也不知道史诗和冻疮。

“矮子，我已经把你剥皮死了。自从我到达代亚海滩以来，我已经重建了我体内的每一个细胞。我的肉像鞭绳一样粘稠，像响尾蛇的咬一样苦涩而刻薄。几个月前，我会拍拍自己的背写下这样的文字，但我不可能写下它们。我必须先生活它们，现在我生活在它们中，没有必要我是一个真正的、痛苦的、刺痛的人，没有一个登山者可以把任何东西放在我身上而不把它恢复回来。现在，你继续前进，做你最坏的事情，当你都在的时候，我会继续给你半个小时真正的最坏的事情。”
“嗯！”矮子和蔼地冷笑道。 “他的耳后还没干。让开，让你父亲给你演示一下。”
他们半小时一个半小时地交替设定节奏。 他们也没有说太多话。 他们的努力让他们保持温暖，尽管他们的呼吸从嘴唇到下巴的脸上都结冰了。 天气如此寒冷，他们几乎不停地用手套揉鼻子和脸颊。 停止几分钟后，肌肉会变得麻木，然后需要用力摩擦才能产生回流循环的灼烧感。
他们常常认为自己已经领先，但他们总是超越更多在他们之前出发的踩踏者。 偶尔，一群人试图跟上他们的步伐，但总是在一两英里后就灰心丧气，消失在后方的黑暗中。
“我们整个冬天都在路上，”肖蒂评论道。 “这些老头子，因为躺在他们的小屋周围而变得软弱，居然有勇气认为他们能跟上我们的步伐。现在，如果他们是真正的酸面团，那就不一样了。如果说酸面团能做一件事的话，那就肯定是走路了。”
有一次，斯莫克点燃了一根火柴，看了一眼手表。 他没有再重复一遍，因为他裸露的双手上的霜冻得太快了，半个小时过去了，他们才再次感到舒服。
“三百三十八，”肖蒂纠正道。 “我在数数。陌生人，让开。让懂得如何踩踏的人来踩踏吧。”

后者是写给一名男子的，他显然已经筋疲力尽，只能跌跌撞撞地前行，并且挡住了道路。 这个人和另外一个人是他们遇到的唯一的精疲力尽的人，因为他们非常接近踩踏事件的头部。 直到事后他们才知道那天晚上的恐怖。 疲惫不堪的男子顺便坐下来休息，没能起来。 七人被冻死，道森医院对幸存者进行了数十例脚趾、脚和手指截肢手术。 在所有发生踩踏事件的夜晚中，前往斯阔溪的那次发生在一年中最冷的夜晚。早上之前，道森的酒精温度计显示零下七十度。 造成踩踏事件的人，除了少数例外，都是刚到这个国家的人，他们不知道寒冷的方式。

title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: Sherlock Holmes sat for some time in silence, with his head sunk forward and his eyes bent upon the red glow of the fire. Then he lit his pipe, and leaning back in his chair he watched the blue smoke-rings as they chased each other up to the ceiling.
“Well, yes. Save, perhaps, that. And yet this John Openshaw seems to me to be walking amid even greater perils than did the Sholtos.”

Sherlock Holmes closed his eyes and placed his elbows upon the arms of his chair, with his finger-tips together. “The ideal reasoner,” he remarked, “would, when he had once been shown a single fact in all its bearings, deduce from it not only all the chain of events which led up to it but also all the results which would follow from it. As Cuvier could correctly describe a whole animal by the contemplation of a single bone, so the observer who has thoroughly understood one link in a series of incidents should be able to accurately state all the other ones, both before and after. We have not yet grasped the results which the reason alone can attain to. Problems may be solved in the study which have baffled all those who have sought a solution by the aid of their senses. To carry the art, however, to its highest pitch, it is necessary that the reasoner should be able to utilise all the facts which have come to his knowledge; and this in itself implies, as you will readily see, a possession of all knowledge, which, even in these days of free education and encyclopædias, is a somewhat rare accomplishment. It is not so impossible, however, that a man should possess all knowledge which is likely to be useful to him in his work, and this I have endeavoured in my case to do. If I remember rightly, you on one occasion, in the early days of our friendship, defined my limits in a very precise fashion.”

“Yes,” I answered, laughing. “It was a singular document. Philosophy, astronomy, and politics were marked at zero, I remember. Botany variable, geology profound as regards the mud-stains from any region within fifty miles of town, chemistry eccentric, anatomy unsystematic, sensational literature and crime records unique, violin-player, boxer, swordsman, lawyer, and self-poisoner by cocaine and tobacco. Those, I think, were the main points of my analysis.”

Holmes grinned at the last item. “Well,” he said, “I say now, as I said then, that a man should keep his little brain-attic stocked with all the furniture that he is likely to use, and the rest he can put away in the lumber-room of his library, where he can get it if he wants it. Now, for such a case as the one which has been submitted to us to-night, we need certainly to muster all our resources. Kindly hand me down the letter K of the American Encyclopædia which stands upon the shelf beside you. Thank you. Now let us consider the situation and see what may be deduced from it. In the first place, we may start with a strong presumption that Colonel Openshaw had some very strong reason for leaving America. Men at his time of life do not change all their habits and exchange willingly the charming climate of Florida for the lonely life of an English provincial town. His extreme love of solitude in England suggests the idea that he was in fear of someone or something, so we may assume as a working hypothesis that it was fear of someone or something which drove him from America. As to what it was he feared, we can only deduce that by considering the formidable letters which were received by himself and his successors. Did you remark the postmarks of those letters?”

“Excellent. We have already a clue. There can be no doubt that the probability—the strong probability—is that the writer was on board of a ship. And now let us consider another point. In the case of Pondicherry, seven weeks elapsed between the threat and its fulfilment, in Dundee it was only some three or four days. Does that suggest anything?”

“There is at least a presumption that the vessel in which the man or men are is a sailing-ship. It looks as if they always send their singular warning or token before them when starting upon their mission. You see how quickly the deed followed the sign when it came from Dundee. If they had come from Pondicherry in a steamer they would have arrived almost as soon as their letter. But, as a matter of fact, seven weeks elapsed. I think that those seven weeks represented the difference between the mail-boat which brought the letter and the sailing vessel which brought the writer.”

“More than that. It is probable. And now you see the deadly urgency of this new case, and why I urged young Openshaw to caution. The blow has always fallen at the end of the time which it would take the senders to travel the distance. But this one comes from London, and therefore we cannot count upon delay.”

“The papers which Openshaw carried are obviously of vital importance to the person or persons in the sailing-ship. I think that it is quite clear that there must be more than one of them. A single man could not have carried out two deaths in such a way as to deceive a coroner’s jury. There must have been several in it, and they must have been men of resource and determination. Their papers they mean to have, be the holder of them who it may. In this way you see K. K. K. ceases to be the initials of an individual and becomes the badge of a society.”
paragraphsZh: 夏洛克·福尔摩斯沉默地坐了一会儿，他的头向前垂着，眼睛盯着火光的红色光芒。然后他点燃了烟斗，靠在椅子上，看着蓝色的烟圈互相追赶到天花板。
“嗯，是的。也许，除了那个。然而，在我看来，这个约翰·奥彭肖似乎比肖尔托家族面临着更大的危险。”

夏洛克·福尔摩斯闭上眼睛，将手肘放在椅子扶手上，指尖并拢。 “理想的推理者，”他评论道，“一旦向他展示了一个单一事实的所有方面，他不仅会从中推断出导致该事件的所有事件链，而且还会推断出随之而来的所有结果。正如居维叶可以通过对一根骨头的沉思来正确地描述整个动物一样，因此，彻底理解一系列事件中的一个环节的观察者应该能够准确地陈述所有其他事件，无论是之前还是之后。我们还没有掌握结果那些曾经通过感官寻求解决方案的人所困惑的问题，可以在研究中得到解决，然而，为了将艺术发挥到极致，推理者必须能够利用他所知道的所有事实；正如你会看到的，这本身就意味着拥有所有的知识，即使在自由教育和百科全书的时代，这也不是不可能的。然而，一个人应该拥有对他的工作可能有用的所有知识，如果我没记错的话，在我们友谊的早期，你曾以一种非常精确的方式界定了我的界限。
“是的，”我笑着回答。 “这是一份独特的文件。我记得，哲学、天文学和政治学都被标记为零。植物学变量、地质学对城镇五十英里范围内任何地区的泥迹的深刻认识、化学怪异、解剖学不系统、耸人听闻的文学和独特的犯罪记录、小提琴手、拳击手、剑客、律师以及可卡因和烟草的自毒者。我认为这些是我分析的要点。”

福尔摩斯对最后一个项目笑了。 “好吧，”他说，“我现在说，正如我当时所说的那样，一个人应该在他的小大脑阁楼里存放他可能会使用的所有家具，其余的可以放在图书馆的杂物间里，如果他想要的话，他可以在那里得到。现在，对于今晚提交给我们的这样一个案例，我们当然需要集中我们所有的资源。请把美国百科全书上的字母K递给我。现在让我们考虑一下这种情况，看看可以从中推断出什么。首先，我们可以假设，奥彭肖上校离开美国有一些非常充分的理由，他不会愿意改变他们所有的习惯，而愿意用英国偏远小镇的孤独生活来交换他对孤独的热爱，因此我们可以假设这是一个可行的假设。对驱使他离开美国的某人或某事的恐惧，我们只能通过考虑他和他的继任者收到的令人畏惧的信件来推断。”
“很好。我们已经有了线索。毫无疑问，可能性——极强的可能性——作者是在一艘船上。现在让我们考虑另一点。就本地治里而言，威胁与实现之间相隔了七周，而在邓迪则只有大约三四天。这表明了什么吗？”
“至少有一个假设，这个人或这些人所在的船只是一艘帆船。看起来他们在开始执行任务时总是在他们面前发出独特的警告或标志。你看，当它来自邓迪时，契约是多么迅速地跟随标志。如果他们乘轮船从本地治里来，他们几乎会在收到信后就到达。但事实上，七个星期过去了。我认为这七个星期代表了差异在运送信件的邮船和运送作者的帆船之间。”
“不仅如此。很有可能。现在你看到了这个新案件的极其紧迫性，以及为什么我敦促年轻的奥彭肖要小心。打击总是在发件人长途跋涉的时间结束时发生。但这一次来自伦敦，因此我们不能指望延误。”
“奥彭肖携带的文件显然对帆船上的一个或多个人至关重要。我认为很明显，这些文件肯定不止一份。一个人不可能以欺骗验尸官陪审团的方式实施两次死亡。其中一定有好几份文件，而且他们一定是足智多谋、有决心的人。他们想要拥有他们的文件，无论是谁都持有这些文件。这样你就明白了K.K.K.不再是个人的名字首字母，而是成为一个社会的徽章。”

title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes · 选段 2
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: “‘Well, then, you know now. And if you ever put your foot over that threshold again’—here in an instant the smile hardened into a grin of rage, and he glared down at me with the face of a demon—‘I’ll throw you to the mastiff.’

“I was so terrified that I do not know what I did. I suppose that I must have rushed past him into my room. I remember nothing until I found myself lying on my bed trembling all over. Then I thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not live there longer without some advice. I was frightened of the house, of the man, of the woman, of the servants, even of the child. They were all horrible to me. If I could only bring you down all would be well. Of course I might have fled from the house, but my curiosity was almost as strong as my fears. My mind was soon made up. I would send you a wire. I put on my hat and cloak, went down to the office, which is about half a mile from the house, and then returned, feeling very much easier. A horrible doubt came into my mind as I approached the door lest the dog might be loose, but I remembered that Toller had drunk himself into a state of insensibility that evening, and I knew that he was the only one in the household who had any influence with the savage creature, or who would venture to set him free. I slipped in in safety and lay awake half the night in my joy at the thought of seeing you. I had no difficulty in getting leave to come into Winchester this morning, but I must be back before three o’clock, for Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle are going on a visit, and will be away all the evening, so that I must look after the child. Now I have told you all my adventures, Mr. Holmes, and I should be very glad if you could tell me what it all means, and, above all, what I should do.”

Holmes and I had listened spellbound to this extraordinary story. My friend rose now and paced up and down the room, his hands in his pockets, and an expression of the most profound gravity upon his face.

“You seem to me to have acted all through this matter like a very brave and sensible girl, Miss Hunter. Do you think that you could perform one more feat? I should not ask it of you if I did not think you a quite exceptional woman.”

“We shall be at the Copper Beeches by seven o’clock, my friend and I. The Rucastles will be gone by that time, and Toller will, we hope, be incapable. There only remains Mrs. Toller, who might give the alarm. If you could send her into the cellar on some errand, and then turn the key upon her, you would facilitate matters immensely.”

“Excellent! We shall then look thoroughly into the affair. Of course there is only one feasible explanation. You have been brought there to personate someone, and the real person is imprisoned in this chamber. That is obvious. As to who this prisoner is, I have no doubt that it is the daughter, Miss Alice Rucastle, if I remember right, who was said to have gone to America. You were chosen, doubtless, as resembling her in height, figure, and the colour of your hair. Hers had been cut off, very possibly in some illness through which she has passed, and so, of course, yours had to be sacrificed also. By a curious chance you came upon her tresses. The man in the road was undoubtedly some friend of hers—possibly her fiancé—and no doubt, as you wore the girl’s dress and were so like her, he was convinced from your laughter, whenever he saw you, and afterwards from your gesture, that Miss Rucastle was perfectly happy, and that she no longer desired his attentions. The dog is let loose at night to prevent him from endeavouring to communicate with her. So much is fairly clear. The most serious point in the case is the disposition of the child.”

“My dear Watson, you as a medical man are continually gaining light as to the tendencies of a child by the study of the parents. Don’t you see that the converse is equally valid. I have frequently gained my first real insight into the character of parents by studying their children. This child’s disposition is abnormally cruel, merely for cruelty’s sake, and whether he derives this from his smiling father, as I should suspect, or from his mother, it bodes evil for the poor girl who is in their power.”

“I am sure that you are right, Mr. Holmes,” cried our client. “A thousand things come back to me which make me certain that you have hit it. Oh, let us lose not an instant in bringing help to this poor creature.”
“We must be circumspect, for we are dealing with a very cunning man. We can do nothing until seven o’clock. At that hour we shall be with you, and it will not be long before we solve the mystery.”

We were as good as our word, for it was just seven when we reached the Copper Beeches, having put up our trap at a wayside public-house. The group of trees, with their dark leaves shining like burnished metal in the light of the setting sun, were sufficient to mark the house even had Miss Hunter not been standing smiling on the door-step.
paragraphsZh: “‘好吧，那么，你现在知道了。如果你再把脚跨过那个门槛’——刹那间，笑容变成了愤怒的笑容，他用恶魔般的脸瞪着我——‘我会把你扔到獒犬那里。’

“我非常害怕，我不知道自己做了什么。我想我一定是从他身边冲进了我的房间。我什么都不记得了，直到我发现自己躺在床上浑身发抖。然后我想到了你，福尔摩斯先生。如果没有一些建议，我就无法在那里住更长的时间。我害怕房子、男人、女人、仆人，甚至孩子。他们对我来说都很可怕。如果我能把你打倒的话，一切都会好起来的。当然，我可能已经逃离了房子，但我的好奇心几乎和我的恐惧一样强烈。我很快就下定了决心。我会给你发一封电报。我戴上帽子，穿上斗篷，去办公室，距离房子大约半英里，然后回来，感觉轻松多了。当我走到门口时，我心里生出一种可怕的怀疑，生怕狗跑了，但我记得托勒那天晚上喝得酩酊大醉，陷入了昏迷状态，我知道他是家里唯一一个对这只野蛮生物有影响力的人，或者是敢于放他自由的人。我安全地溜了进去，一想到要见到你，我就高兴得半夜没睡。今天早上我顺利地请假来到了温彻斯特，但是我必须在三点之前回来，因为鲁卡斯尔先生和夫人要去拜访，并且整个晚上都会离开，所以我必须照顾孩子。现在我已经告诉你我所有的冒险经历了，福尔摩斯先生，如果你能告诉我这一切意味着什么，尤其是我应该做什么，我会非常高兴。”
福尔摩斯和我听得入迷地听着这个非凡的故事。我的朋友现在站起来，在房间里来回踱步，双手插在口袋里，脸上露出极其严肃的表情。
“在我看来，你在这件事上一直表现得像一个非常勇敢和明智的女孩，亨特小姐。你认为你还能再创一项壮举吗？如果我不认为你是一个非常杰出的女人，我就不应该问你这个问题。”
“我和我的朋友，我们将在七点钟到达铜山毛榉。到那时鲁卡斯尔一家就会消失，我们希望托勒将无法工作。只剩下托勒太太了，她可能会发出警报。如果你能派她到地窖去办点什么差事，然后把钥匙转到她身上，你就会极大地方便事情的发展。”

“太好了！接下来我们将彻底调查这件事。当然，只有一种可行的解释。你被带到那里来扮演某人，而真人被囚禁在这个房间里。这是显而易见的。至于这个囚犯是谁，我毫不怀疑，如果我没记错的话，据说是去了美国的女儿，爱丽丝·鲁卡斯尔小姐。毫无疑问，你被选中是因为你的身高、身材和头发的颜色都与她相似。她的生命被切断了，很可能是因为她所患的某种疾病，所以，当然，你的也必须被牺牲。一个奇怪的机会你看到了她的头发。路上的那个男人无疑是她的某个朋友——可能是她的未婚夫——毫无疑问，因为你穿着那女孩的衣服，而且很像她，每当他看到你时，他都会从你的笑声中，然后从你的手势中，确信鲁卡斯尔小姐非常幸福，她不再需要他的关注。这只狗在晚上被放走，以防止它试图与她交流。这么多是相当清楚的。本案最严重的一点是孩子的性格。”
“我亲爱的华生，作为一名医生，您不断地通过研究父母来了解孩子的倾向。难道你没有看到，反过来也同样有效吗？我经常通过研究父母的孩子来第一次真正了解父母的性格。这个孩子的性情异常残忍，只是为了残忍而残忍，无论他的这种性格是从他微笑的父亲（我应该怀疑）还是从他的母亲那里得到的，这对这个受他们控制的可怜的女孩来说都是邪恶的预兆。”
“我确信你是对的，福尔摩斯先生，”我们的客户喊道。 “我想起了一千件事，这让我确信你已经成功了。哦，让我们立即行动起来，为这个可怜的生物提供帮助。”
“我们必须小心，因为我们面对的是一个非常狡猾的人。七点之前我们什么也做不了。到时候我们就会和你在一起，用不了多久我们就能解开这个谜团。”
我们言出必行，因为我们在路边的一家酒馆里设置了陷阱，到达铜山毛榉酒店时才刚刚七点。即使亨特小姐没有微笑着站在门口，那群树的深色叶子在夕阳的照耀下像抛光的金属一样闪闪发光，也足以成为这座房子的标志。

title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes · 选段 3
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night—it was on the twentieth of March, 1888—I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

His manner was not effusive. It seldom was; but he was glad, I think, to see me. With hardly a word spoken, but with a kindly eye, he waved me to an armchair, threw across his case of cigars, and indicated a spirit case and a gasogene in the corner. Then he stood before the fire and looked me over in his singular introspective fashion.
“Wedlock suits you,” he remarked. “I think, Watson, that you have put on seven and a half pounds since I saw you.”
paragraphsZh: 对于福尔摩斯来说，她永远是女人。我很少听到他用其他名字提到她。在他眼中，她使整个性别黯然失色，并占据主导地位。这并不是说他对艾琳·阿德勒有任何类似于爱的情感。所有的情绪，尤其是那一种，对于他冷酷、精确但又极其平衡的头脑来说都是令人厌恶的。我认为，他是世界上最完美的推理和观察机器，但作为一个情人，他会把自己置于一个错误的位置。他从来不谈及更柔和的激情，除了嘲笑和冷笑。对于观察者来说，它们是令人钦佩的事情——非常适合揭开人们的动机和行为的面纱。但是，对于训练有素的推理者来说，承认这种对他自己微妙和精心调整的气质的侵入，就会引入一个干扰因素，这可能会对他的所有心理结果产生怀疑。敏感仪器上的沙砾，或者他自己的高倍镜片上的裂缝，不会比像他这样的人身上的强烈情绪更令人不安。然而他身边只有一个女人，这个女人就是已故的艾琳·阿德勒，她的记忆是可疑的。

我最近很少见到福尔摩斯。我的婚姻使我们彼此疏远。我自己的完全幸福，以及围绕着这个首先发现自己是自己的主人的人所产生的以家庭为中心的兴趣，足以吸引我所有的注意力，而福尔摩斯，他用他整个波西米亚灵魂厌恶一切形式的社会，留在贝克街的我们的住所里，埋在他的旧书中间，每周都在可卡因和野心，药物的昏昏欲睡和他自己敏锐本性的猛烈能量之间交替。他仍然一如既往地被犯罪研究所深深吸引，并运用他巨大的才能和非凡的观察力来追踪这些线索，并解开那些被官方警察视为无望的谜团。我不时听到一些关于他的所作所为的模糊描述：关于他在特雷波夫谋杀案中被传唤到敖德萨，关于他在亭可马里清理阿特金森兄弟的奇异悲剧，最后关于他为荷兰王室精心而成功地完成的使命。然而，除了他的这些活动迹象（我只是与每日新闻的所有读者分享这些迹象）之外，我对我以前的朋友和同伴知之甚少。

一天晚上——那是 1888 年 3 月 20 日——我从一位病人那里回来（因为我现在已经回到民事诊所），这时我穿过了贝克街。当我经过那扇记忆深刻的门时，我的脑海里一定总是将它与我​​的求爱以及《血字研究》中的黑暗事件联系在一起，我强烈地渴望再次见到福尔摩斯，想知道他是如何运用他非凡的力量的。他的房间灯火辉煌，即使我抬起头，我也能看到他高大瘦削的身影在百叶窗上以黑色的轮廓闪过两次。他在房间里快速、急切地来回踱步，头埋在胸前，双手紧握在身后。对我来说，我了解他的每一种情绪和习惯，他的态度和举止讲述着自己的故事。他又上班了。他已经从毒品造成的梦中醒来，并热衷于发现一些新问题。我按响了门铃，被带到了以前属于我自己的房间。
他的态度并不热情。很少有；但我想他很高兴见到我。他几乎一言不发，但眼神和善，招手让我坐到一张扶手椅上，扔过他的雪茄盒，指着角落里的一个烈酒盒和一瓶汽油。然后他站在火前，以他独特的内省方式打量着我。
“婚姻适合你，”他说。 “华生，我认为自从我见到你以来，你已经增加了七磅半。”

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
paragraphs: I lie here on this great immovable bed—it is nailed down, I believe—and follow that pattern about by the hour. It is as good as gymnastics, I assure you. I start, we’ll say, at the bottom, down in the corner over there where it has not been touched, and I determine for the thousandth time that I will follow that pointless pattern to some sort of a conclusion.
I know a little of the principle of design, and I know this thing was not arranged on any laws of radiation, or alternation, or repetition, or symmetry, or anything else that I ever heard of.
Looked at in one way each breadth stands alone, the bloated curves and flourishes—a kind of “debased Romanesque” with delirium tremens—go waddling up and down in isolated columns of fatuity.
But, on the other hand, they connect diagonally, and the sprawling outlines run off in great slanting waves of optic horror, like a lot of wallowing seaweeds in full chase.
The whole thing goes horizontally, too, at least it seems so, and I exhaust myself in trying to distinguish the order of its going in that direction.

There is one end of the room where it is almost intact, and there, when the cross-lights fade and the low sun shines directly upon it, I can almost fancy radiation after all,—the interminable grotesques seem to form around a common centre and rush off in headlong plunges of equal distraction.
And I know John would think it absurd. But I must say what I feel and think in some way—it is such a relief!
John says I mustn’t lose my strength, and has me take cod-liver oil and lots of tonics and things, to say nothing of ale and wine and rare meat.

Dear John! He loves me very dearly, and hates to have me sick. I tried to have a real earnest reasonable talk with him the other day, and tell him how I wish he would let me go and make a visit to Cousin Henry and Julia.
But he said I wasn’t able to go, nor able to stand it after I got there; and I did not make out a very good case for myself, for I was crying before I had finished.
paragraphsZh: 我躺在这张不可移动的大床上——我相信它是钉牢的——并且每小时都遵循这种模式。我向你保证，它和体操一样好。我们会说，我从底部开始，在那个没有被触及的角落里，我第一千次决定我将遵循这种毫无意义的模式得出某种结论。
我知道一点设计原理，而且我知道这个东西不是按照任何辐射定律、交替定律、重复定律、对称定律或我听说过的任何其他定律排列的。
从某种角度看，每个宽度都是独立的，臃肿的曲线和华丽——一种带有震颤性谵妄的“堕落的罗马式”——在孤立的愚蠢的柱子里摇摇晃晃地走来走去。
但是，另一方面，它们是对角连接的，蔓延的轮廓在视觉恐怖的巨大倾斜波浪中蔓延，就像许多在全力追逐的打滚的海藻。
整个事情也是水平进行的，至少看起来是这样，我竭尽全力试图区分它朝那个方向发展的顺序。
房间的一端几乎完好无损，在那里，当十字光褪去，低矮的阳光直接照射在它上面时，我几乎可以想象出辐射，——那些无休无止的怪诞似乎围绕着一个共同的中心形成，并在同样令人分心的情况下一头扎进去。
我知道约翰会认为这很荒谬。但我必须以某种方式说出我的感受和想法——这真是一种解脱！
约翰说我不能失去体力，并让我服用鱼肝油和大量补品之类的东西，更不用说麦芽酒、葡萄酒和稀有的肉了。
亲爱的约翰！他非常爱我，不愿意让我生病。有一天，我试图与他进行一次真正真诚、合理的交谈，并告诉他我多么希望他能让我走，去拜访表弟亨利和朱莉娅。
但是他说我去不了，到了以后也受不了；我并没有为自己找到一个很好的理由，因为我还没说完就哭了。

title: On the Origin of Species
author: Charles Darwin
paragraphs: Summary: the Law of Unity of Type and of the Conditions of Existence embraced by the Theory of Natural Selection.

We have in this chapter discussed some of the difficulties and objections which may be urged against the theory. Many of them are serious; but I think that in the discussion light has been thrown on several facts, which on the belief of independent acts of creation are utterly obscure. We have seen that species at any one period are not indefinitely variable, and are not linked together by a multitude of intermediate gradations, partly because the process of natural selection is always very slow, and at any one time acts only on a few forms; and partly because the very process of natural selection implies the continual supplanting and extinction of preceding and intermediate gradations. Closely allied species, now living on a continuous area, must often have been formed when the area was not continuous, and when the conditions of life did not insensibly graduate away from one part to another. When two varieties are formed in two districts of a continuous area, an intermediate variety will often be formed, fitted for an intermediate zone; but from reasons assigned, the intermediate variety will usually exist in lesser numbers than the two forms which it connects; consequently the two latter, during the course of further modification, from existing in greater numbers, will have a great advantage over the less numerous intermediate variety, and will thus generally succeed in supplanting and exterminating it.

We have seen in this chapter how cautious we should be in concluding that the most different habits of life could not graduate into each other; that a bat, for instance, could not have been formed by natural selection from an animal which at first only glided through the air.

We have seen that a species under new conditions of life may change its habits, or it may have diversified habits, with some very unlike those of its nearest congeners. Hence we can understand, bearing in mind that each organic being is trying to live wherever it can live, how it has arisen that there are upland geese with webbed feet, ground woodpeckers, diving thrushes, and petrels with the habits of auks.

Although the belief that an organ so perfect as the eye could have been formed by natural selection, is enough to stagger any one; yet in the case of any organ, if we know of a long series of gradations in complexity, each good for its possessor, then under changing conditions of life, there is no logical impossibility in the acquirement of any conceivable degree of perfection through natural selection. In the cases in which we know of no intermediate or transitional states, we should be extremely cautious in concluding that none can have existed, for the metamorphoses of many organs show what wonderful changes in function are at least possible. For instance, a swim-bladder has apparently been converted into an air-breathing lung. The same organ having performed simultaneously very different functions, and then having been in part or in whole specialised for one function; and two distinct organs having performed at the same time the same function, the one having been perfected whilst aided by the other, must often have largely facilitated transitions.

We have seen that in two beings widely remote from each other in the natural scale, organs serving for the same purpose and in external appearance closely similar may have been separately and independently formed; but when such organs are closely examined, essential differences in their structure can almost always be detected; and this naturally follows from the principle of natural selection. On the other hand, the common rule throughout nature is infinite diversity of structure for gaining the same end; and this again naturally follows from the same great principle.

In many cases we are far too ignorant to be enabled to assert that a part or organ is so unimportant for the welfare of a species, that modifications in its structure could not have been slowly accumulated by means of natural selection. In many other cases, modifications are probably the direct result of the laws of variation or of growth, independently of any good having been thus gained. But even such structures have often, as we may feel assured, been subsequently taken advantage of, and still further modified, for the good of species under new conditions of life. We may, also, believe that a part formerly of high importance has frequently been retained (as the tail of an aquatic animal by its terrestrial descendants), though it has become of such small importance that it could not, in its present state, have been acquired by means of natural selection.

Natural selection can produce nothing in one species for the exclusive good or injury of another; though it may well produce parts, organs, and excretions highly useful or even indispensable, or highly injurious to another species, but in all cases at the same time useful to the possessor. In each well-stocked country natural selection acts through the competition of the inhabitants and consequently leads to success in the battle for life, only in accordance with the standard of that particular country. Hence the inhabitants of one country, generally the smaller one, often yield to the inhabitants of another and generally the larger country. For in the larger country there will have existed more individuals, and more diversified forms, and the competition will have been severer, and thus the standard of perfection will have been rendered higher. Natural selection will not necessarily lead to absolute perfection; nor, as far as we can judge by our limited faculties, can absolute perfection be everywhere predicated.
paragraphsZh: 摘要：自然选择理论所拥护的类型和存在条件的统一法则。

我们在本章中讨论了可能反对该理论的一些困难和反对意见。其中许多是严肃的；但我认为，在讨论中已经阐明了几个事实，而根据独立创造行为的信念，这些事实是完全模糊的。我们已经看到，任何一个时期的物种都不是无限变化的，也不是通过众多的中间等级联系在一起的，部分原因是自然选择的过程总是非常缓慢，并且在任何时候都只作用于几种形式；部分原因是自然选择的过程本身意味着先前和中间等级的不断取代和灭绝。现在生活在一个连续地区的密切相关的物种，通常一定是在该地区不连续时形成的，而且当生活条件没有不知不觉地从一个地方转移到另一个地方时就形成了。当一个连续区域的两个区域形成两个品种时，往往会形成一个中间品种，适合中间区域；但由于所指定的原因，中间变体的数量通常少于它所连接的两种形式的数量；因此，后两者在进一步变异的过程中，由于数量较多，将比数量较少的中间品种具有很大的优势，因此通常会成功地取代和消灭它。
在本章中我们已经看到，我们应该多么谨慎地得出这样的结论：最不同的生活习惯不可能相互融合；例如，蝙蝠不可能是通过自然选择从最初只在空中滑翔的动物中形成的。
我们已经看到，一个物种在新的生活条件下可能会改变它的习惯，或者它可能有多样化的习惯，其中一些习惯与它最接近的同类非常不同。因此，我们可以理解，考虑到每个有机生物都试图在它能生存的地方生存，为什么会出现有脚蹼的高地雁、地面啄木鸟、潜水画眉和具有海雀习性的海燕。

尽管认为像眼睛这样完美的器官可能是通过自然选择形成的，这一信念足以让任何人感到震惊；但然而，就任何器官而言，如果我们知道一长串的复杂性等级，每一个等级都对其拥有者有利，那么在不断变化的生命条件下，通过自然选择获得任何可以想象的完美程度在逻辑上就不是不可能的。在我们不知道中间或过渡状态的情况下，我们应该极其谨慎地得出没有任何中间或过渡状态存在的结论，因为许多器官的变形表明功能上至少有可能发生奇妙的变化。例如，鱼鳔显然已转变为呼吸空气的肺。同一器官同时执行截然不同的功能，然后部分或全部专门用于一种功能；两个不同的器官同时执行相同的功能，一个在另一个的帮助下得到完善，通常必须在很大程度上促进过渡。
我们已经看到，在自然尺度上相距甚远的两个生物体中，具有相同目的且外观极为相似的器官可能是分别独立形成的；但当仔细检查这些器官时，几乎总能发现它们结构上的本质差异；这自然是遵循自然选择原理的。另一方面，整个自然界的共同规则是为了达到相同的目的而具有无限的结构多样性；这又自然地遵循同样的伟大原则。

在许多情况下，我们太无知了，无法断言某个部分或器官对于物种的福利如此不重要，以至于其结构的改变不可能通过自然选择的方式慢慢积累。在许多其他情况下，修改可能是变异或增长法则的直接结果，与由此获得的任何好处无关。但正如我们可以确信的那样，即使这样的结构也经常被利用，并进一步修改，以适应新的生活条件下的物种利益。我们还可以相信，以前非常重要的部分经常被保留下来（就像水生动物的尾巴被其陆地后代保留下来一样），尽管它已经变得如此不重要，以至于在目前的状态下不可能通过自然选择获得。

自然选择不能在一个物种中产生任何东西，只为另一个物种带来好处或伤害；尽管它很可能产生对另一个物种非常有用甚至不可或缺的部分、器官和排泄物，或者对另一个物种具有高度伤害性，但在所有情况下同时对拥有者有用。在每个资源丰富的国家，自然选择通过居民的竞争发挥作用，从而导致生命之战的成功，只有符合该特定国家的标准。因此，一个国家（通常是较小国家）的居民常常屈服于另一国家（通常是较大国家）的居民。因为国家越大，个体就越多，形式就越多样化，竞争就越激烈，完美的标准也就越高。自然选择并不一定会带来绝对的完美；就我们有限的能力而言，也不能在任何地方都断言绝对完美。

title: On the Origin of Species · 选段 2
author: Charles Darwin
paragraphs: Hereafter we shall be compelled to acknowledge that the only distinction between species and well-marked varieties is, that the latter are known, or believed to be connected at the present day by intermediate gradations, whereas species were formerly thus connected. Hence, without rejecting the consideration of the present existence of intermediate gradations between any two forms, we shall be led to weigh more carefully and to value higher the actual amount of difference between them. It is quite possible that forms now generally acknowledged to be merely varieties may hereafter be thought worthy of specific names; and in this case scientific and common language will come into accordance. In short, we shall have to treat species in the same manner as those naturalists treat genera, who admit that genera are merely artificial combinations made for convenience. This may not be a cheering prospect; but we shall at least be freed from the vain search for the undiscovered and undiscoverable essence of the term species.

The other and more general departments of natural history will rise greatly in interest. The terms used by naturalists, of affinity, relationship, community of type, paternity, morphology, adaptive characters, rudimentary and aborted organs, &c., will cease to be metaphorical and will have a plain signification. When we no longer look at an organic being as a savage looks at a ship, as something wholly beyond his comprehension; when we regard every production of nature as one which has had a long history; when we contemplate every complex structure and instinct as the summing up of many contrivances, each useful to the possessor, in the same way as any great mechanical invention is the summing up of the labour, the experience, the reason, and even the blunders of numerous workmen; when we thus view each organic being, how far more interesting—I speak from experience—does the study of natural history become!

A grand and almost untrodden field of inquiry will be opened, on the causes and laws of variation, on correlation, on the effects of use and disuse, on the direct action of external conditions, and so forth. The study of domestic productions will rise immensely in value. A new variety raised by man will be a far more important and interesting subject for study than one more species added to the infinitude of already recorded species. Our classifications will come to be, as far as they can be so made, genealogies; and will then truly give what may be called the plan of creation. The rules for classifying will no doubt become simpler when we have a definite object in view. We possess no pedigree or armorial bearings; and we have to discover and trace the many diverging lines of descent in our natural genealogies, by characters of any kind which have long been inherited. Rudimentary organs will speak infallibly with respect to the nature of long-lost structures. Species and groups of species which are called aberrant, and which may fancifully be called living fossils, will aid us in forming a picture of the ancient forms of life. Embryology will often reveal to us the structure, in some degree obscured, of the prototypes of each great class.

When we can feel assured that all the individuals of the same species, and all the closely allied species of most genera, have, within a not very remote period descended from one parent, and have migrated from some one birth-place; and when we better know the many means of migration, then, by the light which geology now throws, and will continue to throw, on former changes of climate and of the level of the land, we shall surely be enabled to trace in an admirable manner the former migrations of the inhabitants of the whole world. Even at present, by comparing the differences between the inhabitants of the sea on the opposite sides of a continent, and the nature of the various inhabitants of that continent in relation to their apparent means of immigration, some light can be thrown on ancient geography.

The noble science of geology loses glory from the extreme imperfection of the record. The crust of the earth, with its embedded remains, must not be looked at as a well-filled museum, but as a poor collection made at hazard and at rare intervals. The accumulation of each great fossiliferous formation will be recognised as having depended on an unusual occurrence of favourable circumstances, and the blank intervals between the successive stages as having been of vast duration. But we shall be able to gauge with some security the duration of these intervals by a comparison of the preceding and succeeding organic forms. We must be cautious in attempting to correlate as strictly contemporaneous two formations, which do not include many identical species, by the general succession of the forms of life. As species are produced and exterminated by slowly acting and still existing causes, and not by miraculous acts of creation; and as the most important of all causes of organic change is one which is almost independent of altered and perhaps suddenly altered physical conditions, namely, the mutual relation of organism to organism—the improvement of one organism entailing the improvement or the extermination of others; it follows, that the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations probably serves as a fair measure of the relative, though not actual lapse of time. A number of species, however, keeping in a body might remain for a long period unchanged, whilst within the same period, several of these species, by migrating into new countries and coming into competition with foreign associates, might become modified; so that we must not overrate the accuracy of organic change as a measure of time.
paragraphsZh: 此后，我们将不得不承认，物种和明显变种之间的唯一区别是，后者在当今是已知的，或被认为通过中间等级联系在一起，而物种以前是这样联系的。因此，在不拒绝考虑任何两种形式之间目前存在中间层次的情况下，我们将更加仔细地权衡并更加重视它们之间的实际差异量。现在普遍认为只是变体的形式很可能在以后被认为值得特定的名称。在这种情况下，科学语言和通用语言就会保持一致。简而言之，我们必须以博物学家对待属的方式对待物种，他们承认属只是为了方便而进行的人为组合。这可能不是一个令人振奋的前景。但我们至少可以摆脱对“物种”一词未被发现和无法发现的本质的徒劳探索。

自然历史的其他更一般的部门将大大引起人们的兴趣。博物学家所使用的术语，如亲和力、关系、类型共同体、亲子关系、形态学、适应性特征、未发育和流产的器官等，将不再是隐喻性的，而是具有简单的含义。当我们不再像野蛮人看待一艘船那样看待一个有机存在时，将其视为完全超出他理解范围的东西；当我们认为自然界的每一种产物都具有悠久的历史时；当我们将每一个复杂的结构和本能视为许多发明的总和，每一个对拥有者都是有用的，就像任何伟大的机械发明都是无数工人的劳动、经验、理性甚至失误的总和一样；当我们这样看待每一个有机存在时，我从经验来看，自然历史的研究变得多么有趣！

一个宏大的、几乎无人涉足的探究领域将被打开，关于变异的原因和规律、相关性、使用和废弃的影响、外部条件的直接作用等等。对国内作品的研究价值将大大提高。人类培育的新品种将成为比在无数已记录物种中添加一个物种更重要和更有趣的研究课题。我们的分类将尽可能地成为谱系；然后才会真正给出所谓的创造计划。当我们有明确的目标时，分类的规则无疑会变得更简单。我们没有血统或徽章；我们必须在我们的自然谱系中发现并追踪许多不同的血统，这些血统是由长期遗传的任何类型的特征组成的。简陋的器官能够准确无误地讲述失落已久的结构的本质。被称为异常的物种和物种群体，可以被奇特地称为活化石，将帮助我们形成古代生命形式的图景。胚胎学常常会向我们揭示每个伟大类别的原型的结构（在某种程度上是模糊的）。

当我们确信同一物种的所有个体，以及大多数属的所有密切相关的物种，在一个不太遥远的时期内，都是来自一个父母的后裔，并且是从某个出生地迁移而来的；当我们更好地了解迁徙的多种方式时，根据地质学现在并将继续对以前的气候和土地水平的变化进行分析，我们一定能够以令人钦佩的方式追踪全世界居民以前的迁徙。即使在今天，通过比较大陆两侧海洋居民之间的差异，以及该大陆不同居民的性质与其明显的移民方式的关系，也可以为古代地理提供一些线索。

高贵的地质学因记录的极度不完美而失去了荣耀。地壳及其埋藏的遗迹绝不能被视为一座塞满的博物馆，而应被视为一个在危险和罕见的时间间隔内制作的糟糕收藏品。每个巨大化石地层的积累将被认为取决于有利环境的不寻常发生，并且连续阶段之间的空白间隔持续时间很长。但是，通过比较前后的有机形式，我们将能够可靠地衡量这些间隔的持续时间。我们必须谨慎地试图通过生命形式的一般演替来将严格同时代的两种形态联系起来，这两种形态不包括许多相同的物种。由于物种的产生和灭绝是由于缓慢作用且仍然存在的原因，而不是通过创造的奇迹行为；由于有机变化的所有原因中最重要的原因几乎独立于改变的甚至可能突然改变的物理条件，即有机体与有机体的相互关系——一种有机体的改进导致其他有机体的改进或消灭；由此可见，连续地层的化石中的有机变化量可能可以作为相对时间流逝的公平衡量标准，尽管不是实际的时间流逝。然而，许多物种在体内可能会长期保持不变，而在同一时期内，其中一些物种可能会通过迁移到新的国家并与外国伙伴竞争而发生改变；因此，我们绝不能高估有机变化作为时间衡量标准的准确性。

title: On the Origin of Species · 选段 3
author: Charles Darwin
paragraphs: Some naturalists have maintained that all variations are connected with the act of sexual reproduction; but this is certainly an error; for I have given in another work a long list of “sporting plants;” as they are called by gardeners; that is, of plants which have suddenly produced a single bud with a new and sometimes widely different character from that of the other buds on the same plant. These bud variations, as they may be named, can be propagated by grafts, offsets, &c., and sometimes by seed. They occur rarely under nature, but are far from rare under culture. As a single bud out of many thousands produced year after year on the same tree under uniform conditions, has been known suddenly to assume a new character; and as buds on distinct trees, growing under different conditions, have sometimes yielded nearly the same variety—for instance, buds on peach-trees producing nectarines, and buds on common roses producing moss-roses—we clearly see that the nature of the conditions is of subordinate importance in comparison with the nature of the organism in determining each particular form of variation; perhaps of not more importance than the nature of the spark, by which a mass of combustible matter is ignited, has in determining the nature of the flames.

Changed habits produce an inherited effect as in the period of the flowering of plants when transported from one climate to another. With animals the increased use or disuse of parts has had a more marked influence; thus I find in the domestic duck that the bones of the wing weigh less and the bones of the leg more, in proportion to the whole skeleton, than do the same bones in the wild duck; and this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more, than its wild parents. The great and inherited development of the udders in cows and goats in countries where they are habitually milked, in comparison with these organs in other countries, is probably another instance of the effects of use. Not one of our domestic animals can be named which has not in some country drooping ears; and the view which has been suggested that the drooping is due to disuse of the muscles of the ear, from the animals being seldom much alarmed, seems probable.

Many laws regulate variation, some few of which can be dimly seen, and will hereafter be briefly discussed. I will here only allude to what may be called correlated variation. Important changes in the embryo or larva will probably entail changes in the mature animal. In monstrosities, the correlations between quite distinct parts are very curious; and many instances are given in Isidore Geoffroy St. Hilaire’s great work on this subject. Breeders believe that long limbs are almost always accompanied by an elongated head. Some instances of correlation are quite whimsical; thus cats which are entirely white and have blue eyes are generally deaf; but it has been lately stated by Mr. Tait that this is confined to the males. Colour and constitutional peculiarities go together, of which many remarkable cases could be given among animals and plants. From facts collected by Heusinger, it appears that white sheep and pigs are injured by certain plants, while dark-coloured individuals escape: Professor Wyman has recently communicated to me a good illustration of this fact; on asking some farmers in Virginia how it was that all their pigs were black, they informed him that the pigs ate the paint-root (Lachnanthes), which coloured their bones pink, and which caused the hoofs of all but the black varieties to drop off; and one of the “crackers” (i.e. Virginia squatters) added, “we select the black members of a litter for raising, as they alone have a good chance of living.” Hairless dogs have imperfect teeth; long-haired and coarse-haired animals are apt to have, as is asserted, long or many horns; pigeons with feathered feet have skin between their outer toes; pigeons with short beaks have small feet, and those with long beaks large feet. Hence if man goes on selecting, and thus augmenting, any peculiarity, he will almost certainly modify unintentionally other parts of the structure, owing to the mysterious laws of correlation.

The results of the various, unknown, or but dimly understood laws of variation are infinitely complex and diversified. It is well worth while carefully to study the several treatises on some of our old cultivated plants, as on the hyacinth, potato, even the dahlia, &c.; and it is really surprising to note the endless points of structure and constitution in which the varieties and sub-varieties differ slightly from each other. The whole organisation seems to have become plastic, and departs in a slight degree from that of the parental type.
paragraphsZh: 一些博物学家坚持认为所有变异都与有性生殖行为有关；但这肯定是一个错误；因为我在另一本书中列出了一长串“运动植物”；园丁们这样称呼它们；也就是说，植物突然长出一个芽，该芽具有新的特征，有时与同一植物上的其他芽的特征有很大不同。这些芽变体，正如它们的名字一样，可以通过嫁接、嫁接等繁殖，有时也可以通过种子繁殖。它们在自然条件下很少出现，但在文化条件下却绝非罕见。正如同一棵树上在统一的条件下年复一年产生的数千个芽中的一个芽突然呈现出新的特性一样；由于不同树木上的芽，在不同的条件下生长，有时会产生几乎相同的品种——例如，桃树上的芽产生油桃，普通玫瑰上的芽产生苔藓玫瑰——我们清楚地看到，在决定每种特定形式的变异时，与生物体的性质相比，条件的性质是次要的；在决定火焰的性质方面，也许并不比火花的性质更重要，火花是通过火花来点燃大量可燃物质的。

习惯的改变会产生遗传效应，就像植物从一种气候转移到另一种气候时的开花期一样。对于动物来说，部件使用或废弃的增加产生了更显着的影响。因此，我发现，与野鸭相同的骨头相比，家鸭的翅膀骨头重量更轻，腿骨头占整个骨架的重量更大。这种变化可以肯定地归因于家鸭比其野生父母飞行的次数少得多，行走的次数多。与其他国家的这些器官相比，在习惯性挤奶的国家中，牛和山羊的乳房具有巨大的遗传性发育，这可能是使用效果的另一个例子。在某些国家，我们家养的动物无一不是下垂的耳朵。有人认为，下垂的原因是由于动物很少受到惊吓而导致耳朵肌肉不使用，这种观点似乎是有可能的。

许多法律规范变异，其中一些法律依稀可见，下文将简要讨论。我在这里仅提及所谓的相关变异。胚胎或幼虫的重要变化可能会导致成熟动物的变化。在怪物中，截然不同的部分之间的相关性非常奇怪。伊西多尔·杰弗里·圣伊莱尔（Isidore Geoffroy St. Hilaire）关于这一主题的伟大著作中给出了许多例子。饲养员认为，长四肢几乎总是伴随着细长的头部。有些相关性的例子是相当异想天开的。因此，全身白色、蓝眼睛的猫通常是聋子；但泰特先生最近表示，这仅限于雄性。颜色和体质特征是相辅相成的，在动物和植物中可以举出许多引人注目的例子。从霍辛格收集的事实来看，白色的羊和猪似乎被某些植物伤害，而深色的个体则逃脱了：怀曼教授最近向我传达了这一事实的一个很好的例证；在询问弗吉尼亚州的一些农民时，为什么他们的猪都是黑色的，他们告诉他，这些猪吃了油漆根（Lachnanthes），这种物质使它们的骨头变成粉红色，导致除了黑色品种之外的所有猪的蹄子都脱落了。一位“破坏者”（即弗吉尼亚占屋者）补充道，“我们选择一窝中的黑人来饲养，因为只有他们才有很好的生存机会。”无毛狗的牙齿不完美；正如所声称的那样，长毛和粗毛动物往往有长角或多角；脚上有羽毛的鸽子的外脚趾之间有皮肤；短喙的鸽子脚小，长喙的鸽子脚大。因此，如果人类继续选择并增强任何特性，由于神秘的相关定律，他几乎肯定会无意中修改结构的其他部分。
各种未知的或模糊理解的变异规律的结果是无限复杂和多样化的。仔细研究有关我们一些古老栽培植物的几篇论文是非常值得的，例如风信子、马铃薯，甚至大丽花等；令人惊讶的是，品种和亚品种之间在结构和组成方面存在无穷无尽的细微差别。整个组织似乎已经变得可塑，与父母型的组织略有不同。

title: The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade
author: Edgar Allan Poe
paragraphs: V. In the inorganic life, as well as in the inorganic matter generally, there is nothing to impede the action of one simple unique law—the Divine Volition. With the view of producing impediment, the organic life and matter, (complex, substantial, and law-encumbered,) were contrived.

V. The result of law inviolate is perfection—right—negative happiness. The result of law violate is imperfection, wrong, positive pain. Through the impediments afforded by the number, complexity, and substantiality of the laws of organic life and matter, the violation of law is rendered, to a certain extent, practicable. Thus pain, which in the inorganic life is impossible, is possible in the organic.

V. All things are either good or bad by comparison. A sufficient analysis will show that pleasure, in all cases, is but the contrast of pain. Positive pleasure is a mere idea. To be happy at any one point we must have suffered at the same. Never to suffer would have been never to have been blessed. But it has been shown that, in the inorganic life, pain cannot be thus the necessity for the organic. The pain of the primitive life of Earth, is the sole basis of the bliss of the ultimate life in Heaven.
P. Still, there is one of your expressions which I find it impossible to comprehend—“the truly substantive vastness of infinity.”

V. This, probably, is because you have no sufficiently generic conception of the term “substance” itself. We must not regard it as a quality, but as a sentiment:—it is the perception, in thinking beings, of the adaptation of matter to their organization. There are many things on the Earth, which would be nihility to the inhabitants of Venus—many things visible and tangible in Venus, which we could not be brought to appreciate as existing at all. But to the inorganic beings—to the angels—the whole of the unparticled matter is substance—that is to say, the whole of what we term “space” is to them the truest substantiality;—the stars, meantime, through what we consider their materiality, escaping the angelic sense, just in proportion as the unparticled matter, through what we consider its immateriality, eludes the organic.

As the sleep-waker pronounced these latter words, in a feeble tone, I observed on his countenance a singular expression, which somewhat alarmed me, and induced me to awake him at once. No sooner had I done this, than, with a bright smile irradiating all his features, he fell back upon his pillow and expired. I noticed that in less than a minute afterward his corpse had all the stern rigidity of stone. His brow was of the coldness of ice. Thus, ordinarily, should it have appeared, only after long pressure from Azrael’s hand. Had the sleep-waker, indeed, during the latter portion of his discourse, been addressing me from out the region of the shadows?

Of course I shall not pretend to consider it any matter for wonder, that the extraordinary case of M. Valdemar has excited discussion. It would have been a miracle had it not—especially under the circumstances. Through the desire of all parties concerned, to keep the affair from the public, at least for the present, or until we had farther opportunities for investigation—through our endeavors to effect this—a garbled or exaggerated account made its way into society, and became the source of many unpleasant misrepresentations; and, very naturally, of a great deal of disbelief.
It is now rendered necessary that I give the facts—as far as I comprehend them myself. They are, succinctly, these:

My attention, for the last three years, had been repeatedly drawn to the subject of Mesmerism; and, about nine months ago it occurred to me, quite suddenly, that in the series of experiments made hitherto, there had been a very remarkable and most unaccountable omission:—no person had as yet been mesmerized in articulo mortis. It remained to be seen, first, whether, in such condition, there existed in the patient any susceptibility to the magnetic influence; secondly, whether, if any existed, it was impaired or increased by the condition; thirdly, to what extent, or for how long a period, the encroachments of Death might be arrested by the process. There were other points to be ascertained, but these most excited my curiosity—the last in especial, from the immensely important character of its consequences.

In looking around me for some subject by whose means I might test these particulars, I was brought to think of my friend, M. Ernest Valdemar, the well-known compiler of the “Bibliotheca Forensica,” and author (under the nom de plume of Issachar Marx) of the Polish versions of “Wallenstein” and “Gargantua.” M. Valdemar, who has resided principally at Harlem, N.Y., since the year 1839, is (or was) particularly noticeable for the extreme spareness of his person—his lower limbs much resembling those of John Randolph; and, also, for the whiteness of his whiskers, in violent contrast to the blackness of his hair—the latter, in consequence, being very generally mistaken for a wig. His temperament was markedly nervous, and rendered him a good subject for mesmeric experiment. On two or three occasions I had put him to sleep with little difficulty, but was disappointed in other results which his peculiar constitution had naturally led me to anticipate. His will was at no period positively, or thoroughly, under my control, and in regard to clairvoyance, I could accomplish with him nothing to be relied upon. I always attributed my failure at these points to the disordered state of his health. For some months previous to my becoming acquainted with him, his physicians had declared him in a confirmed phthisis. It was his custom, indeed, to speak calmly of his approaching dissolution, as of a matter neither to be avoided nor regretted.
paragraphsZh: V. 在无机生命中，以及在一般无机物质中，没有什么可以阻碍一个简单而独特的法则——神圣意志的作用。为了产生障碍，有机生命和物质（复杂的、实质性的、受法律约束的）被设计出来。
五、法律不可侵犯的结果是完美——正确——消极的幸福。违反法律的结果是不完美、错误、积极的痛苦。由于有机生命和物质法则的数量、复杂性和实质性所造成的障碍，在某种程度上，违反法则是可行的。因此，痛苦在无机生命中是不可能的，但在有机生命中却是可能的。
V. 一切事物都是通过比较来判断的，要么是好，要么是坏。充分的分析将表明，在所有情况下，快乐只不过是痛苦的对比。积极的快乐只是一个想法。要想在某一时刻感到幸福，我们就必须经历过同样的痛苦。不曾受苦就永远不会得到祝福。但事实证明，在无机生命中，疼痛不可能成为有机生命的必需品。地球原始生命的痛苦，是天堂终极生命幸福的唯一基础。
P. 尽管如此，你的一个表达方式我觉得无法理解——“无限的真正的实质性浩瀚”。

V. 这可能是因为您对“物质”一词本身没有足够通用的概念。我们不能将其视为一种品质，而应将其视为一种情感：——它是有思想的生物对物质与其组织的适应的感知。地球上有很多东西，对于金星上的居民来说是虚无的——许多在金星上看得见、摸得着的东西，我们根本无法欣赏它们的存在。但对于无机生物——对于天使来说——整个非粒子物质就是实体——也就是说，我们所说的“空间”的整体对他们来说是最真实的实体；——与此同时，星星通过我们认为的物质性而逃脱了天使的感觉，正如非粒子物质通过我们认为的非物质性而逃避了有机物一样。
当那个叫醒者以微弱的语气说出这后面的几个字时，我观察到他脸上有一种奇怪的表情，这让我有些警觉，并促使我立即叫醒他。我刚一做完，他就倒在枕头上，断气了，脸上洋溢着灿烂的笑容。我注意到不到一分钟后，他的尸体就变得像石头一样僵硬。他的眉宇冰冷。所以，按理来说，它应该是在阿兹莉尔的手上长时间施压之后才会出现的。那个叫醒人的人，在他讲话的后半部分，确实是从阴影区域对我说话吗？
当然，我不会假装认为瓦尔德马先生的非凡案例引发了讨论，这有什么奇怪的。如果没有的话，这将是一个奇迹——尤其是在这种情况下。由于有关各方都希望不让公众知道这件事，至少目前如此，或者直到我们有进一步调查的机会——通过我们的努力来实现这一点——一份错误或夸大的报道进入了社会，并成为许多令人不快的歪曲事实的根源；并且，很自然地，非常不相信。
现在我有必要提供事实——就我自己的理解而言。简而言之，它们是：

在过去的三年里，我的注意力不断被催眠术这个主题吸引；大约九个月前，我突然想到，在迄今为止所做的一系列实验中，有一个非常显着且最无法解释的遗漏：——迄今为止，还没有人对尸肢进行催眠。首先，在这种情况下，病人是否对磁力影响敏感，还有待观察。其次，如果存在的话，它是否因该状况而受损或加剧；第三，这个过程可以在多大程度上或持续多长时间来阻止死亡的侵犯。还有其他几点需要确定，但这些最激发了我的好奇心——尤其是最后一点，因为它的后果极其重要。

在环顾四周，寻找一些可以测试这些细节的主题时，我想起了我的朋友，M. Ernest Valdemar，他是《法医图书馆》的著名编者，也是波兰版《华伦斯坦》和《卡冈图亚》的作者（化名伊萨查·马克思）。瓦尔德马先生自 1839 年以来主要居住在纽约州哈莱姆区，他（或曾经）因他的极度瘦削而特别引人注目——他的下肢与约翰·伦道夫的下肢非常相似；而且，他的胡须是白色的，与他黑色的头发形成了强烈的对比——因此，后者通常被误认为是假发。他的性情明显紧张，这使他成为催眠实验的好对象。有两三次，我轻而易举地让他入睡，但对他特殊的体质自然让我预料到的其他结果感到失望。他的意志在任何时期都不受我的明确或彻底的控制，就千里眼而言，我无法与他完成任何值得依赖的事情。我总是把我在这些方面的失败归咎于他的健康状况不佳。在我认识他之前的几个月里，他的医生已宣布他患有肺结核。事实上，他的习惯是平静地谈论他即将到来的解体，就像谈论一件既不回避也不后悔的事情一样。

title: The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade · 选段 2
author: Edgar Allan Poe
paragraphs: I found myself sitting in the library, and again sitting there alone. It seemed that I had newly awakened from a confused and exciting dream. I knew that it was now midnight, and I was well aware, that since the setting of the sun, Berenice had been interred. But of that dreary period which intervened I had no positive, at least no definite comprehension. Yet its memory was replete with horror—horror more horrible from being vague, and terror more terrible from ambiguity. It was a fearful page in the record my existence, written all over with dim, and hideous, and unintelligible recollections. I strived to decypher them, but in vain; while ever and anon, like the spirit of a departed sound, the shrill and piercing shriek of a female voice seemed to be ringing in my ears. I had done a deed—what was it? I asked myself the question aloud, and the whispering echoes of the chamber answered me,—“What was it?”

On the table beside me burned a lamp, and near it lay a little box. It was of no remarkable character, and I had seen it frequently before, for it was the property of the family physician; but how came it there, upon my table, and why did I shudder in regarding it? These things were in no manner to be accounted for, and my eyes at length dropped to the open pages of a book, and to a sentence underscored therein. The words were the singular but simple ones of the poet Ebn Zaiat:—“Dicebant mihi sodales si sepulchrum amicae visitarem, curas meas aliquantulum fore levatas.” Why then, as I perused them, did the hairs of my head erect themselves on end, and the blood of my body become congealed within my veins?

There came a light tap at the library door—and, pale as the tenant of a tomb, a menial entered upon tiptoe. His looks were wild with terror, and he spoke to me in a voice tremulous, husky, and very low. What said he?—some broken sentences I heard. He told of a wild cry disturbing the silence of the night—of the gathering together of the household—of a search in the direction of the sound; and then his tones grew thrillingly distinct as he whispered me of a violated grave—of a disfigured body enshrouded, yet still breathing—still palpitating—still alive!

He pointed to garments;—they were muddy and clotted with gore. I spoke not, and he took me gently by the hand: it was indented with the impress of human nails. He directed my attention to some object against the wall. I looked at it for some minutes: it was a spade. With a shriek I bounded to the table, and grasped the box that lay upon it. But I could not force it open; and in my tremor, it slipped from my hands, and fell heavily, and burst into pieces; and from it, with a rattling sound, there rolled out some instruments of dental surgery, intermingled with thirty-two small, white and ivory-looking substances that were scattered to and fro about the floor.

I am come of a race noted for vigor of fancy and ardor of passion. Men have called me mad; but the question is not yet settled, whether madness is or is not the loftiest intelligence—whether much that is glorious—whether all that is profound—does not spring from disease of thought—from moods of mind exalted at the expense of the general intellect. They who dream by day are cognizant of many things which escape those who dream only by night. In their gray visions they obtain glimpses of eternity, and thrill, in awakening, to find that they have been upon the verge of the great secret. In snatches, they learn something of the wisdom which is of good, and more of the mere knowledge which is of evil. They penetrate, however, rudderless or compassless into the vast ocean of the “light ineffable,” and again, like the adventures of the Nubian geographer, “agressi sunt mare tenebrarum, quid in eo esset exploraturi.”

We will say, then, that I am mad. I grant, at least, that there are two distinct conditions of my mental existence—the condition of a lucid reason, not to be disputed, and belonging to the memory of events forming the first epoch of my life—and a condition of shadow and doubt, appertaining to the present, and to the recollection of what constitutes the second great era of my being. Therefore, what I shall tell of the earlier period, believe; and to what I may relate of the later time, give only such credit as may seem due, or doubt it altogether, or, if doubt it ye cannot, then play unto its riddle the Oedipus.

She whom I loved in youth, and of whom I now pen calmly and distinctly these remembrances, was the sole daughter of the only sister of my mother long departed. Eleonora was the name of my cousin. We had always dwelled together, beneath a tropical sun, in the Valley of the Many-Colored Grass. No unguided footstep ever came upon that vale; for it lay away up among a range of giant hills that hung beetling around about it, shutting out the sunlight from its sweetest recesses. No path was trodden in its vicinity; and, to reach our happy home, there was need of putting back, with force, the foliage of many thousands of forest trees, and of crushing to death the glories of many millions of fragrant flowers. Thus it was that we lived all alone, knowing nothing of the world without the valley—I, and my cousin, and her mother.
paragraphsZh: 我发现自己坐在图书馆里，又独自坐在那里。我似乎刚刚从一场混乱而又激动人心的梦中惊醒。我知道现在已经是午夜了，我也很清楚，自从太阳落山之后，贝蕾妮丝就已经被埋葬了。但对于那段沉闷的时期，我没有明确的、至少没有明确的理解。然而它的记忆却充满了恐惧——恐惧因模糊而更可怕，恐惧因模糊而更可怕。这是我存在的记录中令人恐惧的一页，写满了模糊、可怕、难以理解的回忆。我努力破译它们，但徒劳无功。时不时，我的耳边仿佛响起了尖锐而刺耳的女声，就像逝去的声音的灵魂。我做了一件事情——那是什么？我大声问自己这个问题，房间里的低语回声回答了我：“那是什么？”

我旁边的桌子上点着一盏灯，旁边放着一个小盒子。它没什么了不起的特征，而且我以前经常看到它，因为它是家庭医生的财产。但它是怎么来到我的桌子上的？为什么我一想到它就浑身发抖？这些事情根本无法解释，我的目光最终落到了一本打开的书页上，落在了书中划线的一句话上。这些词是诗人埃本·扎亚特（Ebn Zaiat）的奇异而简单的词：“Dicebant mihi sodales si sepulchrum amicae Visitarem，curas meas aliquantulum fore levatas。”为什么我读着读着，头发就竖了起来，全身的血液都凝结在了血管里呢？
图书馆的门被轻轻敲了一下——一个仆人踮起脚尖走进来，脸色苍白得像坟墓里的住户。他的表情充满恐惧，他对我说话的声音颤抖、沙哑、很低。他说什么？——我听到一些断断续续的句子。他讲述了一声狂野的叫声扰乱了夜晚的寂静，讲述了全家人聚集在一起的故事，以及朝着声音传来的方向进行搜寻的故事。然后他的语气变得异常清晰，低声告诉我一座被破坏的坟墓——一具毁容的尸体被包裹着，但仍在呼吸——仍在心悸——仍然活着！
他指着衣服；——它们沾满泥浆，血迹斑斑。我没有说话，他轻轻地握住我的手：手上刻着人类指甲的痕迹。他将我的注意力引向靠墙的某个物体。我看了几分钟：那是一把黑桃。我尖叫着跳到桌子旁，抓住了放在桌上的盒子。但我无法强行打开它；在我的颤抖中，它从我手中滑落，重重地跌落，摔成碎片。伴随着嘎嘎声，一些牙科手术器械从里面滚了出来，其中混杂着三十二个白色、象牙色的小物质，散落在地板上。

我来自一个以充满幻想和热情而闻名的种族。人们称我为疯子；但问题还没有解决，疯狂是否是最崇高的智力——是否是光荣的——是否是深刻的——不是源于思想疾病——源于以牺牲一般智力为代价的精神情绪。白天做梦的人能够认识到许多只在夜间做梦的人无法察觉的事情。在他们灰色的幻象中，他们瞥见了永恒，并且在醒来时兴奋地发现他们已经处于伟大秘密的边缘。在断断续续的过程中，他们学到了一些善的智慧，也学到了更多的恶的纯粹知识。然而，它们无舵无罗盘地深入“不可言喻的光明”的浩瀚海洋，并再次像努比亚地理学家的冒险一样，“aggressi sunt mare tenebrarum, quid in eo esset exploraturi”。
那么，我们会说我生气了。我至少承认，我的精神存在有两种不同的状态——一种是清晰理性的状态，无可争议，属于对我人生第一个时代的事件的记忆；另一种是阴影和怀疑的状态，与现在有关，与构成我存在的第二个伟大时代的回忆有关。因此，请相信我将要讲述的早期阶段；对于我稍后可能会提到的内容，请只给予看似应有的信任，或者完全怀疑它，或者，如果你不能怀疑它，那么就玩俄狄浦斯之谜吧。

我年轻时所爱的她，我现在冷静而清晰地写下这些回忆的她，是我早已去世的母亲唯一的妹妹的唯一女儿。埃莉奥诺拉是我表弟的名字。我们一直生活在一起，在热带阳光下，在杂草谷里。没有任何未经引导的脚步声来到过那个山谷；因为它坐落在一系列巨大的山丘之中，这些山丘在周围耸立着，将阳光从最美丽的凹处挡住了。附近没有人走过任何道路；为了到达我们幸福的家园，我们需要用武力砍掉成千上万棵森林树木的叶子，压死数以百万计芬芳花朵的荣光。就这样，我们独自生活，对没有山谷的世界一无所知——我、我的表弟和她的母亲。

title: The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade · 选段 3
author: Edgar Allan Poe
paragraphs: Shaking in every limb, I groped my way back to the wall—resolving there to perish rather than risk the terrors of the wells, of which my imagination now pictured many in various positions about the dungeon. In other conditions of mind I might have had courage to end my misery at once by a plunge into one of these abysses; but now I was the veriest of cowards. Neither could I forget what I had read of these pits—that the sudden extinction of life formed no part of their most horrible plan.

Agitation of spirit kept me awake for many long hours, but at length I again slumbered. Upon arousing, I found by my side, as before, a loaf and a pitcher of water. A burning thirst consumed me, and I emptied the vessel at a draught. It must have been drugged—for scarcely had I drunk, before I became irresistibly drowsy. A deep sleep fell upon me—a sleep like that of death. How long it lasted of course, I know not; but when, once again, I unclosed my eyes, the objects around me were visible. By a wild sulphurous lustre, the origin of which I could not at first determine, I was enabled to see the extent and aspect of the prison.

In its size I had been greatly mistaken. The whole circuit of its walls did not exceed twenty-five yards. For some minutes this fact occasioned me a world of vain trouble; vain indeed! for what could be of less importance, under the terrible circumstances which environed me, then the mere dimensions of my dungeon? But my soul took a wild interest in trifles, and I busied myself in endeavors to account for the error I had committed in my measurement. The truth at length flashed upon me. In my first attempt at exploration I had counted fifty-two paces, up to the period when I fell; I must then have been within a pace or two of the fragment of serge; in fact, I had nearly performed the circuit of the vault. I then slept—and, upon awaking, I must have returned upon my steps—thus supposing the circuit nearly double what it actually was. My confusion of mind prevented me from observing that I began my tour with the wall to the left, and ended it with the wall to the right.

I had been deceived, too, in respect to the shape of the enclosure. In feeling my way I had found many angles, and thus deduced an idea of great irregularity; so potent is the effect of total darkness upon one arousing from lethargy or sleep! The angles were simply those of a few slight depressions, or niches, at odd intervals. The general shape of the prison was square. What I had taken for masonry seemed now to be iron, or some other metal, in huge plates, whose sutures or joints occasioned the depression. The entire surface of this metallic enclosure was rudely daubed in all the hideous and repulsive devices to which the charnel superstition of the monks has given rise. The figures of fiends in aspects of menace, with skeleton forms, and other more really fearful images, overspread and disfigured the walls. I observed that the outlines of these monstrosities were sufficiently distinct, but that the colors seemed faded and blurred, as if from the effects of a damp atmosphere. I now noticed the floor, too, which was of stone. In the centre yawned the circular pit from whose jaws I had escaped; but it was the only one in the dungeon.

All this I saw indistinctly and by much effort—for my personal condition had been greatly changed during slumber. I now lay upon my back, and at full length, on a species of low framework of wood. To this I was securely bound by a long strap resembling a surcingle. It passed in many convolutions about my limbs and body, leaving at liberty only my head, and my left arm to such extent that I could, by dint of much exertion, supply myself with food from an earthen dish which lay by my side on the floor. I saw, to my horror, that the pitcher had been removed. I say to my horror—for I was consumed with intolerable thirst. This thirst it appeared to be the design of my persecutors to stimulate—for the food in the dish was meat pungently seasoned.

Looking upward, I surveyed the ceiling of my prison. It was some thirty or forty feet overhead, and constructed much as the side walls. In one of its panels a very singular figure riveted my whole attention. It was the painted figure of Time as he is commonly represented, save that, in lieu of a scythe, he held what, at a casual glance, I supposed to be the pictured image of a huge pendulum such as we see on antique clocks. There was something, however, in the appearance of this machine which caused me to regard it more attentively. While I gazed directly upward at it (for its position was immediately over my own) I fancied that I saw it in motion. In an instant afterward the fancy was confirmed. Its sweep was brief, and of course slow. I watched it for some minutes, somewhat in fear, but more in wonder. Wearied at length with observing its dull movement, I turned my eyes upon the other objects in the cell.
