I was going to the Grange one evening—a dark evening, threatening thunder—and, just at the turn of the Heights, I encountered a little boy with a sheep and two lambs before him; he was crying terribly; and I supposed the lambs were skittish, and would not be guided.

I saw nothing; but neither the sheep nor he would go on, so I bid him take the road lower down. He probably raised the phantoms from thinking, as he traversed the moors alone, on the nonsense he had heard his parents and companions repeat. Yet, still, I don’t like being out in the dark now; and I don’t like being left by myself in this grim house: I cannot help it; I shall be glad when they leave it, and shift to the Grange.
“Why, Joseph will take care of the house, and, perhaps, a lad to keep him company. They will live in the kitchen, and the rest will be shut up.”
“No, Mr. Lockwood,” said Nelly, shaking her head. “I believe the dead are at peace: but it is not right to speak of them with levity.”
“They are afraid of nothing,” I grumbled, watching their approach through the window. “Together, they would brave Satan and all his legions.”

As they stepped on to the door-stones, and halted to take a last look at the moon—or, more correctly, at each other by her light—I felt irresistibly impelled to escape them again; and, pressing a remembrance into the hand of Mrs. Dean, and disregarding her expostulations at my rudeness, I vanished through the kitchen as they opened the house-door; and so should have confirmed Joseph in his opinion of his fellow-servant’s gay indiscretions, had he not fortunately recognised me for a respectable character by the sweet ring of a sovereign at his feet.

My walk home was lengthened by a diversion in the direction of the kirk. When beneath its walls, I perceived decay had made progress, even in seven months: many a window showed black gaps deprived of glass; and slates jutted off, here and there, beyond the right line of the roof, to be gradually worked off in coming autumn storms.
paragraphsZh: “这个恶魔已经夺走了他的灵魂，”他喊道，“他可以把他的尸体拖入交易，不管我在乎什么！哎呀！他看起来多么邪恶，一脸的死神！”老罪人嘲笑地笑了。我以为他打算在床上蹦蹦跳跳。但他突然镇定下来，跪下，举起双手，感谢合法的主人和古老的股票恢复了他们的权利。
我对这可怕的事件感到震惊；我的记忆不可避免地浮现在往日，带着一种压抑的悲伤。但可怜的哈里顿是最受委屈的，也是唯一真正受苦的人。他整夜坐在尸体旁边，伤心地哭泣。他握住它的手，吻了吻那张讽刺而野蛮的脸，其他人都不敢正视它。并用强烈的悲伤来哀悼他，这种悲伤是从一颗慷慨的心自然产生的，尽管它像经过淬炼的钢铁一样坚硬。
肯尼思先生对于主人死于何种疾病感到困惑。我隐瞒了他四天没有吞咽任何东西的事实，担心这会引起麻烦，然后，我相信他不是故意戒酒的：这是他奇怪的疾病的结果，而不是原因。

我们按照他的意愿埋葬了他，这引起了整个社区的丑闻。恩肖和我，教堂司事，以及六名搬运棺材的人，了解了整个出席情况。当他们把它放进坟墓时，六个人就离开了：我们留下来看着它被盖上。哈里顿满脸流着泪，挖了绿色的草皮，亲自把它们铺在棕色的霉菌上：现在它和它的同伴土丘一样光滑、青翠——我希望它的房客也睡得香甜。但如果你问乡下人，他们会根据《圣经》发誓说他行走过：有人说曾在教堂附近、荒野上、甚至在这座房子里见过他。你会说，这是无稽之谈，我也这么说。然而，厨房火旁的那个老人确认，自从他死后的每个雨夜，他都看到有两个人从他房间的窗户里往外看：——大约一个月前，我身上发生了一件奇怪的事情。一天晚上，我正要去田庄——一个漆黑的夜晚，雷声逼人——就在高地的拐角处，我遇到了一个小男孩，他面前牵着一只绵羊和两只小羊羔。他哭得很厉害；我猜想小羊们很容易受惊，不会被引导。
我什么也没看到；但羊和他都不愿意继续前行，所以我吩咐他走更低的路。当他独自穿越荒原时，他可能因听到父母和同伴重复的胡言乱语而产生了幻觉。然而，我现在仍然不喜欢在黑暗中待着。我不喜欢被独自留在这间阴森的房子里：我无法控制；当他们离开这里，转移到田庄时，我会很高兴。
“嘿，约瑟夫会照顾房子，也许还会有一个小伙子陪着他。他们会住在厨房里，其余的都会被关起来。”
“不，洛克伍德先生，”耐莉摇着头说道。 “我相信死者是安息的：但轻率地谈论他们是不对的。”
“他们什么都不怕，”我抱怨道，透过窗户看着他们走近。 “他们将一起勇敢地面对撒旦和他的所有军团。”
当他们踏上门石，停下来最后看了一眼月亮——或者更准确地说，在她的光芒下互相看了一眼——我感到不可抗拒地想要再次逃离他们；当他们打开房门时，我把一份纪念塞到迪安太太手里，不顾她对我粗鲁的劝告，就消失在厨房里。如果不是幸运的是，约瑟夫脚下戴着一枚主权戒指，幸运地认识到我是一个值得尊敬的人，那么他应该会证实他对他的同伴仆人的轻率行为的看法。
由于改道朝柯克方向，我回家的时间延长了。在它的墙下，我感觉到腐烂已经进展，甚至在七个月内：许多窗户都显示出没有玻璃的黑色缝隙；石板到处突出，超出了屋顶的右线，在即将到来的秋季暴风雨中逐渐被拆除。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 3
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: “‘He’s there, is he?’ exclaimed my companion, rushing to the gap. ‘If I can get my arm out I can hit him!’

“I’m afraid, Ellen, you’ll set me down as really wicked; but you don’t know all, so don’t judge. I wouldn’t have aided or abetted an attempt on even his life for anything. Wish that he were dead, I must; and therefore I was fearfully disappointed, and unnerved by terror for the consequences of my taunting speech, when he flung himself on Earnshaw’s weapon and wrenched it from his grasp.

“The charge exploded, and the knife, in springing back, closed into its owner’s wrist. Heathcliff pulled it away by main force, slitting up the flesh as it passed on, and thrust it dripping into his pocket. He then took a stone, struck down the division between two windows, and sprang in. His adversary had fallen senseless with excessive pain and the flow of blood, that gushed from an artery or a large vein. The ruffian kicked and trampled on him, and dashed his head repeatedly against the flags, holding me with one hand, meantime, to prevent me summoning Joseph. He exerted preterhuman self-denial in abstaining from finishing him completely; but getting out of breath, he finally desisted, and dragged the apparently inanimate body on to the settle. There he tore off the sleeve of Earnshaw’s coat, and bound up the wound with brutal roughness; spitting and cursing during the operation as energetically as he had kicked before. Being at liberty, I lost no time in seeking the old servant; who, having gathered by degrees the purport of my hasty tale, hurried below, gasping, as he descended the steps two at once.

“‘There’s this to do,’ thundered Heathcliff, ‘that your master’s mad; and should he last another month, I’ll have him to an asylum. And how the devil did you come to fasten me out, you toothless hound? Don’t stand muttering and mumbling there. Come, I’m not going to nurse him. Wash that stuff away; and mind the sparks of your candle—it is more than half brandy!’
“‘And so ye’ve been murthering on him?’ exclaimed Joseph, lifting his hands and eyes in horror. ‘If iver I seed a seeght loike this! May the Lord—’

“Heathcliff gave him a push on to his knees in the middle of the blood, and flung a towel to him; but instead of proceeding to dry it up, he joined his hands and began a prayer, which excited my laughter from its odd phraseology. I was in the condition of mind to be shocked at nothing: in fact, I was as reckless as some malefactors show themselves at the foot of the gallows.
“‘Oh, I forgot you,’ said the tyrant. ‘You shall do that. Down with you. And you conspire with him against me, do you, viper? There, that is work fit for you!’

“He shook me till my teeth rattled, and pitched me beside Joseph, who steadily concluded his supplications, and then rose, vowing he would set off for the Grange directly. Mr. Linton was a magistrate, and though he had fifty wives dead, he should inquire into this. He was so obstinate in his resolution, that Heathcliff deemed it expedient to compel from my lips a recapitulation of what had taken place; standing over me, heaving with malevolence, as I reluctantly delivered the account in answer to his questions. It required a great deal of labour to satisfy the old man that Heathcliff was not the aggressor; especially with my hardly-wrung replies. However, Mr. Earnshaw soon convinced him that he was alive still; Joseph hastened to administer a dose of spirits, and by their succour his master presently regained motion and consciousness. Heathcliff, aware that his opponent was ignorant of the treatment received while insensible, called him deliriously intoxicated; and said he should not notice his atrocious conduct further, but advised him to get to bed. To my joy, he left us, after giving this judicious counsel, and Hindley stretched himself on the hearthstone. I departed to my own room, marvelling that I had escaped so easily.

“This morning, when I came down, about half an hour before noon, Mr. Earnshaw was sitting by the fire, deadly sick; his evil genius, almost as gaunt and ghastly, leant against the chimney. Neither appeared inclined to dine, and, having waited till all was cold on the table, I commenced alone. Nothing hindered me from eating heartily, and I experienced a certain sense of satisfaction and superiority, as, at intervals, I cast a look towards my silent companions, and felt the comfort of a quiet conscience within me. After I had done, I ventured on the unusual liberty of drawing near the fire, going round Earnshaw’s seat, and kneeling in the corner beside him.

“Heathcliff did not glance my way, and I gazed up, and contemplated his features almost as confidently as if they had been turned to stone. His forehead, that I once thought so manly, and that I now think so diabolical, was shaded with a heavy cloud; his basilisk eyes were nearly quenched by sleeplessness, and weeping, perhaps, for the lashes were wet then: his lips devoid of their ferocious sneer, and sealed in an expression of unspeakable sadness. Had it been another, I would have covered my face in the presence of such grief. In his case, I was gratified; and, ignoble as it seems to insult a fallen enemy, I couldn’t miss this chance of sticking in a dart: his weakness was the only time when I could taste the delight of paying wrong for wrong.”
paragraphsZh: “‘他在那儿，是吗？’我的同伴冲到缺口处喊道。‘如果我能伸出手臂，我就能打他！’
“我担心，艾伦，你会认为我真的很邪恶；但你并不知道全部，所以不要评判。我不会出于任何原因帮助或教唆任何人企图谋害他的生命。我希望他死掉，我必须这么做；因此，当他扑向恩肖的武器并将其从手中夺走时，我对我的嘲讽言论的后果感到非常失望和不安。

“冲锋爆炸，刀子弹回来，卡在了主人的手腕上。希刺克厉夫用主力把它拉开，在刀经过时切开了肉，然后把它塞进了口袋里。然后他拿了一块石头，击中了两扇窗户之间的间隔，跳了进去。他的对手因过度疼痛和从动脉或大静脉中涌出的血液而昏倒了。歹徒踢了一脚，然后把它扔进了口袋。”他踩在他身上，用一只手按住我，同时用一只手按住我，他用超乎常人的克己精神，避免彻底杀死他；但他终于停止了呼吸，并把明显没有生命的尸体拖到长椅上，在手术过程中，他粗鲁地吐口水，咒骂着包扎伤口。我得到自由后，立即寻找那位老仆人；他渐渐明白了我仓促故事的要旨，气喘吁吁地急匆匆地下了两级台阶。
“‘你的主人疯了，’希刺克厉夫咆哮道，‘你的主人疯了；’”如果他还能再坚持一个月，我就会把他送进庇护所。你这没牙齿的猎犬，到底是怎么来把我绑起来的？不要站在那里嘀咕咕咕。来吧，我不会护理他的。把那些东西洗掉；请注意蜡烛的火花——其中一半以上是白兰地！”
“‘所以你们一直在谋杀他？’约瑟夫惊恐地举起双手和眼睛，惊呼道。‘如果我能看到这样的景象！愿主——’
“希刺克厉夫把他推到血泊中的膝盖上，然后扔给他一条毛巾；但他并没有继续把它擦干，而是双手合十开始祈祷，这奇怪的措辞激起了我的笑声。我当时的心情是无动于衷的：事实上，我就像一些在绞刑架下表现出来的罪犯一样鲁莽。
“‘哦，我忘了你，’暴君说。‘你应该这么做。打倒你。你和他密谋反对我，是吗，毒蛇？这就是适合你的工作！’

“他摇晃着我，直到我的牙齿格格作响，然后把我推到约瑟夫身边，约瑟夫坚定地完成了他的恳求，然后站起来，发誓他将直接前往田庄。林惇先生是一名地方法官，虽然他有五十个妻子死去，但他应该调查此事。他的决心如此顽固，希刺克厉夫认为有必要强迫我重述所发生的事情。当我不情愿地回答他的问题时，我站在我身边，充满恶意地起伏着。要让老人确信希刺克厉夫不是侵略者，需要付出很大的努力。尤其是我的回复。然而，恩肖先生很快就让他相信自己还活着。约瑟夫赶紧喝了一剂烈酒，在烈酒的帮助下，他的主人很快就恢复了活动和意识。希斯克利夫意识到他的对手在昏迷不醒的情况下对所接受的治疗一无所知，称他喝醉了。并说他不应该再注意到他的残暴行为，但建议他去睡觉。令我高兴的是，他在给出明智的建议后就离开了我们，辛德雷在炉石上躺了下来。我回到自己的房间，惊讶自己竟然如此轻松地逃脱了。
“今天早上，当我下来时，大约在中午前半小时，恩肖先生坐在火边，病得很重；他的邪恶天才，几乎同样憔悴而可怕，靠在烟囱上。两人似乎都不想吃饭，等桌子上的东西都凉了，我才开始独自一人。没有什么能阻止我尽情地吃东西，我体验到了某种满足感和优越感，因为我时不时地向做完这些之后，我感到内心平静的安慰，冒险靠近火炉，绕过恩肖的座位，跪在他旁边的角落里。

“希刺克厉夫没有看我一眼，我抬起头，凝视着他的面容，几乎自信地凝视着他，仿佛他们已经变成了石头。他的额头，我曾以为他是那么的男子气概，现在我却觉得他是那么的恶魔，被一层厚重的云遮住了。他那双蛇怪般的眼睛几乎因失眠而昏暗，也许还在哭泣，因为当时的睫毛还湿漉漉的：他的嘴唇没有凶猛的冷笑，表情中充满了难以言喻的悲伤。如果是别人，我会在如此悲伤的情况下捂住脸。对于他的情况，我感到很满意。尽管这似乎是在侮辱倒下的敌人，这似乎是不光彩的，但我不能错过这个投镖的机会：他的弱点是我唯一能尝到以错报错的喜悦的时候。”

title: The Innocence of Father Brown
author: G. K. Chesterton
paragraphs: He alighted at Liverpool Street, however, quite conscientiously secure that he had not missed the criminal so far. He then went to Scotland Yard to regularise his position and arrange for help in case of need; he then lit another cigarette and went for a long stroll in the streets of London. As he was walking in the streets and squares beyond Victoria, he paused suddenly and stood. It was a quaint, quiet square, very typical of London, full of an accidental stillness. The tall, flat houses round looked at once prosperous and uninhabited; the square of shrubbery in the centre looked as deserted as a green Pacific islet. One of the four sides was much higher than the rest, like a dais; and the line of this side was broken by one of London’s admirable accidents--a restaurant that looked as if it had strayed from Soho. It was an unreasonably attractive object, with dwarf plants in pots and long, striped blinds of lemon yellow and white. It stood specially high above the street, and in the usual patchwork way of London, a flight of steps from the street ran up to meet the front door almost as a fire-escape might run up to a first-floor window. Valentin stood and smoked in front of the yellow-white blinds and considered them long.

The most incredible thing about miracles is that they happen. A few clouds in heaven do come together into the staring shape of one human eye. A tree does stand up in the landscape of a doubtful journey in the exact and elaborate shape of a note of interrogation. I have seen both these things myself within the last few days. Nelson does die in the instant of victory; and a man named Williams does quite accidentally murder a man named Williamson; it sounds like a sort of infanticide. In short, there is in life an element of elfin coincidence which people reckoning on the prosaic may perpetually miss. As it has been well expressed in the paradox of Poe, wisdom should reckon on the unforeseen.

Aristide Valentin was unfathomably French; and the French intelligence is intelligence specially and solely. He was not “a thinking machine”; for that is a brainless phrase of modern fatalism and materialism. A machine only is a machine because it cannot think. But he was a thinking man, and a plain man at the same time. All his wonderful successes, that looked like conjuring, had been gained by plodding logic, by clear and commonplace French thought. The French electrify the world not by starting any paradox, they electrify it by carrying out a truism. They carry a truism so far--as in the French Revolution. But exactly because Valentin understood reason, he understood the limits of reason. Only a man who knows nothing of motors talks of motoring without petrol; only a man who knows nothing of reason talks of reasoning without strong, undisputed first principles. Here he had no strong first principles. Flambeau had been missed at Harwich; and if he was in London at all, he might be anything from a tall tramp on Wimbledon Common to a tall toast-master at the Hotel Metropole. In such a naked state of nescience, Valentin had a view and a method of his own.

In such cases he reckoned on the unforeseen. In such cases, when he could not follow the train of the reasonable, he coldly and carefully followed the train of the unreasonable. Instead of going to the right places--banks, police stations, rendezvous--he systematically went to the wrong places; knocked at every empty house, turned down every cul de sac, went up every lane blocked with rubbish, went round every crescent that led him uselessly out of the way. He defended this crazy course quite logically. He said that if one had a clue this was the worst way; but if one had no clue at all it was the best, because there was just the chance that any oddity that caught the eye of the pursuer might be the same that had caught the eye of the pursued. Somewhere a man must begin, and it had better be just where another man might stop. Something about that flight of steps up to the shop, something about the quietude and quaintness of the restaurant, roused all the detective’s rare romantic fancy and made him resolve to strike at random. He went up the steps, and sitting down at a table by the window, asked for a cup of black coffee.

It was half-way through the morning, and he had not breakfasted; the slight litter of other breakfasts stood about on the table to remind him of his hunger; and adding a poached egg to his order, he proceeded musingly to shake some white sugar into his coffee, thinking all the time about Flambeau. He remembered how Flambeau had escaped, once by a pair of nail scissors, and once by a house on fire; once by having to pay for an unstamped letter, and once by getting people to look through a telescope at a comet that might destroy the world. He thought his detective brain as good as the criminal’s, which was true. But he fully realised the disadvantage. “The criminal is the creative artist; the detective only the critic,” he said with a sour smile, and lifted his coffee cup to his lips slowly, and put it down very quickly. He had put salt in it.
paragraphsZh: 然而，他在利物浦街下了车，非常认真地确保自己到目前为止没有错过罪犯。随后，他前往苏格兰场调整自己的职位，并安排在需要时提供帮助；然后他又点了一支烟，在伦敦的街道上漫步了很长一段时间。当他走在维多利亚郊外的街道和广场上时，他突然停了下来，站了起来。这是一个古色古香、安静的广场，非常典型的伦敦风格，充满了意外的寂静。周围又高又平的房子看上去既繁华又无人居住。中心的方形灌木丛看起来像太平洋上的一座绿色小岛一样荒凉。四个边的其中一个比其他边高得多，就像一个讲台；而这一边的界线被伦敦的一个令人钦佩的意外所打破——一家看起来好像偏离了苏豪区的餐馆。这是一个非常有吸引力的物体，盆中种植着矮小的植物，还有柠檬黄和白色的长条纹百叶窗。它矗立在街道上方特别高的地方，按照伦敦常见的拼凑方式，一段台阶从街道上延伸到前门，几乎就像防火梯可以延伸到一楼的窗户一样。瓦伦丁站在黄白色的百叶窗前抽烟，认为它们很长。

奇迹最令人难以置信的事情就是它们的发生。天上的几朵云确实聚集在一起，形成了一只人眼凝视的形状。一棵树确实以审讯笔记的精确而精致的形状矗立在一段可疑旅程的风景中。在过去的几天里，我亲眼目睹了这两件事。纳尔逊确实在胜利的那一刻死去了；一个名叫威廉姆斯的人确实意外地谋杀了一个名叫威廉姆森的人；这听起来像是一种杀婴行为。简而言之，生活中存在着一种精灵般的巧合，而那些认为平淡无奇的人可能永远会错过这种巧合。正如爱伦·坡的悖论所充分表达的那样，智慧应该考虑到不可预见的事情。

阿里斯蒂德·瓦伦丁 (Aristide Valentin) 是一位深不可测的法国人；法国的情报是专门的、唯一的情报。他不是“一个思考机器”；他是一个“思考机器”。因为这是现代宿命论和唯物论的无脑短语。机器之所以是机器，是因为它无法思考。但他是一个有思想的人，同时也是一个朴素的人。他所有看似魔术般的奇妙成功，都是通过缓慢的逻辑、通过清晰而平常的法国思想而获得的。法国人不是通过引发任何悖论来让世界充满活力，而是通过执行不言而喻的真理来让世界充满活力。到目前为止，它们都带有不言而喻的道理——就像在法国大革命中一样。但正是因为瓦伦丁了解理性，他也了解理性的局限性。只有对汽车一无所知的人才会谈论没有汽油的汽车；只有对理性一无所知的人才会在没有强有力的、无可争议的首要原则的情况下谈论推理。在这里，他没有强有力的首要原则。弗朗博在哈里奇失踪了。如果他真的在伦敦，他可能是任何人，从温布尔登公园的高个子流浪汉到大都会酒店的高个子主持人。在这种赤裸裸的无知状态下，瓦伦丁有自己的观点和方法。

在这种情况下，他会考虑到不可预见的情况。在这种情况下，当他无法追随理性的轨道时，他就冷酷而小心翼翼地追随非理性的轨道。他没有去正确的地方——银行、警察局、约会地点——而是有系统地去了错误的地方；他敲了敲每一栋空房子，推开了每一个死胡同，走上了每一条被垃圾堵住的小巷，绕过了每一个新月形的弯道，这些新月形的弯道让他毫无用处。他非常合乎逻辑地为这种疯狂的做法辩护。他说，如果有人有线索，这是最糟糕的方法；但如果一个人根本不知道那是最好的，因为任何引起追捕者注意的奇怪现象都有可能与引起被追捕者注意的东西相同。一个人必须从某个地方开始，而且最好是另一个人可能停止的地方。通往商店的那段台阶，餐厅的安静和古雅，激发了侦探罕见的浪漫幻想，让他下定决心随机出击。他走上台阶，在靠窗的一张桌子旁坐下，要了一杯黑咖啡。

上午已经过半了，他还没有吃早餐；桌子上散落着一些其他早餐，提醒他饥饿。他点了一份荷包蛋，然后若有所思地往咖啡里加入了一些白糖，心里一直想着弗朗博。他记得弗朗博是如何逃走的，一次是借助一把指甲剪，一次是借助一座着火的房子。一次是为了支付一封未贴邮票的信件的费用，一次是让人们通过望远镜观察一颗可能毁灭世界的彗星。他认为他的侦探头脑和罪犯的头脑一样好，这是真的。但他充分意识到了劣势。 “罪犯是有创造力的艺术家；侦探只是批评家。”他苦笑着说道，慢慢地将咖啡杯举到唇边，又很快放下。他在里面放了盐。

title: The Innocence of Father Brown · 选段 2
author: G. K. Chesterton
paragraphs: “I was in this room next to them,” she explained; “both doors were closed, but I suddenly heard a voice, such as I had never heard on earth, roaring ‘Hell, hell, hell,’ again and again, and then the two doors shook with the first explosion of the revolver. Thrice again the thing banged before I got the two doors open and found the room full of smoke; but the pistol was smoking in my poor, mad Patrick’s hand; and I saw him fire the last murderous volley with my own eyes. Then he leapt on my father, who was clinging in terror to the window-sill, and, grappling, tried to strangle him with the rope, which he threw over his head, but which slipped over his struggling shoulders to his feet. Then it tightened round one leg and Patrick dragged him along like a maniac. I snatched a knife from the mat, and, rushing between them, managed to cut the rope before I fainted.”

As the girl collapsed under her memories, the priest passed stiffly into the next room, where he found Gilder and Merton alone with Patrick Royce, who sat in a chair, handcuffed. There he said to the Inspector submissively:
“Then I will,” he said. “Private lives are more important than public reputations. I am going to save the living, and let the dead bury their dead.”

“I told you that in this case there were too many weapons and only one death. I tell you now that they were not weapons, and were not used to cause death. All those grisly tools, the noose, the bloody knife, the exploding pistol, were instruments of a curious mercy. They were not used to kill Sir Aaron, but to save him.”

“It is a cruel religion,” said the priest, looking out of the window. “Why couldn’t they let him weep a little, like his fathers before him? His plans stiffened, his views grew cold; behind that merry mask was the empty mind of the atheist. At last, to keep up his hilarious public level, he fell back on that dram-drinking he had abandoned long ago. But there is this horror about alcoholism in a sincere teetotaler: that he pictures and expects that psychological inferno from which he has warned others. It leapt upon poor Armstrong prematurely, and by this morning he was in such a case that he sat here and cried he was in hell, in so crazy a voice that his daughter did not know it. He was mad for death, and with the monkey tricks of the mad he had scattered round him death in many shapes--a running noose and his friend’s revolver and a knife. Royce entered accidentally and acted in a flash. He flung the knife on the mat behind him, snatched up the revolver, and having no time to unload it, emptied it shot after shot all over the floor. The suicide saw a fourth shape of death, and made a dash for the window. The rescuer did the only thing he could--ran after him with the rope and tried to tie him hand and foot. Then it was that the unlucky girl ran in, and misunderstanding the struggle, strove to slash her father free. At first she only slashed poor Royce’s knuckles, from which has come all the little blood in this affair. But, of course, you noticed that he left blood, but no wound, on that servant’s face? Only before the poor woman swooned, she did hack her father loose, so that he went crashing through that window into eternity.”

There was a long stillness slowly broken by the metallic noises of Gilder unlocking the handcuffs of Patrick Royce, to whom he said: “I think I should have told the truth, sir. You and the young lady are worth more than Armstrong’s obituary notices.”
“Confound Armstrong’s notices,” cried Royce roughly. “Don’t you see it was because she mustn’t know?”
“Why, that she killed her father, you fool!” roared the other. “He’d have been alive now but for her. It might craze her to know that.”

“No, I don’t think it would,” remarked Father Brown, as he picked up his hat. “I rather think I should tell her. Even the most murderous blunders don’t poison life like sins; anyhow, I think you may both be the happier now. I’ve got to go back to the Deaf School.”
“I’ve got to get back to the Deaf School,” said Father Brown. “I’m sorry I can’t stop for the inquiry.”
paragraphsZh: “我就在他们旁边的这个房间里，”她解释道； “两扇门都关着，但我突然听到一种声音，一种我在地球上从未听过的声音，一遍又一遍地咆哮着‘地狱，地狱，地狱’，然后两扇门随着左轮手枪的第一次爆炸而震动。在我打开两扇门之前，那东西又砰地响了三次，发现房间里充满了烟雾；但手枪在我可怜的、疯狂的帕特里克手中冒着烟；我亲眼看到他射出了最后一发凶残的齐射。然后他跳了起来。我的父亲惊恐地抓着窗台，扭打着，试图用绳子勒死他，他把绳子扔到了他的头上，但绳子从他挣扎的肩膀上滑到了他的脚上，然后绳子勒住了他的一条腿，帕特里克像个疯子一样拖着他，我从垫子上抓起一把刀，冲到他们中间，在我晕过去之前成功地割断了绳子。
当女孩在她的记忆中崩溃时，神父僵硬地走进隔壁房间，在那里他发现吉尔德和默顿与帕特里克·罗伊斯单独在一起，帕特里克·罗伊斯戴着手铐坐在椅子上。他在那里顺从地对督察说：
“那我会的，”他说。 “私生活比公众声誉更重要。我要拯救生者，让死者埋葬他们的死者。”
“我告诉过你，在这个案件中，武器太多，只有一人死亡。我现在告诉你，它们不是武器，也不是用来致人死亡的。所有那些可怕的工具，绞索，血淋淋的刀，爆炸的手枪，都是一种奇怪的怜悯工具。它们不是用来杀死亚伦爵士的，而是用来拯救他的。”

“这是一个残酷的宗教，”牧师看着窗外说道。 “为什么他们不能让他哭一会儿，就像他的父辈们那样？他的计划僵化了，他的观点变得冷漠了；在那张快乐的面具后面是无神论者的空虚心灵。最后，为了保持他热闹的公众水平，他又回到了他早已放弃的饮酒习惯上。但是，一个真诚的滴酒不沾的人对酗酒有一种恐惧：他想象并期待着他警告过别人的心理地狱。它跳到了可怜的人身上。阿姆斯特朗过早地坐在这里，哭喊着他在地狱里，他的声音如此疯狂，以至于他的女儿都不知道，他用疯狂的猴子把戏以多种形式散布在他周围——一个运行的绞索和他朋友的左轮手枪和一把刀，罗伊斯意外地把刀扔到了身后的垫子上，抓起了左轮手枪。自杀者看到了第四次死亡，他冲向窗户，用绳子追赶他，试图绑住他的手脚。但是，当然，你注意到他在那个仆人的脸上留下了血，但没有伤口？只是在那个可怜的女人昏倒之前，她才把她的父亲砍下来，让他从那扇窗户坠入永恒。”
吉尔德解开帕特里克·罗伊斯手铐的金属声慢慢打破了长久的寂静，他对罗伊斯说：“我想我应该说实话，先生。你和那位年轻女士比阿姆斯特朗的讣告更有价值。”
“阿姆斯特朗的通知令人困惑，”罗伊斯粗暴地喊道。 “你难道没看出这是因为她不应该知道吗？”
“为什么，她杀了她的父亲，你这个傻瓜！”另一个咆哮道。 “如果没有她，他现在还活着。她知道这一点可能会发疯。”
“不，我认为不会，”布朗神父拿起帽子说道。 “我觉得我应该告诉她。即使是最致命的错误也不会像罪孽那样毒害生命；无论如何，我想你们现在可能会更幸福。我得回聋哑学校了。”
“我必须回到聋人学校，”布朗神父说。 “抱歉，我无法停下来询问。”

title: The Innocence of Father Brown · 选段 3
author: G. K. Chesterton
paragraphs: Anyone passing the house on the Thursday before Whit-Sunday at about half-past four p.m. would have seen the front door open, and Father Brown, of the small church of St. Mungo, come out smoking a large pipe in company with a very tall French friend of his called Flambeau, who was smoking a very small cigarette. These persons may or may not be of interest to the reader, but the truth is that they were not the only interesting things that were displayed when the front door of the white-and-green house was opened. There are further peculiarities about this house, which must be described to start with, not only that the reader may understand this tragic tale, but also that he may realise what it was that the opening of the door revealed.

The whole house was built upon the plan of a T, but a T with a very long cross piece and a very short tail piece. The long cross piece was the frontage that ran along in face of the street, with the front door in the middle; it was two stories high, and contained nearly all the important rooms. The short tail piece, which ran out at the back immediately opposite the front door, was one story high, and consisted only of two long rooms, the one leading into the other. The first of these two rooms was the study in which the celebrated Mr. Quinton wrote his wild Oriental poems and romances. The farther room was a glass conservatory full of tropical blossoms of quite unique and almost monstrous beauty, and on such afternoons as these glowing with gorgeous sunlight. Thus when the hall door was open, many a passer-by literally stopped to stare and gasp; for he looked down a perspective of rich apartments to something really like a transformation scene in a fairy play: purple clouds and golden suns and crimson stars that were at once scorchingly vivid and yet transparent and far away.

Leonard Quinton, the poet, had himself most carefully arranged this effect; and it is doubtful whether he so perfectly expressed his personality in any of his poems. For he was a man who drank and bathed in colours, who indulged his lust for colour somewhat to the neglect of form--even of good form. This it was that had turned his genius so wholly to eastern art and imagery; to those bewildering carpets or blinding embroideries in which all the colours seem fallen into a fortunate chaos, having nothing to typify or to teach. He had attempted, not perhaps with complete artistic success, but with acknowledged imagination and invention, to compose epics and love stories reflecting the riot of violent and even cruel colour; tales of tropical heavens of burning gold or blood-red copper; of eastern heroes who rode with twelve-turbaned mitres upon elephants painted purple or peacock green; of gigantic jewels that a hundred negroes could not carry, but which burned with ancient and strange-hued fires.

In short (to put the matter from the more common point of view), he dealt much in eastern heavens, rather worse than most western hells; in eastern monarchs, whom we might possibly call maniacs; and in eastern jewels which a Bond Street jeweller (if the hundred staggering negroes brought them into his shop) might possibly not regard as genuine. Quinton was a genius, if a morbid one; and even his morbidity appeared more in his life than in his work. In temperament he was weak and waspish, and his health had suffered heavily from oriental experiments with opium. His wife--a handsome, hard-working, and, indeed, over-worked woman objected to the opium, but objected much more to a live Indian hermit in white and yellow robes, whom her husband insisted on entertaining for months together, a Virgil to guide his spirit through the heavens and the hells of the east.

It was out of this artistic household that Father Brown and his friend stepped on to the door-step; and to judge from their faces, they stepped out of it with much relief. Flambeau had known Quinton in wild student days in Paris, and they had renewed the acquaintance for a week-end; but apart from Flambeau’s more responsible developments of late, he did not get on well with the poet now. Choking oneself with opium and writing little erotic verses on vellum was not his notion of how a gentleman should go to the devil. As the two paused on the door-step, before taking a turn in the garden, the front garden gate was thrown open with violence, and a young man with a billycock hat on the back of his head tumbled up the steps in his eagerness. He was a dissipated-looking youth with a gorgeous red necktie all awry, as if he had slept in it, and he kept fidgeting and lashing about with one of those little jointed canes.
paragraphsZh: 任何人在圣灵降临节之前的周四下午四点半左右经过这所房子。会看到前门打开，圣蒙戈小教堂的布朗神父抽着一根大烟斗走了出来，他的一个很高的法国朋友名叫弗朗博，他抽着一根很小的香烟。读者可能对这些人感兴趣，也可能不感兴趣，但事实是，当白绿相间的房子的前门打开时，他们并不是唯一有趣的东西。这所房子还有更多的奇特之处，必须首先描述一下，这样读者不仅可以理解这个悲惨的故事，而且可以意识到门的打开揭示了什么。

整个房子是按照T形的平面建造的，但是T形有一个很长的横梁和一个很短的尾梁。长横梁是面向街道的正面，前门在中间。它有两层楼高，几乎包含了所有重要的房间。短尾部分从前门对面的后面伸出，有一层楼高，只有两个长房间组成，一个通向另一个房间。这两个房间中的第一个是书房，著名的昆顿先生在其中写下了他狂野的东方诗歌和浪漫史。远处的房间是一个玻璃温室，里面种满了热带花卉，它们非常独特，美得近乎怪异，在这样的下午，在灿烂的阳光下闪闪发光。因此，当大厅的门打开时，许多过路人都停下来凝视并喘息。因为他从高处俯视一栋栋富丽堂皇的公寓，就像童话剧中的变换场景：紫色的云彩、金色的太阳和深红色的星星，既鲜艳又透明又遥远。

诗人伦纳德·昆顿 (Leonard Quinton) 亲自精心安排了这种效果；值得怀疑的是，他是否在任何一首诗中如此完美地表达了他的个性。因为他是一个沐浴在色彩中的人，他沉溺于对色彩的渴望而忽略了形式——甚至是良好的形式。正是这一点使他的天才完全转向了东方艺术和图像。那些令人眼花缭乱的地毯或令人眼花缭乱的刺绣，其中所有的颜色似乎都陷入了幸运的混乱之中，没有什么可以典型或可以教导的。他也许没有在艺术上取得完全的成功，但凭借公认的想象力和创造力，创作了反映暴力甚至残酷色彩的史诗和爱情故事。燃烧黄金或血红铜的热带天堂的故事；东方英雄骑着十二头巾，骑着涂成紫色或孔雀绿的大象；一百个黑人都搬不动的巨大珠宝，却燃烧着古老而奇异的火焰。

总而言之（从更普遍的角度来看），他在东方天堂做了很多事情，比大多数西方地狱更糟糕；在东方君主中，我们可以称他们为疯子；还有东方珠宝，邦德街的珠宝商（如果有上百个令人震惊的黑人将它们带到他的店里）可能不会认为是真品。昆顿是一位天才，尽管是一位病态的天才。甚至他的病态更多地表现在他的生活中而不是他的工作中。他的性情软弱、脾气暴躁，他的健康也因东方鸦片实验而受到严重损害。他的妻子——一位英俊、勤劳、实际上劳累过度的女人，反对鸦片，但更反对一位穿着白黄相间长袍的印度隐士，她的丈夫坚持要招待他几个月，一位维吉尔引导他的灵魂穿越东方的天堂和地狱。

布朗神父和他的朋友就是从这个艺术之家踏上家门的。从他们的表情来看，他们走出监狱时松了口气。弗朗博在巴黎疯狂的学生时代就认识了昆顿，他们在周末又重新认识了。但除了弗朗博近来更加负责任的发展之外，他现在与诗人相处得并不好。用鸦片噎死自己，在羊皮纸上写一些情色小诗，这并不是他认为君子该怎样走向魔鬼的想法。两人在门口台阶上停了下来，准备在花园里转弯时，花园的前门被猛烈地推开，一个后脑勺戴着斗篷帽的年轻人急切地从台阶上滚了下去。他是一个看上去放荡不羁的年轻人，一条华丽的红色领带全部歪了，好像他睡过觉一样，他不停地坐立不安，用一根小节手杖敲打着。

title: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: I am afraid, Watson, that I shall have to go,” said Holmes, as we sat down together to our breakfast one morning.

I was not surprised. Indeed, my only wonder was that he had not already been mixed up in this extraordinary case, which was the one topic of conversation through the length and breadth of England. For a whole day my companion had rambled about the room with his chin upon his chest and his brows knitted, charging and recharging his pipe with the strongest black tobacco, and absolutely deaf to any of my questions or remarks. Fresh editions of every paper had been sent up by our news agent, only to be glanced over and tossed down into a corner. Yet, silent as he was, I knew perfectly well what it was over which he was brooding. There was but one problem before the public which could challenge his powers of analysis, and that was the singular disappearance of the favourite for the Wessex Cup, and the tragic murder of its trainer. When, therefore, he suddenly announced his intention of setting out for the scene of the drama it was only what I had both expected and hoped for.

“My dear Watson, you would confer a great favour upon me by coming. And I think that your time will not be misspent, for there are points about the case which promise to make it an absolutely unique one. We have, I think, just time to catch our train at Paddington, and I will go further into the matter upon our journey. You would oblige me by bringing with you your very excellent field-glass.”

And so it happened that an hour or so later I found myself in the corner of a first-class carriage flying along en route for Exeter, while Sherlock Holmes, with his sharp, eager face framed in his ear-flapped travelling-cap, dipped rapidly into the bundle of fresh papers which he had procured at Paddington. We had left Reading far behind us before he thrust the last one of them under the seat, and offered me his cigar-case.
“We are going well,” said he, looking out the window and glancing at his watch. “Our rate at present is fifty-three and a half miles an hour.”

“Nor have I. But the telegraph posts upon this line are sixty yards apart, and the calculation is a simple one. I presume that you have looked into this matter of the murder of John Straker and the disappearance of Silver Blaze?”

“It is one of those cases where the art of the reasoner should be used rather for the sifting of details than for the acquiring of fresh evidence. The tragedy has been so uncommon, so complete and of such personal importance to so many people, that we are suffering from a plethora of surmise, conjecture, and hypothesis. The difficulty is to detach the framework of fact—of absolute undeniable fact—from the embellishments of theorists and reporters. Then, having established ourselves upon this sound basis, it is our duty to see what inferences may be drawn and what are the special points upon which the whole mystery turns. On Tuesday evening I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross, the owner of the horse, and from Inspector Gregory, who is looking after the case, inviting my co-operation.”

“Because I made a blunder, my dear Watson—which is, I am afraid, a more common occurrence than any one would think who only knew me through your memoirs. The fact is that I could not believe it possible that the most remarkable horse in England could long remain concealed, especially in so sparsely inhabited a place as the north of Dartmoor. From hour to hour yesterday I expected to hear that he had been found, and that his abductor was the murderer of John Straker. When, however, another morning had come, and I found that beyond the arrest of young Fitzroy Simpson nothing had been done, I felt that it was time for me to take action. Yet in some ways I feel that yesterday has not been wasted.”

“At least I have got a grip of the essential facts of the case. I shall enumerate them to you, for nothing clears up a case so much as stating it to another person, and I can hardly expect your co-operation if I do not show you the position from which we start.”

I lay back against the cushions, puffing at my cigar, while Holmes, leaning forward, with his long, thin forefinger checking off the points upon the palm of his left hand, gave me a sketch of the events which had led to our journey.
paragraphsZh: 华生，恐怕我得走了。”一天早上，当我们一起坐下来吃早餐时，福尔摩斯说道。

我并不感到惊讶。事实上，我唯一感到奇怪的是，他还没有卷入这起非同寻常的案件中，这是全英格兰谈论的一个话题。一整天，我的同伴都在房间里闲逛，下巴抵在胸前，眉头紧锁，用最浓烈的黑烟草给他的烟斗装上又装着，对我的任何问题或评论充耳不闻。每份报纸的新版本都被我们的新闻代理送来了，只是被浏览了一下然后扔到了角落里。然而，尽管他沉默不语，我却很清楚他在沉思什么。摆在公众面前的只有一个问题可以挑战他的分析能力，那就是威塞克斯杯夺冠热门的离奇失踪以及其教练的惨遭谋杀。所以，当他突然宣布要出发去戏场时，这也正是我所期待和希望的。
“我亲爱的华生，你的到来将给我很大的帮助。我认为您的时间不会浪费，因为这个案例的一些要点有望使其成为一个绝对独特的案例。我想，我们正好有时间去帕丁顿赶火车，我将在旅途中进一步讨论这个问题。请您带上您非常出色的望远镜来帮助我。”
就这样，大约一个小时后，我发现自己正坐在一辆飞往埃克塞特的头等车厢的角落里，而夏洛克·福尔摩斯，带着他那张盖着耳朵的旅行帽，面容锐利而热切，迅速地投入到他在帕丁顿买来的一捆新文件中。我们已经把雷丁远远地抛在了身后，他把最后一个人塞到了座位下面，把他的雪茄盒递给了我。
“我们进展顺利，”他看着窗外，看了一眼手表说道。 “我们目前的速度是每小时五十三英里半。”
“我也没有。但是这条线上的电报站相距六十码，计算起来很简单。我想你已经调查过约翰·斯特雷克被谋杀和银焰失踪这件事了吧？”

“在这种情况下，推理者的艺术应该用于筛选细节，而不是用于获取新证据。这场悲剧如此罕见，如此完整，对很多人来说都具有如此重要的个人意义，以至于我们面临着过多的猜测、猜想和假设。困难在于将事实框架——绝对不可否认的事实——与理论家和记者的修饰分开。然后，在建立了这个可靠的基础之后，我们就有责任看看可以得出什么推论，以及整个谜团的特殊要点是什么。周二晚上，我收到了马主罗斯上校和负责此案的格雷戈里督察的电报，邀请我合作。”

“因为我犯了一个错误，亲爱的华生——我担心，这种情况比任何只通过你的回忆录认识我的人想象的更常见。事实上，我无法相信英格兰最出色的马能长期隐藏起来，尤其是在达特穆尔北部这样人烟稀少的地方。昨天，我每时每刻都期待着听到他被发现了，绑架他的人就是杀害约翰·斯特拉克的凶手。然而，当又一个早晨到来时，我发现除了逮捕年轻的菲茨罗伊·辛普森之外什么也没做，我觉得是时候采取行动了。但从某些方面来说，我觉得昨天并没有浪费。”
“至少我掌握了案件的基本事实。我将向你一一列举，因为没有什么比向另一个人陈述更能澄清案件的了，如果我不向你展示我们开始的立场，我就很难指望你的合作。”
我靠在垫子上，吸着雪茄，而福尔摩斯则身体前倾，用细长的食指检查着左手手掌上的点，给我概述了导致我们这次旅行的事件。

title: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes · 选段 2
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: I stood for a minute or two to collect myself, for I was dazed with the horror of the thing. Then I began to think of Holmes’s own methods and to try to practise them in reading this tragedy. It was, alas, only too easy to do. During our conversation we had not gone to the end of the path, and the Alpine-stock marked the place where we had stood. The blackish soil is kept forever soft by the incessant drift of spray, and a bird would leave its tread upon it. Two lines of footmarks were clearly marked along the farther end of the path, both leading away from me. There were none returning. A few yards from the end the soil was all ploughed up into a patch of mud, and the branches and ferns which fringed the chasm were torn and bedraggled. I lay upon my face and peered over with the spray spouting up all around me. It had darkened since I left, and now I could only see here and there the glistening of moisture upon the black walls, and far away down at the end of the shaft the gleam of the broken water. I shouted; but only the same half-human cry of the fall was borne back to my ears.

But it was destined that I should after all have a last word of greeting from my friend and comrade. I have said that his Alpine-stock had been left leaning against a rock which jutted on to the path. From the top of this boulder the gleam of something bright caught my eye, and, raising my hand, I found that it came from the silver cigarette-case which he used to carry. As I took it up a small square of paper upon which it had lain fluttered down on to the ground. Unfolding it, I found that it consisted of three pages torn from his note-book and addressed to me. It was characteristic of the man that the direction was a precise, and the writing as firm and clear, as though it had been written in his study.

“My dear Watson,” he said, “I write these few lines through the courtesy of Mr. Moriarty, who awaits my convenience for the final discussion of those questions which lie between us. He has been giving me a sketch of the methods by which he avoided the English police and kept himself informed of our movements. They certainly confirm the very high opinion which I had formed of his abilities. I am pleased to think that I shall be able to free society from any further effects of his presence, though I fear that it is at a cost which will give pain to my friends, and especially, my dear Watson, to you. I have already explained to you, however, that my career had in any case reached its crisis, and that no possible conclusion to it could be more congenial to me than this. Indeed, if I may make a full confession to you, I was quite convinced that the letter from Meiringen was a hoax, and I allowed you to depart on that errand under the persuasion that some development of this sort would follow. Tell Inspector Patterson that the papers which he needs to convict the gang are in pigeonhole M., done up in a blue envelope and inscribed ‘Moriarty.’ I made every disposition of my property before leaving England, and handed it to my brother Mycroft. Pray give my greetings to Mrs. Watson, and believe me to be, my dear fellow,

A few words may suffice to tell the little that remains. An examination by experts leaves little doubt that a personal contest between the two men ended, as it could hardly fail to end in such a situation, in their reeling over, locked in each other’s arms. Any attempt at recovering the bodies was absolutely hopeless, and there, deep down in that dreadful caldron of swirling water and seething foam, will lie for all time the most dangerous criminal and the foremost champion of the law of their generation. The Swiss youth was never found again, and there can be no doubt that he was one of the numerous agents whom Moriarty kept in his employ. As to the gang, it will be within the memory of the public how completely the evidence which Holmes had accumulated exposed their organization, and how heavily the hand of the dead man weighed upon them. Of their terrible chief few details came out during the proceedings, and if I have now been compelled to make a clear statement of his career it is due to those injudicious champions who have endeavoured to clear his memory by attacks upon him whom I shall ever regard as the best and the wisest man whom I have ever known.
paragraphsZh: 我站了一两分钟才平静下来，因为这件事的恐怖让我头晕目眩。然后我开始思考福尔摩斯自己的方法，并尝试在阅读这部悲剧时加以实践。唉，这太容易做到了。在我们谈话的过程中，我们还没有走到小路的尽头，阿尔卑斯山的木桩标记了我们曾经站过的地方。由于水花不断飘流，黑色的土壤永远保持松软，鸟儿会在上面留下足迹。沿着小路的另一端，有两行脚印清晰可见，都远离我。没有人回来。距离尽头几码远的地方，土壤全部被犁成一片泥巴，裂缝边缘的树枝和蕨类植物都被撕裂，脏兮兮的。我趴在地上，凝视四周，水花在我周围喷涌而出。自从我离开后，天就黑了，现在我只能看到黑色墙壁上到处都是湿气，在远处的竖井尽头看到破碎的水的光芒。我喊道；但我的耳中却只听到了同样的半人摔倒时的哭声。
但注定我终究要得到我的朋友和战友的最后一句问候。我说过他的阿尔卑斯山股票被遗弃在一块突出在路上的岩石上。从这块巨石的顶端，一道明亮的光芒映入了我的眼帘，我一抬手，发现那光芒是从他随身携带的银色烟盒里发出来的。当我把它捡起来时，上面放着的一张小纸片飘落到了地上。打开它，我发现它是从他的笔记本上撕下的三页，写给我的。这个人的特点就是方向准确，字迹坚定清晰，就像是在他的书房里写的一样。

“我亲爱的华生，”他说，“我是受莫里亚蒂先生的好意写下这几行字的，他正在等待我的方便，以便对我们之间的那些问题进行最后的讨论。他一直在向我概述他如何躲避英国警察，并随时了解我们的动向。这些无疑证实了我对他能力的高度评价。我很高兴地认为，我将能够使社会免受他的存在的任何进一步影响，尽管我担心这是然而，我已经向你解释过，我的朋友们，尤其是亲爱的华生，我的职业生涯已经到了危机，没有比这更适合我的结论了。 事实上，如果我可以向你坦白，我非常确信迈林根的信是一个骗局，我允许你离开，因为我相信会有这样的进展。帕特森告诉帕特森，他需要给这伙人定罪的文件就放在M.的文件箱里，装在一个蓝色信封里，上面写着“莫里亚蒂”。在离开英国之前，我对我的财产进行了一切处置，并将其交给了我的兄弟麦克罗夫特，请代我向沃森夫人问好，相信我，我亲爱的朋友，

几句话足以说明剩下的一点点。经过专家的检验，毫无疑问，两人之间的个人较量已经结束了，因为在这样的情况下，他们几乎不可能不以互相拥抱的方式结束。任何打捞尸体的尝试都是绝对没有希望的，而在那个充满漩涡水和沸腾泡沫的可怕大锅深处，将永远躺着最危险的罪犯和他们这一代最重要的法律捍卫者。这位瑞士青年再也没有被发现，毫无疑问，他是莫里亚蒂雇佣的众多特工之一。至于这伙人，公众将记住福尔摩斯所积累的证据是多么彻底地暴露了他们的组织，以及死者的手对他们施加了多么沉重的压力。在诉讼过程中，他们可怕的主要细节很少被透露出来，如果我现在不得不对他的职业生涯做出明确的陈述，那是因为那些不明智的拥护者试图通过攻击他来清除他的记忆，我将认为他是我所认识的最好和最聪明的人。

title: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes · 选段 3
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: “And that’s the story of the Musgrave Ritual, Watson. They have the crown down at Hurlstone—though they had some legal bother and a considerable sum to pay before they were allowed to retain it. I am sure that if you mentioned my name they would be happy to show it to you. Of the woman nothing was ever heard, and the probability is that she got away out of England and carried herself and the memory of her crime to some land beyond the seas.”

It was some time before the health of my friend Mr. Sherlock Holmes recovered from the strain caused by his immense exertions in the spring of ’87. The whole question of the Netherland-Sumatra Company and of the colossal schemes of Baron Maupertuis are too recent in the minds of the public, and are too intimately concerned with politics and finance to be fitting subjects for this series of sketches. They led, however, in an indirect fashion to a singular and complex problem which gave my friend an opportunity of demonstrating the value of a fresh weapon among the many with which he waged his life-long battle against crime.

On referring to my notes I see that it was upon the 14th of April that I received a telegram from Lyons which informed me that Holmes was lying ill in the Hotel Dulong. Within twenty-four hours I was in his sick-room, and was relieved to find that there was nothing formidable in his symptoms. Even his iron constitution, however, had broken down under the strain of an investigation which had extended over two months, during which period he had never worked less than fifteen hours a day, and had more than once, as he assured me, kept to his task for five days at a stretch. Even the triumphant issue of his labours could not save him from reaction after so terrible an exertion, and at a time when Europe was ringing with his name and when his room was literally ankle-deep with congratulatory telegrams I found him a prey to the blackest depression. Even the knowledge that he had succeeded where the police of three countries had failed, and that he had outmanœuvred at every point the most accomplished swindler in Europe, was insufficient to rouse him from his nervous prostration.

Three days later we were back in Baker Street together; but it was evident that my friend would be much the better for a change, and the thought of a week of spring time in the country was full of attractions to me also. My old friend, Colonel Hayter, who had come under my professional care in Afghanistan, had now taken a house near Reigate in Surrey, and had frequently asked me to come down to him upon a visit. On the last occasion he had remarked that if my friend would only come with me he would be glad to extend his hospitality to him also. A little diplomacy was needed, but when Holmes understood that the establishment was a bachelor one, and that he would be allowed the fullest freedom, he fell in with my plans and a week after our return from Lyons we were under the Colonel’s roof. Hayter was a fine old soldier who had seen much of the world, and he soon found, as I had expected, that Holmes and he had much in common.
On the evening of our arrival we were sitting in the Colonel’s gun-room after dinner, Holmes stretched upon the sofa, while Hayter and I looked over his little armoury of fire-arms.
“Yes, we’ve had a scare in this part lately. Old Acton, who is one of our county magnates, had his house broken into last Monday. No great damage done, but the fellows are still at large.”
“None as yet. But the affair is a petty one, one of our little country crimes, which must seem too small for your attention, Mr. Holmes, after this great international affair.”

“I fancy not. The thieves ransacked the library and got very little for their pains. The whole place was turned upside down, drawers burst open, and presses ransacked, with the result that an odd volume of Pope’s ‘Homer,’ two plated candlesticks, an ivory letter-weight, a small oak barometer, and a ball of twine are all that have vanished.”
“You are here for a rest, my dear fellow. For Heaven’s sake don’t get started on a new problem when your nerves are all in shreds.”
Holmes shrugged his shoulders with a glance of comic resignation towards the Colonel, and the talk drifted away into less dangerous channels.
paragraphsZh: “这就是马斯格雷夫仪式的故事，华生。他们在赫尔斯通拥有王冠——尽管他们在被允许保留王冠之前遇到了一些法律麻烦，而且要支付相当大的一笔费用。我相信，如果你提到我的名字，他们会很乐意把它展示给你。关于那个女人，我们什么也没听到，很可能她离开了英格兰，把自己和她的罪行记忆带到了海外的某个地方。”
我的朋友夏洛克·福尔摩斯先生的健康过了一段时间才从 87 年春天的巨大劳累所造成的压力中恢复过来。荷兰-苏门答腊公司的整个问题和莫佩尔蒂男爵的庞大计划在公众心目中都是最近才出现的，而且与政治和金融关系太密切，不适合作为这一系列草图的主题。然而，它们以间接的方式导致了一个单一而复杂的问题，这给了我的朋友一个机会，在他一生与犯罪作斗争的众多武器中展示了一种新武器的价值。

根据我的笔记，我发现我是在 4 月 14 日收到里昂发来的电报，通知我福尔摩斯病倒在杜隆酒店。不到二十四小时，我就到了他的病房，发现他的症状没有什么可怕的，这让我松了口气。然而，即使是他的钢铁般的体质，在长达两个多月的调查压力下也崩溃了，在此期间，他每天的工作时间从未少于十五个小时，而且正如他向我保证的那样，他不止一次连续工作五天。即使是他的劳动的胜利也无法使他在经历了如此可怕的努力后免受反应，当欧洲响起他的名字时，当他的房间里充满了齐脚踝的祝贺电报时，我发现他是最黑暗的抑郁症的牺牲品。即使知道他在三个国家的警察失败的地方取得了成功，并且他在每一点上都战胜了欧洲最熟练的骗子，也不足以让他从紧张的沮丧中醒来。

三天后我们一起回到贝克街；但很明显，我的朋友如果换个环境会更好，而且想到在乡下度过一周的春天也对我充满了吸引力。我的老朋友海特上校在阿富汗受到我的专业照顾，现在他在萨里赖盖特附近租了一栋房子，并经常邀请我去拜访他。上次他曾说过，如果我的朋友愿意和我一起去，他也很乐意向他表示热情的款待。需要一点外交手段，但是当福尔摩斯明白这个机构是一个单身汉，并且他将被允许最充分的自由时，他同意了我的计划，从里昂回来一周后，我们就在上校的屋檐下。海特是一位优秀的老兵，见识过很多世界，他很快就发现，正如我所料，福尔摩斯和他有很多共同点。
我们到达的那天晚上，晚饭后我们坐在上校的枪械室里，福尔摩斯在沙发上伸了个懒腰，而海特和我则在检查他的小枪械库。
“是的，我们最近在这方面遇到了恐慌。老阿克顿是我们县的一位大亨，上周一他的房子被闯入了。没有造成重大损失，但这些家伙仍然在逃。”
“目前还没有。但这件事是一件小事，是我们国家的小罪行之一，在这件伟大的国际事件之后，福尔摩斯先生，这对你来说一定太小了。”
“我想不会。窃贼洗劫了图书馆，却一无所获。整个地方被翻了个底朝天，抽屉被炸开，印刷机被洗劫一空，结果一本奇怪的教皇的《荷马史诗》卷、两个镀金烛台、一个象牙信重、一个小橡木气压计和一团麻线都消失了。”
“亲爱的朋友，你在这里休息一下。看在上帝的份上，不要在你的神经都崩溃的时候开始解决新问题。”
福尔摩斯耸了耸肩，用一种滑稽的无奈的眼神看着上校，话题就转移到了不太危险的话题上。

title: The Return of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: It was in the spring of the year 1894 that all London was interested, and the fashionable world dismayed, by the murder of the Honourable Ronald Adair under most unusual and inexplicable circumstances. The public has already learned those particulars of the crime which came out in the police investigation, but a good deal was suppressed upon that occasion, since the case for the prosecution was so overwhelmingly strong that it was not necessary to bring forward all the facts. Only now, at the end of nearly ten years, am I allowed to supply those missing links which make up the whole of that remarkable chain. The crime was of interest in itself, but that interest was as nothing to me compared to the inconceivable sequel, which afforded me the greatest shock and surprise of any event in my adventurous life. Even now, after this long interval, I find myself thrilling as I think of it, and feeling once more that sudden flood of joy, amazement, and incredulity which utterly submerged my mind. Let me say to that public, which has shown some interest in those glimpses which I have occasionally given them of the thoughts and actions of a very remarkable man, that they are not to blame me if I have not shared my knowledge with them, for I should have considered it my first duty to do so, had I not been barred by a positive prohibition from his own lips, which was only withdrawn upon the third of last month.

It can be imagined that my close intimacy with Sherlock Holmes had interested me deeply in crime, and that after his disappearance I never failed to read with care the various problems which came before the public. And I even attempted, more than once, for my own private satisfaction, to employ his methods in their solution, though with indifferent success. There was none, however, which appealed to me like this tragedy of Ronald Adair. As I read the evidence at the inquest, which led up to a verdict of willful murder against some person or persons unknown, I realized more clearly than I had ever done the loss which the community had sustained by the death of Sherlock Holmes. There were points about this strange business which would, I was sure, have specially appealed to him, and the efforts of the police would have been supplemented, or more probably anticipated, by the trained observation and the alert mind of the first criminal agent in Europe. All day, as I drove upon my round, I turned over the case in my mind and found no explanation which appeared to me to be adequate. At the risk of telling a twice-told tale, I will recapitulate the facts as they were known to the public at the conclusion of the inquest.

The Honourable Ronald Adair was the second son of the Earl of Maynooth, at that time governor of one of the Australian colonies. Adair’s mother had returned from Australia to undergo the operation for cataract, and she, her son Ronald, and her daughter Hilda were living together at 427, Park Lane. The youth moved in the best society—had, so far as was known, no enemies and no particular vices. He had been engaged to Miss Edith Woodley, of Carstairs, but the engagement had been broken off by mutual consent some months before, and there was no sign that it had left any very profound feeling behind it. For the rest, the man’s life moved in a narrow and conventional circle, for his habits were quiet and his nature unemotional. Yet it was upon this easy-going young aristocrat that death came, in most strange and unexpected form, between the hours of ten and eleven-twenty on the night of March 30, 1894.

Ronald Adair was fond of cards—playing continually, but never for such stakes as would hurt him. He was a member of the Baldwin, the Cavendish, and the Bagatelle card clubs. It was shown that, after dinner on the day of his death, he had played a rubber of whist at the latter club. He had also played there in the afternoon. The evidence of those who had played with him—Mr. Murray, Sir John Hardy, and Colonel Moran—showed that the game was whist, and that there was a fairly equal fall of the cards. Adair might have lost five pounds, but not more. His fortune was a considerable one, and such a loss could not in any way affect him. He had played nearly every day at one club or other, but he was a cautious player, and usually rose a winner. It came out in evidence that, in partnership with Colonel Moran, he had actually won as much as four hundred and twenty pounds in a sitting, some weeks before, from Godfrey Milner and Lord Balmoral. So much for his recent history as it came out at the inquest.
paragraphsZh: 1894 年春天，罗纳德·阿岱尔阁下在最不寻常和莫名其妙的情况下被谋杀，整个伦敦都在关注，而时尚界则感到沮丧。公众已经了解了警方调查中发现的犯罪细节，但当时很多内容都被压制了，因为检方的案情非常充分，没有必要提出所有事实。直到现在，在近十年结束时，我才被允许提供那些缺失的环节，这些环节构成了整个非凡的链条。犯罪本身就很有趣，但与难以想象的续集相比，这种兴趣对我来说根本算不了什么，它给我带来了我冒险生活中任何事件中最大的震惊和惊喜。即使是现在，经过这么长时间的间隔，我一想到这件事就感到激动不已，并再次感受到突然涌来的喜悦、惊讶和怀疑，它们完全淹没了我的心灵。让我对公众说，他们对我偶尔瞥见的一位非常杰出的人的思想和行为表现出了一些兴趣，如果我没有与他们分享我的知识，他们不会责怪我，因为如果不是他自己亲口发出的明确禁令（上个月三号才撤回），我应该认为这样做是我的首要职责。

可以想象，我与夏洛克·福尔摩斯的亲密关系使我对犯罪产生了浓厚的兴趣，在他失踪后，我从未忘记仔细阅读摆在公众面前的各种问题。为了满足我个人的满足，我什至不止一次尝试采用他的方法来解决问题，尽管成功程度并不高。然而，没有一个像罗纳德·阿代尔的悲剧那样吸引我。当我读到审讯中的证据时，我比以往任何时候都更清楚地认识到夏洛克·福尔摩斯的死给社区带来的损失。我确信，这件奇怪的事情有一些要点对他特别有吸引力，而欧洲第一个犯罪特工训练有素的观察力和警觉的头脑会补充警察的努力，或者更可能预见到这一点。一整天，当我开车兜风时，我在脑子里翻来覆去地思考这个案子，但没有找到我认为合适的解释。冒着重复讲述的风险，我将重述调查结束时公众所了解的事实。

罗纳德·阿代尔阁下是梅努斯伯爵的次子，梅努斯伯爵当时是澳大利亚殖民地之一的总督。阿代尔的母亲从澳大利亚回来接受白内障手术，她、儿子罗纳德和女儿希尔达一起住在公园巷 427 号。年轻人生活在上流社会——据我们所知，没有敌人，也没有什么特别的恶习。他曾与卡斯泰尔斯的伊迪丝·伍德利小姐订婚，但几个月前经双方同意解除了婚约，而且没有任何迹象表明它留下了任何深刻的感情。其余的时间里，这个人的生活都在一个狭窄而传统的圈子里进行，因为他的习惯很安静，天性也不带感情。然而，1894 年 3 月 30 日晚上 10 点到 11 点 20 分之间，死亡以最奇怪和最出乎意料的形式降临在这位随和的年轻贵族身上。

罗纳德·阿代尔（Ronald Adair）喜欢牌——不断地玩牌，但从来不玩会伤害他的赌注。他是鲍德温、卡文迪什和巴加特尔纸牌俱乐部的成员。据显示，在他去世当天的晚餐后，他曾在后者的俱乐部玩过一盘惠斯特棋。下午他也在那里玩过。那些和他一起玩过的人的证据——先生。穆雷、约翰·哈迪爵士和莫兰上校——表明了这场比赛是惠斯特游戏，而且牌面的分配相当平等。阿代尔可能减掉了五磅，但也不会更多。他的财产已经相当可观了，这样的损失对他没有任何影响。他几乎每天都在某个俱乐部或其他俱乐部踢球，但他是一名谨慎的球员，并且通常会成为胜利者。有证据表明，几周前，他与莫兰上校合作，实际上从戈弗雷·米尔纳和巴尔莫勒尔勋爵那里赢得了四百二十英镑。关于他最近的历史就这么多了，因为它是在审讯中公布的。

title: The Return of Sherlock Holmes · 选段 2
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: “Now, Watson, the fair sex is your department,” said Holmes, with a smile, when the dwindling frou-frou of skirts had ended in the slam of the front door. “What was the fair lady’s game? What did she really want?”
“Hum! Think of her appearance, Watson—her manner, her suppressed excitement, her restlessness, her tenacity in asking questions. Remember that she comes of a caste who do not lightly show emotion.”

“Remember also the curious earnestness with which she assured us that it was best for her husband that she should know all. What did she mean by that? And you must have observed, Watson, how she manœuvred to have the light at her back. She did not wish us to read her expression.”

“And yet the motives of women are so inscrutable. You remember the woman at Margate whom I suspected for the same reason. No powder on her nose—that proved to be the correct solution. How can you build on such a quicksand? Their most trivial action may mean volumes, or their most extraordinary conduct may depend upon a hairpin or a curling tongs. Good-morning, Watson.”

“Yes, I will while away the morning at Godolphin Street with our friends of the regular establishment. With Eduardo Lucas lies the solution of our problem, though I must admit that I have not an inkling as to what form it may take. It is a capital mistake to theorize in advance of the facts. Do you stay on guard, my good Watson, and receive any fresh visitors. I’ll join you at lunch if I am able.”

All that day and the next and the next Holmes was in a mood which his friends would call taciturn, and others morose. He ran out and ran in, smoked incessantly, played snatches on his violin, sank into reveries, devoured sandwiches at irregular hours, and hardly answered the casual questions which I put to him. It was evident to me that things were not going well with him or his quest. He would say nothing of the case, and it was from the papers that I learned the particulars of the inquest, and the arrest with the subsequent release of John Mitton, the valet of the deceased. The coroner’s jury brought in the obvious Wilful Murder, but the parties remained as unknown as ever. No motive was suggested. The room was full of articles of value, but none had been taken. The dead man’s papers had not been tampered with. They were carefully examined, and showed that he was a keen student of international politics, an indefatigable gossip, a remarkable linguist, and an untiring letter writer. He had been on intimate terms with the leading politicians of several countries. But nothing sensational was discovered among the documents which filled his drawers. As to his relations with women, they appeared to have been promiscuous but superficial. He had many acquaintances among them, but few friends, and no one whom he loved. His habits were regular, his conduct inoffensive. His death was an absolute mystery and likely to remain so.

As to the arrest of John Mitton, the valet, it was a council of despair as an alternative to absolute inaction. But no case could be sustained against him. He had visited friends in Hammersmith that night. The alibi was complete. It is true that he started home at an hour which should have brought him to Westminster before the time when the crime was discovered, but his own explanation that he had walked part of the way seemed probable enough in view of the fineness of the night. He had actually arrived at twelve o’clock, and appeared to be overwhelmed by the unexpected tragedy. He had always been on good terms with his master. Several of the dead man’s possessions—notably a small case of razors—had been found in the valet’s boxes, but he explained that they had been presents from the deceased, and the housekeeper was able to corroborate the story. Mitton had been in Lucas’s employment for three years. It was noticeable that Lucas did not take Mitton on the Continent with him. Sometimes he visited Paris for three months on end, but Mitton was left in charge of the Godolphin Street house. As to the housekeeper, she had heard nothing on the night of the crime. If her master had a visitor he had himself admitted him.

So for three mornings the mystery remained, so far as I could follow it in the papers. If Holmes knew more, he kept his own counsel, but, as he told me that Inspector Lestrade had taken him into his confidence in the case, I knew that he was in close touch with every development. Upon the fourth day there appeared a long telegram from Paris which seemed to solve the whole question.
paragraphsZh: “现在，华生，女性是你的部门，”福尔摩斯笑着说，当前门关上时，裙子的褶皱逐渐减少。 “这位窈窕淑女的把戏是什么？她到底想要什么？”
“嗯！想想她的外表，华生——她的举止，她压抑的兴奋，她的焦躁不安，她问问题的坚韧。记住，她来自一个不会轻易表露情感的种姓。”
“还记得她向我们保证，她应该知道一切对她的丈夫来说是最好的。她这是什么意思？你一定已经观察到，华生，她如何巧妙地让灯光照在她的背后。她不希望我们读到她的表情。”
“然而，女人的动机却如此难以捉摸。你还记得我出于同样原因怀疑的马盖特女人吗？她鼻子上没有粉——事实证明这是正确的解决方案。你怎么能在这样的流沙上继续发展呢？她们最微不足道的行为可能意味着很大的事情，或者她们最非凡的行为可能取决于一根发夹或卷发钳。早上好，华生。”
“是的，我会在戈多芬街和我们的老朋友一起消磨早晨的时光。爱德华多·卢卡斯就是我们问题的解决方案，尽管我必须承认我对它可能采取什么形式一无所知。提前对事实进行推理是一个致命的错误。你要保持警惕吗，我的好华生，接待新来的访客。如果可以的话，我会和你一起吃午餐。”

那天以及接下来的每一天，福尔摩斯都处于一种他的朋友们称之为沉默寡言的情绪，而其他人则称之为忧郁。他跑出跑进，不停地抽烟，拉小提琴，陷入沉思，不定时地吃三明治，几乎不回答我向他提出的漫不经心的问题。对我来说，很明显，他或他的追求进展并不顺利。他对这个案子只字未提，我就是从报纸上了解到调查的细节，以及逮捕的细节以及死者的贴身男仆约翰·米顿随后被释放的情况。验尸官陪审团认定这是明显的故意谋杀，但当事人仍然像以前一样不为人知。没有暗示任何动机。房间里堆满了贵重物品，但没有一件被拿走。死者的文件没有被篡改。经过仔细检查，结果表明他是一位热衷于国际政治的学生、一位不知疲倦的八卦者、一位杰出的语言学家和一位不知疲倦的写信人。他与多个国家的主要政治家关系密切。但在他抽屉里堆满的文件中，并没有发现任何耸人听闻的东西。至于他与女性的关系，似乎是混杂但肤浅的。他们当中他熟人不少，但朋友却很少，也没有一个他所爱的人。他的习惯很规律，行为也没有冒犯性。他的死绝对是一个谜，而且很可能仍然如此。

至于逮捕男仆约翰·米顿，这是一次绝望的会议，而不是绝对不作为。但对他来说，没有任何案件能够成立。那天晚上他拜访了哈默史密斯的朋友。不在场证据已经齐全。确实，他在一个小时开始回家，这应该让他在犯罪发现之前到达威斯敏斯特，但考虑到夜色很好，他自己解释说他走了一部分路似乎很可能。他实际上是在十二点钟到达的，似乎被这突如其来的悲剧压垮了。他和他的主人一直关系很好。在男仆的箱子里发现了死者的几件物品，特别是一小箱剃须刀，但他解释说，这些物品是死者送给他的礼物，管家也证实了这一说法。米顿已经受雇于卢卡斯三年了。值得注意的是，卢卡斯并没有带着米顿一起前往欧洲大陆。有时他会连续三个月访问巴黎，但米顿则负责管理戈多芬街的房子。至于管家，案发当晚她什么也没听到。如果她的主人有访客，他会亲自接待他。
因此，就我在报纸上所能追踪到的情况而言，这个谜团持续了三个早晨。如果福尔摩斯知道更多的话，他保留了自己的建议，但是，当他告诉我莱斯特雷德督察已经将他视为案件的秘密时，我知道他密切关注着每一个进展。第四天，从巴黎发来的一封长电报似乎解决了整个问题。

title: The Return of Sherlock Holmes · 选段 3
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: “Well, I will tell you,” he said. “Why should I not? And yet I hate to think of this old scandal gaining a new lease of life. Did you ever hear of Dawson and Neligan?”
“You mean the West Country bankers,” said he. “They failed for a million, ruined half the county families of Cornwall, and Neligan disappeared.”

At last we were getting something positive, and yet it seemed a long gap between an absconding banker and Captain Peter Carey pinned against the wall with one of his own harpoons. We all listened intently to the young man’s words.

“It was my father who was really concerned. Dawson had retired. I was only ten years of age at the time, but I was old enough to feel the shame and horror of it all. It has always been said that my father stole all the securities and fled. It is not true. It was his belief that if he were given time in which to realize them, all would be well and every creditor paid in full. He started in his little yacht for Norway just before the warrant was issued for his arrest. I can remember that last night when he bade farewell to my mother. He left us a list of the securities he was taking, and he swore that he would come back with his honour cleared, and that none who had trusted him would suffer. Well, no word was ever heard from him again. Both the yacht and he vanished utterly. We believed, my mother and I, that he and it, with the securities that he had taken with him, were at the bottom of the sea. We had a faithful friend, however, who is a business man, and it was he who discovered some time ago that some of the securities which my father had with him had reappeared on the London market. You can imagine our amazement. I spent months in trying to trace them, and at last, after many doubtings and difficulties, I discovered that the original seller had been Captain Peter Carey, the owner of this hut.

“Naturally, I made some inquiries about the man. I found that he had been in command of a whaler which was due to return from the Arctic seas at the very time when my father was crossing to Norway. The autumn of that year was a stormy one, and there was a long succession of southerly gales. My father’s yacht may well have been blown to the north, and there met by Captain Peter Carey’s ship. If that were so, what had become of my father? In any case, if I could prove from Peter Carey’s evidence how these securities came on the market it would be a proof that my father had not sold them, and that he had no view to personal profit when he took them.

“I came down to Sussex with the intention of seeing the captain, but it was at this moment that his terrible death occurred. I read at the inquest a description of his cabin, in which it stated that the old logbooks of his vessel were preserved in it. It struck me that if I could see what occurred in the month of August, 1883, on board the Sea Unicorn, I might settle the mystery of my father’s fate. I tried last night to get at these logbooks, but was unable to open the door. To-night I tried again and succeeded, but I find that the pages which deal with that month have been torn from the book. It was at that moment I found myself a prisoner in your hands.”
“Then how do you account for that?” cried Hopkins, as he held up the damning notebook, with the initials of our prisoner on the first leaf and the blood-stain on the cover.

“That is enough,” said Hopkins, sternly. “Whatever else you have to say, you must say in court. You will walk down with me now to the police-station. Well, Mr. Holmes, I am very much obliged to you and to your friend for coming down to help me. As it turns out your presence was unnecessary, and I would have brought the case to this successful issue without you, but, none the less, I am grateful. Rooms have been reserved for you at the Brambletye Hotel, so we can all walk down to the village together.”

“Oh, yes, my dear Watson, I am perfectly satisfied. At the same time, Stanley Hopkins’s methods do not commend themselves to me. I am disappointed in Stanley Hopkins. I had hoped for better things from him. One should always look for a possible alternative, and provide against it. It is the first rule of criminal investigation.”
“The line of investigation which I have myself been pursuing. It may give us nothing. I cannot tell. But at least I shall follow it to the end.”
paragraphsZh: “好吧，我会告诉你，”他说。 “我为什么不应该呢？但我不愿意想到这个古老的丑闻会获得新的生命。你听说过道森和内利根吗？”
“你指的是西部地区的银行家，”他说。 “他们一百万都失败了，毁掉了康沃尔郡一半的家庭，内利根也消失了。”
最后我们得到了一些积极的结果，然而潜逃的银行家和用自己的鱼叉钉在墙上的彼得·凯里船长之间似乎存在着很长的差距。我们都聚精会神地听着年轻人的话。

“真正担心的是我父亲。道森已经退休了。当时我只有十岁，但我已经足够大了，能够感受到这一切的耻辱和恐怖。人们总是说我父亲偷了所有证券并逃跑了。这不是真的。他相信，如果给他时间来实现这些目标，一切都会好起来，每个债权人都会全额偿还。就在逮捕令发出之前，他开着他的小游艇前往挪威。我记得昨晚，他向我母亲告别时，发誓他会带着自己的名誉回来，再也不会听到他的消息了。我和母亲都相信，他和它以及他所带的证券都已经沉入海底了。正是他不久前发现我父亲随身携带的一些证券又出现在伦敦市场上，你可以想象我们的惊讶之情，我花了几个月的时间试图追踪它们，最后，在经过许多怀疑和困难后，我发现原来的卖家是这间小屋的主人彼得·凯里上尉。
“当然，我对这个人做了一些询问。我发现，当我父亲穿越挪威时，他正在指挥一艘即将从北冰洋返回的捕鲸船。那年秋天，风雨交加，南风连绵不绝。我父亲的游艇很可能被风吹向北方，在那里与彼得·凯里船长的船相遇。如果真是这样，我父亲又怎么样了？无论如何，如果我能从彼得·凯里的证据中证明这些证券是如何进入市场的，那就可以证明我父亲没有出售它们，而且他在购买这些证券时并没有考虑个人利益。
“我来到苏塞克斯本想见见船长，但就在此时，他可怕的死亡发生了。我在审讯中读到了他的船舱的描述，其中说里面保存着他船上的旧航海日志。我突然想到，如果我能看到 1883 年 8 月在“海洋独角兽”号上发生的事情，我可能会解开我父亲命运之谜。昨晚我试图了解这些今晚我再次尝试并成功了，但我发现有关那个月份的页面已从书中撕下，就在那一刻我发现自己成为了你手中的囚犯。
“那你怎么解释呢？”霍普金斯喊道，他举起那本该死的笔记本，第一页上写着我们囚犯名字的首字母，封面上有血迹。
“够了，”霍普金斯严厉地说。 “无论你还有什么话要说，你都必须在法庭上说。你现在要跟我一起去警察局。好吧，福尔摩斯先生，我非常感谢你和你的朋友下来帮助我。事实证明，你的存在是不必要的，如果没有你，我也会把案子带到这个成功的问题上，但是，尽管如此，我很感激。布兰布尔泰酒店已经为你预订了房间，所以我们可以一起步行到村子里。”
“哦，是的，我亲爱的华生，我非常满意。同时，斯坦利·霍普金斯的方法并不适合我。我对斯坦利·霍普金斯很失望。我本来希望他能得到更好的东西。人们应该总是寻找可能的替代方案，并反对它。这是刑事调查的第一规则。“
“我自己一直在追寻的调查路线。它可能不会给我们带来什么。我不能说。但至少我会追随到底。”

title: The Moonstone
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: Of all the deities worshipped in the temple, the moon-god alone escaped the rapacity of the conquering Mohammedans. Preserved by three Brahmins, the inviolate deity, bearing the Yellow Diamond in its forehead, was removed by night, and was transported to the second of the sacred cities of India—the city of Benares.

Here, in a new shrine—in a hall inlaid with precious stones, under a roof supported by pillars of gold—the moon-god was set up and worshipped. Here, on the night when the shrine was completed, Vishnu the Preserver appeared to the three Brahmins in a dream.

The deity breathed the breath of his divinity on the Diamond in the forehead of the god. And the Brahmins knelt and hid their faces in their robes. The deity commanded that the Moonstone should be watched, from that time forth, by three priests in turn, night and day, to the end of the generations of men. And the Brahmins heard, and bowed before his will. The deity predicted certain disaster to the presumptuous mortal who laid hands on the sacred gem, and to all of his house and name who received it after him. And the Brahmins caused the prophecy to be written over the gates of the shrine in letters of gold.

One age followed another—and still, generation after generation, the successors of the three Brahmins watched their priceless Moonstone, night and day. One age followed another until the first years of the eighteenth Christian century saw the reign of Aurungzebe, Emperor of the Moguls. At his command havoc and rapine were let loose once more among the temples of the worship of Brahmah. The shrine of the four-handed god was polluted by the slaughter of sacred animals; the images of the deities were broken in pieces; and the Moonstone was seized by an officer of rank in the army of Aurungzebe.

Powerless to recover their lost treasure by open force, the three guardian priests followed and watched it in disguise. The generations succeeded each other; the warrior who had committed the sacrilege perished miserably; the Moonstone passed (carrying its curse with it) from one lawless Mohammedan hand to another; and still, through all chances and changes, the successors of the three guardian priests kept their watch, waiting the day when the will of Vishnu the Preserver should restore to them their sacred gem. Time rolled on from the first to the last years of the eighteenth Christian century. The Diamond fell into the possession of Tippoo, Sultan of Seringapatam, who caused it to be placed as an ornament in the handle of a dagger, and who commanded it to be kept among the choicest treasures of his armoury. Even then—in the palace of the Sultan himself—the three guardian priests still kept their watch in secret. There were three officers of Tippoo’s household, strangers to the rest, who had won their master’s confidence by conforming, or appearing to conform, to the Mussulman faith; and to those three men report pointed as the three priests in disguise.

So, as told in our camp, ran the fanciful story of the Moonstone. It made no serious impression on any of us except my cousin—whose love of the marvellous induced him to believe it. On the night before the assault on Seringapatam, he was absurdly angry with me, and with others, for treating the whole thing as a fable. A foolish wrangle followed; and Herncastle’s unlucky temper got the better of him. He declared, in his boastful way, that we should see the Diamond on his finger, if the English army took Seringapatam. The sally was saluted by a roar of laughter, and there, as we all thought that night, the thing ended.

My cousin and I were separated at the outset. I never saw him when we forded the river; when we planted the English flag in the first breach; when we crossed the ditch beyond; and, fighting every inch of our way, entered the town. It was only at dusk, when the place was ours, and after General Baird himself had found the dead body of Tippoo under a heap of the slain, that Herncastle and I met.

We were each attached to a party sent out by the general’s orders to prevent the plunder and confusion which followed our conquest. The camp-followers committed deplorable excesses; and, worse still, the soldiers found their way, by an unguarded door, into the treasury of the Palace, and loaded themselves with gold and jewels. It was in the court outside the treasury that my cousin and I met, to enforce the laws of discipline on our own soldiers. Herncastle’s fiery temper had been, as I could plainly see, exasperated to a kind of frenzy by the terrible slaughter through which we had passed. He was very unfit, in my opinion, to perform the duty that had been entrusted to him.

There was riot and confusion enough in the treasury, but no violence that I saw. The men (if I may use such an expression) disgraced themselves good-humouredly. All sorts of rough jests and catchwords were bandied about among them; and the story of the Diamond turned up again unexpectedly, in the form of a mischievous joke. “Who’s got the Moonstone?” was the rallying cry which perpetually caused the plundering, as soon as it was stopped in one place, to break out in another. While I was still vainly trying to establish order, I heard a frightful yelling on the other side of the courtyard, and at once ran towards the cries, in dread of finding some new outbreak of the pillage in that direction.
paragraphsZh: 在寺庙里崇拜的所有神灵中，只有月​​神逃脱了征服者穆罕默德的贪婪。额头上镶有黄钻的神圣神祇由三位婆罗门保存着，在夜间被移走，并被运送到印度第二圣城——贝拿勒斯城。
在这里，在一座新的神殿里——在一个镶嵌着宝石的大厅里，在金柱支撑的屋顶下——月神被设立和崇拜。在这里，在神殿竣工的那天晚上，守护者毗湿奴在梦中出现在三个婆罗门面前。
神将他的神性气息吹在神额头上的钻石上。婆罗门们跪下，把脸藏在长袍里。神命令从那时起，必须由三位祭司日夜轮流看守月光石，直到人类世世代代的终结。婆罗门闻之，臣服于他的旨意。这位神祇预言，对于拿到这颗神圣宝石的自以为是的凡人，以及在他之后收到这颗宝石的他的整个家族和名字来说，将会遭遇灾难。婆罗门人用金字将预言写在神殿的大门上。
一个时代接着一个时代，但一代又一代，三个婆罗门的继承者日日夜夜地守护着他们无价的月光石。一个时代接着一个时代，直到公元十八世纪初期，莫卧儿皇帝奥龙则贝统治时期。在他的命令下，崇拜梵天的神庙再次遭到破坏和掠夺。四手神的神殿因屠宰神圣动物而受到污染；神像被打碎了；月光石被奥朗则贝军队中的一名高级军官夺取。

三位守护神官无法通过公开武力夺回丢失的宝藏，只好乔装尾随观看。世代相传；犯下亵渎罪的战士惨遭杀害。月光石（带着它的诅咒）从一位无法无天的穆斯林手中传到了另一位；尽管如此，尽管经历了种种机遇和变化，三位守护祭司的继任者仍然保持着警惕，等待着保护者毗湿奴的意志将他们的神圣宝石恢复给他们的那一天。时间从公元十八世纪的最初几年一直持续到最后几年。这颗钻石落入了塞林加帕坦苏丹蒂普 (Tippoo) 的手中，他将其作为装饰品放置在匕首柄上，并下令将其保留在他的军械库中最珍贵的宝藏中。即便如此，在苏丹本人的宫殿里，三位守护神父仍然秘密地守卫着。蒂普家里有三名军官，其他人对他们并不陌生，他们通过遵守或表面上遵守穆斯林信仰而赢得了主人的信任。报告指出那三人是三名乔装的牧师。

因此，正如我们营地中所讲述的那样，流传着月光石的奇特故事。除了我表弟之外，这件事没有给我们任何人留下深刻的印象——他对奇妙事物的热爱使他相信了这一点。在袭击 Seringapatam 的前一天晚上，他对我和其他人感到荒谬的愤怒，因为我把整件事当作寓言。接下来是一场愚蠢的争吵。赫恩卡斯尔的坏脾气控制住了他。他以自夸的方式宣称，如果英国军队占领了塞林加帕坦，我们就应该看到他手指上的钻石。这场突袭引起了一阵笑声，正如那天晚上我们都认为的那样，事情就结束了。
我和表弟一开始就分开了。当我们涉水时我从未见过他；当我们在第一个突破口插上英国国旗时；当我们跨过那条沟渠时；我们一路奋战，进入了城镇。直到黄昏时分，这个地方就属于我们了，贝尔德将军亲自在一堆死者下面发现了蒂波的尸体，赫恩卡斯尔和我才见面。
我们每个人都隶属于将军命令派出的队伍，以防止我们征服后发生的掠夺和混乱。追随营地的人犯下了令人遗憾的过分行为。更糟糕的是，士兵们通过一扇无人看守的门进入了宫殿的金库，并为自己装满了黄金和珠宝。我和表弟就是在金库外的法庭里见面的，目的是对我们自己的士兵执行纪律法规。正如我可以清楚地看到的那样，赫恩卡斯尔的脾气因我们所经历的可怕屠杀而变得疯狂。在我看来，他非常不适合履行赋予他的职责。

金库里有足够的骚乱和混乱，但我没有看到暴力。这些人（如果我可以用这样的表达方式的话）幽默地自取其辱。他们之间流传着各种粗俗的笑话和流行语。钻石的故事意外地再次出现，以恶作剧的形式出现。 “谁有月光石？”这是一种战斗口号，它永远导致掠夺一旦在一个地方停止，就会在另一个地方爆发。当我还在徒劳地试图建立秩序时，我听到院子的另一边传来可怕的叫喊声，我立即向叫喊声的方向跑去，生怕在那个方向发现新的掠夺事件。

title: The Moonstone · 选段 2
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: Finding myself, for the second time, in these romantic regions, I resolved not to leave Kattiawar, without looking once more on the magnificent desolation of Somnauth. At the place where I planned to do this, I was (as nearly as I could calculate it) some three days distant, journeying on foot, from the sacred city.
I had not been long on the road, before I noticed that other people—by twos and threes—appeared to be travelling in the same direction as myself.

To such of these as spoke to me, I gave myself out as a Hindoo-Boodhist, from a distant province, bound on a pilgrimage. It is needless to say that my dress was of the sort to carry out this description. Add, that I know the language as well as I know my own, and that I am lean enough and brown enough to make it no easy matter to detect my European origin—and you will understand that I passed muster with the people readily: not as one of themselves, but as a stranger from a distant part of their own country.

On the second day, the number of Hindoos travelling in my direction had increased to fifties and hundreds. On the third day, the throng had swollen to thousands; all slowly converging to one point—the city of Somnauth.

A trifling service which I was able to render to one of my fellow-pilgrims, during the third day’s journey, proved the means of introducing me to certain Hindoos of the higher caste. From these men I learnt that the multitude was on its way to a great religious ceremony, which was to take place on a hill at a little distance from Somnauth. The ceremony was in honour of the god of the Moon; and it was to be held at night.

The crowd detained us as we drew near to the place of celebration. By the time we reached the hill the moon was high in the heaven. My Hindoo friends possessed some special privileges which enabled them to gain access to the shrine. They kindly allowed me to accompany them. When we arrived at the place, we found the shrine hidden from our view by a curtain hung between two magnificent trees. Beneath the trees a flat projection of rock jutted out, and formed a species of natural platform. Below this, I stood, in company with my Hindoo friends.

Looking back down the hill, the view presented the grandest spectacle of Nature and Man, in combination, that I have ever seen. The lower slopes of the eminence melted imperceptibly into a grassy plain, the place of the meeting of three rivers. On one side, the graceful winding of the waters stretched away, now visible, now hidden by trees, as far as the eye could see. On the other, the waveless ocean slept in the calm of the night. People this lovely scene with tens of thousands of human creatures, all dressed in white, stretching down the sides of the hill, overflowing into the plain, and fringing the nearer banks of the winding rivers. Light this halt of the pilgrims by the wild red flames of cressets and torches, streaming up at intervals from every part of the innumerable throng. Imagine the moonlight of the East, pouring in unclouded glory over all—and you will form some idea of the view that met me when I looked forth from the summit of the hill.
A strain of plaintive music, played on stringed instruments and flutes, recalled my attention to the hidden shrine.

I turned, and saw on the rocky platform the figures of three men. In the central figure of the three I recognised the man to whom I had spoken in England, when the Indians appeared on the terrace at Lady Verinder’s house. The other two who had been his companions on that occasion were no doubt his companions also on this.
One of the spectators, near whom I was standing, saw me start. In a whisper, he explained to me the apparition of the three figures on the platform of rock.
paragraphsZh: 在这些浪漫的地区第二次发现自己，我决定在没有再次看到索姆诺斯壮丽的荒凉之前就不会离开卡蒂亚瓦。在我计划这样做的地方，我距离圣城大约三天路程（据我计算）。
我在路上没走多久，就注意到其他三三两两的人似乎和我朝同一个方向行驶。
对于这些与我交谈的人，我表明自己是一名来自遥远省份、即将踏上朝圣之旅的印度菩萨。不用说，我的衣服正是符合这种描述的。另外，我对当地语言的了解和我对自己语言的了解一样，而且我很瘦，肤色也足够深，因此很难查出我的欧洲血统——你会明白，我很容易就通过了人民的考验：不是作为他们自己的一员，而是作为来自他们国家遥远地区的陌生人。
第二天，朝我方向行驶的印度人数量增加到五十和数百人。第三天，人群已增至数千人。所有的一切都慢慢地汇聚到一个点——索姆诺斯市。
在第三天的旅程中，我为一位朝圣同伴提供了一项微不足道的服务，这证明了将我介绍给某些较高种姓的印度人的方法。从这些人那里我得知，群众正在前往一场盛大的宗教仪式，仪式将在距离索姆诺斯不远的一座小山上举行。这个仪式是为了纪念月神。会议定于晚上举行。
当我们接近庆祝地点时，人群拦住了我们。当我们到达山上时，月亮已经高高挂在天上了。我的印度朋友拥有一些特殊的特权，使他们能够进入神社。他们好心地允许我陪伴他们。当我们到达这个地方时，我们发现神社被两棵参天大树之间挂着的窗帘遮住了。树下有一块平坦的岩石突出，形成了一个天然平台。下面，我和我的印度朋友一起站着。

回望山下，景色呈现出我所见过的最宏伟的自然与人类结合的奇观。高地的较低斜坡不知不觉地融化成一片草地，是三条河流的交汇处。一侧，优美蜿蜒的河水一直延伸到远处，时而可见，时而被树木遮掩，一望无际。另一方面，无波无澜的大海在平静的夜晚沉睡着。数以万计的人类生物，全都身着白衣，沿着山坡延伸至平原，环绕着蜿蜒河流的近岸，构成了这一可爱的场景。灯盏和火把的狂野红色火焰照亮了朝圣者的这个停留点，这些火焰从无数人群的各个部分不时地涌出。想象一下东方的月光，在万里无云的光辉中倾泻而下——你就会对我从山顶向外眺望时所看到的景色产生一些想法。
弦乐器和长笛演奏的一段悲伤的音乐唤起了我对隐藏神殿的注意。
我转身，看到岩石平台上有三个男人的身影。在这三个人的中心人物中，我认出了我在英国与之交谈过的那个人，当时印第安人出现在维林德夫人家的露台上。另外两个当时是他同伴的人无疑也是他这次的同伴。
我站在旁边的一位观众看到我开始了。他低声向我解释了岩石平台上三个人影的出现。

title: The Moonstone · 选段 3
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: With those words he hurried out. In equal haste on my side, I ran upstairs to compose myself in my own room before meeting Aunt Ablewhite and Rachel at the luncheon-table.

I am well aware—to dwell for a moment yet on the subject of Mr. Godfrey—that the all-profaning opinion of the world has charged him with having his own private reasons for releasing Rachel from her engagement, at the first opportunity she gave him. It has also reached my ears, that his anxiety to recover his place in my estimation has been attributed in certain quarters, to a mercenary eagerness to make his peace (through me) with a venerable committee-woman at the Mothers’ Small-Clothes, abundantly blessed with the goods of this world, and a beloved and intimate friend of my own. I only notice these odious slanders for the sake of declaring that they never had a moment’s influence on my mind. In obedience to my instructions, I have exhibited the fluctuations in my opinion of our Christian Hero, exactly as I find them recorded in my diary. In justice to myself, let me here add that, once reinstated in his place in my estimation, my gifted friend never lost that place again. I write with the tears in my eyes, burning to say more. But no—I am cruelly limited to my actual experience of persons and things. In less than a month from the time of which I am now writing, events in the money-market (which diminished even my miserable little income) forced me into foreign exile, and left me with nothing but a loving remembrance of Mr. Godfrey which the slander of the world has assailed, and assailed in vain.
I went downstairs to luncheon, naturally anxious to see how Rachel was affected by her release from her marriage engagement.

It appeared to me—but I own I am a poor authority in such matters—that the recovery of her freedom had set her thinking again of that other man whom she loved, and that she was furious with herself for not being able to control a revulsion of feeling of which she was secretly ashamed. Who was the man? I had my suspicions—but it was needless to waste time in idle speculation. When I had converted her, she would, as a matter of course, have no concealments from Me. I should hear all about the man; I should hear all about the Moonstone. If I had had no higher object in stirring her up to a sense of spiritual things, the motive of relieving her mind of its guilty secrets would have been enough of itself to encourage me to go on.

Aunt Ablewhite took her exercise in the afternoon in an invalid chair. Rachel accompanied her. “I wish I could drag the chair,” she broke out, recklessly. “I wish I could fatigue myself till I was ready to drop.”

She was in the same humour in the evening. I discovered in one of my friend’s precious publications—the Life, Letters, and Labours of Miss Jane Ann Stamper, forty-fourth edition—passages which bore with a marvellous appropriateness on Rachel’s present position. Upon my proposing to read them, she went to the piano. Conceive how little she must have known of serious people, if she supposed that my patience was to be exhausted in that way! I kept Miss Jane Ann Stamper by me, and waited for events with the most unfaltering trust in the future.

Old Mr. Ablewhite never made his appearance that night. But I knew the importance which his worldly greed attached to his son’s marriage with Miss Verinder—and I felt a positive conviction (do what Mr. Godfrey might to prevent it) that we should see him the next day. With his interference in the matter, the storm on which I had counted would certainly come, and the salutary exhaustion of Rachel’s resisting powers would as certainly follow. I am not ignorant that old Mr. Ablewhite has the reputation generally (especially among his inferiors) of being a remarkably good-natured man. According to my observation of him, he deserves his reputation as long as he has his own way, and not a moment longer.

The next day, exactly as I had foreseen, Aunt Ablewhite was as near to being astonished as her nature would permit, by the sudden appearance of her husband. He had barely been a minute in the house, before he was followed, to my astonishment this time, by an unexpected complication in the shape of Mr. Bruff.

I never remember feeling the presence of the lawyer to be more unwelcome than I felt it at that moment. He looked ready for anything in the way of an obstructive proceeding—capable even of keeping the peace with Rachel for one of the combatants!
paragraphsZh: 说完他就急忙出去了。我这边也同样匆忙，跑上楼，在自己的房间里让自己平静下来，然后在午餐桌上见到艾伯怀特姨妈和雷切尔。
