That is the conclusion, I said; and, if a true conclusion, then the souls must always be the same, for if none be destroyed they will not diminish in number. Neither will they increase, for the increase of the immortal natures must come from something mortal, and all things would thus end in immortality.
But this we cannot believe—reason will not allow us—any more than we can believe the soul, in her truest nature, to be full of variety and difference and dissimilarity.
The soul, I said, being, as is now proven, immortal, must be the fairest of compositions and cannot be compounded of many elements?

Her immortality is demonstrated by the previous argument, and there are many other proofs; but to see her as she really is, not as we now behold her, marred by communion with the body and other miseries, you must contemplate her with the eye of reason, in her original purity; and then her beauty will be revealed, and justice and injustice and all the things which we have described will be manifested more clearly. Thus far, we have spoken the truth concerning her as she appears at present, but we must remember also that we have seen her only in a condition which may be compared to that of the sea-god Glaucus, whose original image can hardly be discerned because his natural members are broken off and crushed and damaged by the waves in all sorts of ways, and incrustations have grown over them of seaweed and shells and stones, so that he is more like some monster than he is to his own natural form. And the soul which we behold is in a similar condition, disfigured by ten thousand ills. But not there, Glaucon, not there must we look.

At her love of wisdom. Let us see whom she affects, and what society and converse she seeks in virtue of her near kindred with the immortal and eternal and divine; also how different she would become if wholly following this superior principle, and borne by a divine impulse out of the ocean in which she now is, and disengaged from the stones and shells and things of earth and rock which in wild variety spring up around her because she feeds upon earth, and is overgrown by the good things of this life as they are termed: then you would see her as she is, and know whether she have one shape only or many, or what her nature is. Of her affections and of the forms which she takes in this present life I think that we have now said enough.

And thus, I said, we have fulfilled the conditions of the argument; we have not introduced the rewards and glories of justice, which, as you were saying, are to be found in Homer and Hesiod; but justice in her own nature has been shown to be best for the soul in her own nature. Let a man do what is just, whether he have the ring of Gyges or not, and even if in addition to the ring of Gyges he put on the helmet of Hades.

And now, Glaucon, there will be no harm in further enumerating how many and how great are the rewards which justice and the other virtues procure to the soul from gods and men, both in life and after death.

The assumption that the just man should appear unjust and the unjust just: for you were of opinion that even if the true state of the case could not possibly escape the eyes of gods and men, still this admission ought to be made for the sake of the argument, in order that pure justice might be weighed against pure injustice. Do you remember?

Then, as the cause is decided, I demand on behalf of justice that the estimation in which she is held by gods and men and which we acknowledge to be her due should now be restored to her by us; since she has been shown to confer reality, and not to deceive those who truly possess her, let what has been taken from her be given back, that so she may win that palm of appearance which is hers also, and which she gives to her own.
paragraphsZh: 但是，不能被邪恶所摧毁的灵魂，无论是内在的还是外在的，都必须永远存在，如果永远存在，就一定是不朽的？
这就是结论，我说；而且，如果结论正确，那么灵魂必定永远是一样的，因为即使没有一个被毁灭，它们的数量也不会减少。它们也不会增加，因为不朽本质的增加必须来自于必死的事物，因此所有事物都会以不朽而告终。
但我们不能相信这一点——理性不允许我们——就像我们不能相信灵魂在其最真实的本性中充满多样性、差异性和相异性一样。
我说，灵魂，正如现在所证明的那样，是不朽的，一定是最美丽的组合物，并且不能由许多元素混合而成？

她的不朽是由前面的论证证明的，还有很多其他的证明；但要看到她真实的样子，而不是像我们现在看到的那样，因与身体的交流和其他痛苦而受到损害，你必须用理性的眼睛来观察她最初的纯洁；然后她的美丽就会显露出来，正义与非正义以及我们所描述的一切都会更加清晰地显现出来。到目前为止，我们已经说出了她目前的真相，但我们也必须记住，我们所看到的她只能与海神格劳克斯相媲美，格劳克斯的原始形象几乎无法辨认，因为他的自然成员被海浪以各种方式折断、压碎和损坏，并且在他们上面长出了海藻、贝壳和石头的硬壳，因此他比他自己的自然形态更像一个怪物。我们所看到的灵魂也处于类似的状况，被万种疾病所毁容。但格劳孔，我们必须看的不是那里。

她对智慧的热爱。让我们看看她影响了谁，以及她凭借与不朽、永恒和神圣的近亲而寻求什么样的社交和交谈；而且，如果她完全遵循这一至高无上的原则，并被一种神圣的冲动带离她现在所在的海洋，脱离石头、贝壳以及泥土和岩石的东西，这些东西在她周围涌现，因为她以泥土为食，并且被今生的美好事物所覆盖，正如它们所称的那样，那么她将会变得多么不同：然后你就会看到她的本来面目，知道她是只有一种形状还是多种形状，或者她的本性是什么。关于她的感情和她今生所采取的形式，我想我们现在已经说得够多了。
因此，我说，我们已经满足了论证的条件；我们还没有介绍正义的奖赏和荣耀，正如您所说，这些可以在荷马和赫西奥德那里找到；但她本性中的正义已被证明对她本性中的灵魂来说是最好的。让一个人做正义的事，无论他是否有盖吉斯戒指，即使除了盖吉斯戒指之外还戴上了哈迪斯的头盔。
现在，格劳孔，进一步列举正义和其他美德在生前和死后从诸神和人类那里为灵魂带来多少和多大的回报是没有坏处的。
正义的人应该显得不正义，不正义的人应该正义：因为你认为，即使案件的真实情况不可能逃过神和人的眼睛，为了论证的目的，仍然应该承认这一点，以便可以权衡纯粹的正义与纯粹的不正义。你是否记得？
然后，当案情已经确定时，我代表正义要求我们现在应该恢复她对众神和人类的评价，以及我们承认她应有的评价；既然她已被证明能够赋予现实，而不是欺骗那些真正拥有她的人，那么就让从她身上夺走的东西归还吧，这样她就可以赢得那只属于她的外表的手掌，并且她把它送给了自己。

title: The Wind in the Willows
author: Kenneth Grahame
paragraphs: The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First with brooms, then with dusters; then on ladders and steps and chairs, with a brush and a pail of whitewash; till he had dust in his throat and eyes, and splashes of whitewash all over his black fur, and an aching back and weary arms. Spring was moving in the air above and in the earth below and around him, penetrating even his dark and lowly little house with its spirit of divine discontent and longing. It was small wonder, then, that he suddenly flung down his brush on the floor, said “Bother!” and “O blow!” and also “Hang spring-cleaning!” and bolted out of the house without even waiting to put on his coat. Something up above was calling him imperiously, and he made for the steep little tunnel which answered in his case to the gravelled carriage-drive owned by animals whose residences are nearer to the sun and air. So he scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged and then he scrooged again and scrabbled and scratched and scraped, working busily with his little paws and muttering to himself, “Up we go! Up we go!” till at last, pop! his snout came out into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.

“This is fine!” he said to himself. “This is better than whitewashing!” The sunshine struck hot on his fur, soft breezes caressed his heated brow, and after the seclusion of the cellarage he had lived in so long the carol of happy birds fell on his dulled hearing almost like a shout. Jumping off all his four legs at once, in the joy of living and the delight of spring without its cleaning, he pursued his way across the meadow till he reached the hedge on the further side.

“Hold up!” said an elderly rabbit at the gap. “Sixpence for the privilege of passing by the private road!” He was bowled over in an instant by the impatient and contemptuous Mole, who trotted along the side of the hedge chaffing the other rabbits as they peeped hurriedly from their holes to see what the row was about. “Onion-sauce! Onion-sauce!” he remarked jeeringly, and was gone before they could think of a thoroughly satisfactory reply. Then they all started grumbling at each other. “How stupid you are! Why didn’t you tell him——” “Well, why didn’t you say——” “You might have reminded him——” and so on, in the usual way; but, of course, it was then much too late, as is always the case.

It all seemed too good to be true. Hither and thither through the meadows he rambled busily, along the hedgerows, across the copses, finding everywhere birds building, flowers budding, leaves thrusting—everything happy, and progressive, and occupied. And instead of having an uneasy conscience pricking him and whispering “whitewash!” he somehow could only feel how jolly it was to be the only idle dog among all these busy citizens. After all, the best part of a holiday is perhaps not so much to be resting yourself, as to see all the other fellows busy working.

He thought his happiness was complete when, as he meandered aimlessly along, suddenly he stood by the edge of a full-fed river. Never in his life had he seen a river before—this sleek, sinuous, full-bodied animal, chasing and chuckling, gripping things with a gurgle and leaving them with a laugh, to fling itself on fresh playmates that shook themselves free, and were caught and held again. All was a-shake and a-shiver—glints and gleams and sparkles, rustle and swirl, chatter and bubble. The Mole was bewitched, entranced, fascinated. By the side of the river he trotted as one trots, when very small, by the side of a man who holds one spell-bound by exciting stories; and when tired at last, he sat on the bank, while the river still chattered on to him, a babbling procession of the best stories in the world, sent from the heart of the earth to be told at last to the insatiable sea.

As he sat on the grass and looked across the river, a dark hole in the bank opposite, just above the water’s edge, caught his eye, and dreamily he fell to considering what a nice snug dwelling-place it would make for an animal with few wants and fond of a bijou riverside residence, above flood level and remote from noise and dust. As he gazed, something bright and small seemed to twinkle down in the heart of it, vanished, then twinkled once more like a tiny star. But it could hardly be a star in such an unlikely situation; and it was too glittering and small for a glow-worm. Then, as he looked, it winked at him, and so declared itself to be an eye; and a small face began gradually to grow up round it, like a frame round a picture.
“Oh, its all very well to talk,” said the Mole, rather pettishly, he being new to a river and riverside life and its ways.

The Rat said nothing, but stooped and unfastened a rope and hauled on it; then lightly stepped into a little boat which the Mole had not observed. It was painted blue outside and white within, and was just the size for two animals; and the Mole’s whole heart went out to it at once, even though he did not yet fully understand its uses.

The Rat sculled smartly across and made fast. Then he held up his forepaw as the Mole stepped gingerly down. “Lean on that!” he said. “Now then, step lively!” and the Mole to his surprise and rapture found himself actually seated in the stern of a real boat.
paragraphsZh: 鼹鼠整个早上都在非常努力地工作，对他的小家进行春季大扫除。先用扫帚，然后用掸子；然后用刷子和一桶粉刷在梯子、台阶和椅子上；直到他的喉咙和眼睛里充满了灰尘，黑色的皮毛上溅满了白色的油漆，背部疼痛，手臂疲惫不堪。春天在他的上方、下方和周围的空气中流动，带着神圣的不满和渴望的精神甚至渗透到他黑暗而卑微的小房子里。难怪他突然把画笔扔在地板上，说：“打扰了！”和“哦打击！”还有“进行春季大扫除！”甚至还没等穿上外套就冲出了家门。上面有什么东西在专横地呼唤他，他朝陡峭的小隧道走去，这条隧道对他来说是一条碎石马车车道，动物们的住所离阳光和空气更近。于是他又刮又刮，又刮又刮，然后又又刮又刮，用小爪子忙着干活，一边自言自语道：“我们上去！我们上去！”直到最后，流行！他的鼻子暴露在阳光下，他发现自己在一片大草地温暖的草地上打滚。
“这很好！”他对自己说。 “这比洗白好！”阳光灼热地照在他的皮毛上，微风轻抚着他发热的额头，在他生活了这么久的地窖与世隔绝之后，快乐的鸟儿的歌声几乎像一声喊叫一样落在他迟钝的耳朵里。他立刻从四条腿上跳下来，带着生活的快乐和春天没有被清理的喜悦，他沿着草地追去，直到到达另一边的树篱。

“坚持住！”缺口处一只老兔子说道。 “六便士就可以通过私人道路！”鼹鼠立刻就被不耐烦又轻蔑的鼹鼠撞倒了，鼹鼠沿着树篱边小跑，逗弄其他兔子，而其他兔子则急忙从洞里偷看，想看看到底发生了什么。 “洋葱酱！洋葱酱！”他嘲讽地说，还没等他们想出一个完全令人满意的答复，他就走了。然后他们都开始互相抱怨。 “你真傻！你为什么不告诉他——”“好吧，你为什么不说——”“你可能已经提醒他了——”等等，一如往常；但是，当然，那时已经太晚了，情况总是如此。
这一切似乎美好得令人难以置信。他忙碌地在草地上到处走动，沿着树篱，穿过灌木丛，发现到处都有鸟儿在筑巢，花儿在含苞待放，树叶在抽动——一切都是快乐的、进步的、忙碌的。而不是良心不安地刺痛他并低声说“粉饰！”不知怎的，他只能感觉到，在这些忙碌的市民中，成为唯一一只无所事事的狗是多么快乐。毕竟，假期最好的部分也许不是让自己休息，而是看到其他人忙着工作。

当他漫无目的地蜿蜒前行时，他以为自己的幸福已经圆满，突然，他站在一条水满了的河边。他一生中从未见过河——这种光滑、蜿蜒、体态丰满的动物，一边追逐一边咯咯地笑着，咯咯地抓住东西，然后笑着离开，然后扑向新的玩伴，这些玩伴挣脱了束缚，然后又被抓住并抓住。一切都在摇晃和颤抖——闪烁、闪烁、闪闪发光、沙沙作响、旋转、颤抖和泡沫。鼹鼠被迷住了，着迷了，着迷了。当他还很小的时候，他就在河边像小跑一样小跑，旁边的一个男人抱着他，手里拿着一个被激动人心的故事迷住了的人；当他终于累了的时候，他坐在岸边，河水仍在对他喋喋不休，就像一队喋喋不休的队列，讲述着世界上最好的故事，从地心发出，最终被讲述到永不满足的大海。

当他坐在草地上眺望河对岸时，对面河岸上一个黑洞洞的地方就在水边之上，引起了他的注意，他恍惚地开始思考，对于一只没有什么欲望、喜欢在洪水位以上、远离噪音和灰尘的河边住所的动物来说，这将是一个多么舒适的住所。当他凝视时，有什么明亮而微小的东西似乎在它的中心闪烁，消失了，然后又像一颗小星星一样闪烁。但在这种不太可能的情况下，它很难成为明星。对于萤火虫来说，它太闪闪发光了，也太小了。然后，当他看的时候，它对他眨了眨眼，表明自己是一只眼睛。一张小脸开始在它周围逐渐长大，就像画框周围一样。
“哦，聊得很好，”鼹鼠相当生气地说，他对河流和河边的生活及其方式还很陌生。
老鼠什么也没说，只是弯下腰，解开一根绳子，用力拉着。然后轻轻地踏上了一条鼹鼠没有注意到的小船。它外面漆成蓝色，里面漆成白色，大小正好适合两只动物。鼹鼠立刻全心全意地投入其中，尽管他还没有完全理解它的用途。
老鼠巧妙地划过河，速度很快。然后，当鼹鼠小心翼翼地走下来时，他举起了前爪。 “靠那个！”他说。 「那么，现在就行动起来吧！」令鼹鼠惊讶又狂喜的是，他发现自己竟然坐在一艘真正的船的船尾。

title: The Wind in the Willows · 选段 2
author: Kenneth Grahame
paragraphs: The Toad—came—home! There was panic in the parlours and howling in the halls, There was crying in the cow-sheds and shrieking in the stalls, When the Toad—came—home!
When the Toad—came—home! There was smashing in of window and crashing in of door, There was chivvying of weasels that fainted on the floor, When the Toad—came—home!
Bang! go the drums! The trumpeters are tooting and the soldiers are saluting, And the cannon they are shooting and the motor-cars are hooting, As the—Hero—comes!
Shout—Hoo-ray! And let each one of the crowd try and shout it very loud, In honour of an animal of whom you’re justly proud, For it’s Toad’s—great—day!
He sang this very loud, with great unction and expression; and when he had done, he sang it all over again.

Then he dipped his hairbrush in the water-jug, parted his hair in the middle, and plastered it down very straight and sleek on each side of his face; and, unlocking the door, went quietly down the stairs to greet his guests, who he knew must be assembling in the drawing-room.

All the animals cheered when he entered, and crowded round to congratulate him and say nice things about his courage, and his cleverness, and his fighting qualities; but Toad only smiled faintly, and murmured, “Not at all!” Or, sometimes, for a change, “On the contrary!” Otter, who was standing on the hearthrug, describing to an admiring circle of friends exactly how he would have managed things had he been there, came forward with a shout, threw his arm round Toad’s neck, and tried to take him round the room in triumphal progress; but Toad, in a mild way, was rather snubby to him, remarking gently, as he disengaged himself, “Badger’s was the mastermind; the Mole and the Water Rat bore the brunt of the fighting; I merely served in the ranks and did little or nothing.” The animals were evidently puzzled and taken aback by this unexpected attitude of his; and Toad felt, as he moved from one guest to the other, making his modest responses, that he was an object of absorbing interest to every one.

The Badger had ordered everything of the best, and the banquet was a great success. There was much talking and laughter and chaff among the animals, but through it all Toad, who of course was in the chair, looked down his nose and murmured pleasant nothings to the animals on either side of him. At intervals he stole a glance at the Badger and the Rat, and always when he looked they were staring at each other with their mouths open; and this gave him the greatest satisfaction. Some of the younger and livelier animals, as the evening wore on, got whispering to each other that things were not so amusing as they used to be in the good old days; and there were some knockings on the table and cries of “Toad! Speech! Speech from Toad! Song! Mr. Toad’s song!” But Toad only shook his head gently, raised one paw in mild protest, and, by pressing delicacies on his guests, by topical small-talk, and by earnest inquiries after members of their families not yet old enough to appear at social functions, managed to convey to them that this dinner was being run on strictly conventional lines.

After this climax, the four animals continued to lead their lives, so rudely broken in upon by civil war, in great joy and contentment, undisturbed by further risings or invasions. Toad, after due consultation with his friends, selected a handsome gold chain and locket set with pearls, which he dispatched to the gaoler’s daughter with a letter that even the Badger admitted to be modest, grateful, and appreciative; and the engine-driver, in his turn, was properly thanked and compensated for all his pains and trouble. Under severe compulsion from the Badger, even the barge-woman was, with some trouble, sought out and the value of her horse discreetly made good to her; though Toad kicked terribly at this, holding himself to be an instrument of Fate, sent to punish fat women with mottled arms who couldn’t tell a real gentleman when they saw one. The amount involved, it was true, was not very burdensome, the gipsy’s valuation being admitted by local assessors to be approximately correct.

Sometimes, in the course of long summer evenings, the friends would take a stroll together in the Wild Wood, now successfully tamed so far as they were concerned; and it was pleasing to see how respectfully they were greeted by the inhabitants, and how the mother-weasels would bring their young ones to the mouths of their holes, and say, pointing, “Look, baby! There goes the great Mr. Toad! And that’s the gallant Water Rat, a terrible fighter, walking along o’ him! And yonder comes the famous Mr. Mole, of whom you so often have heard your father tell!” But when their infants were fractious and quite beyond control, they would quiet them by telling how, if they didn’t hush them and not fret them, the terrible grey Badger would up and get them. This was a base libel on Badger, who, though he cared little about Society, was rather fond of children; but it never failed to have its full effect.
paragraphsZh: 蟾蜍——回家了！客厅里一片恐慌，大厅里一片嚎叫，牛棚里一片哭声，马厩里一片尖叫，当蟾蜍——回来——回家时！
当蟾蜍——回家——回家时！窗子被砸碎，门被撞进，黄鼠狼在地板上叽叽喳喳，昏倒在地，当蟾蜍——回来——回家时！
砰！鼓起来吧！号手吹响，士兵敬礼，大炮鸣响，汽车鸣响，英雄来了！
呼喊——万岁！让人群中的每一个人都尝试大声喊叫，以纪念一种让你感到自豪的动物，因为这是蟾蜍的——伟大的——一天！
他唱得很大声，充满了涂油和表情；当他唱完后，他又唱了一遍。
然后，他把发刷浸入水壶中，将头发从中间分开，然后将其笔直、光滑地贴在脸的两侧；然后，打开门，悄悄地下楼去迎接他的客人，他知道他们一定正在客厅里聚集。

当他进来时，所有的动物都欢呼起来，围拢过来祝贺他，称赞他的勇气、他的聪明、他的战斗能力；蟾蜍却只是淡淡一笑，低声说道：“才不是呢！”或者，有时，为了改变一下，“恰恰相反！”奥特站在壁炉边的地毯上，向一圈钦佩的朋友描述如果他在场的话，他会如何处理事情，他大喊一声走上前来，用手臂搂住蟾蜍的脖子，试图带着他胜利地绕着房间转一圈。但蟾蜍却对他表现得相当冷淡，待他摆脱束缚后，温和地说道：“獾是幕后黑手；鼹鼠和水鼠在战斗中首当其冲；我只是在队伍中服役，几乎什么也没做。”动物们显然对他这种意想不到的态度感到困惑和惊讶。蟾蜍觉得，当他从一位客人转向另一位客人并做出谦虚的回应时，他感到自己是每个人都感兴趣的对象。

獾点了最好的一切，宴会非常成功。动物们之间有很多谈话、笑声和闲聊，但在整个过程中，坐在椅子上的蟾蜍一直低着鼻子，对他两侧的动物低声说着愉快的话。他时不时地偷偷瞄一眼獾和老鼠，当他看的时候，它们总是张着嘴互相凝视。这给了他最大的满足。随着夜幕的降临，一些更年轻、更活泼的动物开始互相窃窃私语，说事情不再像过去的美好时光那么有趣；它们变得更加有趣。桌子上传来敲击声和“蟾蜍！演讲！蟾蜍演讲！歌曲！蟾蜍先生的歌曲！”的叫喊声。但蟾蜍只是轻轻摇了摇头，举起一只爪子表示温和的抗议，并通过向客人们强行提供美味佳肴，通过话题性的闲聊，以及对还没有到参加社交活动的年龄的家庭成员的认真询问，成功地向他们传达了这次晚宴是按照严格的传统方式进行的。

在这个高潮之后，四只动物继续过着被内战粗暴地打断的生活，充满喜悦和满足，没有受到进一步的起义或入侵的干扰。蟾蜍在与朋友们充分协商后，选择了一条漂亮的金链子和镶嵌珍珠的挂坠盒，并把它寄给了狱卒的女儿，并附上了一封信，连獾也承认这封信是谦虚的、感激的和欣赏的。轮到火车司机，他的所有痛苦和麻烦也得到了适当的感谢和补偿。在獾的严厉强迫下，甚至费了一番周折才找到了驳船女，并谨慎地以她的马的价值卖给了她。尽管蟾蜍对此非常不以为然，他认为自己是命运的工具，被派来惩罚那些手臂有斑驳的胖女人，她们在看到一个真正的绅士时无法辨别出真正的绅士。诚然，所涉及的金额并不是很大，当地评估人员承认吉普赛人的估价大致正确。

有时，在漫长的夏日夜晚，朋友们会一起在野林中漫步，对他们来说，现在已经成功驯服了；令人高兴的是，他们受到居民们的恭敬欢迎，黄鼠狼妈妈如何将幼崽带到洞口，并指着说：“看，宝贝！伟大的蟾蜍先生来了！那是勇敢的水鼠，一个可怕的战士，沿着他走！那边还有著名的鼹鼠先生，你经常听你的父亲讲起他！”但当他们的婴儿变得暴躁、完全无法控制时，他们会告诉他们，如果他们不让他们安静，不让他们烦恼，可怕的灰獾会如何站起来抓住他们，从而让他们安静下来。这是对巴杰的卑鄙诽谤，他虽然不关心社会，但却很喜欢孩子。但它从未未能充分发挥其作用。

title: Heidi
author: Johanna Spyri
paragraphs: "Up above, right up above. We have a long way to go yet, so come along! And on the topmost peak of all the old bird of prey sits and croaks."
That did it. Heidi immediately sprang to her feet and ran up to Peter with her apron full of flowers.

"You have got enough now," said the boy as they began climbing up again together. "You will stay here forever if you go on picking, and if you gather all the flowers now there will be none for to-morrow."

This last argument seemed a convincing one to Heidi, and moreover her apron was already so full that there was hardly room for another flower, and it would never do to leave nothing to pick for another day. So she now kept with Peter, and the goats also became more orderly in their behavior, for they were beginning to smell the plants they loved that grew on the higher slopes and clambered up now without pause in their anxiety to reach them. The spot where Peter generally halted for his goats to pasture and where he took up his quarters for the day lay at the foot of the high rocks, which were covered for some distance up by bushes and fir trees, beyond which rose their bare and rugged summits. On one side of the mountain the rock was split into deep clefts, and the grandfather had reason to warn Peter of danger. Having climbed as far as the halting-place, Peter unslung his wallet and put it carefully in a little hollow of the ground, for he knew what the wind was like up there and did not want to see his precious belongings sent rolling down the mountain by a sudden gust. Then be threw himself at full length on the warm ground, for he was tired after all his exertions.

Heidi meanwhile had unfastened her apron and rolling it carefully round the flowers laid it beside Peter's wallet inside the hollow; she then sat down beside his outstretched figure and looked about her. The valley lay far below bathed in the morning sun. In front of her rose a broad snow-field, high against the dark-blue sky, while to the left was a huge pile of rocks on either side of which a bare lofty peak, that seemed to pierce the blue, looked frowningly down upon, her. The child sat without moving, her eyes taking in the whole scene, and all around was a great stillness, only broken by soft, light puffs of wind that swayed the light bells of the blue flowers, and the shining gold heads of the cistus, and set them nodding merrily on their slender stems. Peter had fallen asleep after his fatigue and the goats were climbing about among the bushes overhead. Heidi had never felt so happy in her life before. She drank in the golden sunlight, the fresh air, the sweet smell of the flowers, and wished for nothing better than to remain there forever. So the time went on, while to Heidi, who had so often looked up from the valley at the mountains above, these seemed now to have faces, and to be looking down at her like old friends. Suddenly she heard a loud harsh cry overhead and lifting her eyes she saw a bird, larger than any she had ever seen before, with great, spreading wings, wheeling round and round in wide circles, and uttering a piercing, croaking kind of sound above her.
Peter got up on hearing her call, and together they sat and watched the bird, which rose higher and higher in the blue air till it disappeared behind the grey mountain-tops.

"Oh! oh! oh!" exclaimed Peter, his disapproval of Heidi's suggestion becoming more marked with each ejaculation, "why even the goats cannot climb as high as that, besides didn't Uncle say that you were not to fall over the rocks?"

Peter now began suddenly whistling and calling in such a loud manner that Heidi could not think what was happening; but the goats evidently understood his voice, for one after the other they came springing down the rocks until they were all assembled on the green plateau, some continuing to nibble at the juicy stems, others skipping about here and there or pushing at each other with their horns for pastime.

Heidi jumped up and ran in and out among them, for it was new to her to see the goats playing together like this and her delight was beyond words as she joined in their frolics; she made personal acquaintance with them all in turn, for they were like separate individuals to her, each single goat having a particular way of behavior of its own. Meanwhile Peter had taken the wallet out of the hollow and placed the pieces of bread and cheese on the ground in the shape of a square, the larger two on Heidi's side and the smaller on his own, for he knew exactly which were hers and which his. Then he took the little bowl and milked some delicious fresh milk into it from the white goat, and afterwards set the bowl in the middle of the square. Now he called Heidi to come, but she wanted more calling than the goats, for the child was so excited and amused at the capers and lively games of her new playfellows that she saw and heard nothing else. But Peter knew how to make himself heard, for he shouted till the very rocks above echoed his voice, and at last Heidi appeared, and when she saw the inviting repast spread out upon the ground she went skipping round it for joy.
paragraphsZh: “在上面，就在上面。我们还有很长的路要走，所以来吧！在所有猛禽的最高峰上，坐着并呱呱叫。”
就这样了。海蒂立即跳了起来，围裙上装满了鲜花，跑到彼得身边。
“你们现在已经受够了，”当他们开始再次一起攀爬时，男孩说道。 “如果你继续采摘，你就会永远留在这里，如果你现在收集了所有的花，明天就不会再有花了。”

这最后的论点对海蒂来说似乎是有说服力的，而且她的围裙已经塞满了，几乎没有空间再放一朵花，再不留任何东西再采摘是不行的。所以她现在和彼得在一起，山羊的行为也变得更加有序，因为它们开始闻到生长在较高斜坡上的它们喜爱的植物的气味，并且现在毫不犹豫地爬上山坡，渴望到达它们。彼得通常停下来放羊放牧，并在高高的岩石脚下休息，那里是他白天住宿的地方，岩石上有一段距离被灌木和冷杉树覆盖，远处耸立着光秃秃的崎岖山峰。山的一侧岩石裂开了深深的裂缝，祖父有理由警告彼得有危险。爬到停下的地方后，彼得解下钱包，小心翼翼地把它放在地上的一个小凹处，因为他知道上面的风有多大，他不想看到他的贵重物品被一阵突如其来的狂风吹滚下山。然后他全身扑倒在温暖的地面上，因为经过一番努力，他已经累了。

与此同时，海蒂解开了围裙，小心地将它绕着花卷起来，放在空洞里彼得的钱包旁边；然后她在他伸展的身体旁边坐下，环顾四周。下方的山谷沐浴在早晨的阳光下。她的面前是一片宽阔的雪原，高高地映衬着深蓝色的天空，左边是一大堆岩石，两侧是一座光秃秃的高耸山峰，似乎刺穿了蓝色，皱着眉头俯视着她。孩子一动不动地坐着，她的眼睛注视着整个场景，周围一片寂静，只有一阵阵轻柔的风打破了这一切，风吹动了蓝色花朵的光铃和岩蔷薇闪亮的金色花序，让它们在细长的茎上快乐地点头。彼得疲惫不堪后已经睡着了，山羊们正在头顶的灌木丛中爬来爬去。海蒂一生中从未感到如此幸福。她沐浴着金色的阳光、新鲜的空气、芬芳的花香，巴不得永远留在那里。时间就这样过去了，而对于海蒂来说，她经常从山谷里抬头看上面的山，现在这些山似乎有了面孔，并且像老朋友一样俯视着她。突然，她听到头顶上传来一声刺耳的叫声，抬起头，她看到一只鸟，比她以前见过的任何鸟都大，张开巨大的翅膀，绕着大圈旋转，在她上方发出刺耳的呱呱叫声。
听到她的叫声，彼得站了起来，他们一起坐下来看着那只鸟，它在蓝色的天空中越飞越高，直到消失在灰色的山顶后面。
“哦！哦！哦！”彼得大声说道，他对海蒂的建议的不满随着每次的射精而变得更加明显，“为什么连山羊都爬不了那么高，况且叔叔不是说过你不能从岩石上摔下来吗？”
彼得突然开始吹口哨，大声喊叫，海蒂根本无法想象发生了什么事；但山羊们显然听懂了他的声音，它们一只接一只地从岩石上跳下来，直到全部聚集在绿色的高原上，一些山羊继续啃着多汁的茎，另一些则到处跳来跳去，或者用角互相推挤以取乐。

海蒂跳了起来，在他们中间跑来跑去，因为她第一次看到山羊们这样一起玩耍，加入到他们的嬉闹中，她的喜悦之情难以言表；她依次结识了他们，因为他们对她来说就像是不同的个体，每只山羊都有自己独特的行为方式。与此同时，彼得从坑里拿出钱包，把面包片和奶酪片摆成正方形，放在地上，较大的两片放在海蒂这边，较小的放在他自己的一边，因为他清楚地知道哪些是她的，哪些是他的。然后他拿起小碗，从白山羊身上挤了一些美味的新鲜牛奶，然后把碗放在广场中央。现在他叫海蒂来，但她想要的不仅仅是山羊的呼唤，因为孩子对她的新伙伴的嬉戏和活泼的游戏感到非常兴奋和有趣，以至于她什么也没有看到和听到。但彼得知道如何让自己的声音被听到，因为他大声喊叫，直到上面的岩石都回响着他的声音，最后海蒂出现了，当她看到诱人的食物铺在地上时，她高兴地围着它跳来跳去。

title: Heidi · 选段 2
author: Johanna Spyri
paragraphs: This was just what Heidi enjoyed, and so the children sat down in the midst of the flowers, Clara for the first time on the dry, warm mountain grass, and she found it indescribably delightful. Around her were the blue flowers softly waving to and fro, and beyond the gleaming patches of the cistus flowers and the red centaury, while the sweet scent of the brown blossoms and of the fragrant prunella enveloped her as she sat. Everything was so lovely! so lovely! And Heidi, who was beside her, thought she had never seen it so perfectly beautiful up here before, and she did not know herself why she felt so glad at heart that she longed to shout for joy. Then she suddenly remembered that Clara was cured; that was the crowning delight of all that made life so delightful in the midst of all this surrounding beauty. Clara sat silent, overcome with the enchantment of all that her eye rested upon, and with the anticipation of all the happiness that was now before her. There seemed hardly room in her heart for all her joyful emotions, and these and the ecstasy aroused by the sunlight and the scent of the flowers, held her dumb.

Peter also lay among the flowers without moving or speaking, for he was fast asleep. The breeze came blowing softly and caressingly from behind the sheltering rocks, and passed whisperingly through the bushes overhead. Heidi got up now and then to run about, for the flowers waving in the warm wind seemed to smell sweeter and to grow more thickly whichever way she went, and she felt she must sit down at each fresh spot to enjoy the sight and scent. So the hours went by.

It was long past noon when a small troop of goats advanced solemnly towards the plain of flowers. It was not a feeding place of theirs, for they did not care to graze on flowers. They looked like an embassy arriving, with Greenfinch as their leader. They had evidently come in search of their companions who had left them in the lurch, and who had, contrary to all custom, remained away so long, for the goats could tell the time without mistake. As soon as Greenfinch caught sight of the three missing friends amid the flowers she set up an extra loud bleat, whereupon all the others joined in a chorus of bleats, and the whole company came trotting towards the children. Peter woke up, rubbing his eyes, for he had been dreaming that he saw the chair again with its beautiful red padding standing whole and uninjured before the grandfather's door, and indeed just as he awoke he thought he was looking at the brass-headed nails that studded it all round, but it was only the bright yellow flowers beside him. He experienced again a dreadful fear of mind that he had lost in this dream of the uninjured chair. Even though Heidi had promised not to do anything, there still remained the lively dread that his deed might be found out in some other way. He allowed Heidi to do what she liked with him, for he was reduced to such a state of low spirits and meekness that he was ready to give his help to Clara without murmur or resistance.

When all three had got back to their old quarters Heidi ran and brought forward the bag, and proceeded to fulfil her promise, for her threat of the morning had been concerned with Peter's dinner. She had seen her grandfather putting in all sorts of good things, and had been pleased to think of Peter having a large share of them, and she had meant him to understand when he refused at first to help her that he would get nothing for his dinner, but Peter's conscience had put another interpretation upon her words. Heidi took the food out of the bag and divided it into three portions, and each was of such a goodly size that she thought to herself, "There will be plenty of ours left for him to have more still."
paragraphsZh: 这正是海蒂所享受的，于是孩子们坐在花丛中，克拉拉第一次坐在干燥温暖的山草上，她觉得有说不出的愉悦。她周围是蓝色的花朵轻轻地来回摇曳，远处还有闪闪发光的岩蔷薇花和红色的百里香，而当她坐着时，棕色花朵和夏枯草的甜美香气笼罩着她。一切都是那么可爱！太可爱了！而身旁的海蒂，觉得自己从来没有见过这里如此美丽，自己也不知道为什么心里高兴得想要欢呼。然后她突然想起克拉拉已经痊愈了；这是一切使生活在这一切周围的美景中变得如此令人愉快的最大的快乐。克莱拉静静地坐着，她的目光所见的一切都让她着迷，她对眼前的幸福充满了期待。她的心里似乎几乎没有空间容纳她所有的快乐情绪，这些以及阳光和花香所引起的狂喜让她哑口无言。
彼得也躺在花丛中，一动不动，也不说话，因为他睡得很熟。微风从遮风挡雨的岩石后面轻轻地吹来，轻柔地吹过，低语着穿过头顶的灌木丛。海蒂时不时地起身跑来跑去，因为无论她走到哪里，那些在暖风中摇曳的花朵似乎都更香甜，也越茂盛，她觉得自己必须在每一个新鲜的地方坐下来欣赏美景和香气。时间就这样过去了。

正午已过，一小群山羊庄严地向花丛走去。这不是它们进食的地方，因为它们不喜欢吃花。他们看起来就像一个使节到来，以绿翅雀为首。他们显然是来寻找那些让他们陷入困境的同伴的，而这些同伴却违反了惯例，离开了这么久，因为山羊能够准确无误地说出时间。绿翅雀一看到花丛中失踪的三个朋友，她就发出更大的咩咩叫声，其他所有的鸟儿也跟着齐声咩咩叫，整个公司都小跑着向孩子们走来。彼得揉着眼睛醒来，因为他一直在梦中看到那把椅子，上面有漂亮的红色衬垫，完好无损地站在祖父的门前，事实上，当他醒来时，他以为自己看到的是镶嵌在椅子周围的黄铜头钉子，但他身边只是亮黄色的花朵。他再次体验到了一种可怕的恐惧感，这种恐惧感在梦到那张没有受伤的椅子时已经消失了。尽管海蒂保证不会做任何事，但他仍然担心自己的行为可能会以其他方式被发现。他允许海蒂对他做她喜欢做的事，因为他已经陷入了如此低落和温顺的状态，以至于他准备好毫无怨言或抵抗地帮助克拉拉。
当三个人都回到他们的老住处时，海蒂跑着把包拿了过来，并开始履行她的诺言，因为她早上的威胁是关于彼得的晚餐。她看到她的祖父放入了各种各样的好东西，并且很高兴想到彼得拥有其中的很大一部分，当他一开始拒绝帮助她时，她想让他明白，他将一无所获，但彼得的良心对她的话有了另一种解释。海蒂从袋子里拿出食物，分成三份，份量都很大，她心里想：“我们的还有很多，可以给他吃。”

title: The Voyage of the Beagle
author: Charles Darwin
paragraphs: One day, two of the officers and myself rode to Ribeira Grande, a village a few miles eastward of Porto Praya.  Until we reached the valley of St. Martin, the country presented its usual dull brown appearance; but here, a very small rill of water produces a most refreshing margin of luxuriant vegetation.  In the course of an hour we arrived at Ribeira Grande, and were surprised at the sight of a large ruined fort and cathedral.  This little town, before its harbour was filled up, was the principal place in the island: it now presents a melancholy, but very picturesque appearance.  Having procured a black Padre for a guide, and a Spaniard who had served in the Peninsular war as an interpreter, we visited a collection of buildings, of which an ancient church formed the principal part.  It is here the governors and captain-generals of the islands have been buried.  Some of the tombstones recorded dates of the sixteenth century. [2]

The heraldic ornaments were the only things in this retired place that reminded us of Europe.  The church or chapel formed one side of a quadrangle, in the middle of which a large clump of bananas were growing.  On another side was a hospital, containing about a dozen miserable-looking inmates.

We returned to the Venda to eat our dinners.  A considerable number of men, women, and children, all as black as jet, collected to watch us. Our companions were extremely merry; and everything we said or did was followed by their hearty laughter.  Before leaving the town we visited the cathedral.  It does not appear so rich as the smaller church, but boasts of a little organ, which sent forth singularly inharmonious cries.  We presented the black priest with a few shillings, and the Spaniard, patting him on the head, said, with much candour, he thought his colour made no great difference.  We then returned, as fast as the ponies would go, to Porto Praya.

Another day we rode to the village of St. Domingo, situated near the centre of the island.  On a small plain which we crossed, a few stunted acacias were growing; their tops had been bent by the steady trade-wind, in a singular manner--some of them even at right angles to their trunks. The direction of the branches was exactly N. E. by N., and S. W. by S., and these natural vanes must indicate the prevailing direction of the force of the trade-wind.  The travelling had made so little impression on the barren soil, that we here missed our track, and took that to Fuentes.  This we did not find out till we arrived there; and we were afterwards glad of our mistake.  Fuentes is a pretty village, with a small stream; and everything appeared to prosper well, excepting, indeed, that which ought to do so most--its inhabitants. The black children, completely naked, and looking very wretched, were carrying bundles of firewood half as big as their own bodies.

Near Fuentes we saw a large flock of guinea-fowl--probably fifty or sixty in number.  They were extremely wary, and could not be approached.  They avoided us, like partridges on a rainy day in September, running with their heads cocked up; and if pursued, they readily took to the wing.

The scenery of St. Domingo possesses a beauty totally unexpected, from the prevalent gloomy character of the rest of the island.  The village is situated at the bottom of a valley, bounded by lofty and jagged walls of stratified lava. The black rocks afford a most striking contrast with the bright green vegetation, which follows the banks of a little stream of clear water.  It happened to be a grand feast-day, and the village was full of people.  On our return we overtook a party of about twenty young black girls, dressed in excellent taste; their black skins and snow-white linen being set off by coloured turbans and large shawls.  As soon as we approached near, they suddenly all turned round, and covering the path with their shawls, sung with great energy a wild song, beating time with their hands upon their legs. We threw them some vintems, which were received with screams of laughter, and we left them redoubling the noise of their song.

One morning the view was singularly clear; the distant mountains being projected with the sharpest outline on a heavy bank of dark blue clouds.  Judging from the appearance, and from similar cases in England, I supposed that the air was saturated with moisture.  The fact, however, turned out quite the contrary.  The hygrometer gave a difference of 29.6 degs., between the temperature of the air, and the point at which dew was precipitated.  This difference was nearly double that which I had observed on the previous mornings.  This unusual degree of atmospheric dryness was accompanied by continual flashes of lightning.  Is it not an uncommon case, thus to find a remarkable degree of aerial transparency with such a state of weather?
paragraphsZh: 有一天，我和两名军官骑马前往大里贝拉，这是普拉亚港以东几英里处的一个村庄。 在我们到达圣马丁山谷之前，这个国家呈现出平常的暗棕色外观。但在这里，一条很小的溪流却孕育出茂密的植被，令人耳目一新。 一个小时后，我们到达了大里贝拉，惊讶地看到一座巨大的堡垒和大教堂的废墟。 这个小镇在港口被填满之前是岛上的主要地方：现在它呈现出忧郁但风景如画的外观。 我们找了一位黑人教士当导游，又请了一位曾在半岛战争中服役的西班牙人担任翻译，我们参观了一系列建筑，其中一座古老的教堂构成了主体部分。 岛上的总督和总督都埋葬在这里。 一些墓碑记录了十六世纪的日期。 [2]
在这个僻静的地方，纹章装饰品是唯一让我们想起欧洲的东西。 教堂或礼拜堂形成了一个四边形的一侧，中间长着一大丛香蕉。 另一边是一家医院，里面关着十几名表情痛苦的囚犯。
我们回到文达吃晚餐。 相当多的男人、女人和孩子，全都黑如墨玉，聚集在一起观看我们。我们的同伴非常高兴。我们所说或所做的一切都会引起他们爽朗的​​笑声。 离开小镇之前，我们参观了大教堂。 它看上去并不像那个小教堂那样富丽堂皇，但却拥有一个小管风琴，能发出异常不和谐的叫声。 我们递给黑人牧师几先令，西班牙人拍拍他的头，非常坦诚地说，他认为他的肤色没有多大区别。 然后我们以小马最快的速度返回普拉亚港。

另一天，我们骑车前往位于岛中心附近的圣多明戈村。 我们穿过的一小片平原上，长着一些发育不良的金合欢树。它们的顶部被稳定的信风以一种奇特的方式弯曲——其中一些甚至与树干成直角。树枝的方向恰好是北东靠北，西南靠南，这些自然风向标必定表明了信风的主要方向。 这次旅行在贫瘠的土地上没有留下什么印象，所以我们在这里迷失了踪迹，并把它带到了富恩特斯。 直到我们到达那里才发现这一点。后来我们为自己的错误感到高兴。 富恩特斯是一个美丽的村庄，有一条小溪；一切似乎都很繁荣，除了最应该繁荣的人——它的居民。黑人孩子们一丝不挂，样子十分可怜，手里提着一捆捆有自己身体一半大的柴草。
在富恩特斯附近，我们看到了一大群珍珠鸡——数量可能有五十或六十只。 他们极为警惕，不敢靠近。 他们躲着我们，像九月雨天的鹧鸪，昂着头奔跑；如果遭到追击，他们会立即躲到侧翼。

圣多明各的风景拥有一种完全出乎意料的美丽，与岛上其他地方普遍的阴郁性格相比。 该村庄位于山谷底部，周围是高耸且锯齿状的分层熔岩墙。黑色的岩石与清澈的小溪沿岸的鲜绿色植被形成了鲜明的对比。 那天正好是一个盛大的节日，村子里挤满了人。 返回时，我们遇到了一群大约二十名年轻的黑人女孩，她们穿着非常有品位。他们的黑色皮肤和雪白亚麻布与彩色头巾和大披肩相映衬。 当我们走近时，他们突然全部转过身来，用披肩遮住道路，精力充沛地唱着一首狂野的歌曲，双手放在腿上打拍子。我们向他们扔了一些酒，他们收到了尖叫声，然后我们就让他们的歌声加倍了。
一天早上，景色异常清晰；远处的山脉在厚重的深蓝色云层上投射出最清晰的轮廓。 从外观以及英国的类似情况来看，我认为空气中充满了湿气。 然而事实却恰恰相反。 湿度计显示空气温度与结露点之间存在 29.6 度的差异。 这个差异几乎是我前几天早上观察到的两倍。 这种异常程度的大气干燥伴随着持续不断的闪电。 在这样的天气条件下，空气透明度达到了惊人的程度，这不是很罕见吗？

title: The Voyage of the Beagle · 选段 2
author: Charles Darwin
paragraphs: Many of the losses which must be experienced are obvious; such as that of the society of every old friend, and of the sight of those places with which every dearest remembrance is so intimately connected.  These losses, however, are at the time partly relieved by the exhaustless delight of anticipating the long wished-for day of return.  If, as poets say, life is a dream, I am sure in a voyage these are the visions which best serve to pass away the long night.  Other losses, although not at first felt, tell heavily after a period: these are the want of room, of seclusion, of rest; the jading feeling of constant hurry; the privation of small luxuries, the loss of domestic society and even of music and the other pleasures of imagination.  When such trifles are mentioned, it is evident that the real grievances, excepting from accidents, of a sea-life are at an end.  The short space of sixty years has made an astonishing difference in the facility of distant navigation.  Even in the time of Cook, a man who left his fireside for such expeditions underwent severe privations. A yacht now, with every luxury of life, can circumnavigate the globe.  Besides the vast improvements in ships and naval resources, the whole western shores of America are thrown open, and Australia has become the capital of a rising continent.  How different are the circumstances to a man shipwrecked at the present day in the Pacific, to what they were in the time of Cook!  Since his voyage a hemisphere has been added to the civilized world.

If a person suffer much from sea-sickness, let him weigh it heavily in the balance.  I speak from experience: it is no trifling evil, cured in a week.  If, on the other hand, he take pleasure in naval tactics, he will assuredly have full scope for his taste.  But it must be borne in mind, how large a proportion of the time, during a long voyage, is spent on the water, as compared with the days in harbour.  And what are the boasted glories of the illimitable ocean.  A tedious waste, a desert of water, as the Arabian calls it.  No doubt there are some delightful scenes.  A moonlight night, with the clear heavens and the dark glittering sea, and the white sails filled by the soft air of a gently blowing trade-wind, a dead calm, with the heaving surface polished like a mirror, and all still except the occasional flapping of the canvas. It is well once to behold a squall with its rising arch and coming fury, or the heavy gale of wind and mountainous waves.  I confess, however, my imagination had painted something more grand, more terrific in the full-grown storm. It is an incomparably finer spectacle when beheld on shore, where the waving trees, the wild flight of the birds, the dark shadows and bright lights, the rushing of the torrents all proclaim the strife of the unloosed elements.  At sea the albatross and little petrel fly as if the storm were their proper sphere, the water rises and sinks as if fulfilling its usual task, the ship alone and its inhabitants seem the objects of wrath.  On a forlorn and weather-beaten coast, the scene is indeed different, but the feelings partake more of horror than of wild delight.

Let us now look at the brighter side of the past time.  The pleasure derived from beholding the scenery and the general aspect of the various countries we have visited, has decidedly been the most constant and highest source of enjoyment.  It is probable that the picturesque beauty of many parts of Europe exceeds anything which we beheld.  But there is a growing pleasure in comparing the character of the scenery in different countries, which to a certain degree is distinct from merely admiring its beauty.  It depends chiefly on an acquaintance with the individual parts of each view.  I am strongly induced to believe that as in music, the person who understands every note will, if he also possesses a proper taste, more thoroughly enjoy the whole, so he who examines each part of a fine view, may also thoroughly comprehend the full and combined effect.  Hence, a traveller should be a botanist, for in all views plants form the chief embellishment.  Group masses of naked rock, even in the wildest forms, and they may for a time afford a sublime spectacle, but they will soon grow monotonous.  Paint them with bright and varied colours, as in Northern Chile, they will become fantastic; clothe them with vegetation, they must form a decent, if not a beautiful picture.

When I say that the scenery of parts of Europe is probably superior to anything which we beheld, I except, as a class by itself, that of the intertropical zones.  The two classes cannot be compared together; but I have already often enlarged on the grandeur of those regions.  As the force of impressions generally depends on preconceived ideas, I may add, that mine were taken from the vivid descriptions in the Personal Narrative of Humboldt, which far exceed in merit anything else which I have read.  Yet with these high-wrought ideas, my feelings were far from partaking of a tinge of disappointment on my first and final landing on the shores of Brazil.
paragraphsZh: 许多必须经历的损失是显而易见的；比如每一位老朋友的交往，以及那些与每一个最亲密的记忆都紧密相连的地方的景象。 然而，这些损失在当时因期待已久的归来而感到无尽的喜悦而得到了部分缓解。 如果真如诗人们所说，人生是一场梦，那么我确信，在航行中，这些幻象最能帮助消磨长夜。 其他一些损失，虽然一开始并没有感觉到，但在一段时间后就会显露出来：这些是缺乏空间、隐居、休息；持续匆忙的疲惫感；小奢侈品的匮乏，家庭社会的丧失，甚至音乐和其他想象乐趣的丧失。 当提到这些琐事时，很明显，除了意外事件之外，海洋生物的真正不满已经结束了。 短短六十年的时间，使远航的设施发生了惊人的变化。 即使在库克时代，离开炉边进行此类探险的人也会经历严重的贫困。现在，游艇可以环球航行，享受各种奢华的生活。 除了舰船和海军资源的巨大改进之外，美国的整个西海岸也完全开放，澳大利亚也成为了新兴大陆的首都。 如今，一个在太平洋遭遇海难的人的处境与库克时代是多么不同啊！ 自从他的航行以来，文明世界又增加了一个半球。

如果一个人晕船很严重，让他权衡一下。 我的经验告诉我：这不是小病，一周就能治愈。 另一方面，如果他喜欢海军战术，他肯定会充分发挥自己的品味。 但必须记住，与在港口的日子相比，在长途航行中，有很大一部分时间是在水上度过的。 无边无际的海洋有什么值得夸耀的荣耀。 正如阿拉伯人所说，这是一片乏味的浪费，一片水的沙漠。 毫无疑问，其中有一些令人愉快的场景。 月光之夜，晴空万里，大海波光粼粼，白色的船帆被轻柔的信风吹拂，一片死寂，波涛起伏的水面像镜子一样光滑，一切都静止了，除了帆布偶尔拍打的声音。目睹暴风雨升腾、狂怒即将来临，或者是狂风巨浪，是再好不过的事了。 然而，我承认，我的想象力在这场成熟的风暴中描绘了更宏伟、更可怕的东西。在岸上看，那景象是无与伦比的，树木摇曳，鸟儿狂飞，黑影明亮，激流湍急，无不宣告着大自然的争斗。 在海上，信天翁和小海燕飞翔，仿佛暴风雨就是它们的专属领域，海水起起落落，仿佛在完成其平常的任务，船和船上的居民似乎是愤怒的对象。 在荒凉、饱经风霜的海岸上，景色确实不同，但感觉更多的是恐怖而不是狂野的喜悦。

现在让我们看看过去的光明的一面。 欣赏我们所访问的各个国家的风景和总体面貌所带来的乐趣无疑是最持久和最高的享受源泉。 欧洲许多地方的风景如画的美丽可能超出了我们所看到的任何东西。 但比较不同国家风景的特点越来越令人愉悦，这在某种程度上不同于仅仅欣赏其美丽。 这主要取决于对每个视图各个部分的熟悉。 我强烈地相信，就像在音乐中一样，理解每个音符的人，如果他也有适当的品味，就会更彻底地享受整体，因此，审视美景的每个部分的人，也可以彻底理解完整和综合的效果。 因此，一个旅行者应该是一个植物学家，因为在所有的观点中，植物都是主要的点缀。 裸露的岩石群，即使是最狂野的形式，它们可能会在一段时间内提供令人惊叹的奇观，但它们很快就会变得单调。 给它们涂上鲜艳多彩的颜色，就像在智利北部一样，它们会变得很梦幻；如果给它们披上植被，它们就必须形成一幅像样的图画，即使不是一幅美丽的图画。
当我说欧洲部分地区的风景可能比我们所看到的任何地方都优越时，我排除了热带地区的风景。 两个类不能放在一起比较；但我已经经常夸大这些地区的宏伟。 由于印象的力量通常取决于先入为主的想法，我可以补充一点，我的印象取自洪堡《个人叙述》中生动的描述，其价值远远超过我读过的任何其他内容。 然而，有了这些高深的想法，当我第一次也是最后一次登陆巴西海岸时，我的感受远没有一丝失望。

title: The Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
paragraphs: The annual labour of every nation is the fund which originally supplies it with all the necessaries and conveniencies of life which it annually consumes, and which consist always either in the immediate produce of that labour, or in what is purchased with that produce from other nations.

According, therefore, as this produce, or what is purchased with it, bears a greater or smaller proportion to the number of those who are to consume it, the nation will be better or worse supplied with all the necessaries and conveniencies for which it has occasion.

But this proportion must in every nation be regulated by two different circumstances: first, by the skill, dexterity, and judgment with which its labour is generally applied; and, secondly, by the proportion between the number of those who are employed in useful labour, and that of those who are not so employed. Whatever be the soil, climate, or extent of territory of any particular nation, the abundance or scantiness of its annual supply must, in that particular situation, depend upon those two circumstances.

The abundance or scantiness of this supply, too, seems to depend more upon the former of those two circumstances than upon the latter. Among the savage nations of hunters and fishers, every individual who is able to work is more or less employed in useful labour, and endeavours to provide, as well as he can, the necessaries and conveniencies of life, for himself, and such of his family or tribe as are either too old, or too young, or too infirm, to go a-hunting and fishing. Such nations, however, are so miserably poor, that, from mere want, they are frequently reduced, or at least think themselves reduced, to the necessity sometimes of directly destroying, and sometimes of abandoning their infants, their old people, and those afflicted with lingering diseases, to perish with hunger, or to be devoured by wild beasts. Among civilized and thriving nations, on the contrary, though a great number of people do not labour at all, many of whom consume the produce of ten times, frequently of a hundred times, more labour than the greater part of those who work; yet the produce of the whole labour of the society is so great, that all are often abundantly supplied; and a workman, even of the lowest and poorest order, if he is frugal and industrious, may enjoy a greater share of the necessaries and conveniencies of life than it is possible for any savage to acquire.

The causes of this improvement in the productive powers of labour, and the order according to which its produce is naturally distributed among the different ranks and conditions of men in the society, make the subject of the first book of this Inquiry.

Whatever be the actual state of the skill, dexterity, and judgment, with which labour is applied in any nation, the abundance or scantiness of its annual supply must depend, during the continuance of that state, upon the proportion between the number of those who are annually employed in useful labour, and that of those who are not so employed. The number of useful and productive labourers, it will hereafter appear, is everywhere in proportion to the quantity of capital stock which is employed in setting them to work, and to the particular way in which it is so employed. The second book, therefore, treats of the nature of capital stock, of the manner in which it is gradually accumulated, and of the different quantities of labour which it puts into motion, according to the different ways in which it is employed.

Nations tolerably well advanced as to skill, dexterity, and judgment, in the application of labour, have followed very different plans in the general conduct or direction of it; and those plans have not all been equally favourable to the greatness of its produce. The policy of some nations has given extraordinary encouragement to the industry of the country; that of others to the industry of towns. Scarce any nation has dealt equally and impartially with every sort of industry. Since the down-fall of the Roman empire, the policy of Europe has been more favourable to arts, manufactures, and commerce, the industry of towns, than to agriculture, the Industry of the country. The circumstances which seem to have introduced and established this policy are explained in the third book.

Though those different plans were, perhaps, first introduced by the private interests and prejudices of particular orders of men, without any regard to, or foresight of, their consequences upon the general welfare of the society; yet they have given occasion to very different theories of political economy; of which some magnify the importance of that industry which is carried on in towns, others of that which is carried on in the country. Those theories have had a considerable influence, not only upon the opinions of men of learning, but upon the public conduct of princes and sovereign states. I have endeavoured, in the fourth book, to explain as fully and distinctly as I can those different theories, and the principal effects which they have produced in different ages and nations.
paragraphsZh: 每个国家的年度劳动是最初为其每年消费的所有生活必需品和便利设施提供的资金，并且总是要么包含在该劳动的直接产品中，要么包含在用该产品从其他国家购买的东西中。
因此，根据这种产品，或者用它购买的东西，在消费它的人数中所占的比例或多或少，国家在其需要的所有必需品和便利设施方面的供应会更好或更差。
但是，每个国家的这一比例都必须受到两种不同情况的调节：首先，取决于其劳动普遍应用的技能、灵巧性和判断力；其次，取决于其劳动的技能、灵巧性和判断力；其次，是从事有用劳动的人数与不从事有用劳动的人数之间的比例。无论任何特定国家的土壤、气候或领土范围如何，在该特定情况下，其年度供应的丰富或不足都必须取决于这两种情况。

这种供应的丰富或不足似乎也更多地取决于这两种情况中的前者而不是后者。在狩猎和渔民的野蛮民族中，每一个能够工作的人都或多或少地从事有用的劳动，并尽力为自己以及他的家庭或部落的那些太老、太年轻或太虚弱而无法打猎和捕鱼的人提供生活必需品和便利。然而，这些国家却极度贫穷，以至于他们常常从单纯的匮乏，或者至少认为自己被削弱，有时不得不直接毁灭，有时不得不抛弃他们的婴儿、老人和那些患有挥之不去的疾病的人，让他们死于饥饿，或者被野兽吞噬。相反，在文明和繁荣的国家中，尽管有很多人根本不劳动，但他们中的许多人消耗的产品比大多数劳动者多十倍，常常是一百倍；然而，整个社会劳动的产品是如此之多，以至于所有的产品往往都可以充足地供应。一个工人，即使是最低级和最贫穷的工人，如果他节俭和勤劳，也可以享受到比任何野蛮人更多的生活必需品和便利。
劳动生产力提高的原因，以及其产品在社会中不同阶层和条件的人们中自然分配的顺序，构成了本研究第一本书的主题。

无论任何国家应用劳动的技能、灵巧性和判断力的实际状况如何，在这种状况持续期间，其年度供应量的丰富或不足必定取决于每年从事有用劳动的人数与不从事有用劳动的人数之间的比例。下文将表明，有用的、生产性的劳动者的数量在任何地方都与用于让他们工作的资本存量的数量以及资本存量的特定使用方式成正比。因此，第二本书讨论了资本存量的性质、资本逐渐积累的方式，以及资本存量根据其使用方式的不同而投入运转的不同数量的劳动。
在劳动应用方面，在技能、灵巧性和判断力方面相当先进的国家，在劳动的一般行为或方向上却遵循着截然不同的计划；但这些计划并非都同样有利于其产品的伟大发展。一些国家的政策对本国工业给予了极大的鼓励；其他人的产业转向城镇的工业。很少有哪个国家能够平等、公正地对待各种行业。自罗马帝国灭亡以来，欧洲的政策对艺术、制造业和商业（城镇工业）比农业（国家工业）更有利。第三本书解释了引入和确立这一政策的情况。

尽管这些不同的计划最初可能是由特定人群的私人利益和偏见提出的，没有考虑或预见到它们对社会总体福利的影响；然而，它们却催生了截然不同的政治经济学理论。其中一些人夸大了在城镇进行的工业的重要性，另一些人则夸大了在乡村进行的工业的重要性。这些理论不仅对学者的观点产生了相当大的影响，而且对君主和主权国家的公共行为也产生了相当大的影响。在第四本书中，我尽力尽可能全面、清晰地解释这些不同的理论，以及它们在不同时代和国家中产生的主要影响。

title: The Wealth of Nations · 选段 2
author: Adam Smith
paragraphs: When the public expense is defrayed by funding, it is defrayed by the annual destruction of some capital which had before existed in the country; by the perversion of some portion of the annual produce which had before been destined for the maintenance of productive labour, towards that of unproductive labour. As in this case, however, the taxes are lighter than they would have been, had a revenue sufficient for defraying the same expense been raised within the year; the private revenue of individuals is necessarily less burdened, and consequently their ability to save and accumulate some part of that revenue into capital, is a good deal less impaired. If the method of funding destroys more old capital, it, at the same time, hinders less the accumulation or acquisition of new capital, than that of defraying the public expense by a revenue raised within the year. Under the system of funding, the frugality and industry of private people can more easily repair the breaches which the waste and extravagance of government may occasionally make in the general capital of the society.

It is only during the continuance of war, however, that the system of funding has this advantage over the other system. Were the expense of war to be defrayed always by a revenue raised within the year, the taxes from which that extraordinary revenue was drawn would last no longer than the war. The ability of private people to accumulate, though less during the war, would have been greater during the peace, than under the system of funding. War would not necessarily have occasioned the destruction of any old capitals, and peace would have occasioned the accumulation of many more new. Wars would, in general, be more speedily concluded, and less wantonly undertaken. The people feeling, during continuance of war, the complete burden of it, would soon grow weary of it; and government, in order to humour them, would not be under the necessity of carrying it on longer than it was necessary to do so. The foresight of the heavy and unavoidable burdens of war would hinder the people from wantonly calling for it when there was no real or solid interest to fight for. The seasons during which the ability of private people to accumulate was somewhat impaired, would occur more rarely, and be of shorter continuance. Those, on the contrary, during which that ability was in the highest vigour would be of much longer duration than they can well be under the system of funding.

When funding, besides, has made a certain progress, the multiplication of taxes which it brings along with it, sometimes impairs as much the ability of private people to accumulate, even in time of peace, as the other system would in time of war. The peace revenue of Great Britain amounts at present to more than ten millions a-year. If free and unmortgaged, it might be sufficient, with proper management, and without contracting a shilling of new debt, to carry on the most vigorous war. The private revenue of the inhabitants of Great Britain is at present as much incumbered in time of peace, their ability to accumulate is as much impaired, as it would have been in the time of the most expensive war, had the pernicious system of funding never been adopted.

In the payment of the interest of the public debt, it has been said, it is the right hand which pays the left. The money does not go out of the country. It is only a part of the revenue of one set of the inhabitants which is transferred to another; and the nation is not a farthing the poorer. This apology is founded altogether in the sophistry of the mercantile system; and, after the long examination which I have already bestowed upon that system, it may, perhaps, be unnecessary to say anything further about it. It supposes, besides, that the whole public debt is owing to the inhabitants of the country, which happens not to be true; the Dutch, as well as several other foreign nations, having a very considerable share in our public funds. But though the whole debt were owing to the inhabitants of the country, it would not, upon that account, be less pernicious.

Land and capital stock are the two original sources of all revenue, both private and public. Capital stock pays the wages of productive labour, whether employed in agriculture, manufactures, or commerce. The management of those two original sources of revenue belongs to two different sets of people; the proprietors of land, and the owners or employers of capital stock.

The proprietor of land is interested, for the sake of his own revenue, to keep his estate in as good condition as he can, by building and repairing his tenants houses, by making and maintaining the necessary drains and inclosures, and all those other expensive improvements which it properly belongs to the landlord to make and maintain. But, by different land taxes, the revenue of the landlord may be so much diminished, and, by different duties upon the necessaries and conveniencies of life, that diminished revenue may be rendered of so little real value, that he may find himself altogether unable to make or maintain those expensive improvements. When the landlord, however, ceases to do his part, it is altogether impossible that the tenant should continue to do his. As the distress of the landlord increases, the agriculture of the country must necessarily decline.
paragraphsZh: 当公共开支通过资金来支付时，它是通过每年销毁该国以前存在的一些资本来支付的；以前用于维持生产性劳动的年产品的某些部分被扭曲为非生产性劳动。然而，在这种情况下，如果一年内筹集到足以支付相同费用的收入，则税收会比本来应有的税收要少；个人私人收入的负担必然减轻，因此他们将部分收入储蓄和积累为资本的能力受到的损害也小得多。如果这种筹资方法破坏了更多的旧资本，那么它同时对新资本的积累或获取的阻碍就小于通过一年内筹集的收入来支付公共开支的阻碍。在资金体系下，私人的节俭和勤劳可以更容易地修复政府的浪费和奢侈有时对社会总资本造成的缺口。

然而，只有在战争持续期间，资助制度才比其他制度具有这种优势。如果战争费用总是由当年增加的收入来支付，那么从这些额外收入中提取的税收将不会比战争持续得更久。私人积累的能力虽然在战争期间较小，但在和平时期会比在资助体系下更大。战争不一定会导致任何旧首都的毁灭，而和平则会导致更多新首都的积累。一般来说，战争会更快地结束，并且不会那么肆意地进行。人们在战争持续期间感到自己是战争的全部负担，很快就会厌倦。为了迎合他们，政府不会有必要将其延续得比必要的时间更长。对战争的沉重和不可避免的负担的预见，会阻碍人们在没有真正的、坚实的利益可以争取的情况下肆意地呼吁战争。私人积累能力受到一定程度削弱的季节会更加罕见，并且持续时间较短。相反，那些能力处于最高活力期间的持续时间将比资助系统下的持续时间长得多。
此外，当资金投入取得一定进展时，随之而来的税收倍增有时会损害私人积累的能力，即使在和平时期也是如此，就像其他制度在战时一样。英国目前每年的和平收入达千万以上。如果自由且未抵押，在适当的管理下，并且无需签订一先令的新债务，它可能足以进行最激烈的战争。目前，如果从未采用有害的筹资制度，英国居民的私人收入在和平时期就受到了同样严重的困扰，他们的积累能力也受到了损害，就像在最昂贵的战争时期一样。

在公共债务利息的支付中，有人说，是右手支付左手。钱不会出国。这只是一组居民的一部分收入转移到另一组居民的情况；这个国家一点也不穷。这种辩解完全是建立在重商体系的诡辩之上。而且，在我已经对这个系统进行了长时间的考察之后，也许没有必要再进一步谈论它了。此外，它还假定全部公共债务都是该国居民所欠的，但事实并非如此。荷兰以及其他几个国家在我们的公共资金中占有相当大的份额。但是，尽管全部债务都是该国居民欠下的，但其危害性也不会因此而减轻。
土地和资本存量是所有收入（无论是私人收入还是公共收入）的两个原始来源。资本存量支付生产性劳动的工资，无论是农业、制造业还是商业。这两种原始收入来源的管理属于两类不同的人；土地所有者以及资本存量的所有者或雇主。

土地所有者有兴趣，为了自己的收入，通过建造和修理他的租户房屋，通过建造和维护必要的排水沟和围墙，以及所有其他理应由地主建造和维护的昂贵的改进，使他的财产尽可能保持良好状态。但是，由于不同的土地税，地主的收入可能会大大减少，而且，由于对生活必需品和便利设施征收不同的税，减少的收入可能没有什么实际价值，以至于他可能会发现自己完全无法进行或维持这些昂贵的改进。然而，当房东不再尽自己的职责时，租客就完全不可能继续尽自己的职责。地主的苦难增加，国家的农业必然衰落。

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: He told me some queer things that explained a lot that had puzzled me—things that happened in the Balkan War, how one state suddenly came out on top, why alliances were made and broken, why certain men disappeared, and where the sinews of war came from. The aim of the whole conspiracy was to get Russia and Germany at loggerheads.

When I asked why, he said that the anarchist lot thought it would give them their chance. Everything would be in the melting-pot, and they looked to see a new world emerge. The capitalists would rake in the shekels, and make fortunes by buying up wreckage. Capital, he said, had no conscience and no fatherland. Besides, the Jew was behind it, and the Jew hated Russia worse than hell.

“Do you wonder?” he cried. “For three hundred years they have been persecuted, and this is the return match for the pogroms. The Jew is everywhere, but you have to go far down the backstairs to find him. Take any big Teutonic business concern. If you have dealings with it the first man you meet is Prince von und zu Something, an elegant young man who talks Eton-and-Harrow English. But he cuts no ice. If your business is big, you get behind him and find a prognathous Westphalian with a retreating brow and the manners of a hog. He is the German business man that gives your English papers the shakes. But if you’re on the biggest kind of job and are bound to get to the real boss, ten to one you are brought up against a little white-faced Jew in a bath-chair with an eye like a rattlesnake. Yes, sir, he is the man who is ruling the world just now, and he has his knife in the Empire of the Tsar, because his aunt was outraged and his father flogged in some one-horse location on the Volga.”

“Yes and no,” he said. “They won up to a point, but they struck a bigger thing than money, a thing that couldn’t be bought, the old elemental fighting instincts of man. If you’re going to be killed you invent some kind of flag and country to fight for, and if you survive you get to love the thing. Those foolish devils of soldiers have found something they care for, and that has upset the pretty plan laid in Berlin and Vienna. But my friends haven’t played their last card by a long sight. They’ve gotten the ace up their sleeves, and unless I can keep alive for a month they are going to play it and win.”

“Mors janua vitæ,” he smiled. (I recognized the quotation: it was about all the Latin I knew.) “I’m coming to that, but I’ve got to put you wise about a lot of things first. If you read your newspaper, I guess you know the name of Constantine Karolides?”

“He is the man that has wrecked all their games. He is the one big brain in the whole show, and he happens also to be an honest man. Therefore he has been marked down these twelve months past. I found that out—not that it was difficult, for any fool could guess as much. But I found out the way they were going to get him, and that knowledge was deadly. That’s why I have had to decease.”

“They can’t get him in his own land, for he has a bodyguard of Epirotes that would skin their grandmothers. But on the 15th day of June he is coming to this city. The British Foreign Office has taken to having international tea-parties, and the biggest of them is due on that date. Now Karolides is reckoned the principal guest, and if my friends have their way he will never return to his admiring countrymen.”

“And play their game?” he asked sharply. “If he does not come they win, for he’s the only man that can straighten out the tangle. And if his Government are warned he won’t come, for he does not know how big the stakes will be on June the 15th.”
“What about the British Government?” I said. “They’re not going to let their guests be murdered. Tip them the wink, and they’ll take extra precautions.”

“No good. They might stuff your city with plain-clothes detectives and double the police and Constantine would still be a doomed man. My friends are not playing this game for candy. They want a big occasion for the taking off, with the eyes of all Europe on it. He’ll be murdered by an Austrian, and there’ll be plenty of evidence to show the connivance of the big folk in Vienna and Berlin. It will all be an infernal lie, of course, but the case will look black enough to the world. I’m not talking hot air, my friend. I happen to know every detail of the hellish contrivance, and I can tell you it will be the most finished piece of blackguardism since the Borgias. But it’s not going to come off if there’s a certain man who knows the wheels of the business alive right here in London on the 15th day of June. And that man is going to be your servant, Franklin P. Scudder.”
paragraphsZh: 他告诉我一些奇怪的事情，解释了很多让我困惑的事情——巴尔干战争中发生的事情，一个国家如何突然占据上风，为什么联盟建立和破裂，为什么某些人消失，以及战争的根源来自哪里。整个阴谋的目的是让俄罗斯和德国发生争执。
当我问为什么时，他说无政府主义者认为这会给他们机会。一切都将进入熔炉，他们期待看到一个新世界的出现。资本家会大肆捞取谢克尔，并通过购买残骸来发财。他说，资本没有良心，也没有祖国。再说了，背后还有犹太人在背后操纵，犹太人对俄罗斯恨之入骨。

“你想知道吗？”他哭了。 “三百年来，他们一直受到迫害，这是大屠杀的报复。犹太人无处不在，但你必须从后楼走很远才能找到他。以任何大型日耳曼商业公司为例。如果你与它打交道，你遇到的第一个人就是冯·德·祖·普林斯王子，一个优雅的年轻人，说着伊顿公学和哈罗公学的英语。但他不冷不热。如果你的生意很大，你就躲在他身后，找到一个下颌突出的威斯特伐利亚人。他是一个德国商人，他的眉头向后退，举止像猪一样，但如果你从事的是最重要的工作，并且注定会遇到真正的老板，你会遇到一个坐在浴椅上、眼睛像响尾蛇的小白脸犹太人。他被激怒了，他的父亲在伏尔加河畔的某个只有一匹马的地方受到了鞭打。”
“是又不是，”他说。 “他们在一定程度上赢了，但他们击中了比金钱更重要的东西，这是买不来的东西，是人类古老的基本战斗本能。如果你要被杀，你就发明某种旗帜和国家来战斗，如果你活下来，你就会爱上它。那些愚蠢的士兵找到了他们关心的东西，这打乱了柏林和维也纳制定的美好计划。但我的朋友们还没有打出最后一张牌。他们已经拿到了王牌。他们会袖手旁观，除非我能活一个月，否则他们就会赢。”
“Mors janua vitæ，”他微笑着。 （我认出了这句话：它是关于我所知道的所有拉丁语的。）“我正要说到这一点，但我必须首先让你了解很多事情。如果你读报纸，我猜你知道康斯坦丁·卡罗利德斯的名字？”
“他是那个毁掉了他们所有比赛的人。他是整个节目中的一个大大脑，而且他碰巧也是一个诚实的人。因此他在过去的十二个月里被标记了。我发现了这一点——这并不困难，因为任何傻瓜都可以猜到。但我发现了他们要抓住他的方法，而这种知识是致命的。这就是为什么我不得不死。”
“他们无法让他回到自己的土地，因为他有一个伊庇鲁斯保镖，会剥他们祖母的皮。但在 6 月 15 日，他将来到这座城市。英国外交部已经开始举办国际茶会，其中最大的一场将于那天举行。现在卡罗里德斯被认为是主要客人，如果我的朋友们按他们的方式行事，他将永远不会回到他钦佩的同胞身边。”
“然后玩他们的游戏？”他尖锐地问道。 “如果他不来，他们就赢了，因为他是唯一能够理顺混乱的人。如果他的政府受到警告，他就不会来，因为他不知道 6 月 15 日的赌注有多大。”
“英国政府呢？”我说。 “他们不会让他们的客人被谋杀。给他们眨眼，他们就会采取额外的预防措施。”

“不好。他们可能会在你的城市里塞满便衣侦探，加倍警察，康斯坦丁仍然是一个注定要失败的人。我的朋友们玩这个游戏不是为了糖果。他们想要一个起飞的大场合，全欧洲的目光都集中在它身上。他会被一个奥地利人谋杀，而且会有大量证据表明维也纳和柏林大人物的纵容。这将是一个地狱般的谎言，当然，但这个案子对世人来说并不是空话，我碰巧知道这个地狱般的阴谋的每一个细节，我可以告诉你，这将是自博吉亚家族以来最彻底的恶行，但如果 6 月 15 日有一个知道这件事的人就在伦敦，那么这个人就是你的仆人，富兰克林·P·斯卡德。”

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 2
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: That did something to reassure me, but as we rowed back to Bradgate my obstinate doubts would not be dismissed. The thing that worried me was the reflection that my enemies knew that I had got my knowledge from Scudder, and it was Scudder who had given me the clue to this place. If they knew that Scudder had this clue, would they not be certain to change their plans? Too much depended on their success for them to take any risks. The whole question was how much they understood about Scudder’s knowledge. I had talked confidently last night about Germans always sticking to a scheme, but if they had any suspicions that I was on their track they would be fools not to cover it. I wondered if the man last night had seen that I recognized him. Somehow I did not think he had, and to that I had clung. But the whole business had never seemed so difficult as that afternoon when by all calculations I should have been rejoicing in assured success.
In the hotel I met the commander of the destroyer, to whom Scaife introduced me, and with whom I had a few words. Then I thought I would put in an hour or two watching Trafalgar Lodge.

I found a place farther up the hill, in the garden of an empty house. From there I had a full view of the court, on which two figures were having a game of tennis. One was the old man, whom I had already seen; the other was a younger fellow, wearing some club colours in the scarf round his middle. They played with tremendous zest, like two city gents who wanted hard exercise to open their pores. You couldn’t conceive a more innocent spectacle. They shouted and laughed and stopped for drinks, when a maid brought out two tankards on a salver. I rubbed my eyes and asked myself if I was not the most immortal fool on earth. Mystery and darkness had hung about the men who hunted me over the Scotch moor in aeroplane and motor-car, and notably about that infernal antiquarian. It was easy enough to connect those folk with the knife that pinned Scudder to the floor, and with fell designs on the world’s peace. But here were two guileless citizens taking their innocuous exercise, and soon about to go indoors to a humdrum dinner, where they would talk of market prices and the last cricket scores and the gossip of their native Surbiton. I had been making a net to catch vultures and falcons, and lo and behold! two plump thrushes had blundered into it.

Presently a third figure arrived, a young man on a bicycle, with a bag of golf-clubs slung on his back. He strolled round to the tennis lawn and was welcomed riotously by the players. Evidently they were chaffing him, and their chaff sounded horribly English. Then the plump man, mopping his brow with a silk handkerchief, announced that he must have a tub. I heard his very words—“I’ve got into a proper lather,” he said. “This will bring down my weight and my handicap, Bob. I’ll take you on tomorrow and give you a stroke a hole.” You couldn’t find anything much more English than that.

They all went into the house, and left me feeling a precious idiot. I had been barking up the wrong tree this time. These men might be acting; but if they were, where was their audience? They didn’t know I was sitting thirty yards off in a rhododendron. It was simply impossible to believe that these three hearty fellows were anything but what they seemed—three ordinary, game-playing, suburban Englishmen, wearisome, if you like, but sordidly innocent.

And yet there were three of them; and one was old, and one was plump, and one was lean and dark; and their house chimed in with Scudder’s notes; and half a mile off was lying a steam yacht with at least one German officer. I thought of Karolides lying dead and all Europe trembling on the edge of earthquake, and the men I had left behind me in London who were waiting anxiously for the events of the next hours. There was no doubt that hell was afoot somewhere. The Black Stone had won, and if it survived this June night would bank its winnings.

There seemed only one thing to do—go forward as if I had no doubts, and if I was going to make a fool of myself to do it handsomely. Never in my life have I faced a job with greater disinclination. I would rather in my then mind have walked into a den of anarchists, each with his Browning handy, or faced a charging lion with a popgun, than enter that happy home of three cheerful Englishmen and tell them that their game was up. How they would laugh at me!

But suddenly I remembered a thing I once heard in Rhodesia from old Peter Pienaar. I have quoted Peter already in this narrative. He was the best scout I ever knew, and before he had turned respectable he had been pretty often on the windy side of the law, when he had been wanted badly by the authorities. Peter once discussed with me the question of disguises, and he had a theory which struck me at the time. He said, barring absolute certainties like fingerprints, mere physical traits were very little use for identification if the fugitive really knew his business. He laughed at things like dyed hair and false beards and such childish follies. The only thing that mattered was what Peter called “atmosphere”.
paragraphsZh: 这让我放心了，但当我们划回布拉德盖特时，我顽固的怀疑并没有被消除。让我担心的是，我的敌人知道我是从斯卡德那里得到知识的，而正是斯卡德给了我这个地方的线索。如果他们知道斯卡德有这个线索，他们不就肯定要改变计划了吗？他们的成功很大程度上取决于他们的成功，因此他们无法承担任何风险。整个问题在于他们对斯卡德的知识了解多少。昨晚我曾自信地谈到德国人总是坚持某个计划，但如果他们怀疑我正在追踪他们的踪迹，他们就不去报道它，那他们就是傻瓜了。我想知道昨晚那个男人是否看出我认出了他。不知怎的，我不认为他有，但我一直坚持这一点。但整个事情似乎从未像那天下午那样困难，从各方面来看，我本应为确定的成功而感到高兴。
在旅馆里，我遇到了驱逐舰的指挥官，斯凯夫向他介绍了我，并与他交谈了几句。然后我想我应该花一两个小时观看特拉法加洛奇。

我在山上更远的地方找到了一个地方，在一座空房子的花园里。从那里我可以看到球场的全景，两个人影正在球场上打网球。其中一个是那位老人，我已经见过他了；另一个是我见过的老人。另一个是个年轻小伙子，中间围着俱乐部颜色的围巾。他们玩得很投入，就像两个想要通过剧烈运动来打开毛孔的城市绅士。你无法想象比这更天真无邪的景象了。他们又喊又笑，停下来喝饮料，这时一名女仆从托盘上拿出了两个酒杯。我揉揉眼睛，问自己是不是世界上最不朽的傻瓜。那些乘飞机和汽车在苏格兰荒原上追捕我的人，尤其是那个可恶的古物收藏家，一直笼罩着神秘和黑暗。很容易将这些人与将斯卡德按在地板上的刀联系起来，并与世界和平的邪恶计划联系起来。但这里有两个朴实无华的公民正在进行无害的锻炼，很快就要进屋去吃一顿单调的晚餐，在那里他们会谈论市场价格和最后的板球比分以及他们家乡瑟比顿的八卦。我一直在制作一张网来捕捉秃鹰和猎鹰，你瞧！两只胖乎乎的画眉鸟跌跌撞撞地掉了进去。
不久，第三个人影到来，一个骑着自行车的年轻人，背上背着一袋高尔夫球杆。他漫步来到网球场，受到了球员们的热烈欢迎。显然他们是在嘲笑他，而且他们的嘲笑听起来很糟糕。然后，胖男人用丝帕擦着额头，宣布他必须有一个浴缸。我听到了他的原话——“我已经起了泡沫了，”他说。 “这会减轻我的体重和我的障碍，鲍勃。明天我会带你去比赛，给你一个洞打一杆。”你找不到比这更英语的东西了。
他们都进了屋子，让我感觉自己像一个珍贵的白痴。这次我找错了树。这些人可能是在演戏，也可能是在演戏。但如果是的话，他们的观众在哪里？他们不知道我正坐在三十码外的杜鹃花丛中。简直难以置信，这三个热心的家伙其实和他们看上去的样子不一样——三个普通的、爱玩游戏的郊区英国人，如果你愿意的话，他们很令人厌烦，但他们却非常天真。
然而他们是三个人；一个老了，一个胖了，一个又瘦又黑。他们的房子里响起了斯卡德的音符。半英里外停泊着一艘蒸汽游艇，船上至少有一名德国军官。我想起卡罗利德斯已经死了，整个欧洲都在地震的边缘颤抖，而我留在伦敦的那些人正在焦急地等待接下来几个小时的事件。毫无疑问，地狱正在某处发生。黑石赢了，如果它能在这个六月的夜晚幸存下来，它的奖金就会存入银行。
似乎只有一件事要做——向前迈进，就好像我毫无疑问一样，如果我要出丑的话，也要做得漂亮。在我的一生中，我从来没有遇到过比这更令人厌恶的工作。在我当时的脑海里，我宁愿走进一个无政府主义者的巢穴，每个人都拿着他的勃朗宁，或者面对一头拿着爆弹枪的狮子，也不愿走进那个由三个快乐的英国人组成的幸福之家，告诉他们他们的游戏已经结束了。他们会多么嘲笑我啊！

但突然我想起了我曾经在罗德西亚从老彼得·皮纳尔那里听到的一件事。我已经在这篇叙述中引用了彼得的话。他是我认识的最好的侦察员，在他变得受人尊敬之前，当他被当局通缉时，他经常处于法律的不利地位。彼得曾经和我讨论过伪装的问题，他有一个理论让我当时印象深刻。他说，除非有指纹等绝对确定的信息，如果逃亡者真的了解自己的生意，那么单纯的身体特征对于识别身份来说几乎没有什么用处。他嘲笑染头发、假胡须等幼稚的愚蠢行为。唯一重要的是彼得所说的“气氛”。

title: A Little Princess
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: To which Lottie agreed quite cheerfully, and trotted out of the room and upstairs with her, without seeming even to remember that the whole of the last hour's tragedy had been caused by the fact that she had refused to be washed and brushed for lunch and Miss Minchin had been called in to use her majestic authority.

Of course the greatest power Sara possessed and the one which gained her even more followers than her luxuries and the fact that she was "the show pupil," the power that Lavinia and certain other girls were most envious of, and at the same time most fascinated by in spite of themselves, was her power of telling stories and of making everything she talked about seem like a story, whether it was one or not.

Anyone who has been at school with a teller of stories knows what the wonder means--how he or she is followed about and besought in a whisper to relate romances; how groups gather round and hang on the outskirts of the favored party in the hope of being allowed to join in and listen.  Sara not only could tell stories, but she adored telling them. When she sat or stood in the midst of a circle and began to invent wonderful things, her green eyes grew big and shining, her cheeks flushed, and, without knowing that she was doing it, she began to act and made what she told lovely or alarming by the raising or dropping of her voice, the bend and sway of her slim body, and the dramatic movement of her hands. She forgot that she was talking to listening children; she saw and lived with the fairy folk, or the kings and queens and beautiful ladies, whose adventures she was narrating. Sometimes when she had finished her story, she was quite out of breath with excitement, and would lay her hand on her thin, little, quick-rising chest, and half laugh as if at herself.

"When I am telling it," she would say, "it doesn't seem as if it was only made up.  It seems more real than you are--more real than the schoolroom.  I feel as if I were all the people in the story--one after the other.  It is queer."

She had been at Miss Minchin's school about two years when, one foggy winter's afternoon, as she was getting out of her carriage, comfortably wrapped up in her warmest velvets and furs and looking very much grander than she knew, she caught sight, as she crossed the pavement, of a dingy little figure standing on the area steps, and stretching its neck so that its wide-open eyes might peer at her through the railings. Something in the eagerness and timidity of the smudgy face made her look at it, and when she looked she smiled because it was her way to smile at people.

But the owner of the smudgy face and the wide-open eyes evidently was afraid that she ought not to have been caught looking at pupils of importance.  She dodged out of sight like a jack-in-the-box and scurried back into the kitchen, disappearing so suddenly that if she had not been such a poor little forlorn thing, Sara would have laughed in spite of herself.  That very evening, as Sara was sitting in the midst of a group of listeners in a corner of the schoolroom telling one of her stories, the very same figure timidly entered the room, carrying a coal box much too heavy for her, and knelt down upon the hearth rug to replenish the fire and sweep up the ashes.

She was cleaner than she had been when she peeped through the area railings, but she looked just as frightened.  She was evidently afraid to look at the children or seem to be listening. She put on pieces of coal cautiously with her fingers so that she might make no disturbing noise, and she swept about the fire irons very softly.  But Sara saw in two minutes that she was deeply interested in what was going on, and that she was doing her work slowly in the hope of catching a word here and there. And realizing this, she raised her voice and spoke more clearly.
"The Mermaids swam softly about in the crystal-green water, and dragged after them a fishing-net woven of deep-sea pearls," she said.  "The Princess sat on the white rock and watched them."
It was a wonderful story about a princess who was loved by a Prince Merman, and went to live with him in shining caves under the sea.

The small drudge before the grate swept the hearth once and then swept it again.  Having done it twice, she did it three times; and, as she was doing it the third time, the sound of the story so lured her to listen that she fell under the spell and actually forgot that she had no right to listen at all, and also forgot everything else. She sat down upon her heels as she knelt on the hearth rug, and the brush hung idly in her fingers.  The voice of the storyteller went on and drew her with it into winding grottos under the sea, glowing with soft, clear blue light, and paved with pure golden sands. Strange sea flowers and grasses waved about her, and far away faint singing and music echoed.
paragraphsZh: 洛蒂很高兴地同意了，然后小跑着走出房间，和她一起上楼，似乎根本不记得最后一小时的悲剧是由于她拒绝洗澡和刷牙吃午饭而造成的，明钦小姐被叫来使用她的威严。
当然，莎拉所拥有的最伟大的力量，以及比她的奢侈品和她是“表演学生”这一事实为她赢得更多追随者的力量，拉维尼娅和其他某些女孩最羡慕的力量，同时也是最令她们着迷的力量，就是她讲故事的力量，以及让她谈论的一切看起来像一个故事的力量，无论它是否是一个故事。

任何一个在学校里和讲故事的人在一起的人都知道这意味着什么——他或她如何被跟踪并低声恳求讲述浪漫故事；团体如何聚集在受青睐一方的郊区，希望能够加入并倾听。 萨拉不仅会讲故事，而且还喜欢讲故事。当她坐在或站在一个圆圈中间，开始发明奇妙的东西时，她的绿眼睛变得又大又闪亮，脸颊通红，在不知不觉中，她开始行动，通过声音的升高或降低、苗条身体的弯曲和摇摆以及双手的戏剧性动作，使她所说的变得可爱或令人震惊。她忘记了自己是在和倾听的孩子们说话；她看到并与仙女、国王、王后和美丽的女士们一起生活，她正在讲述他们的冒险经历。有时，她讲完故事后，激动得上气不接下气，就把手放在那瘦小、快速挺起的胸口上，半笑半笑，仿佛在自嘲。
“当我讲这个故事时，”她会说，“它看起来并不只是编造的。它看起来比你更真实——比教室更真实。我觉得我好像就是故事中的所有人——一个接一个。这很奇怪。”
她在明钦小姐的学校就读大约两年了，一个有雾的冬日下午，当她从马车里下来时，舒适地裹着最温暖的天鹅绒和毛皮，看起来比她想象的要宏伟得多，当她穿过人行道时，她看到一个肮脏的小身影站在区域台阶上，伸长脖子，以便它睁大的眼睛可以透过栏杆看着她。那张脏兮兮的脸上的急切和胆怯让她看了一眼，当她看的时候，她笑了，因为这是她对人微笑的方式。
但那张脏兮兮的脸和睁大的眼睛的主人显然是担心她不应该被人发现在看重要的瞳孔。 她像个玩偶盒子一样躲开视线，然后急匆匆地跑回厨房，消失得那么突然，如果她不是一个可怜的、被遗弃的小东西，莎拉一定会不由自主地笑起来。 那天晚上，当萨拉坐在教室一角的一群听众中间讲述她的一个故事时，同一个人胆怯地走进房间，提着一个对她来说太重的煤箱，跪在壁炉地毯上补充火并扫灰。
她比透过栏杆往外看时干净多了，但她看起来同样害怕。 她显然不敢看孩子们，也不敢听他们讲话。她小心翼翼地用手指放上煤块，以免发出令人不安的声音，然后非常轻柔地扫动熨斗。 但萨拉在两分钟内就发现她对正在发生的事情非常感兴趣，并且她正在慢慢地做她的工作，希望能听到一些单词。意识到这一点，她提高了声音，说得更清楚。
“美人鱼在碧绿的海水中轻轻游动，身后拖着一张深海珍珠编织的渔网，”她说。 “公主坐在白色的岩石上看着他们。”
这是一个关于一位公主的精彩故事，她被人鱼王子所爱，并与他一起住在海底闪亮的洞穴里。
炉排前的小苦力把炉灶扫了一遍，又扫了一遍。 做了两次之后，她又做了第三次；当她第三遍的时候，故事的声音如此引诱她去听，以至于她被迷住了，实际上忘记了她根本没有权利听，也忘记了其他一切。她跪在炉边地毯上，脚后跟坐下，刷子闲散地挂在她的手指上。 说书人的声音继续说着，带着她走进了海底蜿蜒的洞穴，闪烁着柔和、清澈的蓝色光芒，铺满了纯金色的沙子。奇异的海花海草在她身边摇曳，远处隐约传来歌声和音乐。

title: A Little Princess · 选段 2
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: "She doesn't understand why Lottie is doing her sums so well," she said; "but it is because she creeps up here, too, and I help her." She glanced round the room.  "The attic would be rather nice--if it wasn't so dreadful," she said, laughing again.  "It's a good place to pretend in."

The truth was that Ermengarde did not know anything of the sometimes almost unbearable side of life in the attic and she had not a sufficiently vivid imagination to depict it for herself. On the rare occasions that she could reach Sara's room she only saw the side of it which was made exciting by things which were "pretended" and stories which were told.  Her visits partook of the character of adventures; and though sometimes Sara looked rather pale, and it was not to be denied that she had grown very thin, her proud little spirit would not admit of complaints. She had never confessed that at times she was almost ravenous with hunger, as she was tonight.  She was growing rapidly, and her constant walking and running about would have given her a keen appetite even if she had had abundant and regular meals of a much more nourishing nature than the unappetizing, inferior food snatched at such odd times as suited the kitchen convenience. She was growing used to a certain gnawing feeling in her young stomach.

"I suppose soldiers feel like this when they are on a long and weary march," she often said to herself.  She liked the sound of the phrase, "long and weary march."  It made her feel rather like a soldier. She had also a quaint sense of being a hostess in the attic.

"If I lived in a castle," she argued, "and Ermengarde was the lady of another castle, and came to see me, with knights and squires and vassals riding with her, and pennons flying, when I heard the clarions sounding outside the drawbridge I should go down to receive her, and I should spread feasts in the banquet hall and call in minstrels to sing and play and relate romances.  When she comes into the attic I can't spread feasts, but I can tell stories, and not let her know disagreeable things.  I dare say poor chatelaines had to do that in time of famine, when their lands had been pillaged." She was a proud, brave little chatelaine, and dispensed generously the one hospitality she could offer--the dreams she dreamed--the visions she saw--the imaginings which were her joy and comfort.

So, as they sat together, Ermengarde did not know that she was faint as well as ravenous, and that while she talked she now and then wondered if her hunger would let her sleep when she was left alone. She felt as if she had never been quite so hungry before.
"I wish I was as thin as you, Sara," Ermengarde said suddenly.  "I believe you are thinner than you used to be.  Your eyes look so big, and look at the sharp little bones sticking out of your elbow!"

"I love your queer eyes," said Ermengarde, looking into them with affectionate admiration.  "They always look as if they saw such a long way.  I love them--and I love them to be green--though they look black generally."

It was just at this minute that something happened at the skylight which neither of them saw.  If either of them had chanced to turn and look, she would have been startled by the sight of a dark face which peered cautiously into the room and disappeared as quickly and almost as silently as it had appeared.  Not QUITE as silently, however.  Sara, who had keen ears, suddenly turned a little and looked up at the roof.
"Perhaps I didn't," said Sara; "but I thought I did.  It sounded as if something was on the slates--something that dragged softly."

She broke off in the middle of her words.  They both heard the sound that checked her.  It was not on the slates, but on the stairs below, and it was Miss Minchin's angry voice.  Sara sprang off the bed, and put out the candle.
