Look closely, however, and you may note that there are here seven large trees, each with a hole in its hollow trunk as large as a boy. These are the seven entrances to the home under the ground, for which Hook has been searching in vain these many moons. Will he find it tonight?
paragraphsZh: 现在让我们杀死一个海盗，来展示胡克的方法。天窗就可以了。当他们经过时，天窗笨拙地靠在他身上，弄乱了他的蕾丝衣领。钩子射出，一声撕裂声和一声尖叫，然后尸体被踢到一边，海盗们继续前行。他甚至没有从嘴里取出雪茄。

在海盗的踪迹中，红皮们悄无声息地沿着没有经验的眼睛看不见的战争路线悄悄走来，他们每个人都睁着眼睛。他们携带战斧和刀子，赤裸的身体因油漆和油而闪闪发光。他们周围挂着男孩和海盗的头皮，因为他们是皮卡尼尼部落，不要与心肠软弱的特拉华人或休伦人混淆。货车里趴着的是大大小小的黑豹，他是一只勇敢的人，有这么多的头皮，以他目前的位置，这些头皮在某种程度上阻碍了他的前进。冲在最后，最危险的地方，是虎百合，骄傲地挺立着，她本身就是一位公主。她是肤色黝黑的戴安娜中最美丽的一个，也是皮卡尼尼家族中最美丽的一个，时而风骚，时而冷漠，时而多情。没有一个勇敢的人不会有任性的妻子，但她却用斧头避开了祭坛。观察它们如何越过倒下的树枝而不发出丝毫声音。唯一能听到的就是他们有些粗重的呼吸声。事实上，在大吃大喝之后，他们现在都有点胖了，但随着时间的推移，他们会解决这个问题。然而，就目前而言，这构成了他们的主要危险。
红皮人像影子一样来时就消失了，很快他们的位置就被野兽取代了，这是一个庞大而杂乱的队伍：狮子、老虎、熊，以及无数逃离它们的较小的野蛮生物，因为各种野兽，更具体地说，所有的食人动物，都在这个受青睐的岛屿上紧密地生活在一起。他们的舌头伸出来，他们今晚很饿。
当他们过去后，出现了最后一个人物，一只巨大的鳄鱼。我们要看看她现在在找谁。
鳄鱼经过，但很快男孩们又出现了，因为游行队伍必须无限期地继续下去，直到其中一方停止或改变步伐。然后很快他们就会互相超越。
所有人都在警惕地注视着前方，但没有人怀疑危险可能正在从后面悄悄袭来。由此可见这座岛屿是多么真实。
最先跌出移动圈的是男生们。他们扑倒在靠近地下家园的草地上。
“我真希望彼得能回来。”他们每个人都紧张地说，尽管他们的身高和宽度都比他们的队长还要大。
只有在彼得缺席的情况下，他们才能谈论母亲，这个话题被他认为很愚蠢而禁止。
当他们说话时，他们听到远处有声音。你或我，不是森林里的野兽，不会听到任何声音，但他们听到了，那是一首阴森的歌：
失踪的男孩们立刻——但他们在哪里？他们已经不在那儿了。兔子消失得太快了。

我会告诉你他们在哪里。除了跑去侦察的尼布斯之外，他们都已经在地下的家中了，这是一个非常令人愉快的住所，我们很快就会看到很多。但他们是如何达到这个目标的呢？因为看不到任何入口，连一块大石头也看不到，如果把它滚开，就会露出洞口。然而，仔细观察，你可能会发现这里有七棵大树，每棵树的中空树干上都有一个像男孩那么大的洞。这些是通往地下家园的七个入口，胡克在月球上一直在寻找这些入口，但始终没有成功。今晚他能找到吗？

title: Peter Pan · 选段 7
author: J. M. Barrie
paragraphs: “I heard nothing,” said Starkey, raising the lantern over the waters, and as the pirates looked they saw a strange sight. It was the nest I have told you of, floating on the lagoon, and the Never bird was sitting on it.
“See,” said Hook in answer to Smee’s question, “that is a mother. What a lesson! The nest must have fallen into the water, but would the mother desert her eggs? No.”
There was a break in his voice, as if for a moment he recalled innocent days when—but he brushed away this weakness with his hook.

“It is a princely scheme,” cried Hook, and at once it took practical shape in his great brain. “We will seize the children and carry them to the boat: the boys we will make walk the plank, and Wendy shall be our mother.”
But they could see nothing. They thought it must have been a leaf in the wind. “Do you agree, my bullies?” asked Hook.

“Brimstone and gall,” thundered Hook, “what cozening is going on here!” His face had gone black with rage, but he saw that they believed their words, and he was startled. “Lads,” he said, shaking a little, “I gave no such order.”
“It is passing queer,” Smee said, and they all fidgeted uncomfortably. Hook raised his voice, but there was a quiver in it.
Of course Peter should have kept quiet, but of course he did not. He immediately answered in Hook’s voice:
In that supreme moment Hook did not blanch, even at the gills, but Smee and Starkey clung to each other in terror.
Hook tried a more ingratiating manner. “If you are Hook,” he said almost humbly, “come tell me, who am I?”
“A codfish!” Hook echoed blankly, and it was then, but not till then, that his proud spirit broke. He saw his men draw back from him.

They were his dogs snapping at him, but, tragic figure though he had become, he scarcely heeded them. Against such fearful evidence it was not their belief in him that he needed, it was his own. He felt his ego slipping from him. “Don’t desert me, bully,” he whispered hoarsely to it.
In his dark nature there was a touch of the feminine, as in all the great pirates, and it sometimes gave him intuitions. Suddenly he tried the guessing game.
Hook was completely puzzled. “You ask him some questions,” he said to the others, wiping his damp brow.
“Now we have him,” Hook shouted. “Into the water, Smee. Starkey, mind the boat. Take him dead or alive!”

The fight was short and sharp. First to draw blood was John, who gallantly climbed into the boat and held Starkey. There was fierce struggle, in which the cutlass was torn from the pirate’s grasp. He wriggled overboard and John leapt after him. The dinghy drifted away.

Here and there a head bobbed up in the water, and there was a flash of steel followed by a cry or a whoop. In the confusion some struck at their own side. The corkscrew of Smee got Tootles in the fourth rib, but he was himself pinked in turn by Curly. Farther from the rock Starkey was pressing Slightly and the twins hard.
The others were all brave boys, and they must not be blamed for backing from the pirate captain. His iron claw made a circle of dead water round him, from which they fled like affrighted fishes.

Strangely, it was not in the water that they met. Hook rose to the rock to breathe, and at the same moment Peter scaled it on the opposite side. The rock was slippery as a ball, and they had to crawl rather than climb. Neither knew that the other was coming. Each feeling for a grip met the other’s arm: in surprise they raised their heads; their faces were almost touching; so they met.
paragraphsZh: “我什么也没听到，”斯塔基一边说，一边在水面上举起灯笼，当海盗们看去时，他们看到了奇怪的景象。这就是我告诉过你的鸟巢，漂浮在泻湖上，永不鸟坐在上面。
“看，”胡克在回答斯密的问题时说道，“那是一位母亲。这是一个多么好的教训啊！鸟巢肯定掉进了水里，但是母亲会抛弃她的蛋吗？不会。”
他的声音有些断断续续，仿佛有一瞬间他回忆起了天真无邪的日子——但他用钩子扫掉了这个弱点。
“这是一个高贵的计划，”胡克喊道，这个计划立即在他伟大的大脑中成形。 “我们会抓住孩子们，把他们带到船上：我们会让男孩们走上木板，温迪将成为我们的母亲。”
但他们什么也看不见。他们认为那一定是风中的一片叶子。 “你们同意吗，我的恶霸们？”胡克问道。
“硫磺和胆汁，”胡克雷鸣般地说，“这里发生了什么事！”他的脸已经气得黑了，但见他们相信了自己的话，他心中一惊。 “伙计们，”他说，身体微微颤抖，“我没有下达这样的命令。”
“这真是太奇怪了，”斯密说，他们都不安地坐立不安。胡克提高了声音，但声音里带着颤抖。
彼得当然应该保持沉默，但他当然没有。他立即用胡克的声音回答：
在那个至高无上的时刻，胡克没有脸色变白，甚至连鳃都没有变白，但斯密和斯塔基却惊恐地抱在一起。
胡克尝试了一种更讨好的方式。 “如果你是胡克，”他几乎谦虚地说，“请告诉我，我是谁？”
“鳕鱼！”胡克茫然地应了一声，就在那时，但直到那时，他骄傲的精神才崩溃了。他看到他的手下从他身边退开。
他们是他的狗，正在扑向他，但是，尽管他变成了悲剧人物，他却几乎没有理睬它们。面对如此可怕的证据，他需要的不是他们对他的信任，而是他自己的信任。他感到他的自我意识正在从他身上消失。 “别抛弃我，恶霸。”他嘶哑地对它低声说道。
在他黑暗的本性中，有一丝女性的气息，就像所有伟大的海盗一样，这有时给了他直觉。突然他尝试了猜谜游戏。
胡克完全困惑了。 “你们问他一些问题，”他对其他人说，擦了擦湿漉漉的额头。
“现在我们抓住了他，”胡克喊道。 “下水吧，斯密。斯塔基，看好船。不管他是死是活，都要把他杀死！”
战斗短暂而激烈。第一个抽血的是约翰，他英勇地爬上船并抓住了斯塔基。经过一番激烈的搏斗，海盗手中的弯刀被夺走了。他扭动着跳下船，约翰也跟着跳了下去。小艇漂走了。
时不时地有一个头在水中浮起，伴随着一声钢铁闪光，然后是一声尖叫或一声呼喊。在混乱中，有些人站到了自己一边。斯米的开瓶器击中了图特尔斯的第四根肋骨，但他自己也被科利粉红了。距离岩石更远的地方，斯塔基正用力地压着斯莱特利和双胞胎。
其他人都是勇敢的孩子，不能怪他们得到了海盗船长的支持。他的铁爪在他周围形成了一圈死水，他们像受惊的鱼一样逃离了死水。
奇怪的是，他们并不是在水里相遇的。胡克爬到岩石上呼吸，与此同时，彼得也从对面爬了上去。岩石像球一样滑，他们不得不爬行而不是攀爬。两人都不知道对方会来。每一次握紧的感觉都与对方的手臂相遇：惊讶地抬起头；他们的脸几乎贴在一起了。于是他们相遇了。

title: Peter Pan · 选段 8
author: J. M. Barrie
paragraphs: Steadily the waters rose till they were nibbling at his feet; and to pass the time until they made their final gulp, he watched the only thing on the lagoon. He thought it was a piece of floating paper, perhaps part of the kite, and wondered idly how long it would take to drift ashore.

Presently he noticed as an odd thing that it was undoubtedly out upon the lagoon with some definite purpose, for it was fighting the tide, and sometimes winning; and when it won, Peter, always sympathetic to the weaker side, could not help clapping; it was such a gallant piece of paper.

It was not really a piece of paper; it was the Never bird, making desperate efforts to reach Peter on the nest. By working her wings, in a way she had learned since the nest fell into the water, she was able to some extent to guide her strange craft, but by the time Peter recognised her she was very exhausted. She had come to save him, to give him her nest, though there were eggs in it. I rather wonder at the bird, for though he had been nice to her, he had also sometimes tormented her. I can suppose only that, like Mrs. Darling and the rest of them, she was melted because he had all his first teeth.

She called out to him what she had come for, and he called out to her what she was doing there; but of course neither of them understood the other’s language. In fanciful stories people can talk to the birds freely, and I wish for the moment I could pretend that this were such a story, and say that Peter replied intelligently to the Never bird; but truth is best, and I want to tell you only what really happened. Well, not only could they not understand each other, but they forgot their manners.

Nevertheless the bird was determined to save him if she could, and by one last mighty effort she propelled the nest against the rock. Then up she flew; deserting her eggs, so as to make her meaning clear.

Then at last he understood, and clutched the nest and waved his thanks to the bird as she fluttered overhead. It was not to receive his thanks, however, that she hung there in the sky; it was not even to watch him get into the nest; it was to see what he did with her eggs.

There were two large white eggs, and Peter lifted them up and reflected. The bird covered her face with her wings, so as not to see the last of them; but she could not help peeping between the feathers.

I forget whether I have told you that there was a stave on the rock, driven into it by some buccaneers of long ago to mark the site of buried treasure. The children had discovered the glittering hoard, and when in a mischievous mood used to fling showers of moidores, diamonds, pearls and pieces of eight to the gulls, who pounced upon them for food, and then flew away, raging at the scurvy trick that had been played upon them. The stave was still there, and on it Starkey had hung his hat, a deep tarpaulin, watertight, with a broad brim. Peter put the eggs into this hat and set it on the lagoon. It floated beautifully.

The Never bird saw at once what he was up to, and screamed her admiration of him; and, alas, Peter crowed his agreement with her. Then he got into the nest, reared the stave in it as a mast, and hung up his shirt for a sail. At the same moment the bird fluttered down upon the hat and once more sat snugly on her eggs. She drifted in one direction, and he was borne off in another, both cheering.
paragraphsZh: 水渐渐上涨，直到侵蚀他的脚；为了打发时间，直到他们最后咽下一口，他看着泻湖上唯一的东西。他以为那是一张漂浮的纸，也许是风筝的一部分，并漫不经心地想知道​​要花多长时间才能漂到岸上。
不久，他注意到一件奇怪的事情，毫无疑问，它出现在泻湖上有某种明确的目的，因为它正在对抗潮水，有时甚至获胜;当它获胜时，一向同情弱者的彼得忍不住鼓起掌来。这是一张多么华丽的纸啊。
这实际上并不是一张纸；它是一张纸。那是从未有过的鸟，拼尽全力想要到达巢穴上的彼得。通过运作她的翅膀，以一种自从巢落入水中她就学会的方式，她能够在某种程度上引导她奇怪的飞行器，但当彼得认出她时，她已经非常疲惫了。她是来救他的，给他自己的巢，尽管里面有蛋。我对那只鸟感到很奇怪，因为虽然他对她很好，但有时也会折磨她。我只能猜测，就像达林太太和其他人一样，她被融化了，因为他长出了第一颗牙齿。
她向他喊出她来这里的目的，他也向她喊出她在那里做什么；但当然，他们都听不懂对方的语言。在奇特的故事中，人们可以自由地与鸟儿交谈，我希望此刻我可以假装这是这样一个故事，并说彼得聪明地回答了那只从未见过的鸟；但事实是最好的，我只想告诉你真正发生的事情。好吧，他们不仅无法理解对方，还忘记了礼貌。
尽管如此，这只鸟决心尽可能地拯救他，并通过最后的巨大努力，她将巢推到了岩石上。然后她飞了起来；抛弃她的蛋，以便明确她的意思。
然后他终于明白了，抓住鸟巢，向鸟儿挥手致谢，鸟儿在头顶上扑腾着翅膀。然而，她挂在天上并不是为了接受他的感谢。甚至不是为了看着他进入巢穴；是为了看看他对她的蛋做了什么。
有两个白色的大蛋，彼得把它们举起来思考。那只鸟用翅膀遮住了脸，以免看到最后一个。但她还是忍不住往羽毛之间偷看。
我忘了我是否告诉过你，岩石上有一根木棍，很久以前被一些海盗打入其中，以标记埋藏宝藏的地点。孩子们发现了闪闪发光的宝藏，当心情不好时，他们习惯性地向海鸥扔大量的莫多雷、钻石、珍珠和八块碎片，海鸥扑向他们寻找食物，然后飞走了，对他们所玩的坏血病把戏感到愤怒。木棍还在那儿，斯塔基把帽子挂在上面，那是一顶深防水布，防水，宽边。彼得把鸡蛋放进这顶帽子里，然后把它放在泻湖上。它飘得很漂亮。
从未有过的鸟立刻就明白了他的意图，尖叫着表达了她对他的钦佩；唉，彼得高调同意了她的观点。然后他钻进鸟巢，把里面的木板竖起来当桅杆，把衬衫挂起来当帆。与此同时，小鸟扑通扑通地落在帽子上，再次紧紧地坐在她的蛋上。她朝一个方向飘去，而他则朝另一个方向飞去，两人都欢呼雀跃。

title: Peter Pan · 选段 9
author: J. M. Barrie
paragraphs: A few of the pirates leant over the bulwarks, drinking in the miasma of the night; others sprawled by barrels over games of dice and cards; and the exhausted four who had carried the little house lay prone on the deck, where even in their sleep they rolled skillfully to this side or that out of Hook’s reach, lest he should claw them mechanically in passing.

Hook trod the deck in thought. O man unfathomable. It was his hour of triumph. Peter had been removed for ever from his path, and all the other boys were in the brig, about to walk the plank. It was his grimmest deed since the days when he had brought Barbecue to heel; and knowing as we do how vain a tabernacle is man, could we be surprised had he now paced the deck unsteadily, bellied out by the winds of his success?
But there was no elation in his gait, which kept pace with the action of his sombre mind. Hook was profoundly dejected.

He was often thus when communing with himself on board ship in the quietude of the night. It was because he was so terribly alone. This inscrutable man never felt more alone than when surrounded by his dogs. They were socially inferior to him.

Hook was not his true name. To reveal who he really was would even at this date set the country in a blaze; but as those who read between the lines must already have guessed, he had been at a famous public school; and its traditions still clung to him like garments, with which indeed they are largely concerned. Thus it was offensive to him even now to board a ship in the same dress in which he grappled her, and he still adhered in his walk to the school’s distinguished slouch. But above all he retained the passion for good form.
Good form! However much he may have degenerated, he still knew that this is all that really matters.

From far within him he heard a creaking as of rusty portals, and through them came a stern tap-tap-tap, like hammering in the night when one cannot sleep. “Have you been good form to-day?” was their eternal question.

His vitals were tortured by this problem. It was a claw within him sharper than the iron one; and as it tore him, the perspiration dripped down his tallow countenance and streaked his doublet. Ofttimes he drew his sleeve across his face, but there was no damming that trickle.

There came to him a presentiment of his early dissolution. It was as if Peter’s terrible oath had boarded the ship. Hook felt a gloomy desire to make his dying speech, lest presently there should be no time for it.
“Better for Hook,” he cried, “if he had had less ambition!” It was in his darkest hours only that he referred to himself in the third person.

Strange that he should think of this, which had never troubled him before; perhaps the sewing machine brought it to his mind. For long he muttered to himself, staring at Smee, who was hemming placidly, under the conviction that all children feared him.

Feared him! Feared Smee! There was not a child on board the brig that night who did not already love him. He had said horrid things to them and hit them with the palm of his hand, because he could not hit with his fist, but they had only clung to him the more. Michael had tried on his spectacles.

To tell poor Smee that they thought him lovable! Hook itched to do it, but it seemed too brutal. Instead, he revolved this mystery in his mind: why do they find Smee lovable? He pursued the problem like the sleuth-hound that he was. If Smee was lovable, what was it that made him so? A terrible answer suddenly presented itself—“Good form?”
paragraphsZh: 一些海盗靠在舷墙上，喝着夜晚的瘴气；其他人则趴在桶边玩骰子和纸牌游戏；搬运小房子的四个人筋疲力尽地躺在甲板上，即使在睡梦中，他们也熟练地滚到胡克够不到的地方，以免他在路过时机械地抓起他们。
胡克在甲板上沉思。噢，深不可测的人。这是他胜利的时刻。彼得已经永远离开了他的道路，所有其他男孩都在双桅船里，正要走木板。这是他自从让烧烤业屈服以来最残酷的行为。正如我们所知，人的圣体是多么虚荣，如果他现在在甲板上摇摇晃晃地踱步，被他的成功之风吹得精疲力尽，我们会感到惊讶吗？
但他的步态中没有任何兴高采烈的情绪，这与他阴沉的思想的行动保持同步。胡克深感沮丧。
在夜深人静的船上，他经常这样自言自语。这是因为他实在是太孤独了。这个神秘的男人从来没有比被他的狗包围时感到更孤独的了。他们在社会地位上不如他。
胡克不是他的真名。即使在这个时候，揭露他的真实身份也会让整个国家陷入大火。但那些从字里行间读到的人一定已经猜到了，他曾就读于一所著名的公立学校。它的传统仍然像衣服一样紧紧地贴在他身上，他们确实非常关心这一点。因此，即使是现在，穿着他抓住她时穿的那件衣服登上一艘船，对他来说也是一种冒犯，而且他走路时仍然坚持学校特有的懒散的风格。但最重要的是，他保留了对良好状态的热情。
状态好！无论他堕落到什么程度，他仍然知道这才是真正重要的。
他听到内心深处传来一阵吱吱作响的声音，就像是生锈的传送门发出的，从门缝里传来一阵严厉的敲击声，就像夜里睡不着觉时的敲击声。 “你今天状态好吗？”是他们永恒的问题。
他的生命体受到这个问题的折磨。他体内有一只比铁爪更锋利的爪子。当它撕扯着他时，汗水从他油脂般的脸上滴下来，流淌在他的紧身衣上。他时常用袖子遮住脸，但那股细流却无法阻挡。
他预感到自己早早解体了。就好像彼得的可怕誓言已经登上了船。胡克隐隐约约地想要发表临终演讲，生怕现在没有时间了。
“对胡克来说更好，”他喊道，“如果他没有那么大的野心！”只有在他最黑暗的时刻，他才会以第三人称来称呼自己。
奇怪的是，他会想到这个，这以前从未困扰过他；也许是缝纫机让他想到了这一点。他盯着斯密，自言自语了很长一段时间，斯密正在平静地支支吾吾，相信所有的孩子都害怕他。
怕他！害怕斯密！那天晚上，双桅船上没有一个孩子不爱他。他对他们说了一些可怕的话，并用手掌打他们，因为他不能用拳头打，但他们只是更紧地粘着他。迈克尔试戴过他的眼镜。
告诉可怜的 Smee，他们认为他很可爱！胡克很想这么做，但这似乎太残酷了。相反，他在心里盘旋着这个谜团：为什么他们觉得斯密可爱？他像侦探猎犬一样追寻这个问题。如果斯密很可爱，那么是什么让他如此可爱呢？一个可怕的答案突然出现——“状态不错？”

title: Peter Pan · 选段 10
author: J. M. Barrie
paragraphs: Fine gentlemen though he was, the intensity of his communings had soiled his ruff, and suddenly he knew that she was gazing at it. With a hasty gesture he tried to hide it, but he was too late.
“They are,” he snarled. “Silence all,” he called gloatingly, “for a mother’s last words to her children.”

At this moment Wendy was grand. “These are my last words, dear boys,” she said firmly. “I feel that I have a message to you from your real mothers, and it is this: ‘We hope our sons will die like English gentlemen.’”
Even the pirates were awed, and Tootles cried out hysterically, “I am going to do what my mother hopes. What are you to do, Nibs?”
It was Smee who tied her to the mast. “See here, honey,” he whispered, “I’ll save you if you promise to be my mother.”
But not even for Smee would she make such a promise. “I would almost rather have no children at all,” she said disdainfully.

It is sad to know that not a boy was looking at her as Smee tied her to the mast; the eyes of all were on the plank: that last little walk they were about to take. They were no longer able to hope that they would walk it manfully, for the capacity to think had gone from them; they could stare and shiver only.

Hook smiled on them with his teeth closed, and took a step toward Wendy. His intention was to turn her face so that she should see the boys walking the plank one by one. But he never reached her, he never heard the cry of anguish he hoped to wring from her. He heard something else instead.

They all heard it—pirates, boys, Wendy; and immediately every head was blown in one direction; not to the water whence the sound proceeded, but toward Hook. All knew that what was about to happen concerned him alone, and that from being actors they were suddenly become spectators.
Very frightful was it to see the change that came over him. It was as if he had been clipped at every joint. He fell in a little heap.

Even the iron claw hung inactive; as if knowing that it was no intrinsic part of what the attacking force wanted. Left so fearfully alone, any other man would have lain with his eyes shut where he fell: but the gigantic brain of Hook was still working, and under its guidance he crawled on the knees along the deck as far from the sound as he could go. The pirates respectfully cleared a passage for him, and it was only when he brought up against the bulwarks that he spoke.
They gathered round him, all eyes averted from the thing that was coming aboard. They had no thought of fighting it. It was Fate.

Only when Hook was hidden from them did curiosity loosen the limbs of the boys so that they could rush to the ship’s side to see the crocodile climbing it. Then they got the strangest surprise of the Night of Nights; for it was no crocodile that was coming to their aid. It was Peter.
He signed to them not to give vent to any cry of admiration that might rouse suspicion. Then he went on ticking.

Odd things happen to all of us on our way through life without our noticing for a time that they have happened. Thus, to take an instance, we suddenly discover that we have been deaf in one ear for we don’t know how long, but, say, half an hour. Now such an experience had come that night to Peter. When last we saw him he was stealing across the island with one finger to his lips and his dagger at the ready. He had seen the crocodile pass by without noticing anything peculiar about it, but by and by he remembered that it had not been ticking. At first he thought this eerie, but soon concluded rightly that the clock had run down.
paragraphsZh: 尽管他是一位优秀的绅士，但他的交流强度弄脏了他的领子，突然他知道她正在凝视它。他急忙想掩饰自己的想法，但为时已晚。
“他们是，”他咆哮道。 “全体安静，”他幸灾乐祸地喊道，“听听一位母亲对孩子们说的最后一句话。”
这一刻的温蒂很伟大。 “这是我的最后一句话，亲爱的孩子们，”她坚定地说。 “我觉得我从你的亲生母亲那里给你传达了一条信息，那就是：‘我们希望我们的儿子能像英国绅士一样死去。’”
连海盗们都敬畏不已，图图歇斯底里地喊道：“我要做我妈妈希望的事。你要做什么，尼布斯？”
是斯密把她绑在桅杆上的。 “看这里，亲爱的，”他低声说道，“如果你答应做我的母亲，我就会救你。”
但即使是对于 Smee，她也不会做出这样的承诺。 “我几乎宁愿没有孩子，”她轻蔑地说。
令人难过的是，当斯密将她绑在桅杆上时，没有一个男孩在看着她；所有人的目光都集中在木板上：这是他们即将进行的最后一段步行。他们不再希望自己能勇敢地走下去，因为他们已经失去了思考的能力。他们只能凝视着，颤抖着。
胡克咬紧牙关对他们笑了笑，朝温蒂走了一步。他的目的是把她的脸转过来，让她看到男孩们一一走在木板上。但他从未联系到她，也从未听到他希望从她身上榨取的痛苦呼喊。相反，他听到了别的声音。
他们都听到了——海盗、男孩、温迪；立刻，每个人的头都被吹向一个方向。不是朝着声音发出的水域，而是朝着胡克。所有人都知道，即​​将发生的事情只与他一人有关，他们从演员突然变成了观众。
看到他身上发生的变化非常可怕。就好像他的每个关节都被夹住了。他摔成了一小堆。
连铁爪都挂着不动；就好像知道这不是进攻方想要的内在部分。留下如此可怕的孤独，任何其他人都会闭着眼睛躺在他倒下的地方：但胡克巨大的大脑仍在工作，在它的指导下，他沿着甲板跪着爬行，尽可能远离声音。海盗们毕恭毕敬地为他让出一条通道，直到他走到舷墙上才开口说话。
他们聚集在他周围，所有的目光都从那个正在上船的东西身上移开。他们没有想到要与之抗争。这是命运。
只有当胡克被隐藏起来时，孩子们的好奇心才松开了四肢，以便他们能够冲到船边看鳄鱼爬上船。然后他们得到了夜夜里最奇怪的惊喜：因为没有鳄鱼来帮助他们。是彼得。
他示意他们不要发出任何可能引起怀疑的钦佩呼声。然后他继续滴答作响。
在我们的一生中，奇怪的事情发生在我们所有人身上，而我们却暂时没有注意到它们的发生。比如，我们突然发现自己的一只耳朵聋了，不知道多久了，比如说半个小时。那天晚上彼得就有了这样的经历。当我们最后一次见到他时，他正偷偷穿过小岛，一根手指放在嘴唇上，匕首已准备就绪。他曾看到鳄鱼经过，并没有注意到它有什么异常，但渐渐地他记起它并没有滴答作响。起初他觉得这很奇怪，但很快就得出正确的结论：时间已经到了。

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 4
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: “What do we talk of marks and brands, whether on the bodice of her gown or the flesh of her forehead?” cried another female, the ugliest as well as the most pitiless of these self-constituted judges. “This woman has brought shame upon us all, and ought to die; is there not law for it? Truly there is, both in the Scripture and the statute-book. Then let the magistrates, who have made it of no effect, thank themselves if their own wives and daughters go astray.”

“Mercy on us, goodwife!” exclaimed a man in the crowd, “is there no virtue in woman, save what springs from a wholesome fear of the gallows? That is the hardest word yet! Hush now, gossips for the lock is turning in the prison-door, and here comes Mistress Prynne herself.”

The door of the jail being flung open from within there appeared, in the first place, like a black shadow emerging into sunshine, the grim and grisly presence of the town-beadle, with a sword by his side, and his staff of office in his hand. This personage prefigured and represented in his aspect the whole dismal severity of the Puritanic code of law, which it was his business to administer in its final and closest application to the offender. Stretching forth the official staff in his left hand, he laid his right upon the shoulder of a young woman, whom he thus drew forward, until, on the threshold of the prison-door, she repelled him, by an action marked with natural dignity and force of character, and stepped into the open air as if by her own free will. She bore in her arms a child, a baby of some three months old, who winked and turned aside its little face from the too vivid light of day; because its existence, heretofore, had brought it acquaintance only with the grey twilight of a dungeon, or other darksome apartment of the prison.

When the young woman—the mother of this child—stood fully revealed before the crowd, it seemed to be her first impulse to clasp the infant closely to her bosom; not so much by an impulse of motherly affection, as that she might thereby conceal a certain token, which was wrought or fastened into her dress. In a moment, however, wisely judging that one token of her shame would but poorly serve to hide another, she took the baby on her arm, and with a burning blush, and yet a haughty smile, and a glance that would not be abashed, looked around at her townspeople and neighbours. On the breast of her gown, in fine red cloth, surrounded with an elaborate embroidery and fantastic flourishes of gold thread, appeared the letter A. It was so artistically done, and with so much fertility and gorgeous luxuriance of fancy, that it had all the effect of a last and fitting decoration to the apparel which she wore, and which was of a splendour in accordance with the taste of the age, but greatly beyond what was allowed by the sumptuary regulations of the colony.

The young woman was tall, with a figure of perfect elegance on a large scale. She had dark and abundant hair, so glossy that it threw off the sunshine with a gleam; and a face which, besides being beautiful from regularity of feature and richness of complexion, had the impressiveness belonging to a marked brow and deep black eyes. She was ladylike, too, after the manner of the feminine gentility of those days; characterised by a certain state and dignity, rather than by the delicate, evanescent, and indescribable grace which is now recognised as its indication. And never had Hester Prynne appeared more ladylike, in the antique interpretation of the term, than as she issued from the prison. Those who had before known her, and had expected to behold her dimmed and obscured by a disastrous cloud, were astonished, and even startled, to perceive how her beauty shone out, and made a halo of the misfortune and ignominy in which she was enveloped. It may be true that, to a sensitive observer, there was some thing exquisitely painful in it. Her attire, which indeed, she had wrought for the occasion in prison, and had modelled much after her own fancy, seemed to express the attitude of her spirit, the desperate recklessness of her mood, by its wild and picturesque peculiarity. But the point which drew all eyes, and, as it were, transfigured the wearer—so that both men and women who had been familiarly acquainted with Hester Prynne were now impressed as if they beheld her for the first time—was that SCARLET LETTER, so fantastically embroidered and illuminated upon her bosom. It had the effect of a spell, taking her out of the ordinary relations with humanity, and enclosing her in a sphere by herself.
paragraphsZh: “我们谈论什么标记和品牌，无论是在她礼服的紧身胸衣上还是在她额头的肉上？”另一位女性叫道，她是这些自封法官中最丑陋、也是最无情的。 “这个女人给我们大家带来了耻辱，应该死。难道没有法律规定吗？圣经和法典上确实有相关规定。那么，如果自己的妻子和女儿误入歧途，让那些使这一切无效的地方官们感谢自己吧。”
“可怜我们吧，好妻子！”人群中的一个男人喊道，“除了对绞刑架的健康恐惧之外，女人就没有美德了吗？这是迄今为止最难的词！现在安静，流言蜚语是监狱门的锁正在转动，白兰夫人本人也来了。”

监狱的门从里面猛地打开，首先出现的，就像一个黑影出现在阳光下，镇长的冷酷而可怕的存在，他身边有一把剑，手里拿着他的办公室工作人员。这个人物在他的外表上预示并代表了清教徒法典的全部令人沮丧的严厉性，他的职责是将其最终和最接近地应用于罪犯。他伸出左手的权杖，右手搭在一位年轻女子的肩膀上，她就这样被拉向前，直到她在监狱门口，以一种自然的尊严和性格力量推开了他，仿佛出于自己的自由意志，走到了露天。她怀里怀着一个孩子，一个大约三个月大的婴儿，他眨着眼睛，把小脸转开，避开过于明亮的日光。因为迄今为止，它的存在只让它熟悉了地牢或监狱其他黑暗房间的灰色暮色。

当这位年轻女子——这个孩子的母亲——完全暴露在人群面前时，她的第一冲动似乎是将婴儿紧紧地抱在怀里；与其说是出于母爱的冲动，不如说她可能因此隐藏了某种标记，该标记被制作或固定在她的衣服上。然而，过了一会儿，她明智地判断出，她的一个羞耻的表现并不足以掩盖另一个羞耻的表现，她把婴儿抱在手臂上，脸红得通红，脸上带着傲慢的微笑，眼神毫不羞愧，环顾四周的镇民和邻居。在她那件用精美的红布制成的长袍胸前，出现了一个字母A，周围有精致的刺绣和华丽的金线。它做得如此艺术，充满了如此多的生育力和华丽的幻想，它对她所穿的服装起到了最后和合适的装饰的作用，它的辉煌符合那个时代的品味，但远远超出了殖民地奢华规定所允许的范围。

少妇身材高挑，身材大尺度完美优雅。她有一头浓密的黑发，光泽亮丽，在阳光下闪闪发亮。这张脸除了五官端正、肤色丰富之外，还拥有令人印象深刻的眉毛和深邃的黑眼睛。她也很淑女，符合当时女性的优雅风格。其特征是某种状态和尊严，而不是现在被认为是其标志的精致、转瞬即逝和难以形容的优雅。从这个词的古老解释来看，海丝特·白兰从监狱里出来的时候从来没有像现在这样显得更加淑女。那些以前认识她的人，本以为会看到她被灾难性的乌云遮住，变得黯淡无光，但当他们发现她的美丽光芒四射，并为她所笼罩的不幸和耻辱制造出光环时，他们感到惊讶，甚至震惊。对于敏感的观察者来说，这可能确实是一种极其痛苦的事情。她的服装确实是她为监狱里的场合而制作的，而且很大程度上是按照她自己的想象设计的，似乎以其狂野而美丽的独特性表达了她的精神态度，她绝望的鲁莽情绪。但最吸引所有人目光的一点是那个红字，它绣在她的胸前，闪闪发光，让那些熟悉海丝特·白兰的男人和女人现在都印象深刻，就像第一次见到她一样。它具有咒语的效果，使她脱离了与人类的正常关系，并将她独自封闭在一个球体中。

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 5
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: Hester Prynne, therefore, did not flee. On the outskirts of the town, within the verge of the peninsula, but not in close vicinity to any other habitation, there was a small thatched cottage. It had been built by an earlier settler, and abandoned, because the soil about it was too sterile for cultivation, while its comparative remoteness put it out of the sphere of that social activity which already marked the habits of the emigrants. It stood on the shore, looking across a basin of the sea at the forest-covered hills, towards the west. A clump of scrubby trees, such as alone grew on the peninsula, did not so much conceal the cottage from view, as seem to denote that here was some object which would fain have been, or at least ought to be, concealed. In this little lonesome dwelling, with some slender means that she possessed, and by the licence of the magistrates, who still kept an inquisitorial watch over her, Hester established herself, with her infant child. A mystic shadow of suspicion immediately attached itself to the spot. Children, too young to comprehend wherefore this woman should be shut out from the sphere of human charities, would creep nigh enough to behold her plying her needle at the cottage-window, or standing in the doorway, or labouring in her little garden, or coming forth along the pathway that led townward, and, discerning the scarlet letter on her breast, would scamper off with a strange contagious fear.

Lonely as was Hester’s situation, and without a friend on earth who dared to show himself, she, however, incurred no risk of want. She possessed an art that sufficed, even in a land that afforded comparatively little scope for its exercise, to supply food for her thriving infant and herself. It was the art, then, as now, almost the only one within a woman’s grasp—of needle-work. She bore on her breast, in the curiously embroidered letter, a specimen of her delicate and imaginative skill, of which the dames of a court might gladly have availed themselves, to add the richer and more spiritual adornment of human ingenuity to their fabrics of silk and gold. Here, indeed, in the sable simplicity that generally characterised the Puritanic modes of dress, there might be an infrequent call for the finer productions of her handiwork. Yet the taste of the age, demanding whatever was elaborate in compositions of this kind, did not fail to extend its influence over our stern progenitors, who had cast behind them so many fashions which it might seem harder to dispense with.

Public ceremonies, such as ordinations, the installation of magistrates, and all that could give majesty to the forms in which a new government manifested itself to the people, were, as a matter of policy, marked by a stately and well-conducted ceremonial, and a sombre, but yet a studied magnificence. Deep ruffs, painfully wrought bands, and gorgeously embroidered gloves, were all deemed necessary to the official state of men assuming the reins of power, and were readily allowed to individuals dignified by rank or wealth, even while sumptuary laws forbade these and similar extravagances to the plebeian order. In the array of funerals, too—whether for the apparel of the dead body, or to typify, by manifold emblematic devices of sable cloth and snowy lawn, the sorrow of the survivors—there was a frequent and characteristic demand for such labour as Hester Prynne could supply. Baby-linen—for babies then wore robes of state—afforded still another possibility of toil and emolument.

By degrees, not very slowly, her handiwork became what would now be termed the fashion. Whether from commiseration for a woman of so miserable a destiny; or from the morbid curiosity that gives a fictitious value even to common or worthless things; or by whatever other intangible circumstance was then, as now, sufficient to bestow, on some persons, what others might seek in vain; or because Hester really filled a gap which must otherwise have remained vacant; it is certain that she had ready and fairly requited employment for as many hours as she saw fit to occupy with her needle. Vanity, it may be, chose to mortify itself, by putting on, for ceremonials of pomp and state, the garments that had been wrought by her sinful hands. Her needle-work was seen on the ruff of the Governor; military men wore it on their scarfs, and the minister on his band; it decked the baby’s little cap; it was shut up, to be mildewed and moulder away, in the coffins of the dead. But it is not recorded that, in a single instance, her skill was called in to embroider the white veil which was to cover the pure blushes of a bride. The exception indicated the ever relentless vigour with which society frowned upon her sin.
paragraphsZh: 因此，海丝特·白兰没有逃跑。在小镇的郊区，在半岛的边缘，但离任何其他居住地都不近的地方，有一座小茅草屋。它是由一位早期定居者建造的，后来被遗弃了，因为它周围的土壤太贫瘠，不适合耕种，而它的相对偏远又使其脱离了已经成为移民习惯的社会活动范围。它矗立在岸边，眺望着西边的一片海盆和森林覆盖的山丘。半岛上生长着的一丛茂密的树木，与其说是把小屋遮住了，不如说是表明这里有某种本来应该被隐藏的物体，或者至少应该被隐藏起来。在这个偏僻的小住所里，海丝特凭借她所拥有的一些微薄的财产，并在仍然对她保持着审问式监视的地方法官的许可下，带着她的婴儿安顿下来。一股神秘的怀疑之影立刻就附着在了现场。孩子们还太小，无法理解为什么这个女人应该被排除在人类慈善事业的范围之外，他们会爬近，看到她在小屋的窗户前穿针引线，或者站在门口，或者在她的小花园里劳作，或者沿着通向城镇的小路走出来，当看到她胸前的红字时，就会带着一种奇怪的、传染性的恐惧跑开。

海丝特的处境虽然孤独，世上没有一个敢于露面的朋友，但她却没有遭受匮乏的风险。她拥有一门艺术，即使在一个施展空间相对较小的土地上，也足以为她和她自己茁壮成长的婴儿提供食物。无论是当时还是现在，这都是一门几乎女性唯一掌握的艺术——针线活。她胸前那封绣着奇特的信，是她精致而富有想象力的技艺的典范，宫廷里的贵妇们可能会很乐意利用这一技艺，为她们的丝绸和黄金织物增添人类聪明才智的更丰富、更精神的装饰。确实，在清教徒着装风格的普遍特点的黑貂色简约中，可能很少有人要求她的手工作品更加精美。然而，那个时代的品味，要求在这类作品中精雕细琢，并没有没有对我们严肃的祖先产生影响，他们在他们身后留下了如此多的时尚，这些时尚似乎很难摆脱。

公共仪式，例如任命、地方法官就职，以及所有能够给新政府向人民展示自己的形式带来威严的仪式，作为一项政策，都以庄严和良好的仪式为标志，是一种庄严但又刻意的华丽。深领子、精心制作的带子和华丽刺绣的手套，都被认为是掌握权力的官方国家所必需的，并且很容易被允许具有地位或财富尊严的个人使用，尽管奢侈法禁止这些以及类似的平民秩序的奢侈行为。在一系列的葬礼中，无论是死者的服装，还是通过紫貂布和雪草坪等多种象征性装置来体现幸存者的悲伤，对海丝特·白兰能够提供的劳动力的频繁且典型的需求。婴儿亚麻布——当时婴儿穿着国袍——还提供了另一种辛劳和报酬的可能性。

渐渐地，不是很慢，她的手工作品变成了现在所谓的时尚。是否出于对一个命运如此悲惨的女人的同情；或者是出于病态的好奇心，甚至对普通或无价值的事物也赋予了虚构的价值；或者通过当时和现在一样的任何其他无形环境，足以赋予某些人一些其他人可能徒劳地寻求的东西；或者因为海丝特确实填补了一个本来肯定是空缺的空白；可以肯定的是，她已经准备好并得到公平的报酬，可以在她认为适合做针线活的时间内工作。也许是虚荣心选择了自我羞辱，在盛大的仪式上穿上她用罪恶之手制作的衣服。总督的领子上可以看到她的针线活。军人把它戴在围巾上，部长则把它戴在腰带上。它装饰了婴儿的小帽子；它被关在死者的棺材里，等待发霉、腐烂。但没有记录表明，有一次她的技艺被用来刺绣白色面纱，以遮盖新娘纯净的脸红。这一例外表明社会对她的罪行始终不屑一顾。

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 6
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: “Hush, Pearl, hush! Thou must not talk so!” answered the mother, suppressing a groan. “He sent us all into the world. He sent even me, thy mother. Then, much more thee! Or, if not, thou strange and elfish child, whence didst thou come?”
“Tell me! Tell me!” repeated Pearl, no longer seriously, but laughing and capering about the floor. “It is thou that must tell me!”

But Hester could not resolve the query, being herself in a dismal labyrinth of doubt. She remembered—betwixt a smile and a shudder—the talk of the neighbouring townspeople, who, seeking vainly elsewhere for the child’s paternity, and observing some of her odd attributes, had given out that poor little Pearl was a demon offspring: such as, ever since old Catholic times, had occasionally been seen on earth, through the agency of their mother’s sin, and to promote some foul and wicked purpose. Luther, according to the scandal of his monkish enemies, was a brat of that hellish breed; nor was Pearl the only child to whom this inauspicious origin was assigned among the New England Puritans.

Hester Prynne went one day to the mansion of Governor Bellingham, with a pair of gloves which she had fringed and embroidered to his order, and which were to be worn on some great occasion of state; for, though the chances of a popular election had caused this former ruler to descend a step or two from the highest rank, he still held an honourable and influential place among the colonial magistracy.

Another and far more important reason than the delivery of a pair of embroidered gloves, impelled Hester, at this time, to seek an interview with a personage of so much power and activity in the affairs of the settlement. It had reached her ears that there was a design on the part of some of the leading inhabitants, cherishing the more rigid order of principles in religion and government, to deprive her of her child. On the supposition that Pearl, as already hinted, was of demon origin, these good people not unreasonably argued that a Christian interest in the mother’s soul required them to remove such a stumbling-block from her path. If the child, on the other hand, were really capable of moral and religious growth, and possessed the elements of ultimate salvation, then, surely, it would enjoy all the fairer prospect of these advantages by being transferred to wiser and better guardianship than Hester Prynne’s. Among those who promoted the design, Governor Bellingham was said to be one of the most busy. It may appear singular, and, indeed, not a little ludicrous, that an affair of this kind, which in later days would have been referred to no higher jurisdiction than that of the select men of the town, should then have been a question publicly discussed, and on which statesmen of eminence took sides. At that epoch of pristine simplicity, however, matters of even slighter public interest, and of far less intrinsic weight than the welfare of Hester and her child, were strangely mixed up with the deliberations of legislators and acts of state. The period was hardly, if at all, earlier than that of our story, when a dispute concerning the right of property in a pig not only caused a fierce and bitter contest in the legislative body of the colony, but resulted in an important modification of the framework itself of the legislature.

Full of concern, therefore—but so conscious of her own right that it seemed scarcely an unequal match between the public on the one side, and a lonely woman, backed by the sympathies of nature, on the other—Hester Prynne set forth from her solitary cottage. Little Pearl, of course, was her companion. She was now of an age to run lightly along by her mother’s side, and, constantly in motion from morn till sunset, could have accomplished a much longer journey than that before her. Often, nevertheless, more from caprice than necessity, she demanded to be taken up in arms; but was soon as imperious to be let down again, and frisked onward before Hester on the grassy pathway, with many a harmless trip and tumble. We have spoken of Pearl’s rich and luxuriant beauty—a beauty that shone with deep and vivid tints, a bright complexion, eyes possessing intensity both of depth and glow, and hair already of a deep, glossy brown, and which, in after years, would be nearly akin to black. There was fire in her and throughout her: she seemed the unpremeditated offshoot of a passionate moment. Her mother, in contriving the child’s garb, had allowed the gorgeous tendencies of her imagination their full play, arraying her in a crimson velvet tunic of a peculiar cut, abundantly embroidered in fantasies and flourishes of gold thread. So much strength of colouring, which must have given a wan and pallid aspect to cheeks of a fainter bloom, was admirably adapted to Pearl’s beauty, and made her the very brightest little jet of flame that ever danced upon the earth.
paragraphsZh: “嘘，珀尔，嘘！你不可以这样说话！”母亲强忍着一声呻吟回答道。 “他把我们所有人都送到了这个世界上。他甚至把我，你的母亲送到了这个世界上。那么，更何况你呢！或者，如果不是的话，你这个奇怪而小精灵的孩子，你从哪里来？”
“告诉我！告诉我！”珀尔重复道，她不再认真，而是笑着在地板上蹦蹦跳跳。 “必须由你来告诉我！”

但海丝特无法解决这个问题，因为她自己陷入了令人沮丧的怀疑迷宫。她微笑着，颤抖着想起了邻近镇民的谈话，他们徒劳地在别处寻找孩子的父亲，并观察到她的一些奇怪的特征，已经指出可怜的小珀尔是恶魔的后代：从古老的天主教时代开始，这种恶魔的后代就偶尔在地球上出现，通过他们母亲的罪孽，并促进一些肮脏和邪恶的目的。根据他的修士敌人的丑闻，路德是那种地狱般的孩子。珀尔并不是新英格兰清教徒中唯一被赋予这种不吉利出身的孩子。
有一天，海丝特·白兰带着一副手套来到贝灵厄姆总督的官邸，这副手套是她按照他的命令镶上流苏和刺绣的，准备在一些重大的国家场合佩戴。因为，尽管普选的机会使这位前统治者的最高级别下降了一两级，但他在殖民地治安官中仍然享有光荣且有影响力的地位。

另一个比送一双绣花手套更重要的原因促使海丝特此时寻求采访一位在定居点事务中拥有如此大权力和活跃度的人物。她听到了一些主要居民的阴谋，他们珍视宗教和政府中更严格的原则秩序，想要剥夺她的孩子。正如已经暗示的那样，珀尔是恶魔出身，这些好心人不无道理地辩称，基督徒对母亲灵魂的兴趣要求他们清除她道路上的绊脚石。另一方面，如果这个孩子确实有能力在道德和宗教上成长，并具备最终救赎的要素，那么，通过将其转移到比海丝特·白兰更明智、更好的监护下，他肯定会享受到这些优势的更公平的前景。在推广该设计的人中，贝灵厄姆州长据说是最忙碌的人之一。类似的事件，在后来的日子里，不会被提交给比城里的精英人士更高的管辖权，但在那时，却成为一个公开讨论的问题，而且杰出的政治家也站在了一边，这可能显得很奇怪，而且确实有点可笑。然而，在那个原始简单的时代，公共利益甚至比海丝特和她孩子的福利更微不足道的问题，也比海丝特和她孩子的福利更不重要，奇怪地与立法者的审议和国家行为混在一起。这个时期即使有的话，也几乎不早于我们的故事，当时有关猪的财产权的争端不仅在殖民地的立法机构中引起了激烈而激烈的争论，而且导致了立法机构本身框架的重大修改。

因此，海丝特·白兰满怀忧虑地从她孤独的小屋里出发，但她也非常清楚自己的权利，一方面是公众，另一方面是一个受到大自然同情的孤独女人，这似乎并不是不平等的匹配。小珍珠当然是她的同伴。她现在已经到了可以在母亲身边轻轻奔跑的年龄，从早到晚不断地运动，本来可以完成比她之前更长的旅程。然而，她常常要求拿起武器，更多的是出于任性而不是迫不得已。但很快又再次失望了，在绿草如茵的小路上，在海丝特面前向前跳跃，有很多次无害的绊倒和摔倒。我们已经谈到了珍珠丰富而华丽的美丽——一种闪耀着深邃而生动的色彩的美丽，明亮的肤色，拥有深邃和光芒的眼睛，头发已经是深而有光泽的棕色，多年后，它几乎接近黑色。她的内心和全身充满了火焰：她似乎是激情时刻的意外产物。她的母亲在设计孩子的服装时，充分发挥了她想象力的华丽倾向，给她穿上了一件剪裁奇特的深红色天鹅绒外衣，上面绣满了幻想和华丽的金线。如此强烈的色彩，一定会让淡色花朵的脸颊显得苍白无力，却与珍珠的美丽完美地相适应，使她成为地球上舞动的最明亮的小火焰。

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 7
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: Sometimes a light glimmered out of the physician’s eyes, burning blue and ominous, like the reflection of a furnace, or, let us say, like one of those gleams of ghastly fire that darted from Bunyan’s awful doorway in the hillside, and quivered on the pilgrim’s face. The soil where this dark miner was working had perchance shown indications that encouraged him.

“This man,” said he, at one such moment, to himself, “pure as they deem him—all spiritual as he seems—hath inherited a strong animal nature from his father or his mother. Let us dig a little further in the direction of this vein!”

Then after long search into the minister’s dim interior, and turning over many precious materials, in the shape of high aspirations for the welfare of his race, warm love of souls, pure sentiments, natural piety, strengthened by thought and study, and illuminated by revelation—all of which invaluable gold was perhaps no better than rubbish to the seeker—he would turn back, discouraged, and begin his quest towards another point. He groped along as stealthily, with as cautious a tread, and as wary an outlook, as a thief entering a chamber where a man lies only half asleep—or, it may be, broad awake—with purpose to steal the very treasure which this man guards as the apple of his eye. In spite of his premeditated carefulness, the floor would now and then creak; his garments would rustle; the shadow of his presence, in a forbidden proximity, would be thrown across his victim. In other words, Mr. Dimmesdale, whose sensibility of nerve often produced the effect of spiritual intuition, would become vaguely aware that something inimical to his peace had thrust itself into relation with him. But Old Roger Chillingworth, too, had perceptions that were almost intuitive; and when the minister threw his startled eyes towards him, there the physician sat; his kind, watchful, sympathising, but never intrusive friend.

Yet Mr. Dimmesdale would perhaps have seen this individual’s character more perfectly, if a certain morbidness, to which sick hearts are liable, had not rendered him suspicious of all mankind. Trusting no man as his friend, he could not recognize his enemy when the latter actually appeared. He therefore still kept up a familiar intercourse with him, daily receiving the old physician in his study, or visiting the laboratory, and, for recreation’s sake, watching the processes by which weeds were converted into drugs of potency.

One day, leaning his forehead on his hand, and his elbow on the sill of the open window, that looked towards the graveyard, he talked with Roger Chillingworth, while the old man was examining a bundle of unsightly plants.

“Even in the graveyard here at hand,” answered the physician, continuing his employment. “They are new to me. I found them growing on a grave, which bore no tombstone, no other memorial of the dead man, save these ugly weeds, that have taken upon themselves to keep him in remembrance. They grew out of his heart, and typify, it may be, some hideous secret that was buried with him, and which he had done better to confess during his lifetime.”

“That, good sir, is but a phantasy of yours,” replied the minister. “There can be, if I forbode aright, no power, short of the Divine mercy, to disclose, whether by uttered words, or by type or emblem, the secrets that may be buried in the human heart. The heart, making itself guilty of such secrets, must perforce hold them, until the day when all hidden things shall be revealed. Nor have I so read or interpreted Holy Writ, as to understand that the disclosure of human thoughts and deeds, then to be made, is intended as a part of the retribution. That, surely, were a shallow view of it. No; these revelations, unless I greatly err, are meant merely to promote the intellectual satisfaction of all intelligent beings, who will stand waiting, on that day, to see the dark problem of this life made plain. A knowledge of men’s hearts will be needful to the completest solution of that problem. And, I conceive moreover, that the hearts holding such miserable secrets as you speak of, will yield them up, at that last day, not with reluctance, but with a joy unutterable.”
paragraphsZh: 有时，医生的眼睛里会闪出一丝光芒，燃烧着蓝色，不祥，就像熔炉的倒影，或者，我们可以说，就像从山坡上班扬可怕的门口射出的可怕火焰之一，在朝圣者的脸上颤抖。这位黑暗矿工工作的土壤可能显示出鼓舞他的迹象。
“这个人，”在这样的时刻，他对自己说，“尽管他们认为他很纯洁，但他看起来很有灵性，但他从他的父亲或母亲那里继承了强烈的动物本性。让我们沿着这条脉络的方向进一步挖掘一点！”

然后，经过对牧师暗淡内心的长期探索，并翻出了许多珍贵的材料，表现为对种族福祉的崇高愿望、对灵魂的热烈热爱、纯洁的情感、自然的虔诚，通过思想和研究加强，并通过启示照亮——所有这些无价的黄金对探索者来说也许并不比垃圾更好——他会灰心丧气地回头，开始他对另一个点的探索。他像小偷一样偷偷地摸索着，脚步小心翼翼，目光警惕，就像一个小偷进入一个半睡半醒的人的房间，或者，可能是完全清醒的，目的是偷走这个人视如掌上明珠的宝藏。尽管他预先很小心，地板还是时不时地吱吱作响。他的衣服会沙沙作响；他的存在的阴影，在禁止接近的地方，会投射在他的受害者身上。换句话说，丁梅斯代尔先生的神经敏感常常产生精神直觉的效果，他会隐约意识到有一些不利于他平静的东西已经与他发生了关系。但老罗杰·奇林沃思也有近乎直觉的感知。当牧师用惊讶的目光看向他时，医生就坐在那里。他善良、警惕、富有同情心，但从不打扰别人。
然而，丁梅斯代尔先生也许会更清楚地看到这个人的性格，如果病态的心灵容易产生某种病态，没有使他对全人类产生怀疑的话。他不相信任何人是他的朋友，当敌人真正出现时，他无法认出他的敌人。因此，他仍然与他保持着熟悉的交往，每天接待老医生到他的书房，或者参观实验室，为了消遣，观察杂草转化为有效药物的过程。
有一天，他用手撑着额头，肘部撑在面向墓地的开着的窗台上，与罗杰·奇林沃思交谈，而老人正在检查一捆难看的植物。
“即使是在附近的墓地里，”医生回答道，继续他的工作。 “它们对我来说是新的。我发现它们生长在一座坟墓上，坟墓上没有墓碑，也没有其他对死者的纪念，除了这些丑陋的杂草，它们长出了自己，以纪念他。它们从他的心里生长出来，可能代表着一些与他一起埋葬的可怕秘密，他最好在有生之年坦白这些秘密。”

“那，好先生，这只是您的幻想，”部长回答道。 “如果我禁止正确的话，没有任何力量，缺乏神圣的仁慈，可以披露可能埋在人心中的秘密，无论是通过言语，还是通过类型或象征。心，使自己对这些秘密感到内疚，必须强迫保守它们，直到所有隐藏的事情都被揭露的那一天。我也没有如此阅读或解释圣经，以至于理解人类思想和行为的披露，然后被做出，旨在作为上帝的一部分。不，这当然是一种肤浅的看法；除非我犯了很大的错误，否则这些启示只是为了促进所有聪明人的智力满足，他们会等待着看到这一生的黑暗问题变得清晰，而且，我认为，那些持有你所说的悲惨秘密的人不会放弃它们。虽然很不情愿，但心里却有说不出的喜悦。”

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 8
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: With a chill despondency, like one awakening, all nerveless, from an ugly dream, he yielded himself to the physician, and was led away.

The next day, however, being the Sabbath, he preached a discourse which was held to be the richest and most powerful, and the most replete with heavenly influences, that had ever proceeded from his lips. Souls, it is said, more souls than one, were brought to the truth by the efficacy of that sermon, and vowed within themselves to cherish a holy gratitude towards Mr. Dimmesdale throughout the long hereafter. But as he came down the pulpit steps, the grey-bearded sexton met him, holding up a black glove, which the minister recognised as his own.

“It was found,” said the Sexton, “this morning on the scaffold where evil-doers are set up to public shame. Satan dropped it there, I take it, intending a scurrilous jest against your reverence. But, indeed, he was blind and foolish, as he ever and always is. A pure hand needs no glove to cover it!”

“Thank you, my good friend,” said the minister, gravely, but startled at heart; for so confused was his remembrance, that he had almost brought himself to look at the events of the past night as visionary.

“And, since Satan saw fit to steal it, your reverence must needs handle him without gloves henceforward,” remarked the old sexton, grimly smiling. “But did your reverence hear of the portent that was seen last night? a great red letter in the sky—the letter A, which we interpret to stand for Angel. For, as our good Governor Winthrop was made an angel this past night, it was doubtless held fit that there should be some notice thereof!”

In her late singular interview with Mr. Dimmesdale, Hester Prynne was shocked at the condition to which she found the clergyman reduced. His nerve seemed absolutely destroyed. His moral force was abased into more than childish weakness. It grovelled helpless on the ground, even while his intellectual faculties retained their pristine strength, or had perhaps acquired a morbid energy, which disease only could have given them. With her knowledge of a train of circumstances hidden from all others, she could readily infer that, besides the legitimate action of his own conscience, a terrible machinery had been brought to bear, and was still operating, on Mr. Dimmesdale’s well-being and repose. Knowing what this poor fallen man had once been, her whole soul was moved by the shuddering terror with which he had appealed to her—the outcast woman—for support against his instinctively discovered enemy. She decided, moreover, that he had a right to her utmost aid. Little accustomed, in her long seclusion from society, to measure her ideas of right and wrong by any standard external to herself, Hester saw—or seemed to see—that there lay a responsibility upon her in reference to the clergyman, which she owned to no other, nor to the whole world besides. The links that united her to the rest of humankind—links of flowers, or silk, or gold, or whatever the material—had all been broken. Here was the iron link of mutual crime, which neither he nor she could break. Like all other ties, it brought along with it its obligations.

Hester Prynne did not now occupy precisely the same position in which we beheld her during the earlier periods of her ignominy. Years had come and gone. Pearl was now seven years old. Her mother, with the scarlet letter on her breast, glittering in its fantastic embroidery, had long been a familiar object to the townspeople. As is apt to be the case when a person stands out in any prominence before the community, and, at the same time, interferes neither with public nor individual interests and convenience, a species of general regard had ultimately grown up in reference to Hester Prynne. It is to the credit of human nature that, except where its selfishness is brought into play, it loves more readily than it hates. Hatred, by a gradual and quiet process, will even be transformed to love, unless the change be impeded by a continually new irritation of the original feeling of hostility. In this matter of Hester Prynne there was neither irritation nor irksomeness. She never battled with the public, but submitted uncomplainingly to its worst usage; she made no claim upon it in requital for what she suffered; she did not weigh upon its sympathies. Then, also, the blameless purity of her life during all these years in which she had been set apart to infamy was reckoned largely in her favour. With nothing now to lose, in the sight of mankind, and with no hope, and seemingly no wish, of gaining anything, it could only be a genuine regard for virtue that had brought back the poor wanderer to its paths.
paragraphsZh: 带着一种寒冷的沮丧，就像从一场丑陋的梦中醒来一样，他毫无勇气，向医生屈服了，然后被带走了。
然而，第二天是安息日，他宣讲了一篇被认为是他口中最丰富、最有力、最充满天国影响力的演讲。据说，更多的灵魂因那次布道的功效而认识到了真理，并发誓在今后的漫长岁月里对丁梅斯代尔先生怀有神圣的感激之情。但当他走下讲坛台阶时，灰胡子的司事遇见了他，举着一只黑色手套，牧师认出那是他自己的。
“今天早上在断头台上发现了它，”教堂司事说，“邪恶之徒被公开羞辱的地方。撒旦把它扔在那里，我想，是想对你的尊敬开一个粗俗的玩笑。但是，事实上，他是盲目和愚蠢的，一如既往。一只纯洁的手不需要手套来遮盖它！”
“谢谢你，我的好朋友，”部长严肃地说，但心里却吃了一惊；因为他的记忆如此混乱，以至于他几乎让自己把昨晚发生的事情视为幻觉。
“而且，既然撒旦认为有必要偷走它，那么从今以后，您的尊者必须不戴手套地对待他，”老教堂司事冷酷地微笑着说道。 “但是尊敬的阁下听说了昨晚看到的预兆吗？天空中出现了一个巨大的红色字母——字母A，我们将其解释为代表天使。因为，当我们善良的温思罗普总督昨晚被任命为天使时，毫无疑问，应该对此有所通知！”

在她最近对丁梅斯代尔先生的独特采访中，海丝特·白兰对她发现牧师沦落到这样的境地感到震惊。他的神经似乎完全被摧毁了。他的道德力量已经退化到不仅仅是幼稚的弱点。它无助地跪在地上，尽管他的智力仍然保持着原始的力量，或者可能已经获得了一种病态的能量，而这种能量只有疾病才能赋予它们。凭借她对一系列不为人所知的情况的了解，她可以很容易地推断出，除了丁梅斯代尔先生自己良心的合法行为之外，还有一个可怕的机器已经开始运作，并且仍在运作，影响着丁梅斯代尔先生的健康和休息。她知道这个可怜的堕落男人曾经是什么样子，她的整个灵魂都被他向她——这个被遗弃的女人——求助以对抗他本能地发现的敌人时所产生的颤抖的恐惧所感动。此外，她认为他有权获得她最大的帮助。海丝特长期与社会隔绝，不太习惯用任何外在的标准来衡量自己的是非观念，她看到——或者似乎看到——她对牧师负有责任，她不拥有任何其他人，也不拥有整个世界。将她与其他人类联系在一起的联系——鲜花、丝绸、黄金或任何材料的联系——都被打破了。这是相互犯罪的铁环，他和她都无法打破。与所有其他关系一样，它也带来了义务。

海丝特·白兰现在的处境与我们在她受辱初期所看到的完全不同。岁月已经过去了。珀尔此时已经七岁了。她的母亲胸前有红字，精美的刺绣闪闪发光，长期以来一直是镇上人们熟悉的对象。当一个人在社区中脱颖而出，同时又不干涉公共或个人的利益和便利时，通常会出现这样的情况，一种普遍的尊重最终会在海丝特·白兰的影响下产生。值得赞扬的是，人性除了自私发挥作用外，人性都更容易去爱，而不是去恨。仇恨甚至会通过一个渐进而安静的过程转化为爱，除非这种变化受到对原始敌对感觉的持续新刺激的阻碍。在海丝特·白兰的这件事上，既没有恼怒，也没有令人厌烦。她从不与公众抗争，但毫无怨言地接受了最恶劣的使用。她并没有要求它来补偿她所遭受的痛苦；她并没有引起人们的同情。此外，这些年来她的生活无可指摘的纯洁性，在这些年里她被指为臭名昭著，这在很大程度上被认为对她有利。在人类看来，现在已经没有什么可失去的了，而且没有希望，似乎也没有希望获得任何东西，只有对美德的真正尊重才能把这个可怜的流浪者带回正轨。

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 9
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: Slowly as the minister walked, he had almost gone by before Hester Prynne could gather voice enough to attract his observation. At length she succeeded.

“Who speaks?” answered the minister. Gathering himself quickly up, he stood more erect, like a man taken by surprise in a mood to which he was reluctant to have witnesses. Throwing his eyes anxiously in the direction of the voice, he indistinctly beheld a form under the trees, clad in garments so sombre, and so little relieved from the gray twilight into which the clouded sky and the heavy foliage had darkened the noontide, that he knew not whether it were a woman or a shadow. It may be that his pathway through life was haunted thus by a spectre that had stolen out from among his thoughts.
“Even so.” she answered. “In such life as has been mine these seven years past! And thou, Arthur Dimmesdale, dost thou yet live?”

It was no wonder that they thus questioned one another’s actual and bodily existence, and even doubted of their own. So strangely did they meet in the dim wood that it was like the first encounter in the world beyond the grave of two spirits who had been intimately connected in their former life, but now stood coldly shuddering in mutual dread, as not yet familiar with their state, nor wonted to the companionship of disembodied beings. Each a ghost, and awe-stricken at the other ghost. They were awe-stricken likewise at themselves, because the crisis flung back to them their consciousness, and revealed to each heart its history and experience, as life never does, except at such breathless epochs. The soul beheld its features in the mirror of the passing moment. It was with fear, and tremulously, and, as it were, by a slow, reluctant necessity, that Arthur Dimmesdale put forth his hand, chill as death, and touched the chill hand of Hester Prynne. The grasp, cold as it was, took away what was dreariest in the interview. They now felt themselves, at least, inhabitants of the same sphere.

Without a word more spoken—neither he nor she assuming the guidance, but with an unexpressed consent—they glided back into the shadow of the woods whence Hester had emerged, and sat down on the heap of moss where she and Pearl had before been sitting. When they found voice to speak, it was at first only to utter remarks and inquiries such as any two acquaintances might have made, about the gloomy sky, the threatening storm, and, next, the health of each. Thus they went onward, not boldly, but step by step, into the themes that were brooding deepest in their hearts. So long estranged by fate and circumstances, they needed something slight and casual to run before and throw open the doors of intercourse, so that their real thoughts might be led across the threshold.

“None—nothing but despair!” he answered. “What else could I look for, being what I am, and leading such a life as mine? Were I an atheist—a man devoid of conscience—a wretch with coarse and brutal instincts—I might have found peace long ere now. Nay, I never should have lost it. But, as matters stand with my soul, whatever of good capacity there originally was in me, all of God’s gifts that were the choicest have become the ministers of spiritual torment. Hester, I am most miserable!”
“The people reverence thee,” said Hester. “And surely thou workest good among them! Doth this bring thee no comfort?”

“More misery, Hester!—Only the more misery!” answered the clergyman with a bitter smile. “As concerns the good which I may appear to do, I have no faith in it. It must needs be a delusion. What can a ruined soul like mine effect towards the redemption of other souls?—or a polluted soul towards their purification? And as for the people’s reverence, would that it were turned to scorn and hatred! Canst thou deem it, Hester, a consolation that I must stand up in my pulpit, and meet so many eyes turned upward to my face, as if the light of heaven were beaming from it!—must see my flock hungry for the truth, and listening to my words as if a tongue of Pentecost were speaking!—and then look inward, and discern the black reality of what they idolise? I have laughed, in bitterness and agony of heart, at the contrast between what I seem and what I am! And Satan laughs at it!”
paragraphsZh: 牧师慢慢地走着，在海丝特·白兰能够聚集足够的声音来吸引他的注意之前，他几乎已经过去了。最后她成功了。
“谁说话？”部长回答道。他迅速站起身来，站得更直了，就像一个受了惊吓的人，他不愿意让别人看到他的心情。他焦急地朝声音传来的方向望去，隐隐约约看到树下有一个人影，穿着阴暗的衣服，在灰色的暮色中几乎没有任何缓解，乌云密布的天空和茂密的树叶使正午变得暗淡，他不知道那是一个女人还是一个影子。也许他的人生道路就这样被一个从他的思想中偷出来的幽灵所困扰。
“即便如此。”她回答道。 “这七年里我一直过着这样的生活！而你，阿瑟·丁梅斯代尔，你还活着吗？”

难怪他们会如此质疑彼此的真实存在和身体存在，甚至怀疑自己的存在。他们在昏暗的树林里相遇是如此奇怪，就像是两个灵魂在坟墓之外的世界中第一次相遇，这两个灵魂在前世有着密切的联系，但现在却站在彼此的恐惧中冷冷地颤抖，因为还不熟悉他们的状态，也不习惯与无形存在的陪伴。每个人都是鬼魂，并且对另一个鬼魂感到敬畏。他们同样对自己感到敬畏，因为这场危机让他们恢复了意识，并向每颗心揭示了自己的历史和经历，除了在这样令人窒息的时代之外，生活从来没有这样做过。灵魂在过去的时刻的镜子中看到了自己的面容。阿瑟·丁梅斯代尔怀着恐惧和颤抖，似乎是出于一种缓慢的、不情愿的必要，伸出了他的手，冰冷得像死人一样，触碰了海丝特·白兰冰冷的手。尽管那股冰冷的抓握带走了采访中最沉闷的东西。他们现在至少感觉自己是同一领域的居民。

没有再多说一句话——他和她都没有接受引导，但没有表达出同意——他们滑回到海丝特出现的树林的阴影里，坐在她和珀尔之前坐过的苔藓堆上。当他们找到说话的声音时，一开始只是像任何两个熟人一样发表评论和询问，关于阴沉的天空、威胁性的风暴，以及接下来的每个人的健康状况。就这样，他们不是大胆地，而是一步一步地前进，进入了他们内心最深处的主题。因命运和环境的疏远，他们需要一些轻微的、随意的跑在前面，打开交往的大门，让他们真正的思想跨过门槛。
“没有——只有绝望！”他回答道。 “既然我是这样的人，过着这样的生活，我还能指望什么呢？如果我是一个无神论者——一个没有良心的人——一个有着粗俗和残酷本能的可怜虫——我可能早就找到了平静。不，我永远不会失去它。但是，就我的灵魂而言，无论我最初有什么良好的能力，所有上帝最精选的礼物都变成了精神折磨的使者。海丝特，我最惨了！
“人们尊敬你，”海丝特说。 “你在他们中间确实做得很好！这不会给你带来安慰吗？”

“更多的痛苦，海丝特！——只会更多的痛苦！”牧师苦笑着回答道。 “至于我可能做的善事，我对它没有信心。这一定是一种幻觉。像我这样一个被毁坏的灵魂对其他灵魂的救赎有什么作用？——或者一个被污染的灵魂对他们的净化有什么作用？至于人们的崇敬，希望它变成轻蔑和仇恨！你能认为这是一种安慰吗，海丝特，我必须站在讲坛上，面对这么多眼睛向上看我的脸，你能认为这是一种安慰吗？如果天上的光从其中射出！——一定会看到我的羊群渴望真理，聆听我的话，就像五旬节的舌头在说话一样！——然后向内看，辨别他们所崇拜的黑暗现实？我在内心的痛苦和痛苦中嘲笑我的外表和我的本质之间的对比！”

title: The Scarlet Letter · 选段 10
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
paragraphs: “Yes, to another world,” replied the minister with pious resignation. “Heaven grant it be a better one; for, in good sooth, I hardly think to tarry with my flock through the flitting seasons of another year! But touching your medicine, kind sir, in my present frame of body I need it not.”

“I joy to hear it,” answered the physician. “It may be that my remedies, so long administered in vain, begin now to take due effect. Happy man were I, and well deserving of New England’s gratitude, could I achieve this cure!”
“I thank you from my heart, most watchful friend,” said the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale with a solemn smile. “I thank you, and can but requite your good deeds with my prayers.”

“A good man’s prayers are golden recompense!” rejoined old Roger Chillingworth, as he took his leave. “Yea, they are the current gold coin of the New Jerusalem, with the King’s own mint mark on them!”

Left alone, the minister summoned a servant of the house, and requested food, which, being set before him, he ate with ravenous appetite. Then flinging the already written pages of the Election Sermon into the fire, he forthwith began another, which he wrote with such an impulsive flow of thought and emotion, that he fancied himself inspired; and only wondered that Heaven should see fit to transmit the grand and solemn music of its oracles through so foul an organ pipe as he. However, leaving that mystery to solve itself, or go unsolved for ever, he drove his task onward with earnest haste and ecstasy.

Thus the night fled away, as if it were a winged steed, and he careering on it; morning came, and peeped, blushing, through the curtains; and at last sunrise threw a golden beam into the study, and laid it right across the minister’s bedazzled eyes. There he was, with the pen still between his fingers, and a vast, immeasurable tract of written space behind him!

Betimes in the morning of the day on which the new Governor was to receive his office at the hands of the people, Hester Prynne and little Pearl came into the market-place. It was already thronged with the craftsmen and other plebeian inhabitants of the town, in considerable numbers, among whom, likewise, were many rough figures, whose attire of deer-skins marked them as belonging to some of the forest settlements, which surrounded the little metropolis of the colony.

On this public holiday, as on all other occasions for seven years past, Hester was clad in a garment of coarse gray cloth. Not more by its hue than by some indescribable peculiarity in its fashion, it had the effect of making her fade personally out of sight and outline; while again the scarlet letter brought her back from this twilight indistinctness, and revealed her under the moral aspect of its own illumination. Her face, so long familiar to the townspeople, showed the marble quietude which they were accustomed to behold there. It was like a mask; or, rather like the frozen calmness of a dead woman’s features; owing this dreary resemblance to the fact that Hester was actually dead, in respect to any claim of sympathy, and had departed out of the world with which she still seemed to mingle.

It might be, on this one day, that there was an expression unseen before, nor, indeed, vivid enough to be detected now; unless some preternaturally gifted observer should have first read the heart, and have afterwards sought a corresponding development in the countenance and mien. Such a spiritual seer might have conceived, that, after sustaining the gaze of the multitude through several miserable years as a necessity, a penance, and something which it was a stern religion to endure, she now, for one last time more, encountered it freely and voluntarily, in order to convert what had so long been agony into a kind of triumph. “Look your last on the scarlet letter and its wearer!”—the people’s victim and lifelong bond-slave, as they fancied her, might say to them. “Yet a little while, and she will be beyond your reach! A few hours longer and the deep, mysterious ocean will quench and hide for ever the symbol which ye have caused to burn on her bosom!” Nor were it an inconsistency too improbable to be assigned to human nature, should we suppose a feeling of regret in Hester’s mind, at the moment when she was about to win her freedom from the pain which had been thus deeply incorporated with her being. Might there not be an irresistible desire to quaff a last, long, breathless draught of the cup of wormwood and aloes, with which nearly all her years of womanhood had been perpetually flavoured. The wine of life, henceforth to be presented to her lips, must be indeed rich, delicious, and exhilarating, in its chased and golden beaker, or else leave an inevitable and weary languor, after the lees of bitterness wherewith she had been drugged, as with a cordial of intensest potency.
paragraphsZh: “是的，去另一个世界，”部长虔诚地听天由命地回答道。 “上天保佑它会更好；因为，说实话，我几乎不想和我的羊群一起度过另一年的转瞬即逝的季节！但是，仁慈的先生，以我目前的身体状况，我不需要它。”
“我很高兴听到这个消息，”医生回答道。 “也许我的治疗方法，长期以来一直徒劳无功，现在开始发挥应有的效果。我是幸福的人，完全值得新英格兰的感激之情，我能治愈这种病吗！”
“我发自内心地感谢你，最细心的朋友，”丁梅斯代尔牧师先生带着庄严的微笑说道。 “我感谢你们，只能用我的祈祷来回报你们的善行。”
“善人的祈祷是金的回报！”老罗杰·奇林沃思离开时又回到了他身边。 “是的，它们就是新耶路撒冷现在的金币，上面有国王自己的铸币标记！”
大臣独自一人，召来了仆人，要了食物，食物摆在他面前，他狼吞虎咽地吃了起来。然后，他把已经写好的选举讲道扔进火里，立即开始写下另一篇，他的思想和情感如此冲动，以至于他以为自己受到了启发；但他并没有这样做。只是想知道上天是否认为适合通过像他这样肮脏的风琴管来传递其神谕的宏伟而庄严的音乐。然而，他让这个谜团自行解决，或者永远无法解开，他以诚挚的匆忙和狂喜推动着他的任务。
黑夜就这样逃走了，就像一匹长翅膀的骏马，他在上面狂奔；早晨来临了，从窗帘里探出头来，脸红了。最后，太阳升起，一道金色的光芒射入书房，正好照射在牧师迷惑的眼睛上。他就在那里，手指间还握着笔，身后是一片广阔无边的书写空间！
新总督即将从人民手中接过职位的那天早上，海丝特·白兰和小珀尔走进了市场。那里已经挤满了镇上的工匠和其他平民居民，数量相当可观，其中也有许多粗野的人物，他们穿着鹿皮服装，表明他们属于一些森林定居点，这些定居点围绕着殖民地的小都市。

在这个公众假期，与过去七年的所有其他场合一样，海丝特穿着粗灰布的衣服。与其说是因为它的色调，不如说是因为它的时尚有某种难以形容的特殊性，它的效果是让她从视线和轮廓中消失。而红字再次将她从暮色中的模糊中拉了回来，并在其自身的光芒下揭示了她的道德一面。她的脸对镇上的人们来说已经很熟悉了，脸上呈现出他们在那里惯常看到的大理石般的平静。它就像一个面具；或者，更确切地说，就像一个死去的女人脸上冰冷的平静；由于这种沉闷的相似性，就任何同情而言，海丝特实际上已经死了，并且已经离开了她似乎仍然与之交往的世界。

也许，在这一天，有一种以前从未见过的表情，实际上也不够生动，现在无法被察觉；除非某个具有超凡天赋的观察者首先能读懂人心，然后在面容和神情上寻求相应的发展。这样一位精神先知可能会设想，在经历了几年悲惨的岁月之后，她作为一种必需品、一种忏悔以及一种严格的宗教必须忍受的东西而维持了大众的目光，现在，她最后一次自由地、自愿地面对它，以便将长久以来的痛苦转化为一种胜利。 “最后看看红字和它的佩戴者！”——人民的受害者和终生的奴隶，正如他们所想象的那样，可能会对他们说。 “再过一会儿，你就够不到她了！再过几个小时，深邃而神秘的海洋就会熄灭并永远隐藏你在她怀里燃烧的符号！”就在海丝特即将从深深融入她存在的痛苦中获得自由的那一刻，如果我们假设海丝特心里有一种遗憾的感觉，那么这也不是一种太不可能归咎于人性的矛盾。难道没有一种不可抗拒的欲望，想喝掉最后一杯艾草和芦荟，长长地、气喘吁吁地喝下去吗？她几乎所有的女性岁月都用这杯艾草和芦荟来调味。从此以后送到她唇边的生命之酒，一定是浓郁的、美味的、令人兴奋的，在它刻纹的金色烧杯里，否则，在她被麻醉的苦酒酒糟之后，就会留下一种不可避免的、疲倦的倦怠，就像一种效力最强的甘露水一样。

title: The Time Machine · 选段 4
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “In which case they would certainly plough you for the Little-go. The German scholars have improved Greek so much.”
“Then there is the future,” said the Very Young Man. “Just think! One might invest all one’s money, leave it to accumulate at interest, and hurry on ahead!”

The Time Traveller smiled round at us. Then, still smiling faintly, and with his hands deep in his trousers pockets, he walked slowly out of the room, and we heard his slippers shuffling down the long passage to his laboratory.

“Some sleight-of-hand trick or other,” said the Medical Man, and Filby tried to tell us about a conjuror he had seen at Burslem, but before he had finished his preface the Time Traveller came back, and Filby’s anecdote collapsed.

The thing the Time Traveller held in his hand was a glittering metallic framework, scarcely larger than a small clock, and very delicately made. There was ivory in it, and some transparent crystalline substance. And now I must be explicit, for this that follows—unless his explanation is to be accepted—is an absolutely unaccountable thing. He took one of the small octagonal tables that were scattered about the room, and set it in front of the fire, with two legs on the hearthrug. On this table he placed the mechanism. Then he drew up a chair, and sat down. The only other object on the table was a small shaded lamp, the bright light of which fell full upon the model. There were also perhaps a dozen candles about, two in brass candlesticks upon the mantel and several in sconces, so that the room was brilliantly illuminated. I sat in a low arm-chair nearest the fire, and I drew this forward so as to be almost between the Time Traveller and the fireplace. Filby sat behind him, looking over his shoulder. The Medical Man and the Provincial Mayor watched him in profile from the right, the Psychologist from the left. The Very Young Man stood behind the Psychologist. We were all on the alert. It appears incredible to me that any kind of trick, however subtly conceived and however adroitly done, could have been played upon us under these conditions.

“This little affair,” said the Time Traveller, resting his elbows upon the table and pressing his hands together above the apparatus, “is only a model. It is my plan for a machine to travel through time. You will notice that it looks singularly askew, and that there is an odd twinkling appearance about this bar, as though it was in some way unreal.” He pointed to the part with his finger. “Also, here is one little white lever, and here is another.”
The Medical Man got up out of his chair and peered into the thing. “It’s beautifully made,” he said.

“It took two years to make,” retorted the Time Traveller. Then, when we had all imitated the action of the Medical Man, he said: “Now I want you clearly to understand that this lever, being pressed over, sends the machine gliding into the future, and this other reverses the motion. This saddle represents the seat of a time traveller. Presently I am going to press the lever, and off the machine will go. It will vanish, pass into future Time, and disappear. Have a good look at the thing. Look at the table too, and satisfy yourselves there is no trickery. I don’t want to waste this model, and then be told I’m a quack.”

There was a minute’s pause perhaps. The Psychologist seemed about to speak to me, but changed his mind. Then the Time Traveller put forth his finger towards the lever. “No,” he said suddenly. “Lend me your hand.” And turning to the Psychologist, he took that individual’s hand in his own and told him to put out his forefinger. So that it was the Psychologist himself who sent forth the model Time Machine on its interminable voyage. We all saw the lever turn. I am absolutely certain there was no trickery. There was a breath of wind, and the lamp flame jumped. One of the candles on the mantel was blown out, and the little machine suddenly swung round, became indistinct, was seen as a ghost for a second perhaps, as an eddy of faintly glittering brass and ivory; and it was gone—vanished! Save for the lamp the table was bare.
paragraphsZh: “这样的话，他们肯定会把你逼成Little-go。德国学者已经把希腊语改进了很多。”
“那就有未来了，”非常年轻人说道。 “你想一想！可以把所有的钱都投入进去，积累利息，然后赶紧走！”
时间旅行者对我们微笑。然后，他仍然微笑着，双手深深地插在裤兜里，慢慢地走出房间，我们听到他的拖鞋拖着脚步沿着长长的通道走向他的实验室。
“一些花招或其他的，”医生说，菲尔比试图告诉我们他在布尔斯勒姆见过的魔术师，但在他完成序言之前，时间旅行者回来了，菲尔比的轶事崩溃了。

时间旅行者手里拿着的是一个闪闪发光的金属框架，比一个小钟大不了多少，而且做工非常精致。里面有象牙，还有一些透明的晶体物质。现在我必须明确指出，因为接下来的事情——除非他的解释被接受——是一件绝对无法解释的事情。他拿起房间里散落的一张八角形小桌，把它放在火前，两条腿放在炉边地毯上。他把这个装置放在这张桌子上。然后他拉过一把椅子，坐了下来。桌子上唯一的其他物体是一盏带灯罩的小灯，明亮的光线照在模特身上。周围大约还有十几根蜡烛，两根放在壁炉架上的黄铜烛台上，还有几根放在壁灯座上，所以房间被照亮了。我坐在离火最近的一把矮扶手椅上，把椅子向前拉，几乎位于时间旅行者和壁炉之间。菲尔比坐在他身后，越过他的肩膀往外看。医生和省长从右边侧视着他，心理学家从左边侧视着他。非常年轻的男子站在心理学家身后。我们都保持警惕。在我看来，令人难以置信的是，在这种情况下，任何一种诡计，无论构思多么巧妙，做得多么巧妙，都可能对我们起作用。
“这个小东西，”时间旅行者说，他的胳膊肘靠在桌子上，双手合十放在设备上方，“只是一个模型。这是我的机器穿越时间的计划。你会注意到它看起来非常歪斜，而且这个酒吧有一种奇怪的闪烁外观，好像它在某种程度上不真实。”他用手指指着那部分。 “还有，这是一个白色的小杠杆，这是另一个。”
医生从椅子上站起来，凝视着那个东西。 “它制作得很漂亮，”他说。
“花了两年时间制作，”时间旅行者反驳道。然后，当我们都模仿了医生的动作时，他说：“现在我想让你们清楚地明白，这个杠杆被压下去，使机器滑向未来，而另一个则反转运动。这个马鞍代表时间旅行者的座位。现在我要按下杠杆，机器就会离开。它会消失，进入未来的时间，然后消失。仔细看看这个东西。也看看桌子，让自己确信没有我不想浪费这个模型，然后被告知我是个庸医。”

或许有一分钟的停顿。心理学家似乎想跟我说话，但后来改变了主意。然后时间旅行者将手指伸向控制杆。 “不，”他突然说道。 “把手借给我。”然后转向心理学家，他握住那个人的手，让他伸出食指。因此，正是心理学家本人将模型时间机器送上了无尽的航行。我们都看到杠杆转动了。我绝对确定没有任何诡计。一阵风吹过，灯火跳动。壁炉架上的一支蜡烛被吹灭了，那台小机器突然旋转起来，变得模糊不清，一瞬间被视为幽灵，就像一个微弱闪光的黄铜和象牙的漩涡；然后它就消失了——消失了！除了台灯，桌子上空无一物。

title: The Time Machine · 选段 5
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “The landscape was misty and vague. I was still on the hillside upon which this house now stands, and the shoulder rose above me grey and dim. I saw trees growing and changing like puffs of vapour, now brown, now green; they grew, spread, shivered, and passed away. I saw huge buildings rise up faint and fair, and pass like dreams. The whole surface of the earth seemed changed—melting and flowing under my eyes. The little hands upon the dials that registered my speed raced round faster and faster. Presently I noted that the sun belt swayed up and down, from solstice to solstice, in a minute or less, and that consequently my pace was over a year a minute; and minute by minute the white snow flashed across the world, and vanished, and was followed by the bright, brief green of spring.

“The unpleasant sensations of the start were less poignant now. They merged at last into a kind of hysterical exhilaration. I remarked, indeed, a clumsy swaying of the machine, for which I was unable to account. But my mind was too confused to attend to it, so with a kind of madness growing upon me, I flung myself into futurity. At first I scarce thought of stopping, scarce thought of anything but these new sensations. But presently a fresh series of impressions grew up in my mind—a certain curiosity and therewith a certain dread—until at last they took complete possession of me. What strange developments of humanity, what wonderful advances upon our rudimentary civilisation, I thought, might not appear when I came to look nearly into the dim elusive world that raced and fluctuated before my eyes! I saw great and splendid architecture rising about me, more massive than any buildings of our own time, and yet, as it seemed, built of glimmer and mist. I saw a richer green flow up the hillside, and remain there, without any wintry intermission. Even through the veil of my confusion the earth seemed very fair. And so my mind came round to the business of stopping.

“The peculiar risk lay in the possibility of my finding some substance in the space which I, or the machine, occupied. So long as I travelled at a high velocity through time, this scarcely mattered: I was, so to speak, attenuated—was slipping like a vapour through the interstices of intervening substances! But to come to a stop involved the jamming of myself, molecule by molecule, into whatever lay in my way; meant bringing my atoms into such intimate contact with those of the obstacle that a profound chemical reaction—possibly a far-reaching explosion—would result, and blow myself and my apparatus out of all possible dimensions—into the Unknown. This possibility had occurred to me again and again while I was making the machine; but then I had cheerfully accepted it as an unavoidable risk—one of the risks a man has got to take! Now the risk was inevitable, I no longer saw it in the same cheerful light. The fact is that, insensibly, the absolute strangeness of everything, the sickly jarring and swaying of the machine, above all, the feeling of prolonged falling, had absolutely upset my nerves. I told myself that I could never stop, and with a gust of petulance I resolved to stop forthwith. Like an impatient fool, I lugged over the lever, and incontinently the thing went reeling over, and I was flung headlong through the air.

“There was the sound of a clap of thunder in my ears. I may have been stunned for a moment. A pitiless hail was hissing round me, and I was sitting on soft turf in front of the overset machine. Everything still seemed grey, but presently I remarked that the confusion in my ears was gone. I looked round me. I was on what seemed to be a little lawn in a garden, surrounded by rhododendron bushes, and I noticed that their mauve and purple blossoms were dropping in a shower under the beating of the hailstones. The rebounding, dancing hail hung in a little cloud over the machine, and drove along the ground like smoke. In a moment I was wet to the skin. ‘Fine hospitality,’ said I, ‘to a man who has travelled innumerable years to see you.’
paragraphsZh: “景色朦朦胧胧，模糊不清。我还在这座房子现在矗立的山坡上，山肩在我上方升起，灰色而昏暗。我看到树木像一阵阵蒸汽一样生长和变化，时而棕色，时而绿色；它们生长、蔓延、颤抖，然后消失。我看到巨大的建筑隐约而美丽地拔地而起，然后像梦一样过去。整个地球表面似乎发生了变化——在我的眼前融化和流动。表盘上的小指针记录着我的速度。不久，我注意到太阳带在一分钟或更短的时间内从一个至日到另一个至日上下摆动，因此我的速度超过了一年一分钟；白雪一分钟一分钟地闪过世界，然后消失了，随之而来的是春天的明亮而短暂的绿色。

“开始时的不愉快感觉现在不再那么令人痛苦了。他们最终陷入了一种歇斯底里的兴奋之中。我确实注意到机器笨拙地摇晃，但我无法解释原因。但我的头脑太混乱了，无法关注它，因此，随着一种疯狂的情绪在我身上滋长，我把自己抛向了未来。起初我几乎没有想过要停下来，除了这些新的感觉之外几乎没有想到任何事情。但不久之后，一系列新的印象在我的脑海中涌现——一种好奇，随之而来的一种恐惧——直到最后它们完全占据了我。我想，当我仔细观察眼前这个瞬息万变、难以捉摸的世界时，人类多么奇怪的发展，我们原始文明的多么奇妙的进步，可能都不会出现！我看到伟大而辉煌的建筑在我周围升起，比我们这个时代的任何建筑都要庞大，但看起来却是由微光和薄雾建造的。我看到更浓郁的绿色沿着山坡流淌，一直留在那里，没有任何冬季的间歇。即使透过我困惑的面纱，地球也显得非常公平。于是我的心思转向了停下来的事情。

“特殊的风险在于我可能会在我或机器所占据的空间中找到某种物质。只要我在时间中高速旅行，这几乎不重要：可以说，我被削弱了——像蒸汽一样滑过中间物质的间隙！但是要停下来，我自己，一个分子接一个分子，塞进任何挡在我路上的东西；意味着让我的原子与那些原子进行如此密切的接触。在我制造机器时，我一次又一次地想到了这种可能性；但后来我欣喜地接受了它作为一个人必须承担的风险之一！机器的震动和摇晃，尤其是长时间坠落的感觉，绝对让我心烦意乱，我告诉自己，我永远无法停下来，我像一个不耐烦的傻瓜一样，决定立即停下来，然后那东西不由自主地翻倒了，我被抛到了空中。

“我耳边响起了雷鸣之声。我可能愣了一下。无情的冰雹在我周围嘶嘶作响，我坐在翻倒的机器前柔软的草坪上。一切看起来仍然是灰色的，但不久我发现我耳朵里的混乱消失了。我环顾四周。我站在花园里的一块小草坪上，周围环绕着杜鹃花丛，我注意到它们的淡紫色和紫色花朵在冰雹的袭击下如阵雨般落下。反弹、舞动的冰雹悬浮在机器上方的一小片云中，像烟雾一样沿着地面移动。一会儿我的皮肤就湿透了。 “对一个千里迢迢来见你的人来说，真是太好了。”我说。

title: The Time Machine · 选段 6
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “So watching, I began to put my interpretation upon the things I had seen, and as it shaped itself to me that evening, my interpretation was something in this way. (Afterwards I found I had got only a half truth—or only a glimpse of one facet of the truth.)

“It seemed to me that I had happened upon humanity upon the wane. The ruddy sunset set me thinking of the sunset of mankind. For the first time I began to realise an odd consequence of the social effort in which we are at present engaged. And yet, come to think, it is a logical consequence enough. Strength is the outcome of need; security sets a premium on feebleness. The work of ameliorating the conditions of life—the true civilising process that makes life more and more secure—had gone steadily on to a climax. One triumph of a united humanity over Nature had followed another. Things that are now mere dreams had become projects deliberately put in hand and carried forward. And the harvest was what I saw!

“After all, the sanitation and the agriculture of today are still in the rudimentary stage. The science of our time has attacked but a little department of the field of human disease, but, even so, it spreads its operations very steadily and persistently. Our agriculture and horticulture destroy a weed just here and there and cultivate perhaps a score or so of wholesome plants, leaving the greater number to fight out a balance as they can. We improve our favourite plants and animals—and how few they are—gradually by selective breeding; now a new and better peach, now a seedless grape, now a sweeter and larger flower, now a more convenient breed of cattle. We improve them gradually, because our ideals are vague and tentative, and our knowledge is very limited; because Nature, too, is shy and slow in our clumsy hands. Some day all this will be better organised, and still better. That is the drift of the current in spite of the eddies. The whole world will be intelligent, educated, and co-operating; things will move faster and faster towards the subjugation of Nature. In the end, wisely and carefully we shall readjust the balance of animal and vegetable life to suit our human needs.

“This adjustment, I say, must have been done, and done well; done indeed for all Time, in the space of Time across which my machine had leapt. The air was free from gnats, the earth from weeds or fungi; everywhere were fruits and sweet and delightful flowers; brilliant butterflies flew hither and thither. The ideal of preventive medicine was attained. Diseases had been stamped out. I saw no evidence of any contagious diseases during all my stay. And I shall have to tell you later that even the processes of putrefaction and decay had been profoundly affected by these changes.

“Social triumphs, too, had been effected. I saw mankind housed in splendid shelters, gloriously clothed, and as yet I had found them engaged in no toil. There were no signs of struggle, neither social nor economical struggle. The shop, the advertisement, traffic, all that commerce which constitutes the body of our world, was gone. It was natural on that golden evening that I should jump at the idea of a social paradise. The difficulty of increasing population had been met, I guessed, and population had ceased to increase.

“But with this change in condition comes inevitably adaptations to the change. What, unless biological science is a mass of errors, is the cause of human intelligence and vigour? Hardship and freedom: conditions under which the active, strong, and subtle survive and the weaker go to the wall; conditions that put a premium upon the loyal alliance of capable men, upon self-restraint, patience, and decision. And the institution of the family, and the emotions that arise therein, the fierce jealousy, the tenderness for offspring, parental self-devotion, all found their justification and support in the imminent dangers of the young. Now, where are these imminent dangers? There is a sentiment arising, and it will grow, against connubial jealousy, against fierce maternity, against passion of all sorts; unnecessary things now, and things that make us uncomfortable, savage survivals, discords in a refined and pleasant life.
paragraphsZh: “所以看着，我开始把我的解释放在我所看到的事情上，当那天晚上它在我身上形成时，我的解释就是这样的。（后来我发现我只得到了一半的真相——或者只是真相的一个方面的一瞥。）

“在我看来，我碰巧遇到了正在衰落的人类。红润的夕阳让我想起了人类的夕阳。我第一次开始意识到我们目前所从事的社会努力产生了一个奇怪的后果。然而，仔细想想，这是一个足够合乎逻辑的结果。力量是需要的结果；安全性比脆弱性更重要。改善生活条件的工作——让生活变得越来越安全的真正的文明进程——已经稳步走向高潮。团结一致的人类战胜自然的胜利接踵而至。现在仅仅是梦想的事情已经变成了刻意投入并推进的项目。而收获就是我所看到的！

“毕竟，今天的卫生和农业仍处于初级阶段。我们这个时代的科学只攻击了人类疾病领域的一小部分，但即便如此，它的运作仍然非常稳定和持久。我们的农业和园艺只是在这里或那里消灭杂草，并培育大约二十种有益健康的植物，留下更多的植物来尽可能地争取平衡。我们改善了我们最喜欢的植物和动物——而它们是多么的少。逐渐地，通过选择性培育；现在是一种新的、更好的桃子，现在是一种更甜、更大的花，现在是一种更方便的牛品种，因为我们的理想是模糊的、试探性的，而我们的知识也非常有限；因为有一天，这一切都会变得更好，尽管有漩涡，但整个世界都会变得聪明、有教养。合作；事物将越来越快地走向征服自然。最终，我们将明智而谨慎地重新调整动植物生命的平衡，以适应人类的需求。
“我说这个调整一定要做，而且做得很好；确实是在我的机器所跨越的时间空间中永远完成的。空气中没有蚊虫，土地上没有杂草或真菌。到处都是水果和甜美可爱的花朵。绚丽的蝴蝶飞来飞去。预防医学的理想已经达到。疾病已被消灭。在我逗留期间，我没有看到任何传染病的证据。稍后我必须告诉你，甚至腐烂和腐烂的过程也受到了这些变化的深刻影响。
“社会的胜利也已经实现。我看到人类住在华丽的住所里，衣着华丽，但我还没有发现他们从事任何劳作。没有任何斗争的迹象，无论是社会斗争还是经济斗争。商店、广告、交通以及构成我们世界主体的所有商业都消失了。在那个金色的夜晚，我很自然地想到了一个社会天堂的想法。人口增长的困难已经解决了，我猜想，人口已经停止增长了。

“但是随着条件的变化，不可避免地会出现对变化的适应。除非生物科学存在大量错误，否则人类智慧和活力的原因是什么？艰难与自由：积极、强者、微妙者生存，弱者濒临绝境的条件；这些条件重视有能力的人的忠诚联盟、自我克制、耐心和决心。家庭制度以及其中产生的情感、强烈的嫉妒、对后代的温柔、父母的自我奉献，都在年轻人迫在眉睫的危险中找到了合理性和支持。现在，这些迫在眉睫的危险在哪里？人们会产生一种情绪，并且这种情绪将会增长，反对夫妻间的嫉妒，反对激烈的母性，反对各种激情；现在不必要的事情，以及让我们不舒服的事情，野蛮的生存，与精致愉快的生活的不和谐。

title: The Time Machine · 选段 7
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “Under the new conditions of perfect comfort and security, that restless energy, that with us is strength, would become weakness. Even in our own time certain tendencies and desires, once necessary to survival, are a constant source of failure. Physical courage and the love of battle, for instance, are no great help—may even be hindrances—to a civilised man. And in a state of physical balance and security, power, intellectual as well as physical, would be out of place. For countless years I judged there had been no danger of war or solitary violence, no danger from wild beasts, no wasting disease to require strength of constitution, no need of toil. For such a life, what we should call the weak are as well equipped as the strong, are indeed no longer weak. Better equipped indeed they are, for the strong would be fretted by an energy for which there was no outlet. No doubt the exquisite beauty of the buildings I saw was the outcome of the last surgings of the now purposeless energy of mankind before it settled down into perfect harmony with the conditions under which it lived—the flourish of that triumph which began the last great peace.
