This has ever been the fate of energy in security; it takes to art and to eroticism, and then come languor and decay.

“Even this artistic impetus would at last die away—had almost died in the Time I saw. To adorn themselves with flowers, to dance, to sing in the sunlight: so much was left of the artistic spirit, and no more. Even that would fade in the end into a contented inactivity. We are kept keen on the grindstone of pain and necessity, and it seemed to me that here was that hateful grindstone broken at last!

“As I stood there in the gathering dark I thought that in this simple explanation I had mastered the problem of the world—mastered the whole secret of these delicious people. Possibly the checks they had devised for the increase of population had succeeded too well, and their numbers had rather diminished than kept stationary. That would account for the abandoned ruins. Very simple was my explanation, and plausible enough—as most wrong theories are!

“As I stood there musing over this too perfect triumph of man, the full moon, yellow and gibbous, came up out of an overflow of silver light in the north-east. The bright little figures ceased to move about below, a noiseless owl flitted by, and I shivered with the chill of the night. I determined to descend and find where I could sleep.

“I looked for the building I knew. Then my eye travelled along to the figure of the White Sphinx upon the pedestal of bronze, growing distinct as the light of the rising moon grew brighter. I could see the silver birch against it. There was the tangle of rhododendron bushes, black in the pale light, and there was the little lawn. I looked at the lawn again. A queer doubt chilled my complacency. ‘No,’ said I stoutly to myself, ‘that was not the lawn.’
“But it was the lawn. For the white leprous face of the sphinx was towards it. Can you imagine what I felt as this conviction came home to me? But you cannot. The Time Machine was gone!

“At once, like a lash across the face, came the possibility of losing my own age, of being left helpless in this strange new world. The bare thought of it was an actual physical sensation. I could feel it grip me at the throat and stop my breathing. In another moment I was in a passion of fear and running with great leaping strides down the slope. Once I fell headlong and cut my face; I lost no time in stanching the blood, but jumped up and ran on, with a warm trickle down my cheek and chin. All the time I ran I was saying to myself: ‘They have moved it a little, pushed it under the bushes out of the way.’ Nevertheless, I ran with all my might. All the time, with the certainty that sometimes comes with excessive dread, I knew that such assurance was folly, knew instinctively that the machine was removed out of my reach. My breath came with pain. I suppose I covered the whole distance from the hill crest to the little lawn, two miles perhaps, in ten minutes. And I am not a young man. I cursed aloud, as I ran, at my confident folly in leaving the machine, wasting good breath thereby. I cried aloud, and none answered. Not a creature seemed to be stirring in that moonlit world.
paragraphsZh: “在完美舒适和安全的新条件下，那种不安分的能量，对我们来说就是力量，将成为弱点。即使在我们这个时代，某些倾向和欲望一旦成为生存所必需的，就会成为失败的持续根源。例如，身体的勇气和对战斗的热爱，对一个文明人来说并没有多大帮助，甚至可能是障碍。在身体平衡和安全的状态下，力量，智力和身体，都会显得格格不入。无数年来，我判断没有战争的危险，没有野兽的危险，没有消耗体力的疾病，不需要劳作，对于这样的生活，我们所说的弱者和强者一样装备精良，事实上，他们不再是弱者，因为强者会被一种没有出口的能量所困扰，毫无疑问，我所看到的建筑物的精美是人类现在无目的的能量最后汹涌澎湃的结果。与它所处的环境完美和谐——开启最后伟大和平的胜利的繁荣一直是安全的能量的命运；它带来了艺术和色情，然后是疲倦和衰落。
“即使是这种艺术动力最终也会消失——在我看到的时代几乎消失了。用鲜花装饰自己，在阳光下跳舞、唱歌：艺术精神就只剩这么多了，仅此而已。即便如此，最终也会变成心满意足的无所事事。我们一直热衷于痛苦和必然性的磨刀石，在我看来，这块可恶的磨刀石终于被打破了！
“当我站在逐渐变暗的夜色中时，我想，在这个简单的解释中，我已经掌握了世界的问题——掌握了这些可爱的人们的全部秘密。可能他们为人口增长而设计的控制太成功了，他们的数量反而减少了，而不是保持不变。这就是被遗弃的废墟的原因。我的解释非常简单，而且足够合理——就像大多数错误的理论一样！
当我站在那里沉思人类这一过于完美的胜利时，黄色的凸月满月从东北方溢出的银光中升起。下面那些明亮的小人物停止了移动，一只无声的猫头鹰飞过，我因夜色的寒冷而颤抖。我决定下去寻找可以睡觉的地方。
“我寻找着我所熟悉的建筑。然后我的目光移到青铜底座上的白色狮身人面像上，随着初升的月亮越来越亮，它变得越来越清晰。我可以看到它旁边的银桦树。那里是一丛丛的杜鹃花丛，在苍白的光线下呈黑色，还有那片小草坪。我又看了看那片草坪。一种奇怪的怀疑使我的自满情绪冷了下来。‘不，’说。我坚定地对自己说：“那不是草坪。”
“但那是草坪。因为狮身人面像那张患麻风病的白色脸正对着它。你能想象当我意识到这一信念时我的感受吗？但你不能。时间机器不见了！

“立刻，就像脸上挨了一记鞭子，我失去了自己的年龄，在这个陌生的新世界中感到无助。光是想到它就是一种真实的身体感觉。我能感觉到它掐住了我的喉咙，让我停止了呼吸。转眼间，我充满了恐惧，大步地跑下斜坡。有一次我一头栽倒，割伤了我的脸；我不失时机地止血，但跳起来继续跑，带着温暖的感觉。我一边跑一边对自己说：“他们把它移到了灌木丛下面。”尽管如此，我还是竭尽全力地跑着，有时带着过度的恐惧，我知道这种保证是愚蠢的，我本能地知道我的呼吸已经离开了我的范围，我想我在十英里内跑完了从山顶到小草坪的整个距离。我已经不是年轻人了，一边跑，一边大声咒骂着自己的愚蠢行为，浪费了好大口气，但月光下的世界里似乎没有一个人在动。

title: The Time Machine · 选段 8
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “I thought of the flickering pillars and of my theory of an underground ventilation. I began to suspect their true import. And what, I wondered, was this Lemur doing in my scheme of a perfectly balanced organisation? How was it related to the indolent serenity of the beautiful Overworlders? And what was hidden down there, at the foot of that shaft? I sat upon the edge of the well telling myself that, at any rate, there was nothing to fear, and that there I must descend for the solution of my difficulties. And withal I was absolutely afraid to go! As I hesitated, two of the beautiful upperworld people came running in their amorous sport across the daylight in the shadow. The male pursued the female, flinging flowers at her as he ran.

“They seemed distressed to find me, my arm against the overturned pillar, peering down the well. Apparently it was considered bad form to remark these apertures; for when I pointed to this one, and tried to frame a question about it in their tongue, they were still more visibly distressed and turned away. But they were interested by my matches, and I struck some to amuse them. I tried them again about the well, and again I failed. So presently I left them, meaning to go back to Weena, and see what I could get from her. But my mind was already in revolution; my guesses and impressions were slipping and sliding to a new adjustment. I had now a clue to the import of these wells, to the ventilating towers, to the mystery of the ghosts; to say nothing of a hint at the meaning of the bronze gates and the fate of the Time Machine! And very vaguely there came a suggestion towards the solution of the economic problem that had puzzled me.

“Here was the new view. Plainly, this second species of Man was subterranean. There were three circumstances in particular which made me think that its rare emergence above ground was the outcome of a long-continued underground habit. In the first place, there was the bleached look common in most animals that live largely in the dark—the white fish of the Kentucky caves, for instance. Then, those large eyes, with that capacity for reflecting light, are common features of nocturnal things—witness the owl and the cat. And last of all, that evident confusion in the sunshine, that hasty yet fumbling awkward flight towards dark shadow, and that peculiar carriage of the head while in the light—all reinforced the theory of an extreme sensitiveness of the retina.

“Beneath my feet, then, the earth must be tunnelled enormously, and these tunnellings were the habitat of the New Race. The presence of ventilating shafts and wells along the hill slopes—everywhere, in fact, except along the river valley—showed how universal were its ramifications. What so natural, then, as to assume that it was in this artificial Underworld that such work as was necessary to the comfort of the daylight race was done? The notion was so plausible that I at once accepted it, and went on to assume the how of this splitting of the human species. I dare say you will anticipate the shape of my theory; though, for myself, I very soon felt that it fell far short of the truth.

“At first, proceeding from the problems of our own age, it seemed clear as daylight to me that the gradual widening of the present merely temporary and social difference between the Capitalist and the Labourer was the key to the whole position. No doubt it will seem grotesque enough to you—and wildly incredible!—and yet even now there are existing circumstances to point that way. There is a tendency to utilise underground space for the less ornamental purposes of civilisation; there is the Metropolitan Railway in London, for instance, there are new electric railways, there are subways, there are underground workrooms and restaurants, and they increase and multiply. Evidently, I thought, this tendency had increased till Industry had gradually lost its birthright in the sky. I mean that it had gone deeper and deeper into larger and ever larger underground factories, spending a still-increasing amount of its time therein, till, in the end—! Even now, does not an East-end worker live in such artificial conditions as practically to be cut off from the natural surface of the earth?
paragraphsZh: “我想到了闪烁的柱子和我的地下通风理论。我开始怀疑它们的真正重要性。我想知道，这只狐猴在我的完美平衡组织计划中做了什么？它与美丽的主世界者的懒惰宁静有什么关系？那根竖井的脚下隐藏着什么？我坐在井边告诉自己，无论如何，没有什么可害怕的，我必须下降到那里来解决我的问题。就在我犹豫不决的时候，两个美丽的上层世界的人在阳光下跑来，在阴影中追逐着雌性，一边跑一边向她扔花。

“他们似乎很沮丧地发现我，我的手臂靠在翻倒的柱子上，朝井下看。显然，评论这些孔被认为是不礼貌的；因为当我指着这个孔，并试图用他们的舌头提出一个有关它的问题时，他们仍然更加痛苦并转过身去。但他们对我的火柴很感兴趣，我划了一些来逗他们。我再次向他们尝试关于井的事，但我再次失败了。所以不久我离开了他们，打算回到维纳，看看但我的思绪已经开始转变；我现在对这些井、通风塔、鬼魂的神秘有了一些线索；更不用说关于青铜门的意义和时间机器的命运的暗示了！

“这是新的观点。显然，第二种人类是在地下生活的。有三种情况让我认为，它在地面上的罕见出现是长期持续的地下习性的结果。首先，大多数生活在黑暗中的动物都有一种常见的漂白外观——例如肯塔基州洞穴中的白鱼。然后，那些具有反射光线能力的大眼睛是夜行动物的共同特征——猫头鹰和猫头鹰就是证明。最后，猫在阳光下明显的混乱，仓促而又笨拙地向黑暗阴影飞去，以及在光线下头部的奇特姿势——所有这些都强化了视网膜极度敏感的理论。
“那么，在我的脚下，大地一定有巨大的隧道，而这些隧道是新种族的栖息地。沿着山坡的通风井和井的存在——事实上，除了河谷沿线——无处不在，这表明它的影响是多么普遍。那么，假设在这个人造地下世界中完成了白天种族舒适所必需的工作，这是多么自然的事情呢？这个想法是如此合理，以至于我我立刻接受了它，并继续推测人类物种的分裂是如何发生的，我敢说你会预料到我的理论的形式；但我很快就觉得它与事实相去甚远。

“首先，从我们这个时代的问题出发，我觉得很明显，资本家和劳动者之间目前只是暂时的和社会的差异的逐渐扩大是整个立场的关键。毫无疑问，这对你来说已经够怪诞的了——而且难以置信！——但即使是现在，现有的情况也表明了这一点。有一种趋势是利用地下空间来实现不太装饰性的文明目的；例如，伦敦有大都会铁路，有新的铁路。我想，显然，这种趋势一直在增加，直到工业逐渐失去了它与生俱来的天空权利，我的意思是，它已经越来越深入到越来越大的地下工厂，在其中度过的时间越来越多，直到最后——！即使是现在，东部工人不是生活在几乎与地球自然表面隔绝的人造环境中吗？

title: The Time Machine · 选段 9
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “I had at that time very vague ideas as to the course I should pursue. My first was to secure some safe place of refuge, and to make myself such arms of metal or stone as I could contrive. That necessity was immediate. In the next place, I hoped to procure some means of fire, so that I should have the weapon of a torch at hand, for nothing, I knew, would be more efficient against these Morlocks. Then I wanted to arrange some contrivance to break open the doors of bronze under the White Sphinx. I had in mind a battering ram. I had a persuasion that if I could enter those doors and carry a blaze of light before me I should discover the Time Machine and escape. I could not imagine the Morlocks were strong enough to move it far away. Weena I had resolved to bring with me to our own time. And turning such schemes over in my mind I pursued our way towards the building which my fancy had chosen as our dwelling.

“I found the Palace of Green Porcelain, when we approached it about noon, deserted and falling into ruin. Only ragged vestiges of glass remained in its windows, and great sheets of the green facing had fallen away from the corroded metallic framework. It lay very high upon a turfy down, and looking north-eastward before I entered it, I was surprised to see a large estuary, or even creek, where I judged Wandsworth and Battersea must once have been. I thought then—though I never followed up the thought—of what might have happened, or might be happening, to the living things in the sea.

“The material of the Palace proved on examination to be indeed porcelain, and along the face of it I saw an inscription in some unknown character. I thought, rather foolishly, that Weena might help me to interpret this, but I only learnt that the bare idea of writing had never entered her head. She always seemed to me, I fancy, more human than she was, perhaps because her affection was so human.

“Within the big valves of the door—which were open and broken—we found, instead of the customary hall, a long gallery lit by many side windows. At the first glance I was reminded of a museum. The tiled floor was thick with dust, and a remarkable array of miscellaneous objects was shrouded in the same grey covering. Then I perceived, standing strange and gaunt in the centre of the hall, what was clearly the lower part of a huge skeleton. I recognised by the oblique feet that it was some extinct creature after the fashion of the Megatherium. The skull and the upper bones lay beside it in the thick dust, and in one place, where rain-water had dropped through a leak in the roof, the thing itself had been worn away. Further in the gallery was the huge skeleton barrel of a Brontosaurus. My museum hypothesis was confirmed. Going towards the side I found what appeared to be sloping shelves, and clearing away the thick dust, I found the old familiar glass cases of our own time. But they must have been air-tight to judge from the fair preservation of some of their contents.

“Clearly we stood among the ruins of some latter-day South Kensington! Here, apparently, was the Palæontological Section, and a very splendid array of fossils it must have been, though the inevitable process of decay that had been staved off for a time, and had, through the extinction of bacteria and fungi, lost ninety-nine hundredths of its force, was nevertheless, with extreme sureness if with extreme slowness at work again upon all its treasures. Here and there I found traces of the little people in the shape of rare fossils broken to pieces or threaded in strings upon reeds. And the cases had in some instances been bodily removed—by the Morlocks, as I judged. The place was very silent. The thick dust deadened our footsteps. Weena, who had been rolling a sea urchin down the sloping glass of a case, presently came, as I stared about me, and very quietly took my hand and stood beside me.
paragraphsZh: “当时我对自己应该采取的行动有非常模糊的想法。我的第一件事是确保找到一个安全的避难所，并尽我所能为自己制造这样的金属或石头手臂。这种必要性是迫在眉睫的。其次，我希望获得一些火器，这样我手边就有火炬这样的武器，因为我知道，对抗这些莫洛克人，没有什么比这更有效的了。然后我想安排一些装置来打开白色狮身人面像下的青铜门。我心中有一个攻城锤，如果我能进入那些门并在我面前携带一道光，我就可以发现时间机器并逃脱我无法想象威娜我决定把它带到我们自己的时代，并在我的脑海中思考着这样的计划，我朝着我的幻想选择作为我们的住所的方向前进。
“中午我们接近时，我发现了青瓷宫，它已经荒废了，变成了废墟。窗户上只剩下了破烂的玻璃痕迹，大块的绿色饰面已经从腐蚀的金属框架上脱落了。它位于草皮上很高的地方，在我进入它之前向东北方向看，我惊讶地看到了一个大河口，甚至是小溪，我判断旺兹沃斯和巴特西一定曾经在那里。我当时我就想到——虽然我没有继续思考——海洋中的生物可能发生了什么，或者可能正在发生什么。
“经过检查，宫殿的材料证明确实是瓷器，沿着它的表面，我看到了一些未知字符的铭文。我相当愚蠢地认为维娜可能会帮助我解释这一点，但我只知道她的头脑中从未有过书写的想法。在我看来，她总是比她本身更人性化，也许是因为她的感情是如此人性化。

“在门的大阀门打开且破损的情况下，我们发现，不是通常的大厅，而是一条被许多侧窗照亮的长廊。乍一看，我想起了一个博物馆。瓷砖地板上积满了灰尘，一堆杂七杂八的物品被同样的灰色覆盖物所笼罩。然后我发现，奇怪而憔悴地站在大厅中央，显然是一个巨大骨架的下半部分。我从斜脚认出这是一个什么东西。头骨和上部骨头躺在它旁边的厚厚的灰尘中，在一个地方，雨水从屋顶的缝隙中掉下来，在画廊的更远处，我的博物馆假设得到了证实，我发现了一个似乎是倾斜的架子，清除了厚厚的灰尘，我发现了我们这个时代熟悉的旧玻璃柜。从其中一些内容的合理保存来判断，它们是密不透风的。

“显然，我们站在现代南肯辛顿的废墟之中！显然，这里是古生物区，而且一定有一系列非常精彩的化石，虽然不可避免的腐烂过程已经被推迟了一段时间，并且通过细菌和真菌的灭绝，失去了百分之九十九的力量，但无论如何，非常肯定的是，尽管极其缓慢，它的所有宝藏再次发挥作用。到处都是我我发现了一些小人的痕迹，这些化石的形状是破碎的，或者是串在芦苇上的，据我判断，这些箱子已经被莫洛克人搬走了。 厚厚的灰尘使我们的脚步声变得沉闷，当时威娜正在把海胆滚到箱子的倾斜玻璃上，当我环顾四周时，她悄悄地握住了我的手，站在我旁边。

title: The Time Machine · 选段 10
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “And now came a most unexpected thing. As I approached the pedestal of the sphinx I found the bronze valves were open. They had slid down into grooves.

“Within was a small apartment, and on a raised place in the corner of this was the Time Machine. I had the small levers in my pocket. So here, after all my elaborate preparations for the siege of the White Sphinx, was a meek surrender. I threw my iron bar away, almost sorry not to use it.

“A sudden thought came into my head as I stooped towards the portal. For once, at least, I grasped the mental operations of the Morlocks. Suppressing a strong inclination to laugh, I stepped through the bronze frame and up to the Time Machine. I was surprised to find it had been carefully oiled and cleaned. I have suspected since that the Morlocks had even partially taken it to pieces while trying in their dim way to grasp its purpose.

“Now as I stood and examined it, finding a pleasure in the mere touch of the contrivance, the thing I had expected happened. The bronze panels suddenly slid up and struck the frame with a clang. I was in the dark—trapped. So the Morlocks thought. At that I chuckled gleefully.

“I could already hear their murmuring laughter as they came towards me. Very calmly I tried to strike the match. I had only to fix on the levers and depart then like a ghost. But I had overlooked one little thing. The matches were of that abominable kind that light only on the box.

“You may imagine how all my calm vanished. The little brutes were close upon me. One touched me. I made a sweeping blow in the dark at them with the levers, and began to scramble into the saddle of the machine. Then came one hand upon me and then another. Then I had simply to fight against their persistent fingers for my levers, and at the same time feel for the studs over which these fitted. One, indeed, they almost got away from me. As it slipped from my hand, I had to butt in the dark with my head—I could hear the Morlock’s skull ring—to recover it. It was a nearer thing than the fight in the forest, I think, this last scramble.

“But at last the lever was fixed and pulled over. The clinging hands slipped from me. The darkness presently fell from my eyes. I found myself in the same grey light and tumult I have already described.

“I have already told you of the sickness and confusion that comes with time travelling. And this time I was not seated properly in the saddle, but sideways and in an unstable fashion. For an indefinite time I clung to the machine as it swayed and vibrated, quite unheeding how I went, and when I brought myself to look at the dials again I was amazed to find where I had arrived. One dial records days, and another thousands of days, another millions of days, and another thousands of millions. Now, instead of reversing the levers, I had pulled them over so as to go forward with them, and when I came to look at these indicators I found that the thousands hand was sweeping round as fast as the seconds hand of a watch—into futurity.

“As I drove on, a peculiar change crept over the appearance of things. The palpitating greyness grew darker; then—though I was still travelling with prodigious velocity—the blinking succession of day and night, which was usually indicative of a slower pace, returned, and grew more and more marked. This puzzled me very much at first. The alternations of night and day grew slower and slower, and so did the passage of the sun across the sky, until they seemed to stretch through centuries. At last a steady twilight brooded over the earth, a twilight only broken now and then when a comet glared across the darkling sky. The band of light that had indicated the sun had long since disappeared; for the sun had ceased to set—it simply rose and fell in the west, and grew ever broader and more red. All trace of the moon had vanished. The circling of the stars, growing slower and slower, had given place to creeping points of light. At last, some time before I stopped, the sun, red and very large, halted motionless upon the horizon, a vast dome glowing with a dull heat, and now and then suffering a momentary extinction. At one time it had for a little while glowed more brilliantly again, but it speedily reverted to its sullen red heat. I perceived by this slowing down of its rising and setting that the work of the tidal drag was done. The earth had come to rest with one face to the sun, even as in our own time the moon faces the earth. Very cautiously, for I remembered my former headlong fall, I began to reverse my motion. Slower and slower went the circling hands until the thousands one seemed motionless and the daily one was no longer a mere mist upon its scale. Still slower, until the dim outlines of a desolate beach grew visible.
paragraphsZh: “现在发生了最意想不到的事情。当我接近狮身人面像的基座时，我发现青铜阀门打开了。它们滑入了凹槽。
“里面有一个小公寓，在这个角落的一个凸起的地方是时间机器。我的口袋里有小杠杆。所以，在我为围攻白色狮身人面像所做的一切精心准备之后，我屈服了。我把铁棒扔掉了，几乎后悔没有使用它。
“当我弯腰走向传送门时，我的脑海中突然浮现出一个念头。至少这一次，我掌握了莫洛克人的心理运作。我强忍着大笑的冲动，穿过青铜框架，走到时间机器前。我惊讶地发现它已经被仔细地涂油和清洁了。从那时起我就怀疑莫洛克人甚至在以模糊的方式试图掌握其目的时将其部分地拆成了碎片。
“现在，当我站起来检查它时，仅仅触摸这个装置就感到高兴，我所期望的事情发生了。青铜板猛然滑起，撞在框架上，发出“叮”的一声。我在黑暗中——被困住了。莫洛克人就是这么想的。说到这里我高兴地笑了。
“当他们向我走来时，我已经能听到他们低声的笑声。我非常平静地试图划火柴。我只需固定住杠杆，然后像幽灵一样离开。但我忽略了一件小事。火柴是那种只在盒子上点燃的令人讨厌的火柴。

“你可以想象我所有的平静是如何消失的。这些小畜生离我很近。有一个触动了我。我在黑暗中用操纵杆向他们猛击了一下，然后开始爬上机器的鞍座。然后一只手伸到我身上，然后另一只手伸到我身上。然后我只需与他们顽固的手指搏斗，寻找我的杠杆，同时摸索安装这些杠杆的螺柱。确实，他们差点就从我身边逃脱了。当它从我手中滑落时，我不得不在黑暗中用头撞——我能听到莫洛克的头骨响声——才能把它找回来。我想，这比森林里的战斗更接近，这最后的争夺。
“但最后控制杆被固定并拉了过来。紧紧抓住的手从我身上滑落。黑暗立即从我的眼睛中消失。我发现自己处于我已经描述过的同样的灰色光线和混乱之中。

“我已经告诉过你时间旅行带来的疾病和混乱。这次我没有正确地坐在马鞍上，而是侧身坐在马鞍上，而且坐姿不稳定。在一段不确定的时间里，我紧紧抓住机器，看着它摇摆和振动，完全没有注意到我是如何走的，当我再次看向表盘时，我惊讶地发现我已经到达了哪里。一个表盘记录了几天，另一个表盘记录了数千天，另一个记录了数百万天，又一个记录了数亿天。现在，我没有反转杠杆，而是将它们拉到一边，以便与它们一起前进，当我看这些指示器时，我发现千分表的指针正像手表的秒针一样快速地旋转——进入未来。

“当我继续前行时，事物的外观发生了一种奇特的变化。令人心悸的灰色变得越来越暗；然后——尽管我仍在以惊人的速度行驶——通常表明速度较慢的白天和黑夜的闪烁又回来了，而且变得越来越明显。这起初让我非常困惑。黑夜和白天的交替变得越来越慢，太阳划过天空的速度也越来越慢，直到它们看起来像最后，暮色笼罩着大地，只有当一颗彗星划过黑暗的天空时，那道光带早已消失了——太阳只是在西边升起又落下，月亮的轨迹变得越来越宽，越来越红，最后，所有的星星都消失了。在我停下来之前的一段时间，红色的、巨大的太阳一动不动地停在地平线上，一个巨大的圆顶闪烁着暗淡的热量，有时它会再次发出更明亮的光芒，但它很快又恢复到阴暗的红色热量，通过它的升起和落下的速度，我感觉到潮汐阻力的作用已经完成了，就像我们自己的一样。当月亮面向地球时，我开始小心翼翼地转动旋转的指针，直到数千颗指针似乎一动不动，而日常的指针不再只是其规模上的一层薄雾，而是变得越来越慢，直到荒凉的海滩的模糊轮廓变得清晰可见。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 4
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: “It’s a-movin’,” he said to me as he passed; “a-screwin’ and a-screwin’ out. I don’t like it. I’m a-goin’ ’ome, I am.”
I went on to the crowd. There were really, I should think, two or three hundred people elbowing and jostling one another, the one or two ladies there being by no means the least active.
The crowd swayed a little, and I elbowed my way through. Every one seemed greatly excited. I heard a peculiar humming sound from the pit.
“I say!” said Ogilvy; “help keep these idiots back. We don’t know what’s in the confounded thing, you know!”
I saw a young man, a shop assistant in Woking I believe he was, standing on the cylinder and trying to scramble out of the hole again. The crowd had pushed him in.

The end of the cylinder was being screwed out from within. Nearly two feet of shining screw projected. Somebody blundered against me, and I narrowly missed being pitched onto the top of the screw. I turned, and as I did so the screw must have come out, for the lid of the cylinder fell upon the gravel with a ringing concussion. I stuck my elbow into the person behind me, and turned my head towards the Thing again. For a moment that circular cavity seemed perfectly black. I had the sunset in my eyes.

I think everyone expected to see a man emerge—possibly something a little unlike us terrestrial men, but in all essentials a man. I know I did. But, looking, I presently saw something stirring within the shadow: greyish billowy movements, one above another, and then two luminous disks—like eyes. Then something resembling a little grey snake, about the thickness of a walking stick, coiled up out of the writhing middle, and wriggled in the air towards me—and then another.

A sudden chill came over me. There was a loud shriek from a woman behind. I half turned, keeping my eyes fixed upon the cylinder still, from which other tentacles were now projecting, and began pushing my way back from the edge of the pit. I saw astonishment giving place to horror on the faces of the people about me. I heard inarticulate exclamations on all sides. There was a general movement backwards. I saw the shopman struggling still on the edge of the pit. I found myself alone, and saw the people on the other side of the pit running off, Stent among them. I looked again at the cylinder, and ungovernable terror gripped me. I stood petrified and staring.
A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear, was rising slowly and painfully out of the cylinder. As it bulged up and caught the light, it glistened like wet leather.

Two large dark-coloured eyes were regarding me steadfastly. The mass that framed them, the head of the thing, was rounded, and had, one might say, a face. There was a mouth under the eyes, the lipless brim of which quivered and panted, and dropped saliva. The whole creature heaved and pulsated convulsively. A lank tentacular appendage gripped the edge of the cylinder, another swayed in the air.

Those who have never seen a living Martian can scarcely imagine the strange horror of its appearance. The peculiar V-shaped mouth with its pointed upper lip, the absence of brow ridges, the absence of a chin beneath the wedgelike lower lip, the incessant quivering of this mouth, the Gorgon groups of tentacles, the tumultuous breathing of the lungs in a strange atmosphere, the evident heaviness and painfulness of movement due to the greater gravitational energy of the earth—above all, the extraordinary intensity of the immense eyes—were at once vital, intense, inhuman, crippled and monstrous. There was something fungoid in the oily brown skin, something in the clumsy deliberation of the tedious movements unspeakably nasty. Even at this first encounter, this first glimpse, I was overcome with disgust and dread.
paragraphsZh: “它在动，”他经过时对我说； “一拧一拧。我不喜欢这样。我要走了，我是。”
我走向人群。我想，确实有两三百人互相推搡、推搡，那里的一两个女士绝不是最不活跃的。
人群稍微晃动了一下，我挤了过去。每个人都显得非常兴奋。我听到坑里传来一种奇特的嗡嗡声。
“我说！”奥格维说； “帮助阻止这些白痴。我们不知道这个混乱的东西里有什么，你知道！”
我看到一个年轻人，我相信他是沃金的一名店员，站在圆柱体上，试图再次从洞里爬出来。众人把他推了进去。
圆柱体的末端被从内部旋出。近两英尺的闪亮螺丝伸出。有人对我犯了一个错误，我险些被推到了螺丝的顶部。我转过身来，当我这样做的时候，螺丝肯定已经出来了，因为圆筒的盖子掉在砾石上，发出一声巨响。我用肘部抵住身后的人，然后再次把头转向那个东西。有一瞬间，那个圆形空洞显得漆黑一片。我的眼里有夕阳。
我想每个人都期望看到一个男人的出现——可能与我们地球人有点不同，但本质上是一个男人。我知道我做到了。但是，我一看，很快就看到阴影里有什么东西在搅动：灰色的波涛般的运动，一个在另一个之上，然后是两个发光的圆盘——就像眼睛一样。然后，有一条类似灰色小蛇的东西，大约有一根手杖那么粗，从中间扭动着，在空中扭动着朝我这边爬来——然后又是一条。
我突然感到一阵寒意。身后传来女人的大声尖叫。我半转过身，眼睛仍然盯着圆柱体，其他触手现在从圆柱体上伸出，然后开始从坑的边缘向后推。我看到我周围的人脸上的惊讶变成了恐惧。我听到四面八方发出含糊不清的惊呼声。人们普遍向后退。我看见店主还在坑边挣扎。我发现自己孤身一人，看到坑另一边的人都跑开了，斯坦特也在其中。我再次看着圆柱体，无法抑制的恐惧抓住了我。我惊呆了，呆呆地站着。
一个巨大的灰色圆形物体，大概有熊那么大，正在缓慢而痛苦地从圆柱体中升起。当它鼓起并接受光线时，它像湿皮革一样闪闪发光。
两只黑色的大眼睛坚定地看着我。包围它们的物体，即那个东西的头部，是圆形的，并且有人可能会说，有一张脸。眼睛下面有一张嘴，没有嘴唇的边缘颤抖着，喘息着，流着口水。整个生物剧烈地起伏和搏动。一根细长的触手附肢抓住了圆柱体的边缘，另一根触手在空中摇晃。

那些从未见过活生生的火星人的人几乎无法想象它的外表是多么的诡异恐怖。那张奇特的V形嘴，尖尖的上唇，没有眉骨，楔形下唇下面没有下巴，这张嘴不停地颤抖，戈尔贡群的触手，肺部在奇怪的气氛中汹涌的呼吸，由于地球的更大引力而明显的沉重和痛苦的运动，尤其是那双巨大的眼睛的非凡的强度，立刻是生机勃勃的，强烈的，不人道、残废且可怕。油腻的棕色皮肤里有某种真菌，在笨拙的、沉思的、乏味的动作中，有一种难以形容的令人厌恶的东西。即使在第一次见面、第一次瞥见时，我还是感到厌恶和恐惧。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 5
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: Even as I beheld this a lurid green glare lit the road about me and showed the distant woods towards Addlestone. I felt a tug at the reins. I saw that the driving clouds had been pierced as it were by a thread of green fire, suddenly lighting their confusion and falling into the field to my left. It was the third falling star!

Close on its apparition, and blindingly violet by contrast, danced out the first lightning of the gathering storm, and the thunder burst like a rocket overhead. The horse took the bit between his teeth and bolted.

A moderate incline runs towards the foot of Maybury Hill, and down this we clattered. Once the lightning had begun, it went on in as rapid a succession of flashes as I have ever seen. The thunderclaps, treading one on the heels of another and with a strange crackling accompaniment, sounded more like the working of a gigantic electric machine than the usual detonating reverberations. The flickering light was blinding and confusing, and a thin hail smote gustily at my face as I drove down the slope.

At first I regarded little but the road before me, and then abruptly my attention was arrested by something that was moving rapidly down the opposite slope of Maybury Hill. At first I took it for the wet roof of a house, but one flash following another showed it to be in swift rolling movement. It was an elusive vision—a moment of bewildering darkness, and then, in a flash like daylight, the red masses of the Orphanage near the crest of the hill, the green tops of the pine trees, and this problematical object came out clear and sharp and bright.

And this Thing I saw! How can I describe it? A monstrous tripod, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees, and smashing them aside in its career; a walking engine of glittering metal, striding now across the heather; articulate ropes of steel dangling from it, and the clattering tumult of its passage mingling with the riot of the thunder. A flash, and it came out vividly, heeling over one way with two feet in the air, to vanish and reappear almost instantly as it seemed, with the next flash, a hundred yards nearer. Can you imagine a milking stool tilted and bowled violently along the ground? That was the impression those instant flashes gave. But instead of a milking stool imagine it a great body of machinery on a tripod stand.

Then suddenly the trees in the pine wood ahead of me were parted, as brittle reeds are parted by a man thrusting through them; they were snapped off and driven headlong, and a second huge tripod appeared, rushing, as it seemed, headlong towards me. And I was galloping hard to meet it! At the sight of the second monster my nerve went altogether. Not stopping to look again, I wrenched the horse’s head hard round to the right and in another moment the dog cart had heeled over upon the horse; the shafts smashed noisily, and I was flung sideways and fell heavily into a shallow pool of water.

I crawled out almost immediately, and crouched, my feet still in the water, under a clump of furze. The horse lay motionless (his neck was broken, poor brute!) and by the lightning flashes I saw the black bulk of the overturned dog cart and the silhouette of the wheel still spinning slowly. In another moment the colossal mechanism went striding by me, and passed uphill towards Pyrford.

Seen nearer, the Thing was incredibly strange, for it was no mere insensate machine driving on its way. Machine it was, with a ringing metallic pace, and long, flexible, glittering tentacles (one of which gripped a young pine tree) swinging and rattling about its strange body. It picked its road as it went striding along, and the brazen hood that surmounted it moved to and fro with the inevitable suggestion of a head looking about. Behind the main body was a huge mass of white metal like a gigantic fisherman’s basket, and puffs of green smoke squirted out from the joints of the limbs as the monster swept by me. And in an instant it was gone.
paragraphsZh: 就在我看到这一点的时候，一道刺眼的绿色光芒照亮了我周围的道路，向阿德尔斯通展示了远处的树林。我感到缰绳被拉了一下。只见疾驰的云彩仿佛被一道绿色的火线刺穿，顿时点燃了他们的迷惑，落入了我左边的田野里。这是第三颗流星！
接近它的幻影，与它形成对比的是令人眼花缭乱的紫罗兰色，舞动着正在聚集的风暴中的第一道闪电，雷霆像火箭一样在头顶上爆发。马用牙齿咬住嚼子，拔腿就跑。
一个缓和的斜坡通向梅伯里山脚，我们沿着这条斜坡走下去。闪电一开始，就以我所见过的最快速的连续闪光持续下去。雷声接二连三地响起，伴随着一种奇怪的噼啪声，听起来更像是一台巨大的电机在工作，而不是通常的爆炸性回响。闪烁的灯光令人眼花缭乱，令人困惑，当我驶下斜坡时，一阵细细的冰雹猛烈地打在我​​的脸上。
起初我只关注前方的道路，然后突然我的注意力被沿着梅伯里山对面的斜坡快速移动的东西吸引了。起初我以为这是一座房子的湿屋顶，但一闪接着一闪，显示它正在快速滚动。那是一种难以捉摸的景象——一片令人迷惑的黑暗，然后，像白昼一样一闪而过，山顶附近孤儿院的红色群落、松树的绿色树顶，以及这个有问题的物体清晰、锐利、明亮。

我看到了这个东西！我该如何描述呢？一个巨大的鼎，比许多房屋还高，跨过幼小的松树，在它的职业生涯中将它们砸碎；一辆闪闪发光的金属行走引擎，正大步穿过石南花丛；其上悬挂着铰接的钢索，其通过时发出的咔哒声和雷声交织在一起。一道闪光，它生动地出现了，在空中两英尺处倾斜，几乎立即消失并重新出现，下一次闪光，距离近了一百码。你能想象一个挤奶凳倾斜并沿着地面猛烈滚动吗？这就是那些瞬间的闪光给人的印象。但想象它不是一个挤奶凳，而是一个放在三脚架上的巨大机械体。
突然，我前面的松树林里的树木被分开了，就像脆弱的芦苇被一个人穿过它们分开一样；它们被折断并被猛烈地驱赶，第二个巨大的三脚架出现了，似乎猛烈地冲向我。而我则奋力疾驰去迎接它！当看到第二个怪物时，我的神经完全崩溃了。我没有停下来再看一眼，用力把马头向右扭去，不一会儿，狗车就翻倒在马身上了。轴发出巨大的撞击声，我被抛到一边，重重地掉进了一个浅水池里。
我几乎立即爬了出来，蹲在一丛荆豆下面，双脚仍然浸在水中。那匹马一动不动地躺着（他的脖子被折断了，可怜的畜生！），借着闪电，我看到翻倒的狗车的黑色主体和仍在缓慢旋转的车轮的轮廓。又过了一会儿，巨大的机械装置从我身边大步走过，朝皮尔福德上坡而去。

近距离观察，这个东西非常奇怪，因为它不仅仅是行驶在路上的毫无知觉的机器。它是一台机器，带着金属般的节奏，长长的、灵活的、闪闪发光的触手（其中一根抓住了一棵小松树）在它奇怪的身体周围摆动和嘎嘎作响。它在大步前进时选择了自己的道路，上面的黄铜兜帽来回移动，不可避免地暗示着一个头在四处张望。本体背后是一团巨大的白色金属，就像一个巨大的渔篮，四肢的关节处喷出一股股绿色的烟雾，怪物从我身边掠过。瞬间它就消失了。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 6
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: I heard answering shouts from the people in the water about me. I could have leaped out of the water with that momentary exultation.

The decapitated colossus reeled like a drunken giant; but it did not fall over. It recovered its balance by a miracle, and, no longer heeding its steps and with the camera that fired the Heat-Ray now rigidly upheld, it reeled swiftly upon Shepperton. The living intelligence, the Martian within the hood, was slain and splashed to the four winds of heaven, and the Thing was now but a mere intricate device of metal whirling to destruction. It drove along in a straight line, incapable of guidance. It struck the tower of Shepperton Church, smashing it down as the impact of a battering ram might have done, swerved aside, blundered on and collapsed with tremendous force into the river out of my sight.

A violent explosion shook the air, and a spout of water, steam, mud, and shattered metal shot far up into the sky. As the camera of the Heat-Ray hit the water, the latter had immediately flashed into steam. In another moment a huge wave, like a muddy tidal bore but almost scaldingly hot, came sweeping round the bend upstream. I saw people struggling shorewards, and heard their screaming and shouting faintly above the seething and roar of the Martian’s collapse.

For a moment I heeded nothing of the heat, forgot the patent need of self-preservation. I splashed through the tumultuous water, pushing aside a man in black to do so, until I could see round the bend. Half a dozen deserted boats pitched aimlessly upon the confusion of the waves. The fallen Martian came into sight downstream, lying across the river, and for the most part submerged.

Thick clouds of steam were pouring off the wreckage, and through the tumultuously whirling wisps I could see, intermittently and vaguely, the gigantic limbs churning the water and flinging a splash and spray of mud and froth into the air. The tentacles swayed and struck like living arms, and, save for the helpless purposelessness of these movements, it was as if some wounded thing were struggling for its life amid the waves. Enormous quantities of a ruddy-brown fluid were spurting up in noisy jets out of the machine.

My attention was diverted from this death flurry by a furious yelling, like that of the thing called a siren in our manufacturing towns. A man, knee-deep near the towing path, shouted inaudibly to me and pointed. Looking back, I saw the other Martians advancing with gigantic strides down the riverbank from the direction of Chertsey. The Shepperton guns spoke this time unavailingly.

At that I ducked at once under water, and, holding my breath until movement was an agony, blundered painfully ahead under the surface as long as I could. The water was in a tumult about me, and rapidly growing hotter.

When for a moment I raised my head to take breath and throw the hair and water from my eyes, the steam was rising in a whirling white fog that at first hid the Martians altogether. The noise was deafening. Then I saw them dimly, colossal figures of grey, magnified by the mist. They had passed by me, and two were stooping over the frothing, tumultuous ruins of their comrade.

The third and fourth stood beside him in the water, one perhaps two hundred yards from me, the other towards Laleham. The generators of the Heat-Rays waved high, and the hissing beams smote down this way and that.

The air was full of sound, a deafening and confusing conflict of noises—the clangorous din of the Martians, the crash of falling houses, the thud of trees, fences, sheds flashing into flame, and the crackling and roaring of fire. Dense black smoke was leaping up to mingle with the steam from the river, and as the Heat-Ray went to and fro over Weybridge its impact was marked by flashes of incandescent white, that gave place at once to a smoky dance of lurid flames. The nearer houses still stood intact, awaiting their fate, shadowy, faint and pallid in the steam, with the fire behind them going to and fro.
paragraphsZh: 我听到水中的人们对我的呼喊声。那一瞬间的狂喜让我恨不得跳出水面。

被斩首的巨像像醉酒的巨人一样摇摇晃晃；但它并没有倒下。它奇迹般地恢复了平衡，不再注意自己的脚步，并且紧紧握住发射热射线的摄像机，它迅速向谢珀顿扑来。活生生的智慧，引擎盖里的火星人，被杀死并溅到天堂的四风中，而那个东西现在只是一个复杂的金属装置，旋转着走向毁灭。它沿直线行驶，无法引导。它击中了谢珀顿教堂的塔楼，像攻城锤的撞击一样将其撞倒，然后转向一边，跌跌撞撞地以巨大的力量倒塌到河里，从我的视线中消失了。
剧烈的爆炸震动了空气，一股水流、蒸汽、泥土和破碎的金属喷射到了遥远的天空。当热射线的相机落入水中时，后者立即冒出蒸汽。又过了一会儿，一股巨大的波浪，像泥泞的潮汐一样，但又几乎滚烫，席卷了上游的弯道。我看到人们挣扎着向岸边走去，听到他们的尖叫声和叫喊声盖过火星人崩溃的沸腾和轰鸣声。
有一瞬间，我没有注意到炎热，忘记了自我保护的专利需求。我在汹涌的水中溅起水花，推开一个黑衣人，直到我能看到拐角处。六艘废弃的小船漫无目的地在混乱的海浪上颠簸。坠落的火星人出现在下游的视野中，它躺在河对岸，大部分都被淹没了。
厚厚的蒸汽云从残骸上倾泻而下，透过那些喧嚣旋转的缕缕，我可以断断续续地、模糊地看到巨大的肢体在搅动着水面，并向空中喷射出泥浆和泡沫。触手像活生生的手臂一样摇摆和攻击，除了这些动作的无助和漫无目的之外，就好像有什么受伤的东西在波浪中挣扎着求生。大量的红棕色液体从机器中喷出，发出嘈杂的声音。
我的注意力被一阵愤怒的叫喊声从这场死亡狂潮中转移了，就像我们制造业城镇中那种被称为警报器的东西一样。一个男人站在拖道附近齐膝深的地方，对我大声喊叫，并指着我。回头一看，我看到其他火星人从彻特西方向沿着河岸大步前进。谢珀顿炮这次没有说话。
听到这个消息，我立即潜入水下，屏住呼吸，直到移动变得痛苦为止，尽可能地在水面下痛苦地前行。海水在我周围翻腾，并且迅速变得越来越热。
当我抬起头喘口气，甩掉眼睛里的头发和水时，蒸汽在旋转的白雾中升起，起初完全遮住了火星人。噪音震耳欲聋。然后我隐约看到它们，巨大的灰色人物，被雾气放大了。他们从我身边经过，其中有两个人正弯腰站在他们战友那座冒着泡沫、混乱不堪的废墟上。
第三个和第四个站在他旁边的水中，一个距离我大约两百码，另一个朝向拉勒姆。热射线发生器高高挥舞，发出嘶嘶声的光束从这边或那边猛击下来。
空气中充满了声音，震耳欲聋、令人困惑的噪音冲突——火星人的喧闹声、倒塌房屋的撞击声、树木、栅栏、棚屋着火的轰鸣声，以及火焰的噼啪声和轰鸣声。浓浓的黑烟袅袅升起，与河里的蒸汽混合在一起，当热射线在威布里奇上空来回穿梭时，它的冲击力就被白炽灯的闪光所标记，立刻就被一种烟雾缭绕的可怕火焰所取代。近处的房屋依然完好无损地矗立着，等待着它们的命运，在蒸汽中显得阴暗、微弱、苍白，身后的火光来回闪烁。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 7
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: In another moment the huge wave, well-nigh at the boiling-point had rushed upon me. I screamed aloud, and scalded, half blinded, agonised, I staggered through the leaping, hissing water towards the shore. Had my foot stumbled, it would have been the end. I fell helplessly, in full sight of the Martians, upon the broad, bare gravelly spit that runs down to mark the angle of the Wey and Thames. I expected nothing but death.

I have a dim memory of the foot of a Martian coming down within a score of yards of my head, driving straight into the loose gravel, whirling it this way and that and lifting again; of a long suspense, and then of the four carrying the debris of their comrade between them, now clear and then presently faint through a veil of smoke, receding interminably, as it seemed to me, across a vast space of river and meadow. And then, very slowly, I realised that by a miracle I had escaped.

After getting this sudden lesson in the power of terrestrial weapons, the Martians retreated to their original position upon Horsell Common; and in their haste, and encumbered with the debris of their smashed companion, they no doubt overlooked many such a stray and negligible victim as myself. Had they left their comrade and pushed on forthwith, there was nothing at that time between them and London but batteries of twelve-pounder guns, and they would certainly have reached the capital in advance of the tidings of their approach; as sudden, dreadful, and destructive their advent would have been as the earthquake that destroyed Lisbon a century ago.

But they were in no hurry. Cylinder followed cylinder on its interplanetary flight; every twenty-four hours brought them reinforcement. And meanwhile the military and naval authorities, now fully alive to the tremendous power of their antagonists, worked with furious energy. Every minute a fresh gun came into position until, before twilight, every copse, every row of suburban villas on the hilly slopes about Kingston and Richmond, masked an expectant black muzzle. And through the charred and desolated area—perhaps twenty square miles altogether—that encircled the Martian encampment on Horsell Common, through charred and ruined villages among the green trees, through the blackened and smoking arcades that had been but a day ago pine spinneys, crawled the devoted scouts with the heliographs that were presently to warn the gunners of the Martian approach. But the Martians now understood our command of artillery and the danger of human proximity, and not a man ventured within a mile of either cylinder, save at the price of his life.

It would seem that these giants spent the earlier part of the afternoon in going to and fro, transferring everything from the second and third cylinders—the second in Addlestone Golf Links and the third at Pyrford—to their original pit on Horsell Common. Over that, above the blackened heather and ruined buildings that stretched far and wide, stood one as sentinel, while the rest abandoned their vast fighting-machines and descended into the pit. They were hard at work there far into the night, and the towering pillar of dense green smoke that rose therefrom could be seen from the hills about Merrow, and even, it is said, from Banstead and Epsom Downs.

And while the Martians behind me were thus preparing for their next sally, and in front of me Humanity gathered for the battle, I made my way with infinite pains and labour from the fire and smoke of burning Weybridge towards London.

I saw an abandoned boat, very small and remote, drifting down-stream; and throwing off the most of my sodden clothes, I went after it, gained it, and so escaped out of that destruction. There were no oars in the boat, but I contrived to paddle, as well as my parboiled hands would allow, down the river towards Halliford and Walton, going very tediously and continually looking behind me, as you may well understand. I followed the river, because I considered that the water gave me my best chance of escape should these giants return.
paragraphsZh: 又过了一会儿，几乎达到沸点的巨浪向我扑来。我大声尖叫，浑身被烫伤，半目失明，痛苦不堪，我摇摇晃晃地穿过跳跃、嘶嘶作响的海水，向岸边走去。如果我的脚绊倒了，那就完了。在火星人的众目睽睽之下，我无助地倒在宽阔、光秃秃的砾石沙嘴上，沙嘴向下延伸，标志着威伊河和泰晤士河的角度。除了死亡，我别无所求。
我依稀记得有一个火星人的脚落在距我头几十码的地方，径直踩进松散的砾石上，左右旋转，然后又抬起；一段漫长的悬念，然后是四个人夹着战友的残骸，这些残骸时而清晰，时而在烟雾中变得微弱，在我看来，穿过一片广阔的河流和草地，无休无止地后退。然后，非常缓慢地，我意识到我奇迹般地逃脱了。
在突然了解到地面武器的威力之后，火星人撤退到霍塞尔公地原来的位置；在他们的匆忙中，加上他们被砸碎的同伴的残骸，他们无疑忽视了许多像我这样的流浪和微不足道的受害者。如果他们离开他们的战友并立即继续前进，那么当时他们和伦敦之间除了十二磅炮的炮台之外就什么也没有了，他们肯定会在即将到来的消息之前到达首都。它们的到来就像一个世纪前摧毁里斯本的地震一样突然、可怕和具有破坏性。

但他们并不着急。在星际飞行中，气缸一个接着一个；每二十四小时就会给他们带来增援。与此同时，陆军和海军当局充分认识到对手的巨大力量，并以极大的精力开展工作。每一分钟都有一支新的枪就位，直到黄昏之前，金斯敦和里士满周围山坡上的每一片树林、每一排郊区别墅都掩盖了期待的黑色枪口。穿过霍塞尔公地火星营地周围的烧焦而荒凉的地区——大概总共二十平方英里——穿过绿树丛中烧焦和毁坏的村庄，穿过一天前还是松树的黑色和冒烟的拱廊，虔诚的侦察兵带着日光仪爬行，这些日光仪即将警告炮手火星的逼近。但火星人现在了解了我们对火炮的指挥以及人类接近的危险，没有人冒险进入这两个圆柱体一英里之内，除非付出生命的代价。
这些巨人似乎花了下午早些时候的时间来回移动，将第二个和第三个圆柱体（第二个在阿德尔斯通高尔夫球场，第三个在皮尔福德）的所有东西转移到他们在霍塞尔公共球场的原始维修站。在那之上，在焦黑的石南花和绵延不断的废墟建筑之上，站着一个哨兵，而其余的人则放弃了他们巨大的战斗机器，掉进了坑里。他们在那里辛勤工作到深夜，从梅罗周围的山上，甚至据说从班斯特德和埃普索姆唐斯都可以看到从中升起的高耸的浓绿烟雾柱。
当我身后的火星人正在为他们的下一次突袭做准备，而在我面前，人类聚集在一起准备战斗时，我带着无限的痛苦和劳作，从燃烧的威布里奇的火焰和烟雾中向伦敦前进。
我看到一艘废弃的船，很小很偏僻，顺流而下；我扔掉了大部分湿透的衣服，去追寻它，得到了它，从而逃离了那场毁灭。船上没有桨，但我设法在我那双煮熟的手允许的情况下划桨，顺河而下，向哈利福德和沃尔顿驶去，非常乏味地不断地看着我身后，你可能很理解。我顺着河走，因为我认为如果这些巨人回来的话，水是我最好的逃跑机会。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 8
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: Then the fourth cylinder fell—a brilliant green meteor—as I learned afterwards, in Bushey Park. Before the guns on the Richmond and Kingston line of hills began, there was a fitful cannonade far away in the southwest, due, I believe, to guns being fired haphazard before the black vapour could overwhelm the gunners.

So, setting about it as methodically as men might smoke out a wasps’ nest, the Martians spread this strange stifling vapour over the Londonward country. The horns of the crescent slowly moved apart, until at last they formed a line from Hanwell to Coombe and Malden. All night through their destructive tubes advanced. Never once, after the Martian at St. George’s Hill was brought down, did they give the artillery the ghost of a chance against them. Wherever there was a possibility of guns being laid for them unseen, a fresh canister of the black vapour was discharged, and where the guns were openly displayed the Heat-Ray was brought to bear.

By midnight the blazing trees along the slopes of Richmond Park and the glare of Kingston Hill threw their light upon a network of black smoke, blotting out the whole valley of the Thames and extending as far as the eye could reach. And through this two Martians slowly waded, and turned their hissing steam jets this way and that.

They were sparing of the Heat-Ray that night, either because they had but a limited supply of material for its production or because they did not wish to destroy the country but only to crush and overawe the opposition they had aroused. In the latter aim they certainly succeeded. Sunday night was the end of the organised opposition to their movements. After that no body of men would stand against them, so hopeless was the enterprise. Even the crews of the torpedo-boats and destroyers that had brought their quick-firers up the Thames refused to stop, mutinied, and went down again. The only offensive operation men ventured upon after that night was the preparation of mines and pitfalls, and even in that their energies were frantic and spasmodic.

One has to imagine, as well as one may, the fate of those batteries towards Esher, waiting so tensely in the twilight. Survivors there were none. One may picture the orderly expectation, the officers alert and watchful, the gunners ready, the ammunition piled to hand, the limber gunners with their horses and waggons, the groups of civilian spectators standing as near as they were permitted, the evening stillness, the ambulances and hospital tents with the burned and wounded from Weybridge; then the dull resonance of the shots the Martians fired, and the clumsy projectile whirling over the trees and houses and smashing amid the neighbouring fields.

One may picture, too, the sudden shifting of the attention, the swiftly spreading coils and bellyings of that blackness advancing headlong, towering heavenward, turning the twilight to a palpable darkness, a strange and horrible antagonist of vapour striding upon its victims, men and horses near it seen dimly, running, shrieking, falling headlong, shouts of dismay, the guns suddenly abandoned, men choking and writhing on the ground, and the swift broadening-out of the opaque cone of smoke. And then night and extinction—nothing but a silent mass of impenetrable vapour hiding its dead.

Before dawn the black vapour was pouring through the streets of Richmond, and the disintegrating organism of government was, with a last expiring effort, rousing the population of London to the necessity of flight.

So you understand the roaring wave of fear that swept through the greatest city in the world just as Monday was dawning—the stream of flight rising swiftly to a torrent, lashing in a foaming tumult round the railway stations, banked up into a horrible struggle about the shipping in the Thames, and hurrying by every available channel northward and eastward. By ten o’clock the police organisation, and by midday even the railway organisations, were losing coherency, losing shape and efficiency, guttering, softening, running at last in that swift liquefaction of the social body.
paragraphsZh: 然后第四个圆柱体坠落——一颗明亮的绿色流星——据我后来所知，在布希公园。在里士满和金斯敦山线的炮火开始之前，西南方向远处传来一阵断断续续的炮轰声，我相信，这是因为在黑色蒸汽压倒炮手之前，枪支被随意开火。
因此，火星人像人们熏出黄蜂巢一样有条不紊，将这种奇怪的令人窒息的蒸气散布在伦敦地区。新月形的角慢慢地分开，直到最后它们从汉韦尔到库姆和马尔登形成一条线。整个晚上，他们都在通过破坏性的管道前进。在圣乔治山的火星人被击落之后，他们再也没有给炮兵任何对抗他们的机会。只要有可能在不被发现的情况下为他们放置枪支，就会释放一罐新的黑色蒸汽，而在公开展示枪支的地方，热射线就会发挥作用。
到了午夜，里士满公园山坡上燃烧的树木和金斯顿山的耀眼光芒将它们的光芒投射在黑色的烟雾网络上，遮盖了整个泰晤士河谷，一直延伸到眼睛所能看到的地方。两个火星人慢慢涉水穿过这里，并左右转动他们嘶嘶作响的蒸汽喷射器。

那天晚上他们没有使用热射线，要么是因为他们的生产材料供应有限，要么是因为他们不想摧毁这个国家，而只是为了镇压和震慑他们所激起的反对派。他们的后一个目标确实成功了。周日晚上，有组织地反对他们的行动结束了。从此以后，没有人敢与他们作对，这项事业就变得毫无希望了。就连那些在泰晤士河上开着速射炮的鱼雷艇和驱逐舰的船员也拒绝停下来，发生叛变，然后又沉没了。那天晚上之后，人们冒险进行的唯一进攻性行动就是布设地雷和陷阱，即便如此，他们的精力仍然是疯狂和痉挛的。
人们必须想象，也可以想象，那些在暮色中紧张等待的前往伊舍尔的炮台的命运。没有幸存者。人们可以想象有序的等待，军官们警觉而警惕，炮手准备就绪，弹药堆积如山，灵活的炮手带着他们的马匹和货车，一群群在允许的范围内尽可能靠近的平民观众，夜晚的寂静，救护车和医院帐篷里满是来自威布里奇的烧伤者和伤员；然后火星人发射的炮弹发出沉闷的共鸣，笨拙的射弹在树木和房屋上空盘旋，粉碎在邻近的田野中。
人们也可以想象，注意力的突然转移，迅速蔓延的黑暗的盘绕和腹部，一头扎进，高耸入云，把暮色变成了明显的黑暗，一种奇怪而可怕的蒸汽对手大步跨在它的受害者身上，模糊地看到附近的人和马，奔跑，尖叫，一头倒下，沮丧的呼喊，枪突然被放弃，人们在地上窒息和扭动，而不透明的锥形烟雾迅速扩大。然后是黑夜和灭绝——除了一团无声无息、难以穿透的蒸气隐藏着死者之外什么也没有。
黎明前，黑色的蒸汽涌过里士满的街道，而正在瓦解的政府组织正在用最后的努力，唤醒伦敦人民逃离的必要性。
因此，你可以理解周一拂晓时席卷世界上最伟大城市的恐惧浪潮——逃亡者的洪流迅速上升，在火车站周围掀起泡沫般的骚动，在泰晤士河上陷入了一场可怕的航运斗争，并通过每一个可用的航道向北和向东急速前进。到了十点钟，警察组织，甚至到了中午，铁路组织都失去了连贯性，失去了形状和效率，变得低沉、软化，最终在社会团体迅速液化的情况下运转。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 9
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: The bare idea of this is no doubt horribly repulsive to us, but at the same time I think that we should remember how repulsive our carnivorous habits would seem to an intelligent rabbit.

The physiological advantages of the practice of injection are undeniable, if one thinks of the tremendous waste of human time and energy occasioned by eating and the digestive process. Our bodies are half made up of glands and tubes and organs, occupied in turning heterogeneous food into blood. The digestive processes and their reaction upon the nervous system sap our strength and colour our minds. Men go happy or miserable as they have healthy or unhealthy livers, or sound gastric glands. But the Martians were lifted above all these organic fluctuations of mood and emotion.

Their undeniable preference for men as their source of nourishment is partly explained by the nature of the remains of the victims they had brought with them as provisions from Mars. These creatures, to judge from the shrivelled remains that have fallen into human hands, were bipeds with flimsy, silicious skeletons (almost like those of the silicious sponges) and feeble musculature, standing about six feet high and having round, erect heads, and large eyes in flinty sockets. Two or three of these seem to have been brought in each cylinder, and all were killed before earth was reached. It was just as well for them, for the mere attempt to stand upright upon our planet would have broken every bone in their bodies.

And while I am engaged in this description, I may add in this place certain further details which, although they were not all evident to us at the time, will enable the reader who is unacquainted with them to form a clearer picture of these offensive creatures.

In three other points their physiology differed strangely from ours. Their organisms did not sleep, any more than the heart of man sleeps. Since they had no extensive muscular mechanism to recuperate, that periodical extinction was unknown to them. They had little or no sense of fatigue, it would seem. On earth they could never have moved without effort, yet even to the last they kept in action. In twenty-four hours they did twenty-four hours of work, as even on earth is perhaps the case with the ants.

In the next place, wonderful as it seems in a sexual world, the Martians were absolutely without sex, and therefore without any of the tumultuous emotions that arise from that difference among men. A young Martian, there can now be no dispute, was really born upon earth during the war, and it was found attached to its parent, partially budded off, just as young lilybulbs bud off, or like the young animals in the fresh-water polyp.

In man, in all the higher terrestrial animals, such a method of increase has disappeared; but even on this earth it was certainly the primitive method. Among the lower animals, up even to those first cousins of the vertebrated animals, the Tunicates, the two processes occur side by side, but finally the sexual method superseded its competitor altogether. On Mars, however, just the reverse has apparently been the case.

It is worthy of remark that a certain speculative writer of quasi-scientific repute, writing long before the Martian invasion, did forecast for man a final structure not unlike the actual Martian condition. His prophecy, I remember, appeared in November or December, 1893, in a long-defunct publication, the Pall Mall Budget, and I recall a caricature of it in a pre-Martian periodical called Punch. He pointed out—writing in a foolish, facetious tone—that the perfection of mechanical appliances must ultimately supersede limbs; the perfection of chemical devices, digestion; that such organs as hair, external nose, teeth, ears, and chin were no longer essential parts of the human being, and that the tendency of natural selection would lie in the direction of their steady diminution through the coming ages. The brain alone remained a cardinal necessity. Only one other part of the body had a strong case for survival, and that was the hand, “teacher and agent of the brain.” While the rest of the body dwindled, the hands would grow larger.
paragraphsZh: 这个想法无疑让我们感到非常厌恶，但同时我认为我们应该记住，我们的肉食习惯对于一只聪明的兔子来说是多么令人厌恶。
考虑到饮食和消化过程对人类时间和精力的巨大浪费，注射实践的生理优势是不可否认的。我们的身体一半由腺体、管道和器官组成，负责将异质食物转化为血液。消化过程及其对神经系统的反应会削弱我们的力量并影响我们的思想。男人的幸福或痛苦取决于他们的肝脏健康或不健康，或胃腺健康。但火星人却超越了所有这些情绪和情感的有机波动。
他们不可否认地偏爱男性作为营养来源，部分原因是他们从火星带来的受害者遗骸的性质。从落入人类手中的枯萎遗骸来看，这些生物是两足动物，具有脆弱的硅质骨骼（几乎像硅质海绵的骨骼）和无力的肌肉组织，站立约六英尺高，有圆而直立的头，在坚硬的眼窝中长着大眼睛。每个圆筒中似乎都带了两三个这样的人，在抵达地球之前全部被杀死。这对他们来说也是好事，因为仅仅尝试在我们的星球上直立就会折断他们身上的每一根骨头。
在我进行这个描述的同时，我可能会在这个地方添加一些进一步的细节，尽管它们当时对我们来说并不明显，但将使不熟悉它们的读者对这些令人讨厌的生物形成更清晰的了解。
在其他三点上，他们的生理机能与我们的有奇怪的不同。它们的有机体不睡觉，就像人的心脏不睡觉一样。由于它们没有广泛的肌肉机制来恢复，所以它们不知道周期性的灭绝。他们似乎很少或根本没有疲劳感。在地球上，他们永远不可能不费力地移动，但直到最后他们仍然坚持行动。在二十四小时内，他们做了二十四小时的工作，就像在地球上的蚂蚁一样。
其次，尽管在性世界中看起来很美妙，但火星人完全没有性，因此没有任何因男人之间的差异而产生的混乱情绪。毫无疑问，一个年轻的火星人确实是在战争期间在地球上出生的，人们发现它附着在其父母身上，部分发芽，就像年轻的百合花发芽一样，或者像淡水水螅体内的幼年动物一样。
在人类中，在所有高等陆生动物中，这种增加的方法已经消失了；但即使在这个地球上，这也无疑是最原始的方法。在低等动物中，甚至到脊椎动物的近亲被囊动物，这两个过程同时发生，但最终性方法完全取代了它的竞争对手。然而，在火星上，情况显然恰恰相反。

值得一提的是，一位具有准科学声誉的思辨作家，早在火星入侵之前就已写作，确实预测了人类的最终结构，与火星的实际情况没有什么不同。我记得，他的预言出现在 1893 年 11 月或 12 月，发表在一份早已停刊的出版物《Pall Mall Budget》上，我还记得一本名为《Punch》的前火星期刊上对它的漫画。他以一种愚蠢、滑稽的语气写道，机械器具的完美最终必须取代四肢；化学装置的完善、消化；头发、外鼻、牙齿、耳朵和下巴等器官不再是人类的重要组成部分，自然选择的趋势将是它们在未来的岁月中不断减少。大脑仍然是最基本的必需品。身体只有另一个部分有足够的生存理由，那就是手，“大脑的老师和代理人”。虽然身体的其他部分缩小了，但双手却变大了。

title: The War of the Worlds · 选段 10
author: H. G. Wells
paragraphs: I stared about me, scarcely believing my eyes. All the machinery had gone. Save for the big mound of greyish-blue powder in one corner, certain bars of aluminium in another, the black birds, and the skeletons of the killed, the place was merely an empty circular pit in the sand.

Slowly I thrust myself out through the red weed, and stood upon the mound of rubble. I could see in any direction save behind me, to the north, and neither Martians nor sign of Martians were to be seen. The pit dropped sheerly from my feet, but a little way along the rubbish afforded a practicable slope to the summit of the ruins. My chance of escape had come. I began to tremble.
I hesitated for some time, and then, in a gust of desperate resolution, and with a heart that throbbed violently, I scrambled to the top of the mound in which I had been buried so long.

When I had last seen this part of Sheen in the daylight it had been a straggling street of comfortable white and red houses, interspersed with abundant shady trees. Now I stood on a mound of smashed brickwork, clay, and gravel, over which spread a multitude of red cactus-shaped plants, knee-high, without a solitary terrestrial growth to dispute their footing. The trees near me were dead and brown, but further a network of red thread scaled the still living stems.

The neighbouring houses had all been wrecked, but none had been burned; their walls stood, sometimes to the second story, with smashed windows and shattered doors. The red weed grew tumultuously in their roofless rooms. Below me was the great pit, with the crows struggling for its refuse. A number of other birds hopped about among the ruins. Far away I saw a gaunt cat slink crouchingly along a wall, but traces of men there were none.

The day seemed, by contrast with my recent confinement, dazzlingly bright, the sky a glowing blue. A gentle breeze kept the red weed that covered every scrap of unoccupied ground gently swaying. And oh! the sweetness of the air!

For some time I stood tottering on the mound regardless of my safety. Within that noisome den from which I had emerged I had thought with a narrow intensity only of our immediate security. I had not realised what had been happening to the world, had not anticipated this startling vision of unfamiliar things. I had expected to see Sheen in ruins—I found about me the landscape, weird and lurid, of another planet.

For that moment I touched an emotion beyond the common range of men, yet one that the poor brutes we dominate know only too well. I felt as a rabbit might feel returning to his burrow and suddenly confronted by the work of a dozen busy navvies digging the foundations of a house. I felt the first inkling of a thing that presently grew quite clear in my mind, that oppressed me for many days, a sense of dethronement, a persuasion that I was no longer a master, but an animal among the animals, under the Martian heel. With us it would be as with them, to lurk and watch, to run and hide; the fear and empire of man had passed away.

But so soon as this strangeness had been realised it passed, and my dominant motive became the hunger of my long and dismal fast. In the direction away from the pit I saw, beyond a red-covered wall, a patch of garden ground unburied. This gave me a hint, and I went knee-deep, and sometimes neck-deep, in the red weed. The density of the weed gave me a reassuring sense of hiding. The wall was some six feet high, and when I attempted to clamber it I found I could not lift my feet to the crest. So I went along by the side of it, and came to a corner and a rockwork that enabled me to get to the top, and tumble into the garden I coveted. Here I found some young onions, a couple of gladiolus bulbs, and a quantity of immature carrots, all of which I secured, and, scrambling over a ruined wall, went on my way through scarlet and crimson trees towards Kew—it was like walking through an avenue of gigantic blood drops—possessed with two ideas: to get more food, and to limp, as soon and as far as my strength permitted, out of this accursed unearthly region of the pit.
paragraphsZh: 我环顾四周，几乎不敢相信自己的眼睛。所有的机器都不见了。除了一个角落里的一大堆灰蓝色粉末、另一个角落里的几根铝条、黑色的鸟和被杀死的骷髅之外，这个地方只是沙子里的一个空的圆形坑。
我慢慢地从红色杂草中伸出身子，站在瓦砾堆上。我可以看到除了我身后的北方之外的任何方向，既看不到火星人，也看不到火星人的迹象。坑从我的脚边陡然下降，但沿着垃圾堆走一小段路，就有了一个通往废墟顶峰的可行斜坡。我逃脱的机会来了。我开始颤抖。
我犹豫了一会儿，然后，带着一股绝望的决心，带着一颗剧烈跳动的心，我爬到了我被埋了这么久的土堆顶上。
当我最后一次在白天看到希恩的这一部分时，那是一条蜿蜒的街道，两旁是舒适的白色和红色房屋，散布着茂密的树荫。现在我站在一个由碎砖、粘土和砾石组成的土堆上，上面散布着许多齐膝高的红色仙人掌形状的植物，没有任何一个单独的陆地植物来质疑它们的立足点。我附近的树木已经死了，变成了棕色，但还活着的树干上还布满了红色的线网。
邻近的房屋全部被毁，但没有被烧毁；他们的墙壁直立，有时直达二楼，窗户和门都被打碎。红色的杂草在他们没有屋顶的房间里狂乱地生长。我下面是一个大坑，乌鸦们在为它的垃圾而挣扎。许多其他鸟儿在废墟中跳跃。远远地我看见一只瘦弱的猫蹲在墙上，但那里没有人类的踪迹。
与我最近的监禁相比，这一天似乎明亮得耀眼，天空泛着蓝光。微风徐徐，覆盖着每一片空地上的红色杂草轻轻摇曳。还有哦！空气的甜蜜！
有一段时间，我不顾自己的安全，摇摇晃晃地站在土丘上。在我走出那个肮脏的巢穴时，我只以一种狭隘的强度想到了我们眼前的安全。我没有意识到世界上发生了什么，也没有预料到陌生事物的令人震惊的景象。我原以为会看到希恩变成废墟，但我发现周围的风景怪异而恐怖，就像另一个星球一样。

在那一刻，我感受到了一种超出人类一般范围的情感，但我们所统治的可怜的野兽却非常了解这种情感。我的感觉就像一只兔子回到了自己的洞穴，突然面临着十几个正在忙着挖房子地基的勤杂工的工作。我第一次感觉到有件事在我的脑海中变得非常清晰，它压抑了我很多天，一种被废黜的感觉，一种说服力，我不再是一个主人，而是动物中的动物，在火星的脚下。对我们来说就像对他们一样，潜伏和观察，奔跑和隐藏；人类的恐惧和帝国已经过去。

但一旦意识到这种奇怪的感觉，它就过去了，我的主要动机变成了我漫长而惨淡的禁食的饥饿感。在远离坑的方向，我看到，在红色覆盖的墙壁之外，有一块未被掩埋的花园地面。这给了我一个暗示，我就走进了齐膝深、有时齐脖子深的红色杂草里。杂草的密度给了我一种令人安心的隐藏感。这堵墙大约有六英尺高，当我试图爬上去时，我发现我无法把脚抬到山顶。于是我沿着它的一侧走，来到一个角落和一个岩石结构，使我能够到达顶部，并跌入我梦寐以求的花园。在这里，我找到了一些嫩洋葱、几个唐菖蒲球茎和一些未成熟的胡萝卜，我把所有这些都固定下来，然后爬过一堵毁坏的墙，穿过猩红和深红色的树林，前往邱园——就像走过一条巨大的血滴大道——我有两个想法：获取更多食物，以及在我的力量允许的情况下，尽快、尽可能地一瘸一拐地离开这个被诅咒的神秘地区。坑。

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 4
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: From that time forward, Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the by-street of shops. In the morning before office hours, at noon when business was plenty and time scarce, at night under the face of the fogged city moon, by all lights and at all hours of solitude or concourse, the lawyer was to be found on his chosen post.

And at last his patience was rewarded. It was a fine dry night; frost in the air; the streets as clean as a ballroom floor; the lamps, unshaken by any wind, drawing a regular pattern of light and shadow. By ten o’clock, when the shops were closed, the by-street was very solitary and, in spite of the low growl of London from all round, very silent. Small sounds carried far; domestic sounds out of the houses were clearly audible on either side of the roadway; and the rumour of the approach of any passenger preceded him by a long time. Mr. Utterson had been some minutes at his post, when he was aware of an odd light footstep drawing near. In the course of his nightly patrols, he had long grown accustomed to the quaint effect with which the footfalls of a single person, while he is still a great way off, suddenly spring out distinct from the vast hum and clatter of the city. Yet his attention had never before been so sharply and decisively arrested; and it was with a strong, superstitious prevision of success that he withdrew into the entry of the court.

The steps drew swiftly nearer, and swelled out suddenly louder as they turned the end of the street. The lawyer, looking forth from the entry, could soon see what manner of man he had to deal with. He was small and very plainly dressed and the look of him, even at that distance, went somehow strongly against the watcher’s inclination. But he made straight for the door, crossing the roadway to save time; and as he came, he drew a key from his pocket like one approaching home.

Mr. Hyde shrank back with a hissing intake of the breath. But his fear was only momentary; and though he did not look the lawyer in the face, he answered coolly enough: “That is my name. What do you want?”

“I see you are going in,” returned the lawyer. “I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard of my name; and meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might admit me.”
“You will not find Dr. Jekyll; he is from home,” replied Mr. Hyde, blowing in the key. And then suddenly, but still without looking up, “How did you know me?” he asked.

Mr. Hyde appeared to hesitate, and then, as if upon some sudden reflection, fronted about with an air of defiance; and the pair stared at each other pretty fixedly for a few seconds. “Now I shall know you again,” said Mr. Utterson. “It may be useful.”
“Yes,” returned Mr. Hyde, “it is as well we have met; and à propos, you should have my address.” And he gave a number of a street in Soho.
“Good God!” thought Mr. Utterson, “can he, too, have been thinking of the will?” But he kept his feelings to himself and only grunted in acknowledgment of the address.
The other snarled aloud into a savage laugh; and the next moment, with extraordinary quickness, he had unlocked the door and disappeared into the house.

The lawyer stood awhile when Mr. Hyde had left him, the picture of disquietude. Then he began slowly to mount the street, pausing every step or two and putting his hand to his brow like a man in mental perplexity. The problem he was thus debating as he walked, was one of a class that is rarely solved. Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish, he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation, he had a displeasing smile, he had borne himself to the lawyer with a sort of murderous mixture of timidity and boldness, and he spoke with a husky, whispering and somewhat broken voice; all these were points against him, but not all of these together could explain the hitherto unknown disgust, loathing and fear with which Mr. Utterson regarded him. “There must be something else,” said the perplexed gentleman. “There is something more, if I could find a name for it. God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say? or can it be the old story of Dr. Fell? or is it the mere radiance of a foul soul that thus transpires through, and transfigures, its clay continent? The last, I think; for, O my poor old Harry Jekyll, if ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend.”
paragraphsZh: 从那时起，厄特森先生开始在街边商店的门口出没。在办公时间之前的早晨，在业务繁忙而时间稀缺的中午，在雾蒙蒙的城市月光下的夜晚，在所有灯光下，在孤独或大厅的任何时间里，律师都在他所选择的岗位上。

他的耐心终于得到了回报。这是一个晴朗干燥的夜晚。空气中结霜；街道像舞厅地板一样干净；灯不受风吹动，描绘出规则的光影图案。到了十点钟，商店关门了，小街就变得非常冷清，尽管四面八方都传来伦敦低沉的咆哮声，但街道上却十分寂静。微小的声音传得很远；道路两侧都能清楚地听到房屋外的家庭声响；早在他之前就有关于任何乘客接近的谣言。厄特森先生在岗位上待了几分钟，这时他意识到有一阵奇怪的轻微脚步声正在靠近。在夜间巡逻的过程中，他早已习惯了这样一种奇特的效果：一个人的脚步声，虽然距离他还很远，但突然从城市的喧嚣和喧嚣中脱颖而出。然而，他的注意力以前从未如此强烈和果断地被吸引过。他带着一种强烈的、迷信的成功预感，退出了宫廷。
脚步声迅速靠近，当他们拐过街道尽头时，声音突然变得更大。律师从入口向外望去，很快就看出他要面对的是一个什么样的人。他身材矮小，衣着朴素，即使在那么远的距离，他的样子也与观察者的倾向产生了强烈的反差。但他直接向门口走去，穿过马路以节省时间。当他到达时，他像回家一样从口袋里掏出一把钥匙。
海德先生吸了一口气，向后退了一步。但他的恐惧只是暂时的；尽管他没有直视律师的脸，但他还是冷静地回答道：“这是我的名字。你想要什么？”
“我看到你要进去了，”律师回答道。 “我是杰基尔博士的老朋友——冈特街的厄特森先生——你一定听说过我的名字；而且这么方便地见到你，我想你可能会接纳我。”
“你不会找到杰基尔博士；他是从家里来的，”海德先生吹着钥匙回答道。然后突然，但仍然没有抬头，“你是怎么认识我的？”他问道。
海德先生似乎犹豫了一下，然后，仿佛突然想到了什么，带着一种蔑视的神气走上前去；两人目不转睛地对视了几秒钟。 “现在我又认识你了，”厄特森先生说。 “也许有用。”
“是的，”海德先生回答道，“我们已经见过面了；而且，按建议，你应该知道我的地址。”他还给出了苏豪区的一条街道的号码。
“天啊！”厄特森先生想，“难道他也一直在考虑遗嘱吗？”但他没有表达自己的感受，只是咕哝了一声，承认了这个地址。
另一个人大声咆哮，发出野蛮的笑声；下一刻，他以惊人的速度打开了门，消失在屋子里。

当海德先生离开时，律师站了一会儿，一副不安的样子。然后他开始慢慢地走上街道，每走一两步就停下来，把手放在额头上，就像一个精神困惑的人。他边走边争论的问题属于很少能解决的问题之一。海德先生脸色苍白，身材矮小，给人一种畸形的印象，没有任何明显的畸形，他的笑容令人不快，他在律师面前表现出一种胆怯和大胆的凶残混合体，说话的声音沙哑、低语，有些断断续续；所有这些都是对他不利的，但并不是所有这些加起来就能解释厄特森先生对他前所未有的厌恶、厌恶和恐惧。 “一定还有别的事。”这位困惑的绅士说道。 “如果我能为它找到一个名字的话，还有更多的东西。上帝保佑我，这个人看起来不像人类！我们可以说是穴居人吗？或者它可能是菲尔博士的古老故事吗？或者它仅仅是一个肮脏的灵魂的光辉，从而在它的粘土大陆中散发出来，并变形了它的粘土大陆？我想最后一个；因为，哦，我可怜的老哈利杰基尔，如果我在一张脸上看到了撒旦的签名，那是在你的新面孔上。朋友。”

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 5
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: “I will see, Mr. Utterson,” said Poole, admitting the visitor, as he spoke, into a large, low-roofed, comfortable hall paved with flags, warmed (after the fashion of a country house) by a bright, open fire, and furnished with costly cabinets of oak. “Will you wait here by the fire, sir? or shall I give you a light in the dining-room?”

“Here, thank you,” said the lawyer, and he drew near and leaned on the tall fender. This hall, in which he was now left alone, was a pet fancy of his friend the doctor’s; and Utterson himself was wont to speak of it as the pleasantest room in London. But tonight there was a shudder in his blood; the face of Hyde sat heavy on his memory; he felt (what was rare with him) a nausea and distaste of life; and in the gloom of his spirits, he seemed to read a menace in the flickering of the firelight on the polished cabinets and the uneasy starting of the shadow on the roof. He was ashamed of his relief, when Poole presently returned to announce that Dr. Jekyll was gone out.
“I saw Mr. Hyde go in by the old dissecting room door, Poole,” he said. “Is that right, when Dr. Jekyll is from home?”
“Your master seems to repose a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole,” resumed the other musingly.
“O, dear no, sir. He never dines here,” replied the butler. “Indeed we see very little of him on this side of the house; he mostly comes and goes by the laboratory.”

And the lawyer set out homeward with a very heavy heart. “Poor Harry Jekyll,” he thought, “my mind misgives me he is in deep waters! He was wild when he was young; a long while ago to be sure; but in the law of God, there is no statute of limitations. Ah, it must be that; the ghost of some old sin, the cancer of some concealed disgrace: punishment coming, pede claudo, years after memory has forgotten and self-love condoned the fault.” And the lawyer, scared by the thought, brooded awhile on his own past, groping in all the corners of memory, lest by chance some Jack-in-the-Box of an old iniquity should leap to light there. His past was fairly blameless; few men could read the rolls of their life with less apprehension; yet he was humbled to the dust by the many ill things he had done, and raised up again into a sober and fearful gratitude by the many he had come so near to doing yet avoided. And then by a return on his former subject, he conceived a spark of hope. “This Master Hyde, if he were studied,” thought he, “must have secrets of his own; black secrets, by the look of him; secrets compared to which poor Jekyll’s worst would be like sunshine. Things cannot continue as they are. It turns me cold to think of this creature stealing like a thief to Harry’s bedside; poor Harry, what a wakening! And the danger of it; for if this Hyde suspects the existence of the will, he may grow impatient to inherit. Ah, I must put my shoulder to the wheel—if Jekyll will but let me,” he added, “if Jekyll will only let me.” For once more he saw before his mind’s eye, as clear as transparency, the strange clauses of the will.

A fortnight later, by excellent good fortune, the doctor gave one of his pleasant dinners to some five or six old cronies, all intelligent, reputable men and all judges of good wine; and Mr. Utterson so contrived that he remained behind after the others had departed. This was no new arrangement, but a thing that had befallen many scores of times. Where Utterson was liked, he was liked well. Hosts loved to detain the dry lawyer, when the light-hearted and loose-tongued had already their foot on the threshold; they liked to sit a while in his unobtrusive company, practising for solitude, sobering their minds in the man’s rich silence after the expense and strain of gaiety. To this rule, Dr. Jekyll was no exception; and as he now sat on the opposite side of the fire—a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something of a slyish cast perhaps, but every mark of capacity and kindness—you could see by his looks that he cherished for Mr. Utterson a sincere and warm affection.
paragraphsZh: “我会看到的，厄特森先生，”普尔一边说，一边让来访者进入一个宽敞、低顶、舒适的大厅，大厅里铺满了旗帜，（按照乡间别墅的风格）用明亮的明火取暖，并配有昂贵的橡木柜子。 “先生，您要在火边等吗？还是我去餐厅给您点灯？”

“在这里，谢谢你，”律师说道，他走近并靠在高高的挡泥板上。现在只剩下他一个人呆在这个大厅里，这是他的医生朋友的最爱。厄特森本人也习惯说它是伦敦最令人愉快的房间。但今晚他的血液里颤抖着；海德的脸庞深深地印在他的记忆里。他感到（这对他来说是罕见的）一种恶心和对生活的厌恶。在他心情低落的时候，他似乎从擦亮的橱柜上闪烁的火光和屋顶上不安的阴影中读出了一种威胁。当普尔不久回来宣布杰基尔博士出去时，他为自己的轻松感到羞愧。
“我看到海德先生从旧的解剖室门进来，普尔，”他说。 “是吗，杰基尔博士不在家的时候？”
“你的主人似乎对那个年轻人普尔非常信任，”另一个若有所思地继续说道。
“噢，亲爱的，不，先生。他从来不在这里用餐，”管家回答道。 “事实上，我们在房子的这一边很少见到他；他大部分时间都经过实验室。”

律师怀着沉重的心情踏上回家的路。 “可怜的哈利·杰基尔，”他想，“我的心怀疑他是在深水里！他年轻时很狂野；当然是很久以前了；但在上帝的法律中，没有诉讼时效。啊，一定是这样；一些旧罪的幽灵，一些隐藏的耻辱的癌症：惩罚即将到来，克劳多，在记忆忘记和自爱宽恕过错多年之后。”律师被这个想法吓坏了，在自己的过去中沉思了一会儿，在记忆的各个角落里摸索着，以免某个旧罪孽的杰克盒子偶然跳出来。他的过去是相当无可指责的。很少有人能够不那么忧心忡忡地阅读自己的人生经历。然而，他因自己做过的许多恶事而被降为尘埃，而他又因许多他差点就要做却又避免做的事而重新站起来，陷入清醒而可怕的感激之中。然后，通过回到之前的主题，他萌生了一线希望的火花。 “这个海德大师，如果有人对他进行研究的话，”他想，“一定有他自己的秘密；从他的外表来看，是黑色的秘密；与那些可怜的杰基尔最糟糕的秘密相比，这些秘密就像阳光一样。事情不能再这样继续下去了。一想到这个生物像小偷一样偷到哈利的床边，我就感到寒冷；可怜的哈利，这是多么大的觉醒！还有它的危险；因为如果这个海德怀疑遗嘱的存在，他可能会变得不耐烦继承。啊，我必须把我的肩膀放在方向盘上——如果杰基尔愿意的话，”他补充道，“如果杰基尔愿意的话。”他再一次在脑海中看到了遗嘱中奇怪的条款，清晰如透明。

两周后，由于运气好，医生为五六个老朋友提供了一顿愉快的晚餐，他们都是聪明、有信誉的人，也是美酒的评判者；厄特森先生故意在其他人离开后留下来。这并不是什么新的安排，而是已经发生过很多次的事情了。厄特森受到人们的喜爱，他也受到人们的喜爱。当那些无忧无虑、口无遮拦的人已经踏上门槛时，主人喜欢扣留这位干巴巴的律师。他们喜欢在他低调的陪伴下坐上一会儿，练习独处，在度过了欢乐的花费和紧张之后，在这个男人丰富的沉默中清醒头脑。杰基尔博士也不例外。现在他坐在火炉的对面——一个五十岁的高大、身材匀称、面容光滑的男人，也许带着一丝狡猾，但处处体现着能力和善良——你可以从他的表情看出他对厄特森先生怀有真诚而温暖的感情。

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 6
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: The lawyer listened gloomily; he did not like his friend’s feverish manner. “You seem pretty sure of him,” said he; “and for your sake, I hope you may be right. If it came to a trial, your name might appear.”

“I am quite sure of him,” replied Jekyll; “I have grounds for certainty that I cannot share with any one. But there is one thing on which you may advise me. I have—I have received a letter; and I am at a loss whether I should show it to the police. I should like to leave it in your hands, Utterson; you would judge wisely, I am sure; I have so great a trust in you.”
“No,” said the other. “I cannot say that I care what becomes of Hyde; I am quite done with him. I was thinking of my own character, which this hateful business has rather exposed.”
Utterson ruminated awhile; he was surprised at his friend’s selfishness, and yet relieved by it. “Well,” said he, at last, “let me see the letter.”

The letter was written in an odd, upright hand and signed “Edward Hyde”: and it signified, briefly enough, that the writer’s benefactor, Dr. Jekyll, whom he had long so unworthily repaid for a thousand generosities, need labour under no alarm for his safety, as he had means of escape on which he placed a sure dependence. The lawyer liked this letter well enough; it put a better colour on the intimacy than he had looked for; and he blamed himself for some of his past suspicions.
“I burned it,” replied Jekyll, “before I thought what I was about. But it bore no postmark. The note was handed in.”
“Well, I shall consider,” returned the lawyer. “And now one word more: it was Hyde who dictated the terms in your will about that disappearance?”
“I have had what is far more to the purpose,” returned the doctor solemnly: “I have had a lesson—O God, Utterson, what a lesson I have had!” And he covered his face for a moment with his hands.

On his way out, the lawyer stopped and had a word or two with Poole. “By the bye,” said he, “there was a letter handed in to-day: what was the messenger like?” But Poole was positive nothing had come except by post; “and only circulars by that,” he added.

This news sent off the visitor with his fears renewed. Plainly the letter had come by the laboratory door; possibly, indeed, it had been written in the cabinet; and if that were so, it must be differently judged, and handled with the more caution. The newsboys, as he went, were crying themselves hoarse along the footways: “Special edition. Shocking murder of an M.P.” That was the funeral oration of one friend and client; and he could not help a certain apprehension lest the good name of another should be sucked down in the eddy of the scandal. It was, at least, a ticklish decision that he had to make; and self-reliant as he was by habit, he began to cherish a longing for advice. It was not to be had directly; but perhaps, he thought, it might be fished for.

Presently after, he sat on one side of his own hearth, with Mr. Guest, his head clerk, upon the other, and midway between, at a nicely calculated distance from the fire, a bottle of a particular old wine that had long dwelt unsunned in the foundations of his house. The fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city, where the lamps glimmered like carbuncles; and through the muffle and smother of these fallen clouds, the procession of the town’s life was still rolling in through the great arteries with a sound as of a mighty wind. But the room was gay with firelight. In the bottle the acids were long ago resolved; the imperial dye had softened with time, as the colour grows richer in stained windows; and the glow of hot autumn afternoons on hillside vineyards, was ready to be set free and to disperse the fogs of London. Insensibly the lawyer melted. There was no man from whom he kept fewer secrets than Mr. Guest; and he was not always sure that he kept as many as he meant. Guest had often been on business to the doctor’s; he knew Poole; he could scarce have failed to hear of Mr. Hyde’s familiarity about the house; he might draw conclusions: was it not as well, then, that he should see a letter which put that mystery to rights? and above all since Guest, being a great student and critic of handwriting, would consider the step natural and obliging? The clerk, besides, was a man of counsel; he could scarce read so strange a document without dropping a remark; and by that remark Mr. Utterson might shape his future course.
paragraphsZh: 律师听得郁闷；他不喜欢他朋友的狂热态度。 “看来你对他很有信心，”他说。 “为了你的缘故，我希望你是对的。如果进行审判，你的名字可能会出现。”
“我对他很有信心，”杰基尔回答道； “我有理由确信这一点，但我不能与任何人分享。但是有一件事你可以给我建议。我已经——我收到了一封信；我不知道是否应该把它交给警察。我想把它交给你，厄特森；我相信你会做出明智的判断；我非常信任你。”
“不，”另一个说。 “我不能说我关心海德的结局；我已经受够了他。我在想我自己的性格，这件可恶的事情已经暴露了我的性格。”
厄特森沉思了一会儿；他对朋友的自私感到惊讶，但同时也松了口气。 “好吧，”他最后说道，“让我看看这封信。”
这封信是用一种奇怪的、正直的字体写的，署名是“爱德华·海德”：它很简短地表明，作者的恩人杰基尔博士长期以来一直不值得地报答他的一千次慷慨，为了他的安全，他需要毫无顾忌的劳动，因为他有可靠的逃生手段。律师很喜欢这封信。这给两人的亲密关系增添了比他想象中更好的色彩。他为自己过去的一些怀疑而自责。
“我烧掉了它，”杰基尔回答道，“在我思考我要做什么之前，它没有盖上邮戳。纸条已经上交了。”
“好吧，我会考虑的，”律师回答道。 “现在再说一句：是海德在你的遗嘱中规定了关于那次失踪的条款？”
“我已经得到了更符合目的的东西，”医生严肃地回答道：“我得到了教训——上帝啊，厄特森，我得到了多么好的教训啊！”他用手捂住脸一会儿。
在出去的路上，律师停下来与普尔说了一两句话。 “再见，”他说，“今天有一封信递过来，信使怎么样？”但普尔确信除了邮寄之外什么也没有收到。 “而且只是通告，”他补充道。

这个消息让来访者再次感到恐惧。显然，这封信是从实验室门口寄来的。事实上，它可能已经写在内阁里了；如果真是这样，就必须做出不同的判断，并更加谨慎地处理。当他走的时候，报童们在人行道上声嘶力竭地哭着：“特别版。令人震惊的国会议员谋杀案。”这是一位朋友兼客户的葬礼致辞；他不禁心生忧虑，生怕另一个人的好名声被卷入丑闻的漩涡中。至少，这是他必须做出的一个棘手的决定。尽管他习惯于自力更生，但他开始渴望寻求建议。它不是可以直接得到的，而是可以直接得到的。但他想，也许有人会钓鱼。

不久之后，他坐在自家壁炉的一边，他的首席办事员盖斯特先生坐在另一边，在中间，与火保持着精心计算的距离，有一瓶特殊的陈年葡萄酒，这种酒长期存放在他房子的地基里，没有阳光照射。雾气仍然沉睡在这座被淹没的城市上空，那里的灯光像红宝石一样闪闪发光。透过这些落下的云层的闷热和窒息，小镇的生命之行仍在大动脉中滚滚而过，声音如同狂风一般。但房间里却充满了火光。瓶子里的酸早已溶解；皇家染料随着时间的推移而变软，窗户上的颜色变得更加丰富。炎热的秋日午后，山坡上的葡萄园所散发出的光芒，即将被释放出来，驱散伦敦的雾气。律师不知不觉地融化了。没有人比格斯特先生保守的秘密更少。而且他并不总是确定自己保留了他想要的数量。客人经常去医生那里出差。他认识普尔；他不可能不知道海德先生对这座房子很熟悉。他可能会得出结论：那么，他应该看到一封信来澄清这个谜团，不是更好吗？最重要的是，作为一名出色的学生和笔迹批评家，格斯特会认为这一步自然且乐于助人吗？此外，店员还是一位顾问。读到如此奇怪的文件，他几乎不可能不留下评论。厄特森先生可能会通过这句话来决定他未来的道路。

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 7
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: The court was very cool and a little damp, and full of premature twilight, although the sky, high up overhead, was still bright with sunset. The middle one of the three windows was half-way open; and sitting close beside it, taking the air with an infinite sadness of mien, like some disconsolate prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
“I am very low, Utterson,” replied the doctor drearily, “very low. It will not last long, thank God.”

“You stay too much indoors,” said the lawyer. “You should be out, whipping up the circulation like Mr. Enfield and me. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come now; get your hat and take a quick turn with us.”

“You are very good,” sighed the other. “I should like to very much; but no, no, no, it is quite impossible; I dare not. But indeed, Utterson, I am very glad to see you; this is really a great pleasure; I would ask you and Mr. Enfield up, but the place is really not fit.”

“That is just what I was about to venture to propose,” returned the doctor with a smile. But the words were hardly uttered, before the smile was struck out of his face and succeeded by an expression of such abject terror and despair, as froze the very blood of the two gentlemen below. They saw it but for a glimpse for the window was instantly thrust down; but that glimpse had been sufficient, and they turned and left the court without a word. In silence, too, they traversed the by-street; and it was not until they had come into a neighbouring thoroughfare, where even upon a Sunday there were still some stirrings of life, that Mr. Utterson at last turned and looked at his companion. They were both pale; and there was an answering horror in their eyes.
Mr. Utterson was sitting by his fireside one evening after dinner, when he was surprised to receive a visit from Poole.
“Take a seat, and here is a glass of wine for you,” said the lawyer. “Now, take your time, and tell me plainly what you want.”

“You know the doctor’s ways, sir,” replied Poole, “and how he shuts himself up. Well, he’s shut up again in the cabinet; and I don’t like it, sir—I wish I may die if I like it. Mr. Utterson, sir, I’m afraid.”

The man’s appearance amply bore out his words; his manner was altered for the worse; and except for the moment when he had first announced his terror, he had not once looked the lawyer in the face. Even now, he sat with the glass of wine untasted on his knee, and his eyes directed to a corner of the floor. “I can bear it no more,” he repeated.
“Come,” said the lawyer, “I see you have some good reason, Poole; I see there is something seriously amiss. Try to tell me what it is.”
“Foul play!” cried the lawyer, a good deal frightened and rather inclined to be irritated in consequence. “What foul play! What does the man mean?”

Mr. Utterson’s only answer was to rise and get his hat and greatcoat; but he observed with wonder the greatness of the relief that appeared upon the butler’s face, and perhaps with no less, that the wine was still untasted when he set it down to follow.

It was a wild, cold, seasonable night of March, with a pale moon, lying on her back as though the wind had tilted her, and flying wrack of the most diaphanous and lawny texture. The wind made talking difficult, and flecked the blood into the face. It seemed to have swept the streets unusually bare of passengers, besides; for Mr. Utterson thought he had never seen that part of London so deserted. He could have wished it otherwise; never in his life had he been conscious of so sharp a wish to see and touch his fellow-creatures; for struggle as he might, there was borne in upon his mind a crushing anticipation of calamity. The square, when they got there, was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees in the garden were lashing themselves along the railing. Poole, who had kept all the way a pace or two ahead, now pulled up in the middle of the pavement, and in spite of the biting weather, took off his hat and mopped his brow with a red pocket-handkerchief. But for all the hurry of his coming, these were not the dews of exertion that he wiped away, but the moisture of some strangling anguish; for his face was white and his voice, when he spoke, harsh and broken.
