paragraphsZh: 球场非常凉爽，有点潮湿，充满了过早的暮色，尽管头顶上的天空仍然明亮地伴随着日落。三扇窗户中，中间的一扇半开着。厄特森坐在它旁边，带着无限悲伤的神情呼吸着空气，就像某个郁郁寡欢的囚犯一样，厄特森看到了杰基尔博士。
“我的情绪非常低落，厄特森，”医生沉闷地回答道，“非常低落。感谢上帝，这种情况不会持续太久。”
“你呆在室内的时间太多了，”律师说。 “你应该出去，像恩菲尔德先生和我一样促进流通。（这是我的表弟——恩菲尔德先生——杰基尔博士。）来吧，拿上你的帽子，和我们一起快速转一圈。”
“你很好，”另一个叹了口气。 “我很想去；但是不，不，不，这是完全不可能的；我不敢。但是说实话，厄特森，我很高兴见到你；这真的是一个很大的荣幸；我想邀请你和恩菲尔德先生一起去，但是这个地方实在不合适。”

“这正是我要冒险提出的，”医生微笑着回答道。但话刚说完，他脸上的笑容就消失了，取而代之的是一种卑鄙的恐惧和绝望的表情，让下面两位先生的血液都凝固了。他们看到了，但只是瞥了一眼，因为窗户立即被推了下来。但那一瞥已经足够了，他们一言不发地转身离开了法庭。他们也默默地穿过小街。直到他们来到附近的一条大道上，即使在周日，这里仍然充满了生机，厄特森先生才终于转过身来看着他的同伴。他们的脸色都很苍白。他们的眼中充满了恐惧。
一天晚上，厄特森先生晚饭后坐在炉边，惊讶地发现普尔来访。
“请坐，这里有一杯酒，”律师说道。 “现在，慢慢来，清楚地告诉我你想要什么。”
“您知道医生的做法，先生，”普尔回答道，“以及他如何把自己关起来。好吧，他又被关在柜子里了；我不喜欢这样，先生——如果我喜欢的话，我希望我可以死掉。厄特森先生，先生，我担心。”
这个男人的外表充分证实了他的话；他的态度变得更糟了。除了他第一次宣布他的恐惧那一刻之外，他一次也没有正视过律师的脸。即使现在，他仍将那杯未尝的酒放在膝盖上，眼睛盯着地板的一角。 “我再也无法忍受了，”他重复道。
“来吧，”律师说，“我看到你有一些充分的理由，普尔；我看到有一些严重的问题。试着告诉我它是什么。”
“犯规！”律师喊道，他非常害怕，结果很容易生气。 “什么肮脏的行为！这个人是什么意思？”
厄特森先生唯一的回答是站起来拿帽子和大衣；但他惊讶地发现管家脸上露出了极大的轻松，也许同样重要的是，当他放下酒时，酒还没有品尝。

那是三月里一个狂野、寒冷、季节适宜的夜晚，一轮苍白的月亮仰面躺着，仿佛风把她倾斜了，飞行着最透明、最草坪质地的残骸。风使说话变得困难，血迹溅到脸上。除此之外，街道上似乎少有乘客。因为厄特森先生认为他从未见过伦敦的那个地区如此荒凉。他本可以不这样希望的；但事实却是这样。他一生中从来没有如此强烈地渴望看到并触摸他的同胞。尽管他竭尽全力地挣扎，但他的心中却充满了对灾难的强烈预感。他们到达的时候，广场上风沙很大，花园里的细树正沿着栏杆抽打着。普尔一直领先一两步，现在把车停在人行道中间，尽管天气刺骨，他还是摘下帽子，用红色手帕擦了擦额头。尽管他来得匆忙，但他擦去的并不是劳累时的露水，而是某种令人窒息的痛苦的湿气。因为他的脸色苍白，说话时声音刺耳而破碎。

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 8
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: “These are all very strange circumstances,” said Mr. Utterson, “but I think I begin to see daylight. Your master, Poole, is plainly seized with one of those maladies that both torture and deform the sufferer; hence, for aught I know, the alteration of his voice; hence the mask and the avoidance of his friends; hence his eagerness to find this drug, by means of which the poor soul retains some hope of ultimate recovery—God grant that he be not deceived! There is my explanation; it is sad enough, Poole, ay, and appalling to consider; but it is plain and natural, hangs well together, and delivers us from all exorbitant alarms.”

“Sir,” said the butler, turning to a sort of mottled pallor, “that thing was not my master, and there’s the truth. My master”—here he looked round him and began to whisper—“is a tall, fine build of a man, and this was more of a dwarf.” Utterson attempted to protest. “O, sir,” cried Poole, “do you think I do not know my master after twenty years? Do you think I do not know where his head comes to in the cabinet door, where I saw him every morning of my life? No, sir, that thing in the mask was never Dr. Jekyll—God knows what it was, but it was never Dr. Jekyll; and it is the belief of my heart that there was murder done.”

“Poole,” replied the lawyer, “if you say that, it will become my duty to make certain. Much as I desire to spare your master’s feelings, much as I am puzzled by this note which seems to prove him to be still alive, I shall consider it my duty to break in that door.”
The lawyer took that rude but weighty instrument into his hand, and balanced it. “Do you know, Poole,” he said, looking up, “that you and I are about to place ourselves in a position of some peril?”
“It is well, then that we should be frank,” said the other. “We both think more than we have said; let us make a clean breast. This masked figure that you saw, did you recognise it?”

“Well, sir, it went so quick, and the creature was so doubled up, that I could hardly swear to that,” was the answer. “But if you mean, was it Mr. Hyde?—why, yes, I think it was! You see, it was much of the same bigness; and it had the same quick, light way with it; and then who else could have got in by the laboratory door? You have not forgot, sir, that at the time of the murder he had still the key with him? But that’s not all. I don’t know, Mr. Utterson, if you ever met this Mr. Hyde?”

“Quite so, sir,” returned Poole. “Well, when that masked thing like a monkey jumped from among the chemicals and whipped into the cabinet, it went down my spine like ice. O, I know it’s not evidence, Mr. Utterson; I’m book-learned enough for that; but a man has his feelings, and I give you my bible-word it was Mr. Hyde!”

“Ay, ay,” said the lawyer. “My fears incline to the same point. Evil, I fear, founded—evil was sure to come—of that connection. Ay truly, I believe you; I believe poor Harry is killed; and I believe his murderer (for what purpose, God alone can tell) is still lurking in his victim’s room. Well, let our name be vengeance. Call Bradshaw.”

“Pull yourself together, Bradshaw,” said the lawyer. “This suspense, I know, is telling upon all of you; but it is now our intention to make an end of it. Poole, here, and I are going to force our way into the cabinet. If all is well, my shoulders are broad enough to bear the blame. Meanwhile, lest anything should really be amiss, or any malefactor seek to escape by the back, you and the boy must go round the corner with a pair of good sticks and take your post at the laboratory door. We give you ten minutes to get to your stations.”
paragraphsZh: “这些都是非常奇怪的情况，”厄特森先生说，“但我想我开始看到曙光了。你的主人普尔显然患有一种既折磨患者又使患者变形的疾病；因此，据我所知，他的声音发生了变化；因此他戴上了面具并回避了他的朋友；因此他渴望找到这种药物，通过这种药物，可怜的灵魂保留了最终康复的希望——上帝保佑他不我的解释是受骗了；普尔，是的，想想就很令人震惊，但它很简单，很自然，而且使我们摆脱了所有过度的恐慌。

“先生，”管家说道，脸色变得有些斑驳，脸色苍白，“那东西不是我的主人，这是事实。我的主人”——此时他环顾四周，开始低声说道——“他是一个身材高大、身材匀称的人，而这个人更像是一个侏儒。”厄特森试图抗议。 “哦，先生，”普尔喊道，“你以为二十年后我不认识我的主人了吗？你以为我不知道他的头在柜门的什么地方，我一生中每天早上都在哪里看到他吗？不，先生，那个戴着面具的东西从来就不是杰基尔博士——上帝知道它是什么，但它从来都不是杰基尔博士；而且我内心相信这是谋杀。”
“普尔，”律师答道，“如果你这么说，我就有责任去确认。尽管我很想不伤害你主人的感情，也尽管我对这张似乎证明他还活着的字条感到困惑，但我认为我有责任破门而入。”
律师将那件粗鲁但却沉甸甸的工具拿在手里，平衡了一下。 “你知道吗，普尔，”他抬起头说道，“你和我即将把自己置于危险的境地？”
“好吧，那么我们应该坦白地说，”另一个说。 “我们想的比说的多；让我们坦白说吧。你看到的这个蒙面人，你认得吗？”
“嗯，先生，事情发生得太快了，而且这个生物被折叠起来了，我几乎无法发誓，”这是答案。 “但如果你的意思是，是海德先生吗？——为什么，是的，我认为是！你看，它同样大；而且它有同样快速、轻便的方式；那么还有谁能从实验室门进来？你没有忘记，先生，在谋杀时他还带着钥匙？但这还不是全部。我不知道，厄特森先生，你是否见过这个海德先生？”
“确实如此，先生，”普尔回答道。 “好吧，当那个像猴子一样的蒙面东西从化学品中跳出来并被鞭打进柜子时，它像冰一样顺着我的脊椎。哦，我知道这不是证据，厄特森先生；我在书本上学到了足够多的知识；但是一个人有他的感情，我给你我的圣经词，那就是海德先生！”
“哎呀，”律师说。 “我的恐惧倾向于同一点。邪恶，我担心，邪恶一定会到来。是的，我相信你；我相信可怜的哈利被杀了；我相信凶手（出于什么目的，只有上帝知道）仍然潜伏在受害者的房间里。好吧，让我们的名字报仇。打电话给布拉德肖。”
“振作起来，布拉德肖，”律师说。 “我知道，这个悬念正在告诉你们所有人；但现在我们打算结束这一切。普尔，在这里，我要强行进入内阁。如果一切顺利，我的肩膀足够宽广，可以承担责任。同时，为了避免出现任何问题，或者有恶棍想从后面逃跑，你和那个男孩必须拿着一双好棍子绕过拐角，在实验室门口就职。我们给你十分钟的时间到达你的电台。”

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 9
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: “So it will walk all day, sir,” whispered Poole; “ay, and the better part of the night. Only when a new sample comes from the chemist, there’s a bit of a break. Ah, it’s an ill conscience that’s such an enemy to rest! Ah, sir, there’s blood foully shed in every step of it! But hark again, a little closer—put your heart in your ears, Mr. Utterson, and tell me, is that the doctor’s foot?”

The steps fell lightly and oddly, with a certain swing, for all they went so slowly; it was different indeed from the heavy creaking tread of Henry Jekyll. Utterson sighed. “Is there never anything else?” he asked.
“Weeping like a woman or a lost soul,” said the butler. “I came away with that upon my heart, that I could have wept too.”

But now the ten minutes drew to an end. Poole disinterred the axe from under a stack of packing straw; the candle was set upon the nearest table to light them to the attack; and they drew near with bated breath to where that patient foot was still going up and down, up and down, in the quiet of the night.

“Jekyll,” cried Utterson, with a loud voice, “I demand to see you.” He paused a moment, but there came no reply. “I give you fair warning, our suspicions are aroused, and I must and shall see you,” he resumed; “if not by fair means, then by foul—if not of your consent, then by brute force!”

Poole swung the axe over his shoulder; the blow shook the building, and the red baize door leaped against the lock and hinges. A dismal screech, as of mere animal terror, rang from the cabinet. Up went the axe again, and again the panels crashed and the frame bounded; four times the blow fell; but the wood was tough and the fittings were of excellent workmanship; and it was not until the fifth, that the lock burst and the wreck of the door fell inwards on the carpet.

The besiegers, appalled by their own riot and the stillness that had succeeded, stood back a little and peered in. There lay the cabinet before their eyes in the quiet lamplight, a good fire glowing and chattering on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin strain, a drawer or two open, papers neatly set forth on the business table, and nearer the fire, the things laid out for tea; the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glazed presses full of chemicals, the most commonplace that night in London.

Right in the middle there lay the body of a man sorely contorted and still twitching. They drew near on tiptoe, turned it on his back and beheld the face of Edward Hyde. He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes of the doctor’s bigness; the cords of his face still moved with a semblance of life, but life was quite gone; and by the crushed phial in the hand and the strong smell of kernels that hung upon the air, Utterson knew that he was looking on the body of a self-destroyer.
“We have come too late,” he said sternly, “whether to save or punish. Hyde is gone to his account; and it only remains for us to find the body of your master.”

The far greater proportion of the building was occupied by the theatre, which filled almost the whole ground storey and was lighted from above, and by the cabinet, which formed an upper storey at one end and looked upon the court. A corridor joined the theatre to the door on the by-street; and with this the cabinet communicated separately by a second flight of stairs. There were besides a few dark closets and a spacious cellar. All these they now thoroughly examined. Each closet needed but a glance, for all were empty, and all, by the dust that fell from their doors, had stood long unopened. The cellar, indeed, was filled with crazy lumber, mostly dating from the times of the surgeon who was Jekyll’s predecessor; but even as they opened the door they were advertised of the uselessness of further search, by the fall of a perfect mat of cobweb which had for years sealed up the entrance. Nowhere was there any trace of Henry Jekyll, dead or alive.
paragraphsZh: “所以它会走一整天，先生，”普尔低声说道； “哎呀，还有晚上的大部分时间。只有当化学家送来新的样本时，才会有一点休息。啊，这是一个良心不安的敌人，不能休息！啊，先生，每一步都在流血！但是再听一次，靠近一点——把你的心放在耳边，厄特森先生，告诉我，那是医生的脚吗？”
脚步轻盈而奇怪地落下，虽然走得很慢，但还是有一定的摆动。这确实与亨利·杰基尔沉重的嘎吱嘎吱的脚步声不同。厄特森叹了口气。 “就没有别的事了吗？”他问道。
“像个女人或迷失的灵魂一样哭泣，”管家说。 “我离开时心里一直有这样的想法，我也可能会哭。”
但现在十分钟结束了。普尔从一堆包装稻草下挖出了斧头；蜡烛放在最近的桌子上，为他们的进攻提供照明。他们屏息凝神地走近那只脚仍在静谧的夜色中不断上上下下的地方。
“杰基尔，”厄特森大声喊道，“我要求见你。”他停顿了一会儿，但没有回应。 “我给你公平的警告，我们的怀疑已经引起了，我必须而且将会见到你，”他继续说道。 “如果不以正当手段，那就以邪恶手段——如果未经你的同意，那就以暴力手段！”
普尔将斧头举在肩上；这一击震动了大楼，红色粗呢门突然撞到了锁和铰链。柜子里传来一阵凄凉的尖叫声，仿佛纯粹是动物的恐惧。斧头再次举起，面板再次崩裂，框架再次弹起。四次打击；但木材坚韧，配件做工精良。直到第五天，门锁突然爆裂，门的残骸向内掉到了地毯上。
围攻者们对自己的骚乱和随之而来的寂静感到震惊，退后了一点，向里面张望。在安静的灯光下，柜子就摆在他们眼前，壁炉里熊熊燃烧着熊熊的火，水壶在唱着它细细的旋律，一两个抽屉打开了，文件整齐地放在办公桌上，靠近火的地方，摆着泡茶的东西；你可能会说，这是最安静的房间，而且，如果没有装满化学品的玻璃压榨机，那是伦敦当晚最常见的房间。
正中间躺着一个男人的尸体，他的身体严重扭曲，还在抽搐。他们踮起脚尖走近，把脚翻到背上，看到了爱德华·海德的脸。他穿的衣服对他来说太大了，是医生的大衣服。他脸上的纹路还带着生命的气息，但生命已然消失。厄特森从手中压碎的小瓶和空气中弥漫的玉米粒的强烈气味知道，他看到的是一具自我毁灭者的尸体。
“我们来得太晚了，”他严厉地说，“无论是拯救还是惩罚。海德已经到了他的账上；我们只剩下找到你主人的尸体了。”

这座建筑的大部分面积被剧院占据，剧院几乎占据了整个底层，并从上方照明，而橱柜则在一端形成了上层，面向庭院。一条走廊将剧院与小街的门口连接起来。由此，内阁通过第二段楼梯单独连通。除此之外还有几个黑暗的壁橱和一个宽敞的地窖。他们现在对所有这些进行了彻底的检查。每个壁橱都只需看一眼，因为所有壁橱都是空的，而且从门上落下的灰尘来看，所有壁橱都已经长期没有打开过。事实上，地窖里堆满了疯狂的木材，大部分都是杰基尔的前任外科医生时代的。但当他们打开门时，多年来封锁入口的完美蜘蛛网掉落下来，表明进一步的搜索是无用的。到处都没有亨利·杰基尔的踪迹，无论是死的还是活着的。

title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde · 选段 10
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: He turned a dreadful smile to me, and as if with the decision of despair, plucked away the sheet. At sight of the contents, he uttered one loud sob of such immense relief that I sat petrified. And the next moment, in a voice that was already fairly well under control, “Have you a graduated glass?” he asked.

He thanked me with a smiling nod, measured out a few minims of the red tincture and added one of the powders. The mixture, which was at first of a reddish hue, began, in proportion as the crystals melted, to brighten in colour, to effervesce audibly, and to throw off small fumes of vapour. Suddenly and at the same moment, the ebullition ceased and the compound changed to a dark purple, which faded again more slowly to a watery green. My visitor, who had watched these metamorphoses with a keen eye, smiled, set down the glass upon the table, and then turned and looked upon me with an air of scrutiny.

“And now,” said he, “to settle what remains. Will you be wise? will you be guided? will you suffer me to take this glass in my hand and to go forth from your house without further parley? or has the greed of curiosity too much command of you? Think before you answer, for it shall be done as you decide. As you decide, you shall be left as you were before, and neither richer nor wiser, unless the sense of service rendered to a man in mortal distress may be counted as a kind of riches of the soul. Or, if you shall so prefer to choose, a new province of knowledge and new avenues to fame and power shall be laid open to you, here, in this room, upon the instant; and your sight shall be blasted by a prodigy to stagger the unbelief of Satan.”

“Sir,” said I, affecting a coolness that I was far from truly possessing, “you speak enigmas, and you will perhaps not wonder that I hear you with no very strong impression of belief. But I have gone too far in the way of inexplicable services to pause before I see the end.”

“It is well,” replied my visitor. “Lanyon, you remember your vows: what follows is under the seal of our profession. And now, you who have so long been bound to the most narrow and material views, you who have denied the virtue of transcendental medicine, you who have derided your superiors—behold!”

He put the glass to his lips and drank at one gulp. A cry followed; he reeled, staggered, clutched at the table and held on, staring with injected eyes, gasping with open mouth; and as I looked there came, I thought, a change—he seemed to swell—his face became suddenly black and the features seemed to melt and alter—and the next moment, I had sprung to my feet and leaped back against the wall, my arms raised to shield me from that prodigy, my mind submerged in terror.

“O God!” I screamed, and “O God!” again and again; for there before my eyes—pale and shaken, and half fainting, and groping before him with his hands, like a man restored from death—there stood Henry Jekyll!

What he told me in the next hour, I cannot bring my mind to set on paper. I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it; and yet now when that sight has faded from my eyes, I ask myself if I believe it, and I cannot answer. My life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me; the deadliest terror sits by me at all hours of the day and night; and I feel that my days are numbered, and that I must die; and yet I shall die incredulous. As for the moral turpitude that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror. I will say but one thing, Utterson, and that (if you can bring your mind to credit it) will be more than enough. The creature who crept into my house that night was, on Jekyll’s own confession, known by the name of Hyde and hunted for in every corner of the land as the murderer of Carew.
paragraphsZh: 他对我露出了可怕的微笑，仿佛绝望的决定，撕开了床单。看到里面的内容，他大声抽泣起来，我如释重负，我坐在那儿吓呆了。下一刻，用已经相当控制的声音问道：“你有刻度镜吗？”他问道。
他微笑着点头感谢我，量出了几微量的红色酊剂并添加了一种粉末。混合物最初呈淡红色，随着晶体的熔化，颜色开始变亮，发出气泡声，并散发出少量蒸汽。突然，在同一时刻，沸腾停止了，化合物变成了深紫色，然后又慢慢地褪成了水绿色。我的来访者敏锐地观察到了这些变化，他微笑着，把玻璃杯放在桌子上，然后转过身来，用审视的目光看着我。

“现在，”他说，“解决剩下的问题。你会明智吗？你会被引导吗？你愿意让我拿着这块玻璃杯，不经进一步谈判就离开你的房子吗？还是贪婪的好奇心太多了？在你回答之前先想一想，因为它将按照你的决定去做。当你决定时，你将像以前一样，既不会变得更富有，也不会变得更聪明，除非为一个处于致命困境的人提供的服务感可能会受到影响。或者，如果你愿意选择的话，一个新的知识领域和通向名誉和权力的新途径将在此时此刻向你敞开，在这个房间里，你的视野将被一个神童震撼，以震慑撒旦的不信。
“先生，”我装出一副远非真正拥有的冷静说道，“你说的是谜语，你也许不会奇怪我听到你的话时并没有非常强烈的信仰印象。但我在莫名其妙的服务方面已经走得太远了，在我看到结局之前不能停下来。”
“很好，”我的访客回答道。 “兰宁，你记住你的誓言：接下来的事情是在我们职业的印记下的。现在，你们这些长期受最狭隘和物质观点束缚的人，你们否认超验医学的美德，你们嘲笑你们的上级——看哪！”
他把酒杯放到唇边，一口气喝了下去。随之而来的是一声哭喊。他摇摇晃晃，踉踉跄跄地抓着桌子不放，眼睛瞪得大大的，张着嘴喘着粗气。当我看着那里时，我想，发生了变化——他似乎肿胀了——他的脸突然变黑了，五官似乎融化并改变了——下一刻，我猛地站起来，向后跳到墙上，我举起双臂，保护我免受那个神童的伤害，我的思绪陷入了恐惧。
“上帝啊！”我尖叫起来，“上帝啊！”一次又一次；因为在我眼前——脸色苍白，浑身颤抖，半昏厥，双手在他面前摸索，就像死而复生的人一样——亨利·杰基尔就站在那里！

他在接下来的一个小时里告诉我的话，我无法把我的想法写在纸上。我看到了我所看到的，我听到了我所听到的，我的灵魂为此感到恶心；然而现在，当那景象从我眼前消失时，我问自己是否相信它，但我无法回答。我的生命彻底动摇了；睡眠已离我而去；最致命的恐惧不分昼夜地伴随着我；我觉得我的日子屈指可数了，我必须死去；但我仍将难以置信地死去。至于人们向我揭露的道德败坏，即使带着忏悔的泪水，我也无法在记忆中不感到恐惧。我只想说一件事，厄特森，（如果你能相信这一点的话）就足够了。据杰基尔自己的供述，那天晚上潜入我家的生物名叫海德，并作为谋杀卡鲁的凶手在这片土地的每个角落被追捕。

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 4
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: The “Avenue,” so called by the Newbridge people, was a stretch of road four or five hundred yards long, completely arched over with huge, wide-spreading apple-trees, planted years ago by an eccentric old farmer. Overhead was one long canopy of snowy fragrant bloom. Below the boughs the air was full of a purple twilight and far ahead a glimpse of painted sunset sky shone like a great rose window at the end of a cathedral aisle.

Its beauty seemed to strike the child dumb. She leaned back in the buggy, her thin hands clasped before her, her face lifted rapturously to the white splendor above. Even when they had passed out and were driving down the long slope to Newbridge she never moved or spoke. Still with rapt face she gazed afar into the sunset west, with eyes that saw visions trooping splendidly across that glowing background. Through Newbridge, a bustling little village where dogs barked at them and small boys hooted and curious faces peered from the windows, they drove, still in silence. When three more miles had dropped away behind them the child had not spoken. She could keep silence, it was evident, as energetically as she could talk.

“I guess you’re feeling pretty tired and hungry,” Matthew ventured to say at last, accounting for her long visitation of dumbness with the only reason he could think of. “But we haven’t very far to go now--only another mile.”
She came out of her reverie with a deep sigh and looked at him with the dreamy gaze of a soul that had been wondering afar, star-led.
“Well now, you must mean the Avenue,” said Matthew after a few moments’ profound reflection. “It is a kind of pretty place.”

“Pretty? Oh, pretty doesn’t seem the right word to use. Nor beautiful, either. They don’t go far enough. Oh, it was wonderful--wonderful. It’s the first thing I ever saw that couldn’t be improved upon by imagination. It just satisfied me here”--she put one hand on her breast--“it made a queer funny ache and yet it was a pleasant ache. Did you ever have an ache like that, Mr. Cuthbert?”

“I have it lots of times--whenever I see anything royally beautiful. But they shouldn’t call that lovely place the Avenue. There is no meaning in a name like that. They should call it--let me see--the White Way of Delight. Isn’t that a nice imaginative name? When I don’t like the name of a place or a person I always imagine a new one and always think of them so. There was a girl at the asylum whose name was Hepzibah Jenkins, but I always imagined her as Rosalia DeVere. Other people may call that place the Avenue, but I shall always call it the White Way of Delight. Have we really only another mile to go before we get home? I’m glad and I’m sorry. I’m sorry because this drive has been so pleasant and I’m always sorry when pleasant things end. Something still pleasanter may come after, but you can never be sure. And it’s so often the case that it isn’t pleasanter. That has been my experience anyhow. But I’m glad to think of getting home. You see, I’ve never had a real home since I can remember. It gives me that pleasant ache again just to think of coming to a really truly home. Oh, isn’t that pretty!”

They had driven over the crest of a hill. Below them was a pond, looking almost like a river so long and winding was it. A bridge spanned it midway and from there to its lower end, where an amber-hued belt of sand-hills shut it in from the dark blue gulf beyond, the water was a glory of many shifting hues--the most spiritual shadings of crocus and rose and ethereal green, with other elusive tintings for which no name has ever been found. Above the bridge the pond ran up into fringing groves of fir and maple and lay all darkly translucent in their wavering shadows. Here and there a wild plum leaned out from the bank like a white-clad girl tiptoeing to her own reflection. From the marsh at the head of the pond came the clear, mournfully-sweet chorus of the frogs. There was a little gray house peering around a white apple orchard on a slope beyond and, although it was not yet quite dark, a light was shining from one of its windows.
paragraphsZh: 纽布里奇人所谓的“大道”是一段四五百码长的道路，道路完全呈拱形，上面长满了巨大的、分布广泛的苹果树，这些苹果树是多年前由一位古怪的老农种植的。头顶上是一长长的树冠，开满了雪白的芬芳花朵。树枝下方的空气中弥漫着紫色的暮色，前方远处瞥见彩绘落日的天空，像大教堂过道尽头的一扇巨大的玫瑰窗一样闪闪发光。

它的美丽似乎让孩子目瞪口呆。她靠在马车上，瘦弱的双手紧握在身前，脸上欣喜若狂地仰望着头顶白色的光彩。即使他们昏倒了，沿着长长的斜坡开车前往新桥，她也没有动弹，也没有说话。她仍然全神贯注地凝视着远处的夕阳西下，眼睛里看到了在发光的背景上华丽地游行的景象。他们开车穿过纽布里奇，这是一个熙熙攘攘的小村庄，那里有狗对着他们吠叫，小男孩在叫着，好奇的面孔从车窗里张望。当他们身后又走了三英里时，孩子还是没有说话。很明显，她可以保持沉默，就像她可以说话一样充满活力。
“我猜你感觉很累又饿了，”马修最后大胆地说，这是他能想到的唯一原因，解释了她长期以来的沉默。 “但我们现在还没有走多远——只剩下一英里了。”
她深深地叹了口气，从沉思中醒来，用一颗星辰为首的灵魂在远方徘徊的梦幻般的目光看着他。
“好吧，你指的是大街，”马修沉思了一会儿后说道。 “这是一个美丽的地方。”
“漂亮？哦，漂亮这个词似乎不太合适。也不漂亮。它们还不够远。哦，太棒了——太棒了。这是我见过的第一件无法通过想象来改进的东西。它让我很满意”——她把一只手放在胸前——“它产生了一种奇怪有趣的疼痛，但又是一种愉快的疼痛。你有过这样的疼痛吗，先生。卡斯伯特？”

“我有很多次——每当我看到任何皇家美丽的东西时。但他们不应该称那个可爱的地方为大道。这样的名字没有任何意义。他们应该称它——让我想想——白色的喜悦之路。这不是一个很好的富有想象力的名字吗？当我不喜欢一个地方或一个人的名字时，我总是想象一个新的名字，并且总是这样想他们。精神病院里有一个女孩，她的名字是赫普兹巴·詹金斯，但我一直把她想象成罗莎莉亚·德维尔，但我总是称它为“快乐的白色之路”。我很高兴，也很抱歉，因为这段旅程是如此愉快，当愉快的事情结束时，我总是感到遗憾，但你永远不能确定情况并非如此。无论如何，那是我的经历，但我很高兴想到回家，自从我记事以来，我就再也没有过真正的家了，哦，那不是很漂亮吗？

他们已经驶过山顶。他们下面是一个池塘，看起来几乎像一条河，又长又蜿蜒。一座桥横跨在中间，从那里一直延伸到低端，那里有一条琥珀色的沙丘带将它与远处的深蓝色海湾隔开，海水呈现出多种变幻色彩的光彩——最有灵性的番红花色、玫瑰色和空灵的绿色，还有其他难以捉摸、至今无人知晓的色彩。桥上的池塘一直延伸到边缘的冷杉和枫树林，在它们摇曳的阴影中呈现出黑暗的半透明状态。岸边时不时地探出一株野梅，像一个白衣少女蹑手蹑脚地走向自己的倒影。池塘头的沼泽地里传来青蛙们清脆、哀伤、甜美的合唱。一座灰色的小房子俯瞰着远处山坡上的一片白色苹果园，虽然天还没有完全黑，但它的一扇窗户却透出一丝光亮。

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 5
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: “You’re only Anne of Green Gables,” she said earnestly, “and I see you, just as you are looking now, whenever I try to imagine I’m the Lady Cordelia. But it’s a million times nicer to be Anne of Green Gables than Anne of nowhere in particular, isn’t it?”

“Dear Snow Queen, good afternoon. And good afternoon, dear birches down in the hollow. And good afternoon, dear gray house up on the hill. I wonder if Diana is to be my bosom friend. I hope she will, and I shall love her very much. But I must never quite forget Katie Maurice and Violetta. They would feel so hurt if I did and I’d hate to hurt anybody’s feelings, even a little bookcase girl’s or a little echo girl’s. I must be careful to remember them and send them a kiss every day.”
Anne blew a couple of airy kisses from her fingertips past the cherry blossoms and then, with her chin in her hands, drifted luxuriously out on a sea of daydreams.

ANNE had been a fortnight at Green Gables before Mrs. Lynde arrived to inspect her. Mrs. Rachel, to do her justice, was not to blame for this. A severe and unseasonable attack of grippe had confined that good lady to her house ever since the occasion of her last visit to Green Gables. Mrs. Rachel was not often sick and had a well-defined contempt for people who were; but grippe, she asserted, was like no other illness on earth and could only be interpreted as one of the special visitations of Providence. As soon as her doctor allowed her to put her foot out-of-doors she hurried up to Green Gables, bursting with curiosity to see Matthew and Marilla’s orphan, concerning whom all sorts of stories and suppositions had gone abroad in Avonlea.

Anne had made good use of every waking moment of that fortnight. Already she was acquainted with every tree and shrub about the place. She had discovered that a lane opened out below the apple orchard and ran up through a belt of woodland; and she had explored it to its furthest end in all its delicious vagaries of brook and bridge, fir coppice and wild cherry arch, corners thick with fern, and branching byways of maple and mountain ash.

She had made friends with the spring down in the hollow--that wonderful deep, clear icy-cold spring; it was set about with smooth red sandstones and rimmed in by great palm-like clumps of water fern; and beyond it was a log bridge over the brook.

That bridge led Anne’s dancing feet up over a wooded hill beyond, where perpetual twilight reigned under the straight, thick-growing firs and spruces; the only flowers there were myriads of delicate “June bells,” those shyest and sweetest of woodland blooms, and a few pale, aerial starflowers, like the spirits of last year’s blossoms. Gossamers glimmered like threads of silver among the trees and the fir boughs and tassels seemed to utter friendly speech.

All these raptured voyages of exploration were made in the odd half hours which she was allowed for play, and Anne talked Matthew and Marilla half-deaf over her discoveries. Not that Matthew complained, to be sure; he listened to it all with a wordless smile of enjoyment on his face; Marilla permitted the “chatter” until she found herself becoming too interested in it, whereupon she always promptly quenched Anne by a curt command to hold her tongue.

Anne was out in the orchard when Mrs. Rachel came, wandering at her own sweet will through the lush, tremulous grasses splashed with ruddy evening sunshine; so that good lady had an excellent chance to talk her illness fully over, describing every ache and pulse beat with such evident enjoyment that Marilla thought even grippe must bring its compensations. When details were exhausted Mrs. Rachel introduced the real reason of her call.
paragraphsZh: “你只是绿山墙的安妮，”她认真地说，“每当我试图想象自己是科迪莉亚夫人时，我就能看到你，就像你现在看到的那样。但是，成为绿山墙的安妮比无处可去的安妮好一百万倍，不是吗？”
“亲爱的雪之女王，下午好。下午好，山谷里亲爱的白桦树。下午好，山上亲爱的灰色房子。我想知道戴安娜是否会成为我的知己。我希望她会，我会非常爱她。但我永远不能完全忘记凯蒂·莫里斯和维奥莱塔。如果我这样做，他们会感到很受伤，我不想伤害任何人的感情，即使是一个小书柜女孩或一个小回声我一定要小心地记住他们，每天给他们一个吻。”
安妮用指尖飞过樱花，飞过几个轻吻，然后双手托着下巴，奢华地飘浮在白日梦的海洋中。

林德夫人来检查安妮之前，她已经在绿山墙呆了两周了。公平地说，雷切尔夫人不应为此承担责任。自从上次访问绿山墙以来，一场严重的、不合时宜的流行性感冒发作，让那位好心的女士一直待在家里。雷切尔夫人并不经常生病，而且对生病的人怀有明显的蔑视。但她断言，流行性感冒与地球上任何其他疾病都不一样，只能被解释为上帝的特殊降临之一。医生一允许她出门，她就急忙赶到绿山墙，满怀好奇地想看看马修和玛丽拉的孤儿，关于他的各种故事和猜测已经在埃文利流传开来。
安妮充分利用了这两周的每一个醒着的时刻。她已经熟悉了这个地方的每一棵树和灌木。她发现苹果园下面有一条小路，穿过一片林地向上延伸。她已经探索到了它的最远的尽头，那里有小溪和桥梁、冷杉灌木丛和野樱桃拱门、长满蕨类植物的角落、枫树和山梣树的分支小道，所有奇妙的变幻莫测。
她和山谷里的泉水成了朋友——那美妙的深泉、清澈的冰冷泉水；它周围铺着光滑的红色砂岩，周围是大片棕榈状的水蕨丛。远处是小溪上的一座独木桥。
那座桥引导着安妮舞动的双脚越过远处树木繁茂的小山，那里永远的暮色笼罩在笔直、茂密的冷杉和云杉下；唯一的花朵是无数精致的“六月钟声”，那些最害羞、最甜美的林地花朵，还有一些苍白的空中星花，就像去年花朵的精灵。薄纱在树林中闪闪发光，像银丝一样，冷杉的树枝和流苏似乎在说着友好的话。
所有这些令人兴奋的探索之旅都是在她被允许玩耍的零星半小时内完成的，安妮对她的发现半聋地与马修和玛丽拉交谈。可以肯定的是，马修并不是在抱怨。他听着这一切，脸上挂着无言的享受的微笑。玛丽拉允许她“喋喋不休”，直到她发现自己对此太感兴趣，于是她总是立即简短地命令安妮不要说话，以此来压制住她。
当雷切尔夫人来时，安妮正在果园里，她按照自己的甜蜜意愿在郁郁葱葱的草丛中漫步，草地上洒满了红润的晚霞；这样，这位善良的女士就有了一个绝佳的机会来详细地谈论她的病情，用如此明显的乐趣描述每一次疼痛和脉搏，以至于玛丽拉认为即使是流行性感冒也必须带来它的补偿。当详细信息耗尽后，雷切尔夫人介绍了她打电话的真正原因。

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 6
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: “Spelled with an E,” gasped Anne, who, tremulous and excited as she was, was determined there should be no misunderstanding on that important point.

“I am well in body although considerable rumpled up in spirit, thank you ma’am,” said Anne gravely. Then aside to Marilla in an audible whisper, “There wasn’t anything startling in that, was there, Marilla?”

Diana was sitting on the sofa, reading a book which she dropped when the callers entered. She was a very pretty little girl, with her mother’s black eyes and hair, and rosy cheeks, and the merry expression which was her inheritance from her father.

“This is my little girl Diana,” said Mrs. Barry. “Diana, you might take Anne out into the garden and show her your flowers. It will be better for you than straining your eyes over that book. She reads entirely too much--” this to Marilla as the little girls went out--“and I can’t prevent her, for her father aids and abets her. She’s always poring over a book. I’m glad she has the prospect of a playmate--perhaps it will take her more out-of-doors.”

Outside in the garden, which was full of mellow sunset light streaming through the dark old firs to the west of it, stood Anne and Diana, gazing bashfully at each other over a clump of gorgeous tiger lilies.

The Barry garden was a bowery wilderness of flowers which would have delighted Anne’s heart at any time less fraught with destiny. It was encircled by huge old willows and tall firs, beneath which flourished flowers that loved the shade. Prim, right-angled paths neatly bordered with clamshells, intersected it like moist red ribbons and in the beds between old-fashioned flowers ran riot. There were rosy bleeding-hearts and great splendid crimson peonies; white, fragrant narcissi and thorny, sweet Scotch roses; pink and blue and white columbines and lilac-tinted Bouncing Bets; clumps of southernwood and ribbon grass and mint; purple Adam-and-Eve, daffodils, and masses of sweet clover white with its delicate, fragrant, feathery sprays; scarlet lightning that shot its fiery lances over prim white musk-flowers; a garden it was where sunshine lingered and bees hummed, and winds, beguiled into loitering, purred and rustled.

“Why, I guess so,” she said frankly. “I’m awfully glad you’ve come to live at Green Gables. It will be jolly to have somebody to play with. There isn’t any other girl who lives near enough to play with, and I’ve no sisters big enough.”

“We must join hands--so,” said Anne gravely. “It ought to be over running water. We’ll just imagine this path is running water. I’ll repeat the oath first. I solemnly swear to be faithful to my bosom friend, Diana Barry, as long as the sun and moon shall endure. Now you say it and put my name in.”
“You’re a queer girl, Anne. I heard before that you were queer. But I believe I’m going to like you real well.”

When Marilla and Anne went home Diana went with them as far as the log bridge. The two little girls walked with their arms about each other. At the brook they parted with many promises to spend the next afternoon together.
“Well, did you find Diana a kindred spirit?” asked Marilla as they went up through the garden of Green Gables.

“Oh yes,” sighed Anne, blissfully unconscious of any sarcasm on Marilla’s part. “Oh Marilla, I’m the happiest girl on Prince Edward Island this very moment. I assure you I’ll say my prayers with a right good-will tonight. Diana and I are going to build a playhouse in Mr. William Bell’s birch grove tomorrow. Can I have those broken pieces of china that are out in the woodshed? Diana’s birthday is in February and mine is in March. Don’t you think that is a very strange coincidence? Diana is going to lend me a book to read. She says it’s perfectly splendid and tremendously exciting. She’s going to show me a place back in the woods where rice lilies grow. Don’t you think Diana has got very soulful eyes? I wish I had soulful eyes. Diana is going to teach me to sing a song called ‘Nelly in the Hazel Dell.’ She’s going to give me a picture to put up in my room; it’s a perfectly beautiful picture, she says--a lovely lady in a pale blue silk dress. A sewing-machine agent gave it to her. I wish I had something to give Diana. I’m an inch taller than Diana, but she is ever so much fatter; she says she’d like to be thin because it’s so much more graceful, but I’m afraid she only said it to soothe my feelings. We’re going to the shore some day to gather shells. We have agreed to call the spring down by the log bridge the Dryad’s Bubble. Isn’t that a perfectly elegant name? I read a story once about a spring called that. A dryad is sort of a grown-up fairy, I think.”
paragraphsZh: “拼写为 E，”安妮气喘吁吁地说，尽管她颤抖而兴奋，但她决定在这一重要点上不应该有任何误解。
“我身体很好，虽然精神上有些不舒服，谢谢你，女士。”安妮严肃地说。然后用可听见的低语声对玛丽拉说道：“这并没有什么令人吃惊的，不是吗，玛丽拉？”
戴安娜坐在沙发上看一本书，当打电话的人进来时，她把书掉在了地上。她是一个非常漂亮的小女孩，有着她母亲的黑色眼睛和头发，红润的脸颊，还有她从父亲那里继承的快乐的表情。
“这是我的小女儿戴安娜，”巴里夫人说。 “戴安娜，你可以带安妮去花园，给她看你的花。这对你来说比盯着那本书更好。她读得太多了——”小女孩们出去时，这是对玛丽拉说的——“我无法阻止她，因为她父亲帮助和怂恿她。她总是埋头读书。我很高兴她有一个玩伴——也许这会让她更多地户外活动。”
外面的花园里，充满了柔和的夕阳光线，透过西边深色的老冷杉，安妮和戴安娜站在那里，在一丛华丽的虎百合面前羞涩地凝视着对方。

巴里花园是一片开满鲜花的包房荒野，只要不那么充满命运，安妮的心随时都会感到高兴。周围环绕着巨大的老柳树和高大的冷杉，树下开满了喜荫的花朵。整齐的直角小路整齐地镶着蛤壳，像潮湿的红丝带一样将其交叉，老式花朵之间的花坛里乱七八糟。这里有玫瑰色的血心花和绚丽的深红色牡丹。白色芬芳的水仙花和带刺的甜美苏格兰玫瑰；粉色、蓝色和白色的耧斗菜和淡紫色的弹跳赌注；丛生的南方木、带状草和薄荷；紫色的亚当和夏娃、水仙花和一大片白色的甜三叶草，上面有精致、芬芳、羽毛状的花朵；猩红色的闪电将其炽热的长矛射向古板的白麝香花；这是一座花园，阳光灿烂，蜜蜂嗡嗡作响，风儿在花园中徘徊，发出咕噜声和沙沙声。
“为什么，我想是这样，”她坦白地说。 “我非常高兴你能来绿山墙住。能有人和你一起玩真是太开心了。没有其他女孩住得足够近可以一起玩，而且我也没有足够大的姐妹。”
“我们必须携起手来——所以，”安妮严肃地说。 “应该是在流水之上。我们就想象这条路是流水吧。我先重复一下誓言。我郑重宣誓，日月长存，我将忠于我的知己戴安娜·巴里。现在你说吧，把我的名字写进去。”
“你是个酷儿女孩，安妮。我之前听说你是个酷儿。但我相信我会非常喜欢你。”
当玛丽拉和安妮回家时，戴安娜和他们一起走到了独木桥。两个小女孩互相搂着对方走路。在小溪边，他们告别时许下许多诺言，要一起度过第二天下午。
“那么，你觉得戴安娜志趣相投吗？”当他们穿过绿山墙花园时，玛丽拉问道。

“哦，是的，”安妮叹了口气，幸福地没有意识到玛丽拉的任何讽刺。 “哦，玛丽拉，此时此刻，我是爱德华王子岛最幸福的女孩。我向你保证，今晚我会怀着正确的善意进行祈祷。明天，戴安娜和我将在威廉·贝尔先生的白桦林里建造一座剧场。我可以把木棚里的那些碎瓷器拿走吗？戴安娜的生日是二月，我的生日是三月。你不觉得这是一个非常奇怪的巧合吗？戴安娜要借给我一个她说这本书非常精彩，非常令人兴奋。你不觉得戴安娜有一双充满深情的眼睛吗？我希望戴安娜会教我唱一首名叫《榛树山谷里的耐莉》的歌。她说，这是一幅非常美丽的画。一位缝纫机经纪人送给她的东西，我比戴安娜高一英寸，但她说她想要瘦一点，因为这样更优雅，但我担心她这么说只是为了安抚我的情绪。这是一个非常优雅的名字吗？我曾经读过一个关于春天的故事，我认为树妖是一个成年仙女。”

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 7
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: She did more than look. She sprang to her feet, her bright fancies fallen into cureless ruin. She flashed one indignant glance at Gilbert from eyes whose angry sparkle was swiftly quenched in equally angry tears.
And then--thwack! Anne had brought her slate down on Gilbert’s head and cracked it--slate not head--clear across.

Avonlea school always enjoyed a scene. This was an especially enjoyable one. Everybody said “Oh” in horrified delight. Diana gasped. Ruby Gillis, who was inclined to be hysterical, began to cry. Tommy Sloane let his team of crickets escape him altogether while he stared open-mouthed at the tableau.

“Anne Shirley, what does this mean?” he said angrily. Anne returned no answer. It was asking too much of flesh and blood to expect her to tell before the whole school that she had been called “carrots.” Gilbert it was who spoke up stoutly.

“I am sorry to see a pupil of mine displaying such a temper and such a vindictive spirit,” he said in a solemn tone, as if the mere fact of being a pupil of his ought to root out all evil passions from the hearts of small imperfect mortals. “Anne, go and stand on the platform in front of the blackboard for the rest of the afternoon.”

Anne would have infinitely preferred a whipping to this punishment under which her sensitive spirit quivered as from a whiplash. With a white, set face she obeyed. Mr. Phillips took a chalk crayon and wrote on the blackboard above her head.
“Ann Shirley has a very bad temper. Ann Shirley must learn to control her temper,” and then read it out loud so that even the primer class, who couldn’t read writing, should understand it.

Anne stood there the rest of the afternoon with that legend above her. She did not cry or hang her head. Anger was still too hot in her heart for that and it sustained her amid all her agony of humiliation. With resentful eyes and passion-red cheeks she confronted alike Diana’s sympathetic gaze and Charlie Sloane’s indignant nods and Josie Pye’s malicious smiles. As for Gilbert Blythe, she would not even look at him. She would never look at him again! She would never speak to him!!
When school was dismissed Anne marched out with her red head held high. Gilbert Blythe tried to intercept her at the porch door.
“I’m awfully sorry I made fun of your hair, Anne,” he whispered contritely. “Honest I am. Don’t be mad for keeps, now.”

Anne swept by disdainfully, without look or sign of hearing. “Oh how could you, Anne?” breathed Diana as they went down the road half reproachfully, half admiringly. Diana felt that she could never have resisted Gilbert’s plea.
“I shall never forgive Gilbert Blythe,” said Anne firmly. “And Mr. Phillips spelled my name without an e, too. The iron has entered into my soul, Diana.”

“You mustn’t mind Gilbert making fun of your hair,” she said soothingly. “Why, he makes fun of all the girls. He laughs at mine because it’s so black. He’s called me a crow a dozen times; and I never heard him apologize for anything before, either.”
“There’s a great deal of difference between being called a crow and being called carrots,” said Anne with dignity. “Gilbert Blythe has hurt my feelings excruciatingly, Diana.”
It is possible the matter might have blown over without more excruciation if nothing else had happened. But when things begin to happen they are apt to keep on.

Avonlea scholars often spent noon hour picking gum in Mr. Bell’s spruce grove over the hill and across his big pasture field. From there they could keep an eye on Eben Wright’s house, where the master boarded. When they saw Mr. Phillips emerging therefrom they ran for the schoolhouse; but the distance being about three times longer than Mr. Wright’s lane they were very apt to arrive there, breathless and gasping, some three minutes too late.
paragraphsZh: 她所做的不仅仅是看起来。她猛地站了起来，她的美好幻想陷入了无可救药的毁灭之中。她愤怒地看了吉尔伯特一眼，那双眼睛里愤怒的光芒很快就被同样愤怒的泪水浇灭了。
然后——猛击！安妮把她的石板放在吉尔伯特的头上，把它——石板而不是头部——完全打碎了。
Avonlea 学校总是风景如画。这是一件特别令人愉快的事。大家都惊恐万分地“哦”了一声。戴安娜喘着气。鲁比·吉利斯快要歇斯底里了，她哭了起来。汤米·斯隆目瞪口呆地看着这一幕，让他的蟋蟀队完全逃离了他的视线。
“安妮·雪莉，这是什么意思？”他愤怒地说。安妮没有回答。指望她在全校面前告诉大家她被称为“胡萝卜”，这对有血有肉的人要求太高了。大声说道的正是吉尔伯特。
“我很遗憾看到我的一个学生表现出这样的脾气和这样的斗气，”他语气严肃地说，仿佛仅仅作为他的学生这一事实就应该根除不完美的小凡人心中的所有邪恶激情。 “安妮，下午剩下的时间，你就站在黑板前的讲台上吧。”
安妮宁愿接受鞭打，也不愿接受这种惩罚，因为在这种惩罚下，她敏感的灵魂会像受到鞭打一样颤抖。她脸色苍白，表情坚定，服从了。菲利普斯先生拿起一支粉笔，在她头顶的黑板上写下了一些字。
“安·雪莉的脾气很坏。安·雪莉必须学会控制自己的脾气”，然后大声朗读出来，这样即使是不会读写的初级班也能理解。
整个下午，安妮都站在那儿，那个传奇就在她的上方。她没有哭，也没有低下头。她心中的愤怒仍然太强烈，无法承受这种痛苦，这让她在羞辱的痛苦中支撑着她。她用怨恨的眼神和热情的红色脸颊面对着戴安娜同情的目光、查理·斯隆愤怒的点头和乔西·派伊恶意的微笑。至于吉尔伯特·布莱斯，她连看都不看他一眼。她再也不会看他一眼！她绝对不会跟他说话！！
学校放学时，安妮高举着红头走出去。吉尔伯特·布莱斯试图在门廊门口拦截她。
“我非常抱歉我取笑了你的头发，安妮，”他悔恨地低声说道。 “我是诚实的。现在别再生气了。”
安妮轻蔑地掠过，看也不看，也听不见。 “噢，安妮，你怎么能这样？”当他们走在路上时，戴安娜半是责备半是钦佩地喘着气。戴安娜觉得她永远无法抗拒吉尔伯特的恳求。
“我永远不会原谅吉尔伯特·布莱斯，”安妮坚定地说。 “菲利普斯先生也把我的名字拼写成没有e。戴安娜，铁已经进入了我的灵魂。”
“你一定不要介意吉尔伯特取笑你的头发，”她安慰道。 “为什么，他取笑所有的女孩。他嘲笑我的女孩，因为它太黑了。他已经多次称我为乌鸦；而且我以前也从未听他为任何事情道歉过。”
“被称为乌鸦和被称为胡萝卜之间有很大的区别。”安妮尊严地说。 “吉尔伯特·布莱斯极大地伤害了我的感情，戴安娜。”
如果没有发生其他事情，这件事可能会结束，而不会造成更多痛苦。但当事情开始发生时，它们很容易继续下去。
埃文利的学者们经常在中午的时间里在贝尔先生的云杉林里采摘口香糖，林子位于山上，穿过他的大牧场。从那里他们可以监视埃本赖特的房子，主人就在那里登船。当他们看到菲利普斯先生从里面出来时，他们就跑向校舍。但这段距离大约比赖特先生的车道长三倍，他们很可能气喘吁吁地到达那里，大约晚了三分钟。

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 8
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: “Fiddlesticks! There is no such thing as a haunted wood anywhere. Who has been telling you such stuff?”

“Nobody,” confessed Anne. “Diana and I just imagined the wood was haunted. All the places around here are so--so--commonplace. We just got this up for our own amusement. We began it in April. A haunted wood is so very romantic, Marilla. We chose the spruce grove because it’s so gloomy. Oh, we have imagined the most harrowing things. There’s a white lady walks along the brook just about this time of the night and wrings her hands and utters wailing cries. She appears when there is to be a death in the family. And the ghost of a little murdered child haunts the corner up by Idlewild; it creeps up behind you and lays its cold fingers on your hand--so. Oh, Marilla, it gives me a shudder to think of it. And there’s a headless man stalks up and down the path and skeletons glower at you between the boughs. Oh, Marilla, I wouldn’t go through the Haunted Wood after dark now for anything. I’d be sure that white things would reach out from behind the trees and grab me.”
“Did ever anyone hear the like!” ejaculated Marilla, who had listened in dumb amazement. “Anne Shirley, do you mean to tell me you believe all that wicked nonsense of your own imagination?”
“Not believe exactly,” faltered Anne. “At least, I don’t believe it in daylight. But after dark, Marilla, it’s different. That is when ghosts walk.”

“Oh, but there are, Marilla,” cried Anne eagerly. “I know people who have seen them. And they are respectable people. Charlie Sloane says that his grandmother saw his grandfather driving home the cows one night after he’d been buried for a year. You know Charlie Sloane’s grandmother wouldn’t tell a story for anything. She’s a very religious woman. And Mrs. Thomas’s father was pursued home one night by a lamb of fire with its head cut off hanging by a strip of skin. He said he knew it was the spirit of his brother and that it was a warning he would die within nine days. He didn’t, but he died two years after, so you see it was really true. And Ruby Gillis says--”

“Anne Shirley,” interrupted Marilla firmly, “I never want to hear you talking in this fashion again. I’ve had my doubts about that imagination of yours right along, and if this is going to be the outcome of it, I won’t countenance any such doings. You’ll go right over to Barry’s, and you’ll go through that spruce grove, just for a lesson and a warning to you. And never let me hear a word out of your head about haunted woods again.”

Anne might plead and cry as she liked--and did, for her terror was very real. Her imagination had run away with her and she held the spruce grove in mortal dread after nightfall. But Marilla was inexorable. She marched the shrinking ghost-seer down to the spring and ordered her to proceed straightway over the bridge and into the dusky retreats of wailing ladies and headless specters beyond.
“Oh, Marilla, how can you be so cruel?” sobbed Anne. “What would you feel like if a white thing did snatch me up and carry me off?”
“I’ll risk it,” said Marilla unfeelingly. “You know I always mean what I say. I’ll cure you of imagining ghosts into places. March, now.”

Anne marched. That is, she stumbled over the bridge and went shuddering up the horrible dim path beyond. Anne never forgot that walk. Bitterly did she repent the license she had given to her imagination. The goblins of her fancy lurked in every shadow about her, reaching out their cold, fleshless hands to grasp the terrified small girl who had called them into being. A white strip of birch bark blowing up from the hollow over the brown floor of the grove made her heart stand still. The long-drawn wail of two old boughs rubbing against each other brought out the perspiration in beads on her forehead. The swoop of bats in the darkness over her was as the wings of unearthly creatures. When she reached Mr. William Bell’s field she fled across it as if pursued by an army of white things, and arrived at the Barry kitchen door so out of breath that she could hardly gasp out her request for the apron pattern. Diana was away so that she had no excuse to linger. The dreadful return journey had to be faced. Anne went back over it with shut eyes, preferring to take the risk of dashing her brains out among the boughs to that of seeing a white thing. When she finally stumbled over the log bridge she drew one long shivering breath of relief.
paragraphsZh: “胡说八道！世界上根本不存在闹鬼的树林。谁告诉你这些事情的？”

“没有人，”安妮承认。 “黛安娜和我只是想象这片树林闹鬼。这里周围的所有地方都那么——那么——平常。我们只是为了自己的娱乐而做这个。我们从四月开始。闹鬼的树林非常浪漫，玛丽拉。我们选择云杉林，因为它太阴暗了。哦，我们想象了最痛苦的事情。就在晚上的这个时候，有一位白人女士沿着小溪散步，扭着双手当家里有人要死的时候，她就会出现，一个被谋杀的小孩子的鬼魂会爬到你身后，把冰冷的手指放在你的手上——哦，玛丽拉，一想到这个，我就感到不寒而栗，还有一个骷髅在树枝间怒视着你。天黑后我不会再去鬼林了，我确信白色的东西会从树后伸出来抓住我。”
“有没有人听过类似的话！”玛丽拉惊呼道，她听得目瞪口呆。 “安妮·雪莉，你的意思是告诉我你相信你自己想象的那些邪恶的废话吗？”
“不太相信，”安妮结结巴巴地说。 “至少，白天我不相信。但天黑后，玛丽拉，情况就不一样了。那时鬼魂就会出来。”

“哦，但是有，玛丽拉，”安妮急切地喊道。 “我认识一些见过它们的人。他们都是受人尊敬的人。查理·斯隆说，他的祖母在他被埋葬一年后，有一天晚上看到他的祖父赶着牛回家。你知道查理·斯隆的祖母不会讲任何故事。她是一个非常虔诚的女人。托马斯夫人的父亲有一天晚上被一只火焰羔羊追赶回家，它的头被一条皮割下来。他说他知道那是他哥哥的灵魂，那是一个警告他会在九天内死去，但他没有，但两年后他就去世了，所以你看，鲁比·吉利斯说的是真的——”
“安妮·雪莉，”玛丽拉坚定地打断道，“我再也不想听到你用这种方式说话了。我一直对你的想象力表示怀疑，如果结果是这样，我不会支持任何这样的行为。你会直接去巴里家，你会穿过那片云杉林，只是为了给你一个教训和警告。永远不要让我听到任何声音。”你的脑子里又出现了关于闹鬼森林的消息。”
安妮可以随心所欲地恳求和哭泣——她确实这么做了，因为她的恐惧是非常真实的。她的想象力已经消失，夜幕降临后，她对云杉林抱有致命的恐惧。但玛丽拉却毫不留情。她把这个畏缩的幽灵先知带到了泉水边，命令她直接过桥，进入远处哭泣的女士和无头幽灵的昏暗隐居处。
“哦，玛丽拉，你怎么可以这么残忍？”安妮抽泣着。 “如果有一个白色的东西把我抓起来并带走，你会有什么感觉？”
“我愿意冒险，”玛丽拉无情地说。 “你知道我总是说到做到。我会治愈你想象鬼魂到某个地方的毛病。三月，现在。”

安妮游行。也就是说，她跌跌撞撞地跨过桥，颤抖着沿着远处可怕的昏暗小路走去。安妮永远不会忘记那次散步。她痛苦地后悔自己放纵了自己的想象力。她想象中的妖精潜伏在她周围的每一个阴影中，伸出冰冷、没有肉的手去抓住那个召唤它们的恐惧的小女孩。一条白色的白桦树皮从树林棕色地面上的空洞中吹起，让她的心停止了跳动。两根老树枝相互摩擦发出的长长的哀嚎声，衬托出了她额头上的汗珠。黑暗中，蝙蝠在她上方俯冲，就像超凡脱俗的生物的翅膀。当她到达威廉·贝尔先生的田地时，她像被一群白色的东西追赶一样穿过田地，到达巴里厨房门口时，气喘吁吁，几乎无法说出要围裙图案的要求。戴安娜不在，所以她没有借口逗留。必须面对可怕的回程。安妮闭上眼睛重新审视它，宁愿冒把脑袋撞到树枝上的风险，也不愿看到一个白色的东西。当她终于跌跌撞撞地走上独木桥时，她颤抖着长长地松了一口气。

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 9
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: For a moment Anne hesitated. She had an odd, newly awakened consciousness under all her outraged dignity that the half-shy, half-eager expression in Gilbert’s hazel eyes was something that was very good to see. Her heart gave a quick, queer little beat. But the bitterness of her old grievance promptly stiffened up her wavering determination. That scene of two years before flashed back into her recollection as vividly as if it had taken place yesterday. Gilbert had called her “carrots” and had brought about her disgrace before the whole school. Her resentment, which to other and older people might be as laughable as its cause, was in no whit allayed and softened by time seemingly. She hated Gilbert Blythe! She would never forgive him!
“All right!” Gilbert sprang into his skiff with an angry color in his cheeks. “I’ll never ask you to be friends again, Anne Shirley. And I don’t care either!”

He pulled away with swift defiant strokes, and Anne went up the steep, ferny little path under the maples. She held her head very high, but she was conscious of an odd feeling of regret. She almost wished she had answered Gilbert differently. Of course, he had insulted her terribly, but still--! Altogether, Anne rather thought it would be a relief to sit down and have a good cry. She was really quite unstrung, for the reaction from her fright and cramped clinging was making itself felt.

Halfway up the path she met Jane and Diana rushing back to the pond in a state narrowly removed from positive frenzy. They had found nobody at Orchard Slope, both Mr. and Mrs. Barry being away. Here Ruby Gillis had succumbed to hysterics, and was left to recover from them as best she might, while Jane and Diana flew through the Haunted Wood and across the brook to Green Gables. There they had found nobody either, for Marilla had gone to Carmody and Matthew was making hay in the back field.

“Oh, Anne,” gasped Diana, fairly falling on the former’s neck and weeping with relief and delight, “oh, Anne--we thought--you were--drowned--and we felt like murderers--because we had made--you be--Elaine. And Ruby is in hysterics--oh, Anne, how did you escape?”
“I climbed up on one of the piles,” explained Anne wearily, “and Gilbert Blythe came along in Mr. Andrews’s dory and brought me to land.”
“Oh, Anne, how splendid of him! Why, it’s so romantic!” said Jane, finding breath enough for utterance at last. “Of course you’ll speak to him after this.”

“Of course I won’t,” flashed Anne, with a momentary return of her old spirit. “And I don’t want ever to hear the word ‘romantic’ again, Jane Andrews. I’m awfully sorry you were so frightened, girls. It is all my fault. I feel sure I was born under an unlucky star. Everything I do gets me or my dearest friends into a scrape. We’ve gone and lost your father’s flat, Diana, and I have a presentiment that we’ll not be allowed to row on the pond any more.”
Anne’s presentiment proved more trustworthy than presentiments are apt to do. Great was the consternation in the Barry and Cuthbert households when the events of the afternoon became known.

“Oh, yes, I think I will, Marilla,” returned Anne optimistically. A good cry, indulged in the grateful solitude of the east gable, had soothed her nerves and restored her to her wonted cheerfulness. “I think my prospects of becoming sensible are brighter now than ever.”

“Well,” explained Anne, “I’ve learned a new and valuable lesson today. Ever since I came to Green Gables I’ve been making mistakes, and each mistake has helped to cure me of some great shortcoming. The affair of the amethyst brooch cured me of meddling with things that didn’t belong to me. The Haunted Wood mistake cured me of letting my imagination run away with me. The liniment cake mistake cured me of carelessness in cooking. Dyeing my hair cured me of vanity. I never think about my hair and nose now--at least, very seldom. And today’s mistake is going to cure me of being too romantic. I have come to the conclusion that it is no use trying to be romantic in Avonlea. It was probably easy enough in towered Camelot hundreds of years ago, but romance is not appreciated now. I feel quite sure that you will soon see a great improvement in me in this respect, Marilla.”
paragraphsZh: 安妮犹豫了一会儿。在她那愤怒的尊严之下，她有一种奇怪的、新近觉醒的意识：吉尔伯特淡褐色眼睛里一半害羞、一半渴望的表情是非常好看的。她的心快速而奇怪地跳动着。但旧日积怨的苦涩很快就坚定了她动摇的决心。两年前的那一幕，历历在目，仿佛就发生在昨天。吉尔伯特称她为“胡萝卜”，让她在全校面前蒙羞。对于其他人和年长的人来说，她的怨恨可能与其起因一样可笑，但时间似乎丝毫没有减轻和软化。她恨吉尔伯特·布莱斯！她永远不会原谅他！
“好吧！”吉尔伯特跳上小船，脸颊上浮现出愤怒之色。 “我永远不会再要求你成为朋友了，安妮·雪莉。我也不在乎！”
他迅速而挑衅地离开，安妮走上枫树下那条陡峭、长满蕨类植物的小路。她把头昂得很高，但心里却有一种奇怪的遗憾。她几乎希望自己当时能以不同的方式回答吉尔伯特。当然，他已经严重侮辱了她，但是——！总而言之，安妮觉得坐下来好好哭一场会是一种解脱。她真的很紧张，因为她的恐惧和局促的依恋所带来的反应是显而易见的。
在半路上，她遇到了简和戴安娜，他们正冲回池塘，他们的状态几乎脱离了积极的疯狂。他们在果园坡没有发现任何人，巴里先生和夫人都不在。在这里，鲁比·吉利斯陷入了歇斯底里，只能尽其所能地恢复过来，而简和戴安娜则飞过鬼林，穿过小溪，到达绿山墙。在那里他们也没有发现任何人，因为玛丽拉已经去了卡莫迪，而马修正在后田里晒干草。
“哦，安妮，”黛安娜气喘吁吁地倒在前者的脖子上，欣喜若狂地哭泣，“哦，安妮——我们以为——你被——淹死了——我们感觉自己像杀人犯——因为我们让——你成为了——伊莱恩。而鲁比则歇斯底里——哦，安妮，你是怎么逃出来的？”
“我爬上了其中一个桩，”安妮疲倦地解释道，“吉尔伯特·布莱斯开着安德鲁斯先生的平底船过来，把我带到了陆地上。”
“哦，安妮，他真是太棒了！哎呀，太浪漫了！”简终于喘口气了，终于可以说话了。 “当然，这之后你会和他说话的。”
“我当然不会，”安妮闪现，她的精神瞬间恢复了。 “我不想再听到‘浪漫’这个词了，简·安德鲁斯。我很抱歉你们这么害怕，女孩们。这都是我的错。我确信我出生在一个不幸的星象下。我所做的一切都让我或我最亲爱的朋友陷入困境。我们已经走了，失去了你父亲的公寓，戴安娜，我有一种预感，我们将不再被允许在池塘上划船。”
事实证明，安妮的预感比一般预感更值得信赖。当下午发生的事情被知道后，巴里和卡斯伯特一家非常惊愕。
“哦，是的，我想我会的，玛丽拉，”安妮乐观地回答。沉浸在东山墙令人感激的孤独中，痛哭一场，舒缓了她的神经，让她恢复了往日的快乐。 “我认为我变得明智的前景比以往任何时候都更加光明。”

“好吧，”安妮解释道，“今天我学到了新的、宝贵的一课。自从我来到绿山墙以来，我一直在犯错误，而每一个错误都帮助我弥补了一些重大缺点。紫水晶胸针的事件治愈了我对不属于我的东西的干涉。鬼林的错误治愈了我让我的想象力随心所欲。搽剂蛋糕的错误治愈了我烹饪时的粗心大意。染色我的头发治愈了我的虚荣心——至少，很少，今天的错误会治愈我的过于浪漫，我得出的结论是，在数百年前的埃文利，浪漫可能很容易，但我确信你很快就会看到我在这方面有了很大的进步。

title: Anne of Green Gables · 选段 10
author: L. M. Montgomery
paragraphs: Anne, by dint of talking over her shoulder to the girls and occasionally passing a sop of civility to Billy--who grinned and chuckled and never could think of any reply until it was too late--contrived to enjoy the drive in spite of all. It was a night for enjoyment. The road was full of buggies, all bound for the hotel, and laughter, silver clear, echoed and reechoed along it. When they reached the hotel it was a blaze of light from top to bottom. They were met by the ladies of the concert committee, one of whom took Anne off to the performers’ dressing room which was filled with the members of a Charlottetown Symphony Club, among whom Anne felt suddenly shy and frightened and countrified. Her dress, which, in the east gable, had seemed so dainty and pretty, now seemed simple and plain--too simple and plain, she thought, among all the silks and laces that glistened and rustled around her. What were her pearl beads compared to the diamonds of the big, handsome lady near her? And how poor her one wee white rose must look beside all the hothouse flowers the others wore! Anne laid her hat and jacket away, and shrank miserably into a corner. She wished herself back in the white room at Green Gables.

It was still worse on the platform of the big concert hall of the hotel, where she presently found herself. The electric lights dazzled her eyes, the perfume and hum bewildered her. She wished she were sitting down in the audience with Diana and Jane, who seemed to be having a splendid time away at the back. She was wedged in between a stout lady in pink silk and a tall, scornful-looking girl in a white-lace dress. The stout lady occasionally turned her head squarely around and surveyed Anne through her eyeglasses until Anne, acutely sensitive of being so scrutinized, felt that she must scream aloud; and the white-lace girl kept talking audibly to her next neighbor about the “country bumpkins” and “rustic belles” in the audience, languidly anticipating “such fun” from the displays of local talent on the program. Anne believed that she would hate that white-lace girl to the end of life.

Unfortunately for Anne, a professional elocutionist was staying at the hotel and had consented to recite. She was a lithe, dark-eyed woman in a wonderful gown of shimmering gray stuff like woven moonbeams, with gems on her neck and in her dark hair. She had a marvelously flexible voice and wonderful power of expression; the audience went wild over her selection. Anne, forgetting all about herself and her troubles for the time, listened with rapt and shining eyes; but when the recitation ended she suddenly put her hands over her face. She could never get up and recite after that--never. Had she ever thought she could recite? Oh, if she were only back at Green Gables!

At this unpropitious moment her name was called. Somehow Anne--who did not notice the rather guilty little start of surprise the white-lace girl gave, and would not have understood the subtle compliment implied therein if she had--got on her feet, and moved dizzily out to the front. She was so pale that Diana and Jane, down in the audience, clasped each other’s hands in nervous sympathy.

Anne was the victim of an overwhelming attack of stage fright. Often as she had recited in public, she had never before faced such an audience as this, and the sight of it paralyzed her energies completely. Everything was so strange, so brilliant, so bewildering--the rows of ladies in evening dress, the critical faces, the whole atmosphere of wealth and culture about her. Very different this from the plain benches at the Debating Club, filled with the homely, sympathetic faces of friends and neighbors. These people, she thought, would be merciless critics. Perhaps, like the white-lace girl, they anticipated amusement from her “rustic” efforts. She felt hopelessly, helplessly ashamed and miserable. Her knees trembled, her heart fluttered, a horrible faintness came over her; not a word could she utter, and the next moment she would have fled from the platform despite the humiliation which, she felt, must ever after be her portion if she did so.
paragraphsZh: 安妮通过她的肩膀与女孩们交谈，并偶尔向比利表示礼貌——比利咧着嘴笑，直到为时已晚才想出任何答复——尽管如此，安妮仍设法享受开车的乐趣。这是一个享受的夜晚。路上满是马车，全都是开往旅馆的，清脆的笑声在路上回荡。当他们到达酒店时，从上到下都是一片灯光。他们遇到了音乐会委员会的女士们，其中一位带安妮去了表演者更衣室，里面挤满了夏洛特敦交响乐俱乐部的成员，安妮突然感到害羞、害怕和乡土气息。她的衣服，在东山墙，看起来是那么精致和漂亮，现在显得简单和朴素——她想，在她周围闪闪发光、沙沙作响的丝绸和花边中，太简单和朴素了。与她身边那个大而英俊的​​女士的钻石相比，她的珍珠珠算什么？与其他人所戴的所有温室花朵相比，她那一朵小小的白玫瑰显得多么可怜啊！安妮把帽子和夹克收起来，痛苦地缩到了角落里。她希望自己能回到绿山墙的白色房间里。

在酒店大音乐厅的平台上，她现在发现自己在那里，情况更糟。电灯使她眼花缭乱，香水味和嗡嗡声让她困惑。她希望自己能和戴安娜和简一起坐在观众席上，他们似乎在后面度过了一段美好的时光。她夹在一位穿着粉红色丝绸的胖女人和一位穿着白色蕾丝连衣裙、身材高大、神情轻蔑的女孩中间。这位矮胖的女士偶尔会转过头来，透过眼镜打量着安妮，直到安妮对被如此审视的目光极为敏感，觉得自己必须大声尖叫；白蕾丝女孩不停地向旁边的邻居大声谈论着台下的“土包子”和“土气美女”，慵懒地期待着节目中本地才艺的展示“真有趣”。安妮相信，她会对那个白蕾丝女孩恨之入骨。

对于安妮来说不幸的是，一位专业的演讲家住在酒店并同意朗诵。她是一位身体轻盈、黑眼睛的女人，穿着一件精美的长袍，长袍是用闪闪发光的灰色材料制成的，就像编织的月光一样，脖子上和黑发上都戴着宝石。她有着极其灵活的声音和出色的表达能力。观众对她的选择感到疯狂。安妮暂时忘记了自己和烦恼，全神贯注地听着，眼睛闪闪发亮。但当朗诵结束时，她突然用手捂住了脸。从那以后她再也不能站起来背诵了——永远不能。她有没有想过自己会背诵？哦，如果她回到绿山墙就好了！
在这个不吉利的时刻，她的名字被叫到了。不知怎的，安妮——她没有注意到那个白色蕾丝女孩表现出的相当内疚的惊讶，如果她注意到的话，她也不会理解其中暗示的微妙的恭维——站起来，头晕地走到前面。她脸色苍白，观众席上的戴安娜和简紧张地同情地紧握彼此的双手。

安妮是严重怯场的受害者。正如她经常在公开场合朗诵的那样，她以前从未面对过这样的观众，这一景象让她的精力完全瘫痪了。一切都是那么奇怪，那么辉煌，那么令人困惑——一排排穿着晚礼服的女士，挑剔的面孔，她周围的整个财富和文化氛围。这与辩论俱乐部朴素的长凳截然不同，那里摆满了朋友和邻居的朴素而富有同情心的面孔。她认为这些人会是无情的批评者。也许，就像那个白色蕾丝女孩一样，他们期待着她“质朴”的努力带来的乐趣。她感到无助、无助、羞愧和痛苦。她的双膝在颤抖，她的心在狂跳，一种可怕的虚弱感笼罩着她。她一句话也说不出来，下一刻她就会从站台上逃走，尽管她觉得如果她这样做的话，她将永远受到羞辱。

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz · 选段 2
author: L. Frank Baum
paragraphs: Folklore, legends, myths and fairy tales have followed childhood through the ages, for every healthy youngster has a wholesome and instinctive love for stories fantastic, marvelous and manifestly unreal. The winged fairies of Grimm and Andersen have brought more happiness to childish hearts than all other human creations.

Yet the old time fairy tale, having served for generations, may now be classed as “historical” in the children’s library; for the time has come for a series of newer “wonder tales” in which the stereotyped genie, dwarf and fairy are eliminated, together with all the horrible and blood-curdling incidents devised by their authors to point a fearsome moral to each tale. Modern education includes morality; therefore the modern child seeks only entertainment in its wonder tales and gladly dispenses with all disagreeable incident.

Having this thought in mind, the story of “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz” was written solely to please children of today. It aspires to being a modernized fairy tale, in which the wonderment and joy are retained and the heartaches and nightmares are left out.

Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer’s wife. Their house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one room; and this room contained a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in another corner. There was no garret at all, and no cellar—except a small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose, mighty enough to crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap door in the middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark hole.

When Dorothy stood in the doorway and looked around, she could see nothing but the great gray prairie on every side. Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country that reached to the edge of the sky in all directions. The sun had baked the plowed land into a gray mass, with little cracks running through it. Even the grass was not green, for the sun had burned the tops of the long blades until they were the same gray color to be seen everywhere. Once the house had been painted, but the sun blistered the paint and the rains washed it away, and now the house was as dull and gray as everything else.

When Aunt Em came there to live she was a young, pretty wife. The sun and wind had changed her, too. They had taken the sparkle from her eyes and left them a sober gray; they had taken the red from her cheeks and lips, and they were gray also. She was thin and gaunt, and never smiled now. When Dorothy, who was an orphan, first came to her, Aunt Em had been so startled by the child’s laughter that she would scream and press her hand upon her heart whenever Dorothy’s merry voice reached her ears; and she still looked at the little girl with wonder that she could find anything to laugh at.

Uncle Henry never laughed. He worked hard from morning till night and did not know what joy was. He was gray also, from his long beard to his rough boots, and he looked stern and solemn, and rarely spoke.
paragraphsZh: 民间传说、传说、神话和童话故事一直伴随着童年，每个健康的年轻人都对奇幻、奇妙和明显不真实的故事有着健康和本能的热爱。格林和安徒生的带翅膀的仙女比所有其他人类创造物给孩子们的心灵带来更多的快乐。
然而，古老的童话故事，已经服务了几代人，现在可能在儿童图书馆中被归类为“历史童话”；现在是时候推出一系列更新的“奇幻故事”了，其中消除了刻板印象的精灵、侏儒和仙女，以及作者设计的所有可怕和令人毛骨悚然的事件，为每个故事指明了可怕的寓意。现代教育包括道德；因此，现代儿童只在奇幻故事中寻求娱乐，并乐意避开所有不愉快的事件。
考虑到这一点，《绿野仙踪》的故事只是为了取悦今天的孩子而写的。它渴望成为一个现代化的童话故事，其中保留了惊奇和欢乐，而省略了心痛和噩梦。

多萝西和亨利叔叔（农民）和埃姆婶婶（农民的妻子）住在堪萨斯大草原的中央。他们的房子很小，建造房子的木材必须用马车运来好几英里。有四堵墙、一层地板和一个屋顶，组成了一个房间。这个房间里有一个看起来生锈的炉灶、一个碗柜、一张桌子、三四把椅子和床。亨利叔叔和埃姆婶婶在一个角落里有一张大床，多萝西在另一个角落里有一张小床。根本没有阁楼，也没有地窖——除了在地上挖的一个小洞，称为旋风地窖，一家人可以去那里，以防大旋风刮起，其威力足以摧毁沿途的任何建筑物。地板中间有一扇活板门，从那里有一架梯子通向那个又小又黑的洞。
当多萝西站在门口环顾四周时，除了四面都是灰色的大草原，她什么也看不见。没有一棵树或一栋房子能打破这片广阔的平原，四面八方都延伸到天空的边缘。太阳把耕过的土地烤成了一片灰色，上面布满了细小的裂缝。就连草也不是绿色的，因为太阳已经把长长的叶片顶端烤得灰蒙蒙的，随处可见。房子曾经粉刷过，但阳光使油漆起泡，雨水将其冲走，现在房子和其他一切一样暗淡和灰色。
当艾姆阿姨来这里住的时候，她是一位年轻漂亮的妻子。阳光和风也改变了她。他们夺去了她眼睛里的光芒，让她的眼睛变成了严肃的灰色。他们去掉了她脸颊和嘴唇上的红色，也变成了灰色。她又瘦又憔悴，现在再也没有笑容了。当孤儿多萝西第一次来到她身边时，埃姆婶婶被孩子的笑声吓了一跳，每当多萝西快乐的声音传到她耳边时，她就会尖叫，并用手捂住心口。她仍然惊奇地看着小女孩，她能找到什么可笑的东西。
亨利叔叔从来不笑。他从早忙到晚，不知道什么是快乐。从长长的胡须到粗糙的靴子，他也是灰色的，看上去严肃而严肃，很少说话。

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz · 选段 3
author: L. Frank Baum
paragraphs: Dorothy leaned her chin upon her hand and gazed thoughtfully at the Scarecrow. Its head was a small sack stuffed with straw, with eyes, nose, and mouth painted on it to represent a face. An old, pointed blue hat, that had belonged to some Munchkin, was perched on his head, and the rest of the figure was a blue suit of clothes, worn and faded, which had also been stuffed with straw. On the feet were some old boots with blue tops, such as every man wore in this country, and the figure was raised above the stalks of corn by means of the pole stuck up its back.

While Dorothy was looking earnestly into the queer, painted face of the Scarecrow, she was surprised to see one of the eyes slowly wink at her. She thought she must have been mistaken at first, for none of the scarecrows in Kansas ever wink; but presently the figure nodded its head to her in a friendly way. Then she climbed down from the fence and walked up to it, while Toto ran around the pole and barked.
“No, for this pole is stuck up my back. If you will please take away the pole I shall be greatly obliged to you.”
Dorothy reached up both arms and lifted the figure off the pole, for, being stuffed with straw, it was quite light.
“Thank you very much,” said the Scarecrow, when he had been set down on the ground. “I feel like a new man.”
Dorothy was puzzled at this, for it sounded queer to hear a stuffed man speak, and to see him bow and walk along beside her.
“Who are you?” asked the Scarecrow when he had stretched himself and yawned. “And where are you going?”
“No, indeed. I don’t know anything. You see, I am stuffed, so I have no brains at all,” he answered sadly.
“I cannot tell,” she returned, “but you may come with me, if you like. If Oz will not give you any brains you will be no worse off than you are now.”

“That is true,” said the Scarecrow. “You see,” he continued confidentially, “I don’t mind my legs and arms and body being stuffed, because I cannot get hurt. If anyone treads on my toes or sticks a pin into me, it doesn’t matter, for I can’t feel it. But I do not want people to call me a fool, and if my head stays stuffed with straw instead of with brains, as yours is, how am I ever to know anything?”
“I understand how you feel,” said the little girl, who was truly sorry for him. “If you will come with me I’ll ask Oz to do all he can for you.”
They walked back to the road. Dorothy helped him over the fence, and they started along the path of yellow brick for the Emerald City.

Toto did not like this addition to the party at first. He smelled around the stuffed man as if he suspected there might be a nest of rats in the straw, and he often growled in an unfriendly way at the Scarecrow.

“Oh, I’m not afraid,” replied the Scarecrow. “He can’t hurt the straw. Do let me carry that basket for you. I shall not mind it, for I can’t get tired. I’ll tell you a secret,” he continued, as he walked along. “There is only one thing in the world I am afraid of.”

After a few hours the road began to be rough, and the walking grew so difficult that the Scarecrow often stumbled over the yellow bricks, which were here very uneven. Sometimes, indeed, they were broken or missing altogether, leaving holes that Toto jumped across and Dorothy walked around. As for the Scarecrow, having no brains, he walked straight ahead, and so stepped into the holes and fell at full length on the hard bricks. It never hurt him, however, and Dorothy would pick him up and set him upon his feet again, while he joined her in laughing merrily at his own mishap.
paragraphsZh: 多萝西用手托着下巴，若有所思地凝视着稻草人。它的头是一个塞满稻草的小麻袋，上面画着眼睛、鼻子和嘴巴，代表着一张脸。他的头上戴着一顶旧的尖顶蓝色帽子，那是某个芒奇金人的东西，而人物的其余部分是一套蓝色的衣服，破旧褪色，里面也塞满了稻草。脚上穿着一双蓝色鞋头的旧靴子，就像这个国家每个男人都穿的那样，这个人物通过背上竖起的杆子被举在玉米秆上方。
当多萝西认真地看着稻草人那张奇怪的、彩绘的脸时，她惊讶地发现其中一只眼睛慢慢地向她眨眼。她以为自己一开始一定是弄错了，因为堪萨斯州的稻草人从来不眨眼。但很快那个人影友好地向她点了点头。然后她从栅栏上爬下来，朝栅栏走去，而托托则绕着栅栏跑去并吠叫。
“不，因为这根杆子插在我的背上。如果你愿意，请把杆子拿走，我将非常感激你。”
多萝西伸出双臂，将人物从柱子上抬起，因为里面塞满了稻草，所以很轻。
“非常感谢，”稻草人被放在地上后说道。 “我感觉自己像个新人了。”
多萝西对此感到困惑，因为听到一个毛绒玩具人说话，看到他鞠躬并走在她身边，听起来很奇怪。
“你是谁？”稻草人伸了个懒腰，打了个哈欠，问道。 “那你要去哪里？”
“不，确实。我什么都不知道。你看，我吃饱了，所以我根本没有大脑，”他悲伤地回答。
“我不知道，”她回答道，“但如果你愿意的话，你可以跟我一起去。如果奥兹不给你任何大脑，你的处境不会比现在更糟。”
“确实如此，”稻草人说。 “你看，”他继续保密地说，“我不介意我的腿、手臂和身体被塞满，因为我不会受伤。如果有人踩到我的脚趾或用针扎我，那没关系，因为我感觉不到。但我不想让人们称我为傻瓜，如果我的头塞满了稻草而不是大脑，就像你的一样，我怎么能知道任何事情呢？”
“我理解你的感受。”小女孩真心为他感到难过。 “如果你愿意跟我一起去，我会请奥兹为你竭尽全力。”
他们走回路上。多萝西帮助他翻过栅栏，他们沿着黄砖小路出发，前往翡翠城。
托托一开始并不喜欢这个聚会。他在毛绒玩具周围闻了闻，好像他怀疑稻草里可能有一窝老鼠，而且他经常对稻草人不友好地咆哮。
“哦，我不怕，”稻草人回答道。 “他伤不到稻草。让我帮你拎那个篮子吧。我不会介意的，因为我不会累。我会告诉你一个秘密，”他边走边继续说道。 “世界上只有一件事让我害怕。”
几个小时后，路开始变得崎岖不平，行走变得越来越困难，稻草人经常被黄色砖块绊倒，这里的黄色砖块非常凹凸不平。确实，有时它们会损坏或完全丢失，留下洞，托托跳过，多萝西走过去。至于稻草人，没有脑子，径直往前走，结果一脚踩进了洞里，整个人摔在了坚硬的砖块上。然而，这并没有伤害到他，多萝西会把他抱起来，让他重新站起来，而他则和她一起为自己的不幸而开心地大笑。

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz · 选段 4
author: L. Frank Baum
paragraphs: “I always did like flowers,” said the Lion. “They seem so helpless and frail. But there are none in the forest so bright as these.”

They now came upon more and more of the big scarlet poppies, and fewer and fewer of the other flowers; and soon they found themselves in the midst of a great meadow of poppies. Now it is well known that when there are many of these flowers together their odor is so powerful that anyone who breathes it falls asleep, and if the sleeper is not carried away from the scent of the flowers, he sleeps on and on forever. But Dorothy did not know this, nor could she get away from the bright red flowers that were everywhere about; so presently her eyes grew heavy and she felt she must sit down to rest and to sleep.

“We must hurry and get back to the road of yellow brick before dark,” he said; and the Scarecrow agreed with him. So they kept walking until Dorothy could stand no longer. Her eyes closed in spite of herself and she forgot where she was and fell among the poppies, fast asleep.
“If we leave her here she will die,” said the Lion. “The smell of the flowers is killing us all. I myself can scarcely keep my eyes open, and the dog is asleep already.”
It was true; Toto had fallen down beside his little mistress. But the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, not being made of flesh, were not troubled by the scent of the flowers.

“Run fast,” said the Scarecrow to the Lion, “and get out of this deadly flower bed as soon as you can. We will bring the little girl with us, but if you should fall asleep you are too big to be carried.”
So the Lion aroused himself and bounded forward as fast as he could go. In a moment he was out of sight.

“Let us make a chair with our hands and carry her,” said the Scarecrow. So they picked up Toto and put the dog in Dorothy’s lap, and then they made a chair with their hands for the seat and their arms for the arms and carried the sleeping girl between them through the flowers.

On and on they walked, and it seemed that the great carpet of deadly flowers that surrounded them would never end. They followed the bend of the river, and at last came upon their friend the Lion, lying fast asleep among the poppies. The flowers had been too strong for the huge beast and he had given up at last, and fallen only a short distance from the end of the poppy bed, where the sweet grass spread in beautiful green fields before them.
“We can do nothing for him,” said the Tin Woodman, sadly; “for he is much too heavy to lift. We must leave him here to sleep on forever, and perhaps he will dream that he has found courage at last.”
“I’m sorry,” said the Scarecrow. “The Lion was a very good comrade for one so cowardly. But let us go on.”

They carried the sleeping girl to a pretty spot beside the river, far enough from the poppy field to prevent her breathing any more of the poison of the flowers, and here they laid her gently on the soft grass and waited for the fresh breeze to waken her.

The Tin Woodman was about to reply when he heard a low growl, and turning his head (which worked beautifully on hinges) he saw a strange beast come bounding over the grass toward them. It was, indeed, a great yellow Wildcat, and the Woodman thought it must be chasing something, for its ears were lying close to its head and its mouth was wide open, showing two rows of ugly teeth, while its red eyes glowed like balls of fire. As it came nearer the Tin Woodman saw that running before the beast was a little gray field mouse, and although he had no heart he knew it was wrong for the Wildcat to try to kill such a pretty, harmless creature.
paragraphsZh: “我一直很喜欢花，”狮子说。 “它们看起来如此无助和脆弱。但森林里没有比它们更明亮的了。”
他们现在看到越来越多的大猩红色罂粟花，而其他花越来越少；很快他们就发现自己置身于一大片罂粟花田之中。现在众所周知，当许多这种花聚集在一起时，它们的气味是如此强烈，以至于任何呼吸到这种花的人都会入睡，如果睡眠者没有被花香带走，他就会永远睡下去。但多萝西并不知道这一点，她也无法摆脱周围随处可见的鲜红花朵；因此，她的眼睛很快就变得沉重，她觉得自己必须坐下来休息、睡觉。
“我们必须赶快在天黑之前回到黄砖路，”他说；稻草人同意他的观点。于是他们继续走，直到多萝西再也站不住了。她不由自主地闭上了眼睛，忘记了自己身在何处，倒在罂粟花丛中睡着了。
“如果我们把她留在这里，她就会死，”狮子说。 “花香熏死了我们所有人。我自己都快睁不开眼睛了，而狗已经睡着了。”
这是真的；托托倒在了他的小情妇身边。但稻草人和铁皮樵夫不是肉做的，并没有被花香所困扰。
“快跑，”稻草人对狮子说，“尽快离开这个致命的花坛。我们会带上小女孩，但如果你睡着了，你就太大了，无法携带。”
于是狮子猛地醒来，尽其所能地向前跳跃。一会儿他就看不见了。
“让我们亲手做一把椅子来抱她吧。”稻草人说。于是他们抱起托托，把狗放在多萝西的腿上，然后他们用手当座位，胳膊当扶手，做了一把椅子，抱着熟睡的女孩穿过花丛。
他们走啊走啊，似乎包围着他们的致命花朵的大地毯永远不会结束。他们沿着河湾前行，最后找到了他们的朋友狮子，它正躺在罂粟花丛中熟睡。这些花对这只巨大的野兽来说太强大了，他最终放弃了，落在距离罂粟花床尽头不远的地方，那里甜甜的草在他们面前铺满了美丽的绿色田野。
“我们对他无能为力，”铁皮樵夫悲伤地说； “因为他太重了，抬不动。我们必须把他留在这里永远长眠，也许他会梦想自己终于找到了勇气。”
“对不起，”稻草人说。 “对于如此胆怯的人来说，狮子是一位非常好的同志。但让我们继续吧。”
他们把熟睡的女孩抱到河边一处漂亮的地方，离罂粟田足够远，不让她再吸入花朵的毒，然后把她轻轻放在柔软的草地上，等待清新的微风将她唤醒。
铁皮樵夫正要回答，突然听到一声低沉的咆哮，他转过头（铰链上的效果很好），他看到一只奇怪的野兽从草地上跳向他们。那确实是一只巨大的黄色野猫，樵夫认为它一定是在追什么东西，因为它的耳朵贴着头，嘴巴张得大大的，露出两排丑陋的牙齿，红色的眼睛像火球一样闪闪发光。当它走近时，铁皮樵夫看到在野兽面前跑的是一只灰色的小田鼠，虽然他没有心，但他知道野猫试图杀死这样一个美丽而无害的生物是错误的。

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz · 选段 5
author: L. Frank Baum
paragraphs: She left Dorothy alone and went back to the others. These she also led to rooms, and each one of them found himself lodged in a very pleasant part of the Palace. Of course this politeness was wasted on the Scarecrow; for when he found himself alone in his room he stood stupidly in one spot, just within the doorway, to wait till morning. It would not rest him to lie down, and he could not close his eyes; so he remained all night staring at a little spider which was weaving its web in a corner of the room, just as if it were not one of the most wonderful rooms in the world. The Tin Woodman lay down on his bed from force of habit, for he remembered when he was made of flesh; but not being able to sleep, he passed the night moving his joints up and down to make sure they kept in good working order. The Lion would have preferred a bed of dried leaves in the forest, and did not like being shut up in a room; but he had too much sense to let this worry him, so he sprang upon the bed and rolled himself up like a cat and purred himself asleep in a minute.

The next morning, after breakfast, the green maiden came to fetch Dorothy, and she dressed her in one of the prettiest gowns, made of green brocaded satin. Dorothy put on a green silk apron and tied a green ribbon around Toto’s neck, and they started for the Throne Room of the Great Oz.

First they came to a great hall in which were many ladies and gentlemen of the court, all dressed in rich costumes. These people had nothing to do but talk to each other, but they always came to wait outside the Throne Room every morning, although they were never permitted to see Oz. As Dorothy entered they looked at her curiously, and one of them whispered:

“Oh, he will see you,” said the soldier who had taken her message to the Wizard, “although he does not like to have people ask to see him. Indeed, at first he was angry and said I should send you back where you came from. Then he asked me what you looked like, and when I mentioned your silver shoes he was very much interested. At last I told him about the mark upon your forehead, and he decided he would admit you to his presence.”
Just then a bell rang, and the green girl said to Dorothy, “That is the signal. You must go into the Throne Room alone.”

She opened a little door and Dorothy walked boldly through and found herself in a wonderful place. It was a big, round room with a high arched roof, and the walls and ceiling and floor were covered with large emeralds set closely together. In the center of the roof was a great light, as bright as the sun, which made the emeralds sparkle in a wonderful manner.

But what interested Dorothy most was the big throne of green marble that stood in the middle of the room. It was shaped like a chair and sparkled with gems, as did everything else. In the center of the chair was an enormous Head, without a body to support it or any arms or legs whatever. There was no hair upon this head, but it had eyes and a nose and mouth, and was much bigger than the head of the biggest giant.
As Dorothy gazed upon this in wonder and fear, the eyes turned slowly and looked at her sharply and steadily. Then the mouth moved, and Dorothy heard a voice say:
paragraphsZh: 她留下多萝西独自一人，回到其他人身边。她还把这些房间带进了房间，每一间房间都住在宫殿里一个非常宜人的地方。当然，这种礼貌在稻草人身上就浪费了；因为当他发现自己独自一人在自己的房间里时，他就傻乎乎地站在门口的一个地方，等到早上。躺下他也无法休息，他也无法闭上眼睛。于是他整晚都盯着房间角落里一只正在织网的小蜘蛛，仿佛这不是世界上最美妙的房间之一。铁皮樵夫出于习惯的力量躺在床上，因为他记得自己是由肉身制成的。但由于无法入睡，他整晚都在上下活动关节，以确保它们保持良好的工作状态。狮子更喜欢森林里的干树叶床，不喜欢被关在房间里。但他有足够的理智，不会让这件事让他担心，所以他跳到床上，像猫一样把自己卷起来，一分钟后就睡着了。
第二天早上，早餐后，绿色少女来接多萝西，她给她穿上了一件最漂亮的礼服，由绿色锦缎制成。多萝西穿上绿色的丝绸围裙，在托托的脖子上系上一条绿色的丝带，他们出发前往大奥兹国的王座室。
首先他们来到了一个大厅，里面有很多宫廷贵妇，都穿着华丽的服饰。这些人除了互相交谈之外无事可做，但每天早上他们总是来到王座室外等候，尽管他们从未被允许见到奥兹。当多萝西进来时，他们好奇地看着她，其中一个低声说道：
“哦，他会见到你，”给巫师带去信息的士兵说道，“虽然他不喜欢有人要求见他。事实上，一开始他很生气，说我应该把你送回你来自的地方。然后他问我你长什么样，当我提到你的银鞋时，他非常感兴趣。最后我告诉他你额头上的标记，他决定承认你在场。”
就在这时，铃声响起，绿色少女对多萝西说道：“这是信号，你必须独自进入王座室。”
她打开了一扇小门，多萝西大胆地走了进去，发现自己身处一个美妙的地方。这是一个又大又圆的房间，有着高高的拱形屋顶，墙壁、天花板和地板上都铺满了紧密镶嵌在一起的大块祖母绿。屋顶中央有一盏巨大的光，如太阳般明亮，将祖母绿照得闪闪发光，奇妙极了。
但最让多萝西感兴趣的是房间中央的绿色大理石大宝座。它的形状像一把椅子，和其他东西一样，镶嵌着宝石。椅子的中央有一个巨大的头，没有身体支撑它，也没有任何手臂或腿。这颗头上没有头发，但却有眼睛、鼻子和嘴巴，比最大的巨人的头还要大得多。
当多萝西惊奇而恐惧地看着这一幕时，那双眼睛缓缓转动，锐利而坚定地看着她。然后嘴巴动了，多萝西听到一个声音说：

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz · 选段 6
author: L. Frank Baum
paragraphs: “If he is a Beast when I go to see him, I shall roar my loudest, and so frighten him that he will grant all I ask. And if he is the lovely Lady, I shall pretend to spring upon her, and so compel her to do my bidding. And if he is the great Head, he will be at my mercy; for I will roll this head all about the room until he promises to give us what we desire. So be of good cheer, my friends, for all will yet be well.”
The next morning the soldier with the green whiskers led the Lion to the great Throne Room and bade him enter the presence of Oz.

The Lion at once passed through the door, and glancing around saw, to his surprise, that before the throne was a Ball of Fire, so fierce and glowing he could scarcely bear to gaze upon it. His first thought was that Oz had by accident caught on fire and was burning up; but when he tried to go nearer, the heat was so intense that it singed his whiskers, and he crept back tremblingly to a spot nearer the door.
And the Lion answered, “I am a Cowardly Lion, afraid of everything. I came to you to beg that you give me courage, so that in reality I may become the King of Beasts, as men call me.”
“Because of all Wizards you are the greatest, and alone have power to grant my request,” answered the Lion.

The Ball of Fire burned fiercely for a time, and the voice said, “Bring me proof that the Wicked Witch is dead, and that moment I will give you courage. But as long as the Witch lives, you must remain a coward.”

The Lion was angry at this speech, but could say nothing in reply, and while he stood silently gazing at the Ball of Fire it became so furiously hot that he turned tail and rushed from the room. He was glad to find his friends waiting for him, and told them of his terrible interview with the Wizard.

Therefore it was decided to start upon their journey the next morning, and the Woodman sharpened his axe on a green grindstone and had all his joints properly oiled. The Scarecrow stuffed himself with fresh straw and Dorothy put new paint on his eyes that he might see better. The green girl, who was very kind to them, filled Dorothy’s basket with good things to eat, and fastened a little bell around Toto’s neck with a green ribbon.

They went to bed quite early and slept soundly until daylight, when they were awakened by the crowing of a green cock that lived in the back yard of the Palace, and the cackling of a hen that had laid a green egg.

The soldier with the green whiskers led them through the streets of the Emerald City until they reached the room where the Guardian of the Gates lived. This officer unlocked their spectacles to put them back in his great box, and then he politely opened the gate for our friends.

“Oh, that is different,” said the Guardian of the Gates. “No one has ever destroyed her before, so I naturally thought she would make slaves of you, as she has of the rest. But take care; for she is wicked and fierce, and may not allow you to destroy her. Keep to the West, where the sun sets, and you cannot fail to find her.”

They thanked him and bade him good-bye, and turned toward the West, walking over fields of soft grass dotted here and there with daisies and buttercups. Dorothy still wore the pretty silk dress she had put on in the palace, but now, to her surprise, she found it was no longer green, but pure white. The ribbon around Toto’s neck had also lost its green color and was as white as Dorothy’s dress.
paragraphsZh: “如果他是野兽，当我去看他时，我会大声咆哮，吓唬他，让他满足我的一切要求。如果他是可爱的女士，我会假装跳到她身上，强迫她听从我的命令。如果他是伟大的头，他会听从我的怜悯；因为我会在房间里滚动这个头，直到他答应给我们我们想要的东西。所以，请放心，我的朋友们，因为所有人都会但愿你一切都好。”
第二天早上，长着绿色胡须的士兵将狮子带到了宏伟的王座室，并请他进入奥兹国的面前。
狮子立刻推门而入，环顾四周，惊讶地发现王座前有一团火球，凶猛而耀眼，让他几乎不忍直视。他的第一个念头是奥兹不小心着火了，正在烧毁。但当他试图走近时，热量太高了，烧焦了他的胡须，他颤抖着爬回靠近门的地方。
狮子回答说：“我是一头胆怯的狮子，什么都害怕。我来找你是为了请求你给我勇气，这样我就可以成为现实中的百兽之王，就像人们称呼我的那样。”
“因为在所有巫师中你是最伟大的，只有你有能力满足我的请求，”狮子回答道。
火球猛烈燃烧了一会，那个声音说道：“给我证据，证明恶女巫已经死了，那一刻我会给你勇气。但只要女巫还活着，你就必须一直是个胆小鬼。”
狮子对这番话很生气，但无话可说，当他静静地站着，凝视着火球时，火球变得非常热，他转身冲出了房间。他很高兴发现他的朋友们在等他，并向他们讲述了他与巫师的可怕会面。
因此，他们决定第二天早上开始他们的旅程，樵夫在绿色磨石上磨利他的斧子，并给他所有的关节涂上适当的油。稻草人用新鲜的稻草塞满了自己，多萝西在他的眼睛上涂了新颜料，这样他就可以看得更清楚了。绿姑娘对他们非常友善，她给多萝西的篮子里装满了好吃的东西，并用一条绿丝带在托托的脖子上系了一个小铃铛。
他们很早就上床睡觉，睡得很香，一直睡到天亮，然后被宫殿后院一只绿色公鸡的啼叫声和下了绿色鸡蛋的母鸡的咯咯叫声吵醒。
绿须士兵带着他们穿过翡翠城的街道，来到了城门守护者居住的房间。这位警官打开他们的眼镜，把它们放回他的大盒子里，然后他礼貌地为我们的朋友打开了大门。
“哦，那不一样，”大门守护者说道。 “以前没有人消灭过她，所以我自然认为她会成为你的奴隶，就像她对待其他人一样。但是你要小心，因为她邪恶而凶猛，可能不允许你消灭她。继续向西，太阳落山的地方，你一定会找到她的。”
他们感谢了他，向他告别，然后转向西方，走在柔软的草地上，那里点缀着雏菊和毛茛。多萝西还穿着她在宫殿里穿的那件漂亮的丝质连衣裙，但现在，她惊讶地发现，它不再是绿色的，而是纯白色的。托托脖子上的丝带也失去了绿色，变成了和多萝西的裙子一样的白色。

title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz · 选段 7
author: L. Frank Baum
paragraphs: Promptly at nine o’clock the next morning the green-whiskered soldier came to them, and four minutes later they all went into the Throne Room of the Great Oz.

Of course each one of them expected to see the Wizard in the shape he had taken before, and all were greatly surprised when they looked about and saw no one at all in the room. They kept close to the door and closer to one another, for the stillness of the empty room was more dreadful than any of the forms they had seen Oz take.

“I am everywhere,” answered the Voice, “but to the eyes of common mortals I am invisible. I will now seat myself upon my throne, that you may converse with me.” Indeed, the Voice seemed just then to come straight from the throne itself; so they walked toward it and stood in a row while Dorothy said:
“Dear me,” said the Voice, “how sudden! Well, come to me tomorrow, for I must have time to think it over.”

The Lion thought it might be as well to frighten the Wizard, so he gave a large, loud roar, which was so fierce and dreadful that Toto jumped away from him in alarm and tipped over the screen that stood in a corner. As it fell with a crash they looked that way, and the next moment all of them were filled with wonder. For they saw, standing in just the spot the screen had hidden, a little old man, with a bald head and a wrinkled face, who seemed to be as much surprised as they were. The Tin Woodman, raising his axe, rushed toward the little man and cried out, “Who are you?”
“I am Oz, the Great and Terrible,” said the little man, in a trembling voice. “But don’t strike me—please don’t—and I’ll do anything you want me to.”
“Hush, my dear,” he said. “Don’t speak so loud, or you will be overheard—and I should be ruined. I’m supposed to be a Great Wizard.”
