“Good Lord!” exclaimed poor Mrs. Medlock with her eyes almost starting out of her head. “Good Lord!”

Then Mary was reminded of the boy Rajah again. Colin answered as if neither the doctor’s alarm nor Mrs. Medlock’s terror were of the slightest consequence. He was as little disturbed or frightened as if an elderly cat and dog had walked into the room.
“This is my cousin, Mary Lennox,” he said. “I asked her to come and talk to me. I like her. She must come and talk to me whenever I send for her.”
“Oh, sir” she panted. “I don’t know how it’s happened. There’s not a servant on the place tha’d dare to talk—they all have their orders.”
“Nobody told her anything,” said Colin. “She heard me crying and found me herself. I am glad she came. Don’t be silly, Medlock.”
Mary saw that Dr. Craven did not look pleased, but it was quite plain that he dare not oppose his patient. He sat down by Colin and felt his pulse.

“I should be excited if she kept away,” answered Colin, his eyes beginning to look dangerously sparkling. “I am better. She makes me better. The nurse must bring up her tea with mine. We will have tea together.”
Mrs. Medlock and Dr. Craven looked at each other in a troubled way, but there was evidently nothing to be done.
“He does look rather better, sir,” ventured Mrs. Medlock. “But”—thinking the matter over—“he looked better this morning before she came into the room.”

“She came into the room last night. She stayed with me a long time. She sang a Hindustani song to me and it made me go to sleep,” said Colin. “I was better when I wakened up. I wanted my breakfast. I want my tea now. Tell nurse, Medlock.”

Dr. Craven did not stay very long. He talked to the nurse for a few minutes when she came into the room and said a few words of warning to Colin. He must not talk too much; he must not forget that he was ill; he must not forget that he was very easily tired. Mary thought that there seemed to be a number of uncomfortable things he was not to forget.

Dr. Craven did not look happy when he left the room. He gave a puzzled glance at the little girl sitting on the large stool. She had become a stiff, silent child again as soon as he entered and he could not see what the attraction was. The boy actually did look brighter, however—and he sighed rather heavily as he went down the corridor.

“They are always wanting me to eat things when I don’t want to,” said Colin, as the nurse brought in the tea and put it on the table by the sofa. “Now, if you’ll eat I will. Those muffins look so nice and hot. Tell me about Rajahs.”

After another week of rain the high arch of blue sky appeared again and the sun which poured down was quite hot. Though there had been no chance to see either the secret garden or Dickon, Mistress Mary had enjoyed herself very much. The week had not seemed long. She had spent hours of every day with Colin in his room, talking about Rajahs or gardens or Dickon and the cottage on the moor. They had looked at the splendid books and pictures and sometimes Mary had read things to Colin, and sometimes he had read a little to her. When he was amused and interested she thought he scarcely looked like an invalid at all, except that his face was so colorless and he was always on the sofa.
paragraphsZh: 奇怪的是，他们说了这么多却从来不记得这么简单的事情，他们笑得比以往任何时候都多，因为他们已经陷入了嘲笑任何事情的幽默之中。正当大家高兴的时候，门开了，克雷文医生和梅德洛克夫人走了进来。
克雷文医生吓了一跳，梅德洛克夫人差点向后退去，因为他不小心撞到了她。
“上帝啊！”可怜的梅德劳克太太惊呼道，她的眼睛几乎要从脑袋里掉出来了。 “天哪！”
然后玛丽再次想起了男孩拉贾。科林回答道，仿佛医生的惊慌和梅德洛克夫人的恐惧都无关紧要。他一点也不感到不安或害怕，就像一只年长的猫和狗走进了房间一样。
“这是我的表弟，玛丽·伦诺克斯，”他说。 “我让她来跟我说话。我喜欢她。每当我叫她来的时候，她都必须来跟我说话。”
“哦，先生，”她气喘吁吁。 “我不知道怎么会这样，这里没有一个仆人敢说话，他们都有命令。”
“没有人告诉她任何事情，”科林说。 “她听到我的哭声，亲自找到了我。我很高兴她来了。别傻了，梅德洛克。”
玛丽看到克雷文医生看上去不太高兴，但很明显他不敢反对他的病人。他在科林身边坐下，摸了摸他的脉搏。
“如果她远离我，我会很兴奋，”科林回答道，他的眼睛开始闪烁着危险的光芒。 “我好多了。她让我好多了。护士必须把她的茶和我的一起端上来。我们一起喝茶。”
梅德洛克夫人和克雷文博士困惑地看着对方，但显然没有什么可做的。
“他看起来确实好多了，先生，”梅德洛克夫人大胆地说。 “但是”——仔细想想——“今天早上她进房间之前，他看起来好多了。”
“她昨晚走进房间。她和我待了很长时间。她给我唱了一首印度斯坦歌曲，这让我入睡，”科林说。 “醒来后我好多了。我想吃早餐。我现在想喝茶。告诉护士，梅德洛克。”
克雷文博士没有停留很长时间。当护士走进房间时，他和她聊了几分钟，并向科林说了几句警告的话。他不能说太多；他不能忘记自己病了；他一定不能忘记他很容易疲倦。玛丽认为似乎有很多不舒服的事情他不能忘记。
克雷文博士离开房间时看上去并不高兴。他疑惑地看了一眼坐在大凳子上的小女孩。他一进来，她又变成了一个僵硬、沉默的孩子，他看不出有什么吸引力。然而，这个男孩实际上看起来确实更聪明了——当他沿着走廊走时，他重重地叹了口气。
“当我不想吃的时候，他们总是想让我吃东西，”科林说，护士把茶端了进来，放在沙发旁边的桌子上。 “现在，如果你愿意吃，我就吃。那些松饼看起来又好吃又热。告诉我关于拉贾的事。”
又过了一周的雨，又出现了高高的蓝天，倾盆而下的阳光相当炎热。虽然没有机会参观秘密花园和迪肯，但玛丽小姐却玩得很开心。这一周似乎并不长。她每天都会花几个小时和科林待在他的房间里，谈论王公、花园、迪肯和沼泽上的小屋。他们看了精彩的书籍和图画，有时玛丽给科林读了一些东西，有时他也给她读了一点。当他感到有趣和感兴趣时，她觉得他看起来根本不像一个病人，除了他的脸色毫无血色，而且他总是坐在沙发上。

title: The Secret Garden · 选段 8
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: When he was very much interested he often spoke quite broad Yorkshire though at other times he tried to modify his dialect so that Mary could better understand. But she loved his broad Yorkshire and had in fact been trying to learn to speak it herself. So she spoke a little now.

“Aye, that we mun,” she said (which meant “Yes, indeed, we must”). “I’ll tell thee what us’ll do first,” she proceeded, and Dickon grinned, because when the little wench tried to twist her tongue into speaking Yorkshire it amused him very much. “He’s took a graidely fancy to thee. He wants to see thee and he wants to see Soot an’ Captain. When I go back to the house to talk to him I’ll ax him if tha’ canna’ come an’ see him tomorrow mornin’—an’ bring tha’ creatures wi’ thee—an’ then—in a bit, when there’s more leaves out, an’ happen a bud or two, we’ll get him to come out an’ tha’ shall push him in his chair an’ we’ll bring him here an’ show him everything.”
When she stopped she was quite proud of herself. She had never made a long speech in Yorkshire before and she had remembered very well.

“Tha’ mun talk a bit o’ Yorkshire like that to Mester Colin,” Dickon chuckled. “Tha’ll make him laugh an’ there’s nowt as good for ill folk as laughin’ is. Mother says she believes as half a hour’s good laugh every mornin’ ’ud cure a chap as was makin’ ready for typhus fever.”

The garden had reached the time when every day and every night it seemed as if Magicians were passing through it drawing loveliness out of the earth and the boughs with wands. It was hard to go away and leave it all, particularly as Nut had actually crept on to her dress and Shell had scrambled down the trunk of the apple-tree they sat under and stayed there looking at her with inquiring eyes. But she went back to the house and when she sat down close to Colin’s bed he began to sniff as Dickon did though not in such an experienced way.
“You smell like flowers and—and fresh things,” he cried out quite joyously. “What is it you smell of? It’s cool and warm and sweet all at the same time.”

“It’s th’ wind from th’ moor,” said Mary. “It comes o’ sittin’ on th’ grass under a tree wi’ Dickon an’ wi’ Captain an’ Soot an’ Nut an’ Shell. It’s th’ springtime an’ out o’ doors an’ sunshine as smells so graidely.”
She said it as broadly as she could, and you do not know how broadly Yorkshire sounds until you have heard someone speak it. Colin began to laugh.

“I’m givin’ thee a bit o’ Yorkshire,” answered Mary triumphantly. “I canna’ talk as graidely as Dickon an’ Martha can but tha’ sees I can shape a bit. Doesn’t tha’ understand a bit o’ Yorkshire when tha’ hears it? An’ tha’ a Yorkshire lad thysel’ bred an’ born! Eh! I wonder tha’rt not ashamed o’ thy face.”

And then she began to laugh too and they both laughed until they could not stop themselves and they laughed until the room echoed and Mrs. Medlock opening the door to come in drew back into the corridor and stood listening amazed.

“Well, upon my word!” she said, speaking rather broad Yorkshire herself because there was no one to hear her and she was so astonished. “Whoever heard th’ like! Whoever on earth would ha’ thought it!”

There was so much to talk about. It seemed as if Colin could never hear enough of Dickon and Captain and Soot and Nut and Shell and the pony whose name was Jump. Mary had run round into the wood with Dickon to see Jump. He was a tiny little shaggy moor pony with thick locks hanging over his eyes and with a pretty face and a nuzzling velvet nose. He was rather thin with living on moor grass but he was as tough and wiry as if the muscle in his little legs had been made of steel springs. He had lifted his head and whinnied softly the moment he saw Dickon and he had trotted up to him and put his head across his shoulder and then Dickon had talked into his ear and Jump had talked back in odd little whinnies and puffs and snorts. Dickon had made him give Mary his small front hoof and kiss her on her cheek with his velvet muzzle.
paragraphsZh: 当他非常感兴趣时，他经常说相当广泛的约克郡话，尽管有时他试图修改他的方言，以便玛丽能更好地理解。但她喜欢他那宽阔的约克郡语，事实上她一直在努力学习说这种语言。所以她现在说了一点。

“是的，我们必须”，她说（意思是“是的，确实，我们必须”）。 “我会告诉你我们先做什么，”她继续说，迪肯笑了，因为当这个小姑娘试图扭动舌头说约克郡语时，这让他非常好笑。 “他越来越喜欢你了。他想见你，他想见烟灰和船长。当我回到屋子里和他说话时，如果你明天早上能来见他，我会问他——然后把那些生物带到你身边——然后——等一会儿，当有更多的叶子长出来，或者出现一两个花蕾时，我们会让他出来，然后”你将把他推到椅子上，我们将把他带到这里，向他展示一切。”
当她停下来时，她为自己感到非常自豪。她以前从未在约克郡发表过长篇演讲，而且记得很清楚。
“你对科林先生说了一点约克郡的事，”迪肯咯咯地笑道。 “这会让他开怀大笑，对于生病的人来说，没有比笑更有益的了。母亲说，她相信每天早上笑半个小时就能治愈一个小伙子，就像为斑疹伤寒做好准备一样。”
花园已经到了每天每夜都仿佛有魔术师穿过它，用魔杖从大地和树枝中汲取可爱的时候。离开这一切是很困难的，尤其是当坚果实际上已经爬上她的衣服，而谢尔则爬下他们坐在下面的苹果树的树干上并留在那里用询问的眼神看着她时。但她回到了房子，当她坐在科林床边时，科林开始像迪肯那样吸鼻子，尽管没有那么有经验。
“你闻起来像花和——还有新鲜的东西，”他非常高兴地喊道。 “你闻到了什么味道？凉爽、温暖、甜蜜。”
“这是来自荒野的风，”玛丽说。 “它和迪肯、船长、烟灰、坚果和贝壳一起坐在树下的草地上。现在是春天，户外和阳光，闻起来如此柔和。”
她尽可能广泛地说了这句话，除非你听到有人这么说，否则你不会知道约克郡听起来有多广泛。科林开始大笑。
“我给你一点约克郡，”玛丽得意洋洋地回答道。 “我不能像迪肯和玛莎那样彬彬有礼地说话，但你看我能塑造一点。你听的时候难道不明白一点约克郡的意思吗？你是一个约克郡的小伙子，你养育和出生的！呃！我不知道你的脸不感到羞耻。”
然后她也开始笑，他们俩都笑到无法停止，笑到房间里回响着，梅德洛克太太打开门进来，退到走廊里，站着惊讶地听着。
“好吧，我保证！”她说，自己说的是粗略的约克郡语，因为没有人听她说话，她感到非常惊讶。 “谁听到了！地球上谁会想到！”

有很多话要说。科林似乎永远听不够迪肯、船长、烟灰、坚果和贝壳以及名叫跳跃的小马。玛丽和迪肯跑到树林里去看詹普。他是一匹毛茸茸的小沼泽小马，浓密的头发垂在眼睛上，有一张漂亮的脸和一个用鼻子蹭蹭的天鹅绒鼻子。由于生活在沼泽草地上，他相当瘦弱，但他的小腿上的肌肉却坚韧而结实，仿佛是钢弹簧制成的。当他看到迪肯时，他抬起头，轻轻地发出呜呜声，然后小跑到迪肯身边，把头靠在迪肯的肩膀上，然后迪肯在他耳边说话，詹姆用奇怪的小呜呜声、气喘吁吁和鼻息声回应了他。迪肯让他把小前蹄给了玛丽，并用天鹅绒的口吻亲吻了她的脸颊。

title: The Secret Garden · 选段 9
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: “You have my permission to go,” he said, and they both disappeared quickly and it must be confessed giggled when they were safely inside the house.

Dickon began to push the wheeled chair slowly and steadily. Mistress Mary walked beside it and Colin leaned back and lifted his face to the sky. The arch of it looked very high and the small snowy clouds seemed like white birds floating on outspread wings below its crystal blueness. The wind swept in soft big breaths down from the moor and was strange with a wild clear scented sweetness. Colin kept lifting his thin chest to draw it in, and his big eyes looked as if it were they which were listening—listening, instead of his ears.
“There are so many sounds of singing and humming and calling out,” he said. “What is that scent the puffs of wind bring?”
“It’s gorse on th’ moor that’s openin’ out,” answered Dickon. “Eh! th’ bees are at it wonderful today.”

Not a human creature was to be caught sight of in the paths they took. In fact every gardener or gardener’s lad had been witched away. But they wound in and out among the shrubbery and out and round the fountain beds, following their carefully planned route for the mere mysterious pleasure of it. But when at last they turned into the Long Walk by the ivied walls the excited sense of an approaching thrill made them, for some curious reason they could not have explained, begin to speak in whispers.
“Is it?” cried Colin, and his eyes began to search the ivy with eager curiousness. “But I can see nothing,” he whispered. “There is no door.”
“Where? Where? There?” he cried, and his eyes were as big as the wolf’s in Red Riding-Hood, when Red Riding-Hood felt called upon to remark on them. Dickon stood still and the wheeled chair stopped.

“And this,” said Mary, stepping on to the bed close to the ivy, “is where I went to talk to him when he chirped at me from the top of the wall. And this is the ivy the wind blew back,” and she took hold of the hanging green curtain.

But Colin had actually dropped back against his cushions, even though he gasped with delight, and he had covered his eyes with his hands and held them there shutting out everything until they were inside and the chair stopped as if by magic and the door was closed. Not till then did he take them away and look round and round and round as Dickon and Mary had done. And over walls and earth and trees and swinging sprays and tendrils the fair green veil of tender little leaves had crept, and in the grass under the trees and the gray urns in the alcoves and here and there everywhere were touches or splashes of gold and purple and white and the trees were showing pink and snow above his head and there were fluttering of wings and faint sweet pipes and humming and scents and scents. And the sun fell warm upon his face like a hand with a lovely touch. And in wonder Mary and Dickon stood and stared at him. He looked so strange and different because a pink glow of color had actually crept all over him—ivory face and neck and hands and all.
“I shall get well! I shall get well!” he cried out. “Mary! Dickon! I shall get well! And I shall live forever and ever and ever!”

One of the strange things about living in the world is that it is only now and then one is quite sure one is going to live forever and ever and ever. One knows it sometimes when one gets up at the tender solemn dawn-time and goes out and stands alone and throws one’s head far back and looks up and up and watches the pale sky slowly changing and flushing and marvelous unknown things happening until the East almost makes one cry out and one’s heart stands still at the strange unchanging majesty of the rising of the sun—which has been happening every morning for thousands and thousands and thousands of years. One knows it then for a moment or so. And one knows it sometimes when one stands by oneself in a wood at sunset and the mysterious deep gold stillness slanting through and under the branches seems to be saying slowly again and again something one cannot quite hear, however much one tries. Then sometimes the immense quiet of the dark blue at night with millions of stars waiting and watching makes one sure; and sometimes a sound of far-off music makes it true; and sometimes a look in someone’s eyes.
paragraphsZh: “我允许你走，”他说，然后他们很快就消失了，当他们安全地进入房子时，必须承认，他们咯咯地笑了。
迪肯开始缓慢而稳定地推着轮椅。玛丽女主人走在它旁边，科林靠在椅背上，仰视着天空。它的拱门看起来很高，晶莹的蓝色下面，小小的雪云就像张开翅膀的白鸟。风从荒野上吹来，带着柔和的气息，带着一种野性的、清甜的、奇异的香气。科林不断地抬起他瘦弱的胸膛，将其收拢，他的大眼睛看起来就像是它们在听——听，而不是他的耳朵。
“有很多唱歌、哼唱和呼喊的声音，”他说。 “一阵阵风带来的气味是什么？”
“这是荒原上的金雀花，正在开放，”迪肯回答道。 “呃！蜜蜂今天干得真棒。”
他们所走的道路上看不到任何人类。事实上，每个园丁或园丁的小伙子都被巫术迷惑了。但他们在灌木丛中蜿蜒进出，在喷泉床周围蜿蜒前行，沿着精心设计的路线，纯粹是为了获得神秘的乐趣。但当他们最后拐进长满常春藤的围墙旁的长路时，一种即将到来的兴奋感让他们兴奋不已，出于某种他们无法解释的奇怪原因，开始低声说话。
“是吗？”科林叫道，他的眼睛开始带着急切的好奇心在常春藤上搜寻。 “但我什么也看不见，”他低声说道。 “没有门。”
“哪里？哪里？那里？”他叫道，当小红帽觉得有必要对他们发表评论时，他的眼睛就和《小红帽》中的狼的眼睛一样大。迪肯站着不动，轮椅也停了下来。
“而这里，”玛丽踏上靠近常春藤的床说道，“当他从墙顶对我叽叽喳喳时，我就去那里和他说话。这就是被风吹回的常春藤，”她抓住了悬挂的绿色窗帘。

但科林实际上已经靠在了他的垫子上，尽管他高兴地喘着粗气，他用手捂住眼睛，把它们放在那里，将一切都隔绝在外，直到他们进入里面，椅子就像魔法一样停了下来，门也关上了。直到那时，他才把它们拿走，像迪肯和玛丽那样四处查看。墙壁、泥土、树木、摇曳的水花和卷须上，柔嫩的小叶子的翠绿面纱已经悄然爬上，树下的草丛里，壁龛里的灰色瓮里，到处都是金色、紫色和白色的点缀或飞溅，树木在他头顶上呈现出粉红色和雪花，翅膀在拍动，微弱甜美的笛声、嗡嗡声、香味和香味。阳光照在他的脸上，温暖如手，触感可爱。玛丽和迪肯惊奇地站起来盯着他。他看起来如此奇怪和不同，因为他全身都散发着粉红色的光芒——象牙色的脸、脖子、手等等。
“我会好起来的！我会好起来的！”他喊道。 “玛丽！迪肯！我会康复的！我会永远活下去！”

生活在这个世界上的一件奇怪的事情是，只有时不时地，人们才确信自己会永远活下去。有时，当一个人在温柔而庄严的黎明时分起床，走出去，独自站着，把头远远地向后仰，向上看，向上看，看着苍白的天空慢慢地变化、泛红，奇妙的未知的事情发生时，直到东方几乎让人大喊大叫，一个人的心静止在太阳升起的奇怪的、不变的威严面前——这已经发生了成千上万年的每天早晨。人们在一瞬间就知道了。有时，当一个人独自站在日落时分的树林里，神秘的深金色寂静在树枝间和树枝下倾斜时，人们就会知道这一点，似乎在一次又一次缓慢地诉说着一些人们无法完全听到的东西，无论人们如何努力。有时，深蓝色的夜晚，数以百万计的星星在等待和观看，一片寂静，让人确信；有时，远处传来的音乐声就证明了这一点；有时还有某人的眼神。

title: The Secret Garden · 选段 10
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
paragraphs: “Tha’ young bad ’un!” he called down at her. “Layin’ tha’ badness on a robin—not but what he’s impidint enow for anythin’. Him showin’ thee th’ way! Him! Eh! tha’ young nowt”—she could see his next words burst out because he was overpowered by curiosity—“however i’ this world did tha’ get in?”
“It was the robin who showed me the way,” she protested obstinately. “He didn’t know he was doing it but he did. And I can’t tell you from here while you’re shaking your fist at me.”
He stopped shaking his fist very suddenly at that very moment and his jaw actually dropped as he stared over her head at something he saw coming over the grass toward him.

At the first sound of his torrent of words Colin had been so surprised that he had only sat up and listened as if he were spellbound. But in the midst of it he had recovered himself and beckoned imperiously to Dickon.

And this, if you please, this is what Ben Weatherstaff beheld and which made his jaw drop. A wheeled chair with luxurious cushions and robes which came toward him looking rather like some sort of State Coach because a young Rajah leaned back in it with royal command in his great black-rimmed eyes and a thin white hand extended haughtily toward him. And it stopped right under Ben Weatherstaff’s nose. It was really no wonder his mouth dropped open.
How Ben Weatherstaff stared! His red old eyes fixed themselves on what was before him as if he were seeing a ghost. He gazed and gazed and gulped a lump down his throat and did not say a word.
Ben Weatherstaff put his gnarled hand up and passed it over his eyes and over his forehead and then he did answer in a queer shaky voice.
“Who tha’ art?” he said. “Aye, that I do—wi’ tha’ mother’s eyes starin’ at me out o’ tha’ face. Lord knows how tha’ come here. But tha’rt th’ poor cripple.”
“He’s not!” cried Mary, almost shouting up the wall in her fierce indignation. “He’s not got a lump as big as a pin! I looked and there was none there—not one!”

Ben Weatherstaff passed his hand over his forehead again and gazed as if he could never gaze enough. His hand shook and his mouth shook and his voice shook. He was an ignorant old man and a tactless old man and he could only remember the things he had heard.

It was too much. The strength which Colin usually threw into his tantrums rushed through him now in a new way. Never yet had he been accused of crooked legs—even in whispers—and the perfectly simple belief in their existence which was revealed by Ben Weatherstaff’s voice was more than Rajah flesh and blood could endure. His anger and insulted pride made him forget everything but this one moment and filled him with a power he had never known before, an almost unnatural strength.
“Come here!” he shouted to Dickon, and he actually began to tear the coverings off his lower limbs and disentangle himself. “Come here! Come here! This minute!”
Dickon was by his side in a second. Mary caught her breath in a short gasp and felt herself turn pale.
“He can do it! He can do it! He can do it! He can!” she gabbled over to herself under her breath as fast as ever she could.

There was a brief fierce scramble, the rugs were tossed on the ground, Dickon held Colin’s arm, the thin legs were out, the thin feet were on the grass. Colin was standing upright—upright—as straight as an arrow and looking strangely tall—his head thrown back and his strange eyes flashing lightning.
paragraphsZh: “你这个年轻人太坏了！”他低头冲她喊道。 “把你的坏事放在知更鸟身上——不是他现在对任何事情都无礼的。他给你指明了道路！他！呃！你这个年轻人”——她可以看到他的下一句话突然爆发，因为他被好奇心压倒了——“但我是怎么进来的？”
“是知更鸟给我带路的，”她固执地抗议道。 “他不知道自己在这么做，但他确实这么做了。当你向我挥舞拳头时，我无法在这里告诉你。”
在那一刻，他突然停止了握拳，当他越过她的头，看到有什么东西从草地上向他走来时，他的下巴实际上掉了下来。
听到他滔滔不绝的话语，科林一听就感到非常惊讶，他只是坐起来听着，仿佛着了迷一样。但在这之中，他恢复了平静，并专横地向迪肯招了招手。
如果你愿意的话，这就是本·韦瑟斯塔夫所看到的，这让他下巴都掉下来了。一张配有豪华坐垫和长袍的轮椅朝他走来，看起来很像某种国家教练，因为年轻的拉贾靠在上面，黑眼圈的大眼睛里带着皇家的命令，一只瘦瘦的白手傲慢地向他伸出。它就停在了本·韦瑟斯塔夫的眼皮子底下。也难怪他张大了嘴巴。
本·韦瑟斯塔夫瞪大了眼睛！他那双红色的老眼，死死地盯着眼前的一切，就像见了鬼一样。他凝视着，凝视着，咽了一口喉咙，没有说话。
本·韦瑟斯塔夫举起粗糙的手，抚过眼睛和额头，然后用一种奇怪的、颤抖的声音回答了。
“你是谁？”他说。 “是的，我知道——你母亲的眼睛从脸上盯着我。上帝知道你是怎么来到这里的。但你是个可怜的瘸子。”
“他不是！”玛丽大声喊道，她的愤怒几乎冲墙而去。 “他没有像针那么大的肿块！我看了看，那里没有——一个也没有！”
本·韦瑟斯塔夫再次把手放在额头上，凝视着，仿佛他永远都看不够。他的手在颤抖，他的嘴在颤抖，他的声音也在颤抖。他是一个无知的老人，一个不圆滑的老人，他只能记住自己听到的事情。
太多了。科林平时发脾气时所表现出的力量现在以一种新的方式涌入他的全身。他还从未被指控有弯曲腿——即使是在低声说话中——而本·韦瑟斯塔夫的声音所透露出的对弯曲腿存在的简单信念是拉贾的血肉之躯无法忍受的。他的愤怒和被侮辱的骄傲让他忘记了除了这一刻之外的一切，并让他充满了一种他以前从未了解过的力量，一种近乎不自然的力量。
“过来！”他对迪肯大喊，迪肯实际上开始撕下下肢的覆盖物，解开自己。 “过来！过来！就这一分钟！”
迪肯立刻就到了他身边。玛丽短促地喘了口气，感觉自己脸色苍白。
“他能做到！他能做到！他能做到！他能！”她尽可能快地低声自言自语。
一阵短暂的激烈争抢，地毯被扔在了地上，迪肯抓住了科林的手臂，细腿伸出来，细脚踩在了草地上。科林笔直地站着——笔直——笔直如箭，看上去异常高大——他的头向后仰着，奇怪的眼睛里闪烁着闪电。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 4
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: “Give me the key,” said my mother; and though the lock was very stiff, she had turned it and thrown back the lid in a twinkling.

A strong smell of tobacco and tar rose from the interior, but nothing was to be seen on the top except a suit of very good clothes, carefully brushed and folded. They had never been worn, my mother said. Under that, the miscellany began--a quadrant, a tin canikin, several sticks of tobacco, two brace of very handsome pistols, a piece of bar silver, an old Spanish watch and some other trinkets of little value and mostly of foreign make, a pair of compasses mounted with brass, and five or six curious West Indian shells. I have often wondered since why he should have carried about these shells with him in his wandering, guilty, and hunted life.

In the meantime, we had found nothing of any value but the silver and the trinkets, and neither of these were in our way. Underneath there was an old boat-cloak, whitened with sea-salt on many a harbour-bar. My mother pulled it up with impatience, and there lay before us, the last things in the chest, a bundle tied up in oilcloth, and looking like papers, and a canvas bag that gave forth, at a touch, the jingle of gold.

“I’ll show these rogues that I’m an honest woman,” said my mother. “I’ll have my dues, and not a farthing over. Hold Mrs. Crossley’s bag.” And she began to count over the amount of the captain’s score from the sailor’s bag into the one that I was holding.

It was a long, difficult business, for the coins were of all countries and sizes--doubloons, and louis d’ors, and guineas, and pieces of eight, and I know not what besides, all shaken together at random. The guineas, too, were about the scarcest, and it was with these only that my mother knew how to make her count.

When we were about half-way through, I suddenly put my hand upon her arm, for I had heard in the silent frosty air a sound that brought my heart into my mouth--the tap-tapping of the blind man’s stick upon the frozen road. It drew nearer and nearer, while we sat holding our breath. Then it struck sharp on the inn door, and then we could hear the handle being turned and the bolt rattling as the wretched being tried to enter; and then there was a long time of silence both within and without. At last the tapping recommenced, and, to our indescribable joy and gratitude, died slowly away again until it ceased to be heard.

“Mother,” said I, “take the whole and let’s be going,” for I was sure the bolted door must have seemed suspicious and would bring the whole hornet’s nest about our ears, though how thankful I was that I had bolted it, none could tell who had never met that terrible blind man.

But my mother, frightened as she was, would not consent to take a fraction more than was due to her and was obstinately unwilling to be content with less. It was not yet seven, she said, by a long way; she knew her rights and she would have them; and she was still arguing with me when a little low whistle sounded a good way off upon the hill. That was enough, and more than enough, for both of us.

Next moment we were both groping downstairs, leaving the candle by the empty chest; and the next we had opened the door and were in full retreat. We had not started a moment too soon. The fog was rapidly dispersing; already the moon shone quite clear on the high ground on either side; and it was only in the exact bottom of the dell and round the tavern door that a thin veil still hung unbroken to conceal the first steps of our escape. Far less than half-way to the hamlet, very little beyond the bottom of the hill, we must come forth into the moonlight. Nor was this all, for the sound of several footsteps running came already to our ears, and as we looked back in their direction, a light tossing to and fro and still rapidly advancing showed that one of the newcomers carried a lantern.
paragraphsZh: “给我钥匙，”我妈妈说；虽然锁很硬，但她还是转动了它，眨眼间就把盖子打开了。
一股浓烈的烟草和焦油味从里面升起，但上面什么也看不见，除了一套非常好的衣服，经过仔细的刷洗和折叠。我妈妈说，它们从来没有穿过。下面开始是杂物——一个象限、一个锡罐、几根烟草、两把非常漂亮的手枪、一块银条、一块旧西班牙手表和其他一些价值不大且大多是外国制造的小饰品、一对镶有黄铜的指南针，以及五六个奇怪的西印度贝壳。从那时起，我常常想知道，为什么他要在他流浪、有罪和狩猎的生活中随身携带这些贝壳。
与此同时，除了银子和小饰品之外，我们没有发现任何有价值的东西，而这些都没有妨碍我们。里面有一件旧船斗篷，用许多港口酒吧的海盐涂得发白。母亲不耐烦地把它拉起来，摆在我们面前的是箱子里最后的东西，一个用油布捆着的包裹，看起来像纸，还有一个帆布袋，一碰就发出金叮当的声音。
“我会让这些流氓知道我是一个诚实的女人，”我的母亲说。 “我会得到我的会费，一毛钱也不会多。帮我保管克罗斯利夫人的包。”她开始把水手包里的船长分数算到我手里的包里。
这是一件漫长而困难的事情，因为这些硬币来自不同的国家和大小——达布隆、路易·多布隆、几内亚、八枚硬币，还有我不知道还有什么，全都是随机摇晃在一起的。几尼也是最稀缺的，只有这些，我母亲才知道如何让她算数。
当我们走到一半的时候，我突然把手放在她的手臂上，因为在寂静的霜冻空气中，我听到了一种让我心都提到了嗓子眼的声音——盲人的手杖敲打结冰的道路的声音。它越来越近，我们屏住呼吸。然后它猛烈地敲在旅馆的门上，然后我们可以听到把手转动的声音，当这个可怜虫试图进去时，门闩嘎嘎作响；随后，屋内屋外陷入了良久的沉默。最后，敲击声又开始了，令我们难以形容的喜悦和感激的是，敲击声又慢慢消失，直到听不见。
“妈妈，”我说，“带上所有的东西，我们走吧。”因为我确信那扇锁着的门一定看起来很可疑，会把整个马蜂窝带到我们的耳朵里，尽管我很庆幸我把它锁上了，但没有人知道谁从未见过那个可怕的盲人。
但我的母亲，尽管她很害怕，但她不同意多拿一点她应得的，而且顽固地不愿意满足于少一点。她说，现在还不到七点。她知道自己的权利并且她会拥有这些权利；当她还在和我争论时，远处山上传来了一阵低沉的口哨声。这对我们俩来说已经足够了，而且绰绰有余。

下一刻我们都摸索着下楼，把蜡烛留在了空箱子旁；接下来我们打开门，全线撤退。我们开始的时间还不算太早。雾气正在迅速消散。月亮已经很清楚地照在两边的高地上了。只有在山谷的最底部和酒馆门的周围，一层薄薄的面纱仍然完整地挂着，以掩盖我们逃跑的第一步。距离小村庄还不到一半，离山脚不远，我们就必须来到月光下。不仅如此，我们的耳边已经传来了几声脚步声，当我们回头看向他们的方向时，一盏灯来回摇曳，仍在快速前进，表明其中一个新来的人提着灯笼。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 5
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: I had never seen the squire so near at hand. He was a tall man, over six feet high, and broad in proportion, and he had a bluff, rough-and-ready face, all roughened and reddened and lined in his long travels. His eyebrows were very black, and moved readily, and this gave him a look of some temper, not bad, you would say, but quick and high.
“Good evening, Dance,” says the doctor with a nod. “And good evening to you, friend Jim. What good wind brings you here?”

The supervisor stood up straight and stiff and told his story like a lesson; and you should have seen how the two gentlemen leaned forward and looked at each other, and forgot to smoke in their surprise and interest. When they heard how my mother went back to the inn, Dr. Livesey fairly slapped his thigh, and the squire cried “Bravo!” and broke his long pipe against the grate. Long before it was done, Mr. Trelawney (that, you will remember, was the squire’s name) had got up from his seat and was striding about the room, and the doctor, as if to hear the better, had taken off his powdered wig and sat there looking very strange indeed with his own close-cropped black poll.

“Mr. Dance,” said the squire, “you are a very noble fellow. And as for riding down that black, atrocious miscreant, I regard it as an act of virtue, sir, like stamping on a cockroach. This lad Hawkins is a trump, I perceive. Hawkins, will you ring that bell? Mr. Dance must have some ale.”
The doctor looked it all over, as if his fingers were itching to open it; but instead of doing that, he put it quietly in the pocket of his coat.
So a big pigeon pie was brought in and put on a sidetable, and I made a hearty supper, for I was as hungry as a hawk, while Mr. Dance was further complimented and at last dismissed.

“Heard of him!” cried the squire. “Heard of him, you say! He was the bloodthirstiest buccaneer that sailed. Blackbeard was a child to Flint. The Spaniards were so prodigiously afraid of him that, I tell you, sir, I was sometimes proud he was an Englishman. I’ve seen his top-sails with these eyes, off Trinidad, and the cowardly son of a rum-puncheon that I sailed with put back--put back, sir, into Port of Spain.”
“Money!” cried the squire. “Have you heard the story? What were these villains after but money? What do they care for but money? For what would they risk their rascal carcasses but money?”

“That we shall soon know,” replied the doctor. “But you are so confoundedly hot-headed and exclamatory that I cannot get a word in. What I want to know is this: Supposing that I have here in my pocket some clue to where Flint buried his treasure, will that treasure amount to much?”

“Amount, sir!” cried the squire. “It will amount to this: If we have the clue you talk about, I fit out a ship in Bristol dock, and take you and Hawkins here along, and I’ll have that treasure if I search a year.”
“Very well,” said the doctor. “Now, then, if Jim is agreeable, we’ll open the packet”; and he laid it before him on the table.
The bundle was sewn together, and the doctor had to get out his instrument case and cut the stitches with his medical scissors. It contained two things--a book and a sealed paper.

The squire and I were both peering over his shoulder as he opened it, for Dr. Livesey had kindly motioned me to come round from the side-table, where I had been eating, to enjoy the sport of the search. On the first page there were only some scraps of writing, such as a man with a pen in his hand might make for idleness or practice. One was the same as the tattoo mark, “Billy Bones his fancy”; then there was “Mr. W. Bones, mate,” “No more rum,” “Off Palm Key he got itt,” and some other snatches, mostly single words and unintelligible. I could not help wondering who it was that had “got itt,” and what “itt” was that he got. A knife in his back as like as not.
paragraphsZh: 我从来没有在这么近的地方见过乡绅。他身材高大，六英尺多高，比例宽阔，他有一张直率、粗糙的脸，在长途旅行中变得粗糙、发红、布满皱纹。他的眉毛很黑，而且很容易动，这让他看起来有些脾气，你可以说还不错，但又急又高。
“晚上好，丹斯，”医生点点头说道。 “晚上好，朋友吉姆。是什么好风把你吹到这里来的？”

主管站得笔直，僵硬地讲着他的故事，就像教训一样；你应该看到两位先生如何倾身向前，互相看着对方，却在惊讶和兴趣中忘记了抽烟。当他们听到我母亲如何回到客栈时，利夫西医生狠狠地拍了拍大腿，乡绅喊道：“好极了！”把他的长管子撞到了炉栅上。手术还没结束，特里劳尼先生（你会记得，那是乡绅的名字）就从座位上站起来，在房间里大步走来走去，而医生，好像是为了听清楚，摘下了撒了粉的假发，坐在那里，戴着他自己剪得很短的黑色头发，看上去确实很奇怪。
“丹斯先生，”乡绅说，“你是一个非常高贵的人。至于骑下那个黑色、残暴的恶棍，我认为这是一种美德，先生，就像踩蟑螂一样。我认为，霍金斯这个小伙子是王牌。霍金斯，你能按响那个铃吗？丹斯先生必须喝点麦芽酒。”
医生把它从头到尾地看了一遍，似乎手指都痒痒地想打开；但他没有这样做，而是悄悄地把它放进了外套口袋里。
于是，一个大鸽子馅饼被拿进来，放在了边桌上，我做了一顿丰盛的晚餐，因为我饿得像鹰一样，而丹斯先生则受到了进一步的称赞，最后被打发走了。
“听说过他！”乡绅叫道。 “你听说过他吗！他是航海中最嗜血的海盗。黑胡子是弗林特的孩子。西班牙人非常害怕他，我告诉你，先生，我有时为他是英国人而感到自豪。我用这些眼睛在特立尼达岛见过他的中帆，还有我航行时带着的朗姆酒潘趣酒的胆怯儿子——放回去，先生，进入西班牙港。”
“钱！”乡绅叫道。 “你听过这个故事吗？这些恶棍除了钱之外还追求什么？除了钱他们还关心什么？除了钱他们还愿意用自己的流氓尸体来冒险吗？”
“我们很快就会知道，”医生回答道。 “但你头脑发热，大喊大叫，我根本插不上话。我想知道的是：假设我口袋里有一些关于弗林特埋藏宝藏的线索，那份宝藏会值多少钱吗？”
“金额，先生！”乡绅叫道。 “这相当于：如果我们有你所说的线索，我在布里斯托尔码头布置一艘船，带你和霍金斯一起来这里，如果我搜寻一年，我就会得到那个宝藏。”
“很好，”医生说。 “那么，如果吉姆同意，我们就打开包裹”；他把它放在他面前的桌子上。
包裹被缝合在一起，医生不得不拿出仪器箱并用医用剪刀剪断缝线。里面有两件东西——一本书和一张密封的纸。

当乡绅打开门时，我和他都在他​​的肩膀上凝视着，因为利夫西博士友善地示意我从我一直在吃饭的边桌上过来，享受搜索的乐趣。第一页上只有一些字迹，就像一个人手里拿着笔可能会闲着或练习一样。一个与纹身标记相同，“比利·骨头他的幻想”；然后是“W. Bones 先生，伙计”、“不再有朗姆酒”、“他在棕榈岛得到了它”，以及其他一些片段，大部分是单个单词，难以理解。我不禁想知道是谁“得到了它”，以及他得到了什么“itt”。他的背后就像没有一把刀。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 6
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: I now felt for the first time the joy of exploration. The isle was uninhabited; my shipmates I had left behind, and nothing lived in front of me but dumb brutes and fowls. I turned hither and thither among the trees. Here and there were flowering plants, unknown to me; here and there I saw snakes, and one raised his head from a ledge of rock and hissed at me with a noise not unlike the spinning of a top. Little did I suppose that he was a deadly enemy and that the noise was the famous rattle.

Then I came to a long thicket of these oaklike trees--live, or evergreen, oaks, I heard afterwards they should be called--which grew low along the sand like brambles, the boughs curiously twisted, the foliage compact, like thatch. The thicket stretched down from the top of one of the sandy knolls, spreading and growing taller as it went, until it reached the margin of the broad, reedy fen, through which the nearest of the little rivers soaked its way into the anchorage. The marsh was steaming in the strong sun, and the outline of the Spy-glass trembled through the haze.

All at once there began to go a sort of bustle among the bulrushes; a wild duck flew up with a quack, another followed, and soon over the whole surface of the marsh a great cloud of birds hung screaming and circling in the air. I judged at once that some of my shipmates must be drawing near along the borders of the fen. Nor was I deceived, for soon I heard the very distant and low tones of a human voice, which, as I continued to give ear, grew steadily louder and nearer.
This put me in a great fear, and I crawled under cover of the nearest live-oak and squatted there, hearkening, as silent as a mouse.

Another voice answered, and then the first voice, which I now recognized to be Silver’s, once more took up the story and ran on for a long while in a stream, only now and again interrupted by the other. By the sound they must have been talking earnestly, and almost fiercely; but no distinct word came to my hearing.

At last the speakers seemed to have paused and perhaps to have sat down, for not only did they cease to draw any nearer, but the birds themselves began to grow more quiet and to settle again to their places in the swamp.

And now I began to feel that I was neglecting my business, that since I had been so foolhardy as to come ashore with these desperadoes, the least I could do was to overhear them at their councils, and that my plain and obvious duty was to draw as close as I could manage, under the favourable ambush of the crouching trees.
I could tell the direction of the speakers pretty exactly, not only by the sound of their voices but by the behaviour of the few birds that still hung in alarm above the heads of the intruders.

Crawling on all fours, I made steadily but slowly towards them, till at last, raising my head to an aperture among the leaves, I could see clear down into a little green dell beside the marsh, and closely set about with trees, where Long John Silver and another of the crew stood face to face in conversation.
The sun beat full upon them. Silver had thrown his hat beside him on the ground, and his great, smooth, blond face, all shining with heat, was lifted to the other man’s in a kind of appeal.
paragraphsZh: 我现在第一次感受到探索的乐趣。岛上无人居住。我把我的船友抛在了后面，在我面前除了愚蠢的畜生和家禽，什么也没有。我在树林里转来转去。到处都有我不认识的开花植物；我到处看到蛇，其中一条从岩石壁架上抬起头，对我发出嘶嘶声，发出类似于陀螺旋转的声音。我没想到他是一个致命的敌人，而且那声音就是著名的嘎嘎声。
然后我来到了一片长长的灌木丛，长满了像橡树一样的树——活的，或常绿的橡树，我后来听说它们应该被称为——它们像荆棘一样沿着沙子低矮地生长，树枝奇怪地扭曲，叶子紧凑，像茅草一样。灌木丛从一个沙丘的顶部延伸下来，越延伸越宽，越来越高，直到到达宽阔的芦苇沼泽的边缘，最近的一条小河穿过沼泽流入锚地。沼泽地在强烈的阳光下冒着热气，望远镜的轮廓在薄雾中颤抖。
突然，芦苇丛中开始热闹起来。一只野鸭嘎嘎地飞了起来，另一只野鸭紧随其后，很快整个沼泽地表面就出现了一大群鸟儿，尖叫着，在空中盘旋。我立刻判断，我的一些同船伙伴肯定已经沿着沼泽的边界逼近了。我也没有被欺骗，因为很快我就听到了非常遥远而低沉的人声，随着我继续侧耳倾听，声音逐渐变得越来越大，越来越近。
这让我非常害怕，我爬到最近的一棵活橡树的掩护下，蹲在那里，像老鼠一样安静地听着。
另一个声音回答了，然后第一个声音，我现在认出是西尔弗的声音，再次开始讲述这个故事，并持续了很长一段时间，只是时不时地被另一个声音打断。从声音来看，他们一定是在认真地、几乎激烈地交谈着。但我没有听到任何明确的词。
最后，说话者似乎停了下来，也许已经坐下了，因为他们不仅不再靠近，而且鸟儿本身也开始变得更加安静，并再次安顿在沼泽中的位置。
现在我开始觉得我忽视了我的事情，既然我如此鲁莽地和这些亡命之徒一起上岸，我至少能做的就是在他们的会议上偷听他们的声音，而我明显而明显的职责就是在蹲伏的树木的有利伏击下尽我所能地靠近。
我可以非常准确地辨别说话者的方向，不仅通过他们的声音，还通过仍然惊恐地悬挂在入侵者头顶上方的几只鸟的行为。
我四肢着地爬行，稳步但缓慢地朝他们走去，直到最后，抬起头到树叶间的一个缝隙，我可以清楚地看到沼泽旁边的一个绿色小山谷，周围都是树木，长约翰·西尔弗和另一名船员面对面站着交谈。
阳光照在他们身上。西尔弗把他的帽子扔到了他旁边的地上，他那张光滑的金发大脸，闪烁着热量，带着一种恳求的神情，被举向另一个人的脸。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 7
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: “Well,” said I, “I believe I understand. You have something to propose, and you wish to see the squire or the doctor, and you’re to be found where I found you. Is that all?”

“You won’t forget?” he inquired anxiously. “Precious sight, and reasons of his own, says you. Reasons of his own; that’s the mainstay; as between man and man. Well, then”--still holding me--“I reckon you can go, Jim. And, Jim, if you was to see Silver, you wouldn’t go for to sell Ben Gunn? Wild horses wouldn’t draw it from you? No, says you. And if them pirates camp ashore, Jim, what would you say but there’d be widders in the morning?”

Here he was interrupted by a loud report, and a cannonball came tearing through the trees and pitched in the sand not a hundred yards from where we two were talking. The next moment each of us had taken to his heels in a different direction.

For a good hour to come frequent reports shook the island, and balls kept crashing through the woods. I moved from hiding-place to hiding-place, always pursued, or so it seemed to me, by these terrifying missiles. But towards the end of the bombardment, though still I durst not venture in the direction of the stockade, where the balls fell oftenest, I had begun, in a manner, to pluck up my heart again, and after a long detour to the east, crept down among the shore-side trees.

The sun had just set, the sea breeze was rustling and tumbling in the woods and ruffling the grey surface of the anchorage; the tide, too, was far out, and great tracts of sand lay uncovered; the air, after the heat of the day, chilled me through my jacket.

The HISPANIOLA still lay where she had anchored; but, sure enough, there was the Jolly Roger--the black flag of piracy--flying from her peak. Even as I looked, there came another red flash and another report that sent the echoes clattering, and one more round-shot whistled through the air. It was the last of the cannonade.

I lay for some time watching the bustle which succeeded the attack. Men were demolishing something with axes on the beach near the stockade--the poor jolly-boat, I afterwards discovered. Away, near the mouth of the river, a great fire was glowing among the trees, and between that point and the ship one of the gigs kept coming and going, the men, whom I had seen so gloomy, shouting at the oars like children. But there was a sound in their voices which suggested rum.

At length I thought I might return towards the stockade. I was pretty far down on the low, sandy spit that encloses the anchorage to the east, and is joined at half-water to Skeleton Island; and now, as I rose to my feet, I saw, some distance further down the spit and rising from among low bushes, an isolated rock, pretty high, and peculiarly white in colour. It occurred to me that this might be the white rock of which Ben Gunn had spoken and that some day or other a boat might be wanted and I should know where to look for one.
Then I skirted among the woods until I had regained the rear, or shoreward side, of the stockade, and was soon warmly welcomed by the faithful party.

I had soon told my story and began to look about me. The log-house was made of unsquared trunks of pine--roof, walls, and floor. The latter stood in several places as much as a foot or a foot and a half above the surface of the sand. There was a porch at the door, and under this porch the little spring welled up into an artificial basin of a rather odd kind--no other than a great ship’s kettle of iron, with the bottom knocked out, and sunk “to her bearings,” as the captain said, among the sand.
paragraphsZh: “好吧，”我说，“我想我明白了。你有件事要提出，你想见见乡绅或医生，然后就可以在我找到你的地方找到你。就这些了吗？”
“你不会忘记吧？”他焦急地问道。 “珍贵的视力，还有他自己的理由，你说。他自己的理由；这是人与人之间的支柱。好吧，那么”——仍然抱着我——“我想你可以走了，吉姆。还有，吉姆，如果你要见西尔弗，你不会去卖本·冈恩吗？野马不会从你身上夺走它？不，你说。如果海盗在岸上扎营，吉姆，你会怎么说，但会有更多的人。早上吗？
说到这里，他被一声响亮的报告打断了，一颗炮弹穿过树林飞来，落在距离我们两人谈话的地方不到一百码的沙子里。下一刻，我们每个人都朝不同的方向逃跑了。
接下来的一个小时里，频繁的报道震动了整个岛屿，球不断在树林中坠落。我从一个藏身之处转移到另一个藏身之处，总是被这些可怕的导弹追赶，至少在我看来是这样。但在炮击即将结束时，虽然我仍然不敢冒险向最常落下炮弹的栅栏方向走去，但我在某种程度上又开始鼓起勇气，绕了很长一段路向东，爬到了岸边的树林里。
太阳刚刚落山，海风在树林里沙沙翻滚，吹皱了锚地灰色的地面；潮水也退得很远，大片的沙地裸露在外。经过一天的炎热之后，空气透过夹克让我感到凉爽。
伊斯帕尼奥拉号仍然停泊在她抛锚的地方；但是，果然，海盗旗——海盗的黑旗——从她的巅峰飘扬着。就在我看的时候，又传来了一道红色闪光和另一声发出回声的报告，又一发子弹在空中呼啸而过。这是最后一次炮击。
我躺了一会儿，看着袭击成功后的喧嚣。人们正在栅栏附近的海滩上用斧头拆除一些东西——后来我发现那是可怜的救生艇。远处，在河口附近，树林里熊熊燃烧，在那个点和船之间，一艘平底艇不停地来来往往，我看到的那些人，他们脸色阴沉，像孩子一样对着桨大喊大叫。但他们的声音听起来像是朗姆酒。
最后我想我可以返回寨子了。我在很远的地方，位于低洼的沙嘴上，它包围了东边的锚地，并在半水处与骷髅岛相连。现在，当我站起来时，我看到，在沙嘴下方不远的地方，从低矮的灌木丛中升起一块孤立的岩石，相当高，颜色特别白。我突然想到，这可能就是本·古恩所说的白色岩石，总有一天可能会需要一艘船，而我应该知道去哪里找一艘。
然后我在树林中绕行，直到重新回到栅栏的后方，或者说靠岸的一侧，很快就受到了忠实队伍的热烈欢迎。
我很快就讲述了我的故事并开始审视自己。木屋的屋顶、墙壁和地板都是用不方形的松树干建造的。后者有好几个地方都高出沙子表面一英尺或一英尺半。门口有一个门廊，门廊下的小泉水涌入一个相当奇怪的人造盆地——无非是一艘大船的铁壶，底部被撞坏了，正如船长所说，“向她的方位”沉入沙中。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 8
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: The next thing I laid hold of was a brace of pistols, and as I already had a powder-horn and bullets, I felt myself well supplied with arms.

As for the scheme I had in my head, it was not a bad one in itself. I was to go down the sandy spit that divides the anchorage on the east from the open sea, find the white rock I had observed last evening, and ascertain whether it was there or not that Ben Gunn had hidden his boat, a thing quite worth doing, as I still believe. But as I was certain I should not be allowed to leave the enclosure, my only plan was to take French leave and slip out when nobody was watching, and that was so bad a way of doing it as made the thing itself wrong. But I was only a boy, and I had made my mind up.

Well, as things at last fell out, I found an admirable opportunity. The squire and Gray were busy helping the captain with his bandages, the coast was clear, I made a bolt for it over the stockade and into the thickest of the trees, and before my absence was observed I was out of cry of my companions.
This was my second folly, far worse than the first, as I left but two sound men to guard the house; but like the first, it was a help towards saving all of us.

I took my way straight for the east coast of the island, for I was determined to go down the sea side of the spit to avoid all chance of observation from the anchorage. It was already late in the afternoon, although still warm and sunny. As I continued to thread the tall woods, I could hear from far before me not only the continuous thunder of the surf, but a certain tossing of foliage and grinding of boughs which showed me the sea breeze had set in higher than usual. Soon cool draughts of air began to reach me, and a few steps farther I came forth into the open borders of the grove, and saw the sea lying blue and sunny to the horizon and the surf tumbling and tossing its foam along the beach.

I have never seen the sea quiet round Treasure Island. The sun might blaze overhead, the air be without a breath, the surface smooth and blue, but still these great rollers would be running along all the external coast, thundering and thundering by day and night; and I scarce believe there is one spot in the island where a man would be out of earshot of their noise.
I walked along beside the surf with great enjoyment, till, thinking I was now got far enough to the south, I took the cover of some thick bushes and crept warily up to the ridge of the spit.

Behind me was the sea, in front the anchorage. The sea breeze, as though it had the sooner blown itself out by its unusual violence, was already at an end; it had been succeeded by light, variable airs from the south and south-east, carrying great banks of fog; and the anchorage, under lee of Skeleton Island, lay still and leaden as when first we entered it. The HISPANIOLA, in that unbroken mirror, was exactly portrayed from the truck to the waterline, the Jolly Roger hanging from her peak.

Alongside lay one of the gigs, Silver in the stern-sheets--him I could always recognize--while a couple of men were leaning over the stern bulwarks, one of them with a red cap--the very rogue that I had seen some hours before stride-legs upon the palisade. Apparently they were talking and laughing, though at that distance--upwards of a mile--I could, of course, hear no word of what was said. All at once there began the most horrid, unearthly screaming, which at first startled me badly, though I had soon remembered the voice of Captain Flint and even thought I could make out the bird by her bright plumage as she sat perched upon her master’s wrist.
paragraphsZh: 接下来我拿到的是一对手枪，而且由于我已经有了火药喇叭和子弹，我感觉自己的武器装备充足。
至于我脑子里的这个计划，本身并不坏。我要沿着将东部锚地与公海分开的沙嘴下去，找到我昨晚观察到的白色岩石，并确定本·古恩是否在那里隐藏了他的船，这是一件非常值得做的事情，我仍然相信。但由于我确信我不应该被允许离开围栏，所以我唯一的计划就是在没有人在场的情况下请法国假并溜出去，这是一种非常糟糕的做法，因为这让事情本身变得错误。但我只是个男孩，我已经下定决心了。
好吧，当事情最终失败时，我发现了一个令人钦佩的机会。乡绅和格雷正忙着帮助船长包扎绷带，海岸已经畅通无阻，我在栅栏上拉了一个螺栓，进入了最茂密的树林，在发现我不在之前，我的同伴们已经不再哭泣了。
这是我的第二个愚蠢行为，比第一个更糟糕，因为我只留下了两个健全的人看守房子；但和第一个一样，它有助于拯救我们所有人。
我径直前往岛的东海岸，因为我决定沿着沙嘴的海边走，以避免从锚地观察到的所有机会。虽然已经是下午晚些时候了，但阳光依然温暖。当我继续穿过高大的树林时，我不仅能听到前面远处传来的连续不断的海浪轰鸣声，还有树叶的摇曳声和树枝的摩擦声，这表明海风比平时吹得更强了。很快，凉爽的气流开始吹到我身上，我又走了几步，来到了树林的开阔边界，看到蔚蓝、阳光明媚的大海一直延伸到地平线，海浪翻滚，沿着海滩抛洒泡沫。
我从来没有见过金银岛周围的大海如此安静。太阳可能在头顶上闪耀，空气没有呼吸，表面光滑而蓝色，但这些巨大的滚轴仍然会沿着整个外部海岸运行，白天和晚上都发出雷鸣般的声音；我几乎不相信岛上有一个地方可以让人们听不到他们的噪音。
我非常高兴地沿着海浪走着，直到我以为我现在已经到了南方足够远的地方，我就在一些茂密的灌木丛的掩护下小心翼翼地爬到了沙嘴的山脊上。
身后是大海，前方是锚地。海风仿佛因其异常的猛烈而很快就被吹散了，但现在已经结束了。紧随其后的是来自南方和东南方的微风，多变的气流，带来大片的雾气。位于骷髅岛背风处的锚地一动不动，就像我们第一次进入它时一样。在那面完整的镜子里，伊斯帕尼奥拉号从卡车到吃水线都被准确地描绘出来，海盗旗悬挂在她的船顶上。

旁边躺着一艘平底艇，西尔弗在船尾板上——我总能认出他——同时有几个人靠在船尾舷墙上，其中一个戴着红色帽子——正是我在几个小时前看到的那个大步走在栅栏上的盗贼。显然他们正在有说有笑，尽管在那么远的地方——一英里以上——我当然听不到他们在说什么。突然，最可怕的、超凡脱俗的尖叫声开始了，一开始把我吓了一跳，尽管我很快就想起了弗林特船长的声音，甚至认为我可以通过她明亮的羽毛辨认出那只鸟，因为她坐在主人的手腕上。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 9
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: I opened my eyes at once. All round me were little ripples, combing over with a sharp, bristling sound and slightly phosphorescent. The HISPANIOLA herself, a few yards in whose wake I was still being whirled along, seemed to stagger in her course, and I saw her spars toss a little against the blackness of the night; nay, as I looked longer, I made sure she also was wheeling to the southward.

I glanced over my shoulder, and my heart jumped against my ribs. There, right behind me, was the glow of the camp-fire. The current had turned at right angles, sweeping round along with it the tall schooner and the little dancing coracle; ever quickening, ever bubbling higher, ever muttering louder, it went spinning through the narrows for the open sea.

Suddenly the schooner in front of me gave a violent yaw, turning, perhaps, through twenty degrees; and almost at the same moment one shout followed another from on board; I could hear feet pounding on the companion ladder and I knew that the two drunkards had at last been interrupted in their quarrel and awakened to a sense of their disaster.

I lay down flat in the bottom of that wretched skiff and devoutly recommended my spirit to its Maker. At the end of the straits, I made sure we must fall into some bar of raging breakers, where all my troubles would be ended speedily; and though I could, perhaps, bear to die, I could not bear to look upon my fate as it approached.

So I must have lain for hours, continually beaten to and fro upon the billows, now and again wetted with flying sprays, and never ceasing to expect death at the next plunge. Gradually weariness grew upon me; a numbness, an occasional stupor, fell upon my mind even in the midst of my terrors, until sleep at last supervened and in my sea-tossed coracle I lay and dreamed of home and the old Admiral Benbow.

It was broad day when I awoke and found myself tossing at the south-west end of Treasure Island. The sun was up but was still hid from me behind the great bulk of the Spy-glass, which on this side descended almost to the sea in formidable cliffs.

Haulbowline Head and Mizzenmast Hill were at my elbow, the hill bare and dark, the head bound with cliffs forty or fifty feet high and fringed with great masses of fallen rock. I was scarce a quarter of a mile to seaward, and it was my first thought to paddle in and land.

That notion was soon given over. Among the fallen rocks the breakers spouted and bellowed; loud reverberations, heavy sprays flying and falling, succeeded one another from second to second; and I saw myself, if I ventured nearer, dashed to death upon the rough shore or spending my strength in vain to scale the beetling crags.

Nor was that all, for crawling together on flat tables of rock or letting themselves drop into the sea with loud reports I beheld huge slimy monsters--soft snails, as it were, of incredible bigness--two or three score of them together, making the rocks to echo with their barkings.

I have understood since that they were sea lions, and entirely harmless. But the look of them, added to the difficulty of the shore and the high running of the surf, was more than enough to disgust me of that landing-place. I felt willing rather to starve at sea than to confront such perils.

In the meantime I had a better chance, as I supposed, before me. North of Haulbowline Head, the land runs in a long way, leaving at low tide a long stretch of yellow sand. To the north of that, again, there comes another cape--Cape of the Woods, as it was marked upon the chart--buried in tall green pines, which descended to the margin of the sea.
paragraphsZh: 我立刻睁开了眼睛。我的周围泛起细小的涟漪，伴随着尖锐、刺耳的声音，略带磷光。伊斯帕尼奥拉号本身，在几码远的地方，我仍在她的尾迹中旋转，似乎在她的航向中摇摇欲坠，我看到她的桅杆在夜色的黑暗中轻微地摇晃；不仅如此，当我看得更远时，我确信她也在向南行驶。
我回头看了一眼，我的心猛地跳到了肋骨上。就在我身后，有篝火的光芒。水流已经转了直角，一起扫过那艘高大的纵帆船和那只跳舞的小圆舟。它的速度越来越快，气泡越来越高，咕哝声越来越响，它旋转着穿过狭窄的海域，驶向大海。
突然，我前面的纵帆船猛烈地偏航，大约转了二十度；几乎就在同一时刻，船上又传来一声叫喊。我能听到同伴梯子上的脚步声，我知道这两个酒鬼的争吵终于被打断了，并意识到了他们的灾难。
我平躺在那艘可怜的小船的底部，虔诚地向它的创造者推荐我的灵魂。在海峡的尽头，我确信我们一定会掉进汹涌的海浪中，在那里我所有的麻烦都会很快结束。虽然我也许可以忍受死亡，但我无法忍受看着我的命运即将来临。
所以我一定躺了几个小时，不断地在波涛上来来回回，时不时地被飞溅的水花弄湿，并且从未停止过在下一次跳水时死亡。我渐渐感到疲倦。即使在我的恐惧之中，一种麻木，偶尔的昏迷，也降临在我的脑海里，直到最后我睡着了，我躺在我那被海浪翻腾的小船里，梦见了家乡和老海军上将本博。
当我醒来时，天已经大亮了，我发现自己在金银岛的西南端翻来覆去。太阳已经升起，但我仍然躲在巨大的望远镜后面，望远镜的这一侧几乎在可怕的悬崖上下降到大海。
Haulbowline Head和Mizzenmast Hill就在我的肘部，山上光秃秃的，黑暗的，山头周围是四十或五十英尺高的悬崖，周围是大量的落石。我距离大海还不到四分之一英里，我的第一个念头就是划桨登陆。
这个想法很快就被放弃了。在落下的岩石中，海浪喷水咆哮；巨大的回响、猛烈的水花飞溅、落下，一秒接着一秒接二连三地发生。我看到自己，如果我冒险靠近一点，就会在崎岖的海岸上冲死，或者徒劳地耗尽我的力量去攀登甲虫般的峭壁。
这还不是全部，因为我在平坦的岩石上一起爬行，或者让自己掉进海里，发出响亮的声音，我看到了巨大的粘糊糊的怪物——软蜗牛，可以说是大得令人难以置信——它们有两到三只在一起，让岩石与它们的吠声相呼应。
我从那时起就明白它们是海狮，完全无害。但他们的样子，再加上海岸的困难和海浪的高涨，足以让我对那个登陆地点感到厌恶。我宁愿在海上挨饿，也不愿面对这样的危险。
与此同时，正如我所想，我面前有一个更好的机会。 Haulbowline Head以北，陆地绵延很长，退潮时留下一大片黄沙。在那儿的北面，又出现了另一个海角——海图上标出的“森林海角”——埋藏在高大的绿色松树中，一直延伸到大海的边缘。

title: Treasure Island · 选段 10
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
paragraphs: This brought me near to where I had encountered Ben Gunn, the maroon; and I walked more circumspectly, keeping an eye on every side. The dusk had come nigh hand completely, and as I opened out the cleft between the two peaks, I became aware of a wavering glow against the sky, where, as I judged, the man of the island was cooking his supper before a roaring fire. And yet I wondered, in my heart, that he should show himself so careless. For if I could see this radiance, might it not reach the eyes of Silver himself where he camped upon the shore among the marshes?

Gradually the night fell blacker; it was all I could do to guide myself even roughly towards my destination; the double hill behind me and the Spy-glass on my right hand loomed faint and fainter; the stars were few and pale; and in the low ground where I wandered I kept tripping among bushes and rolling into sandy pits.

Suddenly a kind of brightness fell about me. I looked up; a pale glimmer of moonbeams had alighted on the summit of the Spy-glass, and soon after I saw something broad and silvery moving low down behind the trees, and knew the moon had risen.

With this to help me, I passed rapidly over what remained to me of my journey, and sometimes walking, sometimes running, impatiently drew near to the stockade. Yet, as I began to thread the grove that lies before it, I was not so thoughtless but that I slacked my pace and went a trifle warily. It would have been a poor end of my adventures to get shot down by my own party in mistake.

The moon was climbing higher and higher, its light began to fall here and there in masses through the more open districts of the wood, and right in front of me a glow of a different colour appeared among the trees. It was red and hot, and now and again it was a little darkened--as it were, the embers of a bonfire smouldering.

At last I came right down upon the borders of the clearing. The western end was already steeped in moonshine; the rest, and the block house itself, still lay in a black shadow chequered with long silvery streaks of light. On the other side of the house an immense fire had burned itself into clear embers and shed a steady, red reverberation, contrasted strongly with the mellow paleness of the moon. There was not a soul stirring nor a sound beside the noises of the breeze.

I stopped, with much wonder in my heart, and perhaps a little terror also. It had not been our way to build great fires; we were, indeed, by the captain’s orders, somewhat niggardly of firewood, and I began to fear that something had gone wrong while I was absent.
I stole round by the eastern end, keeping close in shadow, and at a convenient place, where the darkness was thickest, crossed the palisade.

To make assurance surer, I got upon my hands and knees and crawled, without a sound, towards the corner of the house. As I drew nearer, my heart was suddenly and greatly lightened. It is not a pleasant noise in itself, and I have often complained of it at other times, but just then it was like music to hear my friends snoring together so loud and peaceful in their sleep. The sea-cry of the watch, that beautiful “All’s well,” never fell more reassuringly on my ear.

In the meantime, there was no doubt of one thing; they kept an infamous bad watch. If it had been Silver and his lads that were now creeping in on them, not a soul would have seen daybreak. That was what it was, thought I, to have the captain wounded; and again I blamed myself sharply for leaving them in that danger with so few to mount guard.
paragraphsZh: 这让我很接近遇到栗色本·冈恩的地方；我走路更加小心，留意四周。黄昏已经完全来临，当我打开两座山峰之间的裂缝时，我意识到天空中有一道摇曳的光芒，据我判断，岛上的人正在熊熊的炉火前煮晚饭。但我心里却纳闷，他竟然表现得如此粗心。因为如果我能看到这种光芒，它是否不会到达他在沼泽地岸边扎营的西尔弗本人的眼睛？
夜渐渐黑了；我所能做的就是引导自己走向目的地，哪怕只是粗略地引导自己。我身后的双山和我右手上的望远镜变得越来越模糊。星星稀少而苍白；在我徘徊的低地里，我总是在灌木丛中绊倒，滚进沙坑里。
突然，一种光明笼罩着我。我抬头一看；一道苍白的月光落在望远镜的山顶上，不久之后我看到一个宽阔而银色的东西在树后低低地移动，我知道月亮已经升起来了。
有了这个的帮助，我飞快地走过了剩下的路程，时而走，时而跑，不耐烦地靠近了寨子。然而，当我开始穿过它前面的小树林时，我并没有那么粗心，而是放慢了脚步，走得有点小心翼翼。如果我的冒险被我自己的队伍错误地击落，那将是一个糟糕的结局。
月亮爬得越来越高，它的光芒开始大量地穿过树林中更开阔的区域，在我面前的树林中出现了一种不同颜色的光芒。它又红又热，时不时变得有点暗——就像篝火闷烧的余烬。
我终于来到了空地的边界。西端已经沐浴在月光之中。其余部分，以及街区房屋本身，仍然躺在黑色的阴影中，上面布满了长长的银色光线。房子的另一边，一场大火已经烧成了清晰的余烬，发出稳定的红色回响，与柔和苍白的月亮形成鲜明对比。除了微风的声音之外，没有任何灵魂的搅动，也没有任何声音。
我停了下来，心中充满了惊奇，也许还有一点恐惧。这不是我们生火的方式；事实上，按照船长的命令，我们有点吝惜柴火，我开始担心我不在的时候出了什么问题。
我从东端偷偷绕过，紧贴阴影，在一个方便的地方，黑暗最浓的地方，越过了栅栏。
为了更确定，我用手和膝盖爬起来，无声地向房子的角落爬去。当我走近的时候，我的心突然大大地轻松了。这本身并不是一种令人愉快的噪音，我在其他时候也经常抱怨它，但就在那时，听到我的朋友们在睡梦中一起打呼噜，如此响亮而平静，就像音乐一样。腕表的大海呐喊声，那句美丽的“一切都好”，在我耳边响起，从未如此令人安心。
与此同时，有一件事是毫无疑问的：他们的守望不善是臭名昭著的。如果是西尔弗和他的小伙子们正在悄悄向他们袭来，那么没有人会看到黎明。我想，船长受伤就是这样的。我再一次严厉地责备自己，让他们处于危险之中，而护卫的人却如此之少。

title: The Lost World · 选段 4
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: Half an hour later I was seated in the newspaper office with a huge tome in front of me, which had been opened at the article "Weissmann versus Darwin," with the sub heading, "Spirited Protest at Vienna. Lively Proceedings."  My scientific education having been somewhat neglected, I was unable to follow the whole argument, but it was evident that the English Professor had handled his subject in a very aggressive fashion, and had thoroughly annoyed his Continental colleagues.  "Protests," "Uproar," and "General appeal to the Chairman" were three of the first brackets which caught my eye.  Most of the matter might have been written in Chinese for any definite meaning that it conveyed to my brain.

"If I could only get a single good, meaty sentence which seemed to convey some sort of definite human idea, it would serve my turn.  Ah, yes, this one will do.  I seem in a vague way almost to understand it. I'll copy it out.  This shall be my link with the terrible Professor."
"Well, yes; I propose to write to him.  If I could frame the letter here, and use your address it would give atmosphere."
It took some doing, but I flatter myself that it wasn't such a bad job when it was finished.  I read it aloud to the critical bacteriologist with some pride in my handiwork.

"DEAR PROFESSOR CHALLENGER," it said, "As a humble student of Nature, I have always taken the most profound interest in your speculations as to the differences between Darwin and Weissmann.  I have recently had occasion to refresh my memory by re-reading----"

--"by re-reading your masterly address at Vienna.  That lucid and admirable statement seems to be the last word in the matter.  There is one sentence in it, however--namely:  'I protest strongly against the insufferable and entirely dogmatic assertion that each separate id is a microcosm possessed of an historical architecture elaborated slowly through the series of generations.' Have you no desire, in view of later research, to modify this statement?  Do you not think that it is over-accentuated?  With your permission, I would ask the favor of an interview, as I feel strongly upon the subject, and have certain suggestions which I could only elaborate in a personal conversation. With your consent, I trust to have the honor of calling at eleven o'clock the day after to-morrow (Wednesday) morning.
"To get there.  Once I am in his room I may see some opening.  I may even go the length of open confession.  If he is a sportsman he will be tickled."

"Tickled, indeed!  He's much more likely to do the tickling.  Chain mail, or an American football suit--that's what you'll want.  Well, good-bye.  I'll have the answer for you here on Wednesday morning--if he ever deigns to answer you.  He is a violent, dangerous, cantankerous character, hated by everyone who comes across him, and the butt of the students, so far as they dare take a liberty with him.  Perhaps it would be best for you if you never heard from the fellow at all."

My friend's fear or hope was not destined to be realized.  When I called on Wednesday there was a letter with the West Kensington postmark upon it, and my name scrawled across the envelope in a handwriting which looked like a barbed-wire railing.  The contents were as follows:--

"SIR,--I have duly received your note, in which you claim to endorse my views, although I am not aware that they are dependent upon endorsement either from you or anyone else.  You have ventured to use the word 'speculation' with regard to my statement upon the subject of Darwinism, and I would call your attention to the fact that such a word in such a connection is offensive to a degree.  The context convinces me, however, that you have sinned rather through ignorance and tactlessness than through malice, so I am content to pass the matter by.  You quote an isolated sentence from my lecture, and appear to have some difficulty in understanding it.  I should have thought that only a sub-human intelligence could have failed to grasp the point, but if it really needs amplification I shall consent to see you at the hour named, though visits and visitors of every sort are exceeding distasteful to me.  As to your suggestion that I may modify my opinion, I would have you know that it is not my habit to do so after a deliberate expression of my mature views.  You will kindly show the envelope of this letter to my man, Austin, when you call, as he has to take every precaution to shield me from the intrusive rascals who call themselves 'journalists.'
paragraphsZh: 半小时后，我坐在报社办公室里，面前放着一本巨著，打开时是“魏斯曼与达尔文”一文，副标题是“维也纳的激烈抗议。热闹的会议记录。” 我的科学教育在某种程度上被忽视了，我无法理解整个论点，但很明显，英国教授以一种非常激进的方式处理他的主题，并彻底惹恼了他的大陆同事。 “抗议”、“骚乱”和“向主席发出的一般性呼吁”是引起我注意的前三个括号。 大部分内容可能是用中文写的，因为它向我的大脑传达了明确的含义。
“如果我只能得到一个好的、充实的句子，它似乎传达了某种明确的人类思想，那就轮到我了。啊，是的，这个就可以了。我似乎以一种模糊的方式几乎理解了它。我会把它抄下来。这将是我与可怕的教授的联系。”
“嗯，是的；我打算写信给他。如果我能把这封信装在这里，并使用你的地址，那就会营造气氛。”
这需要一些努力，但我自以为完成后这并不是一项糟糕的工作。 我向那位挑剔的细菌学家大声朗读它，对我的手艺感到有些自豪。
“亲爱的挑战者教授，”它说，“作为一名谦虚的自然学生，我一直对您关于达尔文和魏斯曼之间差异的推测抱有最浓厚的兴趣。最近我有机会通过重读来刷新我的记忆——”

——“重读你在维也纳的精彩演讲。那句清晰而令人钦佩的陈述似乎是这件事的定论。然而，其中有一句话——即：‘我强烈反对这种令人难以忍受的、完全教条的断言，即每一个独立的身份都是一个缩影，拥有一个经过几代人慢慢阐述的历史建筑。’鉴于后来的研究，您是否不想修改这个说法？ 你不觉得它被过分强调了吗？ 如果您允许，我会请求接受采访，因为我对这个主题有强烈的感受，并且有一些只能在个人谈话中详细阐述的建议。如果您同意的话，我相信我有幸在后天（星期三）上午十一点钟打电话。
“到达那里。 一旦我进入他的房间，我可能会看到一些空缺。 我什至可能会公开坦白。 如果他是一名运动员，他会被逗乐的。”
“确实很痒！ 他更有可能去挠痒痒。 锁子甲，或者美式橄榄球服——这就是你想要的。 好吧，再见。 周三早上我会在这里给你答案——如果他愿意回答你的话。 他是一个暴力、危险、脾气暴躁的人，每个遇到他的人都讨厌他，而学生们只要胆敢对他出言不逊，他就会成为他们的屁股。 如果你根本没有收到这个家伙的消息，也许对你来说是最好的。”
我朋友的恐惧或希望注定不会实现。 当我周三打电话时，收到了一封带有西肯辛顿邮戳的信，信封上潦草地写着我的名字，字迹看起来像铁丝网栏杆。 内容如下：——

“先生，我已正式收到您的说明，您在其中声称支持我的观点，尽管我不知道这些观点取决于您或其他任何人的认可。您在我关于达尔文主义主题的陈述中大胆使用了“推测”一词，我想提请您注意这样一个事实，即在这种联系中使用这样的词在一定程度上是令人反感的。然而，上下文使我相信，您是由于无知而犯了罪。我很乐意从我的演讲中引用一个孤立的句子，而且似乎很难理解它，但如果确实需要放大，我会同意在指定的时间见到你，尽管各种拜访和访客都让我非常不喜欢，但我想让你知道，在一段时间后这样做不是我的习惯。当你打电话时，请将这封信的信封交给我的人奥斯汀，因为他必须采取一切预防措施来保护我免受那些自称“记者”的流氓的侵扰。

title: The Lost World · 选段 5
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: I began to feel uneasy.  Perhaps, after all, I had been premature in my acquiescence.  Then I had a sudden happy thought.

"He is not a popular person, the genial Challenger," said he.  "A lot of people have accounts to settle with him.  I should say he is about the best-hated man in London.  If the medical students turn out there will be no end of a rag.  I don't want to get into a bear-garden."

When we arrived at the hall we found a much greater concourse than I had expected.  A line of electric broughams discharged their little cargoes of white-bearded professors, while the dark stream of humbler pedestrians, who crowded through the arched door-way, showed that the audience would be popular as well as scientific.  Indeed, it became evident to us as soon as we had taken our seats that a youthful and even boyish spirit was abroad in the gallery and the back portions of the hall.  Looking behind me, I could see rows of faces of the familiar medical student type.  Apparently the great hospitals had each sent down their contingent.  The behavior of the audience at present was good-humored, but mischievous.  Scraps of popular songs were chorused with an enthusiasm which was a strange prelude to a scientific lecture, and there was already a tendency to personal chaff which promised a jovial evening to others, however embarrassing it might be to the recipients of these dubious honors.

Thus, when old Doctor Meldrum, with his well-known curly-brimmed opera-hat, appeared upon the platform, there was such a universal query of "Where DID you get that tile?" that he hurriedly removed it, and concealed it furtively under his chair.  When gouty Professor Wadley limped down to his seat there were general affectionate inquiries from all parts of the hall as to the exact state of his poor toe, which caused him obvious embarrassment.  The greatest demonstration of all, however, was at the entrance of my new acquaintance, Professor Challenger, when he passed down to take his place at the extreme end of the front row of the platform.  Such a yell of welcome broke forth when his black beard first protruded round the corner that I began to suspect Tarp Henry was right in his surmise, and that this assemblage was there not merely for the sake of the lecture, but because it had got rumored abroad that the famous Professor would take part in the proceedings.

There was some sympathetic laughter on his entrance among the front benches of well-dressed spectators, as though the demonstration of the students in this instance was not unwelcome to them.  That greeting was, indeed, a frightful outburst of sound, the uproar of the carnivora cage when the step of the bucket-bearing keeper is heard in the distance.  There was an offensive tone in it, perhaps, and yet in the main it struck me as mere riotous outcry, the noisy reception of one who amused and interested them, rather than of one they disliked or despised.  Challenger smiled with weary and tolerant contempt, as a kindly man would meet the yapping of a litter of puppies.  He sat slowly down, blew out his chest, passed his hand caressingly down his beard, and looked with drooping eyelids and supercilious eyes at the crowded hall before him.  The uproar of his advent had not yet died away when Professor Ronald Murray, the chairman, and Mr. Waldron, the lecturer, threaded their way to the front, and the proceedings began.

Professor Murray will, I am sure, excuse me if I say that he has the common fault of most Englishmen of being inaudible.  Why on earth people who have something to say which is worth hearing should not take the slight trouble to learn how to make it heard is one of the strange mysteries of modern life.  Their methods are as reasonable as to try to pour some precious stuff from the spring to the reservoir through a non-conducting pipe, which could by the least effort be opened. Professor Murray made several profound remarks to his white tie and to the water-carafe upon the table, with a humorous, twinkling aside to the silver candlestick upon his right.  Then he sat down, and Mr. Waldron, the famous popular lecturer, rose amid a general murmur of applause.  He was a stern, gaunt man, with a harsh voice, and an aggressive manner, but he had the merit of knowing how to assimilate the ideas of other men, and to pass them on in a way which was intelligible and even interesting to the lay public, with a happy knack of being funny about the most unlikely objects, so that the precession of the Equinox or the formation of a vertebrate became a highly humorous process as treated by him.
paragraphsZh: 我开始感到不安。 或许，我的默许毕竟为时过早。 然后我突然有一个愉快的想法。
“他不是一个受欢迎的人，一个和蔼可亲的挑战者，”他说。 “很多人都有账要跟他算。我应该说，他是伦敦最令人讨厌的人。如果医学院的学生出来了，那就没有尽头了。我不想进入熊园。”

当我们到达大厅时，我们发现大厅比我想象的要大得多。 一排电动马车卸下了白胡子教授的小货物，而一群卑微的行人则挤进了拱形门口，这表明观众将是受欢迎的和科学的。 事实上，当我们一坐下来，我们就清楚地看到，画廊和大厅的后部充满了一种年轻甚至孩子气的精神。 回头望去，我看到一排排熟悉的医科生面孔。 显然各大医院都派出了自己的特遣队。 目前观众的行为是幽默的，但又是恶作剧的。 流行歌曲的片段被热情地合唱，这是科学讲座的奇怪前奏，而且已经有一种个人闲聊的倾向，这向其他人保证了一个愉快的夜晚，无论这些可疑荣誉的接受者可能会感到尴尬。

因此，当老医生梅尔德鲁姆戴着他著名的卷边歌剧帽出现在平台上时，出现了这样一个普遍的疑问：“你从哪里得到那块瓷砖？”他赶紧把它取下来，偷偷地藏在椅子底下。 当患有痛风病的瓦德利教授一瘸一拐地走到座位上时，大厅里的各个角落都热情地询问他那可怜的脚趾的确切状况，这让他明显感到尴尬。 然而，最伟大的示威是在我的新朋友查林杰教授的入口处，当时他走下来坐在站台前排最末端的位置上。 当他的黑胡子第一次从拐角处伸出时，爆发出如此热烈的欢迎声，我开始怀疑塔普·亨利的猜测是对的，这次聚集不仅仅是为了演讲，而是因为国外有传言说这位著名的教授将参加会议。

他一出场，前排穿着考究的观众席上响起了一些同情的笑声，就好像学生们的示威活动并不受他们欢迎。 那句问候确实是一阵可怕的爆发声，当远处传来提桶饲养员的脚步声时，食肉动物的笼子里发出了一阵骚动。 也许其中有一种冒犯性的语气，但总的来说，我觉得这只是骚乱的抗议，是对那些使他们感到有趣和感兴趣的人的喧闹接待，而不是他们不喜欢或鄙视的人。 查林杰带着疲倦而宽容的轻蔑微笑，就像一个善良的人会面对一窝小狗的吠叫一样。 他缓缓坐下，挺起胸膛，用手抚摸着胡须，垂下眼睑，用白眼看着面前拥挤的大厅。 当主席罗纳德·默里教授和讲师沃尔德伦先生走到前面时，会议的喧嚣尚未平息，会议开始了。

我相信，如果我说穆雷教授有大多数英国人的通病，那就是听不见声音，那么请原谅我。 到底为什么那些有话要说、值得听的话的人不应该花点功夫去学习如何让别人听到它，这是现代生活的奇怪谜团之一。 他们的方法很合理，就像试图通过一根不导电的管道将一些珍贵的东西从泉水倒入蓄水池，而这个管道可以毫不费力地打开。默里教授对他的白领带和桌上的水瓶说了几句深刻的话，并幽默而闪烁地对他右边的银色烛台表示感谢。 然后他坐下来，著名的受欢迎的讲师沃尔德伦先生在一片热烈的掌声中站了起来。 他是一个严厉、憔悴的人，声音粗鲁，态度咄咄逼人，但他的优点是知道如何吸收其他人的思想，并以一种公众可以理解甚至有趣的方式传递它们，并具有对最不可能的物体进行有趣的快乐诀窍，因此春分岁差或脊椎动物的形成在他看来成为一个高度幽默的过程。

title: The Lost World · 选段 6
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: "No doubt, sir," Summerlee answered.  "Like all such tribes, I shall expect to find them of poly-synthetic speech and of Mongolian type."

"Polysynthetic certainly," said Challenger, indulgently.  "I am not aware that any other type of language exists in this continent, and I have notes of more than a hundred.  The Mongolian theory I regard with deep suspicion."
"I should have thought that even a limited knowledge of comparative anatomy would have helped to verify it," said Summerlee, bitterly.

Challenger thrust out his aggressive chin until he was all beard and hat-rim.  "No doubt, sir, a limited knowledge would have that effect. When one's knowledge is exhaustive, one comes to other conclusions." They glared at each other in mutual defiance, while all round rose the distant whisper, "We will kill you--we will kill you if we can."

That night we moored our canoes with heavy stones for anchors in the center of the stream, and made every preparation for a possible attack. Nothing came, however, and with the dawn we pushed upon our way, the drum-beating dying out behind us.  About three o'clock in the afternoon we came to a very steep rapid, more than a mile long--the very one in which Professor Challenger had suffered disaster upon his first journey.  I confess that the sight of it consoled me, for it was really the first direct corroboration, slight as it was, of the truth of his story.  The Indians carried first our canoes and then our stores through the brushwood, which is very thick at this point, while we four whites, our rifles on our shoulders, walked between them and any danger coming from the woods.  Before evening we had successfully passed the rapids, and made our way some ten miles above them, where we anchored for the night.  At this point I reckoned that we had come not less than a hundred miles up the tributary from the main stream.

It was in the early forenoon of the next day that we made the great departure.  Since dawn Professor Challenger had been acutely uneasy, continually scanning each bank of the river.  Suddenly he gave an exclamation of satisfaction and pointed to a single tree, which projected at a peculiar angle over the side of the stream.

"Exactly.  It was an Assai palm which I took for my landmark.  The secret opening is half a mile onwards upon the other side of the river. There is no break in the trees.  That is the wonder and the mystery of it.  There where you see light-green rushes instead of dark-green undergrowth, there between the great cotton woods, that is my private gate into the unknown.  Push through, and you will understand."

It was indeed a wonderful place.  Having reached the spot marked by a line of light-green rushes, we poled out two canoes through them for some hundreds of yards, and eventually emerged into a placid and shallow stream, running clear and transparent over a sandy bottom.  It may have been twenty yards across, and was banked in on each side by most luxuriant vegetation.  No one who had not observed that for a short distance reeds had taken the place of shrubs, could possibly have guessed the existence of such a stream or dreamed of the fairyland beyond.

For a fairyland it was--the most wonderful that the imagination of man could conceive.  The thick vegetation met overhead, interlacing into a natural pergola, and through this tunnel of verdure in a golden twilight flowed the green, pellucid river, beautiful in itself, but marvelous from the strange tints thrown by the vivid light from above filtered and tempered in its fall.  Clear as crystal, motionless as a sheet of glass, green as the edge of an iceberg, it stretched in front of us under its leafy archway, every stroke of our paddles sending a thousand ripples across its shining surface.  It was a fitting avenue to a land of wonders.  All sign of the Indians had passed away, but animal life was more frequent, and the tameness of the creatures showed that they knew nothing of the hunter.  Fuzzy little black-velvet monkeys, with snow-white teeth and gleaming, mocking eyes, chattered at us as we passed.  With a dull, heavy splash an occasional cayman plunged in from the bank.  Once a dark, clumsy tapir stared at us from a gap in the bushes, and then lumbered away through the forest; once, too, the yellow, sinuous form of a great puma whisked amid the brushwood, and its green, baleful eyes glared hatred at us over its tawny shoulder.  Bird life was abundant, especially the wading birds, stork, heron, and ibis gathering in little groups, blue, scarlet, and white, upon every log which jutted from the bank, while beneath us the crystal water was alive with fish of every shape and color.
paragraphsZh: “毫无疑问，先生，”萨默里回答道。 “像所有这样的部落一样，我预计会发现他们具有多种合成语言和蒙古类型。”
“当然是多合成的，”挑战者宽容地说。 “我不知道这片大陆上还存在其他类型的语言，我有一百多个笔记。我对蒙古的理论抱有深深的怀疑。”
“我应该认为，即使是有限的比较解剖学知识也能帮助验证这一点，”萨默里痛苦地说。
查林杰伸出他咄咄逼人的下巴，直到他满脸胡须和帽子。 “毫无疑问，先生，有限的知识也会产生这种效果。当一个人的知识详尽无遗时，就会得出其他结论。”他们互相挑衅地怒视着对方，而四周却传来远处传来的低语：“我们会杀了你——如果可以的话，我们会杀了你。”

那天晚上，我们用沉重的石头作为锚把独木舟停泊在溪流中央，并为可能的袭击做好了一切准备。然而，什么也没发生，黎明时分，我们继续赶路，鼓声在我们身后渐渐消失。 下午三点左右，我们来到了一条非常陡峭的急流，一英里多长——查林杰教授第一次旅行时就在这条急流中遭遇了灾难。 我承认，看到它让我感到安慰，因为这确实是对他故事真实性的第一次直接证实，尽管很轻微。 印第安人首先扛着我们的独木舟，然后是我们的物资穿过灌木丛，此时灌木丛非常茂密，而我们四个白人肩上扛着步枪，在他们和来自树林的任何危险之间行走。 傍晚之前，我们成功地渡过了急流，并在急流上方约十英里处航行，并在那里抛锚过夜。 此时我估计我们已经从干流沿支流逆流而上至少一百英里了。
第二天一早，我们就出发了。 从黎明起，查林杰教授就极度不安，不断地扫视着河的每一岸。 突然，他发出了一声满意的感叹，并指着一棵树，这棵树以一种奇特的角度突出在溪边。
“没错。那是一棵阿塞棕榈树，我把它当作我的地标。秘密的入口就在河对岸半英里处。树木没有中断。这就是它的奇迹和神秘。在那里你看到的是浅绿色的灯心草，而不是深绿色的灌木丛，在巨大的棉花树林之间，那是我通往未知世界的私人大门。推过去，你就会明白。”
这确实是一个很棒的地方。 到达一排浅绿色灯芯草的地方后，我们把两艘独木舟划过它们，行进了数百码，最终出现在一条平静而浅的溪流中，溪流清澈透明地流过沙底。 它可能有二十码宽，两边都长满了茂密的植被。 没有人注意到，在一小段距离内，芦苇取代了灌木，不可能猜到这样一条溪流的存在，也不可能梦想到远处的仙境。

对于仙境来说，这是——人类想象力所能想象到的最美妙的仙境。 茂密的植被在头顶上交汇，交织成一个天然的凉棚，在金色的暮色中，穿过这条青翠的隧道，流淌着绿色、清澈的河流，它本身很美丽，但由于上面的生动光线在秋天的过滤和调和而投射出奇怪的色彩，令人惊叹不已。 它像水晶一样清澈，像玻璃一样静止，像冰山边缘一样绿色，它在绿树成荫的拱门下伸展在我们面前，我们的桨的每一次划动都会在它闪亮的表面上激起一千个涟漪。 这是一条通往奇迹之地的合适大道。 印第安人的所有迹象都消失了，但动物的生活更加频繁，而这些动物的温顺表明它们对猎人一无所知。 当我们经过时，毛茸茸的黑色天鹅绒小猴子，牙齿雪白，眼睛闪闪发亮，嘲讽地对我们叽叽喳喳。 伴随着沉闷而沉重的水花声，偶尔有一只开曼群岛鳄鱼从岸边冲了进来。 有一次，一只黑色、笨拙的貘从灌木丛的缝隙里盯着我们看，然后缓慢地穿过森林走开。还有一次，一头黄色、蜿蜒的大美洲狮在灌木丛中疾驰，它那绿色、恶毒的眼睛在黄褐色的肩膀上仇恨地瞪着我们。 鸟类非常丰富，尤其是涉水鸟、鹳、苍鹭和朱鹮，成群结队地聚集在岸边伸出的每一根木头上，有蓝色、红色和白色，而在我们脚下晶莹剔透的水中，生活着各种形状和颜色的鱼。

title: The Lost World · 选段 7
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: On the ninth day after leaving the canoes, having done, as I reckon, about a hundred and twenty miles, we began to emerge from the trees, which had grown smaller until they were mere shrubs.  Their place was taken by an immense wilderness of bamboo, which grew so thickly that we could only penetrate it by cutting a pathway with the machetes and billhooks of the Indians.  It took us a long day, traveling from seven in the morning till eight at night, with only two breaks of one hour each, to get through this obstacle.  Anything more monotonous and wearying could not be imagined, for, even at the most open places, I could not see more than ten or twelve yards, while usually my vision was limited to the back of Lord John's cotton jacket in front of me, and to the yellow wall within a foot of me on either side.  From above came one thin knife-edge of sunshine, and fifteen feet over our heads one saw the tops of the reeds swaying against the deep blue sky.  I do not know what kind of creatures inhabit such a thicket, but several times we heard the plunging of large, heavy animals quite close to us. From their sounds Lord John judged them to be some form of wild cattle. Just as night fell we cleared the belt of bamboos, and at once formed our camp, exhausted by the interminable day.

Early next morning we were again afoot, and found that the character of the country had changed once again.  Behind us was the wall of bamboo, as definite as if it marked the course of a river.  In front was an open plain, sloping slightly upwards and dotted with clumps of tree-ferns, the whole curving before us until it ended in a long, whale-backed ridge.  This we reached about midday, only to find a shallow valley beyond, rising once again into a gentle incline which led to a low, rounded sky-line.  It was here, while we crossed the first of these hills, that an incident occurred which may or may not have been important.

Professor Challenger, who with the two local Indians was in the van of the party, stopped suddenly and pointed excitedly to the right.  As he did so we saw, at the distance of a mile or so, something which appeared to be a huge gray bird flap slowly up from the ground and skim smoothly off, flying very low and straight, until it was lost among the tree-ferns.
Summerlee burst into derisive laughter "A pter-fiddlestick!" said he. "It was a stork, if ever I saw one."

Challenger was too furious to speak.  He simply swung his pack upon his back and continued upon his march.  Lord John came abreast of me, however, and his face was more grave than was his wont.  He had his Zeiss glasses in his hand.

"I focused it before it got over the trees," said he. "I won't undertake to say what it was, but I'll risk my reputation as a sportsman that it wasn't any bird that ever I clapped eyes on in my life."

So there the matter stands.  Are we really just at the edge of the unknown, encountering the outlying pickets of this lost world of which our leader speaks?  I give you the incident as it occurred and you will know as much as I do.  It stands alone, for we saw nothing more which could be called remarkable.

And now, my readers, if ever I have any, I have brought you up the broad river, and through the screen of rushes, and down the green tunnel, and up the long slope of palm trees, and through the bamboo brake, and across the plain of tree-ferns.  At last our destination lay in full sight of us.  When we had crossed the second ridge we saw before us an irregular, palm-studded plain, and then the line of high red cliffs which I have seen in the picture.  There it lies, even as I write, and there can be no question that it is the same.  At the nearest point it is about seven miles from our present camp, and it curves away, stretching as far as I can see.  Challenger struts about like a prize peacock, and Summerlee is silent, but still sceptical. Another day should bring some of our doubts to an end.  Meanwhile, as Jose, whose arm was pierced by a broken bamboo, insists upon returning, I send this letter back in his charge, and only hope that it may eventually come to hand.  I will write again as the occasion serves.  I have enclosed with this a rough chart of our journey, which may have the effect of making the account rather easier to understand.
paragraphsZh: 离开独木舟后的第九天，据我估计，我们已经走了大约一百二十英里，我们开始从树林中走出来，树林已经变小，直到只剩下灌木。 他们的位置被一片巨大的竹子荒野所取代，竹子生长得非常茂密，我们只能用印第安人的砍刀和尖钩割开一条路才能穿透它。 我们花了整整一天的时间，从早上七点一直赶到晚上八点，中间只有两次休息时间，每次一小时，才克服了这个障碍。 无法想象任何更单调和令人疲惫的事情，因为即使在最开阔的地方，我也只能看到十或十二码，而通常我的视野仅限于我面前约翰勋爵棉袄的背面，以及两侧距我一英尺以内的黄色墙壁。 一道薄薄的阳光从头顶射来，在我们头顶十五英尺的地方，人们看到芦苇的顶部在深蓝色的天空中摇曳。 我不知道这样的灌木丛里栖息着什么样的生物，但有几次我们听到离我们很近的大型、重型动物的猛冲声。约翰勋爵根据它们的声音判断它们是某种野牛。夜幕降临时，我们清理了竹带，立即扎营，因为无休无止的白天而筋疲力尽。
第二天一早，我们再次上路，发现这个国家的面貌再次发生了变化。 我们身后是竹墙，清晰得就像标记着河道一样。 前面是一片开阔的平原，略微向上倾斜，点缀着一丛丛树蕨，整个平原在我们面前弯曲，直到尽头是一条长长的鲸背山脊。 我们大约在中午到达这里，却发现远处有一个浅山谷，再次升起，形成一个平缓的斜坡，通向低矮的圆形天际线。 正是在这里，当我们越过第一座山时，发生了一件可能重要也可能不重要的事件。
查林杰教授和两名当地印第安人一起坐在队伍的前车上，他突然停下来，兴奋地指着右边。 当他这样做时，我们看到，在大约一英里的距离处，有一个似乎是一只巨大的灰色鸟的东西慢慢地从地面上拍打起来，平稳地掠过，飞得很低，笔直，直到消失在树蕨丛中。
萨默里突然发出嘲笑声，“一只翼琴！”他说。 “如果我见过的话，那就是一只鹳鸟。”
查林杰气得说不出话来。 他只是将背包甩在背上，继续前行。 然而，约翰勋爵来到了我身边，他的脸色比平常更加严肃。 他手里拿着蔡司眼镜。
“我在它越过树林之前聚焦它，”他说。 “我不会透露那是什么鸟，但我会拿自己作为运动员的声誉冒险，这不是我一生中见过的任何一只鸟。”
事情就是这样。 我们真的正处于未知的边缘，遇到我们领导人所说的这个失落世界的边远纠察队吗？ 我把事件发生的经过告诉你，你会和我一样了解的。 它是独一无二的，因为我们没有看到任何其他可以称为非凡的东西。

现在，我的读者们，如果我有的话，我已经带你们上了宽阔的河流，穿过灯芯草的屏障，穿过绿色的隧道，爬上长长的棕榈树斜坡，穿过竹林，穿过树蕨平原。 目的地终于在我们的眼前了。 当我们越过第二座山脊时，我们看到前面是一片不规则的、棕榈树丛生的平原，然后是我在照片中看到的一排高高的红色悬崖。 就在我写这篇文章的时候，它就在那里，毫无疑问它是一样的。 最近的地方距离我们现在的营地大约有七英里，并且它呈弧形延伸，一直延伸到我能看到的地方。 挑战者像一只获奖孔雀一样昂首阔步，萨默里沉默不语，但仍然持怀疑态度。另一天应该可以结束我们的一些疑虑。 与此同时，由于手臂被断竹刺穿的何塞坚持要回来，我将这封信寄回给他，只希望它最终能到达我的手中。 有机会我会再写信。 我随信附上了我们旅程的粗略图表，这可能会使叙述更容易理解。

title: The Lost World · 选段 8
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
paragraphs: That night (our third in Maple White Land) we had an experience which left a fearful impression upon our minds, and made us thankful that Lord John had worked so hard in making our retreat impregnable.  We were all sleeping round our dying fire when we were aroused--or, rather, I should say, shot out of our slumbers--by a succession of the most frightful cries and screams to which I have ever listened.  I know no sound to which I could compare this amazing tumult, which seemed to come from some spot within a few hundred yards of our camp.  It was as ear-splitting as any whistle of a railway-engine; but whereas the whistle is a clear, mechanical, sharp-edged sound, this was far deeper in volume and vibrant with the uttermost strain of agony and horror. We clapped our hands to our ears to shut out that nerve-shaking appeal. A cold sweat broke out over my body, and my heart turned sick at the misery of it.  All the woes of tortured life, all its stupendous indictment of high heaven, its innumerable sorrows, seemed to be centered and condensed into that one dreadful, agonized cry.  And then, under this high-pitched, ringing sound there was another, more intermittent, a low, deep-chested laugh, a growling, throaty gurgle of merriment which formed a grotesque accompaniment to the shriek with which it was blended.  For three or four minutes on end the fearsome duet continued, while all the foliage rustled with the rising of startled birds.  Then it shut off as suddenly as it began.  For a long time we sat in horrified silence.  Then Lord John threw a bundle of twigs upon the fire, and their red glare lit up the intent faces of my companions and flickered over the great boughs above our heads.

"We have been privileged to overhear a prehistoric tragedy, the sort of drama which occurred among the reeds upon the border of some Jurassic lagoon, when the greater dragon pinned the lesser among the slime," said Challenger, with more solemnity than I had ever heard in his voice.  "It was surely well for man that he came late in the order of creation.  There were powers abroad in earlier days which no courage and no mechanism of his could have met.
