Supposing you were to say twelve months for the theft, which is mild; and three years for the furious driving, which is lenient; and fifteen years for the cheek, which was pretty bad sort of cheek, judging by what we’ve heard from the witness-box, even if you only believe one-tenth part of what you heard, and I never believe more myself—those figures, if added together correctly, tot up to nineteen years——”

“An excellent suggestion!” said the Chairman approvingly. “Prisoner! Pull yourself together and try and stand up straight. It’s going to be twenty years for you this time. And mind, if you appear before us again, upon any charge whatever, we shall have to deal with you very seriously!”

Then the brutal minions of the law fell upon the hapless Toad; loaded him with chains, and dragged him from the Court House, shrieking, praying, protesting; across the marketplace, where the playful populace, always as severe upon detected crime as they are sympathetic and helpful when one is merely “wanted,” assailed him with jeers, carrots, and popular catch-words; past hooting school children, their innocent faces lit up with the pleasure they ever derive from the sight of a gentleman in difficulties; across the hollow-sounding drawbridge, below the spiky portcullis, under the frowning archway of the grim old castle, whose ancient towers soared high overhead; past guardrooms full of grinning soldiery off duty, past sentries who coughed in a horrid, sarcastic way, because that is as much as a sentry on his post dare do to show his contempt and abhorrence of crime; up time-worn winding stairs, past men-at-arms in casquet and corselet of steel, darting threatening looks through their vizards; across courtyards, where mastiffs strained at their leash and pawed the air to get at him; past ancient warders, their halberds leant against the wall, dozing over a pasty and a flagon of brown ale; on and on, past the rack-chamber and the thumbscrew-room, past the turning that led to the private scaffold, till they reached the door of the grimmest dungeon that lay in the heart of the innermost keep. There at last they paused, where an ancient gaoler sat fingering a bunch of mighty keys.
paragraphsZh: 那辆车停在院子中央，完全无人看管，马厩帮手和其他跟随的人都在吃晚饭。蟾蜍慢慢地绕着它走，仔细检查，批评，并深深地沉思。

下一刻，他几乎不知道这是怎么发生的，发现自己已经握住了把手，并正在转动它。当熟悉的声音响起时，老癖好抓住了癞蛤蟆，完全控制了他的身体和灵魂。仿佛在做梦，他发现自己不知怎的坐在了驾驶座上；仿佛在做梦，他拉动操纵杆，把车在院子里转了弯，驶出拱门；仿佛在做梦，所有的对错感、对明显后果的恐惧，似乎暂时消失了。他加快了脚步，当汽车在街道上飞驰，穿过开阔的乡间道路时，他只意识到自己再次成为了鼹鼠，最好的、最高贵的鼹鼠，令人畏惧的鼹鼠，交通的克星，孤独路径的主人，凡阻挡者，必被击入虚无和永恒的黑暗中。他在飞驰中吟唱，汽车发出低沉的轰鸣；在他脚下，英里在飞速消逝，他不知道自己会去向何方，顺从本能，活在当下，毫不在意将会发生什么。

“在我看来，”治安法官席的主席愉快地说道，“在这个原本非常明了的案件中，唯一出现的困难就是，我们怎么可能对坐在被告席上畏缩不前的这个不可救药的恶棍和硬汉施加足够的惩罚。让我看看：他已经根据最清楚的证据被判有罪，首先是偷一辆贵重的汽车；其次是驾驶危及公共安全；第三是对乡村警察极度无礼。书记员先生，请告诉我们，对于每一项罪行，我们可以施加的最严厉的处罚是什么？当然，不要给犯人任何疑虑的好处，因为根本没有。”
职员用笔挠了挠鼻子。“有些人会认为，”他观察道，“偷汽车是最严重的罪行；确实如此。但顶撞警察无疑会受到最严厉的处罚；而且理应如此。假设你判盗窃罪十二个月，这算轻的；为了疯狂驾驶判三年，这算宽大；而为了顶撞，判十五年，这种顶撞相当严重，从我们在证人席上听到的情况来看，即使你只相信你听到的十分之一，而我自己从来不相信超过这个——如果把这些数字加起来正确，总共是十九年——”
“一个极好的建议！”主席赞许地说。“囚犯！振作起来，尽量站直。这次你将被判二十年。而且记住，如果你再次以任何指控出现在我们面前，我们将不得不非常严肃地处理你！”

然后，法律的残酷爪牙扑向可怜的蟾蜍；给他戴上镣铐，把他从法院拖出来，他尖叫着、祈祷着、抗议着；穿过市场，这里的顽皮民众在抓到罪犯时总是严厉无比，而在有人仅仅是“通缉”时却又充满同情和帮助，他们用嘲笑、胡萝卜和流行语袭击他；经过嘲笑的学童，他们无辜的脸因看到绅士陷入困境而露出愉快的神情；穿过空洞回响的吊桥，经过尖刺门栅，走过阴沉的古堡拱门，这座古老的塔楼高耸在头顶；经过充满笑嘻嘻休假士兵的守卫室，经过嗓音刺耳、带讽刺咳嗽的哨兵，因为守岗的士兵只能做到如此为了显示他对罪行的蔑视和憎恶；顺着陈旧的旋转楼梯，经过身穿钢盔和钢胸甲的武士，透过面罩投来威胁的目光；穿过庭院，那里的獒犬在牵绳下挣扎，挥爪扑向空气试图攻击他；经过古老的狱卒，他们的戟靠在墙上，对着肉饼和一壶棕色啤酒打盹；继续前行，经过拷打室和拇指拧紧器房间，经过通向私人绞刑台的转角，直到他们到达位于最内层城堡中心的最阴森的地牢门口。终于在这里停下，那里一位古老的狱卒坐着，摆弄着一串巨大的钥匙。

title: The Wind in the Willows · 选段 7
author: Kenneth Grahame
paragraphs: In silence Mole rowed steadily, and soon they came to a point where the river divided, a long backwater branching off to one side. With a slight movement of his head Rat, who had long dropped the rudder-lines, directed the rower to take the backwater. The creeping tide of light gained and gained, and now they could see the colour of the flowers that gemmed the water’s edge.
“Clearer and nearer still,” cried the Rat joyously. “Now you must surely hear it! Ah—at last—I see you do!”

Breathless and transfixed the Mole stopped rowing as the liquid run of that glad piping broke on him like a wave, caught him up, and possessed him utterly. He saw the tears on his comrade’s cheeks, and bowed his head and understood. For a space they hung there, brushed by the purple loose-strife that fringed the bank; then the clear imperious summons that marched hand-in-hand with the intoxicating melody imposed its will on Mole, and mechanically he bent to his oars again. And the light grew steadily stronger, but no birds sang as they were wont to do at the approach of dawn; and but for the heavenly music all was marvellously still.

On either side of them, as they glided onwards, the rich meadow-grass seemed that morning of a freshness and a greenness unsurpassable. Never had they noticed the roses so vivid, the willow-herb so riotous, the meadow-sweet so odorous and pervading. Then the murmur of the approaching weir began to hold the air, and they felt a consciousness that they were nearing the end, whatever it might be, that surely awaited their expedition.

A wide half-circle of foam and glinting lights and shining shoulders of green water, the great weir closed the backwater from bank to bank, troubled all the quiet surface with twirling eddies and floating foam-streaks, and deadened all other sounds with its solemn and soothing rumble. In midmost of the stream, embraced in the weir’s shimmering arm-spread, a small island lay anchored, fringed close with willow and silver birch and alder. Reserved, shy, but full of significance, it hid whatever it might hold behind a veil, keeping it till the hour should come, and, with the hour, those who were called and chosen.

Slowly, but with no doubt or hesitation whatever, and in something of a solemn expectancy, the two animals passed through the broken tumultuous water and moored their boat at the flowery margin of the island. In silence they landed, and pushed through the blossom and scented herbage and undergrowth that led up to the level ground, till they stood on a little lawn of a marvellous green, set round with Nature’s own orchard-trees—crab-apple, wild cherry, and sloe.
“This is the place of my song-dream, the place the music played to me,” whispered the Rat, as if in a trance. “Here, in this holy place, here if anywhere, surely we shall find Him!”

Then suddenly the Mole felt a great Awe fall upon him, an awe that turned his muscles to water, bowed his head, and rooted his feet to the ground. It was no panic terror—indeed he felt wonderfully at peace and happy—but it was an awe that smote and held him and, without seeing, he knew it could only mean that some august Presence was very, very near. With difficulty he turned to look for his friend and saw him at his side cowed, stricken, and trembling violently. And still there was utter silence in the populous bird-haunted branches around them; and still the light grew and grew.

Perhaps he would never have dared to raise his eyes, but that, though the piping was now hushed, the call and the summons seemed still dominant and imperious. He might not refuse, were Death himself waiting to strike him instantly, once he had looked with mortal eye on things rightly kept hidden. Trembling he obeyed, and raised his humble head; and then, in that utter clearness of the imminent dawn, while Nature, flushed with fullness of incredible colour, seemed to hold her breath for the event, he looked in the very eyes of the Friend and Helper; saw the backward sweep of the curved horns, gleaming in the growing daylight; saw the stern, hooked nose between the kindly eyes that were looking down on them humourously, while the bearded mouth broke into a half-smile at the corners; saw the rippling muscles on the arm that lay across the broad chest, the long supple hand still holding the pan-pipes only just fallen away from the parted lips; saw the splendid curves of the shaggy limbs disposed in majestic ease on the sward; saw, last of all, nestling between his very hooves, sleeping soundly in entire peace and contentment, the little, round, podgy, childish form of the baby otter. All this he saw, for one moment breathless and intense, vivid on the morning sky; and still, as he looked, he lived; and still, as he lived, he wondered.
paragraphsZh: 默尔默默地划着船，不久他们来到一个河流分岔的地方，一条长长的回水从一侧分出。拉特轻轻点了点头，他早已放下了舵绳，示意划船的人向回水处划去。缓缓上升的光潮渐渐增强，现在他们可以看清点缀在水边的花朵的颜色。
“更清晰，更近了，”老鼠兴高采烈地叫道。“现在你肯定能听见了！啊——终于——我看你确实能听到了！”
气喘吁吁、目不转睛的鼹鼠停止了划桨，因为那欢快的哨声如同海浪般涌向他，吞没了他，完全掌控了他。他看见同伴脸上的泪水，低下头，心领神会。有一会儿，他们停在那里，被河岸边的紫色柳穿草轻拂；然后，那清晰而专横的召唤与这陶醉的旋律携手而来，强加了它的意志于鼹鼠身上，他机械地又低头划起桨来。光线 steadily 变得愈发明亮，但鸟儿却未像往常那样在黎明到来时啼鸣；如果不是天籁之音，一切都静得出奇。
在他们两侧，当他们缓缓前行时，那丰富的草地似乎在那个早晨展现出无与伦比的新鲜与翠绿。他们从未注意到玫瑰如此鲜艳，柳叶菜如此繁茂，蜜草如此芳香且弥漫开来。随后，近水坝的低语声开始充满空气，他们感到一种意识，知道无论结果如何，他们的探险很快就要结束了，终点正静静等待着他们。
一个宽阔的半圆形泡沫，闪闪发光的灯光，以及绿色水面的闪亮波肩，巨大的堰从岸到岸封锁了回水，搅动了所有宁静的水面，泛起旋转的漩涡和漂浮的泡沫痕迹，并以庄重而舒缓的隆隆声掩盖了其他所有声音。在水流的中央，被堰闪烁的臂弯环绕着，一座小岛静静地矗立，岸边环绕着柳树、白桦和赤杨。它内敛、害羞，但充满意义，将它可能拥有的一切隐藏在一层面纱之后，静待时机的到来，并与时机一起，迎来那些被召唤和被拣选的人。
缓慢地，但毫无疑问或犹豫，并带着一种庄重的期待，这两只动物穿过破碎而汹涌的水流，将他们的船停泊在岛的花丛边缘。沉默中，他们上了岸，穿过盛开的花朵、散发香气的草本植物和下层灌木，直到他们站在一片奇妙的绿草坪上，四周环绕着大自然本身的果树——野苹果、野樱桃和黑刺李。
“这是我的歌梦之地，音乐对我演奏的地方，”老鼠低声说道，仿佛出神。“在这里，在这个神圣的地方，如果有地方能找到他，那么就在这里！”

然后，鼹鼠突然感到一股强烈的敬畏降临到他身上，这种敬畏使他的肌肉变得如水般软弱，低下了头，把双脚深深地钉在地上。这不是恐慌的惊惧——实际上他感到异常平静和快乐——但这是一种击打并束缚住他的敬畏，他没有看到，却知道这只能意味着某种庄严的存在非常非常接近。他费力地转过身去寻找他的朋友，看到他在自己身旁显得惧怕、震惊，剧烈地颤抖着。在他们周围那些栖息着众多鸟类的枝头上，仍然一片寂静；光线仍然在不断增强。

也许他从未敢抬起眼睛，但尽管吹奏声现在已经平息，那呼唤和召唤似乎仍然占据主导地位，充满威严。他可能无法拒绝，即使死亡自己正等待着立即击打他，一旦他用凡人的眼睛去看那些理应隐藏的事物。他颤抖着遵从命令，抬起谦卑的头；然后，在那即将到来的黎明的极度清晰中，当大自然因不可思议的色彩的丰满而面露红晕，似乎屏住呼吸等待这一时刻，他直视着朋友与帮手的眼睛；看到弯曲的角向后伸展，在逐渐明亮的光线下闪闪发光；看到那严厉的钩状鼻子在那双幽默地俯视他们的善意眼睛之间，而胡须覆盖的嘴角微微上扬成半笑；看到平放在宽阔胸膛上的手臂上起伏的肌肉，那只仍然握着刚从微张的嘴唇那掉落下来的排箫的长而灵活的手；看到披着毛发的四肢在草地上安然舒展的壮丽曲线；最后看到，栖息在他的蹄子之间，安详沉睡着，完全平静的满足，小小的、圆胖的、孩子气的水獭宝宝的形态。他看到了这一切，在一刻间屏息凝神、强烈而生动地映在晨空中；而且，当他凝视时，他还活着；当他活着时，他还在感到惊奇。

title: The Wind in the Willows · 选段 8
author: Kenneth Grahame
paragraphs: A long half-hour passed, and every minute of it saw Toad getting crosser and crosser. Nothing that he could do to the things seemed to please them or do them good. He tried coaxing, he tried slapping, he tried punching; they smiled back at him out of the tub unconverted, happy in their original sin. Once or twice he looked nervously over his shoulder at the barge-woman, but she appeared to be gazing out in front of her, absorbed in her steering. His back ached badly, and he noticed with dismay that his paws were beginning to get all crinkly. Now Toad was very proud of his paws. He muttered under his breath words that should never pass the lips of either washerwomen or Toads; and lost the soap, for the fiftieth time.
A burst of laughter made him straighten himself and look round. The barge-woman was leaning back and laughing unrestrainedly, till the tears ran down her cheeks.

“I’ve been watching you all the time,” she gasped. “I thought you must be a humbug all along, from the conceited way you talked. Pretty washerwoman you are! Never washed so much as a dish-clout in your life, I’ll lay!”
Toad’s temper which had been simmering viciously for some time, now fairly boiled over, and he lost all control of himself.

“You common, low, fat barge-woman!” he shouted; “don’t you dare to talk to your betters like that! Washerwoman indeed! I would have you to know that I am a Toad, a very well-known, respected, distinguished Toad! I may be under a bit of a cloud at present, but I will not be laughed at by a bargewoman!”

The woman moved nearer to him and peered under his bonnet keenly and closely. “Why, so you are!” she cried. “Well, I never! A horrid, nasty, crawly Toad! And in my nice clean barge, too! Now that is a thing that I will not have.”

She relinquished the tiller for a moment. One big mottled arm shot out and caught Toad by a fore-leg, while the other-gripped him fast by a hind-leg. Then the world turned suddenly upside down, the barge seemed to flit lightly across the sky, the wind whistled in his ears, and Toad found himself flying through the air, revolving rapidly as he went.

The water, when he eventually reached it with a loud splash, proved quite cold enough for his taste, though its chill was not sufficient to quell his proud spirit, or slake the heat of his furious temper. He rose to the surface spluttering, and when he had wiped the duck-weed out of his eyes the first thing he saw was the fat barge-woman looking back at him over the stern of the retreating barge and laughing; and he vowed, as he coughed and choked, to be even with her.

He struck out for the shore, but the cotton gown greatly impeded his efforts, and when at length he touched land he found it hard to climb up the steep bank unassisted. He had to take a minute or two’s rest to recover his breath; then, gathering his wet skirts well over his arms, he started to run after the barge as fast as his legs would carry him, wild with indignation, thirsting for revenge.

The barge-woman was still laughing when he drew up level with her. “Put yourself through your mangle, washerwoman,” she called out, “and iron your face and crimp it, and you’ll pass for quite a decent-looking Toad!”

Toad never paused to reply. Solid revenge was what he wanted, not cheap, windy, verbal triumphs, though he had a thing or two in his mind that he would have liked to say. He saw what he wanted ahead of him. Running swiftly on he overtook the horse, unfastened the towrope and cast off, jumped lightly on the horse’s back, and urged it to a gallop by kicking it vigorously in the sides. He steered for the open country, abandoning the tow-path, and swinging his steed down a rutty lane. Once he looked back, and saw that the barge had run aground on the other side of the canal, and the barge-woman was gesticulating wildly and shouting, “Stop, stop, stop!” “I’ve heard that song before,” said Toad, laughing, as he continued to spur his steed onward in its wild career.
paragraphsZh: 半个小时很慢地过去了，每一分钟，蟾蜍都变得越来越烦躁。他对这些东西做的任何事情似乎都无法让它们高兴或产生效果。他试着哄它们，试着拍它们，试着拳打它们；它们从浴缸里对他微笑，丝毫未被感化，仍旧沉浸在原罪的快乐中。有一两次，他紧张地回头望了望驳船上的女工，但她似乎只是望着前方，专注于掌舵。他的背痛得厉害，并且沮丧地注意到他的爪子开始变得起皱。蟾蜍非常以自己的爪子自豪。他小声地咕哝一些洗衣妇或蟾蜍都绝不该说出的词；结果他第五十次把肥皂都丢了。
一阵笑声让他挺直了身子，四下张望。驳船女正靠着船边放声大笑，笑得眼泪都流了下来。
“我一直在看着你，”她喘着气说。“我一直以为你从一开始就是个骗子，因为你说话太自负了。你可真是个洗衣妇啊！我敢打赌，你一生都没真正洗过一块抹布！”
蟾蜍那已经压抑得很久的坏脾气，这会儿彻底爆发了，他完全控制不住自己。
“你这俗气、低贱、胖乎乎的驳船女！”他大喊，“你不敢这样对你的上级说话！洗衣妇！我要让你知道，我可是蟾蜍，一个非常有名、受人尊敬、杰出的蟾蜍！我现在或许有些不顺，但我不会被一个驳船女嘲笑！”
那名女人走近他，仔细而近距离地往他的帽下看。“哎呀，你居然在这里！”她喊道。“天哪，我才不信呢！一个可怕、讨厌、爬来爬去的蟾蜍！而且还在我干净整洁的驳船上！这可真是我绝对不能容忍的事情。”
她暂时放开了舵。一条大大的斑驳臂膀伸出，抓住蟾蜍的一条前腿，另一条手则紧紧抓住它的一条后腿。然后世界突然翻转过来，驳船似乎轻轻地在天空中掠过，风在他的耳边呼啸，蟾蜍发现自己在空中飞行，一边飞行一边迅速旋转。
当他最终以一声巨响扑入水中时，水的温度对于他的口味来说相当冷，尽管这种寒冷不足以平息他傲慢的心灵，也无法消减他愤怒的脾气。他带着呛水浮出水面，当他擦去眼中的浮萍，看到的第一件事就是那位肥胖的驳船女正从退去的驳船尾部回头看着他笑；他一边咳嗽、一边呛水，一边发誓要向她报复。
他朝岸边游去，但棉质长袍极大地妨碍了他的动作，当他终于触到陆地时，发现没有人帮忙很难爬上陡峭的河岸。他不得不休息一两分钟以恢复呼吸；然后，他把湿漉漉的裙摆收拢到手臂上，开始尽可能快地追赶驳船，愤怒异常，渴望复仇。
当他赶上她时，驳船上的女人还在笑。“去你自己的轧布机里转一圈，洗衣妇，”她喊道，“把你的脸熨熨平，加点褶子，你就能看起来像只相当体面的蟾蜍了！”

蟾蜍从未停下来回应。他想要的是实实在在的复仇，而不是廉价、空洞的口舌之争，尽管他心里确实有几句话想说。他看到了眼前自己想要的东西。他迅速奔跑，赶上了马，解开牵引绳并甩开，轻巧地跳上马背，用力踢它的两侧催它飞奔。他朝开阔地带驶去，离开了拖航道，沿着一条坑洼的小路驾马前行。他曾回头看去，只见驳船已在运河的另一侧搁浅，那位驳船女工正疯狂地挥手叫喊着：“停，停，停！”“我以前听过那首歌，”蟾蜍笑着说，同时继续在这匹狂奔的马背上猛力策马前进。

title: The Wind in the Willows · 选段 9
author: Kenneth Grahame
paragraphs: The driver tried to interfere, but he pinned him down in his seat with one elbow, and put on full speed. The rush of air in his face, the hum of the engines, and the light jump of the car beneath him intoxicated his weak brain. “Washerwoman, indeed!” he shouted recklessly. “Ho! ho! I am the Toad, the motor-car snatcher, the prison-breaker, the Toad who always escapes! Sit still, and you shall know what driving really is, for you are in the hands of the famous, the skilful, the entirely fearless Toad!”

With a cry of horror the whole party rose and flung themselves on him. “Seize him!” they cried, “seize the Toad, the wicked animal who stole our motor-car! Bind him, chain him, drag him to the nearest police-station! Down with the desperate and dangerous Toad!”

Alas! they should have thought, they ought to have been more prudent, they should have remembered to stop the motor-car somehow before playing any pranks of that sort. With a half-turn of the wheel the Toad sent the car crashing through the low hedge that ran along the roadside. One mighty bound, a violent shock, and the wheels of the car were churning up the thick mud of a horse-pond.

Toad found himself flying through the air with the strong upward rush and delicate curve of a swallow. He liked the motion, and was just beginning to wonder whether it would go on until he developed wings and turned into a Toad-bird, when he landed on his back with a thump, in the soft rich grass of a meadow. Sitting up, he could just see the motor-car in the pond, nearly submerged; the gentlemen and the driver, encumbered by their long coats, were floundering helplessly in the water.

He picked himself up rapidly, and set off running across country as hard as he could, scrambling through hedges, jumping ditches, pounding across fields, till he was breathless and weary, and had to settle down into an easy walk. When he had recovered his breath somewhat, and was able to think calmly, he began to giggle, and from giggling he took to laughing, and he laughed till he had to sit down under a hedge. “Ho, ho!” he cried, in ecstasies of self-admiration, “Toad again! Toad, as usual, comes out on the top! Who was it got them to give him a lift? Who managed to get on the front seat for the sake of fresh air? Who persuaded them into letting him see if he could drive? Who landed them all in a horse-pond? Who escaped, flying gaily and unscathed through the air, leaving the narrow-minded, grudging, timid excursionists in the mud where they should rightly be? Why, Toad, of course; clever Toad, great Toad, good Toad!”
“The motor-car went Poop-poop-poop, As it raced along the road. Who was it steered it into a pond? Ingenious Mr. Toad!
A slight noise at a distance behind him made him turn his head and look. O horror! O misery! O despair!
About two fields off, a chauffeur in his leather gaiters and two large rural policemen were visible, running towards him as hard as they could go!

Poor Toad sprang to his feet and pelted away again, his heart in his mouth. O, my!” he gasped, as he panted along, “what an ass I am! What a conceited and heedless ass! Swaggering again! Shouting and singing songs again! Sitting still and gassing again! O my! O my! O my!”

He glanced back, and saw to his dismay that they were gaining on him. On he ran desperately, but kept looking back, and saw that they still gained steadily. He did his best, but he was a fat animal, and his legs were short, and still they gained. He could hear them close behind him now. Ceasing to heed where he was going, he struggled on blindly and wildly, looking back over his shoulder at the now triumphant enemy, when suddenly the earth failed under his feet, he grasped at the air, and, splash! he found himself head over ears in deep water, rapid water, water that bore him along with a force he could not contend with; and he knew that in his blind panic he had run straight into the river!
paragraphsZh: 司机试图干预，但他用一只手肘把他按在座位上，然后全速前进。迎面而来的风声、引擎的轰鸣和车子轻微的跳动让他那脆弱的脑子陶醉。“洗衣妇，真是的！”他鲁莽地大喊。“哈哈！我是蟾蜍，汽车抢夺者，越狱犯，那个总能逃脱的蟾蜍！乖乖坐好，你就会知道什么是真正的驾驶，因为你现在在著名、熟练、完全无畏的蟾蜍手中！”
带着惊恐的叫声，整队人都站起来扑向他。“抓住他！”他们喊道，“抓住蟾蜍，这个偷了我们汽车的邪恶动物！绑住他，锁上他，把他拖到最近的警察局去！打倒这个绝望而危险的蟾蜍！”
唉！他们本该多加考虑，应该更为谨慎，他们本该记得在做那种恶作剧之前想办法停下汽车。蟾蜍轻轻一转方向盘，汽车便撞穿了沿路低矮的篱笆。一跃而起，剧烈的震动，汽车的车轮在马塘的浓厚泥浆中翻滚搅动。
蟾蜍发现自己像燕子一样被强劲的上升气流带着轻盈的弧线在空中飞行。他喜欢这种感觉，正开始想它是否会一直持续下去，直到他长出翅膀变成一只蟾蜍鸟时，他“嘭”地一声落在了草地上柔软而肥沃的草坪上。他坐起身来，只能隐约看到停在池塘里几乎淹没的汽车；那些穿着长外套的绅士和司机在水中无助地挣扎着。

他迅速地站了起来，竭尽全力开始穿越田野奔跑，翻越树篱，跳过沟渠，穿越田地，直到气喘吁吁、疲惫不堪，不得不放慢脚步，轻松地走起来。当他稍微恢复了呼吸，能够冷静思考时，他开始咯咯地笑，从咯咯笑变成大笑，他笑得直到不得不坐在树篱下。“呵，呵！”他欣喜地自我赞叹，“蟾蜍又来了！蟾蜍像往常一样，总是占上风！是谁让他们给他搭便车的？谁为了清新的空气设法坐到前排的？谁说服他们让自己试试开车？是谁把他们全部弄到马池里的？”谁逃走了，欢快地、安然无恙地飞过空中，把那些狭隘、嫉妒、胆小的远足者留在他们应有的泥潭里？当然是蟾蜍；聪明的蟾蜍，伟大的蟾蜍，善良的蟾蜍！”
“汽车嘟嘟嘟地响着，沿着路飞驰。是谁把它开进了池塘？机智的蟾蜍先生！”
身后远处传来一声轻微的响声，他便转过头去看。哦，恐怖！哦，悲惨！哦，绝望！
大约距离两块地之外，一名穿着皮套的司机和两名魁梧的乡村警察正朝他竭尽全力地跑来！
可怜的蟾蜍跳起来又跑开了，心都提到了嗓子眼。他一边气喘吁吁地跑，一边喘着气说：“哦，我的天啊！我真是个笨蛋！多么自负、多么不小心的笨蛋啊！又摇摆着走路！又大喊大叫又唱歌！又坐着说话不干正事！哦，我的天啊！哦，我的天啊！哦，我的天啊！”

他回头一看，沮丧地发现他们正在追上他。他拼命地跑着，但不停地回头看，看到他们仍然稳步逼近。他尽了最大努力，但他是只肥胖的动物，腿又短，他们仍然赶上来。他现在能听到他们就在身后。忽略了前方的去向，他盲目而狂乱地挣扎着，回头望着现在得意的敌人，突然地面在他脚下塌陷，他抓住空气，扑通！他发现自己头朝下跌入深水之中，急流之水，那水以他无法抗拒的力量将他冲走；他明白，在自己盲目的恐慌中，他竟然径直跑进了河里！

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 4
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: This last compromise was a hasty bit of legislation, vague and uncertain in outline. A Bureau was created, “to continue during the present War of Rebellion, and for one year thereafter,” to which was given “the supervision and management of all abandoned lands and the control of all subjects relating to refugees and freedmen,” under “such rules and regulations as may be presented by the head of the Bureau and approved by the President.” A Commissioner, appointed by the President and Senate, was to control the Bureau, with an office force not exceeding ten clerks. The President might also appoint assistant commissioners in the seceded States, and to all these offices military officials might be detailed at regular pay. The Secretary of War could issue rations, clothing, and fuel to the destitute, and all abandoned property was placed in the hands of the Bureau for eventual lease and sale to ex-slaves in forty-acre parcels.

Thus did the United States government definitely assume charge of the emancipated Negro as the ward of the nation. It was a tremendous undertaking. Here at a stroke of the pen was erected a government of millions of men,—and not ordinary men either, but black men emasculated by a peculiarly complete system of slavery, centuries old; and now, suddenly, violently, they come into a new birthright, at a time of war and passion, in the midst of the stricken and embittered population of their former masters. Any man might well have hesitated to assume charge of such a work, with vast responsibilities, indefinite powers, and limited resources. Probably no one but a soldier would have answered such a call promptly; and, indeed, no one but a soldier could be called, for Congress had appropriated no money for salaries and expenses.

Less than a month after the weary Emancipator passed to his rest, his successor assigned Major-Gen. Oliver O. Howard to duty as Commissioner of the new Bureau. He was a Maine man, then only thirty-five years of age. He had marched with Sherman to the sea, had fought well at Gettysburg, and but the year before had been assigned to the command of the Department of Tennessee. An honest man, with too much faith in human nature, little aptitude for business and intricate detail, he had had large opportunity of becoming acquainted at first hand with much of the work before him. And of that work it has been truly said that “no approximately correct history of civilization can ever be written which does not throw out in bold relief, as one of the great landmarks of political and social progress, the organization and administration of the Freedmen’s Bureau.”

On May 12, 1865, Howard was appointed; and he assumed the duties of his office promptly on the 15th, and began examining the field of work. A curious mess he looked upon: little despotisms, communistic experiments, slavery, peonage, business speculations, organized charity, unorganized almsgiving,—all reeling on under the guise of helping the freedmen, and all enshrined in the smoke and blood of the war and the cursing and silence of angry men. On May 19 the new government—for a government it really was—issued its constitution; commissioners were to be appointed in each of the seceded states, who were to take charge of “all subjects relating to refugees and freedmen,” and all relief and rations were to be given by their consent alone. The Bureau invited continued cooperation with benevolent societies, and declared: “It will be the object of all commissioners to introduce practicable systems of compensated labor,” and to establish schools. Forthwith nine assistant commissioners were appointed. They were to hasten to their fields of work; seek gradually to close relief establishments, and make the destitute self-supporting; act as courts of law where there were no courts, or where Negroes were not recognized in them as free; establish the institution of marriage among ex-slaves, and keep records; see that freedmen were free to choose their employers, and help in making fair contracts for them; and finally, the circular said: “Simple good faith, for which we hope on all hands for those concerned in the passing away of slavery, will especially relieve the assistant commissioners in the discharge of their duties toward the freedmen, as well as promote the general welfare.”
paragraphsZh: 这最后的妥协是一项仓促的立法，其轮廓含糊不清、不确定。成立了一个局，“在当前叛乱战争期间及其后一年继续存在”，赋予其“对所有被遗弃土地的监督和管理，以及对与难民和自由民有关的一切事务的控制”，按照“局长提出并由总统批准的规则和条例”进行。局长由总统和参议院任命，负责管理该局，办公室职员不得超过十名文员。总统也可以在脱离联邦的州任命助理局长，并且所有这些职位都可以派驻军事官员，按正常工资领取报酬。战争部长可以向贫困者发放口粮、衣物和燃料，所有被遗弃的财产都由局接管，最终以四十英亩的地块租赁和出售给前奴隶。

就这样，美国政府确实承担起将获得自由的黑人作为国家监护人的责任。这是一项巨大的任务。在一挥笔之间，就建立了一个由数百万人的政府——而且这些人并非普通人，而是被一种历经数百年的极其彻底的奴隶制度阉割的黑人；而现在，他们突然间、猛烈地获得了新的生来权利，正值战争与激情的时期，在他们前任主人的痛苦和愤恨的人口中。任何人都难免会犹豫是否要承担这样一项工作，肩负如此重大的责任、拥有无限的权力，却资源有限。恐怕除了士兵以外，没有人会立即响应这样的号召；事实上，也只有士兵才可能被召集，因为国会并未拨款用于工资和开支。

在那位疲惫的解放者去世不到一个月后，他的继任者任命奥利弗·O·霍华德少将担任新局的专员。他是缅因州人，当时年仅三十五岁。他曾随谢尔曼行军至大海，在葛底斯堡表现出色，并且就在前一年被任命为田纳西军区司令。霍华德是个诚实的人，对人性过于信任，缺乏处理事务和复杂细节的才能，但他有大量机会亲身了解他面前的诸多工作。关于那项工作，人们曾真实地说过：“没有哪部大致正确的文明史能够写成，而不将解放奴隶局的组织和管理作为政治与社会进步的重要里程碑之一，明确突出地呈现出来。”

1865年5月12日，霍华德被任命；他在15日立即履行了职务，并开始审查工作领域。他所看到的情况奇怪而混乱：小型专制、共产主义实验、奴隶制、佃农制度、商业投机、组织化的慈善、非组织化的施舍——这一切都在以帮助解放黑人为名义下摇摇欲坠，而且都镶嵌在战争的烟雾和鲜血中，以及愤怒人们的咒骂和沉默之中。5月19日，新的政府——因为它实际上确实是一个政府——发布了宪法；每个脱离联邦的州都将任命专员，负责“所有与难民和自由黑人有关的事务”，所有救济和配给都必须经其同意才能发放。局方邀请继续与慈善团体合作，并宣称：“所有专员的目标将是引入可行的有偿劳动制度，”并建立学校。随后，任命了九名助理专员。他们应当加快前往他们的工作领域；逐步关闭救济机构，使陷入困境的人能够自力更生；在没有法院或者黑人在其中不被承认为自由人的地方行使法院职能；在前奴隶中建立婚姻制度，并进行登记；确保自由民可以自由选择雇主，并帮助他们订立公平的合同；最后，通告中说道：“我们希望所有参与奴隶制度废除事务的人都能抱有单纯的诚信，这将特别减轻助理专员在履行对自由民职责时的负担，同时促进整体福利。”

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 5
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: Before 1750, while the fire of African freedom still burned in the veins of the slaves, there was in all leadership or attempted leadership but the one motive of revolt and revenge,—typified in the terrible Maroons, the Danish blacks, and Cato of Stono, and veiling all the Americas in fear of insurrection. The liberalizing tendencies of the latter half of the eighteenth century brought, along with kindlier relations between black and white, thoughts of ultimate adjustment and assimilation. Such aspiration was especially voiced in the earnest songs of Phyllis, in the martyrdom of Attucks, the fighting of Salem and Poor, the intellectual accomplishments of Banneker and Derham, and the political demands of the Cuffes.

Stern financial and social stress after the war cooled much of the previous humanitarian ardor. The disappointment and impatience of the Negroes at the persistence of slavery and serfdom voiced itself in two movements. The slaves in the South, aroused undoubtedly by vague rumors of the Haytian revolt, made three fierce attempts at insurrection,—in 1800 under Gabriel in Virginia, in 1822 under Vesey in Carolina, and in 1831 again in Virginia under the terrible Nat Turner. In the Free States, on the other hand, a new and curious attempt at self-development was made. In Philadelphia and New York color-prescription led to a withdrawal of Negro communicants from white churches and the formation of a peculiar socio-religious institution among the Negroes known as the African Church,—an organization still living and controlling in its various branches over a million of men.

Walker’s wild appeal against the trend of the times showed how the world was changing after the coming of the cotton-gin. By 1830 slavery seemed hopelessly fastened on the South, and the slaves thoroughly cowed into submission. The free Negroes of the North, inspired by the mulatto immigrants from the West Indies, began to change the basis of their demands; they recognized the slavery of slaves, but insisted that they themselves were freemen, and sought assimilation and amalgamation with the nation on the same terms with other men. Thus, Forten and Purvis of Philadelphia, Shad of Wilmington, Du Bois of New Haven, Barbadoes of Boston, and others, strove singly and together as men, they said, not as slaves; as “people of color,” not as “Negroes.” The trend of the times, however, refused them recognition save in individual and exceptional cases, considered them as one with all the despised blacks, and they soon found themselves striving to keep even the rights they formerly had of voting and working and moving as freemen. Schemes of migration and colonization arose among them; but these they refused to entertain, and they eventually turned to the Abolition movement as a final refuge.

Here, led by Remond, Nell, Wells-Brown, and Douglass, a new period of self-assertion and self-development dawned. To be sure, ultimate freedom and assimilation was the ideal before the leaders, but the assertion of the manhood rights of the Negro by himself was the main reliance, and John Brown’s raid was the extreme of its logic. After the war and emancipation, the great form of Frederick Douglass, the greatest of American Negro leaders, still led the host. Self-assertion, especially in political lines, was the main programme, and behind Douglass came Elliot, Bruce, and Langston, and the Reconstruction politicians, and, less conspicuous but of greater social significance, Alexander Crummell and Bishop Daniel Payne.

Then came the Revolution of 1876, the suppression of the Negro votes, the changing and shifting of ideals, and the seeking of new lights in the great night. Douglass, in his old age, still bravely stood for the ideals of his early manhood,—ultimate assimilation through self-assertion, and on no other terms. For a time Price arose as a new leader, destined, it seemed, not to give up, but to re-state the old ideals in a form less repugnant to the white South. But he passed away in his prime. Then came the new leader. Nearly all the former ones had become leaders by the silent suffrage of their fellows, had sought to lead their own people alone, and were usually, save Douglass, little known outside their race. But Booker T. Washington arose as essentially the leader not of one race but of two,—a compromiser between the South, the North, and the Negro. Naturally the Negroes resented, at first bitterly, signs of compromise which surrendered their civil and political rights, even though this was to be exchanged for larger chances of economic development. The rich and dominating North, however, was not only weary of the race problem, but was investing largely in Southern enterprises, and welcomed any method of peaceful cooperation. Thus, by national opinion, the Negroes began to recognize Mr. Washington’s leadership; and the voice of criticism was hushed.
paragraphsZh: 在1750年之前，当非洲自由的火焰仍然在奴隶的血脉中燃烧时，所有的领导或试图领导的行动中，唯一的动机就是反抗和复仇——这在可怕的马龙人、丹麦黑奴和圣诺诺的卡托身上得到了体现，也使整个美洲笼罩在起义的恐惧之中。十八世纪下半叶的自由化趋势，伴随着黑人与白人之间更友好的关系，也带来了最终调解与同化的思想。这种愿望尤其体现在菲利斯的深情歌声、阿图克斯的殉难、塞勒姆和普尔的战斗、班内克与德汉的智慧成就，以及卡富家族的政治诉求中。

战争后的严峻经济和社会压力抑制了先前的人道热情。黑人对奴隶制和农奴制持久存在的失望和不耐烦，表现在两场运动中。南方的奴隶，无疑是受到海地革命模糊传闻的刺激，曾三次猛烈尝试起义——1800年弗吉尼亚州的加布里埃尔起义，1822年卡罗来纳州的韦西起义，以及1831年弗吉尼亚州的可怕的纳特·特纳起义。另一方面，在自由州，则出现了一种新的、奇特的自我发展的尝试。在费城和纽约，肤色规定导致黑人领餐者退出白人教堂，形成了一个特殊的社会宗教机构——非洲教会——一个至今仍在各分支中控制着超过一百万男性的组织。

沃克对时代潮流的猛烈反对显示了棉花轧花机出现后世界的变化。到1830年，奴隶制似乎已牢不可破地固定在南方，而奴隶们则完全顺从而被吓服。北方的自由黑人，在来自西印度群岛的混血移民的激励下，开始改变他们诉求的基础；他们承认奴隶的奴役，但坚持认为自己是自由人，并寻求与国家在与其他人同样的条件下同化和融合。因此，费城的福尔顿和珀维斯，威明顿的沙德，新罕布什尔的杜波依斯，波士顿的巴巴多斯等人，既独自也共同努力，他们说，是作为人，而不是奴隶；作为“有色人”，而不是“黑人”。然而，时代的潮流拒绝给予他们认可，除了个别和特殊案例，将他们视为所有被鄙视的黑人中的一员，他们很快发现自己不得不努力争取甚至曾经拥有的投票、工作和以自由人身份行动的权利。他们中间出现了迁移和殖民的计划；但他们拒绝考虑这些，最终转向废奴运动作为最后的庇护所。

在这里，由雷蒙德、内尔、韦尔斯-布朗和道格拉斯领导，一个自我主张和自我发展的新时期开始了。当然，最终的自由和同化是这些领导者心中的理想，但黑人自己争取男子权利才是主要依靠，而约翰·布朗的袭击是其逻辑的极端表现。战争和解放之后，美国黑人领袖中最伟大的弗雷德里克·道格拉斯的伟大身影仍然带领着人群。自我主张，尤其是在政治领域，是主要纲领，而在道格拉斯之后出现了埃利奥特、布鲁斯和朗斯顿，以及重建时期的政治家们，还有不太显眼但社会意义更大的亚历山大·克拉默尔和主教丹尼尔·佩恩。

随后是1876年的革命、对黑人投票权的压制、理念的变化和转移，以及在漫长黑夜中寻求新的光明。杜格拉斯在晚年仍然勇敢地坚持他青年时期的理想——通过自我主张最终实现同化，而且别无他法。曾有一段时间，普赖斯崛起为一位新领导人，似乎注定不会放弃，而是以一种对白人南方不那么令人反感的形式重新表达旧有理想。但他在壮年时去世。随后出现了新领导人。几乎所有以前的领导人都是通过同伴的沉默选票而成为领导者，他们寻求只领导自己的族群，而且通常，除了杜格拉斯之外，在族群外几乎不为人知。但布克·T。华盛顿实际上不是单一种族的领导者，而是两个种族的领导者——南方、北方和黑人之间的妥协者。自然，黑人们起初对放弃公民和政治权利的妥协表示愤怒，尽管这将换取更大的经济发展机会。然而，富有且主导地位的北方不仅对种族问题感到厌倦，还大量投资南方企业，欢迎任何和平合作的方式。因此，按照全国舆论，黑人开始认可华盛顿先生的领导;批评的声音被压制。

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 6
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: And last of all there trickles down that third and darker thought,—the thought of the things themselves, the confused, half-conscious mutter of men who are black and whitened, crying “Liberty, Freedom, Opportunity—vouchsafe to us, O boastful World, the chance of living men!” To be sure, behind the thought lurks the afterthought,—suppose, after all, the World is right and we are less than men? Suppose this mad impulse within is all wrong, some mock mirage from the untrue?

So here we stand among thoughts of human unity, even through conquest and slavery; the inferiority of black men, even if forced by fraud; a shriek in the night for the freedom of men who themselves are not yet sure of their right to demand it. This is the tangle of thought and afterthought wherein we are called to solve the problem of training men for life.

Behind all its curiousness, so attractive alike to sage and dilettante, lie its dim dangers, throwing across us shadows at once grotesque and awful. Plain it is to us that what the world seeks through desert and wild we have within our threshold,—a stalwart laboring force, suited to the semi-tropics; if, deaf to the voice of the Zeitgeist, we refuse to use and develop these men, we risk poverty and loss. If, on the other hand, seized by the brutal afterthought, we debauch the race thus caught in our talons, selfishly sucking their blood and brains in the future as in the past, what shall save us from national decadence? Only that saner selfishness, which Education teaches, can find the rights of all in the whirl of work.

Again, we may decry the color-prejudice of the South, yet it remains a heavy fact. Such curious kinks of the human mind exist and must be reckoned with soberly. They cannot be laughed away, nor always successfully stormed at, nor easily abolished by act of legislature. And yet they must not be encouraged by being let alone. They must be recognized as facts, but unpleasant facts; things that stand in the way of civilization and religion and common decency. They can be met in but one way,—by the breadth and broadening of human reason, by catholicity of taste and culture. And so, too, the native ambition and aspiration of men, even though they be black, backward, and ungraceful, must not lightly be dealt with. To stimulate wildly weak and untrained minds is to play with mighty fires; to flout their striving idly is to welcome a harvest of brutish crime and shameless lethargy in our very laps. The guiding of thought and the deft coordination of deed is at once the path of honor and humanity.

And so, in this great question of reconciling three vast and partially contradictory streams of thought, the one panacea of Education leaps to the lips of all:—such human training as will best use the labor of all men without enslaving or brutalizing; such training as will give us poise to encourage the prejudices that bulwark society, and to stamp out those that in sheer barbarity deafen us to the wail of prisoned souls within the Veil, and the mounting fury of shackled men.

But when we have vaguely said that Education will set this tangle straight, what have we uttered but a truism? Training for life teaches living; but what training for the profitable living together of black men and white? A hundred and fifty years ago our task would have seemed easier. Then Dr. Johnson blandly assured us that education was needful solely for the embellishments of life, and was useless for ordinary vermin. To-day we have climbed to heights where we would open at least the outer courts of knowledge to all, display its treasures to many, and select the few to whom its mystery of Truth is revealed, not wholly by birth or the accidents of the stock market, but at least in part according to deftness and aim, talent and character. This programme, however, we are sorely puzzled in carrying out through that part of the land where the blight of slavery fell hardest, and where we are dealing with two backward peoples. To make here in human education that ever necessary combination of the permanent and the contingent—of the ideal and the practical in workable equilibrium—has been there, as it ever must be in every age and place, a matter of infinite experiment and frequent mistakes.
paragraphsZh: 最后，还有那第三个更黑暗的想法——关于事物本身的念头，那些黑白分明的人们困惑半意识地喃喃自语，喊着“自由、自由、机会——向我们保证，哦，自夸的世界，活着的人的机会！”当然，在思想背后隐藏着附带的思绪——假设，毕竟世界是对的，而我们不如人？假如这种疯狂的冲动全错了，是虚假的幻象？
我们站在人类团结的思想中，即使经历了征服和奴役;黑人的劣势，即使被欺诈所迫;夜晚为那些自己尚未确定是否有权争取自由的人发出的尖叫。这就是我们被召唤解决培养终身人性问题的思想与后悔纠缠之中。

在其所有的奇异性背后，同样吸引着智者与爱好者，隐藏着昏暗的危险，投射在我们身上的阴影既滑稽又可怕。对于我们来说很清楚，世界通过沙漠与荒野所寻找的东西，我们就在门槛之内——一支强壮而勤勉的劳动力，适合半热带地区；如果我们对时代精神的呼声充耳不闻，拒绝利用和培养这些人，我们就有贫困和损失的风险。另一方面，如果受残酷事后的冲动驱使，我们败坏了被我们掌控的种族，自私地像过去一样榨取他们的血液与智慧，将来也是如此，那么有什么能拯救我们免于国家衰退呢？唯有教育所教导那种更理智的自私，才能在工作旋涡中找到人人的权利。

我们可以再次谴责南方的种族偏见，但它依然是一个严峻的事实。人类心灵中存在这种奇特的扭曲，必须冷静地面对。它们不能被一笑了之，也不能总是成功地攻克，也不能轻易通过立法废除。然而，也不能因不理会而纵容它们。它们必须被承认为事实，但却是不愉快的事实；这些东西阻碍了文明、宗教和基本的体面行为。面对它们只有一种办法——通过人类理性的广阔与拓展，通过审美和文化的包容性。同样地，人的天生的雄心与志向，即便他们是黑皮肤、落后、不优雅，也不能轻易对待。刺激极为脆弱和未受训练的心智，就像玩火一般；对他们的努力漫不经心地嘲弄，就是在我们自己的膝上迎接野蛮犯罪和无耻懒惰的丰收。思想的引导与行为的巧妙协调，同时是荣誉与人道的道路。
因此，在调和三股巨大且部分相互矛盾的思想潮流这一重大问题上，教育的唯一灵丹妙药便跃然众人唇边：——这种人类训练将最有效地利用所有人的劳动而不致奴役或残害他们；这种训练将赋予我们平衡，以鼓励支撑社会的偏见，并铲除那些以纯粹野蛮使我们对囚禁灵魂在帷幕后哀嚎以及被束缚之人日益增长的愤怒麻木的偏见。

但是，当我们含糊地说教育将解决这个纠葛时，我们说的不过是一个陈词滥调而已。生活的训练教会人们生活；但对于黑人与白人共同有益的生活，我们有什么样的训练呢？一百五十年前，我们的任务似乎会更容易些。那时，约翰逊博士轻描淡写地告诉我们，教育仅仅是为了生活的装饰，对普通的人无用。今天，我们已经攀登到这样高的高度，我们至少可以向所有人开放知识的外院，向许多人展示其宝藏，并挑选少数人向他们揭示真理的奥秘，这不仅完全靠出身或股市的偶然因素，而至少在某种程度上根据聪明才智与目标、天赋和品格来决定。然而，在那片受奴隶制之害最重的土地上执行这个计划，我们感到非常困惑，因为我们正在与两个落后民族打交道。在这里的人类教育中，要实现那种永远必要的、将永久性与偶然性——理想与实践——在可行的平衡中结合的教育，一直以来，正如在任何时代和地点一样，都是一个无穷无尽的实验，并伴随着频繁的错误。

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 7
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: If it is true that there are an appreciable number of Negro youth in the land capable by character and talent to receive that higher training, the end of which is culture, and if the two and a half thousand who have had something of this training in the past have in the main proved themselves useful to their race and generation, the question then comes, What place in the future development of the South ought the Negro college and college-bred man to occupy? That the present social separation and acute race-sensitiveness must eventually yield to the influences of culture, as the South grows civilized, is clear. But such transformation calls for singular wisdom and patience. If, while the healing of this vast sore is progressing, the races are to live for many years side by side, united in economic effort, obeying a common government, sensitive to mutual thought and feeling, yet subtly and silently separate in many matters of deeper human intimacy,—if this unusual and dangerous development is to progress amid peace and order, mutual respect and growing intelligence, it will call for social surgery at once the delicatest and nicest in modern history. It will demand broad-minded, upright men, both white and black, and in its final accomplishment American civilization will triumph. So far as white men are concerned, this fact is to-day being recognized in the South, and a happy renaissance of university education seems imminent. But the very voices that cry hail to this good work are, strange to relate, largely silent or antagonistic to the higher education of the Negro.

Strange to relate! for this is certain, no secure civilization can be built in the South with the Negro as an ignorant, turbulent proletariat. Suppose we seek to remedy this by making them laborers and nothing more: they are not fools, they have tasted of the Tree of Life, and they will not cease to think, will not cease attempting to read the riddle of the world. By taking away their best equipped teachers and leaders, by slamming the door of opportunity in the faces of their bolder and brighter minds, will you make them satisfied with their lot? or will you not rather transfer their leading from the hands of men taught to think to the hands of untrained demagogues? We ought not to forget that despite the pressure of poverty, and despite the active discouragement and even ridicule of friends, the demand for higher training steadily increases among Negro youth: there were, in the years from 1875 to 1880, 22 Negro graduates from Northern colleges; from 1885 to 1890 there were 43, and from 1895 to 1900, nearly 100 graduates. From Southern Negro colleges there were, in the same three periods, 143, 413, and over 500 graduates. Here, then, is the plain thirst for training; by refusing to give this Talented Tenth the key to knowledge, can any sane man imagine that they will lightly lay aside their yearning and contentedly become hewers of wood and drawers of water?

No. The dangerously clear logic of the Negro’s position will more and more loudly assert itself in that day when increasing wealth and more intricate social organization preclude the South from being, as it so largely is, simply an armed camp for intimidating black folk. Such waste of energy cannot be spared if the South is to catch up with civilization. And as the black third of the land grows in thrift and skill, unless skilfully guided in its larger philosophy, it must more and more brood over the red past and the creeping, crooked present, until it grasps a gospel of revolt and revenge and throws its new-found energies athwart the current of advance. Even to-day the masses of the Negroes see all too clearly the anomalies of their position and the moral crookedness of yours. You may marshal strong indictments against them, but their counter-cries, lacking though they be in formal logic, have burning truths within them which you may not wholly ignore, O Southern Gentlemen! If you deplore their presence here, they ask, Who brought us? When you cry, Deliver us from the vision of intermarriage, they answer that legal marriage is infinitely better than systematic concubinage and prostitution. And if in just fury you accuse their vagabonds of violating women, they also in fury quite as just may reply: The rape which your gentlemen have done against helpless black women in defiance of your own laws is written on the foreheads of two millions of mulattoes, and written in ineffaceable blood. And finally, when you fasten crime upon this race as its peculiar trait, they answer that slavery was the arch-crime, and lynching and lawlessness its twin abortions; that color and race are not crimes, and yet it is they which in this land receive most unceasing condemnation, North, East, South, and West.
paragraphsZh: 如果确实有相当数量的黑人青年凭借品格和才能能够接受这种更高的教育，而其终点是文化，并且过去接受过这种训练的两千五百人大多对他们的种族和世代有所帮助，那么问题就出现了：黑人学院和大学出身的人在南方未来的发展中应占据什么位置？随着南方日益文明，当前的社会隔离和高度的种族敏感性最终必须屈服于文化的影响，这一点显而易见。但这种转变需要非凡的智慧和耐心。如果，在这个巨大创伤的愈合过程中，各族群要在多年中并肩生活，在经济活动中团结一致，服从共同的政府，对彼此的思想和感受保持敏感，同时在许多更深层的人类亲密事务上又微妙而默默地保持分离——如果这种不寻常而危险的发展要在和平与秩序、相互尊重和不断增长的智慧中推进，它将需要进行现代历史上最精细巧妙的社会手术。它将要求宽宏大量、品行端正的人物，不论白人还是黑人，而在最终完成时，美国文明将获得胜利。就白人而言，这一事实今天在南方已经被承认，而大学教育的幸福复兴似乎指日可待。但那些为这项伟大工作致敬的声音，奇怪的是，大多对黑人高等教育保持沉默甚至敌对。

说得真奇怪！因为这是肯定的，南方无法建立一个安全的文明，只有黑人是无知、动荡的无产阶级。假设我们试图通过让他们成为劳工来弥补这一点：他们不是傻瓜，他们尝过生命之树的滋味，他们不会停止思考，不会停止试图解读世界的谜题。通过夺走他们最有能力的教师和领导者，关上机会之门，拒绝他们更大胆、更聪明的头脑，你会让他们满足于自己的处境吗？还是你不愿意把他们的领导权从被教导思考的人手中转移到未经训练的煽动者手中？我们不应忘记，尽管贫困的压力，尽管朋友们受到积极的劝阻甚至嘲笑，黑人青年对高等教育的需求却在稳步增长：1875年至1880年间，北方学院有22名黑人毕业生;1885年至1890年有43人，1895年至1900年近100人。南方黑人学院在同样三个时期共有143人、413人，超过500人。这就是对培训的明显渴望;拒绝将这具才华的第十学院提供知识钥匙，任何理智的人能想象他们会轻易放下渴望，满足地成为砍柴和挑水的人吗？

不。黑人立场的危险清晰逻辑将在那一天愈发高声地彰显出来，当财富不断增长、社会结构更加复杂，南方不再像现在这样，仅仅沦为一个恐吓黑人的武装营地。如果南方想要赶上文明，这种浪费精力是无法被剥夺的。随着黑人三分之一土地在节俭和技能上不断增长，除非在其更大哲学中得到巧妙引导，否则他们必须越来越多地沉思红色过去和逐渐腐败的现在，直到它抓住反抗和复仇的福音，将新获得的能量投掷出逆流而上的进步潮流。即使在今天，黑人大众依然清楚地看到他们处境的异常和你们的道德腐败。你们可以对她们提出强烈指控，但她们的反驳，虽然缺乏形式上的逻辑，却蕴含着你们不能完全忽视的炽热真相，南方的绅士们！如果你们谴责她们的存在，她们会问：是谁带我们来的？当你们喊着，救我们脱离通婚的幻象时，她们回答说，合法婚姻远胜于系统性的妾室和卖淫。如果你愤怒地指责他们的流浪汉侵犯妇女，她们也会愤怒地反驳：你们的绅士们对无助黑人妇女所做的强奸，违抗你们自己的法律，写在两百万混血者的额头上，用不可抹去的鲜血写下。最后，当你把犯罪归咎于这个种族，认为这是它的特有特征时，他们回应说，奴隶制是最严重的罪行，而私刑和无法无天则是其双胞胎产物；肤色和种族不是犯罪，但在这片土地上，它们却受到最持续的谴责，无论是北方、东方、南方还是西方。

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 8
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: Above all, the cabins are crowded. We have come to associate crowding with homes in cities almost exclusively. This is primarily because we have so little accurate knowledge of country life. Here in Dougherty County one may find families of eight and ten occupying one or two rooms, and for every ten rooms of house accommodation for the Negroes there are twenty-five persons. The worst tenement abominations of New York do not have above twenty-two persons for every ten rooms. Of course, one small, close room in a city, without a yard, is in many respects worse than the larger single country room. In other respects it is better; it has glass windows, a decent chimney, and a trustworthy floor. The single great advantage of the Negro peasant is that he may spend most of his life outside his hovel, in the open fields.

There are four chief causes of these wretched homes: First, long custom born of slavery has assigned such homes to Negroes; white laborers would be offered better accommodations, and might, for that and similar reasons, give better work. Secondly, the Negroes, used to such accommodations, do not as a rule demand better; they do not know what better houses mean. Thirdly, the landlords as a class have not yet come to realize that it is a good business investment to raise the standard of living among labor by slow and judicious methods; that a Negro laborer who demands three rooms and fifty cents a day would give more efficient work and leave a larger profit than a discouraged toiler herding his family in one room and working for thirty cents. Lastly, among such conditions of life there are few incentives to make the laborer become a better farmer. If he is ambitious, he moves to town or tries other labor; as a tenant-farmer his outlook is almost hopeless, and following it as a makeshift, he takes the house that is given him without protest.

Looking now at the county black population as a whole, it is fair to characterize it as poor and ignorant. Perhaps ten per cent compose the well-to-do and the best of the laborers, while at least nine per cent are thoroughly lewd and vicious. The rest, over eighty per cent, are poor and ignorant, fairly honest and well meaning, plodding, and to a degree shiftless, with some but not great sexual looseness. Such class lines are by no means fixed; they vary, one might almost say, with the price of cotton. The degree of ignorance cannot easily be expressed. We may say, for instance, that nearly two-thirds of them cannot read or write. This but partially expresses the fact. They are ignorant of the world about them, of modern economic organization, of the function of government, of individual worth and possibilities,—of nearly all those things which slavery in self-defence had to keep them from learning. Much that the white boy imbibes from his earliest social atmosphere forms the puzzling problems of the black boy’s mature years. America is not another word for Opportunity to all her sons.

It is easy for us to lose ourselves in details in endeavoring to grasp and comprehend the real condition of a mass of human beings. We often forget that each unit in the mass is a throbbing human soul. Ignorant it may be, and poverty stricken, black and curious in limb and ways and thought; and yet it loves and hates, it toils and tires, it laughs and weeps its bitter tears, and looks in vague and awful longing at the grim horizon of its life,—all this, even as you and I. These black thousands are not in reality lazy; they are improvident and careless; they insist on breaking the monotony of toil with a glimpse at the great town-world on Saturday; they have their loafers and their rascals; but the great mass of them work continuously and faithfully for a return, and under circumstances that would call forth equal voluntary effort from few if any other modern laboring class. Over eighty-eight per cent of them—men, women, and children—are farmers. Indeed, this is almost the only industry. Most of the children get their schooling after the “crops are laid by,” and very few there are that stay in school after the spring work has begun. Child-labor is to be found here in some of its worst phases, as fostering ignorance and stunting physical development. With the grown men of the county there is little variety in work: thirteen hundred are farmers, and two hundred are laborers, teamsters, etc., including twenty-four artisans, ten merchants, twenty-one preachers, and four teachers. This narrowness of life reaches its maximum among the women: thirteen hundred and fifty of these are farm laborers, one hundred are servants and washerwomen, leaving sixty-five housewives, eight teachers, and six seamstresses.
paragraphsZh: 最重要的是，小屋里人满为患。我们几乎只将拥挤与城市的住宅联系在一起。这主要是因为我们对乡村生活了解极少。在多尔蒂县，八到十口的家庭住在一两个房间里，而黑人每十个房间的住房就有二十五人。纽约最糟糕的贫民公寓，每十个房间的人数都不超过二十二人。当然，城市里一个没有院子的小房间，在许多方面比更大的乡村房间更糟糕。在其他方面，它更好;它有玻璃窗，一个不错的烟囱，还有一个值得信赖的地板。黑人农民唯一的巨大优势是，他可以大部分时间待在茅屋外的开阔田野里。

这些糟糕的住房主要有四个原因：首先，奴隶制养成的长期习俗将这些住房分配给黑人;白人劳工将获得更好的住所，因此可能提供更好的工作。其次，习惯于此类住所的黑人通常不会要求更好的住房;他们不了解更好的住房意味着什么。第三，地主阶层尚未意识到通过缓慢而明智地提高劳动者的生活水平是一种良好的商业投资;一个要求每天三间房五毛钱的黑人劳工，工作效率更高，利润也比一个气馁的劳工把家人赶在一个房间里，只为三毛钱工作。最后，在这样的生活条件下，很少有激励让劳动者成为一个更好的农民。如果他有抱负，他会搬到城里或尝试其他工作；作为佃农，他的前景几乎是绝望的，而作为权宜之计，他接受分配给他的房子而不提出异议。

现在看全县黑人人口，可以说他们贫穷且无知。大约百分之十是富裕和最优秀的劳工，而至少百分之九的人极其猥亵和恶毒。其余超过八成的人贫穷无知，相当诚实且善意，缓慢，有一定程度的闲散，性方面有些许但不甚放荡。这些阶级界限绝非固定;几乎可以说，它们与棉花价格不同。无知程度难以言表。例如，我们可以说近三分之二的黑人不会读写。这只是部分事实。他们对周围的世界、现代经济组织、政府功能、个人价值和可能性一无所知——几乎所有那些奴隶制为了自卫而使他们无法学习的东西。白人男孩从最早的社会氛围中吸收的许多，构成了黑人男孩成熟岁月的复杂问题。美国对她所有儿子来说，不是机会的另一个词。

在努力把握和理解一大群人的真实状况时，我们很容易在细节中迷失自己。我们经常忘记，群体中的每一个个体都是一个跳动的人类灵魂。它可能无知，贫困，四肢和行为及思想奇特；然而它也会爱与恨，它劳作并疲惫，它笑并哭出苦涩的泪水，并以模糊而可怕的渴望凝视生活那严酷的地平线——所有这一切，都和你我一样。这些黑人成千上万的人实际上并不懒惰；他们是缺乏远见和粗心大意的；他们坚持在星期六通过瞥一眼大城市世界来打破劳作的单调；他们有自己的游手好闲者和流氓；但绝大多数人都在持续且忠实地工作以获取报酬，并且在这样的环境下工作，很少有其他现代劳动阶层能够自发地付出同样的努力。他们中有超过88%的人——包括男性、女性和儿童——是农民。实际上，这几乎是唯一的产业。大多数孩子在“庄稼收割完毕”后接受教育，很少有人在春季农活开始后还继续上学。在这里，童工现象存在于其一些最糟糕的阶段，如助长无知和阻碍身体发育。在这个县的成年男性中，工作的种类很少：有一千三百人是农民，两百人是劳工、车夫等，其中包括二十四名工匠、十名商人、二十一名传教士和四名教师。这种生活的单调在女性中达到了极点：其中一千三百五十人是农场女工，一百人是仆人和洗衣妇，剩下六十五名家庭主妇、八名教师和六名女裁缝。

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 9
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: Two characteristic things must be noticed in regard to the church. First, it became almost entirely Baptist and Methodist in faith; secondly, as a social institution it antedated by many decades the monogamic Negro home. From the very circumstances of its beginning, the church was confined to the plantation, and consisted primarily of a series of disconnected units; although, later on, some freedom of movement was allowed, still this geographical limitation was always important and was one cause of the spread of the decentralized and democratic Baptist faith among the slaves. At the same time, the visible rite of baptism appealed strongly to their mystic temperament. To-day the Baptist Church is still largest in membership among Negroes, and has a million and a half communicants. Next in popularity came the churches organized in connection with the white neighboring churches, chiefly Baptist and Methodist, with a few Episcopalian and others. The Methodists still form the second greatest denomination, with nearly a million members. The faith of these two leading denominations was more suited to the slave church from the prominence they gave to religious feeling and fervor. The Negro membership in other denominations has always been small and relatively unimportant, although the Episcopalians and Presbyterians are gaining among the more intelligent classes to-day, and the Catholic Church is making headway in certain sections. After Emancipation, and still earlier in the North, the Negro churches largely severed such affiliations as they had had with the white churches, either by choice or by compulsion. The Baptist churches became independent, but the Methodists were compelled early to unite for purposes of episcopal government. This gave rise to the great African Methodist Church, the greatest Negro organization in the world, to the Zion Church and the Colored Methodist, and to the black conferences and churches in this and other denominations.

The second fact noted, namely, that the Negro church antedates the Negro home, leads to an explanation of much that is paradoxical in this communistic institution and in the morals of its members. But especially it leads us to regard this institution as peculiarly the expression of the inner ethical life of a people in a sense seldom true elsewhere. Let us turn, then, from the outer physical development of the church to the more important inner ethical life of the people who compose it. The Negro has already been pointed out many times as a religious animal,—a being of that deep emotional nature which turns instinctively toward the supernatural. Endowed with a rich tropical imagination and a keen, delicate appreciation of Nature, the transplanted African lived in a world animate with gods and devils, elves and witches; full of strange influences,—of Good to be implored, of Evil to be propitiated. Slavery, then, was to him the dark triumph of Evil over him. All the hateful powers of the Under-world were striving against him, and a spirit of revolt and revenge filled his heart. He called up all the resources of heathenism to aid,—exorcism and witch-craft, the mysterious Obi worship with its barbarious rites, spells, and blood-sacrifice even, now and then, of human victims. Weird midnight orgies and mystic conjurations were invoked, the witch-woman and the voodoo-priest became the centre of Negro group life, and that vein of vague superstition which characterizes the unlettered Negro even to-day was deepened and strengthened.

In spite, however, of such success as that of the fierce Maroons, the Danish blacks, and others, the spirit of revolt gradually died away under the untiring energy and superior strength of the slave masters. By the middle of the eighteenth century the black slave had sunk, with hushed murmurs, to his place at the bottom of a new economic system, and was unconsciously ripe for a new philosophy of life. Nothing suited his condition then better than the doctrines of passive submission embodied in the newly learned Christianity. Slave masters early realized this, and cheerfully aided religious propaganda within certain bounds. The long system of repression and degradation of the Negro tended to emphasize the elements of his character which made him a valuable chattel: courtesy became humility, moral strength degenerated into submission, and the exquisite native appreciation of the beautiful became an infinite capacity for dumb suffering. The Negro, losing the joy of this world, eagerly seized upon the offered conceptions of the next; the avenging Spirit of the Lord enjoining patience in this world, under sorrow and tribulation until the Great Day when He should lead His dark children home,—this became his comforting dream. His preacher repeated the prophecy, and his bards sang,—
paragraphsZh: 教会有两个显著特点需要注意。首先，教会几乎完全信奉浸信会和卫理公会;其次，作为一种社会机构，它比一夫一妻制的黑人家庭早了几十年。从最初的环境开始，教会就局限于种植园内，主要由一系列分散的单位组成;尽管后来允许一定的行动自由，但这种地理限制始终重要，也是奴隶中分散且民主的浸信会信仰传播的原因之一。与此同时，洗礼的可见仪式强烈吸引了他们的神秘气质。如今，浸信会仍是黑人中会员人数最多的，拥有一百五十万圣餐信徒。接下来受欢迎的是与附近的白人教会相关联而组建的教会，主要是浸信会和卫理公会教会，还有少数圣公会和其他教派。卫理公会仍然是人数第二多的教派，拥有近一百万信徒。这两个主要教派的信仰更适合奴隶教会，因为它们强调宗教感受和热情。在其他教派中，黑人成员一直很少，相对不重要，尽管今天圣公会和长老会在较有文化的群体中正在增长，天主教会在某些地区也在取得进展。解放后，甚至更早在北方，黑人教会大多切断了与白人教会的联系，无论是出于选择还是被迫。浸信会教会独立，但卫理公会被迫早早合并以实现主教治理。这催生了伟大的非洲卫理公会——世界上最大的黑人组织，锡安教会和有色卫理公会，以及该教派及其他教派中的黑人会议和教会。

第二个事实，即黑人教会早于黑人家庭，这解释了这个共产主义机构及其成员道德中许多矛盾之处。但尤其让我们将该机构视为一个民族内在伦理生活的独特表达，这种意义在其他地方很少成立。那么，让我们从教会的外部物理发展转向构成教会的人们更重要的内在伦理生活。黑人已被多次指出为宗教动物——一种本能地转向超自然的深层情感生物。拥有丰富的热带想象力和敏锐而细腻的自然欣赏力，这位被带到外地的非洲人生活在一个充满神和魔鬼、精灵和女巫的世界里；充满奇异影响——善的可以祈求，恶的需要安抚。对他而言，奴隶制是恶在他身上的黑暗胜利。所有可恨的冥界力量都在与他作斗争，他的心中充满了反抗和复仇的精神。他召唤异教的一切资源来助力——驱魔和巫术、神秘的奥比崇拜及其野蛮的仪式、咒语，甚至不时有人祭的血祭。奇怪的午夜狂欢和神秘的咒语被召唤出来，女巫和巫毒祭司成为黑人群体生活的中心，而那种即使在今天也特有于未受教育黑人模糊迷信的倾向被加深和强化。

然而，尽管激烈的马龙奴、人丹黑奴以及其他黑奴曾取得过某些成功，奴隶主以其不知疲倦的精力和更强的力量，使反抗精神逐渐消亡。到 eighteenth 世纪中叶，黑人奴隶在低声的抱怨中，已经沉沦到新经济体系的底层，并在不知不觉中为一种新的生活哲学做好了准备。那时，没有什么比新学的基督教中体现的被动顺从教义更适合他们的处境。奴隶主很早就意识到这一点，并在一定范围内欣然支持宗教宣传。长期的压迫和贬低黑人制度，往往强调了他性格中使他成为宝贵财产的元素：礼貌变成了谦卑，道德力量退化为顺从，对美的精致欣赏变成了无尽的愚蠢痛苦能力。黑人失去了这个世界的喜悦，热切地抓住来世所提供的观念;主的复仇之灵在这世间劝诫忍耐，尽管在悲伤和磨难中，直到伟大的日子，他将引领他的黑暗之子回家——这成了他的安慰梦想。他的传教士重复了预言，他的吟游诗人唱道，——

title: The Souls of Black Folk · 选段 10
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
source: Project Gutenberg · W. E. B. Du Bois
paragraphs: The evening sunbeams had set the dust to dancing in the gloomy chapel when he arose. He folded his vestments, put away the hymn-books, and closed the great Bible. He stepped out into the twilight, looked back upon the narrow little pulpit with a weary smile, and locked the door. Then he walked briskly to the Bishop, and told the Bishop what the Bishop already knew. “I have failed,” he said simply. And gaining courage by the confession, he added: “What I need is a larger constituency. There are comparatively few Negroes here, and perhaps they are not of the best. I must go where the field is wider, and try again.” So the Bishop sent him to Philadelphia, with a letter to Bishop Onderdonk.

Bishop Onderdonk lived at the head of six white steps,—corpulent, red-faced, and the author of several thrilling tracts on Apostolic Succession. It was after dinner, and the Bishop had settled himself for a pleasant season of contemplation, when the bell must needs ring, and there must burst in upon the Bishop a letter and a thin, ungainly Negro. Bishop Onderdonk read the letter hastily and frowned. Fortunately, his mind was already clear on this point; and he cleared his brow and looked at Crummell. Then he said, slowly and impressively: “I will receive you into this diocese on one condition: no Negro priest can sit in my church convention, and no Negro church must ask for representation there.”

I sometimes fancy I can see that tableau: the frail black figure, nervously twitching his hat before the massive abdomen of Bishop Onderdonk; his threadbare coat thrown against the dark woodwork of the bookcases, where Fox’s “Lives of the Martyrs” nestled happily beside “The Whole Duty of Man.” I seem to see the wide eyes of the Negro wander past the Bishop’s broadcloth to where the swinging glass doors of the cabinet glow in the sunlight. A little blue fly is trying to cross the yawning keyhole. He marches briskly up to it, peers into the chasm in a surprised sort of way, and rubs his feelers reflectively; then he essays its depths, and, finding it bottomless, draws back again. The dark-faced priest finds himself wondering if the fly too has faced its Valley of Humiliation, and if it will plunge into it,—when lo! it spreads its tiny wings and buzzes merrily across, leaving the watcher wingless and alone.

Then the full weight of his burden fell upon him. The rich walls wheeled away, and before him lay the cold rough moor winding on through life, cut in twain by one thick granite ridge,—here, the Valley of Humiliation; yonder, the Valley of the Shadow of Death. And I know not which be darker,—no, not I. But this I know: in yonder Vale of the Humble stand to-day a million swarthy men, who willingly would

“. . . bear the whips and scorns of time, The oppressor’s wrong, the proud man’s contumely, The pangs of despised love, the law’s delay, The insolence of office, and the spurns That patient merit of the unworthy takes,”—

all this and more would they bear did they but know that this were sacrifice and not a meaner thing. So surged the thought within that lone black breast. The Bishop cleared his throat suggestively; then, recollecting that there was really nothing to say, considerately said nothing, only sat tapping his foot impatiently. But Alexander Crummell said, slowly and heavily: “I will never enter your diocese on such terms.” And saying this, he turned and passed into the Valley of the Shadow of Death. You might have noted only the physical dying, the shattered frame and hacking cough; but in that soul lay deeper death than that. He found a chapel in New York,—the church of his father; he labored for it in poverty and starvation, scorned by his fellow priests. Half in despair, he wandered across the sea, a beggar with outstretched hands. Englishmen clasped them,—Wilberforce and Stanley, Thirwell and Ingles, and even Froude and Macaulay; Sir Benjamin Brodie bade him rest awhile at Queen’s College in Cambridge, and there he lingered, struggling for health of body and mind, until he took his degree in ’53. Restless still, and unsatisfied, he turned toward Africa, and for long years, amid the spawn of the slave-smugglers, sought a new heaven and a new earth.
paragraphsZh: 当他起身时，黄昏的阳光让昏暗的教堂里的灰尘跳起了舞。他叠好礼服，把赞美诗书收好，合上那本大大的圣经。他走到暮光中，回头望了望那狭小的讲台，露出一丝疲惫的微笑，然后锁上了门。接着，他快步走向主教，把主教已经知道的事情告诉了他。“我失败了，”他简单地说。借着坦白获得勇气，他又补充道：“我需要更多的信徒。这里的黑人相对较少，也许品质不是最好。我必须去更广阔的地方，再试一次。”于是主教便派他去了费城，并交给他一封给Onderdonk主教的信。

翁德东克主教住在六级白色台阶的顶端——肥胖、脸红，是多篇关于使徒传承的激动人心的小册子的作者。晚餐后，主教正准备度过一段愉快的沉思时光，这时钟声必须响起，突然一封信和一位瘦削笨拙的黑人闯入主教面前。昂德东克主教匆忙读完信，皱起了眉头。幸运的是，他对这一点已经很清楚;他清了清眉头，看向克拉梅尔。然后他缓慢而有力地说：“我会接纳你进入这个教区，但有一个条件：任何黑人神父不得参加我的教会大会，也不得任何黑人教会请求代表。”

我有时觉得自己能看到那一幕画面：瘦弱的黑人身影，紧张地在昂德东克主教庞大的腹部前扭动帽子;他那件破旧的外套被扔在书架的深色木质上，福克斯的《殉道者的生平》愉快地安放在《人类的全部责任》旁边。我似乎看到黑人睁大的眼睛越过主教的宽布，来到橱柜中在阳光下闪烁的玻璃门。一只小蓝苍蝇正试图穿过那张大嘴的钥匙孔。他快步走向它，惊讶地凝视着深渊，反省地揉了揉触角;然后他探究了深渊，发现它无底，便又收回去。这位黑脸的神父不禁想，这只苍蝇是否也遭遇了屈辱之谷，是否会跳进去——当瞧！它展开微小的翅膀，欢快地嗡嗡飞过，留下观看者一无所有，孤独无助。
然后，他感到了沉重的负担。富丽的墙壁旋转着消失，在他面前展开的是寒冷粗糙的荒原，穿过生活缓缓延伸，被一道厚重的花岗岩山脊一分为二——这里，是卑微之谷；那边，是死亡阴影谷。我不知道哪一边更黑暗——不，我不知道。但我知道：在那卑微之谷中，今天站着一百万肤色黝黑的人，他们自愿
“……承受时间的鞭打与轻蔑，压迫者的伤害，傲慢之人的侮辱，被轻视的爱之痛苦，法律的拖延，权势者的傲慢，以及不配之人对有耐心的才德所施的轻蔑，”——

如果他们知道这是一种牺牲而不是卑微的事情，他们会承受这一切以及更多。孤独的黑色胸膛中涌动着这样的念头。主教含义深长地清了清喉咙；然后，他回想起其实并没有什么可说的，于是体贴地什么也没说，只是坐着不耐烦地跺着脚。但亚历山大·克鲁梅尔缓慢而沉重地说：“我绝不会以这样的条件进入你们的教区。”说完这句话，他转身走入死亡幽谷。你可能只注意到身体上的垂死，破碎的身躯和剧烈的咳嗽；但在他的灵魂里，潜伏着比那更深的死亡。他在纽约找到一座小教堂——那是他父亲的教堂；他在贫困和饥饿中为它劳作，被同僚神父们轻视。半带绝望，他漂泊在海上，像一个伸出双手的乞丐。英国人握着他的手——威尔伯福斯和斯坦利，瑟维尔和英格尔斯，甚至弗劳德和麦考利；本杰明·布罗迪爵士让他在剑桥的皇后学院稍作休息，他在那里停留，为了身体和精神的健康而挣扎，直到他在53年获得学位。仍然不安且不满足，他转向非洲，多年间，在奴隶贩子的后裔中，寻求一个新的天堂和新的地球。

title: Little Women · 选段 4
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: Hither, hither, from thy home, Airy sprite, I bid thee come! Born of roses, fed on dew, Charms and potions canst thou brew? Bring me here, with elfin speed, The fragrant philter which I need. Make it sweet and swift and strong, Spirit, answer now my song!

A soft strain of music sounded, and then at the back of the cave appeared a little figure in cloudy white, with glittering wings, golden hair, and a garland of roses on its head. Waving a wand, it sang...
Hither I come, From my airy home, Afar in the silver moon. Take the magic spell, And use it well, Or its power will vanish soon!

And dropping a small, gilded bottle at the witch’s feet, the spirit vanished. Another chant from Hagar produced another apparition, not a lovely one, for with a bang an ugly black imp appeared and, having croaked a reply, tossed a dark bottle at Hugo and disappeared with a mocking laugh. Having warbled his thanks and put the potions in his boots, Hugo departed, and Hagar informed the audience that as he had killed a few of her friends in times past, she had cursed him, and intends to thwart his plans, and be revenged on him. Then the curtain fell, and the audience reposed and ate candy while discussing the merits of the play.

A good deal of hammering went on before the curtain rose again, but when it became evident what a masterpiece of stage carpentery had been got up, no one murmured at the delay. It was truly superb. A tower rose to the ceiling, halfway up appeared a window with a lamp burning in it, and behind the white curtain appeared Zara in a lovely blue and silver dress, waiting for Roderigo. He came in gorgeous array, with plumed cap, red cloak, chestnut lovelocks, a guitar, and the boots, of course. Kneeling at the foot of the tower, he sang a serenade in melting tones. Zara replied and, after a musical dialogue, consented to fly. Then came the grand effect of the play. Roderigo produced a rope ladder, with five steps to it, threw up one end, and invited Zara to descend. Timidly she crept from her lattice, put her hand on Roderigo’s shoulder, and was about to leap gracefully down when “Alas! Alas for Zara!” she forgot her train. It caught in the window, the tower tottered, leaned forward, fell with a crash, and buried the unhappy lovers in the ruins.

A universal shriek arose as the russet boots waved wildly from the wreck and a golden head emerged, exclaiming, “I told you so! I told you so!” With wonderful presence of mind, Don Pedro, the cruel sire, rushed in, dragged out his daughter, with a hasty aside...

“Don’t laugh! Act as if it was all right!” and, ordering Roderigo up, banished him from the kingdom with wrath and scorn. Though decidedly shaken by the fall from the tower upon him, Roderigo defied the old gentleman and refused to stir. This dauntless example fired Zara. She also defied her sire, and he ordered them both to the deepest dungeons of the castle. A stout little retainer came in with chains and led them away, looking very much frightened and evidently forgetting the speech he ought to have made.

Act third was the castle hall, and here Hagar appeared, having come to free the lovers and finish Hugo. She hears him coming and hides, sees him put the potions into two cups of wine and bid the timid little servant, “Bear them to the captives in their cells, and tell them I shall come anon.” The servant takes Hugo aside to tell him something, and Hagar changes the cups for two others which are harmless. Ferdinando, the ‘minion’, carries them away, and Hagar puts back the cup which holds the poison meant for Roderigo. Hugo, getting thirsty after a long warble, drinks it, loses his wits, and after a good deal of clutching and stamping, falls flat and dies, while Hagar informs him what she has done in a song of exquisite power and melody.
paragraphsZh: 到这里，来到这里，从你的家中来吧，空气精灵，我召唤你！生于玫瑰，饮露水而长，你能调制魔法和药水吗？以精灵般的速度把我所需的芳香药水带来。使它甜美、迅捷而强大，精灵，现在就回应我的歌声吧！
一阵轻柔的音乐响起，然后在洞穴的后面出现了一个身着朦胧白色的小身影，拥有闪亮的翅膀、金色的头发，头上戴着玫瑰花环。它挥动魔杖，唱道……
我来了， 从我 airy 的家， 远在银色的月光下。 接受魔法咒语，并好好使用， 否则它的力量很快就会消失！

当灵魂把一个小小的镀金瓶子扔到女巫的脚下时，就消失了。哈加尔再念一段咒语，又出现了另一个幻影，但这次并不美丽，因为随着一声巨响，一个丑陋的黑色小鬼出现了，它呱呱叫了一声，然后把一个黑色的瓶子扔向雨果，并伴随着嘲讽的笑声消失了。雨果哼唱着谢意，把药水放进靴子里后便离开了，哈加尔告诉观众，由于他过去曾杀死她的一些朋友，她曾诅咒过他，并打算挫败他的计划，并向他复仇。然后，幕布落下，观众放松休息，一边吃糖果，一边讨论这出戏的优劣。

在帷幕再次拉开之前，有不少敲击声响起，但当大家看到舞台木工技艺的杰作时，没有人对耽搁发出抱怨。这真是绝妙的作品。一座塔直冲天花板，中间出现一扇窗户，里面燃着一盏灯，而在白色帷幕后，扎拉穿着一件漂亮的蓝银色连衣裙，等待罗德里戈。他华丽登场，戴着插羽的帽子，红色披风，栗色卷发，带着吉他，当然还有靴子。他在塔脚下跪下，用柔和的声音唱起小夜曲。扎拉回应，经过一段音乐对话后，同意逃跑。接着出现了戏剧的高潮。罗德里戈拿出一架五级绳梯，把一端抛上去，邀请扎拉下来。她胆怯地从格子窗爬出来，把手放在罗德里戈的肩上，正要优雅地跳下去时，“唉！唉，扎拉呀！”她忘记了她的裙摆。裙摆被窗户卡住，塔楼摇晃，向前倾倒，轰然倒下，把不幸的恋人掩埋在废墟中。
当赤褐色的靴子在废墟中疯狂挥舞，一个金色的头冒出来，大声喊道：“我早说过！我早说过！”随着出色的机智，残酷的父亲唐·佩德罗冲了进来，拉出他的女儿，并匆忙地说了一句旁白……
“别笑！装作没事的样子！”他命令罗德里戈站起来，并愤怒且轻蔑地将他驱逐出王国。尽管从塔上摔下让他明显受到了震动，罗德里戈仍然无畏地反抗这位老先生，拒绝动弹。这个无畏的行为点燃了扎拉的勇气。她也反抗了自己的父亲，于是父亲命令将他们两人关进城堡最深的地牢里。一位强壮的小仆人带着镣铐进来，把他们带走，他看起来非常害怕，而且明显忘记了他本该说的话。

第三幕是城堡大厅，这里出现了哈加，来解救恋人并消灭雨果。她听到他走来，便躲起来，看见他将药水倒入两杯葡萄酒中，并吩咐胆小的小仆人：‘把它们带到囚犯的牢房里去，并告诉他们我很快就来。’仆人把雨果带到一旁要告诉他一些事情，而哈加则将这两杯换成另外两杯无害的。‘宠儿’费迪南多把酒带走，哈加将原本装有毒药、要毒死罗德里戈的酒杯放回原处。雨果在长时间的高声歌唱后口渴，喝了下去，失去了理智，经过一番抓挠和跺脚后，倒下并死去，而哈加则在一首极具力量与旋律的歌曲中告诉他她所做的一切。

title: Little Women · 选段 5
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: This spirited burst from Beth electrified the club, and Jo left her seat to shake hands approvingly. “Now then, vote again. Everybody remember it’s our Laurie, and say, ‘Aye!’” cried Snodgrass excitedly.

“Good! Bless you! Now, as there’s nothing like ‘taking time by the fetlock’, as Winkle characteristically observes, allow me to present the new member.” And, to the dismay of the rest of the club, Jo threw open the door of the closet, and displayed Laurie sitting on a rag bag, flushed and twinkling with suppressed laughter.
“You rogue! You traitor! Jo, how could you?” cried the three girls, as Snodgrass led her friend triumphantly forth, and producing both a chair and a badge, installed him in a jiffy.

“The coolness of you two rascals is amazing,” began Mr. Pickwick, trying to get up an awful frown and only succeeding in producing an amiable smile. But the new member was equal to the occasion, and rising, with a grateful salutation to the Chair, said in the most engaging manner, “Mr. President and ladies—I beg pardon, gentlemen—allow me to introduce myself as Sam Weller, the very humble servant of the club.”

“My faithful friend and noble patron,” continued Laurie with a wave of the hand, “who has so flatteringly presented me, is not to be blamed for the base stratagem of tonight. I planned it, and she only gave in after lots of teasing.”
“Come now, don’t lay it all on yourself. You know I proposed the cupboard,” broke in Snodgrass, who was enjoying the joke amazingly.

“Never mind what she says. I’m the wretch that did it, sir,” said the new member, with a Welleresque nod to Mr. Pickwick. “But on my honor, I never will do so again, and henceforth devote myself to the interest of this immortal club.”

“I merely wish to say, that as a slight token of my gratitude for the honor done me, and as a means of promoting friendly relations between adjoining nations, I have set up a post office in the hedge in the lower corner of the garden, a fine, spacious building with padlocks on the doors and every convenience for the mails, also the females, if I may be allowed the expression. It’s the old martin house, but I’ve stopped up the door and made the roof open, so it will hold all sorts of things, and save our valuable time. Letters, manuscripts, books, and bundles can be passed in there, and as each nation has a key, it will be uncommonly nice, I fancy. Allow me to present the club key, and with many thanks for your favor, take my seat.”

Great applause as Mr. Weller deposited a little key on the table and subsided, the warming pan clashed and waved wildly, and it was some time before order could be restored. A long discussion followed, and everyone came out surprising, for everyone did her best. So it was an unusually lively meeting, and did not adjourn till a late hour, when it broke up with three shrill cheers for the new member.

No one ever regretted the admittance of Sam Weller, for a more devoted, well-behaved, and jovial member no club could have. He certainly did add ‘spirit’ to the meetings, and ‘a tone’ to the paper, for his orations convulsed his hearers and his contributions were excellent, being patriotic, classical, comical, or dramatic, but never sentimental. Jo regarded them as worthy of Bacon, Milton, or Shakespeare, and remodeled her own works with good effect, she thought.

The P. O. was a capital little institution, and flourished wonderfully, for nearly as many queer things passed through it as through the real post office. Tragedies and cravats, poetry and pickles, garden seeds and long letters, music and gingerbread, rubbers, invitations, scoldings, and puppies. The old gentleman liked the fun, and amused himself by sending odd bundles, mysterious messages, and funny telegrams, and his gardener, who was smitten with Hannah’s charms, actually sent a love letter to Jo’s care. How they laughed when the secret came out, never dreaming how many love letters that little post office would hold in the years to come.
paragraphsZh: 贝丝这一股充满活力的表现点燃了整个俱乐部的气氛，乔起身走过去赞许地握手。“那么，现在再投一次票。大家记住是我们的劳里，说‘赞成！’”斯诺德格拉斯兴奋地喊道。
“很好！保佑你！现在，正如温克尔一贯所说的，没有什么比‘抓住机会’更重要的了，请允许我介绍新成员。” 然而，让俱乐部的其他人沮丧的是，乔猛地推开衣橱的门，展示出了坐在破布袋上的劳里，他满脸通红，抑制着笑意，眼睛闪闪发光。
“你这个流氓！你这个叛徒！乔，你怎么能这样？”三个女孩喊道，斯诺德格拉斯得意地带着她的朋友走出来，并拿出一把椅子和一枚徽章，迅速把他安置好。
“你们两个小淘气的冷静真是令人惊讶，”皮克威克先生开始说，试图做出一副可怕的皱眉，却只成功地露出了一个友善的笑容。但是，新成员完全适应了这个场合，他起身，向主席表示感激的敬意，并以最迷人的方式说道：“主席先生，各位女士——抱歉，先生们——请允许我自我介绍，我是山姆·韦勒，这个俱乐部非常卑微的仆人。”
“我忠实的朋友和高贵的恩人，”劳里继续挥了挥手说，“如此恭维我的人，不应因今晚卑劣的计谋而受到责怪。是我策划了这一切，而她只是在很多挑逗之后才答应的。”
“来吧，别把所有责任都归咎于自己。你知道是我提议买橱柜的，”斯诺德格拉斯插话道，他对这个玩笑感到非常开心。
“别理她说的什么。我是干这事的可怜人，先生，”新成员说着，向皮克威克先生点了点头，带着韦勒式的神态。“但以我的名誉发誓，我再也不会这样做了，从今以后，我将全心全意为这个不朽俱乐部的利益服务。”

“我只是想说，作为对我获得的荣誉表示一点感激之情，也作为促进邻国友好关系的一种方式，我在花园下角的篱笆里设立了一个邮局，这是一座宽敞精美的建筑，门上装有挂锁，具备处理邮件的各种便利设施，也包括女性专用区，如果我可以这样说的话。它原本是旧的马丁鸟屋，但我堵上了门并把屋顶打开，这样可以放各种东西，也能节省我们宝贵的时间。信件、手稿、书籍和包裹都可以放在里面，每个国家都有一把钥匙，我想这会非常好。请允许我出示俱乐部的钥匙，并对您的厚爱表示衷心感谢，同时就座。”
当韦勒先生将一把小钥匙放在桌子上并坐下时，掌声雷动，暖水壶碰撞并剧烈摇晃，好一会儿才恢复秩序。随后进行了一场长时间的讨论，每个人都表现出惊人的表现，因为大家都尽力了。所以这是一次异常热闹的会议，直到很晚才散会，并以三声尖锐的欢呼声为新成员送行。
没人曾后悔接纳山姆·韦勒，因为没有哪个俱乐部能有比他更忠诚、行为更端正、性格更开朗的成员。他确实为聚会增添了‘活力’，也为报纸增添了‘风格’，他的演讲让听众捧腹大笑，他的投稿也很出色，既爱国、又古典、幽默或富有戏剧性，但从不矫情。乔认为这些作品堪比培根、弥尔顿或莎士比亚，并相信她自己也能在作品的改写中取得良好效果。

那个邮局是一个极好的小机构，而且繁荣得不可思议，因为几乎有和真正邮局一样多的奇怪东西通过它。悲剧和领结，诗歌和泡菜，花园种子和长信，音乐和姜饼，橡胶靴、请柬、训斥和小狗。那位老人喜欢这种乐趣，并通过寄送奇怪的包裹、神秘的讯息和滑稽的电报来娱乐自己，而他的园丁则因被汉娜的魅力吸引，居然给乔托管的地址寄了一封情书。当这个秘密被揭开时，他们笑得前仰后合，根本没想到这个小小的邮局在未来的岁月里会承载多少情书。

title: Little Women · 选段 6
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: “A tall figure, all in white with a veil over its face and a lamp in its wasted hand,” went on Meg. “It beckoned, gliding noiselessly before him down a corridor as dark and cold as any tomb. Shadowy effigies in armor stood on either side, a dead silence reigned, the lamp burned blue, and the ghostly figure ever and anon turned its face toward him, showing the glitter of awful eyes through its white veil. They reached a curtained door, behind which sounded lovely music. He sprang forward to enter, but the specter plucked him back, and waved threateningly before him a...”

“Snuffbox,” said Jo, in a sepulchral tone, which convulsed the audience. “‘Thankee,’ said the knight politely, as he took a pinch and sneezed seven times so violently that his head fell off. ‘Ha! Ha!’ laughed the ghost, and having peeped through the keyhole at the princesses spinning away for dear life, the evil spirit picked up her victim and put him in a large tin box, where there were eleven other knights packed together without their heads, like sardines, who all rose and began to...”

“Dance a hornpipe,” cut in Fred, as Jo paused for breath, “and, as they danced, the rubbishy old castle turned to a man-of-war in full sail. ‘Up with the jib, reef the tops’l halliards, helm hard alee, and man the guns!’ roared the captain, as a Portuguese pirate hove in sight, with a flag black as ink flying from her foremast. ‘Go in and win, my hearties!’ says the captain, and a tremendous fight began. Of course the British beat—they always do.”

“Having taken the pirate captain prisoner, sailed slap over the schooner, whose decks were piled high with dead and whose lee scuppers ran blood, for the order had been ‘Cutlasses, and die hard!’ ‘Bosun’s mate, take a bight of the flying-jib sheet, and start this villain if he doesn’t confess his sins double quick,’ said the British captain. The Portuguese held his tongue like a brick, and walked the plank, while the jolly tars cheered like mad. But the sly dog dived, came up under the man-of-war, scuttled her, and down she went, with all sail set, ‘To the bottom of the sea, sea, sea’ where...”

“Oh, gracious! What shall I say?” cried Sallie, as Fred ended his rigmarole, in which he had jumbled together pell-mell nautical phrases and facts out of one of his favorite books. “Well, they went to the bottom, and a nice mermaid welcomed them, but was much grieved on finding the box of headless knights, and kindly pickled them in brine, hoping to discover the mystery about them, for being a woman, she was curious. By-and-by a diver came down, and the mermaid said, ‘I’ll give you a box of pearls if you can take it up,’ for she wanted to restore the poor things to life, and couldn’t raise the heavy load herself. So the diver hoisted it up, and was much disappointed on opening it to find no pearls. He left it in a great lonely field, where it was found by a...”

“Little goose girl, who kept a hundred fat geese in the field,” said Amy, when Sallie’s invention gave out. “The little girl was sorry for them, and asked an old woman what she should do to help them. ‘Your geese will tell you, they know everything.’ said the old woman. So she asked what she should use for new heads, since the old ones were lost, and all the geese opened their hundred mouths and screamed...”

“‘Cabbages!’” continued Laurie promptly. “‘Just the thing,’ said the girl, and ran to get twelve fine ones from her garden. She put them on, the knights revived at once, thanked her, and went on their way rejoicing, never knowing the difference, for there were so many other heads like them in the world that no one thought anything of it. The knight in whom I’m interested went back to find the pretty face, and learned that the princesses had spun themselves free and all gone and married, but one. He was in a great state of mind at that, and mounting the colt, who stood by him through thick and thin, rushed to the castle to see which was left. Peeping over the hedge, he saw the queen of his affections picking flowers in her garden. ‘Will you give me a rose?’ said he. ‘You must come and get it. I can’t come to you, it isn’t proper,’ said she, as sweet as honey. He tried to climb over the hedge, but it seemed to grow higher and higher. Then he tried to push through, but it grew thicker and thicker, and he was in despair. So he patiently broke twig after twig till he had made a little hole through which he peeped, saying imploringly, ‘Let me in! Let me in!’ But the pretty princess did not seem to understand, for she picked her roses quietly, and left him to fight his way in. Whether he did or not, Frank will tell you.”
paragraphsZh: “一个高大的身影，全身白衣，面上罩着面纱，手中握着一盏灯，”梅格继续说道。“它招手，静静地在他面前顺着一条像任何坟墓一样黑暗寒冷的走廊滑行。两旁站着盔甲里的影子化身，死一般的寂静笼罩着，灯光发出蓝色的光，而那幽灵般的身影不时转过脸来看着他，从白色面纱中透出可怕眼睛的光芒。他们来到一扇挂着帘子的门前，帘子后传来美妙的音乐。他跃身向前想要进去，但幽灵把他拉了回来，并在他面前威胁性地挥动着一个……
“鼻烟盒，”乔以一种阴森的语调说道，这语调让在场的人捧腹大笑。‘谢谢你，’骑士礼貌地说道，他掏了一撮鼻烟打了七个喷嚏，喷得如此猛烈以至于他的头掉了下来。‘哈！哈！’幽灵笑道，看着闪过钥匙孔看到公主们拼命纺纱，邪恶的灵魂抓起她的牺牲者，把他放进一个大锡盒里，那里还有另外十一位没有头的骑士像沙丁鱼一样挤在一起，他们都站了起来开始……”
“跳一支喇叭舞，”弗雷德在乔停下来喘气时插话说，“当他们舞动时，那座破旧的城堡变成了一艘扬满帆的战舰。‘拉起前桅帆，卷起上帆索，舵向远离风的一边，操起炮台！’船长大喊着，这时一名葡萄牙海盗出现了，船首桅杆上飘着黑得像墨汁一样的旗帜。‘去吧，赢下来，我的伙计们！’船长说，于是一场惊天动地的战斗开始了。当然是英国人赢了——他们总是赢。”
“俘虏了海盗船长后，飞过双桅纵帆船，船甲板堆满了尸体，背风舷流血，因为命令是'弯刀，死硬！''水手长，抓住飞帆索，如果他不快点认罪，就开始他的行动，'英国船长说。葡萄牙人像铁头一样咬紧嘴巴，走在木板上，而欢快的塔尔船员们则像疯狂一样欢呼。但狡猾的狗潜入水中，靠近军舰下方，将其击沉，船帆全开，'沉入海底，海底，海底'，那里......”

“哦，天哪！我该说什么呢？”萨莉喊道，当弗雷德结束他那混乱的长篇大论时，他把他最喜欢的一本书里的航海术语和事实杂乱地凑在一起。“好吧，他们沉入海底，一位漂亮的美人鱼迎接了他们，但当她发现那盒无头骑士时，非常难过，于是好心地把他们泡在盐水里，希望能解开其中的奥秘，因为作为一个女人，她很好奇。不久，一个潜水员下来了，美人鱼说：‘如果你能拿上来，我就给你一盒珍珠，’因为她想让可怜的小家伙们复活，但自己无法举起这么重的负担。于是潜水员把它抬了上来，打开时非常失望，因为里面没有珍珠。他把它留在一个荒无人烟的大地里，那里被一个……”
“小鹅姑娘，田里养着一百只胖鹅，”当萨莉的发明坏了时，艾米说道。“小姑娘为它们感到难过，便去问一个老妇人她应该怎么办才能帮助它们。‘你的鹅会告诉你，它们什么都知道。’老妇人说。所以她问应该用什么来做新的头，因为旧的已经丢了，所有的鹅都张开它们的一百张嘴尖叫起来……”

“‘卷心菜！’”劳里立刻接着说。 “‘正是需要的东西，’那个女孩说着，跑去从她的花园里摘了十二个漂亮的。她戴上它们，骑士们立刻恢复了精神，感谢她，然后满心欢喜地继续上路，从未察觉其中的不同，因为世上有那么多与他们相似的头，没有人会在意。 我感兴趣的那位骑士回去寻找那张美丽的面庞，得知公主们已经自己解开了束缚，所有人都去结婚了，只剩下一位。他为此心情大起大落，骑上小马驹，那匹一直忠心陪伴他的马，飞奔到城堡去看看剩下的是哪一位。 他从篱笆上往里偷看，看到他心爱的女王正在花园里采花。 ‘你会给我一朵玫瑰吗？’他说。 ‘你必须自己来取。’“我不能到你那里去，那不合适，”她甜如蜜地说道。他试图翻过树篱，但它似乎越来越高。然后他试着推开它，但它变得越来越厚，他感到绝望。于是他耐心地一根又一根地折断树枝，直到他弄出了一个小洞，通过洞偷偷看着，并乞求地说，‘让我进来！让我进来！’但漂亮的公主似乎并不明白，因为她安静地采着玫瑰花，把他留在外面努力闯入。不管他是否进去了，弗兰克会告诉你的。”

title: Little Women · 选段 7
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: “I’m so full of happiness, that if Father was only here, I couldn’t hold one drop more,” said Beth, quite sighing with contentment as Jo carried her off to the study to rest after the excitement, and to refresh herself with some of the delicious grapes the ‘Jungfrau’ had sent her.
