“I’m sure I am,” echoed Amy, poring over the engraved copy of the Madonna and Child, which her mother had given her in a pretty frame.

“Of course I am!” cried Meg, smoothing the silvery folds of her first silk dress, for Mr. Laurence had insisted on giving it. “How can I be otherwise?” said Mrs. March gratefully, as her eyes went from her husband’s letter to Beth’s smiling face, and her hand caressed the brooch made of gray and golden, chestnut and dark brown hair, which the girls had just fastened on her breast.

Now and then, in this workaday world, things do happen in the delightful storybook fashion, and what a comfort it is. Half an hour after everyone had said they were so happy they could only hold one drop more, the drop came. Laurie opened the parlor door and popped his head in very quietly. He might just as well have turned a somersault and uttered an Indian war whoop, for his face was so full of suppressed excitement and his voice so treacherously joyful that everyone jumped up, though he only said, in a queer, breathless voice, “Here’s another Christmas present for the March family.”

Before the words were well out of his mouth, he was whisked away somehow, and in his place appeared a tall man, muffled up to the eyes, leaning on the arm of another tall man, who tried to say something and couldn’t. Of course there was a general stampede, and for several minutes everybody seemed to lose their wits, for the strangest things were done, and no one said a word.

Mr. March became invisible in the embrace of four pairs of loving arms. Jo disgraced herself by nearly fainting away, and had to be doctored by Laurie in the china closet. Mr. Brooke kissed Meg entirely by mistake, as he somewhat incoherently explained. And Amy, the dignified, tumbled over a stool, and never stopping to get up, hugged and cried over her father’s boots in the most touching manner. Mrs. March was the first to recover herself, and held up her hand with a warning, “Hush! Remember Beth.”

But it was too late. The study door flew open, the little red wrapper appeared on the threshold, joy put strength into the feeble limbs, and Beth ran straight into her father’s arms. Never mind what happened just after that, for the full hearts overflowed, washing away the bitterness of the past and leaving only the sweetness of the present.

It was not at all romantic, but a hearty laugh set everybody straight again, for Hannah was discovered behind the door, sobbing over the fat turkey, which she had forgotten to put down when she rushed up from the kitchen. As the laugh subsided, Mrs. March began to thank Mr. Brooke for his faithful care of her husband, at which Mr. Brooke suddenly remembered that Mr. March needed rest, and seizing Laurie, he precipitately retired. Then the two invalids were ordered to repose, which they did, by both sitting in one big chair and talking hard.

Mr. March told how he had longed to surprise them, and how, when the fine weather came, he had been allowed by his doctor to take advantage of it, how devoted Brooke had been, and how he was altogether a most estimable and upright young man. Why Mr. March paused a minute just there, and after a glance at Meg, who was violently poking the fire, looked at his wife with an inquiring lift of the eyebrows, I leave you to imagine. Also why Mrs. March gently nodded her head and asked, rather abruptly, if he wouldn’t like to have something to eat. Jo saw and understood the look, and she stalked grimly away to get wine and beef tea, muttering to herself as she slammed the door, “I hate estimable young men with brown eyes!”
paragraphsZh: “我心里充满了幸福，如果爸爸在这里，我一点也装不下了，”贝丝说道，满足地叹了口气，乔正把她抱到书房休息，帮她在兴奋之后恢复精神，并吃一些‘少女峰’送来的美味葡萄。
“我也确定是这样的，”艾米应声说道，一边仔细端详着母亲赠送给她的、装在漂亮相框里的《圣母子》。
“当然是啦！”梅格喊道，一边抚平她第一件丝绸连衣裙的银色褶皱，这件衣服是劳伦斯先生坚持送给她的。“我怎么会不开心呢？”玛奇太太感激地说着，目光在丈夫的信和贝丝微笑的脸庞之间来回扫过，她的手抚摸着女孩们刚别在胸前的由灰色和金色、栗色和深棕色头发制成的胸针。
偶尔在这个平凡的世界里，事情确实会以令人愉快的童话方式发生，这真是令人欣慰。在每个人说他们高兴得再也容不下一滴快乐的时候，半小时后，那滴快乐来了。劳里轻轻地推开客厅门，把头探了进来。他不如翻个筋斗大叫一声印第安战歌，因为他的脸上充满了抑制不住的兴奋，声音里透着难以置信的喜悦，以至于每个人都跳了起来，尽管他只是用一种奇怪、气喘吁吁的声音说：“这是送给马奇家的又一份圣诞礼物。”
话音未落，他不知怎的就被迅速带走了，取而代之的是一个高个子男子，全身裹得只露出眼睛，靠在另一个高个子男子的手臂上，后者试图说些什么，但说不出来。当然，随之而来的是一阵混乱的逃窜，几分钟之内，大家似乎都失了智，因为发生了最奇怪的事情，却没有人出声说话。
玛奇先生在四对充满爱意的手臂怀抱中变得隐形。乔差点晕倒，丢了自尊，不得不在瓷器柜里由劳里照料。布鲁克先生完全是误打误撞地亲了梅格，正如他有些语无伦次地解释的那样。而庄重的艾米跌倒在凳子上，从未停下站起来的动作，最动情地抱着父亲的靴子哭泣。玛奇夫人最先恢复过来，举起手示意警告：“嘘！记住贝丝。”
但已经太晚了。书房的门猛地被推开，小小的红色包裹出现在门口，喜悦给了虚弱的四肢以力量，贝丝径直跑进了父亲的怀抱。接下来发生了什么并不重要，因为满溢的心情冲淡了过去的苦涩，只留下现在的甜美。
这根本不浪漫，但一阵爽朗的笑声让大家重新恢复了平静，因为汉娜被发现躲在门后，为那只肥火鸡哭泣——当她从厨房冲上来时忘了把它放下。笑声渐渐消退后，马奇夫人开始感谢布鲁克先生对她丈夫的忠心照料，这时布鲁克先生突然想起马奇先生需要休息，于是抓起劳里匆忙退下。随后，这两位病人被命令休息，他们确实照做了——两个人挤在一把大椅子上，专心聊了起来。

马奇先生讲述了他多么渴望给他们一个惊喜，以及当天气转好时，他的医生允许他利用这个机会，他多么敬业的布鲁克，以及他完全是一个最值得尊敬和正直的年轻人。马奇先生为什么在这里停顿了一分钟，在瞥了一眼正猛烈戳着火炉的梅格之后，又抬起眉毛看着妻子，带着询问的神情，我留给你自行想象。还有为什么马奇太太轻轻点头，然后相当唐突地问他是否想吃点东西。乔看到了并理解了那眼神，她阴沉地走开去准备葡萄酒和牛肉汤，一边重重关上门一边对自己喃喃自语：“我讨厌有棕色眼睛的值得尊敬的年轻人！”

title: Little Women · 选段 8
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: “Don’t feel that I am separated from you, Marmee dear, or that I love you any the less for loving John so much,” she said, clinging to her mother, with full eyes for a moment. “I shall come every day, Father, and expect to keep my old place in all your hearts, though I am married. Beth is going to be with me a great deal, and the other girls will drop in now and then to laugh at my housekeeping struggles. Thank you all for my happy wedding day. Good-by, good-by!”

They stood watching her, with faces full of love and hope and tender pride as she walked away, leaning on her husband’s arm, with her hands full of flowers and the June sunshine brightening her happy face—and so Meg’s married life began.

It takes people a long time to learn the difference between talent and genius, especially ambitious young men and women. Amy was learning this distinction through much tribulation, for mistaking enthusiasm for inspiration, she attempted every branch of art with youthful audacity. For a long time there was a lull in the ‘mud-pie’ business, and she devoted herself to the finest pen-and-ink drawing, in which she showed such taste and skill that her graceful handiwork proved both pleasant and profitable. But over-strained eyes caused pen and ink to be laid aside for a bold attempt at poker-sketching. While this attack lasted, the family lived in constant fear of a conflagration, for the odor of burning wood pervaded the house at all hours, smoke issued from attic and shed with alarming frequency, red-hot pokers lay about promiscuously, and Hannah never went to bed without a pail of water and the dinner bell at her door in case of fire. Raphael’s face was found boldly executed on the underside of the moulding board, and Bacchus on the head of a beer barrel. A chanting cherub adorned the cover of the sugar bucket, and attempts to portray Romeo and Juliet supplied kindling for some time.

From fire to oil was a natural transition for burned fingers, and Amy fell to painting with undiminished ardor. An artist friend fitted her out with his castoff palettes, brushes, and colors, and she daubed away, producing pastoral and marine views such as were never seen on land or sea. Her monstrosities in the way of cattle would have taken prizes at an agricultural fair, and the perilous pitching of her vessels would have produced seasickness in the most nautical observer, if the utter disregard to all known rules of shipbuilding and rigging had not convulsed him with laughter at the first glance. Swarthy boys and dark-eyed Madonnas, staring at you from one corner of the studio, suggested Murillo; oily brown shadows of faces with a lurid streak in the wrong place, meant Rembrandt; buxom ladies and dropiscal infants, Rubens; and Turner appeared in tempests of blue thunder, orange lightning, brown rain, and purple clouds, with a tomato-colored splash in the middle, which might be the sun or a bouy, a sailor’s shirt or a king’s robe, as the spectator pleased.

Charcoal portraits came next, and the entire family hung in a row, looking as wild and crocky as if just evoked from a coalbin. Softened into crayon sketches, they did better, for the likenesses were good, and Amy’s hair, Jo’s nose, Meg’s mouth, and Laurie’s eyes were pronounced ‘wonderfully fine’. A return to clay and plaster followed, and ghostly casts of her acquaintances haunted corners of the house, or tumbled off closet shelves onto people’s heads. Children were enticed in as models, till their incoherent accounts of her mysterious doings caused Miss Amy to be regarded in the light of a young ogress. Her efforts in this line, however, were brought to an abrupt close by an untoward accident, which quenched her ardor. Other models failing her for a time, she undertook to cast her own pretty foot, and the family were one day alarmed by an unearthly bumping and screaming and running to the rescue, found the young enthusiast hopping wildly about the shed with her foot held fast in a pan full of plaster, which had hardened with unexpected rapidity. With much difficulty and some danger she was dug out, for Jo was so overcome with laughter while she excavated that her knife went too far, cut the poor foot, and left a lasting memorial of one artistic attempt, at least.
paragraphsZh: “不要觉得我与你分离，亲爱的妈妈，也不要以为我因为如此爱约翰而减少对你的爱，”她说着，紧紧抱住母亲，眼中充满泪水，片刻停留。“爸爸，我每天都会来，也希望即使结了婚，仍能在你们心中保持我以前的位置。贝丝会常常和我在一起，其余的姐妹们也偶尔会来，笑看我料理家务的笨拙。谢谢你们让我度过了如此幸福的婚礼日。再见，再见！”
她们站在那里看着她，脸上满是爱、希望和柔情的骄傲，看着她依偎在丈夫臂弯上走开，双手捧满鲜花，六月的阳光照亮她幸福的脸庞——于是梅格的婚姻生活开始了。

人们需要很长时间才能分清天赋与天才之间的区别，尤其是雄心勃勃的年轻男女。艾米正在通过许多磨难学习这种区分，因为她将热情误认为灵感，带着年轻的大胆尝试了每一种艺术分支。很长一段时间，“泥饼”事业陷入停滞，她专注于最精致的钢笔画，在其中展现了如此的品味和技巧，她优美的手工既令人愉悦又带来利润。但过度用眼导致她不得不放下钢笔画，转而大胆尝试扑克牌速写。在这次袭击持续期间，这个家庭一直生活在对大火的恐惧中，因为燃烧木头的气味时刻弥漫在屋子里，烟雾频繁地从阁楼和棚屋冒出，烧红的烙铁随意地散落在各处，而汉娜每次上床睡觉前，总要在门口放一桶水和晚餐铃以防火灾。拉斐尔的面孔被大胆地雕刻在模制木板的底面上，而酒桶的桶头上则刻着巴克斯。一位吟唱的小天使装饰着糖桶的盖子，而尝试描绘罗密欧与朱丽叶画作的行为也曾一度成为点燃柴火的材料。

从火漆到油画对于烧伤的手指来说是一个自然的过渡，而艾米依然以不减的热情投入绘画。一位艺术家朋友给她提供了用过的调色板、画笔和颜料，她便不停地涂抹，创作出陆地或海上从未见过的田园和海景画。她那种怪异的牛群画作本可以在农业展览会上赢得奖项，而她的船只那惊险的倾斜姿态会让最有航海经验的观察者感到晕船，如果不是对所有已知造船和装帆规则的完全漠视在第一眼就让他捧腹大笑的话。黝黑的男孩和黑眼睛的圣母像，从画室的一角凝视着你，让人联想到穆里略；带有不合适艳丽条纹的油光棕色脸影，让人想到伦勃朗；丰满的女士和下垂的婴儿，让人想到鲁本斯；而特纳则出现在蓝色闪电、橙色闪电、棕色雨和紫色云的风暴中，中间有一片番茄色的飞溅，可能是太阳或浮标、海员的衬衫或国王的长袍，由观者自行判断。

接下来是炭笔肖像画，整个家庭的成员排成一排，看起来既野性又粗糙，就像刚从煤箱里捞出来的一样。用蜡笔画出来后，画面效果好多了，因为相貌很像，而且艾米的头发、乔的鼻子、梅格的嘴巴和劳里的眼睛都被认为‘极其精美’。随后又回到黏土和石膏上，她熟识之人的鬼魂般的石膏像出现在屋子的角落，或者从衣橱的架子上掉到人们的头上。孩子们也被吸引进来当模特，直到他们对她神秘行为的杂乱叙述使艾米小姐被看作年轻的食人魔。然而，她在这方面的努力被一次不幸的事故突然中断，熄灭了她的热情。其他模型暂时都让她失望，她便决定为自己塑造一只漂亮的脚。一天，全家因听到一阵诡异的撞击声、尖叫声，立即跑去查看，结果发现这位年轻的热心者正狂乱地在棚子里跳跃，脚牢牢地固定在一盆已经意外快速硬化的石膏中。她被挖出来时非常困难，也有些危险，因为乔在挖掘过程中笑得太厉害，以至于刀子滑得太远，割伤了可怜的脚，并且至少为一次艺术尝试留下了永久的纪念。

title: Little Women · 选段 9
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: His very clothes seemed to partake of the hospitable nature of the wearer. They looked as if they were at ease, and liked to make him comfortable. His capacious waistcoat was suggestive of a large heart underneath. His rusty coat had a social air, and the baggy pockets plainly proved that little hands often went in empty and came out full. His very boots were benevolent, and his collars never stiff and raspy like other people’s.

“That’s it!” said Jo to herself, when she at length discovered that genuine good will toward one’s fellow men could beautify and dignify even a stout German teacher, who shoveled in his dinner, darned his own socks, and was burdened with the name of Bhaer.

Jo valued goodness highly, but she also possessed a most feminine respect for intellect, and a little discovery which she made about the Professor added much to her regard for him. He never spoke of himself, and no one ever knew that in his native city he had been a man much honored and esteemed for learning and integrity, till a countryman came to see him. He never spoke of himself, and in a conversation with Miss Norton divulged the pleasing fact. From her Jo learned it, and liked it all the better because Mr. Bhaer had never told it. She felt proud to know that he was an honored Professor in Berlin, though only a poor language-master in America, and his homely, hard-working life was much beautified by the spice of romance which this discovery gave it. Another and a better gift than intellect was shown her in a most unexpected manner. Miss Norton had the entree into most society, which Jo would have had no chance of seeing but for her. The solitary woman felt an interest in the ambitious girl, and kindly conferred many favors of this sort both on Jo and the Professor. She took them with her one night to a select symposium, held in honor of several celebrities.

Jo went prepared to bow down and adore the mighty ones whom she had worshiped with youthful enthusiasm afar off. But her reverence for genius received a severe shock that night, and it took her some time to recover from the discovery that the great creatures were only men and women after all. Imagine her dismay, on stealing a glance of timid admiration at the poet whose lines suggested an ethereal being fed on ‘spirit, fire, and dew’, to behold him devouring his supper with an ardor which flushed his intellectual countenance. Turning as from a fallen idol, she made other discoveries which rapidly dispelled her romantic illusions. The great novelist vibrated between two decanters with the regularity of a pendulum; the famous divine flirted openly with one of the Madame de Staels of the age, who looked daggers at another Corinne, who was amiably satirizing her, after outmaneuvering her in efforts to absorb the profound philosopher, who imbibed tea Johnsonianly and appeared to slumber, the loquacity of the lady rendering speech impossible. The scientific celebrities, forgetting their mollusks and glacial periods, gossiped about art, while devoting themselves to oysters and ices with characteristic energy; the young musician, who was charming the city like a second Orpheus, talked horses; and the specimen of the British nobility present happened to be the most ordinary man of the party.

Before the evening was half over, Jo felt so completely disillusioned, that she sat down in a corner to recover herself. Mr. Bhaer soon joined her, looking rather out of his element, and presently several of the philosophers, each mounted on his hobby, came ambling up to hold an intellectual tournament in the recess. The conversations were miles beyond Jo’s comprehension, but she enjoyed it, though Kant and Hegel were unknown gods, the Subjective and Objective unintelligible terms, and the only thing ‘evolved from her inner consciousness’ was a bad headache after it was all over. It dawned upon her gradually that the world was being picked to pieces, and put together on new and, according to the talkers, on infinitely better principles than before, that religion was in a fair way to be reasoned into nothingness, and intellect was to be the only God. Jo knew nothing about philosophy or metaphysics of any sort, but a curious excitement, half pleasurable, half painful, came over her as she listened with a sense of being turned adrift into time and space, like a young balloon out on a holiday.
paragraphsZh: 他穿的衣服似乎也带有穿戴者的好客本性。衣服看起来很自在，仿佛喜欢让他感到舒适。他那宽大的马甲让人联想到他内心的坦荡。他那件生锈的外套有一种社交气息，而那鼓囊囊的口袋明确表明，小手常常空着伸进去，却能满载而出。他的靴子也充满了善意，他的衣领从不僵硬刺耳，像别人一样。
“就是这样！”乔对自己说，当她终于发现，对同伴的真诚善意甚至可以使一个体态魁梧的德国教师变得美丽而有尊严时——这个教师在吃饭时铲着食物，自己缝补袜子，而且背负着布尔先生（Bhaer）这个名字的负担。

乔高度重视善良，但她同样对智慧怀有极其女性化的尊重，而她对教授的一点小发现更让她对他增添了许多敬意。他从不谈论自己，没有人知道他在故乡是一位因学识和正直而备受尊敬的人，直到有一位同乡来拜访他。他从不谈论自己，在与诺顿小姐的一次谈话中透露了这一令人愉快的事实。乔从她那里得知此事，并且因为巴赫尔先生从未说起而更喜欢这个事实。她为知道他在柏林是一位受人尊敬的教授而感到自豪，尽管在美国他只是一个贫穷的语言教师，他那平凡而勤奋的生活因这一发现所带来的浪漫色彩而增添了许多美感。一个比智慧更好的礼物以一种最意想不到的方式呈现在她面前。诺顿小姐可以进入大多数社交圈，而如果不是她，乔是没有机会见到这些的。这位孤独的女士对这个有抱负的女孩产生了兴趣，并友善地给予乔和教授许多这样的恩惠。她有一晚带他们去参加一个精英座谈会，这是为了几位名人而举办的。

乔准备好去向那些曾经让她年少时满怀热情远远崇拜的伟人们行礼和敬拜。但那天晚上一种对天才的崇敬受到了严重打击，她花了一段时间才从发现这些伟人归根结底不过是普通男女的事实中恢复过来。想象一下她的失望，当她偷偷瞥一眼那位诗人——他笔下的诗句仿佛描述一个以“精神、火焰和露水”为食的超凡存在——却看见他以一种热切的姿态狼吞虎咽地吃着晚餐，那种模样甚至让他的智慧面庞都泛起红晕。像从倒下的偶像前转身一样，她做出了其他发现，这些发现迅速打破了她浪漫的幻想。这位伟大的小说家在两个酒壶之间摇摆不定，如同钟摆般有规律；那位著名的神学家公然与当时的某位德·斯塔尔夫人调情，而这位夫人则怒视另一位柯琳娜，这位柯琳娜在巧妙讽刺她，同时在争取吸引那位深邃哲学家时占了上风，而这位哲学家以约翰逊式的方式品茶，看似沉睡，女士的多话让言语变得不可能。科学界的名人们忘记了他们的软体动物和冰河时期，高谈艺术，同时以特有的精力沉浸于牡蛎和冰品；年轻的音乐家像第二个奥菲斯一样迷住了全城，却在谈论马匹；而在场的英国贵族样本恰恰是聚会中最普通的人。

傍晚还不到一半时，乔感到彻底失望，她坐在一个角落里恢复情绪。巴尔先生很快走到她身边，看起来有些格格不入。不久，几位哲学家各自骑着心爱的“专长”，悠闲地走过来，在这个角落里举行一场智力较量。那些谈话远远超出了乔的理解能力，但她依然觉得有趣，尽管康德和黑格尔是未知的神灵，“主观”和“客观”是难以理解的术语，而从她内心意识中“演化”出的唯一东西，就是这一切结束后头痛得厉害。她逐渐意识到，世界正在被一点点拆解，又按照谈论者所说，用全新的、无限更好的原则重新组合起来，宗教正处在被理性化至虚无的途中，而智慧将成为唯一的上帝。乔对任何形式的哲学或形而上学一无所知，但当她聆听时，一种既愉快又痛苦的奇异激动涌上心头，她感到自己仿佛被放逐到时间和空间中，就像假日里放飞的年轻气球一样。

title: Little Women · 选段 10
author: Louisa May Alcott
paragraphs: Thanks to this inspiration, he got on swimmingly for a time, but gradually the work lost its charm, and he forgot to compose, while he sat musing, pen in hand, or roamed about the gay city to get some new ideas and refresh his mind, which seemed to be in a somewhat unsettled state that winter. He did not do much, but he thought a great deal and was conscious of a change of some sort going on in spite of himself. “It’s genius simmering, perhaps. I’ll let it simmer, and see what comes of it,” he said, with a secret suspicion all the while that it wasn’t genius, but something far more common. Whatever it was, it simmered to some purpose, for he grew more and more discontented with his desultory life, began to long for some real and earnest work to go at, soul and body, and finally came to the wise conclusion that everyone who loved music was not a composer. Returning from one of Mozart’s grand operas, splendidly performed at the Royal Theatre, he looked over his own, played a few of the best parts, sat staring at the busts of Mendelssohn, Beethoven, and Bach, who stared benignly back again. Then suddenly he tore up his music sheets, one by one, and as the last fluttered out of his hand, he said soberly to himself...
“She is right! Talent isn’t genius, and you can’t make it so. That music has taken the vanity out of me as Rome took it out of her, and I won’t be a humbug any longer. Now what shall I do?”

That seemed a hard question to answer, and Laurie began to wish he had to work for his daily bread. Now if ever, occurred an eligible opportunity for ‘going to the devil’, as he once forcibly expressed it, for he had plenty of money and nothing to do, and Satan is proverbially fond of providing employment for full and idle hands. The poor fellow had temptations enough from without and from within, but he withstood them pretty well, for much as he valued liberty, he valued good faith and confidence more, so his promise to his grandfather, and his desire to be able to look honestly into the eyes of the women who loved him, and say “All’s well,” kept him safe and steady.

Very likely some Mrs. Grundy will observe, “I don’t believe it, boys will be boys, young men must sow their wild oats, and women must not expect miracles.” I dare say you don’t, Mrs. Grundy, but it’s true nevertheless. Women work a good many miracles, and I have a persuasion that they may perform even that of raising the standard of manhood by refusing to echo such sayings. Let the boys be boys, the longer the better, and let the young men sow their wild oats if they must. But mothers, sisters, and friends may help to make the crop a small one, and keep many tares from spoiling the harvest, by believing, and showing that they believe, in the possibility of loyalty to the virtues which make men manliest in good women’s eyes. If it is a feminine delusion, leave us to enjoy it while we may, for without it half the beauty and the romance of life is lost, and sorrowful forebodings would embitter all our hopes of the brave, tenderhearted little lads, who still love their mothers better than themselves and are not ashamed to own it.

Laurie thought that the task of forgetting his love for Jo would absorb all his powers for years, but to his great surprise he discovered it grew easier every day. He refused to believe it at first, got angry with himself, and couldn’t understand it, but these hearts of ours are curious and contrary things, and time and nature work their will in spite of us. Laurie’s heart wouldn’t ache. The wound persisted in healing with a rapidity that astonished him, and instead of trying to forget, he found himself trying to remember. He had not foreseen this turn of affairs, and was not prepared for it. He was disgusted with himself, surprised at his own fickleness, and full of a queer mixture of disappointment and relief that he could recover from such a tremendous blow so soon. He carefully stirred up the embers of his lost love, but they refused to burst into a blaze. There was only a comfortable glow that warmed and did him good without putting him into a fever, and he was reluctantly obliged to confess that the boyish passion was slowly subsiding into a more tranquil sentiment, very tender, a little sad and resentful still, but that was sure to pass away in time, leaving a brotherly affection which would last unbroken to the end.
paragraphsZh: 多亏了这种灵感，他一时间进展顺利，但工作逐渐失去了吸引力，他开始忘记作曲，有时坐着沉思，手握钢笔，或漫步在热闹的城市中，以获取新的灵感并振奋心情，而那个冬天，他的心似乎有些不安定。他并没有做太多事情，但思考了很多，并意识到自己身上正在发生某种变化，尽管这是在他无意之间。“也许这是天才在酝酿，”他说，同时暗自怀疑，那并不是天才，而是更为平常的某种东西。不管那是什么，它起到了某种作用，因为他对自己零散的生活越来越不满，开始渴望从事一些真正的、全心全意的工作，最终得出了明智的结论：并非每个热爱音乐的人都是作曲家。从皇家剧院观赏完一场精彩演出的莫扎特宏大歌剧回家后，他翻阅了自己的作品，弹奏了其中几个最好的部分，坐在那里凝视门德尔松、贝多芬和巴赫的半身像，它们也仁慈地回望着他。然后，突然间，他把乐谱一张张撕掉，当最后一张从手中飘落时，他一本正经地对自己说……
“她是对的！才能不是天才，你也无法使它成为天才。那音乐已经把我的虚荣心取走，就像罗马从她身上取走一样，从今以后我不再做虚伪的人。现在我该怎么办呢？”

这个问题似乎很难回答，劳里开始希望自己必须为日常的面包而工作。现在，如果有机会，他就有了‘倒霉’的可能性，正如他曾经强烈地表达过的那样，因为他有很多钱，却无事可做，而俗话说，撒旦特别喜欢给富裕而闲散的人提供麻烦。这个可怜的家伙从外部和内部都受到了足够的诱惑，但他相当坚强地抵抗住了，因为虽然他非常珍惜自由，但他更重视诚信和信任，所以他对祖父的承诺，以及能够诚实地看着爱他的女人的眼睛并说‘一切都好’的愿望，使他保持了安全和稳定。

很可能会有格伦迪夫人说：“我不相信，男孩就是男孩，年轻人必须放纵自己，女人不能指望奇迹。”我敢说你不这么认为，格伦迪夫人，但这话是真的。女人创造了许多奇迹，我相信她们甚至可以通过拒绝重复这些说法来提升男子气概的标准。让男孩做男孩，时间越长越好，年轻人如果必须，就让他们尽情发挥。但母亲、姐妹和朋友们可以通过相信并表现出对让男人在好女人眼中最男子气概的美德忠诚的可能性，帮助让庄稼变得小，避免许多“玉米渣”毁掉收成。如果这是女性的幻想，就让我们趁着还能享受它的时候去享受吧，因为没有它，生活中一半的美丽和浪漫将会消失，而悲伤的不祥预感会使我们对这些勇敢、心地善良的小男孩的所有希望都变得苦涩——他们仍然比自己更爱母亲，并且不以承认这一点为耻。

劳里原以为忘记乔的爱需要耗费他多年的全部精力，但令他大为惊讶的是，他发现每天都变得更容易了。起初，他拒绝相信，生自己的气，也无法理解，但我们的心是奇怪而反复无常的东西，时间和自然会不顾我们而发挥它们的作用。劳里的心不会再痛。伤口以令他震惊的速度持续愈合，与其试图去忘记，他反而发现自己在努力去记住。他没有预料到事情会如此发展，也没有为此做好准备。他对自己感到厌恶，对自己的反复无常感到惊讶，同时充满了一种奇怪的失望与宽慰的混合情绪，因为他能够如此迅速地从如此巨大的打击中恢复过来。他小心翼翼地挑起失去的爱情的余烬，但它们拒绝燃成火焰。只有一种舒适的光芒，温暖着他，对他有益，却没有让他陷入狂热，他不得不勉强承认，少年时期的激情正在慢慢消退，变成一种更平静的情感，非常温柔，仍带一点悲伤和怨恨，但这终将过去，留下兄弟般的情谊，持续不间断直到最后。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 4
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: In this manner I used to look upon my condition with the utmost regret. I had nobody to converse with, but now and then this neighbour; no work to be done, but by the labour of my hands; and I used to say, I lived just like a man cast away upon some desolate island, that had nobody there but himself. But how just has it been—and how should all men reflect, that when they compare their present conditions with others that are worse, Heaven may oblige them to make the exchange, and be convinced of their former felicity by their experience—I say, how just has it been, that the truly solitary life I reflected on, in an island of mere desolation, should be my lot, who had so often unjustly compared it with the life which I then led, in which, had I continued, I had in all probability been exceeding prosperous and rich.

This was so wholesome advice, and looked so friendly, that I could not but be convinced it was the best course I could take; so I accordingly prepared letters to the gentlewoman with whom I had left my money, and a procuration to the Portuguese captain, as he desired.

I wrote the English captain’s widow a full account of all my adventures—my slavery, escape, and how I had met with the Portuguese captain at sea, the humanity of his behaviour, and what condition I was now in, with all other necessary directions for my supply; and when this honest captain came to Lisbon, he found means, by some of the English merchants there, to send over, not the order only, but a full account of my story to a merchant in London, who represented it effectually to her; whereupon she not only delivered the money, but out of her own pocket sent the Portugal captain a very handsome present for his humanity and charity to me.

The merchant in London, vesting this hundred pounds in English goods, such as the captain had written for, sent them directly to him at Lisbon, and he brought them all safe to me to the Brazils; among which, without my direction (for I was too young in my business to think of them), he had taken care to have all sorts of tools, ironwork, and utensils necessary for my plantation, and which were of great use to me.

When this cargo arrived I thought my fortune made, for I was surprised with the joy of it; and my good steward, the captain, had laid out the five pounds, which my friend had sent him for a present for himself, to purchase and bring me over a servant, under bond for six years’ service, and would not accept of any consideration, except a little tobacco, which I would have him accept, being of my own produce.

Neither was this all; for my goods being all English manufacture, such as cloths, stuffs, baize, and things particularly valuable and desirable in the country, I found means to sell them to a very great advantage; so that I might say I had more than four times the value of my first cargo, and was now infinitely beyond my poor neighbour—I mean in the advancement of my plantation; for the first thing I did, I bought me a negro slave, and an European servant also—I mean another besides that which the captain brought me from Lisbon.

But as abused prosperity is oftentimes made the very means of our greatest adversity, so it was with me. I went on the next year with great success in my plantation: I raised fifty great rolls of tobacco on my own ground, more than I had disposed of for necessaries among my neighbours; and these fifty rolls, being each of above a hundredweight, were well cured, and laid by against the return of the fleet from Lisbon: and now increasing in business and wealth, my head began to be full of projects and undertakings beyond my reach; such as are, indeed, often the ruin of the best heads in business. Had I continued in the station I was now in, I had room for all the happy things to have yet befallen me for which my father so earnestly recommended a quiet, retired life, and of which he had so sensibly described the middle station of life to be full of; but other things attended me, and I was still to be the wilful agent of all my own miseries; and particularly, to increase my fault, and double the reflections upon myself, which in my future sorrows I should have leisure to make, all these miscarriages were procured by my apparent obstinate adhering to my foolish inclination of wandering abroad, and pursuing that inclination, in contradiction to the clearest views of doing myself good in a fair and plain pursuit of those prospects, and those measures of life, which nature and Providence concurred to present me with, and to make my duty.
paragraphsZh: 以这种方式，我曾以极大的遗憾看待自己的处境。我没有人可以交谈，偶尔才有这个邻居；没有工作可做，只有靠自己的双手劳作；我常常说，我的生活就像一个被放逐到荒凉孤岛上的人，岛上除了他自己再无他人。但是，这是多么公正——以及所有人都应该反思，当他们将自己目前的处境与更糟糕的处境相比时，天堂可能会迫使他们去经历交换，并通过经验确认他们先前的幸福——我说，这是多么公正啊，我曾反思的那种真正孤独的生活，在一座荒芜的孤岛上，竟成了我的命运，而我曾如此频繁地不公正地将其与我当时过的生活相比，如果我继续那样的生活，我很可能会极其富有和繁荣。
这是如此健康的建议，看起来又如此友好，我不得不相信这是我可以采取的最佳途径；于是我照着准备了给我把钱留下的那位女士的信，以及按葡萄牙船长所要求的委托书。

我给那位英国船长的遗孀写了一份详尽的信，讲述了我所有的经历——我的为奴经历、逃脱的经过，以及我如何在海上遇到葡萄牙船长，他的善良行为，以及我现在的境况，还有所有确保我得到物资的必要指示；当这位正直的船长来到里斯本时，他设法通过那里的几位英国商人，不仅把命令发送过去，还将我的整个故事完整地转交给伦敦的一位商人，这位商人有效地向她转述了事情经过；于是她不仅交付了钱财，还自掏腰包送给那位葡萄牙船长一份非常可观的礼物，以表彰他对我的善行与慈善。
伦敦的商人将这百英镑投资于英国货物，比如船长写信所需的那些，直接寄到里斯本给他，他又把这些货物安全地带到我在巴西的地方；其中，有一些工具、铁器和我种植园所需的器具，都是他在没有我的指示下（因为我在生意上还太年轻，没想到这些）特意准备的，对我非常有用。
当这批货物到达时，我觉得自己的财富已经到手，因为我为此惊喜不已；而我的好管家、船长，用我朋友寄给他为自己的一份礼物的五英镑，买来并带给我一个仆人，签订六年的劳务合同，他不愿接受任何报酬，除了我让他收下的一点烟草，那是我自己出产的。
这也不是全部;因为我的货物全是英国制造的，比如布料、杂物、baize以及乡下特别有价值和受欢迎的东西，我找到了极大的销售手段;因此我可以说，我的价值是我第一批货物的四倍多，现在远远超过了我贫穷的邻居——我指的是在我的种植园发展方面;我做的第一件事，就是买了一个黑人奴隶，还有一个欧洲仆人——我是说除了船长从里斯本带来的那个之外，还有一个。

但是，由于被滥用的繁荣往往成为我们遭遇最大不幸的手段，我的情况也是如此。第二年，我的种植园取得了很大成功：我在自己的地里种了五十大卷烟草，比我为了邻居的生活必需品而处理的还多；这五十卷烟草，每卷都超过一百磅，经过精心烘干，为里斯本船队归来作了储备。此时，随着生意和财富的增长，我的脑子里开始充满了力所不能及的计划和项目；这些计划确实常常是经商头脑最精明者的毁灭之源。如果我继续待在我现在所处的位置，我本可以拥有所有那些美好的事物，这些事物本应在我父亲如此真诚地建议过我过一种安静、隐居生活的情况下发生，而他也如此明智地描述了中年生活的充实；但其他事情找上了我，我仍然要成为自己所有苦难的故意制造者；特别是，为了增加我的过错，加倍我对自己的反思——在我未来的悲痛中，我将有时间去反省——所有这些失败都是因为我表面上固执地坚持自己愚蠢的出游倾向，而追随这种倾向，与清晰的自利视角相违背，偏离了那些自然与天意一同呈现给我的美好前景和生活措施的一条光明而正当的道路。并履行我的职责。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 5
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: This was a fair proposal, it must be confessed, had it been made to any one that had not had a settlement and a plantation of his own to look after, which was in a fair way of coming to be very considerable, and with a good stock upon it; but for me, that was thus entered and established, and had nothing to do but to go on as I had begun, for three or four years more, and to have sent for the other hundred pounds from England; and who in that time, and with that little addition, could scarce have failed of being worth three or four thousand pounds sterling, and that increasing too—for me to think of such a voyage was the most preposterous thing that ever man in such circumstances could be guilty of.

But I, that was born to be my own destroyer, could no more resist the offer than I could restrain my first rambling designs when my father’s good counsel was lost upon me. In a word, I told them I would go with all my heart, if they would undertake to look after my plantation in my absence, and would dispose of it to such as I should direct, if I miscarried. This they all engaged to do, and entered into writings or covenants to do so; and I made a formal will, disposing of my plantation and effects in case of my death, making the captain of the ship that had saved my life, as before, my universal heir, but obliging him to dispose of my effects as I had directed in my will; one half of the produce being to himself, and the other to be shipped to England.

In short, I took all possible caution to preserve my effects and to keep up my plantation. Had I used half as much prudence to have looked into my own interest, and have made a judgment of what I ought to have done and not to have done, I had certainly never gone away from so prosperous an undertaking, leaving all the probable views of a thriving circumstance, and gone upon a voyage to sea, attended with all its common hazards, to say nothing of the reasons I had to expect particular misfortunes to myself.

But I was hurried on, and obeyed blindly the dictates of my fancy rather than my reason; and, accordingly, the ship being fitted out, and the cargo furnished, and all things done, as by agreement, by my partners in the voyage, I went on board in an evil hour, the 1st September 1659, being the same day eight years that I went from my father and mother at Hull, in order to act the rebel to their authority, and the fool to my own interests.

Our ship was about one hundred and twenty tons burden, carried six guns and fourteen men, besides the master, his boy, and myself. We had on board no large cargo of goods, except of such toys as were fit for our trade with the negroes, such as beads, bits of glass, shells, and other trifles, especially little looking-glasses, knives, scissors, hatchets, and the like.

The same day I went on board we set sail, standing away to the northward upon our own coast, with design to stretch over for the African coast when we came about ten or twelve degrees of northern latitude, which, it seems, was the manner of course in those days. We had very good weather, only excessively hot, all the way upon our own coast, till we came to the height of Cape St. Augustino; from whence, keeping further off at sea, we lost sight of land, and steered as if we were bound for the isle Fernando de Noronha, holding our course N.E. by N., and leaving those isles on the east. In this course we passed the line in about twelve days’ time, and were, by our last observation, in seven degrees twenty-two minutes northern latitude, when a violent tornado, or hurricane, took us quite out of our knowledge. It began from the south-east, came about to the north-west, and then settled in the north-east; from whence it blew in such a terrible manner, that for twelve days together we could do nothing but drive, and, scudding away before it, let it carry us whither fate and the fury of the winds directed; and, during these twelve days, I need not say that I expected every day to be swallowed up; nor, indeed, did any in the ship expect to save their lives.
paragraphsZh: 必须承认，这是一个公平的提议，如果它是向那些没有自己需要管理的定居地和种植园的人提出的，而我的种植园正处于一个相当有前途的发展阶段，且有良好的存货；但对于我来说，我已经入宅安居，无需做其他事，只需像开始时一样继续经营三四年，并去从英格兰寄来另外一百英镑；在那段时间里，有了这个小小的增加，几乎不可能不值三四千英镑，而且还会继续增加——对我来说，考虑这样的航行是处在这种情况下的人所能犯下的最荒谬的事情。

但是我，这个生来就是自我毁灭的人，无法抗拒这个提议，就像当我父亲的良言未能影响我时，我无法抑制自己最初的胡思乱想一样。总之，我告诉他们，如果他们愿意在我不在时照料我的庄园，并在我失败时按我的指示处理它，我会全心全意跟随他们。他们都答应这么做，并签署了书面或契约来保证执行；我还立了一份正式遗嘱，规定万一我死去，庄园和财产的处置方式，如同以前一样，将救过我性命的船长作为我的唯一继承人，但要求他按我遗嘱的指示处置我的财产；一半收益归他自己，另一半运往英格兰。
总之，我采取了一切可能的谨慎措施来保护我的财物，并维持我的种植园。如果我曾用一半的谨慎来关心自己的利益，并判断我应该做什么、不应该做什么，我肯定永远不会离开这样一个繁荣的事业，放弃所有可能带来繁荣的前景，而去进行一次充满各种常见风险的海上航行，更不用说我有理由预料到自己会遭遇特殊的不幸。
但是我被催促着前行，盲目地服从了我幻想的指示而不是理智；因此，船只被装备好，货物备齐，一切按约定由我航行的伙伴们完成，我在一个不祥的时刻登上了船——1659年9月1日，正是八年前我离开赫尔的父母之日，为了违抗他们的权威，以及愚蠢地损害我自己的利益。
我们的船约重一百二十吨，载有六门火炮和十四名船员，除了船长、他的儿子和我本人。船上没有大型货物，除了适合与黑人贸易的玩具，比如珠子、玻璃碎片、贝壳和其他小玩意，尤其是小镜子、刀、剪刀、斧头等。

同一天我上船，我们就起航了，沿着我们自己的海岸向北行驶，计划在到达北纬大约十到十二度时向非洲海岸伸展，这似乎是当时的航线方式。我们天气非常好，只是沿着自己的海岸一直非常炎热，直到我们到达圣奥古斯蒂诺角的高度。从那里，我们进一步驶离海岸，失去了陆地的视线，并向着费尔南多·德诺罗尼亚岛的方向航行，航向为东北偏北，并将这些岛屿留在东边。在这条航线上，我们大约在十二天内穿越了赤道，并且根据我们最后一次的观测，我们位于北纬七度二十二分时，一场猛烈的旋风或飓风把我们完全带离了我们的航线。它从东南方开始，转向西北方，然后停留在东北方；从那里它以如此可怕的方式吹来，以至于连续十二天我们除了操纵船只，加速前行之外，无事可做，只能任其将我们带往命运和风暴意志所指的方向；在这十二天里，我不需要说每天都期待被吞没；事实上，船上的任何人也不指望能保住性命。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 6
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: April 22.—The next morning I begin to consider of means to put this resolve into execution; but I was at a great loss about my tools. I had three large axes, and abundance of hatchets (for we carried the hatchets for traffic with the Indians); but with much chopping and cutting knotty hard wood, they were all full of notches, and dull; and though I had a grindstone, I could not turn it and grind my tools too. This cost me as much thought as a statesman would have bestowed upon a grand point of politics, or a judge upon the life and death of a man. At length I contrived a wheel with a string, to turn it with my foot, that I might have both my hands at liberty. Note.—I had never seen any such thing in England, or at least, not to take notice how it was done, though since I have observed, it is very common there; besides that, my grindstone was very large and heavy. This machine cost me a full week’s work to bring it to perfection.
April 28, 29.—These two whole days I took up in grinding my tools, my machine for turning my grindstone performing very well.
April 30.—Having perceived my bread had been low a great while, now I took a survey of it, and reduced myself to one biscuit cake a day, which made my heart very heavy.

May 1.—In the morning, looking towards the sea side, the tide being low, I saw something lie on the shore bigger than ordinary, and it looked like a cask; when I came to it, I found a small barrel, and two or three pieces of the wreck of the ship, which were driven on shore by the late hurricane; and looking towards the wreck itself, I thought it seemed to lie higher out of the water than it used to do. I examined the barrel which was driven on shore, and soon found it was a barrel of gunpowder; but it had taken water, and the powder was caked as hard as a stone; however, I rolled it farther on shore for the present, and went on upon the sands, as near as I could to the wreck of the ship, to look for more.

When I came down to the ship I found it strangely removed. The forecastle, which lay before buried in sand, was heaved up at least six feet, and the stern, which was broke in pieces and parted from the rest by the force of the sea, soon after I had left rummaging her, was tossed as it were up, and cast on one side; and the sand was thrown so high on that side next her stern, that whereas there was a great place of water before, so that I could not come within a quarter of a mile of the wreck without swimming I could now walk quite up to her when the tide was out. I was surprised with this at first, but soon concluded it must be done by the earthquake; and as by this violence the ship was more broke open than formerly, so many things came daily on shore, which the sea had loosened, and which the winds and water rolled by degrees to the land.

This wholly diverted my thoughts from the design of removing my habitation, and I busied myself mightily, that day especially, in searching whether I could make any way into the ship; but I found nothing was to be expected of that kind, for all the inside of the ship was choked up with sand. However, as I had learned not to despair of anything, I resolved to pull everything to pieces that I could of the ship, concluding that everything I could get from her would be of some use or other to me.
paragraphsZh: 4月22日——第二天早晨，我开始考虑如何将这个决定付诸实施；但是我对我的工具感到非常困惑。我有三把大斧头，还有许多小斧头（因为我们带着小斧头是为了与印第安人进行交易）；但是经过大量的劈砍和削切坚硬的结节木，它们全都布满了缺口，而且钝了；虽然我有一块磨石，但我无法同时转动它并磨锐我的工具。这让我费尽心思，就像政治家为一个重大政治问题苦思冥想，或者法官为了一个人的生死而深思一样。最后，我想出了一个用绳子转动的轮子，用脚踩来转动，这样我双手就可以腾出来。注意。——我在英格兰从未见过这样的东西，或者至少，没有注意它是如何制作的，尽管自从我观察之后，我发现那里很常见；此外，我的砂轮非常大而重。这台机器花了我整整一周的时间才弄到完美。
4月28、29日——这整整两天我都花在磨工具上，我用来转磨石的机器表现得非常好。
4月30日——意识到我的面包已经缺了很久，现在我检查了一下，只给自己一天一块饼干，这使我的心情非常沉重。
5月1日——早晨，朝海边望去，潮水很低，我看到岸上有一样比平常大一些的东西，看起来像一个桶；当我走近时，发现是一个小桶，还有两三块被最近的飓风冲到岸上的船只残骸；看向残骸本身，我觉得它似乎比以前高出水面。我检查了冲上岸的小桶，很快发现这是一个火药桶；但它进水了，火药结块得像石头一样硬；不过，我暂且把它滚到岸上更远的地方，然后走到沙地上，尽可能靠近船只残骸，去寻找更多东西。

当我走下船时，我发现它奇怪地被移动了。以前埋在沙子里的前甲板被抬高了至少六英尺，而船尾在我离开后不久，由于海水的冲击而破碎并与船体分离，也仿佛被掀起，扔到了一边；沙子在靠近船尾的一侧被堆得很高，以前那里有一大片水，以至于我无法在不游泳的情况下接近船只四分之一英里，现在潮水退去时，我完全可以走到船边。起初我对此感到惊讶，但很快就得出结论，这一定是地震造成的；而且由于这种剧烈的作用，船比以前更破损，所以每天都有许多东西被冲到岸上，这是海水松动的，而风和水逐渐将它们推动到陆地上。
这完全转移了我将住所搬走的念头，那天尤其如此，我忙得不可开交，寻找是否能找到进入船只的办法；但我发现这种希望根本不存在，因为船的内部全被沙子堵住了。然而，由于我已学会不对任何事情绝望，我决定拆开船上能拆的所有部分，认为从船上得到的一切都会在某种程度上对我有用。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 7
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: I cannot express what a satisfaction it was to me to come into my old hutch, and lie down in my hammock-bed. This little wandering journey, without settled place of abode, had been so unpleasant to me, that my own house, as I called it to myself, was a perfect settlement to me compared to that; and it rendered everything about me so comfortable, that I resolved I would never go a great way from it again while it should be my lot to stay on the island.

I reposed myself here a week, to rest and regale myself after my long journey; during which most of the time was taken up in the weighty affair of making a cage for my Poll, who began now to be a mere domestic, and to be well acquainted with me. Then I began to think of the poor kid which I had penned in within my little circle, and resolved to go and fetch it home, or give it some food; accordingly I went, and found it where I left it, for indeed it could not get out, but was almost starved for want of food. I went and cut boughs of trees, and branches of such shrubs as I could find, and threw it over, and having fed it, I tied it as I did before, to lead it away; but it was so tame with being hungry, that I had no need to have tied it, for it followed me like a dog: and as I continually fed it, the creature became so loving, so gentle, and so fond, that it became from that time one of my domestics also, and would never leave me afterwards.

The rainy season of the autumnal equinox was now come, and I kept the 30th of September in the same solemn manner as before, being the anniversary of my landing on the island, having now been there two years, and no more prospect of being delivered than the first day I came there, I spent the whole day in humble and thankful acknowledgments of the many wonderful mercies which my solitary condition was attended with, and without which it might have been infinitely more miserable. I gave humble and hearty thanks that God had been pleased to discover to me that it was possible I might be more happy in this solitary condition than I should have been in the liberty of society, and in all the pleasures of the world; that He could fully make up to me the deficiencies of my solitary state, and the want of human society, by His presence and the communications of His grace to my soul; supporting, comforting, and encouraging me to depend upon His providence here, and hope for His eternal presence hereafter.

It was now that I began sensibly to feel how much more happy this life I now led was, with all its miserable circumstances, than the wicked, cursed, abominable life I led all the past part of my days; and now I changed both my sorrows and my joys; my very desires altered, my affections changed their gusts, and my delights were perfectly new from what they were at my first coming, or, indeed, for the two years past.

Before, as I walked about, either on my hunting or for viewing the country, the anguish of my soul at my condition would break out upon me on a sudden, and my very heart would die within me, to think of the woods, the mountains, the deserts I was in, and how I was a prisoner, locked up with the eternal bars and bolts of the ocean, in an uninhabited wilderness, without redemption. In the midst of the greatest composure of my mind, this would break out upon me like a storm, and make me wring my hands and weep like a child. Sometimes it would take me in the middle of my work, and I would immediately sit down and sigh, and look upon the ground for an hour or two together; and this was still worse to me, for if I could burst out into tears, or vent myself by words, it would go off, and the grief, having exhausted itself, would abate.
paragraphsZh: 我无法表达回到我那间老窝棚，躺在吊床床上时的满足感。这次小小的流浪旅程，没有固定的居所，对我来说是如此不愉快，以至于我称之为自己的家时，它相比之下简直就是一种完美的安定；它使我周围的一切都感到如此舒适，以至于我下定决心，只要命运让我继续留在岛上，我再也不会离它很远了。

我在这里休息了一周，以在长途旅行后休整并享受自己；这段时间大部分都用在了为我的波尔制作一个笼子这件重要的事情上，它现在几乎成了家养动物，并且与我非常熟悉。然后我开始想起那只可怜的小山羊，它被圈在我的小圈子里，于是决定去把它带回家，或者给它一些食物；于是我去了，发现它仍在那里，因为它确实无法出来，但几乎因缺乏食物而饿死。我去砍了树枝，以及我能找到的灌木枝条，把它扔过去，喂了它之后，我像以前一样把它拴起来，以便牵走它；但它因为饥饿而变得如此驯服，我根本不需要拴它，因为它像狗一样跟着我：随着我不断地喂它，这个生物变得非常亲昵、温顺和依恋，从那时起，它也成了我的一名家养动物，并且之后再也不离开我。

秋分的雨季如今已经到来，我仍然以同样庄重的方式纪念9月30日，这是我登陆这座岛屿的周年纪念。到现在为止，我已经在这里待了两年，但获救的前景仍然和我刚到这里的第一天一样渺茫。我用整整一天的时间，谦卑而感激地承认在我孤独的处境中所蒙受的许多奇妙的恩惠，如果没有这些，我的生活可能会痛苦得多。我怀着谦卑而真诚的心感谢上帝，祂让我明白，我在这种孤独的状态下可能比在社会的自由和世间的各种快乐中更幸福；祂能够通过亲自的同在和将祂的恩典传达给我的灵魂，完全弥补我孤独状态的不足以及缺乏人类社会的空缺；支撑、安慰并鼓励我依靠祂的天意生活在此，并期望将来能永远与祂同在。
正是在那时，我才真正开始感受到自己现在所过的这种生活，纵使环境凄惨，却比过去生命中所过的邪恶、被诅咒、可憎的生活幸福得多；而现在，我既改变了忧愁，也改变了欢乐；我的欲望发生了变化，我的感情的取向改变了，我的快乐与初来此地时，甚至过去两年的感受，截然不同。

以前，每当我四处走动，无论是狩猎还是游览乡野，我的灵魂因自身境遇的痛苦会突然爆发，我的心仿佛在我体内死去，想着我所处的树林、山脉、荒野，以及我如何成为一个囚徒，被大海那永恒的栅栏和闸门锁住，困在无人居住的荒原中，无可救赎。在我心境最平静的时候，这种痛苦也会像风暴般爆发，使我捶手顿足，像孩子一样哭泣。有时它会在我工作到一半的时候袭来，我会立刻坐下叹息，凝视地面一两个小时；这对我来说更糟，因为如果我能爆发出眼泪，或者用言语发泄自己，这种情绪就会消散，而悲伤在耗尽自身后也会减轻。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 8
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: These reflections made me very sensible of the goodness of Providence to me, and very thankful for my present condition, with all its hardships and misfortunes; and this part also I cannot but recommend to the reflection of those who are apt, in their misery, to say, “Is any affliction like mine?” Let them consider how much worse the cases of some people are, and their case might have been, if Providence had thought fit.

I had another reflection, which assisted me also to comfort my mind with hopes; and this was comparing my present situation with what I had deserved, and had therefore reason to expect from the hand of Providence. I had lived a dreadful life, perfectly destitute of the knowledge and fear of God. I had been well instructed by father and mother; neither had they been wanting to me in their early endeavours to infuse a religious awe of God into my mind, a sense of my duty, and what the nature and end of my being required of me. But, alas! falling early into the seafaring life, which of all lives is the most destitute of the fear of God, though His terrors are always before them; I say, falling early into the seafaring life, and into seafaring company, all that little sense of religion which I had entertained was laughed out of me by my messmates; by a hardened despising of dangers, and the views of death, which grew habitual to me by my long absence from all manner of opportunities to converse with anything but what was like myself, or to hear anything that was good or tended towards it.

So void was I of everything that was good, or the least sense of what I was, or was to be, that, in the greatest deliverances I enjoyed—such as my escape from Sallee; my being taken up by the Portuguese master of the ship; my being planted so well in the Brazils; my receiving the cargo from England, and the like—I never had once the words “Thank God!” so much as on my mind, or in my mouth; nor in the greatest distress had I so much as a thought to pray to Him, or so much as to say, “Lord, have mercy upon me!” no, nor to mention the name of God, unless it was to swear by, and blaspheme it.

I had terrible reflections upon my mind for many months, as I have already observed, on account of my wicked and hardened life past; and when I looked about me, and considered what particular providences had attended me since my coming into this place, and how God had dealt bountifully with me—had not only punished me less than my iniquity had deserved, but had so plentifully provided for me—this gave me great hopes that my repentance was accepted, and that God had yet mercy in store for me.

With these reflections I worked my mind up, not only to a resignation to the will of God in the present disposition of my circumstances, but even to a sincere thankfulness for my condition; and that I, who was yet a living man, ought not to complain, seeing I had not the due punishment of my sins; that I enjoyed so many mercies which I had no reason to have expected in that place; that I ought never more to repine at my condition, but to rejoice, and to give daily thanks for that daily bread, which nothing but a crowd of wonders could have brought; that I ought to consider I had been fed even by a miracle, even as great as that of feeding Elijah by ravens, nay, by a long series of miracles; and that I could hardly have named a place in the uninhabitable part of the world where I could have been cast more to my advantage; a place where, as I had no society, which was my affliction on one hand, so I found no ravenous beasts, no furious wolves or tigers, to threaten my life; no venomous creatures, or poisons, which I might feed on to my hurt; no savages to murder and devour me. In a word, as my life was a life of sorrow one way, so it was a life of mercy another; and I wanted nothing to make it a life of comfort but to be able to make my sense of God’s goodness to me, and care over me in this condition, be my daily consolation; and after I did make a just improvement on these things, I went away, and was no more sad. I had now been here so long that many things which I had brought on shore for my help were either quite gone, or very much wasted and near spent.
paragraphsZh: 这些反思让我深切感受到天意对我的恩惠，并对我目前的境遇充满感激，尽管其中有诸多艰难和不幸；这一部分，我也不得不推荐给那些在苦难中容易说“有哪种痛苦像我的痛苦吗？”的人去思考。让他们考虑一下别人处境的糟糕，以及如果天意认为合适，他们的处境可能会怎样更糟。

我又有了另一种反思，这也帮助我以希望来安慰我的心；那就是将我当前的境遇与我应得的情况进行比较，因此我有理由从天意的手中期待。我曾过着可怕的生活，完全缺乏对上帝的知识与敬畏。我曾受到父母的良好教导；他们在早期努力向我灌输对上帝的宗教敬畏、对我职责的意识以及我存在的性质和目的所要求的行为时，都没有忽视我。但，唉！早早投身于航海生活，而在所有生活中，这种生活最缺乏对上帝的敬畏，尽管他们总是面对祂的威严；我说，早早投身于航海生活，进入航海伙伴之间的圈子，我所抱有的那点微不足道的宗教感，被我的同伴们嘲笑殆尽；通过对危险的麻木蔑视，以及对死亡的习以为常，这些都由于我长时间远离任何与我不同的事物，无法与之交流，或者无法听到任何有益或指向善的事物，而逐渐变为习惯。
我对一切美好事物，甚至对自己是什么，或者将成为什么，都感到如此空虚，以至于在我享受的最大解脱中——比如我从萨利逃脱；被船上的葡萄牙船长接纳；在巴西安顿得如此好；从英格兰收到货物，诸如此类——我心中或口中一次也没有出现过“感谢上帝！”的话；即使在最大的苦难中，我也没有想到向他祈祷，甚至没有说过“主啊，怜悯我！”的话，更没有提到上帝的名字，除非是为了发誓或亵渎它。
正如我已经提到的，由于过去我邪恶且顽固的生活，我的心中曾有长达数月的严重反思；当我环顾四周，思考自从来到这个地方以来，上天对我所施的种种特别眷顾，以及上帝如何慷慨待我——不仅惩罚我比我的罪孽应得的少，还如此丰盛地供应我——这让我有很大的希望，相信我的悔改已被接受，上帝仍为我预留怜悯。

带着这些反思，我让自己的心态不仅调整到接受上帝在我现有环境中的旨意，甚至对我的境况心怀真诚的感激；我意识到，作为一个仍然活着的人，我不应该抱怨，因为我还没有受到应有的罪罚；我享受了在那样的地方本不应期望的诸多恩惠；我不应再对自己的境况感到不满，而应欢喜，并每天为那每日的食物心存感激，这食物唯有通过一连串的奇迹才能到手；我应当意识到，我甚至是被奇迹喂养的，正如以利亚被乌鸦喂养的奇迹一样，甚至是一系列的奇迹；我几乎无法说出在世界那片无人居住的地方，我还能被投放到更适合我的地方。优势；一个地方，因为我没有社交，这在一方面是我的痛苦，所以我没有遇到贪婪的野兽，没有凶猛的狼或老虎威胁我的生命；也没有有毒的生物或毒药会让我因食用而受害；没有野蛮人来谋杀或吞食我。总之，我的生活在一方面是悲惨的生活，但在另一方面又是充满仁慈的生活；我所缺少的只是能够将我对上帝恩惠和在这种情况下对我的关怀的感受，作为每日的安慰；而当我确实对这些事情做了公平的改进之后，我离开了，也不再悲伤。我现在已经在这里待了很久，我带上岸以助自己的许多东西，要么已经完全用完，要么严重浪费，快要耗尽。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 9
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: Abundance of such things as these assisted to argue me out of all apprehensions of its being the devil; and I presently concluded then that it must be some more dangerous creature—viz. that it must be some of the savages of the mainland opposite who had wandered out to sea in their canoes, and either driven by the currents or by contrary winds, had made the island, and had been on shore, but were gone away again to sea; being as loath, perhaps, to have stayed in this desolate island as I would have been to have had them.

While these reflections were rolling in my mind, I was very thankful in my thoughts that I was so happy as not to be thereabouts at that time, or that they did not see my boat, by which they would have concluded that some inhabitants had been in the place, and perhaps have searched farther for me. Then terrible thoughts racked my imagination about their having found out my boat, and that there were people here; and that, if so, I should certainly have them come again in greater numbers and devour me; that if it should happen that they should not find me, yet they would find my enclosure, destroy all my corn, and carry away all my flock of tame goats, and I should perish at last for mere want.

Thus my fear banished all my religious hope, all that former confidence in God, which was founded upon such wonderful experience as I had had of His goodness; as if He that had fed me by miracle hitherto could not preserve, by His power, the provision which He had made for me by His goodness. I reproached myself with my laziness, that would not sow any more corn one year than would just serve me till the next season, as if no accident could intervene to prevent my enjoying the crop that was upon the ground; and this I thought so just a reproof, that I resolved for the future to have two or three years’ corn beforehand; so that, whatever might come, I might not perish for want of bread.

How strange a chequer-work of Providence is the life of man! and by what secret different springs are the affections hurried about, as different circumstances present! To-day we love what to-morrow we hate; to-day we seek what to-morrow we shun; to-day we desire what to-morrow we fear, nay, even tremble at the apprehensions of. This was exemplified in me, at this time, in the most lively manner imaginable; for I, whose only affliction was that I seemed banished from human society, that I was alone, circumscribed by the boundless ocean, cut off from mankind, and condemned to what I call silent life; that I was as one whom Heaven thought not worthy to be numbered among the living, or to appear among the rest of His creatures; that to have seen one of my own species would have seemed to me a raising me from death to life, and the greatest blessing that Heaven itself, next to the supreme blessing of salvation, could bestow; I say, that I should now tremble at the very apprehensions of seeing a man, and was ready to sink into the ground at but the shadow or silent appearance of a man having set his foot in the island.

Such is the uneven state of human life; and it afforded me a great many curious speculations afterwards, when I had a little recovered my first surprise. I considered that this was the station of life the infinitely wise and good providence of God had determined for me; that as I could not foresee what the ends of Divine wisdom might be in all this, so I was not to dispute His sovereignty; who, as I was His creature, had an undoubted right, by creation, to govern and dispose of me absolutely as He thought fit; and who, as I was a creature that had offended Him, had likewise a judicial right to condemn me to what punishment He thought fit; and that it was my part to submit to bear His indignation, because I had sinned against Him. I then reflected, that as God, who was not only righteous but omnipotent, had thought fit thus to punish and afflict me, so He was able to deliver me: that if He did not think fit to do so, it was my unquestioned duty to resign myself absolutely and entirely to His will; and, on the other hand, it was my duty also to hope in Him, pray to Him, and quietly to attend to the dictates and directions of His daily providence.
paragraphsZh: 诸如此类的丰富之物帮助我消除了所有对它是魔鬼的怀疑；于是我立刻得出结论，它一定是某种更危险的生物——即一定是对岸本土的某些野人，他们驾着独木舟漂到了海上，要么被洋流，要么被逆风带到这座岛上，并曾上过岸，但又重新出海而去；或许他们像我不愿意他们停留在这荒凉的岛上一样，也不情愿留下来。
当这些思绪在我脑海中翻滚时，我在心里非常感激，因为我当时没有在那个地方，或者他们没有看到我的船，否则他们会以为那里曾有人居住，可能还会进一步寻找我。然后，可怕的念头折磨着我的想象：他们发现了我的船，那里有人；如果真是如此，他们一定会带更多人再来吃掉我；即使他们没有找到我，也会找到我的围栏，摧毁我所有的谷物，带走我所有的家养山羊，而我最终将仅因食物匮乏而死去。

因此，我的恐惧驱散了我所有的宗教希望，驱散了我对上帝以前所建立的信心，而这种信心是建立在我曾经经历过的上帝仁慈的奇妙经历之上的；仿佛那位至今以奇迹养活我的上帝，不能凭借祂的能力保全祂因仁慈而为我准备的供给。我责怪自己懒惰，一年只种足够支撑到下个季节的玉米，好像不会有任何意外发生来阻止我享受地上的收成；而我认为这是非常公正的责备，于是我决定以后要提前备有两三年的谷物；这样，无论发生什么，我也不会因为缺乏面包而灭亡。

人的生活是多么奇异的天意拼图啊！情感是由多么隐秘不同的动力推动的，随着不同的环境而变化！今天我们爱，明天我们恨；今天我们追求，明天我们回避；今天我们渴望，明天我们惧怕，甚至因预感而颤抖。这在我身上得到了最生动的体现；因为我，唯一的痛苦就是似乎被人类社会所排斥，孤独一人，被无边的大海包围，与人类隔绝，被判处我称之为寂静的生活；我如同一个被上天认为不配被列入生者行列，或不配出现在其他生物中的人；看到同类中的任何一个人，对我来说都仿佛是从死亡中复活，是除至高救赎之福之外，上天能够赐予的最大祝福；我说，现在连想到可能看到一个人我都会战栗，甚至在岛上看到一个人影或寂静出现时，我都几乎想要陷入地面。

人类生活就是如此不均衡；当我稍微从最初的惊讶中恢复过来后，这给了我很多有趣的思考。我认为这是上帝那无限智慧和良善的天意为我安排的人生位置；因为我无法预见神圣智慧在这一切中的最终目的，所以我不该质疑祂的主权；作为祂的创造物，祂有无可置疑的权利凭借创造对我进行绝对的统治和处置，按照祂认为合适的方式；同时，作为一名得罪了祂的创造物，我也承认祂有司法上的权利按祂所认为合适的方式惩罚我；而我应尽的本分就是顺从，承受祂的愤怒，因为我曾犯罪于祂。然后我反思到，既然上帝，不仅是公义的，而且是全能的，认为有必要如此惩罚和折磨我，那么他也有能力拯救我：如果他认为不适合这样做，那么完全、彻底地顺从他的旨意就是我无可置疑的责任；另一方面，我的责任也是寄望于他，向他祈祷，并平静地遵从他每日天意的指示和引导。

title: Robinson Crusoe · 选段 10
author: Daniel Defoe
paragraphs: In a little time, however, no more canoes appearing, the fear of their coming wore off; and I began to take my former thoughts of a voyage to the main into consideration; being likewise assured by Friday’s father that I might depend upon good usage from their nation, on his account, if I would go. But my thoughts were a little suspended when I had a serious discourse with the Spaniard, and when I understood that there were sixteen more of his countrymen and Portuguese, who having been cast away and made their escape to that side, lived there at peace, indeed, with the savages, but were very sore put to it for necessaries, and, indeed, for life. I asked him all the particulars of their voyage, and found they were a Spanish ship, bound from the Rio de la Plata to the Havanna, being directed to leave their loading there, which was chiefly hides and silver, and to bring back what European goods they could meet with there; that they had five Portuguese seamen on board, whom they took out of another wreck; that five of their own men were drowned when first the ship was lost, and that these escaped through infinite dangers and hazards, and arrived, almost starved, on the cannibal coast, where they expected to have been devoured every moment. He told me they had some arms with them, but they were perfectly useless, for that they had neither powder nor ball, the washing of the sea having spoiled all their powder but a little, which they used at their first landing to provide themselves with some food.

I asked him what he thought would become of them there, and if they had formed any design of making their escape. He said they had many consultations about it; but that having neither vessel nor tools to build one, nor provisions of any kind, their councils always ended in tears and despair. I asked him how he thought they would receive a proposal from me, which might tend towards an escape; and whether, if they were all here, it might not be done. I told him with freedom, I feared mostly their treachery and ill-usage of me, if I put my life in their hands; for that gratitude was no inherent virtue in the nature of man, nor did men always square their dealings by the obligations they had received so much as they did by the advantages they expected. I told him it would be very hard that I should be made the instrument of their deliverance, and that they should afterwards make me their prisoner in New Spain, where an Englishman was certain to be made a sacrifice, what necessity or what accident soever brought him thither; and that I had rather be delivered up to the savages, and be devoured alive, than fall into the merciless claws of the priests, and be carried into the Inquisition. I added that, otherwise, I was persuaded, if they were all here, we might, with so many hands, build a barque large enough to carry us all away, either to the Brazils southward, or to the islands or Spanish coast northward; but that if, in requital, they should, when I had put weapons into their hands, carry me by force among their own people, I might be ill-used for my kindness to them, and make my case worse than it was before.

He answered, with a great deal of candour and ingenuousness, that their condition was so miserable, and that they were so sensible of it, that he believed they would abhor the thought of using any man unkindly that should contribute to their deliverance; and that, if I pleased, he would go to them with the old man, and discourse with them about it, and return again and bring me their answer; that he would make conditions with them upon their solemn oath, that they should be absolutely under my direction as their commander and captain; and they should swear upon the holy sacraments and gospel to be true to me, and go to such Christian country as I should agree to, and no other; and to be directed wholly and absolutely by my orders till they were landed safely in such country as I intended, and that he would bring a contract from them, under their hands, for that purpose. Then he told me he would first swear to me himself that he would never stir from me as long as he lived till I gave him orders; and that he would take my side to the last drop of his blood, if there should happen the least breach of faith among his countrymen. He told me they were all of them very civil, honest men, and they were under the greatest distress imaginable, having neither weapons nor clothes, nor any food, but at the mercy and discretion of the savages; out of all hopes of ever returning to their own country; and that he was sure, if I would undertake their relief, they would live and die by me.
paragraphsZh: 然而，不久之后，再没有独木舟出现，对他们到来的恐惧便消失了；我开始考虑重新进行一次远航的念头；同时，我也得到了星期五的父亲的保证，如果我愿意去的话，可以因他而信赖他们族群的良好待遇。但当我与那位西班牙人进行一次认真的谈话时，我的想法稍稍中断；当我了解到还有十六个同他国家的人和葡萄牙人，他们曾遇难并逃到那边，在那里与野人和平共处，但在生活必需品上，实际上甚至在生存上，非常困苦的时候，我的想法就更为复杂了。我问了他关于他们航行的所有细节，了解到他们是一艘西班牙船，从拉普拉塔河开往哈瓦那，计划在那里卸下货物，主要是兽皮和银子，并带回他们在那里能找到的欧洲货物；船上有五个葡萄牙水手，是从另一艘沉船中救上来的；当船第一次失事时，他们船上的五个人淹死了，而这些人则历经无数危险和风险幸存下来，几乎饿死地到达食人族海岸，他们预计随时可能被吃掉。他告诉我他们带了一些武器，但完全无用，因为他们既没有火药也没有子弹，海水的冲刷弄坏了他们所有的火药，只剩下一点，他们在首次登陆时用这些火药为自己获取一些食物。

我问他，他认为他们在那里会变成什么样子，以及他们是否有逃跑的打算。他说他们为此进行了很多商议；但由于既没有船只也没有造船工具，也没有任何食物储备，所以他们的会议总是以泪水和绝望结束。我问他，他认为他们会如何看待我提出的可能有助于逃跑的建议；以及如果他们都在这里，这件事是否可以实现。我坦率地告诉他，我最担心的是他们的背叛以及对我不好，如果我把生命交到他们手中；因为感激并非人类天性中的固有美德，人们处理事务时，并不总是根据自己所受的恩惠来衡量，而更多是根据他们所期望获得的利益来衡量。我告诉他，要我成为他们得救的工具将是非常艰难的，而且他们之后会把我变成新西班牙的囚犯，一名英国人无论因何必要或意外被带到那里，肯定会成为牺牲；我宁愿被交给野蛮人，活生生地被吞食，也不愿落入牧师无情的魔爪，被带入宗教裁判所。我补充说，否则的话，我已经被说服了，如果他们都在这里，我们或许可以凭借这么多双手，建造一艘足够大的小船，把我们所有人带走，要么向南去巴西，要么向北去诸岛或西班牙海岸；但是，如果作为回报，当我把武器交到他们手中时，他们强行把我带到自己人中间，我可能会因为对他们的好心而受到虐待，情况比以前还糟。

他回答说，他非常坦率和真诚地认为，他们的处境是如此悲惨，并且他们自己也非常清楚这一点，以至于他相信他们会厌恶任何对协助他们获救的人不友善的想法；如果我愿意，他将和那个老人一起去找他们，与他们谈论此事，然后再回来带来他们的答复；他会与他们订立条件，在他们庄严的誓言下，他们将绝对服从我作为指挥官和船长的指挥；他们将以神圣的圣礼和福音发誓忠于我，前往我同意的基督教国家，而不是其他地方；并且完全绝对按照我的命令行动，直到安全抵达我所打算的国家，而且他将带来一为此目的，他亲笔向他们签订了合同。然后他告诉我，他首先会向我发誓，只要我吩咐，他一生都不会离开我；而如果他的同胞之间发生任何最轻微的背信行为，他会以最后一滴血站在我这边。他告诉我，他们都是非常彬彬有礼、诚实的人，而且他们处于极度困境中，没有武器、衣物，也没有食物，全凭野蛮人的恩赐和决定；对返回本国已完全无望；并且他确信，如果我愿意承担救援他们的责任，他们会生死与我共。

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 3
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: About six o’clock I went home, dressed, dined at the Café Royal, and turned into a music-hall. It was a silly show, all capering women and monkey-faced men, and I did not stay long. The night was fine and clear as I walked back to the flat I had hired near Portland Place. The crowd surged past me on the pavements, busy and chattering, and I envied the people for having something to do. These shop-girls and clerks and dandies and policemen had some interest in life that kept them going. I gave half-a-crown to a beggar because I saw him yawn; he was a fellow-sufferer. At Oxford Circus I looked up into the spring sky and I made a vow. I would give the Old Country another day to fit me into something; if nothing happened, I would take the next boat for the Cape.

My flat was the first floor in a new block behind Langham Place. There was a common staircase, with a porter and a liftman at the entrance, but there was no restaurant or anything of that sort, and each flat was quite shut off from the others. I hate servants on the premises, so I had a fellow to look after me who came in by the day. He arrived before eight o’clock every morning and used to depart at seven, for I never dined at home.

I was just fitting my key into the door when I noticed a man at my elbow. I had not seen him approach, and the sudden appearance made me start. He was a slim man, with a short brown beard and small, gimlety blue eyes. I recognized him as the occupant of a flat on the top floor, with whom I had passed the time of day on the stairs.
“Can I speak to you?” he said. “May I come in for a minute?” He was steadying his voice with an effort, and his hand was pawing my arm.
I got my door open and motioned him in. No sooner was he over the threshold than he made a dash for my back room, where I used to smoke and write my letters. Then he bolted back.

“I’m very sorry,” he said humbly. “It’s a mighty liberty, but you looked the kind of man who would understand. I’ve had you in my mind all this week when things got troublesome. Say, will you do me a good turn?”
“I’ll listen to you,” I said. “That’s all I’ll promise.” I was getting worried by the antics of this nervous little chap.
There was a tray of drinks on a table beside him, from which he filled himself a stiff whisky-and-soda. He drank it off in three gulps, and cracked the glass as he set it down.

A smile flickered over his drawn face. “I’m not mad—yet. Say, sir, I’ve been watching you, and I reckon you’re a cool customer. I reckon, too, you’re an honest man, and not afraid of playing a bold hand. I’m going to confide in you. I need help worse than any man ever needed it, and I want to know if I can count you in.”
He seemed to brace himself for a great effort, and then started on the queerest rigmarole. I didn’t get hold of it at first, and I had to stop and ask him questions. But here is the gist of it:

He was an American, from Kentucky, and after college, being pretty well off, he had started out to see the world. He wrote a bit, and acted as war correspondent for a Chicago paper, and spent a year or two in South-Eastern Europe. I gathered that he was a fine linguist, and had got to know pretty well the society in those parts. He spoke familiarly of many names that I remembered to have seen in the newspapers.
paragraphsZh: 大约六点我回家，穿好衣服，在皇家咖啡馆用餐，然后转进了一个音乐厅。那是一场愚蠢的表演，满是嬉戏的女人和猴脸的男人，我没待太久。夜色晴朗，我走回波特兰广场附近租的公寓。人群在人行道上匆匆经过，忙碌交谈，我羡慕人们有事可做。这些店员、店员、花花公子和警察对生活有些兴趣，维持着他们的生活。我给了一个乞丐半克朗，因为我看到他打哈欠;他也是同苦者。在牛津圆环，我仰望春天的天空，立下誓言。我要再给老家一天时间，好让自己适应些什么;如果什么都没发生，我会坐下一班船去好望角。
我的公寓在朗豪坊后面一栋新楼的一楼。有一个公共楼梯，入口处有门房和电梯员，但没有餐厅或类似的地方，每个公寓都相互隔绝。我讨厌家里有仆人，所以我雇了一个白天来照顾我的人。他每天早上八点前到，通常七点离开，因为我从不在家用餐。
当我正把钥匙插进门锁时，我注意到有一个男人站在我身边。我没有看到他靠近，他的突然出现让我吃了一惊。他是一个瘦削的男人，留着短短的棕色胡子，眼睛小而锐利呈蓝色。我认出了他，他是顶楼一套公寓的住户，我曾在楼梯上和他打过招呼。
“我可以跟你谈谈吗？”他说。“我可以进来一下吗？”他努力稳定声音，手却在碰我的手臂。
我打开门，招手让他进来。他刚一跨进门槛，就冲向我以前用来抽烟和写信的后屋。然后又飞快地跑了回来。
“非常抱歉，”他谦卑地说。“冒昧打扰，但你看起来是那种能理解人的人。这一周事情麻烦的时候，我一直在想着你。请问，你能帮我一个忙吗？”
“我会听你说的，”我说。“我只能答应这个。”这个神经质的小家伙的举动让我开始担心。
他身旁的桌子上有一盘饮料，他从中给自己倒了一杯烈威士忌苏打水。他三口就喝完了，放下杯子时还把玻璃杯碰得啪响。
他那张憔悴的脸上闪过一丝笑意。“我还没疯——至少现在没。先生，我一直在观察你，我觉得你是个冷静的人。我也觉得，你是个诚实的人，不怕走大胆的路。我打算向你吐露心声。我需要的帮助比任何人都急切，我想知道我能否指望你帮忙。”
他似乎在为一次重大努力做准备，然后开始讲述一段最奇怪的离奇故事。我一开始没弄明白，不得不停下来问他问题。但事情的大意是这样的:
他是美国人，来自肯塔基州，大学毕业后，因为家境相当不错，他开始了环游世界的旅程。他写过一些文章，并为一家芝加哥报纸担任战地记者，还在东南欧待了一两年。我了解到他是个优秀的语言学家，并且对那些地方的社会相当了解。他熟悉地提到许多名字，我记得曾在报纸上见过。

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 4
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: “And that’s a’ I get,” he moaned. “A heid better than hell fire, and twae een lookin’ different ways for the Sabbath.”

“A drink they ca’ brandy. Bein’ a teetotaller I keepit off the whisky, but I was nip-nippin’ a’ day at this brandy, and I doubt I’ll no be weel for a fortnicht.” His voice died away into a splutter, and sleep once more laid its heavy hand on him.

My plan had been to get out at some station down the line, but the train suddenly gave me a better chance, for it came to a standstill at the end of a culvert which spanned a brawling porter-coloured river. I looked out and saw that every carriage window was closed and no human figure appeared in the landscape. So I opened the door, and dropped quickly into the tangle of hazels which edged the line.

It would have been all right but for that infernal dog. Under the impression that I was decamping with its master’s belongings, it started to bark, and all but got me by the trousers. This woke up the herd, who stood bawling at the carriage door in the belief that I had committed suicide. I crawled through the thicket, reached the edge of the stream, and in cover of the bushes put a hundred yards or so behind me. Then from my shelter I peered back, and saw the guard and several passengers gathered round the open carriage door and staring in my direction. I could not have made a more public departure if I had left with a bugler and a brass band.

Happily the drunken herd provided a diversion. He and his dog, which was attached by a rope to his waist, suddenly cascaded out of the carriage, landed on their heads on the track, and rolled some way down the bank towards the water. In the rescue which followed the dog bit somebody, for I could hear the sound of hard swearing. Presently they had forgotten me, and when after a quarter of a mile’s crawl I ventured to look back, the train had started again and was vanishing in the cutting.

I was in a wide semicircle of moorland, with the brown river as radius, and the high hills forming the northern circumference. There was not a sign or sound of a human being, only the plashing water and the interminable crying of curlews. Yet, oddly enough, for the first time I felt the terror of the hunted on me. It was not the police that I thought of, but the other folk, who knew that I knew Scudder’s secret and dared not let me live. I was certain that they would pursue me with a keenness and vigilance unknown to the British law, and that once their grip closed on me I should find no mercy.

I looked back, but there was nothing in the landscape. The sun glinted on the metals of the line and the wet stones in the stream, and you could not have found a more peaceful sight in the world. Nevertheless I started to run. Crouching low in the runnels of the bog, I ran till the sweat blinded my eyes. The mood did not leave me till I had reached the rim of mountain and flung myself panting on a ridge high above the young waters of the brown river.

From my vantage-ground I could scan the whole moor right away to the railway line and to the south of it where green fields took the place of heather. I have eyes like a hawk, but I could see nothing moving in the whole countryside. Then I looked east beyond the ridge and saw a new kind of landscape—shallow green valleys with plentiful fir plantations and the faint lines of dust which spoke of highroads. Last of all I looked into the blue May sky, and there I saw that which set my pulses racing....
paragraphsZh: “这就是我得到的一切，”他呻吟道。“头痛得比地狱之火还厉害，两只眼睛在安息日朝不同的方向看。”
“这是一种叫白兰地的酒。因为我不碰酒精，所以一直没喝威士忌，但我整天还是抿着这白兰地，我怀疑我接下来两周身体都不好。”他的声音渐渐消散成喘息，又一次沉重的睡意压在他身上。
我的计划是到线路上的某个车站下车，但火车突然给了我更好的机会，因为它在一条跨过汹涌棕色河流的涵洞尽头停了下来。我向外望去，看到每节车厢的窗户都关着，景色里没有任何人影。于是我打开门，迅速跳进了沿着铁路线生长的榛树丛中。
如果不是那该死的狗，一切本来都没问题。它以为我要带着主人东西逃走，开始狂吠，差点抓住我的裤子。这惊动了那群人，他们站在马车门前大喊大叫，以为我自杀了。我爬过灌木丛，到了小溪边，然后在灌木的掩护下，把大约一百码的距离甩在身后。然后，我从藏身处向后看，看到守卫和几名乘客聚在敞开的马车门旁，盯着我的方向。我如果带着号手和铜管乐队离开，也不可能比这更公开了。
幸好那群醉汉制造了分心。他和他的狗——狗被绳子拴在他腰上——突然从马车上翻了出去，头朝下摔在轨道上，滚了一段距离，向河边的堤岸滚去。在随后的救援中，狗咬了某人，因为我能听到粗鲁的咒骂声。不久他们就忘记了我，而当我在爬行了四分之一英里后胆敢回头看时，火车已经重新启动，正消失在切道里。
我身处一片广阔的荒原半圆中，以棕色的河流为半径，高耸的山丘构成北侧的弧线。四周没有人类的迹象或声音，只有水花拍击的声响和长鸣的烏鴉般的鸟叫声。然而，奇怪的是，我第一次感到被猎捕的恐惧降临到自己身上。我想到的不是警察，而是那些其他人，他们知道我知道斯卡德的秘密，因此不敢让我活着。我确信他们会以英国法律所未知的敏锐和警觉追杀我，一旦他们抓住我，我将无处可逃，也难求宽恕。
我回头看去，但景色中什么也没有。阳光在铁路线的金属和小溪中的湿石上闪烁，你找不到比这更宁静的景象了。尽管如此，我还是开始跑。蹲伏在沼泽的小水沟里，我跑着，直到汗水模糊了我的眼睛。这种心情一直没有离开我，直到我到达山顶的边缘，气喘吁吁地扔自己躺在高高的山脊上，俯瞰褐色河流的年轻水流。
从我的高地上，我可以立即扫描整片荒原，一直到铁路，以及它以南的地方，那里的绿田取代了石南花。我有如鹰般的眼睛，但在整个乡间我什么移动的东西也没看到。然后我向东眺望过山脊，看见了一种新的景象——浅绿的山谷里种满了杉树，还有那微弱的尘土痕迹，暗示着大道的存在。最后，我仰望湛蓝的五月天空，在那里，我看到了让我的脉搏加速的东西……

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 5
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: Just then I heard a noise in the sky, and lo and behold there was that infernal aeroplane, flying low, about a dozen miles to the south and rapidly coming towards me.

I had the sense to remember that on a bare moor I was at the aeroplane’s mercy, and that my only chance was to get to the leafy cover of the valley. Down the hill I went like blue lightning, screwing my head round, whenever I dared, to watch that damned flying machine. Soon I was on a road between hedges, and dipping to the deep-cut glen of a stream. Then came a bit of thick wood where I slackened speed.

Suddenly on my left I heard the hoot of another car, and realized to my horror that I was almost up on a couple of gate-posts through which a private road debouched on the highway. My horn gave an agonized roar, but it was too late. I clapped on my brakes, but my impetus was too great, and there before me a car was sliding athwart my course. In a second there would have been the deuce of a wreck. I did the only thing possible, and ran slap into the hedge on the right, trusting to find something soft beyond.

But there I was mistaken. My car slithered through the hedge like butter, and then gave a sickening plunge forward. I saw what was coming, leapt on the seat and would have jumped out. But a branch of hawthorn got me in the chest, lifted me up and held me, while a ton or two of expensive metal slipped below me, bucked and pitched, and then dropped with an almighty smash fifty feet to the bed of the stream.

Slowly that thorn let me go. I subsided first on the hedge, and then very gently on a bower of nettles. As I scrambled to my feet a hand took me by the arm, and a sympathetic and badly scared voice asked me if I were hurt.

I found myself looking at a tall young man in goggles and a leather ulster, who kept on blessing his soul and whinnying apologies. For myself, once I got my wind back, I was rather glad than otherwise. This was one way of getting rid of the car.
“My blame, sir,” I answered him. “It’s lucky that I did not add homicide to my follies. That’s the end of my Scotch motor tour, but it might have been the end of my life.”

He plucked out a watch and studied it. “You’re the right sort of fellow,” he said. “I can spare a quarter of an hour, and my house is two minutes off. I’ll see you clothed and fed and snug in bed. Where’s your kit, by the way? Is it in the burn along with the car?”
“A colonial,” he cried. “By Gad, you’re the very man I’ve been praying for. Are you by any blessed chance a Free Trader?”

He patted my shoulder and hurried me into his car. Three minutes later we drew up before a comfortable-looking shooting-box set among pine trees, and he ushered me indoors. He took me first to a bedroom and flung half a dozen of his suits before me, for my own had been pretty well reduced to rags. I selected a loose blue serge, which differed most conspicuously from my former garments, and borrowed a linen collar. Then he haled me to the dining-room, where the remnants of a meal stood on the table, and announced that I had just five minutes to feed. “You can take a snack in your pocket, and we’ll have supper when we get back. I’ve got to be at the Masonic Hall at eight o’clock, or my agent will comb my hair.”
paragraphsZh: 就在那时，我听到天空中传来一阵响声，抬头一看，真是那架该死的飞机，低空飞行，离我大约十几英里朝南方飞来，而且快速向我靠近。
我意识到在光秃秃的荒原上，我完全处于飞机的掌控之中，我唯一的机会就是跑到山谷的树荫下去。我像蓝色闪电一样冲下山坡，尽量扭头去偷看那架该死的飞行器。很快我来到一条夹在树篱之间的道路，倾斜向深切的溪谷。然后是一片浓密的树林，我在这里放慢了速度。
突然在我左边，我听到另一辆车的喇叭声，惊恐地意识到我几乎要撞上几根门柱，那是私人道路通向公路的出口。我的喇叭发出痛苦的长鸣，但为时已晚。我猛踩刹车，但惯性太大，而在我面前，一辆车横在我的行驶路线。一秒钟之后，必将发生一场严重的事故。我只能做唯一可能的事，直接撞向右边的篱笆，希望在其后能有东西比较柔软。
但我在那里错了。我的车像黄油一样滑过树篱，然后狠狠地向前扎去。我看到了即将发生的事情，跳到座位上，想要跳出去。但是一根山楂树枝打在我的胸口，把我托起来固定住，而一两吨昂贵的金属在我身下滑行，翻动、颠簸，然后以一声巨响摔落在下方的溪床上，距离大约五十英尺。
那根刺慢慢放开了我。我先是落在树篱上，然后非常轻柔地落在一片荨麻丛中。当我挣扎着站起来时，一只手抓住了我的手臂，一个同情而又惊恐的声音问我是否受伤。
我发现自己正看着一个戴着护目镜、穿着皮大衣的高个年轻人，他不停地为自己的灵魂祈福并发出歉意的声音。至于我自己，一旦我恢复了呼吸，我反而感到相当高兴。这是摆脱汽车的一种方式。
“都是我的错，先生，”我回答他。“幸运的是，我没有把谋杀加入我的愚行。这就是我苏格兰汽车之旅的终点，但它本可能是我生命的终点。”
他掏出一块手表，仔细看了看。“你是个合适的人，”他说。“我可以抽出一刻钟时间，而我的房子就在两分钟路程内。我会让你穿好衣服、吃饱、舒舒服服地上床。顺便问一句，你的行李呢？也和那辆车一起落入河里了吗？”
“一个殖民地来的呀，”他喊道。“天哪，你正是我一直祈求的人。你难道碰巧是自由贸易支持者吗？”

他拍了拍我的肩膀，催我快上车。三分钟后，我们停在一座松林环绕、看起来舒适的狩猎小屋前，他把我领了进去。他先带我到一间卧室，把他半打西装扔到我面前，因为我自己的衣服几乎都破烂不堪了。我挑了一件宽松的蓝色斜纹布西装，与我以前的衣服差别很大，还借了一件亚麻领子。然后他把我拉到餐厅，桌上还剩着一些饭菜，并宣布我只有五分钟时间吃饭。“你可以带点零食放在口袋里，等我们回来再吃晚饭。我得八点到共济会礼堂，否则我的经纪人会帮我梳头。”

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 6
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: I jumped the dyke and followed it, and after a few hundred yards—as soon as it was out of sight of the highway—the grass stopped and it became a very respectable road, which was evidently kept with some care. Clearly it ran to a house, and I began to think of doing the same. Hitherto my luck had held, and it might be that my best chance would be found in this remote dwelling. Anyhow there were trees there, and that meant cover.

I did not follow the road, but the burnside which flanked it on the right, where the bracken grew deep and the high banks made a tolerable screen. It was well I did so, for no sooner had I gained the hollow than, looking back, I saw the pursuit topping the ridge from which I had descended.

After that I did not look back; I had no time. I ran up the burnside, crawling over the open places, and for a large part wading in the shallow stream. I found a deserted cottage with a row of phantom peat-stacks and an overgrown garden. Then I was among young hay, and very soon had come to the edge of a plantation of wind-blown firs. From there I saw the chimneys of the house smoking a few hundred yards to my left. I forsook the burnside, crossed another dyke, and almost before I knew was on a rough lawn. A glance back told me that I was well out of sight of the pursuit, which had not yet passed the first lift of the moor.

The lawn was a very rough place, cut with a scythe instead of a mower, and planted with beds of scrubby rhododendrons. A brace of black-game, which are not usually garden birds, rose at my approach. The house before me was the ordinary moorland farm, with a more pretentious whitewashed wing added. Attached to this wing was a glass veranda, and through the glass I saw the face of an elderly gentleman meekly watching me.

I stalked over the border of coarse hill gravel and entered the open veranda door. Within was a pleasant room, glass on one side, and on the other a mass of books. More books showed in an inner room. On the floor, instead of tables, stood cases such as you see in a museum, filled with coins and queer stone implements.

There was a knee-hole desk in the middle, and seated at it, with some papers and open volumes before him, was the benevolent old gentleman. His face was round and shiny, like Mr Pickwick’s, big glasses were stuck on the end of his nose, and the top of his head was as bright and bare as a glass bottle. He never moved when I entered, but raised his placid eyebrows and waited on me to speak.

It was not an easy job, with about five minutes to spare, to tell a stranger who I was and what I wanted, and to win his aid. I did not attempt it. There was something about the eye of the man before me, something so keen and knowledgeable, that I could not find a word. I simply stared at him and stuttered.
I nodded towards the window. It gave a prospect across the moor through a gap in the plantation, and revealed certain figures half a mile off straggling through the heather.
“Ah, I see,” he said, and took up a pair of field-glasses through which he patiently scrutinized the figures.

“A fugitive from justice, eh? Well, we’ll go into the matter at our leisure. Meantime I object to my privacy being broken in upon by the clumsy rural policeman. Go into my study, and you will see two doors facing you. Take the one on the left and close it behind you. You will be perfectly safe.”
paragraphsZh: 我跳过堤坝沿着它走，几百码之后——一旦离开了公路的视线——草地停止了，取而代之的是一条相当体面的道路，显然得到了相当的维护。很明显，它通向一所房子，于是我开始考虑也去那儿。到目前为止，我的运气还不错，也许在这个偏僻的住处我能找到最好的机会。不管怎样，那儿有树，这意味着可以掩护。
我没有沿着道路走，而是沿着它右侧的溪边走，那里蕨类植物茂盛，高高的河岸形成了一个相当不错的屏障。我这么做是明智的，因为我刚进入洼地，回头一看，就看到追赶者正从我下来的那条山脊上出现。

之后我没有回头；我没有时间。我沿着溪边跑，爬过开阔地带，大部分时间都在浅溪里涉水。我发现了一座废弃的小屋，旁边有一排幽灵般的泥炭堆和一个长满杂草的花园。然后我进入了年轻的干草地，很快就来到了被风吹动的杉树种植园边缘。从那里我看到房子的烟囱在我左边几百码远的地方冒着烟。我离开了溪边，越过另一条堤坝，差点没意识到自己已经走上了一块崎岖的草地。回头一瞥，我发现自己已经完全脱离了追赶者的视线，他们还没有越过荒原的第一道坡道。
草坪是一个非常粗糙的地方，用镰刀而不是割草机割过，并种有丛生杜鹃花。两只黑色的野禽——通常不是花园里的鸟——在我靠近时飞了起来。我面前的房子是普通的荒原农舍，还加建了一翼较为讲究的白灰粉墙。附着在这翼房上的有一个玻璃阳台，通过玻璃我看到一位年长的绅士正温顺地注视着我。
我踩过粗糙的山地砂砾边缘，走进敞开的阳台门。里面是一间令人愉快的房间，一面是玻璃，另一面则是成堆的书。内室里还有更多的书。地板上，不是桌子，而是博物馆里常见的展示柜，里面装满了硬币和奇怪的石制器具。
中间有一张膝下桌，桌前坐着一位慈祥的老人，桌上放着一些文件和打开的书卷。他的脸圆而光亮，像皮克威克先生一样，鼻子上架着一副大眼镜，头顶光亮得像玻璃瓶。他在我进来时一动不动，只是抬起平静的眉毛等我开口。
在大约五分钟的时间里，要向一个陌生人说明我是谁、想要什么，并赢得他的帮助，这并非易事。我没有尝试。眼前这人的目光中有某种东西，如此敏锐而博学，以至于我找不到合适的词语。我只是盯着他看，结结巴巴地说话。
我向窗户点了点头。窗户透过林间的缝隙，可以看到沼泽地的一片景色，还显露出半英里开外某些人在石楠丛中零散前行的身影。
“啊，我明白了，”他说着，拿起一副望远镜，耐心地观察那些人影。
“一个逃犯吗？好吧，我们可以慢慢处理这件事。与此同时，我反对笨拙的乡下警察打扰我的隐私。去我的书房，你会看到两个门在你面前。走左边那扇门，并把它关上。你将完全安全。”

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 7
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: That was one of the hardest jobs I ever took on. My shoulder and arm ached like hell, and I was so sick and giddy that I was always on the verge of falling. But I managed it somehow. By the use of out-jutting stones and gaps in the masonry and a tough ivy root I got to the top in the end. There was a little parapet behind which I found space to lie down. Then I proceeded to go off into an old-fashioned swoon.

I woke with a burning head and the sun glaring in my face. For a long time I lay motionless, for those horrible fumes seemed to have loosened my joints and dulled my brain. Sounds came to me from the house—men speaking throatily and the throbbing of a stationary car. There was a little gap in the parapet to which I wriggled, and from which I had some sort of prospect of the yard. I saw figures come out—a servant with his head bound up, and then a younger man in knickerbockers. They were looking for something, and moved towards the mill. Then one of them caught sight of the wisp of cloth on the nail, and cried out to the other. They both went back to the house, and brought two more to look at it. I saw the rotund figure of my late captor, and I thought I made out the man with the lisp. I noticed that all had pistols.

For half an hour they ransacked the mill. I could hear them kicking over the barrels and pulling up the rotten planking. Then they came outside, and stood just below the dovecot arguing fiercely. The servant with the bandage was being soundly rated. I heard them fiddling with the door of the dovecote and for one horrid moment I fancied they were coming up. Then they thought better of it, and went back to the house.

All that long blistering afternoon I lay baking on the rooftop. Thirst was my chief torment. My tongue was like a stick, and to make it worse I could hear the cool drip of water from the mill-lade.
