I watched the course of the little stream as it came in from the moor, and my fancy followed it to the top of the glen, where it must issue from an icy fountain fringed with cool ferns and mosses. I would have given a thousand pounds to plunge my face into that.

I had a fine prospect of the whole ring of moorland. I saw the car speed away with two occupants, and a man on a hill pony riding east. I judged they were looking for me, and I wished them joy of their quest.

But I saw something else more interesting. The house stood almost on the summit of a swell of moorland which crowned a sort of plateau, and there was no higher point nearer than the big hills six miles off. The actual summit, as I have mentioned, was a biggish clump of trees—firs mostly, with a few ashes and beeches. On the dovecot I was almost on a level with the tree-tops, and could see what lay beyond. The wood was not solid, but only a ring, and inside was an oval of green turf, for all the world like a big cricket-field.

I didn’t take long to guess what it was. It was an aerodrome, and a secret one. The place had been most cunningly chosen. For suppose anyone were watching an aeroplane descending here, he would think it had gone over the hill beyond the trees. As the place was on the top of a rise in the midst of a big amphitheatre, any observer from any direction would conclude it had passed out of view behind the hill. Only a man very close at hand would realize that the aeroplane had not gone over but had descended in the midst of the wood. An observer with a telescope on one of the higher hills might have discovered the truth, but only herds went there, and herds do not carry spy-glasses. When I looked from the dovecot I could see far away a blue line which I knew was the sea, and I grew furious to think that our enemies had this secret conning-tower to rake our waterways.
paragraphsZh: 那是我接手过的最艰难的工作之一。我的肩膀和手臂疼得要命，我又病又头晕，常常险些摔倒。但我还是设法做到了。通过利用凸出的石头、墙体的缝隙和一根结实的常青藤根，我最终爬到了顶部。后面有一小段女儿墙，我找到空间躺下。然后我便开始陷入一种老式的晕厥状态。

我醒来时头疼欲裂，阳光刺入我的眼睛。很长一段时间我一动不动地躺着，因为那些可怕的烟雾似乎让我的关节松弛，头脑迟钝。我听到从房子里传来的声音——男人沙哑地说话，还有一辆停着的车发出的嗡嗡声。我挪到矮墙的小缝隙处，从那里我大概能看到院子的一角。我看见有人出来——一个头上绑着绷带的仆人，然后是一个穿灯笼裤的年轻人。他们在找什么东西，朝磨坊那边走去。然后其中一个人看见钉子上的一丝布条，叫了另一个人。他们都回到屋里，又带了两个人来看。我看到了我那已故俘虏者的圆胖身影，还以为认出了那个口齿不清的男人。我注意到他们全都带着手枪。
他们洗劫了半个小时的磨坊。我能听到他们踢翻桶，掀起腐烂的木板。然后他们走到外面，站在鸽舍下方激烈争论。那个裹着绷带的仆人正被严厉责骂。我听到他们摆弄鸽舍的门，有一瞬间我可怕地以为他们要上来。随后他们改变了主意，回到房子里去了。
那漫长炙热的下午，我整天躺在屋顶上烤晒。口渴是我最大的折磨。我的舌头干得像木棍，而更糟糕的是，我能听到水从水渠里发出的清凉滴水声。我看着那条小溪从荒原流来，它的河道，我的想象一直跟随到山谷的顶端，那里的泉水一定冰凉，周围铺满了凉爽的蕨类和苔藓。我宁愿花一千磅把脸埋进那水里。
我可以很好地眺望整片荒原环形地带。我看到汽车飞驰而去，车里有两名乘客，还有一个骑着小山马的男人向东行。我推测他们是在找我，并祝他们寻找顺利。
但是我看到了更有趣的东西。那座房子几乎矗立在一片荒原的小丘顶上，这片小丘像一种高原的冠冕，而在附近没有比六英里外的大山更高的地方。如我之前提到的，真正的顶峰是一簇较大的树木——大多是杉树，还有几棵白蜡树和榉树。在鸽棚上，我几乎与树梢平齐，可以看到那边的景象。这片树林并不密集，只是一个环状，中间是一个椭圆形的绿色草坪，看上去完全像一个大板球场。

我很快就猜出了那是什么。那是一个飞机场，而且是一个秘密的飞机场。这个地方选得非常巧妙。因为假如有人在看飞机在这里下降，他会以为飞机已经飞过树木后面的山丘。由于这个地方位于一个大型圆形剧场中央的高地上，从任何方向的观察者都会认为飞机已经飞到山后看不见的地方。只有站得非常近的人才能意识到，飞机不是飞过去，而是在林中降下。站在较高的山上的观察者用望远镜可能会发现真相，但那里只有牧群，而牧群是不会带望远镜的。当我从鸽舍往外看时，我能看到远处有一条蓝线，我知道那是大海，我一想到我们的敌人拥有这个秘密的瞭望塔来扫荡我们的水道，就气得发狂。

title: The Thirty-Nine Steps · 选段 8
author: John Buchan
paragraphs: The reply was a wry smile. “It would have been a welcome present, Bullivant. This, I presume, is Mr Richard Hannay, who for some days greatly interested my department.”

“Mr Hannay will interest it again. He has much to tell you, but not today. For certain grave reasons his tale must wait for four hours. Then, I can promise you, you will be entertained and possibly edified. I want you to assure Mr Hannay that he will suffer no further inconvenience.”

This assurance was promptly given. “You can take up your life where you left off,” I was told. “Your flat, which probably you no longer wish to occupy, is waiting for you, and your man is still there. As you were never publicly accused, we considered that there was no need of a public exculpation. But on that, of course, you must please yourself.”

“Come and see me tomorrow, Hannay. I needn’t tell you to keep deadly quiet. If I were you I would go to bed, for you must have considerable arrears of sleep to overtake. You had better lie low, for if one of your Black Stone friends saw you there might be trouble.”

I felt curiously at a loose end. At first it was very pleasant to be a free man, able to go where I wanted without fearing anything. I had only been a month under the ban of the law, and it was quite enough for me. I went to the Savoy and ordered very carefully a very good luncheon, and then smoked the best cigar the house could provide. But I was still feeling nervous. When I saw anybody look at me in the lounge, I grew shy, and wondered if they were thinking about the murder.

After that I took a taxi and drove miles away up into North London. I walked back through fields and lines of villas and terraces and then slums and mean streets, and it took me pretty nearly two hours. All the while my restlessness was growing worse. I felt that great things, tremendous things, were happening or about to happen, and I, who was the cog-wheel of the whole business, was out of it. Royer would be landing at Dover, Sir Walter would be making plans with the few people in England who were in the secret, and somewhere in the darkness the Black Stone would be working. I felt the sense of danger and impending calamity, and I had the curious feeling, too, that I alone could avert it, alone could grapple with it. But I was out of the game now. How could it be otherwise? It was not likely that Cabinet Ministers and Admiralty Lords and Generals would admit me to their councils.

I actually began to wish that I could run up against one of my three enemies. That would lead to developments. I felt that I wanted enormously to have a vulgar scrap with those gentry, where I could hit out and flatten something. I was rapidly getting into a very bad temper.
I didn’t feel like going back to my flat. That had to be faced some time, but as I still had sufficient money I thought I would put it off till next morning, and go to a hotel for the night.

My irritation lasted through dinner, which I had at a restaurant in Jermyn Street. I was no longer hungry, and let several courses pass untasted. I drank the best part of a bottle of Burgundy, but it did nothing to cheer me. An abominable restlessness had taken possession of me. Here was I, a very ordinary fellow, with no particular brains, and yet I was convinced that somehow I was needed to help this business through—that without me it would all go to blazes. I told myself it was sheer silly conceit, that four or five of the cleverest people living, with all the might of the British Empire at their back, had the job in hand. Yet I couldn’t be convinced. It seemed as if a voice kept speaking in my ear, telling me to be up and doing, or I would never sleep again.
paragraphsZh: 回答是一个讽刺的微笑。“这本来会是一个受欢迎的礼物，布利文特。我想，这位是理查德·汉内先生，几天来他使我的部门十分感兴趣。”
“汉内先生将再次引起部门的兴趣。他有很多事情要告诉你，但今天不能说。出于某些严重的原因，他的故事必须等待四个小时。到时候，我可以向你保证，你将既受到娱乐，也可能有所启发。我希望你向汉内先生保证，他不会再受到进一步的不便。”
这个保证很快就给出了。“你可以从你中断的生活继续过下去，”有人告诉我，“你的公寓，虽然你可能不再想住在那里，正等着你，而且你的仆人还在原处。由于你从未被公开指控，我们认为没有必要进行公开的辩解。当然，关于这点，你必须自己决定。”
“明天来见我，汉奈。我不必告诉你保持绝对安静。如果我是你，我现在就该去睡觉了，因为你肯定有不少睡眠欠账需要补。你最好保持低调，因为如果你的某位黑石俱乐部朋友看到你，可能会惹麻烦。”
我感到一种奇怪的无所适从。一开始成为自由人可以随心所欲地去任何地方而不必害怕，感觉非常愉快。我只是被法律禁止行动一个月，这对我来说已经足够了。我去了萨沃伊酒店，非常仔细地点了一顿很好的午餐，然后抽了店里最好的雪茄。但我仍然感到紧张。当我看到有人在休息室里看我时，我会觉得害羞，心想他们是否在想那个谋杀案。

之后，我打了辆出租车，开车行驶数英里，到了伦敦北部。我穿过田野、别墅和排屋之间的道路，然后是贫民区和狭窄的街道，走了将近两个小时。整段时间里，我的焦躁感越来越严重。我感觉到有伟大的事情、极其重要的事情正在发生或即将发生，而我，这整个事件的齿轮，却被排除在外。罗耶将会在多佛尔着陆，沃尔特爵士会和英国少数知情的人制定计划，而在某个黑暗之处，黑石将会发挥作用。我感到一种危险和即将到来的灾难的气息，同时也有一种奇怪的感觉——只有我才能挽救它，才能独自应对它。但我现在已经脱离了这场游戏。还能有别的可能吗？内阁部长、海军上将和将军们不太可能允许我参加他们的会议。
我甚至开始希望能碰上我的三个敌人之一。那样就会有一些进展。我感到非常想和那些上流人士打一场粗俗的架子，让我能够出手打击、压倒什么。我很快就变得脾气非常暴躁。
我不想回去我的公寓。那件事迟早得面对，但因为我仍有足够的钱，我想我可以把它推到第二天早晨，再去酒店过夜。

我的烦躁一直持续到晚餐，那天我在捷明街的一家餐馆吃饭。我已经不再饿了，让几道菜未经品尝就过去了。我喝掉了几乎整整一瓶勃艮第葡萄酒，但这丝毫没有让我高兴起来。一种可恶的不安感占据了我。我就是这样一个非常普通的人，没有特别的才智，但我却确信我 somehow（以某种方式）需要帮助这个事务——如果没有我，一切都会完蛋。我告诉自己这纯属可笑的自负，世上最聪明的四五个人，在整个大英帝国的全力支持下，都已经负责处理这件事了。然而，我就是无法信服。似乎有一个声音一直在我耳边说话，告诉我必须起身去做，否则我将永远无法入睡。

title: The Woman in White · 选段 3
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: I must have been hard to please, indeed, if I had not approved of the room, and of everything about it. The bow-window looked out on the same lovely view which I had admired, in the morning, from my bedroom. The furniture was the perfection of luxury and beauty; the table in the centre was bright with gaily bound books, elegant conveniences for writing, and beautiful flowers; the second table, near the window, was covered with all the necessary materials for mounting water-colour drawings, and had a little easel attached to it, which I could expand or fold up at will; the walls were hung with gaily tinted chintz; and the floor was spread with Indian matting in maize-colour and red. It was the prettiest and most luxurious little sitting-room I had ever seen; and I admired it with the warmest enthusiasm.

The solemn servant was far too highly trained to betray the slightest satisfaction. He bowed with icy deference when my terms of eulogy were all exhausted, and silently opened the door for me to go out into the passage again.

We turned a corner, and entered a long second passage, ascended a short flight of stairs at the end, crossed a small circular upper hall, and stopped in front of a door covered with dark baize. The servant opened this door, and led me on a few yards to a second; opened that also, and disclosed two curtains of pale sea-green silk hanging before us; raised one of them noiselessly; softly uttered the words, “Mr. Hartright,” and left me.

I found myself in a large, lofty room, with a magnificent carved ceiling, and with a carpet over the floor, so thick and soft that it felt like piles of velvet under my feet. One side of the room was occupied by a long book-case of some rare inlaid wood that was quite new to me. It was not more than six feet high, and the top was adorned with statuettes in marble, ranged at regular distances one from the other. On the opposite side stood two antique cabinets; and between them, and above them, hung a picture of the Virgin and Child, protected by glass, and bearing Raphael’s name on the gilt tablet at the bottom of the frame. On my right hand and on my left, as I stood inside the door, were chiffoniers and little stands in buhl and marquetterie, loaded with figures in Dresden china, with rare vases, ivory ornaments, and toys and curiosities that sparkled at all points with gold, silver, and precious stones. At the lower end of the room, opposite to me, the windows were concealed and the sunlight was tempered by large blinds of the same pale sea-green colour as the curtains over the door. The light thus produced was deliciously soft, mysterious, and subdued; it fell equally upon all the objects in the room; it helped to intensify the deep silence, and the air of profound seclusion that possessed the place; and it surrounded, with an appropriate halo of repose, the solitary figure of the master of the house, leaning back, listlessly composed, in a large easy-chair, with a reading-easel fastened on one of its arms, and a little table on the other.

If a man’s personal appearance, when he is out of his dressing-room, and when he has passed forty, can be accepted as a safe guide to his time of life—which is more than doubtful—Mr. Fairlie’s age, when I saw him, might have been reasonably computed at over fifty and under sixty years. His beardless face was thin, worn, and transparently pale, but not wrinkled; his nose was high and hooked; his eyes were of a dim greyish blue, large, prominent, and rather red round the rims of the eyelids; his hair was scanty, soft to look at, and of that light sandy colour which is the last to disclose its own changes towards grey. He was dressed in a dark frock-coat, of some substance much thinner than cloth, and in waistcoat and trousers of spotless white. His feet were effeminately small, and were clad in buff-coloured silk stockings, and little womanish bronze-leather slippers. Two rings adorned his white delicate hands, the value of which even my inexperienced observation detected to be all but priceless. Upon the whole, he had a frail, languidly-fretful, over-refined look—something singularly and unpleasantly delicate in its association with a man, and, at the same time, something which could by no possibility have looked natural and appropriate if it had been transferred to the personal appearance of a woman. My morning’s experience of Miss Halcombe had predisposed me to be pleased with everybody in the house; but my sympathies shut themselves up resolutely at the first sight of Mr. Fairlie.
paragraphsZh: 如果我没有赞同这间房间及其周围的一切，确实说明我一定很难让人满意。凸窗朝向我早上从卧室欣赏过的同样美丽的景色。家具是奢华与美感的极致；中央的桌子上摆放着色彩鲜艳的书籍、优雅的书写用具和美丽的花卉；靠近窗户的第二张桌子上摆满了安装水彩画所需的一切材料，并附有一个小画架，我可以随意展开或折叠；墙壁挂着色彩鲜艳的印花棉布；地板铺着玉米色与红色相间的印度草席。这是我见过的最漂亮、最奢华的小客厅，我满怀最热烈的热情欣赏它。
那位庄重的仆人训练得太过精良，以至于不会流露丝毫的满足感。当我所有的颂词说完时，他以冰冷的恭敬鞠躬，并默默为我开门，让我再次走进走廊。
我们拐过一个角，进入了一条长长的第二通道，在尽头上了一小段楼梯，穿过一个小型圆形上厅，然后停在一扇覆盖着深色毛呢布的门前。仆人打开了这扇门，带我走了几码到第二扇门；也把那扇门打开，显露出两帘淡海绿色丝绸挂在我们面前；悄无声息地掀起其中一帘，轻声说了句：“哈特赖特先生，”然后离开了我。

我发现自己身处一个宽敞、高大的房间里，房顶雕刻华丽，地板上铺着厚厚的地毯，柔软得像一堆堆天鹅绒在脚下。一侧的墙上摆放着一个长长的书柜，用某种我完全陌生的珍贵镶嵌木制成。书柜高不过六英尺，顶部装饰着大理石小雕像，彼此间均匀排列。在对面墙上立着两个古董橱柜；它们之间及上方，挂着一幅圣母与婴孩的画，被玻璃保护着，并在画框底部的镀金牌匾上标有拉斐尔的名字。当我站在门内时，我的右手和左手边放着布尔和镶嵌木工制成的矮柜和小柜台，上面摆满了德累斯顿瓷制的人偶、珍稀花瓶、象牙饰品，以及闪闪发光的玩具和奇珍异宝，点缀着金、银和宝石。房间的另一端，正对着我，窗户被遮住，阳光透过与门上窗帘同样淡海绿色的大百叶窗，被柔和地调节着。由此产生的光线柔和、神秘而低沉；它均匀地落在房间里的所有物体上；它有助于强化深沉的寂静感以及笼罩这个地方的深度隐居气息；它以适当的安宁光环环绕着屋主孤独的身影，他靠在一把大扶手椅上，神情漫不经心地安坐，一只扶手上固定着读书架，另一只扶手旁放着一张小桌子。

如果一个人的外貌，在他离开化妆间之后，且在他超过四十岁时，可以被认为是判断他年龄的可靠依据——这实际上值得怀疑——那么当我见到费尔利先生时，他的年龄可以合理地估计在五十岁以上而六十岁以下。他无须须的脸瘦削、憔悴且苍白透明，但没有皱纹；他的鼻子高而鹰钩；眼睛呈模糊的灰蓝色，较大、突出，眼睑边缘略显红；他的头发稀疏，看起来柔软，呈浅沙色，这种颜色是最晚开始显露灰白变化的。他穿着一件深色短礼服上衣，面料比布料薄得多，还穿着洁白无瑕的马甲和裤子。他的脚纤细得有些女性化，穿着浅黄色丝质长袜，脚上是小巧得近乎女性化的青铜皮革拖鞋。两枚戒指装饰着他白皙精致的手，仅凭我缺乏经验的观察，就可以看出它们的价值几乎是无法估量的。总的来说，他显得脆弱、疲惫而易怒、过于讲究——这种与男人相结合的样貌显得异乎寻常地、不快地精致，同时，如果换到女性身上，这种样貌无论如何都不可能显得自然和适当。我早上与哈尔科姆小姐的经历使我对屋子里的人产生了好感；但在第一次看到费尔里先生时，我的同情心便坚决地关闭了。

title: The Woman in White · 选段 4
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: In external appearance Mr. Gilmore was the exact opposite of the conventional idea of an old lawyer. His complexion was florid—his white hair was worn rather long and kept carefully brushed—his black coat, waistcoat, and trousers fitted him with perfect neatness—his white cravat was carefully tied, and his lavender-coloured kid gloves might have adorned the hands of a fashionable clergyman, without fear and without reproach. His manners were pleasantly marked by the formal grace and refinement of the old school of politeness, quickened by the invigorating sharpness and readiness of a man whose business in life obliges him always to keep his faculties in good working order. A sanguine constitution and fair prospects to begin with—a long subsequent career of creditable and comfortable prosperity—a cheerful, diligent, widely-respected old age—such were the general impressions I derived from my introduction to Mr. Gilmore, and it is but fair to him to add, that the knowledge I gained by later and better experience only tended to confirm them.

I left the old gentleman and Miss Halcombe to enter the house together, and to talk of family matters undisturbed by the restraint of a stranger’s presence. They crossed the hall on their way to the drawing-room, and I descended the steps again to wander about the garden alone.

My hours were numbered at Limmeridge House—my departure the next morning was irrevocably settled—my share in the investigation which the anonymous letter had rendered necessary was at an end. No harm could be done to any one but myself if I let my heart loose again, for the little time that was left me, from the cold cruelty of restraint which necessity had forced me to inflict upon it, and took my farewell of the scenes which were associated with the brief dream-time of my happiness and my love.
The empty silence of the beach struck cold to my heart. I returned to the house and the garden, where traces were left to speak of her at every turn.

On the west terrace walk I met Mr. Gilmore. He was evidently in search of me, for he quickened his pace when we caught sight of each other. The state of my spirits little fitted me for the society of a stranger; but the meeting was inevitable, and I resigned myself to make the best of it.

“You are the very person I wanted to see,” said the old gentleman. “I had two words to say to you, my dear sir; and if you have no objection I will avail myself of the present opportunity. To put it plainly, Miss Halcombe and I have been talking over family affairs—affairs which are the cause of my being here—and in the course of our conversation she was naturally led to tell me of this unpleasant matter connected with the anonymous letter, and of the share which you have most creditably and properly taken in the proceedings so far. That share, I quite understand, gives you an interest which you might not otherwise have felt, in knowing that the future management of the investigation which you have begun will be placed in safe hands. My dear sir, make yourself quite easy on that point—it will be placed in MY hands.”
“You are, in every way, Mr. Gilmore, much fitter to advise and to act in the matter than I am. Is it an indiscretion on my part to ask if you have decided yet on a course of proceeding?”

“So far as it is possible to decide, Mr. Hartright, I have decided. I mean to send a copy of the letter, accompanied by a statement of the circumstances, to Sir Percival Glyde’s solicitor in London, with whom I have some acquaintance. The letter itself I shall keep here to show to Sir Percival as soon as he arrives. The tracing of the two women I have already provided for, by sending one of Mr. Fairlie’s servants—a confidential person—to the station to make inquiries. The man has his money and his directions, and he will follow the women in the event of his finding any clue. This is all that can be done until Sir Percival comes on Monday. I have no doubt myself that every explanation which can be expected from a gentleman and a man of honour, he will readily give. Sir Percival stands very high, sir—an eminent position, a reputation above suspicion—I feel quite easy about results—quite easy, I am rejoiced to assure you. Things of this sort happen constantly in my experience. Anonymous letters—unfortunate woman—sad state of society. I don’t deny that there are peculiar complications in this case; but the case itself is, most unhappily, common—common.”
paragraphsZh: 外表上，吉尔摩先生与传统观念中的老律师完全相反。他的脸色红润——白发偏长，并仔细梳理整齐——黑色的外套、马甲和裤子穿得整整齐齐——白色领巾系得非常讲究，而淡紫色的小羊皮手套，则可以毫无顾虑地佩戴在时髦牧师的手上而不受责备。他的举止带有老派礼仪的正式优雅和精致，同时又因生活事业需要而使思维敏捷、反应迅速，从而增添了一种让人愉快的生气。一开始我对吉尔摩先生的印象是开朗的性格和良好的前景——随后的漫长生涯中充满了体面而舒适的繁荣——晚年快乐、勤奋且备受尊敬——通过对吉尔摩先生的初次接触，我获得了这样的总体印象，而且公平地说，我后来通过更深的了解所得到的认识，只是进一步印证了这些印象。
我留下老先生和哈尔科姆小姐一起进入屋内，谈论家庭事务，不受陌生人在场的拘束。他们穿过大厅前往客厅，而我再次沿着台阶下去，独自一人在花园中漫步。
我在利默里奇庄园的日子已经屈指可数——我第二天早晨的离开已无法更改——匿名信所引发的调查中我所承担的部分也已结束。如果我再次让我的心在剩下的短暂时间里从不得已强加的冷酷约束中释放出来，唯一受到伤害的也不过是我自己。我向那些与我短暂的幸福与爱情梦境相关的场景告别。
海滩的空寂让我的心感到一阵寒意。我回到房子和花园，每一个角落都留下了她的痕迹，仿佛在诉说她的存在。
在西侧露台散步时，我遇到了吉尔摩先生。他显然在寻找我，因为当我们彼此看见时，他加快了脚步。我的心情状态并不适合与陌生人交往；但是相遇是不可避免的，我只好顺从现实，尽力应对。

“您正是我想要见的人，”那位老人说道。“我有两句话想对您说，尊敬的先生；如果您没有异议，我想借此机会说出来。说得直白一些，哈尔科姆小姐和我一直在谈论家事——这些家事正是我来此的原因——在我们的谈话过程中，她自然而然地向我提起了那封匿名信的令人不快的事情，以及您迄今在处理此事中所负责任、恰当地担任的角色。我完全理解，这个角色让您产生了一种兴趣，否则您可能不会有——那就是知道您所开始的调查未来的管理将会被交到可靠的人手中。尊敬的先生，请您对此毫无担忧——它将交由我来处理。”
“在各方面，吉尔莫先生，您比我更适合在此事上提供建议和采取行动。我问一句是否冒犯，是否因为您已经决定了下一步的行动方案？”

“在可能的范围内作出决定的事情上，哈特赖特先生，我已经作出了决定。我的意思是，把信的副本连同情况说明一起寄给伯爵·格莱德爵士在伦敦的律师，我与他有一些交情。信本身我会留在这里，以便格莱德爵士一到就给他看。我已经安排好了对那两个女人的追踪，派了费尔利先生的一名仆人——一个值得信赖的人——去车站打听消息。那个人有他的报酬和指示，如果他找到了任何线索，就会跟踪这两个女人。这就是在格莱德爵士周一到来之前能做的一切。我自己毫不怀疑，每一个一个绅士和荣誉之人的解释，他都会乐意提供。”佩西瓦尔爵士地位非常高，爵士——一个卓越的位置，一个无可置疑的名声——我对结果感到相当放心——相当放心，我很高兴向您保证。这类事情在我的经验中经常发生。匿名信——不幸的女人——社会的悲哀状态。我不否认这个案件中存在特殊的复杂情况；但案件本身，不幸的是，非常普通——普通。”

title: The Woman in White · 选段 5
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: And the magician who has wrought this wonderful transformation—the foreign husband who has tamed this once wayward English woman till her own relations hardly know her again—the Count himself? What of the Count?

This in two words: He looks like a man who could tame anything. If he had married a tigress, instead of a woman, he would have tamed the tigress. If he had married me, I should have made his cigarettes, as his wife does—I should have held my tongue when he looked at me, as she holds hers.

I am almost afraid to confess it, even to these secret pages. The man has interested me, has attracted me, has forced me to like him. In two short days he has made his way straight into my favourable estimation, and how he has worked the miracle is more than I can tell.

It absolutely startles me, now he is in my mind, to find how plainly I see him!—how much more plainly than I see Sir Percival, or Mr. Fairlie, or Walter Hartright, or any other absent person of whom I think, with the one exception of Laura herself! I can hear his voice, as if he was speaking at this moment. I know what his conversation was yesterday, as well as if I was hearing it now. How am I to describe him? There are peculiarities in his personal appearance, his habits, and his amusements, which I should blame in the boldest terms, or ridicule in the most merciless manner, if I had seen them in another man. What is it that makes me unable to blame them, or to ridicule them in HIM?

For example, he is immensely fat. Before this time I have always especially disliked corpulent humanity. I have always maintained that the popular notion of connecting excessive grossness of size and excessive good-humour as inseparable allies was equivalent to declaring, either that no people but amiable people ever get fat, or that the accidental addition of so many pounds of flesh has a directly favourable influence over the disposition of the person on whose body they accumulate. I have invariably combated both these absurd assertions by quoting examples of fat people who were as mean, vicious, and cruel as the leanest and the worst of their neighbours. I have asked whether Henry the Eighth was an amiable character? Whether Pope Alexander the Sixth was a good man? Whether Mr. Murderer and Mrs. Murderess Manning were not both unusually stout people? Whether hired nurses, proverbially as cruel a set of women as are to be found in all England, were not, for the most part, also as fat a set of women as are to be found in all England?—and so on, through dozens of other examples, modern and ancient, native and foreign, high and low. Holding these strong opinions on the subject with might and main as I do at this moment, here, nevertheless, is Count Fosco, as fat as Henry the Eighth himself, established in my favour, at one day’s notice, without let or hindrance from his own odious corpulence. Marvellous indeed!

It may be his face. He is a most remarkable likeness, on a large scale, of the great Napoleon. His features have Napoleon’s magnificent regularity—his expression recalls the grandly calm, immovable power of the Great Soldier’s face. This striking resemblance certainly impressed me, to begin with; but there is something in him besides the resemblance, which has impressed me more. I think the influence I am now trying to find is in his eyes. They are the most unfathomable grey eyes I ever saw, and they have at times a cold, clear, beautiful, irresistible glitter in them which forces me to look at him, and yet causes me sensations, when I do look, which I would rather not feel. Other parts of his face and head have their strange peculiarities. His complexion, for instance, has a singular sallow-fairness, so much at variance with the dark-brown colour of his hair, that I suspect the hair of being a wig, and his face, closely shaven all over, is smoother and freer from all marks and wrinkles than mine, though (according to Sir Percival’s account of him) he is close on sixty years of age. But these are not the prominent personal characteristics which distinguish him, to my mind, from all the other men I have ever seen. The marked peculiarity which singles him out from the rank and file of humanity lies entirely, so far as I can tell at present, in the extraordinary expression and extraordinary power of his eyes.
paragraphsZh: 而创造了这一奇妙变化的魔术师——那个驯服了这位曾经任性的英国妇女，以至于她自己的亲属几乎都认不出来的外国丈夫——伯爵本人呢？伯爵怎么样？
用两个词来说：他看起来像一个可以驯服任何东西的人。如果他娶的是一只母虎，而不是一个女人，他也能驯服那只母虎。如果他娶的是我，我也会像他的妻子那样为他准备香烟——我在他看我的时候会像她那样保持沉默。
甚至对这些秘密仆人，我几乎也害怕承认。这名男子引起了我的兴趣，吸引了我，并迫使我喜欢他。在短短两天内，他就直接赢得了我的好感，而他是如何创造这一奇迹的，我实在无法说明。

这让我感到十分震惊，现在他在我的脑海里，我发现我看他是多么清晰啊！——比我看珀西瓦尔爵士、费尔利先生、沃尔特·哈特赖特，或者任何其他我所思念的缺席之人都要清晰得多，唯一的例外是劳拉本人！我仿佛能听到他的声音，就像他此刻正在说话。我清楚地知道他昨天的谈话，就好像我现在正在听一样。我该如何描述他呢？他的个人外貌、习惯和消遣有一些特殊之处，如果是在其他人身上，我会用最大胆的言辞去指责，或者用最无情的方式去嘲笑。是什么让在他身上我无法指责，也无法嘲笑呢？

例如，他非常胖。在此之前，我一直特别不喜欢肥胖的人性。我一直坚持认为，将过度粗壮的体型和过度的幽默感联系起来，是说，除了和蔼可亲的人，没有人会变胖，或者意外增加那么多磅肉体会直接影响身体上的人性质。我总是通过引用那些像邻居中最瘦、最坏的一样刻薄、凶狠残忍的胖人例子来反驳这两种荒谬的说法。我曾问过亨利八世是否是一个和蔼可亲的人？亚历山大六世教皇是否是一个好人？杀人犯先生和夫人是否......弑母者曼宁难道不是两个异常肥胖的人吗？那些受雇的护士，俗话说，是英国所有女性中最残忍的一群人，也不是大多数情况下，都是英国所有女性中最胖的一群人吗？——如此等等，通过几十个其他例子，现代的和古代的，本土的和外国的，高贵的和卑贱的。我此刻在这里，尽全力持有关于这个话题的这些强烈看法，然而，福斯科伯爵却出现在我面前，他和亨利八世一样胖，在一天之内就在没有自己讨厌的肥胖阻碍的情况下，为我站队。这真是令人惊奇！

可能是他的面容。他是拿破仑的大幅肖像中最为卓越的相似者。他的五官具有拿破仑那种宏伟而均衡的美——他的神情让人联想到伟大士兵面容中那种庄严平静、不可动摇的力量。这种惊人的相似首先确实给我留下了深刻印象；但除了相似之外，他身上还有一些使我更加印象深刻的东西。我想我现在试图寻找的影响力就在他的眼睛里。那是我见过的最难以琢磨的灰色双眼，有时眼中会闪现冷冽、清澈、美丽、不可抗拒的光芒，迫使我注视他，但在我注视时，又会让我产生一些我宁愿不去感受的情绪。他面部和头部的其他部分也有其奇特的特性。例如，他的肤色有一种奇特的黄白色，与他深棕色的头发形成极大的反差，以至于我怀疑他的头发是戴的假发，而他全脸剃得干干净净，比我脸上光滑得多，没有任何痕迹或皱纹，尽管（根据珀西瓦尔爵士对他的描述）他已接近六十岁。但在我看来，这些并不是使他与我见过的所有其他人区别开来的显著个人特征。据我目前所能判断，使他从芸芸众生中脱颖而出的显著特征，完全在于他眼睛的非凡神情和非凡力量。

title: The Woman in White · 选段 6
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: She sighed bitterly. I saw in her face that she was thinking of Hartright—saw it the more plainly because her last words set me thinking of him too. In six months only from her marriage we wanted the faithful service he had offered to us in his farewell words. How little I once thought that we should ever want it at all!
“We must do what we can to help ourselves,” I said. “Let us try to talk it over calmly, Laura—let us do all in our power to decide for the best.”

Putting what she knew of her husband’s embarrassments and what I had heard of his conversation with the lawyer together, we arrived necessarily at the conclusion that the parchment in the library had been drawn up for the purpose of borrowing money, and that Laura’s signature was absolutely necessary to fit it for the attainment of Sir Percival’s object.

The second question, concerning the nature of the legal contract by which the money was to be obtained, and the degree of personal responsibility to which Laura might subject herself if she signed it in the dark, involved considerations which lay far beyond any knowledge and experience that either of us possessed. My own convictions led me to believe that the hidden contents of the parchment concealed a transaction of the meanest and the most fraudulent kind.

I had not formed this conclusion in consequence of Sir Percival’s refusal to show the writing or to explain it, for that refusal might well have proceeded from his obstinate disposition and his domineering temper alone. My sole motive for distrusting his honesty sprang from the change which I had observed in his language and his manners at Blackwater Park, a change which convinced me that he had been acting a part throughout the whole period of his probation at Limmeridge House. His elaborate delicacy, his ceremonious politeness which harmonised so agreeably with Mr. Gilmore’s old-fashioned notions, his modesty with Laura, his candour with me, his moderation with Mr. Fairlie—all these were the artifices of a mean, cunning, and brutal man, who had dropped his disguise when his practised duplicity had gained its end, and had openly shown himself in the library on that very day. I say nothing of the grief which this discovery caused me on Laura’s account, for it is not to be expressed by any words of mine. I only refer to it at all, because it decided me to oppose her signing the parchment, whatever the consequences might be, unless she was first made acquainted with the contents.

Under these circumstances, the one chance for us when to-morrow came was to be provided with an objection to giving the signature, which might rest on sufficiently firm commercial or legal grounds to shake Sir Percival’s resolution, and to make him suspect that we two women understood the laws and obligations of business as well as himself.

After some pondering, I determined to write to the only honest man within reach whom we could trust to help us discreetly in our forlorn situation. That man was Mr. Gilmore’s partner, Mr. Kyrle, who conducted the business now that our old friend had been obliged to withdraw from it, and to leave London on account of his health. I explained to Laura that I had Mr. Gilmore’s own authority for placing implicit confidence in his partner’s integrity, discretion, and accurate knowledge of all her affairs, and with her full approval I sat down at once to write the letter, I began by stating our position to Mr. Kyrle exactly as it was, and then asked for his advice in return, expressed in plain, downright terms which he could comprehend without any danger of misinterpretations and mistakes. My letter was as short as I could possibly make it, and was, I hope, unencumbered by needless apologies and needless details.
paragraphsZh: 她苦涩地叹了口气。我从她的脸上看出她在想哈特赖特——之所以看得更清楚，是因为她的最后几句话也让我开始思考他。自从她结婚才六个月，我们就需要他在告别时所承诺的忠诚服务。我曾经多么没想到我们竟然会需要它！
“我们必须尽力自助，”我说。“劳拉，让我们试着冷静地谈一谈——让我们尽一切可能做出最好的决定。”
把她所知道的关于丈夫的困境与我从律师那里听到的谈话结合起来，我们自然得出结论，图书馆里的羊皮纸是为了借款而拟定的，而劳拉的签名对实现珀西瓦尔爵士的目的绝对是必要的。
第二个问题，关于获取这笔钱所依赖的法律合同的性质，以及劳拉如果在黑暗中签署它可能承担的个人责任程度，涉及的考量远远超出了我们任何一人所掌握的知识和经验。我的信念使我相信，这张羊皮纸上隐藏的内容涉及一种最卑劣和最欺诈的交易。

我并不是因为珀西瓦尔爵士拒绝展示那份文件或解释内容而得出这个结论，因为他的拒绝很可能只是出于他固执的性格和专横的脾性。我怀疑他诚实的唯一动机，是源于我在布莱克沃特庄园观察到的他语言和举止上的变化，这种变化使我确信，他在整个在利默里奇府的试用期中一直在扮演一个角色。他那精心的细腻，他那与吉尔摩先生老派观念如此和谐的礼貌，他对劳拉的谦逊，对我坦诚，以及对先生的克制。法利利——这一切都是一个卑鄙、狡猾而残忍的人的诡计，当他熟练的欺骗达到了目的后，他便放下了伪装，并在那天就在图书馆里公开露面。我没有说这次发现给我在劳拉方面带来的悲痛，因为任何言辞都无法表达。我之所以提到它，仅仅是因为它让我决定反对她签署这份文件，无论后果如何，除非事先让她了解文件的内容。
在这种情况下，当明天到来时，我们唯一的机会是找出一个反对签字的理由，这个理由可能基于足够坚实的商业或法律基础，以动摇珀西瓦尔爵士的决心，并让他怀疑我们两个女人理解商业的法律和义务不亚于他自己。

经过一番思考，我决定写信给我们能够信赖的、在我们绝望处境中可以悄悄帮助我们的唯一诚实的人。那个人是吉尔莫先生的合伙人凯尔先生，他在我们的老朋友因健康原因不得不退出并离开伦敦后，负责经营这项业务。我向劳拉解释说，我有吉尔莫先生本人的授权，对他的合伙人的诚信、谨慎以及对她所有事务的准确了解可以完全信任，并在她完全同意下，我立刻坐下来写信。我开始向凯尔先生如实陈述我们的处境，然后请求他的建议，用明确、直截了当的语言表达，以便他理解而不致出现误解或错误。我的信尽可能地简短，希望没有被不必要的道歉和不必要的细节所累赘。

title: The Woman in White · 选段 7
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: On the next page of the Diary, another entry appears. It is in a man’s handwriting, large, bold, and firmly regular, and the date is “June the 21st.” It contains these lines—]
The illness of our excellent Miss Halcombe has afforded me the opportunity of enjoying an unexpected intellectual pleasure.
There are many hundred pages here. I can lay my hand on my heart, and declare that every page has charmed, refreshed, delighted me.

Yes! these pages are amazing. The tact which I find here, the discretion, the rare courage, the wonderful power of memory, the accurate observation of character, the easy grace of style, the charming outbursts of womanly feeling, have all inexpressibly increased my admiration of this sublime creature, of this magnificent Marian. The presentation of my own character is masterly in the extreme. I certify, with my whole heart, to the fidelity of the portrait. I feel how vivid an impression I must have produced to have been painted in such strong, such rich, such massive colours as these. I lament afresh the cruel necessity which sets our interests at variance, and opposes us to each other. Under happier circumstances how worthy I should have been of Miss Halcombe—how worthy Miss Halcombe would have been of ME.
The sentiments which animate my heart assure me that the lines I have just written express a Profound Truth.

Those sentiments exalt me above all merely personal considerations. I bear witness, in the most disinterested manner, to the excellence of the stratagem by which this unparalleled woman surprised the private interview between Percival and myself—also to the marvellous accuracy of her report of the whole conversation from its beginning to its end.

Those sentiments have induced me to offer to the unimpressionable doctor who attends on her my vast knowledge of chemistry, and my luminous experience of the more subtle resources which medical and magnetic science have placed at the disposal of mankind. He has hitherto declined to avail himself of my assistance. Miserable man!

Finally, those sentiments dictate the lines—grateful, sympathetic, paternal lines—which appear in this place. I close the book. My strict sense of propriety restores it (by the hands of my wife) to its place on the writer’s table. Events are hurrying me away. Circumstances are guiding me to serious issues. Vast perspectives of success unroll themselves before my eyes. I accomplish my destiny with a calmness which is terrible to myself. Nothing but the homage of my admiration is my own. I deposit it with respectful tenderness at the feet of Miss Halcombe.

I condole with her on the inevitable failure of every plan that she has formed for her sister’s benefit. At the same time, I entreat her to believe that the information which I have derived from her Diary will in no respect help me to contribute to that failure. It simply confirms the plan of conduct which I had previously arranged. I have to thank these pages for awakening the finest sensibilities in my nature—nothing more.

Why—I ask everybody—why worry ME? Nobody answers that question, and nobody lets me alone. Relatives, friends, and strangers all combine to annoy me. What have I done? I ask myself, I ask my servant, Louis, fifty times a day—what have I done? Neither of us can tell. Most extraordinary!

The last annoyance that has assailed me is the annoyance of being called upon to write this Narrative. Is a man in my state of nervous wretchedness capable of writing narratives? When I put this extremely reasonable objection, I am told that certain very serious events relating to my niece have happened within my experience, and that I am the fit person to describe them on that account. I am threatened if I fail to exert myself in the manner required, with consequences which I cannot so much as think of without perfect prostration. There is really no need to threaten me. Shattered by my miserable health and my family troubles, I am incapable of resistance. If you insist, you take your unjust advantage of me, and I give way immediately. I will endeavour to remember what I can (under protest), and to write what I can (also under protest), and what I can’t remember and can’t write, Louis must remember and write for me. He is an ass, and I am an invalid, and we are likely to make all sorts of mistakes between us. How humiliating!
paragraphsZh: 在日记的下一页，又出现了一则条目。它是用一位男性的笔迹写成的，字迹大、粗、规整，日期是“6月21日”。内容包括以下几行——]
我们出色的哈尔科姆小姐的病情给了我享受意外智力乐趣的机会。
这里有数百页。我可以将手放在胸口，宣称每一页都让我着迷、振奋、愉悦。

是的！这些页真是太精彩了。我在这里发现的机智、审慎、罕见的勇气、惊人的记忆力、对性格的精准观察、流畅优雅的文风以及迷人的女性情感迸发，无一不无限地增加了我对这位崇高生灵、这位宏伟的玛丽安的敬佩。我对自己性格的描写极其出色。我全心全意地证明这幅肖像的忠实度。我感受到，为了如此生动、如此丰富、如此厚重的色彩所描绘，我一定留下了多么深刻的印象。我再次哀叹那残酷的必要性，它使我们的利益产生冲突，并将我们置于对立面。在更幸福的环境下，我将是多么配得上哈尔科姆小姐——哈尔科姆小姐也将是多么配得上我。
激励我内心的情感使我确信，我刚刚写下的这些文字表达了一个深刻的真理。
这些情感使我凌驾于所有仅仅个人的考虑之上。我以最无私的方式见证了这位无与伦比的女性通过巧妙的策略意外得知我与珀西瓦尔的私人会面——也见证了她对整个对话从开始到结束的惊人准确的报告。
这些情感促使我向那位对她毫无感应的医生提供我广博的化学知识，以及我对医学和磁学科学为人类提供的更微妙手段的卓越经验。他迄今为止拒绝利用我的帮助。这可怜的人！
最后，这些情感决定了这些行——感激、同情、父性的行——出现在这个地方。我合上书。由于我对礼节的严格要求，它（在我妻子的手中）被恢复到作家的桌子上。事件正催促着我离开。环境正在引导我处理严肃的问题。成功的广大前景在我眼前展开。我以一种对自己来说可怕的平静完成我的命运。除了我钦佩的敬意，没有什么是属于我自己的。我怀着尊敬的柔情将它献于哈尔科姆小姐脚下。
我为她为妹妹所制定的每一个计划终将失败而表示哀悼。与此同时，我恳求她相信，我从她的日记中获得的信息在任何方面都不会帮助我促成这种失败。它只是确认了我先前已经安排好的行为计划。我必须感谢这些页面，它唤醒了我性情中最细腻的感受——仅此而已。
为什么——我问每个人——为什么要烦我？没有人回答这个问题，也没有人让我安宁。亲戚、朋友和陌生人都联合起来惹恼我。我做了什么？我问自己，我每天问我的仆人路易斯五十次——我做了什么？我们都说不清。非常奇怪！

最近困扰我的最后一件烦恼是被要求去写这篇叙述。我一个处在神经衰弱状态的人，能写得出叙述吗？当我提出这个极为合理的反对意见时，人们告诉我，我的侄女经历了一些非常严重的事件，而正因为如此，我才是适合去描述这些事件的人。如果我未能以要求的方式努力，人们还威胁说会有一些后果，这些后果一想到就让我完全崩溃。实际上根本没有必要威胁我。在可怜的健康状况和家庭烦恼的摧残下，我已经无力反抗。如果你坚持，你就是在不公正地占我便宜，而我会立即让步。我会努力记住我能记住的东西（虽心存抗议），并写下我能写的东西（同样心存抗议），而那些我既记不住也写不下的，必须由路易斯替我记住并写下。他是个笨蛋，我是个病人，我们之间很可能会犯各种各样的错误。多么令人羞愧啊！

title: The Woman in White · 选段 8
author: Wilkie Collins
paragraphs: As early as the end of October the daily course of our lives had assumed its settled direction, and we three were as completely isolated in our place of concealment as if the house we lived in had been a desert island, and the great network of streets and the thousands of our fellow-creatures all round us the waters of an illimitable sea. I could now reckon on some leisure time for considering what my future plan of action should be, and how I might arm myself most securely at the outset for the coming struggle with Sir Percival and the Count.

I gave up all hope of appealing to my recognition of Laura, or to Marian’s recognition of her, in proof of her identity. If we had loved her less dearly, if the instinct implanted in us by that love had not been far more certain than any exercise of reasoning, far keener than any process of observation, even we might have hesitated on first seeing her.

The outward changes wrought by the suffering and the terror of the past had fearfully, almost hopelessly, strengthened the fatal resemblance between Anne Catherick and herself. In my narrative of events at the time of my residence in Limmeridge House, I have recorded, from my own observation of the two, how the likeness, striking as it was when viewed generally, failed in many important points of similarity when tested in detail. In those former days, if they had both been seen together side by side, no person could for a moment have mistaken them one for the other—as has happened often in the instances of twins. I could not say this now. The sorrow and suffering which I had once blamed myself for associating even by a passing thought with the future of Laura Fairlie, HAD set their profaning marks on the youth and beauty of her face; and the fatal resemblance which I had once seen and shuddered at seeing, in idea only, was now a real and living resemblance which asserted itself before my own eyes. Strangers, acquaintances, friends even who could not look at her as we looked, if she had been shown to them in the first days of her rescue from the Asylum, might have doubted if she were the Laura Fairlie they had once seen, and doubted without blame.

The one remaining chance, which I had at first thought might be trusted to serve us—the chance of appealing to her recollection of persons and events with which no impostor could be familiar, was proved, by the sad test of our later experience, to be hopeless. Every little caution that Marian and I practised towards her—every little remedy we tried, to strengthen and steady slowly the weakened, shaken faculties, was a fresh protest in itself against the risk of turning her mind back on the troubled and the terrible past.

The only events of former days which we ventured on encouraging her to recall were the little trivial domestic events of that happy time at Limmeridge, when I first went there and taught her to draw. The day when I roused those remembrances by showing her the sketch of the summer-house which she had given me on the morning of our farewell, and which had never been separated from me since, was the birthday of our first hope. Tenderly and gradually, the memory of the old walks and drives dawned upon her, and the poor weary pining eyes looked at Marian and at me with a new interest, with a faltering thoughtfulness in them, which from that moment we cherished and kept alive. I bought her a little box of colours, and a sketch-book like the old sketch-book which I had seen in her hands on the morning that we first met. Once again—oh me, once again!—at spare hours saved from my work, in the dull London light, in the poor London room, I sat by her side to guide the faltering touch, to help the feeble hand. Day by day I raised and raised the new interest till its place in the blank of her existence was at last assured—till she could think of her drawing and talk of it, and patiently practise it by herself, with some faint reflection of the innocent pleasure in my encouragement, the growing enjoyment in her own progress, which belonged to the lost life and the lost happiness of past days.
paragraphsZh: 早在十月底，我们日常生活的日程就已经固定下来，我们三人被完全隔离在藏身之处，就好像我们居住的房子是一座荒岛，而周围那纵横交错的街道和成千上万的同类仿佛是无边大海的水面。我现在可以预料有一些闲暇时间来思考未来的行动计划，以及如何在一开始就最安全地为即将到来的与珀西瓦尔爵士和伯爵的斗争做好准备。
我彻底放弃了通过我对劳拉的认知，或通过玛丽安对她的认知，来证明她身份的希望。如果我们对她的爱没有那么深厚，如果那种由爱所植入我们的直觉没有比任何推理更可靠，比任何观察过程更敏锐，即便是我们，在第一次见到她时也可能会犹豫。

过去的痛苦和恐惧带来的外在变化令人惊恐，几乎使人绝望地加强了安妮·凯瑟里克和她自己之间的致命相似。在我叙述我居住在利默里奇庄园时的事件中，我已经根据自己对两人的观察记录了这一点：这种相似性虽然在总体上令人震惊，但在细节上进行考察时，却在许多重要的地方不一致。在那些日子里，如果她们两人并肩而立，没有人会片刻间将她们错认——这在双胞胎的案例中经常发生。但我现在不能这样说了。我曾因为自己甚至只是偶尔地将悲伤和痛苦与劳拉·费尔利的未来联系在一起而自责，而这些悲伤和痛苦已经在她的面庞上留下了亵渎的痕迹，破坏了她的青春与美貌；我曾经在脑海中看到并因而战栗的那种致命的相似，如今已成为真实而生动的相似，直接展现在我眼前。陌生人、熟人，甚至朋友，如果在她从庇护所获救的最初几天被带去看她，而不能像我们一样看待她，可能会怀疑她是否真的是曾经见过的劳拉·费尔利，这种怀疑也无可非议。
唯一剩下的机会——我最初曾认为可以依赖它来帮助我们——即借助她对那些没有冒名者可能熟悉的人物和事件的记忆，但经过我们后来的悲惨经历，这一机会被证明是无望的。我们对她采取的每一点小心谨慎——我们尝试的每一种小小方法，旨在慢慢增强和稳定她那受损、动摇的心智——本身都是对让她的思绪回到那些动荡而可怕的过去的风险的一种新的抗议。

我们唯一敢于让她回忆起的往昔事件，是那段在利默里奇幸福时光里的一些琐碎的家务小事，那时我第一次去那里，并教她画画。那一天，我通过展示她在我们告别的早晨送给我的凉亭素描图唤起了这些回忆，而这幅画自那以后从未离开过我，那一天便成为我们第一份希望的生日。她温柔而逐渐地回想起那些旧日的散步和车游，疲惫而渴望的眼睛以全新的兴趣看向玛丽安和我，眼中流露出犹豫的思绪，从那一刻起，我们珍视并使之持续存在。我给她买了一小盒颜料和一本素描本，和我们初次见面那个早晨我曾见她手中的旧素描本类似。再一次——哦，我啊，再一次！——在从工作中节省出来的闲暇时间里，在伦敦那昏暗的光线下，在那贫乏的伦敦房间里，我坐在她身旁，指导她踉跄的触感，帮助她那无力的手。日复一日，我不断提高新的兴趣，直到它在她生活的空白中终于得以确立——直到她能够思考她的绘画并谈论它，并耐心地独自练习它，带着对我鼓励中纯真乐趣的微弱回忆，对自己进步中逐渐增长的享受，那些属于过去失去的生活和失去的幸福。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 4
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: By this curious turn of disposition I have gained the reputation of deliberate heartlessness; how undeserved, I alone can appreciate.

I took a seat at the end of the hearthstone opposite that towards which my landlord advanced, and filled up an interval of silence by attempting to caress the canine mother, who had left her nursery, and was sneaking wolfishly to the back of my legs, her lip curled up, and her white teeth watering for a snatch. My caress provoked a long, guttural gnarl.

“You’d better let the dog alone,” growled Mr. Heathcliff in unison, checking fiercer demonstrations with a punch of his foot. “She’s not accustomed to be spoiled—not kept for a pet.” Then, striding to a side door, he shouted again, “Joseph!”

Joseph mumbled indistinctly in the depths of the cellar, but gave no intimation of ascending; so his master dived down to him, leaving me vis-à-vis the ruffianly bitch and a pair of grim shaggy sheep-dogs, who shared with her a jealous guardianship over all my movements. Not anxious to come in contact with their fangs, I sat still; but, imagining they would scarcely understand tacit insults, I unfortunately indulged in winking and making faces at the trio, and some turn of my physiognomy so irritated madam, that she suddenly broke into a fury and leapt on my knees. I flung her back, and hastened to interpose the table between us. This proceeding aroused the whole hive: half-a-dozen four-footed fiends, of various sizes and ages, issued from hidden dens to the common centre. I felt my heels and coat-laps peculiar subjects of assault; and parrying off the larger combatants as effectually as I could with the poker, I was constrained to demand, aloud, assistance from some of the household in re-establishing peace.

Mr. Heathcliff and his man climbed the cellar steps with vexatious phlegm: I don’t think they moved one second faster than usual, though the hearth was an absolute tempest of worrying and yelping. Happily, an inhabitant of the kitchen made more dispatch; a lusty dame, with tucked-up gown, bare arms, and fire-flushed cheeks, rushed into the midst of us flourishing a frying-pan: and used that weapon, and her tongue, to such purpose, that the storm subsided magically, and she only remained, heaving like a sea after a high wind, when her master entered on the scene.
“What the devil is the matter?” he asked, eyeing me in a manner that I could ill endure after this inhospitable treatment.

“What the devil, indeed!” I muttered. “The herd of possessed swine could have had no worse spirits in them than those animals of yours, sir. You might as well leave a stranger with a brood of tigers!”
“They won’t meddle with persons who touch nothing,” he remarked, putting the bottle before me, and restoring the displaced table. “The dogs do right to be vigilant. Take a glass of wine?”
“If I had been, I would have set my signet on the biter.” Heathcliff’s countenance relaxed into a grin.

“Come, come,” he said, “you are flurried, Mr. Lockwood. Here, take a little wine. Guests are so exceedingly rare in this house that I and my dogs, I am willing to own, hardly know how to receive them. Your health, sir?”

I bowed and returned the pledge; beginning to perceive that it would be foolish to sit sulking for the misbehaviour of a pack of curs; besides, I felt loth to yield the fellow further amusement at my expense; since his humour took that turn. He—probably swayed by prudential consideration of the folly of offending a good tenant—relaxed a little in the laconic style of chipping off his pronouns and auxiliary verbs, and introduced what he supposed would be a subject of interest to me,—a discourse on the advantages and disadvantages of my present place of retirement. I found him very intelligent on the topics we touched; and before I went home, I was encouraged so far as to volunteer another visit to-morrow. He evidently wished no repetition of my intrusion. I shall go, notwithstanding. It is astonishing how sociable I feel myself compared with him.
paragraphsZh: 由于这种奇特的性情转变，我获得了冷酷无情的名声；这种名声多么不应得，只有我自己能体会。
我在壁炉石的尽头坐下，面对我的房东走来的方向，用试图抚摸那只离开了产床、偷偷溜到我腿后面、嘴唇上翻、白牙垂涎欲咬的小母犬来打发沉默的间隔。我的抚摸引发了一声长长的、喉间的低吼。
“你最好别去打扰那条狗，”希斯克利夫先生同时咆哮道，用脚一踢制止它更激烈的表现，“她不习惯被宠爱——不是供人当宠物养的。” 然后，他大步走到旁边的一扇门前，又喊道：“约瑟夫！”

约瑟夫在地窖深处含糊地嘀咕着，但没有露出要上来的迹象；于是他的主人潜入地下找他，留下我面对那只凶恶的母狗和一对阴森的长毛牧羊犬，它们与她一起对我的一举一动保持着嫉妒般的守护。我不想与它们的獠牙接触，于是静静坐着；但是，想着它们大概难以理解无声的侮辱，我不幸地对这三只动物眨眼和做怪相，结果我面部表情的某个动作惹怒了这位女士，她突然大发狂怒，跳到我膝上。我把她甩开，并迅速把桌子挡在我们之间。这一举动惊动了整个群体：半打各种大小、年龄的四足恶魔从隐藏的巢穴里冲向了公共中心。我觉得我的脚跟和大衣襟是奇怪的攻击对象；尽我所能用火钳挡开那些更大的攻击者后，我不得不大声向屋里的一些人请求帮助，以重新恢复和平。
希思克利夫先生和他的仆人带着恼人的冷漠爬上地窖的台阶：我不认为他们比平时快了一秒，虽然壁炉旁简直是一场令人焦躁和叫嚷的风暴。幸运的是，厨房的一位住户动作更快；一位健壮的妇人，卷起的裙子，赤裸的手臂，脸颊被火光映红，冲到我们中间，挥舞着一个煎锅：她用那武器和她的舌头干得如此有效，风暴神奇地平息了，只剩下她一人，像大风过后的海洋般起伏，当她的主人登场时仍气喘吁吁。
“到底出了什么事？”他问道，用一种我在经历了如此不友好的对待后难以忍受的目光看着我。
“见鬼了，的确如此！”我喃喃说道。“那群被附身的猪群，也不可能比您这些动物更邪恶了，先生。您倒不如把一个陌生人留给一窝老虎！”
“他们不会干涉那些什么都不碰的人，”他评论道，把酒瓶放到我面前，并把移开的桌子放回原处。“这些狗警惕是对的。来杯葡萄酒吗？”
“如果我早知道，我就会在咬人的地方盖上我的印章。” 希斯克利夫的表情放松，露出了笑容。
“来，来，”他说，“你太慌张了，洛克伍德先生。来，喝点酒。在这屋子里客人实在是太少了，我得承认，我和我的狗几乎不知道该如何招待他们。您的健康，先生？”

我鞠了一躬，并归还了誓言；开始意识到，仅仅因为一群杂狗的恶行而生闷气是愚蠢的；此外，我也不愿再让那家伙从我的不快中获得更多乐趣；既然他的情绪朝那个方向发展。他——可能出于对得罪一个好房客的愚蠢行为的审慎考虑——在削减人称代词和助动词的简短风格上稍微放松了一点，并引入了他认为会引起我兴趣的话题——关于我目前隐退之地的利弊的讨论。我发现我们触及的话题上他非常聪明；在我回家之前，我甚至被鼓励，主动提出明天再来拜访。他显然不希望我重复打扰。不过，我还是会去。与他相比，我感到自己社交能力如此之强，真是令人惊讶。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 5
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: Mrs. Dean raised the candle, and I discerned a soft-featured face, exceedingly resembling the young lady at the Heights, but more pensive and amiable in expression. It formed a sweet picture. The long light hair curled slightly on the temples; the eyes were large and serious; the figure almost too graceful. I did not marvel how Catherine Earnshaw could forget her first friend for such an individual. I marvelled much how he, with a mind to correspond with his person, could fancy my idea of Catherine Earnshaw.

Catherine had kept up her acquaintance with the Lintons since her five-weeks’ residence among them; and as she had no temptation to show her rough side in their company, and had the sense to be ashamed of being rude where she experienced such invariable courtesy, she imposed unwittingly on the old lady and gentleman by her ingenious cordiality; gained the admiration of Isabella, and the heart and soul of her brother: acquisitions that flattered her from the first—for she was full of ambition—and led her to adopt a double character without exactly intending to deceive any one. In the place where she heard Heathcliff termed a “vulgar young ruffian,” and “worse than a brute,” she took care not to act like him; but at home she had small inclination to practise politeness that would only be laughed at, and restrain an unruly nature when it would bring her neither credit nor praise.

Mr. Edgar seldom mustered courage to visit Wuthering Heights openly. He had a terror of Earnshaw’s reputation, and shrunk from encountering him; and yet he was always received with our best attempts at civility: the master himself avoided offending him, knowing why he came; and if he could not be gracious, kept out of the way. I rather think his appearance there was distasteful to Catherine; she was not artful, never played the coquette, and had evidently an objection to her two friends meeting at all; for when Heathcliff expressed contempt of Linton in his presence, she could not half coincide, as she did in his absence; and when Linton evinced disgust and antipathy to Heathcliff, she dared not treat his sentiments with indifference, as if depreciation of her playmate were of scarcely any consequence to her. I’ve had many a laugh at her perplexities and untold troubles, which she vainly strove to hide from my mockery. That sounds ill-natured: but she was so proud, it became really impossible to pity her distresses, till she should be chastened into more humility. She did bring herself, finally, to confess, and to confide in me: there was not a soul else that she might fashion into an adviser.

Mr. Hindley had gone from home one afternoon, and Heathcliff presumed to give himself a holiday on the strength of it. He had reached the age of sixteen then, I think, and without having bad features, or being deficient in intellect, he contrived to convey an impression of inward and outward repulsiveness that his present aspect retains no traces of. In the first place, he had by that time lost the benefit of his early education: continual hard work, begun soon and concluded late, had extinguished any curiosity he once possessed in pursuit of knowledge, and any love for books or learning. His childhood’s sense of superiority, instilled into him by the favours of old Mr. Earnshaw, was faded away. He struggled long to keep up an equality with Catherine in her studies, and yielded with poignant though silent regret: but he yielded completely; and there was no prevailing on him to take a step in the way of moving upward, when he found he must, necessarily, sink beneath his former level. Then personal appearance sympathised with mental deterioration: he acquired a slouching gait and ignoble look; his naturally reserved disposition was exaggerated into an almost idiotic excess of unsociable moroseness; and he took a grim pleasure, apparently, in exciting the aversion rather than the esteem of his few acquaintance.
paragraphsZh: 迪恩夫人抬起烛灯，我看清了一张面容柔和的脸，非常像海茨庄园的那位小姐，但表情更显沉思与和善。这构成了一幅可爱的画面。长而浅色的头发在太阳穴处微微卷曲；眼睛又大又深沉；身姿几近优雅得过分。我并不奇怪凯瑟琳·恩肖会为了这样的人而忘记她的第一个朋友。我倒是非常奇怪，他明明有意与自身相符，却能相信我对凯瑟琳·恩肖的想法。

凯瑟琳自从在林顿家住了五周以来，一直保持着与他们的交往；由于在他们的陪伴下她没有展示自己粗鲁一面的诱惑，并且也明白在受到如此一贯礼遇的场合下感到粗鲁是可耻的，她以巧妙而热情的态度无意中让老夫人和绅士产生好感；赢得了伊莎贝拉的钦佩，以及她兄弟的心灵和灵魂：这些收获从一开始就让她感到自豪——因为她充满了野心——并促使她采取双重性格，尽管并不完全打算欺骗任何人。在她听到希斯克利夫被称为“粗俗的年轻无赖”和“比野兽还坏”的地方，她小心翼翼地不去像他那样行事；但在家里，她几乎没有兴趣去练习那些只会被嘲笑的礼貌，也没有兴趣约束那种不会给她带来任何荣誉或赞扬的任性性格。

埃德加先生很少鼓起勇气公开拜访呼啸山庄。他非常害怕恩肖的名声，也畏惧与他相遇；然而，他总是受到我们尽力而为的礼貌接待：主人本人避免冒犯他，因为他知道他来访的原因；如果不能表现得亲切，也总是尽量避开。我倒觉得他出现在那里让凯瑟琳感觉不快；她并不善于心机，从不卖弄风情，而且明显不希望她的两个朋友见面；因为当希斯克利夫在他面前表示对林顿的轻蔑时，她不能像他不在场时那样完全认同；而当林顿表露出对希斯克利夫的厌恶和反感时，她也不敢对他的感受置之不理，好像贬低她的玩伴对她毫无关系一样。我曾对她的困惑和无数的烦恼发过很多次笑，她徒劳地试图掩盖，以躲避我的嘲笑。听起来很刻薄：但她太自负了，以至于真的无法同情她的苦难，直到她被磨炼成更谦逊的人。最终，她确实使自己坦白，并向我倾诉：没有其他人可以成为她的顾问。

欣德利先生有一天下午外出，而希斯克利夫便擅自认为自己可以借此机会休假。我想那时他已经十六岁了，他虽没有丑陋的外貌，也不缺智力，却设法给人一种内外皆令人厌恶的印象，而他现在的外貌已不再带有这种印象。首先，那时他已经失去了早期教育的益处：从小开始并一直到很晚的持续繁重劳动，消灭了他曾经追求知识的好奇心，也消灭了他对书籍或学习的热爱。他童年时期因老欧恩肖先生的宠爱而形成的优越感，也已经消退了。他努力很久才勉强在学业上与凯瑟琳保持平等，并怀着深切却无声的遗憾屈服了：但他完全屈服了；当他发现自己必然会落到从前的水平之下时，没有人能说服他采取任何向上进步的举措。然后，个人外貌也与精神衰退相呼应：他养成了垂头丧气的步态和卑劣的外表；他本来性格内向的特点被夸大成几乎愚蠢的极端孤僻；显然，他在激起少数熟人反感而非尊重方面，感到某种冷峻的乐趣。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 6
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: “It’s a nice place for a young man to fix his dwelling in!” said I. “Have you no fear of the consequences, Mrs. Linton?”

“None for my friend,” she replied: “his strong head will keep him from danger; a little for Hindley: but he can’t be made morally worse than he is; and I stand between him and bodily harm. The event of this evening has reconciled me to God and humanity! I had risen in angry rebellion against Providence. Oh, I’ve endured very, very bitter misery, Nelly! If that creature knew how bitter, he’d be ashamed to cloud its removal with idle petulance. It was kindness for him which induced me to bear it alone: had I expressed the agony I frequently felt, he would have been taught to long for its alleviation as ardently as I. However, it’s over, and I’ll take no revenge on his folly; I can afford to suffer anything hereafter! Should the meanest thing alive slap me on the cheek, I’d not only turn the other, but I’d ask pardon for provoking it; and, as a proof, I’ll go make my peace with Edgar instantly. Good-night! I’m an angel!”

In this self-complacent conviction she departed; and the success of her fulfilled resolution was obvious on the morrow: Mr. Linton had not only abjured his peevishness (though his spirits seemed still subdued by Catherine’s exuberance of vivacity), but he ventured no objection to her taking Isabella with her to Wuthering Heights in the afternoon; and she rewarded him with such a summer of sweetness and affection in return as made the house a paradise for several days; both master and servants profiting from the perpetual sunshine.

Heathcliff—Mr. Heathcliff I should say in future—used the liberty of visiting at Thrushcross Grange cautiously, at first: he seemed estimating how far its owner would bear his intrusion. Catherine, also, deemed it judicious to moderate her expressions of pleasure in receiving him; and he gradually established his right to be expected. He retained a great deal of the reserve for which his boyhood was remarkable; and that served to repress all startling demonstrations of feeling. My master’s uneasiness experienced a lull, and further circumstances diverted it into another channel for a space.

His new source of trouble sprang from the not anticipated misfortune of Isabella Linton evincing a sudden and irresistible attraction towards the tolerated guest. She was at that time a charming young lady of eighteen; infantile in manners, though possessed of keen wit, keen feelings, and a keen temper, too, if irritated. Her brother, who loved her tenderly, was appalled at this fantastic preference. Leaving aside the degradation of an alliance with a nameless man, and the possible fact that his property, in default of heirs male, might pass into such a one’s power, he had sense to comprehend Heathcliff’s disposition: to know that, though his exterior was altered, his mind was unchangeable and unchanged. And he dreaded that mind: it revolted him: he shrank forebodingly from the idea of committing Isabella to its keeping. He would have recoiled still more had he been aware that her attachment rose unsolicited, and was bestowed where it awakened no reciprocation of sentiment; for the minute he discovered its existence he laid the blame on Heathcliff’s deliberate designing.

We had all remarked, during some time, that Miss Linton fretted and pined over something. She grew cross and wearisome; snapping at and teasing Catherine continually, at the imminent risk of exhausting her limited patience. We excused her, to a certain extent, on the plea of ill-health: she was dwindling and fading before our eyes. But one day, when she had been peculiarly wayward, rejecting her breakfast, complaining that the servants did not do what she told them; that the mistress would allow her to be nothing in the house, and Edgar neglected her; that she had caught a cold with the doors being left open, and we let the parlour fire go out on purpose to vex her, with a hundred yet more frivolous accusations, Mrs. Linton peremptorily insisted that she should get to bed; and, having scolded her heartily, threatened to send for the doctor. Mention of Kenneth caused her to exclaim, instantly, that her health was perfect, and it was only Catherine’s harshness which made her unhappy.
paragraphsZh: “这是年轻人安顿住处的好地方！”我说。“林顿太太，您不担心后果吗？”

“我的朋友不需要，”她回答道：“他那坚强的头脑会护他免于危险；给欣德利一点，但他不会比现在道德上更糟；我站在他和身体伤害之间。今晚的事件使我与上帝和人类和解了！我曾对天意发怒反抗。哦，我忍受过非常非常痛苦的苦难，内莉！如果那家伙知道这种痛苦有多深，他会因用无谓的任性来遮掩它而感到羞愧。正是出于对他的善意，我才独自承受；如果我表达我时常感受到的痛苦，他也会同样渴望减轻它。然而，现在一切都过去了，我不会对他的愚行进行报复；以后我能承受任何苦难！”如果世上最卑劣的东西打我的脸，我不仅会转过另一边，还会为激怒它而道歉；作为证明，我现在就去和埃德加和解。晚安！我就是天使！”
带着这种自满的信念，她离开了；而她坚定决心的成功在第二天显而易见：林顿先生不仅放弃了脾气坏的态度（尽管凯瑟琳的活力仍然让他的情绪显得低落），而且也没有反对她下午带伊莎贝拉去呼啸山庄；她以一整个夏天般的甜蜜和爱意回报他，使这座房子几天内都像乐园一样；主人和仆人们都因这持续的阳光受益。
希斯克利夫——我以后应该称他为希斯克利夫先生——最初小心翼翼地利用机会拜访了瑟斯克罗斯庄园：他似乎在衡量庄园主人能忍受他到访的程度。凯瑟琳也认为在接待他时适度表达欣喜是明智的；然后他逐渐建立了自己应受期待的权利。他保留了很多少年时期的矜持；这抑制了所有令人吃惊的情感表现。我的主人感到焦虑的心情暂时平息了，随后又因其他事情转移到另一个方向，有一段时间缓解了压力。

他的新麻烦源于他没有预料到的伊莎贝拉·林顿的不幸——她对那个被容忍的客人产生了突如其来的不可抗拒的吸引力。当时她是一个十八岁的迷人少女；举止稚嫩，但拥有敏锐的机智、敏锐的情感，如果被激怒，也有敏锐的脾气。她的兄长深深爱她，对于这种奇异的偏爱感到震惊。撇开与一个无名男子结盟的耻辱不谈，以及如果没有男性继承人，他的财产可能落入那个人手中的可能性，他还是有头脑能够理解希斯克利夫的性格：他知道，尽管外表有所改变，他的心智是不可改变且未曾改变的。他害怕那种心智：它让他感到厌恶：想到要把伊莎贝拉交给它，他预感中就感到退缩。如果他意识到她的依恋是自发的，而付出的位置却没有唤起任何回报的感情，他本会更加退缩；因为他一旦发现这种依恋的存在，就把责任归咎于希斯克利夫的故意算计。

我们早就注意到，莱顿小姐总是为某事焦躁和憔悴。她变得易怒且令人厌烦，不停地对凯瑟琳发火和戏弄她，几乎到了耗尽她有限耐性的程度。我们在一定程度上原谅她，以她身体不适为理由：她在我们眼前日渐消瘦、憔悴。然而有一天，她特别任性，不吃早餐，抱怨仆人没有按她的吩咐办事；抱怨女主人不允许她在家里有任何权力，且埃德加忽视她；抱怨因为门没关好而感冒，我们故意让客厅火熄，以惹她生气，还有更多无关紧要的指控，夫人。林顿断然坚持她应该上床睡觉；在狠狠地训斥她之后，还威胁要去叫医生。提到肯尼斯时，她立刻喊道，她的健康状况完全良好，只有凯瑟琳的苛刻让她感到不快。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 7
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: I wrung my hands, and cried out; and Mr. Linton hastened his step at the noise. In the midst of my agitation, I was sincerely glad to observe that Catherine’s arms had fallen relaxed, and her head hung down.
“She’s fainted, or dead,” I thought: “so much the better. Far better that she should be dead, than lingering a burden and a misery-maker to all about her.”

Edgar sprang to his unbidden guest, blanched with astonishment and rage. What he meant to do I cannot tell; however, the other stopped all demonstrations, at once, by placing the lifeless-looking form in his arms.

He walked into the parlour, and sat down. Mr. Linton summoned me, and with great difficulty, and after resorting to many means, we managed to restore her to sensation; but she was all bewildered; she sighed, and moaned, and knew nobody. Edgar, in his anxiety for her, forgot her hated friend. I did not. I went, at the earliest opportunity, and besought him to depart; affirming that Catherine was better, and he should hear from me in the morning how she passed the night.

“I shall not refuse to go out of doors,” he answered; “but I shall stay in the garden: and, Nelly, mind you keep your word to-morrow. I shall be under those larch-trees. Mind! or I pay another visit, whether Linton be in or not.”
He sent a rapid glance through the half-open door of the chamber, and, ascertaining that what I stated was apparently true, delivered the house of his luckless presence.

About twelve o’clock that night was born the Catherine you saw at Wuthering Heights: a puny, seven-months’ child; and two hours after the mother died, having never recovered sufficient consciousness to miss Heathcliff, or know Edgar. The latter’s distraction at his bereavement is a subject too painful to be dwelt on; its after-effects showed how deep the sorrow sunk. A great addition, in my eyes, was his being left without an heir. I bemoaned that, as I gazed on the feeble orphan; and I mentally abused old Linton for (what was only natural partiality) the securing his estate to his own daughter, instead of his son’s. An unwelcomed infant it was, poor thing! It might have wailed out of life, and nobody cared a morsel, during those first hours of existence. We redeemed the neglect afterwards; but its beginning was as friendless as its end is likely to be.

Next morning—bright and cheerful out of doors—stole softened in through the blinds of the silent room, and suffused the couch and its occupant with a mellow, tender glow. Edgar Linton had his head laid on the pillow, and his eyes shut. His young and fair features were almost as deathlike as those of the form beside him, and almost as fixed: but his was the hush of exhausted anguish, and hers of perfect peace. Her brow smooth, her lids closed, her lips wearing the expression of a smile; no angel in heaven could be more beautiful than she appeared. And I partook of the infinite calm in which she lay: my mind was never in a holier frame than while I gazed on that untroubled image of Divine rest. I instinctively echoed the words she had uttered a few hours before: “Incomparably beyond and above us all! Whether still on earth or now in heaven, her spirit is at home with God!”

I don’t know if it be a peculiarity in me, but I am seldom otherwise than happy while watching in the chamber of death, should no frenzied or despairing mourner share the duty with me. I see a repose that neither earth nor hell can break, and I feel an assurance of the endless and shadowless hereafter—the Eternity they have entered—where life is boundless in its duration, and love in its sympathy, and joy in its fulness. I noticed on that occasion how much selfishness there is even in a love like Mr. Linton’s, when he so regretted Catherine’s blessed release! To be sure, one might have doubted, after the wayward and impatient existence she had led, whether she merited a haven of peace at last. One might doubt in seasons of cold reflection; but not then, in the presence of her corpse. It asserted its own tranquillity, which seemed a pledge of equal quiet to its former inhabitant.
paragraphsZh: 我扭动着双手，喊了出来；林顿先生听到声音，快步走了过来。在我激动不安之中，我真心感到高兴，看到凯瑟琳的手臂松了下来，头垂了下去。
“她晕倒了，或者死了，”我心想：“那就好。她死比活着拖累和折磨周围的人要好得多。”
埃德加跳向这位不请自来的客人，脸色因震惊和愤怒而变得苍白。我无法确定他打算做什么；然而，对方立刻停止了一切动作，把那副看似无生命的身体抱在怀里。
他走进客厅，坐了下来。林顿先生叫我去，经过极大的努力，并采取许多方法，我们终于让她恢复了知觉；但她完全困惑不解；她叹息、呻吟，并不认识任何人。埃德加因担心她而忘记了她讨厌的朋友。我没有。我抓住最早的机会，去恳求他离开；并且确认凯瑟琳好多了，明天早晨他会从我这里听到她如何度过了夜晚的消息。
“我不会拒绝到户外去，”他回答道；“但我会留在花园里：内莉，你明天一定要守信用。我会在那些落叶松树下。记住！否则，无论林顿在不在，我都会再来一趟。”
他透过半开的房门迅速扫了一眼，并在确认我所说的显然是真的后，交出了他那不幸存在的房子。

那天夜里大约十二点，出生了你在《呼啸山庄》中见到的凯瑟琳：一个虚弱的，七个月大的孩子；母亲在两小时后去世，从未恢复足够的意识去想念希斯克利夫，也无法认出埃德加。他因丧母而感到的心神恍惚，是一个令人痛苦得无法细述的话题；其后遗症显示出悲痛沉得有多深。在我眼里，一个巨大的影响是他没有继承人。我凝视着这个孱弱的孤儿时，为此感到哀叹；并在心里责怪老林顿（那只是自然的偏心）把产业留给自己女儿，而不是儿子。那是个不受欢迎的婴儿，可怜的孩子！在生命的最初几个小时里，它可能哭喊着来到了人世，可没人丝毫关心。我们之后弥补了当初的疏忽；但它的开始是如此孤立无援，就像它的结局可能会一样。

第二天清晨——户外明亮欢快——透过寂静房间的百叶窗，柔和地洒进沙发和坐着的人，散发出柔和温柔的光辉。埃德加·林顿头枕头，闭着眼睛。他年轻而白皙的面容几乎和身旁的身影一样死气沉沉，几乎同样坚定：但他的却是疲惫痛苦的寂静，而她的则是完美的平静。她的眉头平静，眼皮紧闭，嘴唇带着微笑;天堂中没有天使比她看起来更美丽。我享受着她躺着时的无限宁静：当我凝视着那无忧无虑的神圣安息时，我的心灵从未处于如此神圣的境界。我本能地重复了几小时前她说过的话：“无与伦比，超越我们所有人！无论她仍在世上，还是如今在天上，她的灵魂都与上帝同在！”

我不知道这是否是我的一个特性，但在死亡的房间里观看时，我很少有不快乐的时候，只要没有狂乱或绝望的哀悼者与我一起承担这个责任。我看到一种既非世间也非地狱能打破的安宁，我感到对无尽且无影无踪的来世——他们已经进入的永恒——的一种确信，那里的生命在时间上无边无际，爱在同情上无尽，喜悦在充实上圆满。我在那次场合注意到，即使是像林顿先生那样的爱，也有多少自私，当他如此遗憾凯瑟琳的幸福解脱时！当然，在她那种任性而不耐烦的生活方式之后，人们可能会怀疑她是否最终配得上一个平静的港湾。在冷静反思的时刻人们或许会怀疑；但不是在那个时候，在她的尸体面前。它断言了自己的宁静，这似乎是对其前任居民同样安宁的保证。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 8
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: The boy was fully occupied with his own cogitations for the remainder of the ride, till we halted before the farmhouse garden-gate. I watched to catch his impressions in his countenance. He surveyed the carved front and low-browed lattices, the straggling gooseberry-bushes and crooked firs, with solemn intentness, and then shook his head: his private feelings entirely disapproved of the exterior of his new abode. But he had sense to postpone complaining: there might be compensation within. Before he dismounted, I went and opened the door. It was half-past six; the family had just finished breakfast: the servant was clearing and wiping down the table. Joseph stood by his master’s chair telling some tale concerning a lame horse; and Hareton was preparing for the hayfield.
“Hallo, Nelly!” said Mr. Heathcliff, when he saw me. “I feared I should have to come down and fetch my property myself. You’ve brought it, have you? Let us see what we can make of it.”
He got up and strode to the door: Hareton and Joseph followed in gaping curiosity. Poor Linton ran a frightened eye over the faces of the three.

“God! what a beauty! what a lovely, charming thing!” he exclaimed. “Hav’n’t they reared it on snails and sour milk, Nelly? Oh, damn my soul! but that’s worse than I expected—and the devil knows I was not sanguine!”

I bid the trembling and bewildered child get down, and enter. He did not thoroughly comprehend the meaning of his father’s speech, or whether it were intended for him: indeed, he was not yet certain that the grim, sneering stranger was his father. But he clung to me with growing trepidation; and on Mr. Heathcliff’s taking a seat and bidding him “come hither” he hid his face on my shoulder and wept.

“Tut, tut!” said Heathcliff, stretching out a hand and dragging him roughly between his knees, and then holding up his head by the chin. “None of that nonsense! We’re not going to hurt thee, Linton—isn’t that thy name? Thou art thy mother’s child, entirely! Where is my share in thee, puling chicken?”

He took off the boy’s cap and pushed back his thick flaxen curls, felt his slender arms and his small fingers; during which examination Linton ceased crying, and lifted his great blue eyes to inspect the inspector.
“Do you know me?” asked Heathcliff, having satisfied himself that the limbs were all equally frail and feeble.

“No! What a shame of your mother, never to waken your filial regard for me! You are my son, then, I’ll tell you; and your mother was a wicked slut to leave you in ignorance of the sort of father you possessed. Now, don’t wince, and colour up! Though it is something to see you have not white blood. Be a good lad; and I’ll do for you. Nelly, if you be tired you may sit down; if not, get home again. I guess you’ll report what you hear and see to the cipher at the Grange; and this thing won’t be settled while you linger about it.”
“Well,” replied I, “I hope you’ll be kind to the boy, Mr. Heathcliff, or you’ll not keep him long; and he’s all you have akin in the wide world, that you will ever know—remember.”

“I’ll be very kind to him, you needn’t fear,” he said, laughing. “Only nobody else must be kind to him: I’m jealous of monopolising his affection. And, to begin my kindness, Joseph, bring the lad some breakfast. Hareton, you infernal calf, begone to your work. Yes, Nell,” he added, when they had departed, “my son is prospective owner of your place, and I should not wish him to die till I was certain of being his successor. Besides, he’s mine, and I want the triumph of seeing my descendant fairly lord of their estates; my child hiring their children to till their fathers’ lands for wages. That is the sole consideration which can make me endure the whelp: I despise him for himself, and hate him for the memories he revives! But that consideration is sufficient: he’s as safe with me, and shall be tended as carefully as your master tends his own. I have a room upstairs, furnished for him in handsome style; I’ve engaged a tutor, also, to come three times a week, from twenty miles’ distance, to teach him what he pleases to learn. I’ve ordered Hareton to obey him: and in fact I’ve arranged everything with a view to preserve the superior and the gentleman in him, above his associates. I do regret, however, that he so little deserves the trouble: if I wished any blessing in the world, it was to find him a worthy object of pride; and I’m bitterly disappointed with the whey-faced, whining wretch!”
paragraphsZh: 男孩在剩下的行程中完全沉浸在自己的思考中，直到我们在农舍的花园门前停下。我观察他的面部表情，想捕捉他的感受。他庄重而专注地打量着雕花的正面和低矮的格子窗，以及参差不齐的醋栗丛和弯曲的杉树，然后摇了摇头：他内心完全不赞同新居的外观。但他有智慧推迟抱怨：可能里面会有补偿。在他下马之前，我走过去开了门。现在是六点半；家人刚吃完早餐；仆人在收拾并擦拭餐桌。约瑟夫站在主人的椅旁讲述一匹瘸马的故事；哈雷顿正在为干草地做准备。
“你好，奈莉！”希斯克利夫先生看到我时说道。“我还以为我得亲自下来取我的财产呢。你带来了，是吗？让我们看看能从中搞些什么。”
他站起来大步走向门口：哈雷顿和约瑟夫好奇地跟在后面张大了嘴。可怜的林顿害怕地扫视着三张脸。
“天啊！多美啊！多可爱、多迷人的东西！”他喊道。“他们难道是用蜗牛和酸奶养大的么，奈莉？哦，见鬼！这比我预期的还糟——我发誓我以前可没抱有什么乐观期待！”
我示意那颤抖而迷茫的孩子下去，进去。他并不完全理解他父亲的话语的意思，也不确定话语是不是针对他：事实上，他还不确定那个面带严肃、讥笑的陌生人是不是他的父亲。但他带着日益增长的恐惧紧紧抓住我；当希斯克利夫先生坐下并叫他“过来”时，他把脸埋在我的肩上哭了起来。
“嘘，嘘！”希斯克利夫说着，伸手粗暴地把他拉到自己膝盖之间，然后托住他的下巴抬起头。“别胡闹！我们不会伤害你，林顿——你名字是这个吧？你完全是你母亲的孩子！我在你身上有什么份额呢，这个爱哭的小鸡崽？”
他摘下男孩的帽子，拨开他浓密的亚麻色卷发，触了触他纤细的手臂和小手指；在这期间，林顿停止了哭泣，抬起他那双大大的蓝眼睛打量着检查者。
“你认识我吗？”希斯克利夫问道，在确认四肢同样纤弱无力之后。
“不！你母亲真可耻，从来没有唤起你对我的孝顺之心！你是我的儿子，我告诉你；而你母亲是个邪恶的荡妇，把你置于对你拥有怎样的父亲一无所知的境地。现在，别皱眉，脸色红起来！虽然能看出你血统中没有白人的成分还是件值得看的事。做个乖孩子，我会为你搞定的。奈莉，如果你累了可以坐下；如果不累，就回家去吧。我猜你会把所见所闻告诉庄园里的密探；在你绕来绕去之前，这件事是解决不了的。”
“嗯，”我回答道，“海斯克利夫先生，我希望你能对孩子好，否则你可保不长久；他是你在这个广阔世界里唯一的亲近的人——记住。”

“我会对他非常好，你不必害怕，”他说着笑了。“只是其他人不能对他好：我嫉妒独占他的感情。而且，为了开始我的慈爱，约瑟夫，给那孩子准备点早餐去。哈里顿，你这该死的小牛，快去干你的活吧。是的，内尔，”他们离开后，他补充道，“我的儿子将来是你家地产的继承人，我不希望他死去，直到我确定自己能成为他的继承人。此外，他是我的，我想要看到我的后代真正成为这些地产的主人；我孩子雇佣他们的孩子为工资耕种他们父亲的土地。这是唯一能够让我忍受那个小子的重要原因：我鄙视他本身，并且因为他唤醒的回忆而憎恨他！”但这一考虑已经足够：他在我这里很安全，并且将会得到像你的主人照顾自己一样细心的照料。我在楼上给他准备了一间房间，布置得很漂亮；我还请了一位家教，每周来三次，从二十英里外赶来，教他想学的东西。我已经命令哈里顿服从他：实际上，我安排的一切都是为了保持他身上优越和绅士的一面，高于他的同伴。不过，我确实为他如此不值得费心而感到遗憾：如果我希望世界上有什么祝福，那就是找到一个值得自豪的对象；而现在，我对这个面色苍白、爱哭的可怜虫感到深深失望！”

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 9
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: Cathy was a powerful ally at home; and between them they at length persuaded my master to acquiesce in their having a ride or a walk together about once a week, under my guardianship, and on the moors nearest the Grange: for June found him still declining. Though he had set aside yearly a portion of his income for my young lady’s fortune, he had a natural desire that she might retain—or at least return in a short time to—the house of her ancestors; and he considered her only prospect of doing that was by a union with his heir; he had no idea that the latter was failing almost as fast as himself; nor had any one, I believe: no doctor visited the Heights, and no one saw Master Heathcliff to make report of his condition among us. I, for my part, began to fancy my forebodings were false, and that he must be actually rallying, when he mentioned riding and walking on the moors, and seemed so earnest in pursuing his object. I could not picture a father treating a dying child as tyrannically and wickedly as I afterwards learned Heathcliff had treated him, to compel this apparent eagerness: his efforts redoubling the more imminently his avaricious and unfeeling plans were threatened with defeat by death.

Summer was already past its prime, when Edgar reluctantly yielded his assent to their entreaties, and Catherine and I set out on our first ride to join her cousin. It was a close, sultry day: devoid of sunshine, but with a sky too dappled and hazy to threaten rain: and our place of meeting had been fixed at the guide-stone, by the cross-roads. On arriving there, however, a little herd-boy, despatched as a messenger, told us that,—“Maister Linton wer just o’ this side th’ Heights: and he’d be mitch obleeged to us to gang on a bit further.”

But when we reached him, and that was scarcely a quarter of a mile from his own door, we found he had no horse; and we were forced to dismount, and leave ours to graze. He lay on the heath, awaiting our approach, and did not rise till we came within a few yards. Then he walked so feebly, and looked so pale, that I immediately exclaimed,—“Why, Master Heathcliff, you are not fit for enjoying a ramble this morning. How ill you do look!”

Catherine surveyed him with grief and astonishment: she changed the ejaculation of joy on her lips to one of alarm; and the congratulation on their long-postponed meeting to an anxious inquiry, whether he were worse than usual?

“No—better—better!” he panted, trembling, and retaining her hand as if he needed its support, while his large blue eyes wandered timidly over her; the hollowness round them transforming to haggard wildness the languid expression they once possessed.
“I’m tired,” he interrupted, hurriedly. “It is too hot for walking, let us rest here. And, in the morning, I often feel sick—papa says I grow so fast.”

“This is something like your paradise,” said she, making an effort at cheerfulness. “You recollect the two days we agreed to spend in the place and way each thought pleasantest? This is nearly yours, only there are clouds; but then they are so soft and mellow: it is nicer than sunshine. Next week, if you can, we’ll ride down to the Grange Park, and try mine.”

Linton did not appear to remember what she talked of; and he had evidently great difficulty in sustaining any kind of conversation. His lack of interest in the subjects she started, and his equal incapacity to contribute to her entertainment, were so obvious that she could not conceal her disappointment. An indefinite alteration had come over his whole person and manner. The pettishness that might be caressed into fondness, had yielded to a listless apathy; there was less of the peevish temper of a child which frets and teases on purpose to be soothed, and more of the self-absorbed moroseness of a confirmed invalid, repelling consolation, and ready to regard the good-humoured mirth of others as an insult. Catherine perceived, as well as I did, that he held it rather a punishment, than a gratification, to endure our company; and she made no scruple of proposing, presently, to depart. That proposal, unexpectedly, roused Linton from his lethargy, and threw him into a strange state of agitation. He glanced fearfully towards the Heights, begging she would remain another half-hour, at least.
paragraphsZh: 凯茜在家里是一个强大的盟友；在他们的共同努力下，他们最终说服了我的主人同意，让她们每周在我的看护下，在距离庄园最近的荒原上一起骑马或散步一次：因为六月的时候，他的健康依然在衰退。尽管他每年都会从收入中划出一部分作为我小姐的嫁妆，他仍然自然希望她能够保留——或者至少在短时间内回到——祖宅；而他认为她实现这一目标的唯一途径就是与他的继承人结婚；他没有意识到继承人的健康状况几乎和他自己一样在迅速恶化；我相信，也没有人知道：海茨没有医生上门，也没有人来看望希斯克利夫大师向我们汇报他的状况。就我而言，我开始觉得自己的预感是错误的，而且他提到在荒原上骑马和散步时，我认为他实际上一定是在恢复健康，并且他追求目标的神情显得如此认真。我无法想象有哪位父亲会像后来我了解到的希斯克利夫那样，残暴而邪恶地对待垂死的孩子，以迫使他表现出这种明显的急切：他的努力越发加倍，因为当贪婪而冷酷的计划面临死亡威胁而可能失败时，他愈发拼命。
夏天已经过了盛期，埃德加勉强同意了他们的请求，凯瑟琳和我便出发去参加她堂兄的聚会。这是一个闷热的日子：没有阳光，但天空斑驳而朦胧，不会下雨；我们的会面地点定在十字路口的导向石处。然而，到那里时，一个被派来传信的小牧童告诉我们——“林顿先生就在高地这边不远：如果我们能再走一段路，他会非常感激。”
但是当我们赶到他那里时，那距离他自家门口还不到四分之一英里，我们发现他没有马；我们不得不下马，让我们的马去吃草。他躺在荒地上，等待我们的靠近，直到我们走到几码之内他才站起来。然后他走得非常虚弱，面色又苍白，我立刻喊道——“哎呀，希斯克里夫先生，你今天早上可不适合散步啊。你看上去真是很虚弱！”
凯瑟琳既伤心又惊讶地打量着他：她嘴里的喜悦感叹变成了惊恐；对久违重逢的祝贺也变成了焦虑的询问，他是否比平时更糟糕？
“不——更好——更好！”他气喘吁吁地说，颤抖着，握着她的手，好像需要它的支撑，他那双大大的蓝眼睛畏缩地在她身上游移；眼周的凹陷使他原本慵懒的表情变得憔悴而狂乱。
“我累了，”他急切地插话道。“天气太热，不适合走路，我们在这里休息吧。早上我常常感到不适——爸爸说我长得太快了。”
“这有点像你的乐园，”她努力保持开心地说道。“你还记得我们约定花两天时间去那个地方，每个人按照自己最喜欢的方式去度过吗？这里几乎就是你的，只是有些云彩；但它们如此柔软而温暖：比阳光还要好。下周，如果你能去，我们会骑车到格兰奇公园，尝试我的乐园。”

林顿似乎不记得她谈论的内容；而且他显然很难维持任何形式的交谈。他对她提出的话题缺乏兴趣，以及同样不能为她提供娱乐的能力，都是如此明显，以至于她无法掩饰自己的失望。他的整个形象和举止发生了难以言喻的变化。那些可以被宠爱转化为亲昵的任性，已经让位于无精打采的冷淡；那种故意烦恼以求安慰的孩子般的脾气减少了，而更多的是长期患病者的自我封闭的阴郁，排斥安慰，并容易将他人的愉快欢笑视为侮辱。凯瑟琳和我一样察觉到，他把忍受我们的陪伴看作是一种惩罚，而非享受；她毫不犹豫地立即提出要离开。这个提议出乎意料地将林顿从昏睡中唤醒，把他陷入一种奇怪的激动状态。他带着恐惧的目光瞥向高地，恳求她至少再留下半个小时。

title: Wuthering Heights · 选段 10
author: Emily Brontë
paragraphs: “Quite sure,” replied his cousin. “Only Ellen and I were disputing concerning your health. Are you truly stronger, Linton, than when we separated in winter? If you be, I’m certain one thing is not stronger—your regard for me: speak,—are you?”
The tears gushed from Linton’s eyes as he answered, “Yes, yes, I am!” And, still under the spell of the imaginary voice, his gaze wandered up and down to detect its owner.

Cathy rose. “For to-day we must part,” she said. “And I won’t conceal that I have been sadly disappointed with our meeting; though I’ll mention it to nobody but you: not that I stand in awe of Mr. Heathcliff.”

“Hush,” murmured Linton; “for God’s sake, hush! He’s coming.” And he clung to Catherine’s arm, striving to detain her; but at that announcement she hastily disengaged herself, and whistled to Minny, who obeyed her like a dog.
And so we left him, scarcely conscious of our departure, so absorbed was he in anticipating his father’s approach.

Before we reached home, Catherine’s displeasure softened into a perplexed sensation of pity and regret, largely blended with vague, uneasy doubts about Linton’s actual circumstances, physical and social: in which I partook, though I counselled her not to say much; for a second journey would make us better judges. My master requested an account of our ongoings. His nephew’s offering of thanks was duly delivered, Miss Cathy gently touching on the rest: I also threw little light on his inquiries, for I hardly knew what to hide and what to reveal.

Seven days glided away, every one marking its course by the henceforth rapid alteration of Edgar Linton’s state. The havoc that months had previously wrought was now emulated by the inroads of hours. Catherine we would fain have deluded yet; but her own quick spirit refused to delude her: it divined in secret, and brooded on the dreadful probability, gradually ripening into certainty. She had not the heart to mention her ride, when Thursday came round; I mentioned it for her, and obtained permission to order her out of doors: for the library, where her father stopped a short time daily—the brief period he could bear to sit up—and his chamber, had become her whole world. She grudged each moment that did not find her bending over his pillow, or seated by his side. Her countenance grew wan with watching and sorrow, and my master gladly dismissed her to what he flattered himself would be a happy change of scene and society; drawing comfort from the hope that she would not now be left entirely alone after his death.

He had a fixed idea, I guessed by several observations he let fall, that, as his nephew resembled him in person, he would resemble him in mind; for Linton’s letters bore few or no indications of his defective character. And I, through pardonable weakness, refrained from correcting the error; asking myself what good there would be in disturbing his last moments with information that he had neither power nor opportunity to turn to account.

We deferred our excursion till the afternoon; a golden afternoon of August: every breath from the hills so full of life, that it seemed whoever respired it, though dying, might revive. Catherine’s face was just like the landscape—shadows and sunshine flitting over it in rapid succession; but the shadows rested longer, and the sunshine was more transient; and her poor little heart reproached itself for even that passing forgetfulness of its cares.

We discerned Linton watching at the same spot he had selected before. My young mistress alighted, and told me that, as she was resolved to stay a very little while, I had better hold the pony and remain on horseback; but I dissented: I wouldn’t risk losing sight of the charge committed to me a minute; so we climbed the slope of heath together. Master Heathcliff received us with greater animation on this occasion: not the animation of high spirits though, nor yet of joy; it looked more like fear.
paragraphsZh: “相当确定，”他的表弟回答道。“只有艾伦和我在争论你的健康状况。林顿，你真比我们冬天分开时强壮吗？如果是的话，我确信有一件事一点也没有变——那就是你对我的感情：说吧，你还是吗？”
林顿眼泪涌出，回答道：“是的，是的，我强了！”而且，仍被那虚幻的声音迷住，他的目光上下游移，试图寻找声音的主人。
凯西站起身。“今天我们必须分别，”她说。“而且我不会隐瞒我对这次见面感到非常失望；不过我只会向你提起这件事：并不是因为我害怕希斯克利夫先生。”
“嘘，”林顿低声说道；“看在上帝的份上，别出声！他要来了。”他紧紧抓住凯瑟琳的手臂，试图挽留她；但在那一喊声中，她急忙挣脱开来，并吹口哨叫来敏妮，她像狗一样服从了她。
就这样我们离开了他，他几乎没有意识到我们的离去，因为他全神贯注于期待他父亲的到来。
在我们到家之前，凯瑟琳的不悦渐渐化作了一种困惑的怜悯和悔意，这种感情在很大程度上夹杂着对林顿实际情况的模糊不安的怀疑，无论是身体上的还是社会上的；我也参与了这种感受，尽管我劝她少说为妙；因为第二次旅程会让我们成为更好的评判者。我的主人要求我们汇报行程。他侄子的谢意得到了恰当的传达，凯蒂小姐轻描淡写其余的部分：我对他的询问也几乎没有提供什么线索，因为我几乎不知道该隐瞒什么，该透露什么。

七天悄然流逝，每一天都以埃德加·林顿状态的迅速变化为标志。几个月前造成的破坏，如今正被小时的侵袭所效仿。凯瑟琳本想自我欺骗；但她敏捷的心灵拒绝欺骗自己：它在暗中洞察，并沉思着那可怕的可能性，逐渐成熟为确定性。星期四来临时，她没有勇气提起她的骑乘；我替她提及，并获得了允许让她出门：因为图书馆——她父亲每天短暂停留的地方——以及他的卧室，已经成了她的整个世界。她对每一刻未能弯身俯伏在他枕边，或坐在他身旁的时间都心生怨忿。她的面色因熬夜和忧愁而苍白，我的主人高兴地让她去一个他自我安慰地认为会带来快乐景象和社交变化的地方；从希望她在自己死后不会完全孤单中获得安慰。
我通过他随口说出的几句观察，猜到他有一个固定的想法：既然他的侄子在外貌上像他，他的心智也会像他一样；因为林顿的信中几乎看不到他品格上的缺陷。而我出于可原谅的软弱，没有纠正这个错误；自问在他生命的最后时刻告诉他这些既无力也无机会利用的信息，有什么好处呢。
