他的姐姐们非常希望他能拥有自己的产业；但是虽然他现在只是以租户的身份安定下来，宾利小姐却并非不愿意在他的餐桌上主持；赫斯特夫人也不例外，她嫁给了一个比家产更讲究的人，当便利时也愿意把他的房子当作自己的家。宾利先生未满二十岁两年时，因为一次偶然的推荐而被诱使去参观内瑟菲尔德庄园。他确实去看了，而且看了其中半个小时；对地理位置和主要房间感到满意，对房主的夸奖之词表示满意，并立即租下了这所房子。

尽管性格差异很大，他和达西之间仍然有着非常稳固的友谊。宾利因其性情的随和、开朗和柔顺而深受达西的喜欢，尽管他的性格与达西截然不同，而达西自己却从未对自己的性情表现出不满。凭借达西的关爱，宾利有着最坚定的信赖，对他的判断也抱有最高的评价。在理解力方面，达西更为出众。宾利绝非愚钝，但达西聪明。同时，达西傲慢、拘谨并且挑剔；他的举止虽然举止得体，却不讨人喜欢。在这方面，他的朋友有着很大的优势。宾利无论出现在哪里都能被人喜欢；而达西则不断地冒犯他人。
他们谈论梅里顿集会的方式足够具有典型性。宾利从未遇到过如此令人愉快的人或更漂亮的女孩；每个人都对他非常友好和周到；没有任何拘谨，没有任何生硬；他很快就和屋子里的所有人都熟络起来；至于贝内特小姐，他简直无法想象有天使比她更美丽。相反，达西看到的则是一群既不美丽也不时尚的人，他对他们一点兴趣都没有，也没有从任何人那里获得关注或愉悦。他承认贝内特小姐很漂亮；但她笑得太多了。
赫斯特夫人和她的妹妹允许事情如此；但她们仍然钦佩她并喜欢她，并称她为一个可爱的女孩，是一个她们不反对进一步了解的人。因此，贝内特小姐被确立为一个可爱的女孩；她们的兄弟也觉得有了这样的赞扬，可以按照自己的想法去考虑她。

在朗博恩不远处，住着一家人，贝内特家与他们关系尤其亲密。威廉·卢卡斯爵士以前在梅里顿从事商业，在那里赚了一笔还可以的财富，并在担任市长期间向国王致敬，从而获得了骑士荣誉。这种荣誉，也许被他看得过重。它让他对自己的生意和在一个小市场城镇的居住感到厌烦；于是，他辞去了这两者，与家人搬到距离梅里顿约一英里的房子，从那时起称作卢卡斯宅邸；在那里，他可以愉快地思考自己的重要性，并且不受生意束缚，专心致志地对所有人彬彬有礼。因为，虽然他的爵位使他自豪，但并未让他傲慢；恰恰相反，他对每个人都极为关心。他天性无害、友好且乐于助人，他在圣詹姆斯的表现使他变得彬彬有礼。

title: Pride and Prejudice · 选段 5
author: Jane Austen
paragraphs: “No, my dear; I think not. I have great hopes of finding him quite the reverse. There is a mixture of servility and self-importance in his letter which promises well. I am impatient to see him.”
“In point of composition,” said Mary, “his letter does not seem defective. The idea of the olive branch perhaps is not wholly new, yet I think it is well expressed.”

To Catherine and Lydia neither the letter nor its writer were in any degree interesting. It was next to impossible that their cousin should come in a scarlet coat, and it was now some weeks since they had received pleasure from the society of a man in any other colour. As for their mother, Mr. Collins’s letter had done away much of her ill-will, and she was preparing to see him with a degree of composure which astonished her husband and daughters.

Mr. Collins was punctual to his time, and was received with great politeness by the whole family. Mr. Bennet indeed said little; but the ladies were ready enough to talk, and Mr. Collins seemed neither in need of encouragement, nor inclined to be silent himself. He was a tall, heavy-looking young man of five-and-twenty. His air was grave and stately, and his manners were very formal. He had not been long seated before he complimented Mrs. Bennet on having so fine a family of daughters, said he had heard much of their beauty, but that, in this instance, fame had fallen short of the truth; and added, that he did not doubt her seeing them all in due time well disposed of in marriage. This gallantry was not much to the taste of some of his hearers; but Mrs. Bennet, who quarrelled with no compliments, answered most readily,--
“You are very kind, sir, I am sure; and I wish with all my heart it may prove so; for else they will be destitute enough. Things are settled so oddly.”

“Ah, sir, I do indeed. It is a grievous affair to my poor girls, you must confess. Not that I mean to find fault with you, for such things, I know, are all chance in this world. There is no knowing how estates will go when once they come to be entailed.”

“I am very sensible, madam, of the hardship to my fair cousins, and could say much on the subject, but that I am cautious of appearing forward and precipitate. But I can assure the young ladies that I come prepared to admire them. At present I will not say more, but, perhaps, when we are better acquainted----”

He was interrupted by a summons to dinner; and the girls smiled on each other. They were not the only objects of Mr. Collins’s admiration. The hall, the dining-room, and all its furniture, were examined and praised; and his commendation of everything would have touched Mrs. Bennet’s heart, but for the mortifying supposition of his viewing it all as his own future property. The dinner, too, in its turn, was highly admired; and he begged to know to which of his fair cousins the excellence of its cookery was owing. But here he was set right by Mrs. Bennet, who assured him, with some asperity, that they were very well able to keep a good cook, and that her daughters had nothing to do in the kitchen. He begged pardon for having displeased her. In a softened tone she declared herself not at all offended; but he continued to apologize for about a quarter of an hour.

During dinner, Mr. Bennet scarcely spoke at all; but when the servants were withdrawn, he thought it time to have some conversation with his guest, and therefore started a subject in which he expected him to shine, by observing that he seemed very fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes, and consideration for his comfort, appeared very remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen better. Mr. Collins was eloquent in her praise. The subject elevated him to more than usual solemnity of manner; and with a most important aspect he protested that he had never in his life witnessed such behaviour in a person of rank--such affability and condescension, as he had himself experienced from Lady Catherine. She had been graciously pleased to approve of both the discourses which he had already had the honour of preaching before her. She had also asked him twice to dine at Rosings, and had sent for him only the Saturday before, to make up her pool of quadrille in the evening. Lady Catherine was reckoned proud by many people, he knew, but he had never seen anything but affability in her. She had always spoken to him as she would to any other gentleman; she made not the smallest objection to his joining in the society of the neighbourhood, nor to his leaving his parish occasionally for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as he could, provided he chose with discretion; and had once paid him a visit in his humble parsonage, where she had perfectly approved all the alterations he had been making, and had even vouchsafed to suggest some herself,--some shelves in the closets upstairs.
paragraphsZh: “不，亲爱的；我想不会。我非常希望发现他完全相反。他信中混杂的奴性与自负令人期待。我迫不及待想见他。”
“在作曲方面，”玛丽说，“他的信似乎并不缺陷。橄榄枝的想法或许并非全新，但我认为表达得很好。”
对于凯瑟琳和丽迪亚来说，那封信和写信的人一点也不有趣。她们的堂兄几乎不可能穿着一件猩红色的外套出现，而自从几周前以来，她们已经很久没有因为与穿着其他颜色的男子交往而感到愉快了。至于她们的母亲，柯林斯先生的信消除了她很大一部分的恶意，她正在准备以一种让丈夫和女儿都感到惊讶的坦然态度去见他。

柯林斯先生准时到达，受到全家人的热情接待。班纳特先生确实话不多；但女士们却很健谈，而柯林斯先生似乎既不需要鼓励，也不倾向于沉默。他是一个二十五岁左右的高大、体格厚实的年轻人。他的仪态庄重严肃，举止非常正式。他刚坐下不久，就称赞班纳特太太拥有这样一群出色的女儿，说他听过很多关于她们美貌的传闻，但在这次会面中，这些传闻还不及事实；并补充说，他毫不怀疑她会在适当的时候让她们都妥善嫁出。这种殷勤对他的一些听众来说并不很合口味；但班纳特太太班纳特从不为恭维而争辩，他回答得非常干脆，——
“先生，您非常仁慈，我很确定；我衷心希望情况真是如此；否则他们将会相当贫困。事情安排得如此奇怪。”
“啊，先生，我确实有的。这对我可怜的女孩们来说是件悲惨的事，你必须承认。不过，我并不是要责怪你，因为我知道，这世上的事情都是偶然的。谁也无法预料，当地产一旦被继承后会如何发展。”
“夫人，我非常理解对我那些漂亮的堂姐妹们来说的困难，本可以在这个话题上多说一些，但我谨慎，不想显得轻率和过于急切。不过我可以向这些年轻女士保证，我已经准备好去欣赏她们。目前我不打算多说，但也许，当我们更熟悉之后——”

他被召去吃晚饭打断了，而女孩们相视而笑。她们并不是柯林斯先生仰慕的唯一对象。大厅、餐厅以及所有的家具都受到了仔细检查和称赞；他对一切事物的称赞原本会打动贝内特太太的心，但她却因假设他将这些视为自己未来的财产而感到尴尬。同样，晚餐也赢得了极高的赞赏；他恳求知道，这一切美食的烹饪出色归功于哪位美丽的表妹。然而在这里，贝内特太太纠正了他，她带着些许严厉向他保证，她们完全有能力雇一个好厨师，她的女儿们在厨房里毫无事宜。他为使她不快而道歉。她以柔和的语气声称自己一点也不生气；但他仍然连续道歉大约十五分钟。

晚餐时，班内特先生几乎一句话也没说；但当仆人们退下后，他觉得是时候与客人交谈了，因此提出了一个他期望客人擅长的话题，指出他似乎在他的保护人面前非常幸运。德堡夫人的关心他所希望的事，以及对他舒适的考虑，显得非常显著。班内特先生再也无法做出更好的选择。柯林斯先生对她的称赞滔滔不绝。这个话题让他的举止比平时更显庄重；他以一种非常严肃的表情宣称，在他一生中从未见过如此显贵的人表现出像他自己从德堡夫人那里所体验到的那样的和蔼与谦逊。她曾满怀恩宠地赞许他曾有幸在她面前讲授过的两篇讲道。她也曾两次邀请他到罗辛斯用晚餐，而且就在前一个星期六，她还特地请他前来，以便晚上参加她们的四人方块舞局。凯瑟琳夫人被许多人认为很骄傲，他知道，但他从未在她身上看到过除了和蔼以外的任何表现。她总是像对待其他绅士一样对他说话；她对他参加当地的社交活动丝毫没有异议，也不反对他偶尔离开自己的教区一两周去拜访亲戚。她甚至曾屈尊建议他尽快结婚，前提是他要明智地选择；她还曾去过他简陋的牧师住宅拜访，在那里她完全赞同他所做的所有改动，甚至亲自提出了一些建议——比如楼上壁橱里的几块搁板。

title: Pride and Prejudice · 选段 6
author: Jane Austen
paragraphs: In vain did Elizabeth endeavour to check the rapidity of her mother’s words, or persuade her to describe her felicity in a less audible whisper; for to her inexpressible vexation she could perceive that the chief of it was overheard by Mr. Darcy, who sat opposite to them. Her mother only scolded her for being nonsensical.
“What is Mr. Darcy to me, pray, that I should be afraid of him? I am sure we owe him no such particular civility as to be obliged to say nothing he may not like to hear.”
“For heaven’s sake, madam, speak lower. What advantage can it be to you to offend Mr. Darcy? You will never recommend yourself to his friend by so doing.”

Nothing that she could say, however, had any influence. Her mother would talk of her views in the same intelligible tone. Elizabeth blushed and blushed again with shame and vexation. She could not help frequently glancing her eye at Mr. Darcy, though every glance convinced her of what she dreaded; for though he was not always looking at her mother, she was convinced that his attention was invariably fixed by her. The expression of his face changed gradually from indignant contempt to a composed and steady gravity.

At length, however, Mrs. Bennet had no more to say; and Lady Lucas, who had been long yawning at the repetition of delights which she saw no likelihood of sharing, was left to the comforts of cold ham and chicken. Elizabeth now began to revive. But not long was the interval of tranquillity; for when supper was over, singing was talked of, and she had the mortification of seeing Mary, after very little entreaty, preparing to oblige the company. By many significant looks and silent entreaties did she endeavour to prevent such a proof of complaisance,--but in vain; Mary would not understand them; such an opportunity of exhibiting was delightful to her, and she began her song. Elizabeth’s eyes were fixed on her, with most painful sensations; and she watched her progress through the several stanzas with an impatience which was very ill rewarded at their close; for Mary, on receiving amongst the thanks of the table the hint of a hope that she might be prevailed on to favour them again, after the pause of half a minute began another. Mary’s powers were by no means fitted for such a display; her voice was weak, and her manner affected. Elizabeth was in agonies. She looked at Jane to see how she bore it; but Jane was very composedly talking to Bingley. She looked at his two sisters, and saw them making signs of derision at each other, and at Darcy, who continued, however, impenetrably grave. She looked at her father to entreat his interference, lest Mary should be singing all night. He took the hint, and, when Mary had finished her second song, said aloud,--
“That will do extremely well, child. You have delighted us long enough. Let the other young ladies have time to exhibit.”

Mary, though pretending not to hear, was somewhat disconcerted; and Elizabeth, sorry for her, and sorry for her father’s speech, was afraid her anxiety had done no good. Others of the party were now applied to.

“If I,” said Mr. Collins, “were so fortunate as to be able to sing, I should have great pleasure, I am sure, in obliging the company with an air; for I consider music as a very innocent diversion, and perfectly compatible with the profession of a clergyman. I do not mean, however, to assert that we can be justified in devoting too much of our time to music, for there are certainly other things to be attended to. The rector of a parish has much to do. In the first place, he must make such an agreement for tithes as may be beneficial to himself and not offensive to his patron. He must write his own sermons; and the time that remains will not be too much for his parish duties, and the care and improvement of his dwelling, which he cannot be excused from making as comfortable as possible. And I do not think it of light importance that he should have attentive and conciliatory manners towards everybody, especially towards those to whom he owes his preferment. I cannot acquit him of that duty; nor could I think well of the man who should omit an occasion of testifying his respect towards anybody connected with the family.” And with a bow to Mr. Darcy, he concluded his speech, which had been spoken so loud as to be heard by half the room. Many stared--many smiled; but no one looked more amused than Mr. Bennet himself, while his wife seriously commended Mr. Collins for having spoken so sensibly, and observed, in a half-whisper to Lady Lucas, that he was a remarkably clever, good kind of young man.
paragraphsZh: 伊丽莎白徒劳地努力想要制止母亲话语的急促，或者劝她以较低的声音描述自己的幸福；然而令她难以言表的恼火的是，她能察觉到这些话的大部分内容都被坐在她们对面的达西先生听到了。她母亲只是因为她说话不合情理而责备她。
“达西先生对我算什么，我为什么要害怕他？我确信我们并不欠他什么特别的礼遇，并不必说那些他可能不喜欢听的话。”
“看在老天的份上，夫人，请说小声点。冒犯达西先生对您有什么好处？您这样做绝不会让他对您产生好感。”
然而，她说的任何话都没有任何影响。她母亲仍会以同样明白易懂的语气谈论她的观点。伊丽莎白因羞愧和懊恼一次又一次地脸红。她忍不住时常瞥一眼达西先生，虽然每一瞥都让她更加确信她所害怕的事情；因为尽管他并不总是看着她母亲，她却确信他的注意力总是集中在她身上。他的面部表情逐渐从愤慨的轻蔑变为镇定而稳重的严肃。

然而，班纳特夫人最终无话可说；而卢卡斯夫人早已因一再重复的快乐而打呵欠，这些快乐她看不到分享的可能性，只得享受冷火腿和鸡肉的安慰。伊丽莎白这时开始恢复精神。但这片宁静的间隔并不长；因为晚餐结束后，人们谈起唱歌，而她却懊恼地看到玛丽在稍作请求后，就开始准备取悦众人。她用许多意味深长的眼神和无声的恳求试图阻止这种殷勤的表现——但都徒劳无功；玛丽就是不理解，她非常喜欢这种展示自己的机会，并开始唱歌。伊丽莎白的目光紧紧注视着她，满是最痛苦的感受；她焦急地看着她在几个诗节间的进展，而到结束时这种急切几乎没有得到回报；因为当玛丽在收到桌上众人的感谢时，隐约希望她可能会再次宽容她们的演奏，停顿了半分钟后又开始了另一首。玛丽的能力根本不适合如此展示；她的声音很弱，举止也很造作。伊丽莎白痛苦万分。她看向简，想看看她是如何应对的；但简正镇定自若地与宾利交谈。她看向他的两个姐妹，看到她们相互做出嘲弄的手势，又看向达西，他仍然面无表情、神情难以捉摸。她又看向父亲，恳求他干预，生怕玛丽会唱整晚。他明白了暗示，当玛丽唱完第二首歌时，大声说道——
“孩子，你唱得非常好。你已经让我们高兴够久了。让其他年轻女士也有机会展示吧。”
玛丽虽然装作没听见，但有些不安；伊丽莎白为她感到难过，也为她父亲的话感到遗憾，担心她的焦虑没有起到任何作用。聚会的其他人现在也被邀请参与了。

“如果我如此幸运，能够唱歌，我相信我会非常乐意为大家献上一首歌;因为我认为音乐是一种非常纯真的消遣，完全适合牧师的职业。不过，我并不是说我们有理由把太多时间投入音乐，因为肯定还有其他事情需要处理。教区牧师有很多事情要做。首先，他必须就什一税达成对自己有利且不冒犯其赞助人的协议。他必须自己撰写讲道稿;剩下的时间不会太长，既能完成教区职责，也不会让住所变得尽可能舒适。我认为他对每个人都应表现出体贴和和解的态度，尤其是对那些帮助他获得晋升的人，这绝不是一件小事。我无法免除他这方面的责任；我也不会对那个错过向任何与家族有关的人表达尊重的机会的人抱有好感。”说完，他向达西先生鞠了一躬，结束了他的讲话，这番话声音很大，半个房间的人都听到了。许多人都惊讶地看着——许多人微笑；但没有人比班纳特先生自己看起来更感到好笑，而他的妻子则认真地称赞柯林斯先生说话如此明智，并半声对卢卡斯夫人说道，他是个非常聪明、善良的年轻人。

title: Pride and Prejudice · 选段 7
author: Jane Austen
paragraphs: “An excellent consolation in its way,” said Elizabeth; “but it will not do for us. We do not suffer by accident. It does not often happen that the interference of friends will persuade a young man of independent fortune to think no more of a girl whom he was violently in love with only a few days before.”

“But that expression of ‘violently in love’ is so hackneyed, so doubtful, so indefinite, that it gives me very little idea. It is as often applied to feelings which arise only from a half hour’s acquaintance, as to a real, strong attachment. Pray, how violent was Mr. Bingley’s love?”

“I never saw a more promising inclination; he was growing quite inattentive to other people, and wholly engrossed by her. Every time they met, it was more decided and remarkable. At his own ball he offended two or three young ladies by not asking them to dance; and I spoke to him twice myself without receiving an answer. Could there be finer symptoms? Is not general incivility the very essence of love?”

“Oh, yes! of that kind of love which I suppose him to have felt. Poor Jane! I am sorry for her, because, with her disposition, she may not get over it immediately. It had better have happened to you, Lizzy; you would have laughed yourself out of it sooner. But do you think she would be prevailed on to go back with us? Change of scene might be of service--and perhaps a little relief from home may be as useful as anything.”
Elizabeth was exceedingly pleased with this proposal, and felt persuaded of her sister’s ready acquiescence.

“I hope,” added Mrs. Gardiner, “that no consideration with regard to this young man will influence her. We live in so different a part of town, all our connections are so different, and, as you well know, we go out so little, that it is very improbable they should meet at all, unless he really comes to see her.”

“And that is quite impossible; for he is now in the custody of his friend, and Mr. Darcy would no more suffer him to call on Jane in such a part of London! My dear aunt, how could you think of it? Mr. Darcy may, perhaps, have heard of such a place as Gracechurch Street, but he would hardly think a month’s ablution enough to cleanse him from its impurities, were he once to enter it; and, depend upon it, Mr. Bingley never stirs without him.”
“So much the better. I hope they will not meet at all. But does not Jane correspond with his sister? She will not be able to help calling.”

But, in spite of the certainty in which Elizabeth affected to place this point, as well as the still more interesting one of Bingley’s being withheld from seeing Jane, she felt a solicitude on the subject which convinced her, on examination, that she did not consider it entirely hopeless. It was possible, and sometimes she thought it probable, that his affection might be re-animated, and the influence of his friends successfully combated by the more natural influence of Jane’s attractions.

Miss Bennet accepted her aunt’s invitation with pleasure; and the Bingleys were no otherwise in her thoughts at the same time than as she hoped, by Caroline’s not living in the same house with her brother, she might occasionally spend a morning with her, without any danger of seeing him.

The Gardiners stayed a week at Longbourn; and what with the Philipses, the Lucases, and the officers, there was not a day without its engagement. Mrs. Bennet had so carefully provided for the entertainment of her brother and sister, that they did not once sit down to a family dinner. When the engagement was for home, some of the officers always made part of it, of which officers Mr. Wickham was sure to be one; and on these occasions Mrs. Gardiner, rendered suspicious by Elizabeth’s warm commendation of him, narrowly observed them both. Without supposing them, from what she saw, to be very seriously in love, their preference of each other was plain enough to make her a little uneasy; and she resolved to speak to Elizabeth on the subject before she left Hertfordshire, and represent to her the imprudence of encouraging such an attachment.
paragraphsZh: “某种程度上倒是个极好的安慰，”伊丽莎白说；“但对我们来说不管用。我们并非偶然遭遇痛苦。朋友的干预很少能说服一个独立财富的年轻人不再考虑一个几天前他还疯狂爱慕的女孩。”
“但那种‘疯狂爱慕’的说法已经太陈词滥调、太模糊、太不明确，以至于几乎让我无法理解。它常常用来形容仅仅相识半小时产生的情感，也可以用来形容真正强烈的感情。请问，宾利先生的爱到底有多疯狂？”
“我从未见过如此有前途的倾向；他对其他人完全不再注意，全心全意地被她吸引。每次他们见面，这种情形都更加明显和引人注目。在自己的舞会上，他因为没有邀请两三位年轻女士跳舞而冒犯了她们；我亲自和他说了两次话，却没有得到回应。难道还有比这更好的症状吗？难道一般的无礼不是爱的本质吗？”
“哦，是的！正是我猜测他所感受到的那种爱。可怜的简！我为她感到难过，因为以她的性格，她可能不会很快克服那段情感。如果是你，莉齐，倒会好些；你会更快地笑着走出来。但你认为她会被说服和我们一起回去吗？换个环境可能会有帮助——也许远离家一点小小的宽慰，比什么都管用。”
伊丽莎白对这个提议感到非常高兴，并且相信她的妹妹会欣然同意。
“我希望，”加德纳太太补充道，“没有任何关于这个年轻人的考虑会影响她。我们住在城里截然不同的地方，所有的社交圈也都不同，而且，你也很清楚，我们外出很少，因此他们几乎不可能相遇，除非他真的来拜访她。”
“那是完全不可能的；因为他现在在他朋友的看管下，而达西先生绝不会允许他到伦敦的那部分地区去拜访简！我亲爱的阿姨，你怎么会想到这种事？达西先生或许听说过像格雷斯教堂街这样的地方，但他几乎不会认为一个月的洗净足以洗去那里的污染，如果他一旦进入那里；而且，相信我，宾利先生从来不会独自行动。”
“那就更好。我希望他们根本不会见面。但简难道不和他的姐姐通信吗？她到时候肯定会不由自主地去拜访。”
但是，尽管伊丽莎白在此问题上显得非常确定，而且在宾利未能见到简这一更为有趣的问题上显得同样笃定，她在这个问题上仍感到一种关切，这使她经过反复思考后相信，她并不认为完全没有希望。可能，有时她甚至认为很可能，他的感情会重新被唤起，而他朋友的影响也可能被简更自然的吸引力所成功抵消。
班纳特小姐愉快地接受了姑妈的邀请；而宾利家族在她此时的心中也仅仅是作为一种希望——她希望，由于卡罗琳没有和她的哥哥住在同一屋檐下，她有时能够在早上与卡罗琳共度时光，而不会有遇到他那样的危险。

加丁纳一家在朗伯恩住了一周；再加上菲利普一家、卢卡斯一家和那些军官们，每天都有活动安排。贝内特夫人为了招待她的兄妹做了周到的准备，以至于他们一次也没有坐下来一起吃家常晚餐。每当活动在家举行时，总有一些军官参加，而威克姆先生肯定会是其中之一；在这些场合下，加丁纳夫人由于伊丽莎白对他的热情称赞而心生疑虑，便仔细观察着他们两人。虽然她没有假定他们彼此非常深情相爱，但从她所看到的情形来看，他们对彼此的偏爱足够明显，这让她有些不安；于是她决定在离开赫特福德郡之前就这个话题与伊丽莎白谈谈，并向她说明鼓励这种感情的轻率之处。

title: Pride and Prejudice · 选段 8
author: Jane Austen
paragraphs: “Good Heaven! What is to become of us? What are we to do?” would they often exclaim in the bitterness of woe. “How can you be smiling so, Lizzy?”
Their affectionate mother shared all their grief; she remembered what she had herself endured on a similar occasion five-and-twenty years ago.
“I am sure,” said she, “I cried for two days together when Colonel Miller’s regiment went away. I thought I should have broke my heart.”

Such were the kind of lamentations resounding perpetually through Longbourn House. Elizabeth tried to be diverted by them; but all sense of pleasure was lost in shame. She felt anew the justice of Mr. Darcy’s objections; and never had she before been so much disposed to pardon his interference in the views of his friend.

But the gloom of Lydia’s prospect was shortly cleared away; for she received an invitation from Mrs. Forster, the wife of the colonel of the regiment, to accompany her to Brighton. This invaluable friend was a very young woman, and very lately married. A resemblance in good-humour and good spirits had recommended her and Lydia to each other, and out of their three months’ acquaintance they had been intimate two.

The rapture of Lydia on this occasion, her adoration of Mrs. Forster, the delight of Mrs. Bennet, and the mortification of Kitty, are scarcely to be described. Wholly inattentive to her sister’s feelings, Lydia flew about the house in restless ecstasy, calling for everyone’s congratulations, and laughing and talking with more violence than ever; whilst the luckless Kitty continued in the parlour repining at her fate in terms as unreasonable as her accent was peevish.

“I cannot see why Mrs. Forster should not ask me as well as Lydia,” said she, “though I am not her particular friend. I have just as much right to be asked as she has, and more too, for I am two years older.”

In vain did Elizabeth attempt to make her reasonable, and Jane to make her resigned. As for Elizabeth herself, this invitation was so far from exciting in her the same feelings as in her mother and Lydia, that she considered it as the death-warrant of all possibility of common sense for the latter; and detestable as such a step must make her, were it known, she could not help secretly advising her father not to let her go. She represented to him all the improprieties of Lydia’s general behaviour, the little advantage she could derive from the friendship of such a woman as Mrs. Forster, and the probability of her being yet more imprudent with such a companion at Brighton, where the temptations must be greater than at home. He heard her attentively, and then said,--

“Already arisen!” repeated Mr. Bennet. “What! has she frightened away some of your lovers? Poor little Lizzy! But do not be cast down. Such squeamish youths as cannot bear to be connected with a little absurdity are not worth a regret. Come, let me see the list of the pitiful fellows who have been kept aloof by Lydia’s folly.”

“Indeed, you are mistaken. I have no such injuries to resent. It is not of peculiar, but of general evils, which I am now complaining. Our importance, our respectability in the world, must be affected by the wild volatility, the assurance and disdain of all restraint which mark Lydia’s character. Excuse me,--for I must speak plainly. If you, my dear father, will not take the trouble of checking her exuberant spirits, and of teaching her that her present pursuits are not to be the business of her life, she will soon be beyond the reach of amendment. Her character will be fixed; and she will, at sixteen, be the most determined flirt that ever made herself and her family ridiculous;--a flirt, too, in the worst and meanest degree of flirtation; without any attraction beyond youth and a tolerable person; and, from the ignorance and emptiness of her mind, wholly unable to ward off any portion of that universal contempt which her rage for admiration will excite. In this danger Kitty is also comprehended. She will follow wherever Lydia leads. Vain, ignorant, idle, and absolutely uncontrolled! Oh, my dear father, can you suppose it possible that they will not be censured and despised wherever they are known, and that their sisters will not be often involved in the disgrace?”
paragraphsZh: “天哪！我们将会怎么样？我们该怎么办？”他们常在痛苦的苦涩中这样惊呼。“你怎么还能笑得出来，莉齐？”
他们慈爱的母亲分担了他们所有的悲痛；她记得二十五年前自己在类似情况下所经历的一切。
“我确定，” 她说，“米勒上校的团离开的时候，我连续哭了两天。我以为我的心都要碎了。”
这样的哀叹声不断在朗伯恩府回响。伊丽莎白试图从中获得消遣；然而，所有的愉悦感都在羞愧中消失了。她再次感受到达西先生反对的正当性；她从未像现在这样倾向于原谅他在朋友事务上的干涉。
但是莉迪亚前景的阴霾很快消散；因为她收到了弗斯特女士的邀请——那位团长的妻子——邀请她一起去布莱顿。这位无价的朋友是一位非常年轻的女性，并且最近刚结婚。开朗和愉快的性格上的相似使她和莉迪亚互相推荐，在她们三个月的相识中，她们已经亲密无间两个月了。
在这次场合中，莉迪亚的狂喜、她对福斯特夫人的崇拜、班纳特夫人的喜悦，以及小凯蒂的尴尬，几乎无法形容。莉迪亚完全不顾她姐姐的感受，在屋子里焦躁不安地飞来飞去，呼唤大家的祝贺，笑闹说话比以往更加激烈；而不幸的小凯蒂则继续在客厅里抱怨自己的命运，言辞既不合理，声调又尖厉刺耳。
“我不明白福斯特太太为什么不能像问莉迪亚一样问我，”她说，“虽然我不是她的特别朋友。我和她一样有权被邀请，而且我更应该被邀请，因为我比她大两岁。”

伊丽莎白徒劳地试图说服她讲道理，简则试图使她顺从。至于伊丽莎白自己，这份邀请不仅没有在她心中激起与她母亲和莉迪亚相同的感情，反而使她认为这几乎是剥夺后者所有常识的死刑令；而这样一个行为即使被人知道，也必定让她变得可憎，但她仍忍不住暗暗劝父亲不要让她去。她向父亲陈述了莉迪亚一贯行为中的各种不端之处，她可能从福斯特太太这样的女性友情中获得的微小益处，以及她在布赖顿与这样的同伴在一起可能会更加轻率的可能性，因为那里比在家里的诱惑更大。他仔细听了她的意见，然后说道——
“已经发生了！”贝内特先生重复道。“什么！她把你的一些追求者吓跑了吗？可怜的小莉齐！但不要沮丧。那些连一点小荒谬都无法忍受而不愿有所牵连的胆小青年，不值得惋惜。来，让我看看因为莉迪亚的愚行而被疏远的可怜家伙们的名单。”

“确实，你错了。我没有什么伤害需要怨恨。我抱怨的，不是特殊的，而是一般性的邪恶。我们的重要性，我们在社会上的声望，必然会受到莉迪亚性格中那种极端多变、放肆自信和蔑视一切约束的影响。请原谅我——我必须直言。如果你，我亲爱的父亲，不费心去控制她过于奔放的性格，并教导她目前的追求不应该成为她一生的事业，她很快就会无法改正。”她的性格将会固定；十六岁时，她将成为史上最固执的调情者，让自己和家人都显得可笑——而且是以最差、最卑鄙的方式调情的人；除了年轻和尚可的外貌之外，没有任何吸引力；由于她心灵的无知和空虚，完全无法抵挡她对追求赞美的狂热所激起的普遍轻蔑。在这种危险中，Kitty 也包括在内。她会追随 Lydia 的脚步。虚荣、无知、懒散，完全无法控制！哦，我亲爱的父亲，您难道能想象她们在所到之处不会被谴责和轻视，并且她们的姐妹不会经常因此蒙受耻辱吗？”

title: Pride and Prejudice · 选段 9
author: Jane Austen
paragraphs: Elizabeth soon saw that she was herself closely watched by Miss Bingley, and that she could not speak a word, especially to Miss Darcy, without calling her attention. This observation would not have prevented her from trying to talk to the latter, had they not been seated at an inconvenient distance; but she was not sorry to be spared the necessity of saying much: her own thoughts were employing her. She expected every moment that some of the gentlemen would enter the room: she wished, she feared, that the master of the house might be amongst them; and whether she wished or feared it most, she could scarcely determine. After sitting in this manner a quarter of an hour, without hearing Miss Bingley’s voice, Elizabeth was roused by receiving from her a cold inquiry after the health of her family. She answered with equal indifference and brevity, and the other said no more.

The next variation which their visit afforded was produced by the entrance of servants with cold meat, cake, and a variety of all the finest fruits in season; but this did not take place till after many a significant look and smile from Mrs. Annesley to Miss Darcy had been given, to remind her of her post. There was now employment for the whole party; for though they could not all talk, they could all eat; and the beautiful pyramids of grapes, nectarines, and peaches, soon collected them round the table.

While thus engaged, Elizabeth had a fair opportunity of deciding whether she most feared or wished for the appearance of Mr. Darcy, by the feelings which prevailed on his entering the room; and then, though but a moment before she had believed her wishes to predominate, she began to regret that he came.

He had been some time with Mr. Gardiner, who, with two or three other gentlemen from the house, was engaged by the river; and had left him only on learning that the ladies of the family intended a visit to Georgiana that morning. No sooner did he appear, than Elizabeth wisely resolved to be perfectly easy and unembarrassed;--a resolution the more necessary to be made, but perhaps not the more easily kept, because she saw that the suspicions of the whole party were awakened against them, and that there was scarcely an eye which did not watch his behaviour when he first came into the room. In no countenance was attentive curiosity so strongly marked as in Miss Bingley’s, in spite of the smiles which overspread her face whenever she spoke to one of its objects; for jealousy had not yet made her desperate, and her attentions to Mr. Darcy were by no means over. Miss Darcy, on her brother’s entrance, exerted herself much more to talk; and Elizabeth saw that he was anxious for his sister and herself to get acquainted, and forwarded, as much as possible, every attempt at conversation on either side. Miss Bingley saw all this likewise; and, in the imprudence of anger, took the first opportunity of saying, with sneering civility,--
“Pray, Miss Eliza, are not the ----shire militia removed from Meryton? They must be a great loss to your family.”

In Darcy’s presence she dared not mention Wickham’s name: but Elizabeth instantly comprehended that he was uppermost in her thoughts; and the various recollections connected with him gave her a moment’s distress; but, exerting herself vigorously to repel the ill-natured attack, she presently answered the question in a tolerably disengaged tone. While she spoke, an involuntary glance showed her Darcy with a heightened complexion, earnestly looking at her, and his sister overcome with confusion, and unable to lift up her eyes. Had Miss Bingley known what pain she was then giving her beloved friend, she undoubtedly would have refrained from the hint; but she had merely intended to discompose Elizabeth, by bringing forward the idea of a man to whom she believed her partial, to make her betray a sensibility which might injure her in Darcy’s opinion, and, perhaps, to remind the latter of all the follies and absurdities by which some part of her family were connected with that corps. Not a syllable had ever reached her of Miss Darcy’s meditated elopement. To no creature had it been revealed, where secrecy was possible, except to Elizabeth; and from all Bingley’s connections her brother was particularly anxious to conceal it, from that very wish which Elizabeth had long ago attributed to him, of their becoming hereafter her own. He had certainly formed such a plan; and without meaning that it should affect his endeavour to separate him from Miss Bennet, it is probable that it might add something to his lively concern for the welfare of his friend.
paragraphsZh: 伊丽莎白很快就注意到自己正被宾利小姐密切注视着，尤其是每当她对达西小姐说话时，总会引起宾利小姐的注意。若不是她们坐得相距不便，这种观察并不会阻止她尝试与后者交谈；但她并不介意因此而免去说太多话的必要：她自己的思绪正占据着她的心头。她每时每刻都在期待某些绅士进入房间；她既希望又害怕屋主会在其中，而究竟她更希望还是更害怕，这几乎让她无法判断。她就这样坐了十五分钟，没有听到宾利小姐开口，直到宾利小姐冷冷地问起她家人的健康状况，才把她从沉思中唤回。她以同样的冷漠和简短回应，而对方再也没有说什么。
他们的访问带来的下一个变化，是仆人们端着冷盘、蛋糕和各种当季最好水果的进入；但这一切发生在安妮斯利夫人向黛西小姐投去许多意味深长的目光和微笑之后，以提醒她履行自己的职责。现在，全体宾客都有事可做；虽然他们不能都说话，但都可以吃；闪亮的葡萄、油桃和桃子堆成的美丽金字塔，很快就把他们聚集在桌子周围。
在这样忙碌的时候，伊丽莎白有一个很好的机会，通过他进入房间时占据她心头的感情，来判断她到底更害怕还是更希望达西先生的出现；然后，尽管就在片刻之前她还相信自己的愿望占了上风，她开始后悔他来了。

他已经和加德纳先生在一起一段时间了，加德纳先生和来自府上的另外两三位绅士正在河边活动；他只是在得知这家族的女士们打算当天上午去乔乔安娜那儿拜访后才离开他。一旦他出现，伊丽莎白明智地决定保持完全的轻松和不拘束；——这个决定之所以更有必要作出，或许并不是因为更容易坚持，因为她看到整个队伍的怀疑都被引起了，而且几乎没有一双眼睛在他刚进屋时不在观察他的举动。在没有哪个面容上，好奇心表现得像在宾利小姐的脸上那样明显，尽管每当她与其中一个对象说话时，她的脸上总是浮现微笑；因为嫉妒尚未使她绝望，她对达西先生的关注也一点都没有减少。达西小姐在她兄长进来时，努力多说话；伊丽莎白看到，他希望他的妹妹和她熟悉起来，并尽可能推动双方的每一次对话尝试。宾利小姐也看到了这一切；在愤怒的不明智下，她抓住第一个机会，用带着讥讽的礼貌说道——
“请问，伊丽莎小姐，----郡的民兵不是已从梅里顿撤走了吗？他们对你们家一定是很大的损失。”

在达西面前，她不敢提起威克姆的名字；但是伊丽莎白立刻明白，他正占据着她的心头；与他相关的各种回忆让她感到一时的苦恼；但她竭力抵御那恶意的攻击，很快便以相当自然的语气回答了问题。说话间，一个不自觉的目光让她看到了面色略显潮红、认真注视自己的达西，以及尴尬不已、无法抬眼的姐姐。如果宾利小姐知道自己当时正给她心爱的朋友带来多大的痛苦，她无疑会避免那句暗示；但她只是想通过提出一个她认为伊丽莎白偏爱的男子，让伊丽莎白暴露出可能在达西眼中不利的敏感情绪，也许还想提醒达西她家族中有些人与那个团体有关联的所有愚蠢和荒谬之事。从未有任何人告诉过她关于达西小姐计划私奔的事情。这个秘密除了伊丽莎白之外，没有人知道，在可能保持秘密的情况下也没有透露给任何人；而宾利的所有亲戚中，他特别想对她的兄弟隐瞒此事，正是出于伊丽莎白早就归因于他的愿望，即他们将来能成为她自己的家庭的一部分。他确实制定了这样的计划；并且在无意让它影响他将他与班纳特小姐分开的努力的情况下，这很可能会增加他对朋友福祉的热切关心。

title: Pride and Prejudice · 选段 10
author: Jane Austen
paragraphs: “Good gracious! Mr. Darcy!--and so it does, I vow. Well, any friend of Mr. Bingley’s will always be welcome here, to be sure; but else I must say that I hate the very sight of him.”

Jane looked at Elizabeth with surprise and concern. She knew but little of their meeting in Derbyshire, and therefore felt for the awkwardness which must attend her sister, in seeing him almost for the first time after receiving his explanatory letter. Both sisters were uncomfortable enough. Each felt for the other, and of course for themselves; and their mother talked on of her dislike of Mr. Darcy, and her resolution to be civil to him only as Mr. Bingley’s friend, without being heard by either of them. But Elizabeth had sources of uneasiness which could not yet be suspected by Jane, to whom she had never yet had courage to show Mrs. Gardiner’s letter, or to relate her own change of sentiment towards him. To Jane, he could be only a man whose proposals she had refused, and whose merits she had undervalued; but to her own more extensive information, he was the person to whom the whole family were indebted for the first of benefits, and whom she regarded herself with an interest, if not quite so tender, at least as reasonable and just, as what Jane felt for Bingley. Her astonishment at his coming--at his coming to Netherfield, to Longbourn, and voluntarily seeking her again, was almost equal to what she had known on first witnessing his altered behaviour in Derbyshire.

The colour which had been driven from her face returned for half a minute with an additional glow, and a smile of delight added lustre to her eyes, as she thought for that space of time that his affection and wishes must still be unshaken; but she would not be secure.

She sat intently at work, striving to be composed, and without daring to lift up her eyes, till anxious curiosity carried them to the face of her sister as the servant was approaching the door. Jane looked a little paler than usual, but more sedate than Elizabeth had expected. On the gentlemen’s appearing, her colour increased; yet she received them with tolerable ease, and with a propriety of behaviour equally free from any symptom of resentment, or any unnecessary complaisance.

Elizabeth said as little to either as civility would allow, and sat down again to her work, with an eagerness which it did not often command. She had ventured only one glance at Darcy. He looked serious as usual; and, she thought, more as he had been used to look in Hertfordshire, than as she had seen him at Pemberley. But, perhaps, he could not in her mother’s presence be what he was before her uncle and aunt. It was a painful, but not an improbable, conjecture.

Bingley she had likewise seen for an instant, and in that short period saw him looking both pleased and embarrassed. He was received by Mrs. Bennet with a degree of civility which made her two daughters ashamed, especially when contrasted with the cold and ceremonious politeness of her courtesy and address of his friend.

Elizabeth particularly, who knew that her mother owed to the latter the preservation of her favourite daughter from irremediable infamy, was hurt and distressed to a most painful degree by a distinction so ill applied.

Darcy, after inquiring of her how Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner did--a question which she could not answer without confusion--said scarcely anything. He was not seated by her: perhaps that was the reason of his silence; but it had not been so in Derbyshire. There he had talked to her friends when he could not to herself. But now several minutes elapsed, without bringing the sound of his voice; and when occasionally, unable to resist the impulse of curiosity, she raised her eyes to his face, she as often found him looking at Jane as at herself, and frequently on no object but the ground. More thoughtfulness and less anxiety to please, than when they last met, were plainly expressed. She was disappointed, and angry with herself for being so.
paragraphsZh: “天哪！达西先生！——的确如此，我发誓。好吧，宾利先生的任何朋友在这里总会受到欢迎，这是当然的；但除此之外，我必须说我一看到他就讨厌。”

简带着惊讶和担忧看着伊丽莎白。她对她们在德比郡的会面知之甚少，因此对妹妹在几乎第一次见到他，且是在收到他解释信之后所感受到的尴尬表示同情。两姊妹都相当不舒服。她们彼此体会对方的感受，当然也体会自己的感受；而她们的母亲则继续讲述自己对达西先生的不喜欢，以及她决定仅作为宾利先生的朋友礼貌对待他，而没有让任何一个人听到。但是伊丽莎白有一些不安的源头，简尚无法察觉——她至今还没有勇气把加德纳夫人的信展示给简看，也没有勇气讲述自己对他的态度已经发生的变化。对简来说，他不过是一个她曾拒绝过他的求婚、且她曾低估过优点的男人；但在她自己更广泛的认知中，他是那个全家第一次受益于的人，而且她对他怀有的兴趣，如果不完全像简对宾利那样温柔，至少也是合理而公正的。她对他的到来——到内瑟菲尔德、到朗博恩，并主动再次寻求她的到来——的惊讶，几乎与她第一次在德比郡目睹他改变后的行为时的震惊相当。
她脸上曾被驱散的颜色又回来了，持续了半分钟，并带着额外的光彩，喜悦的微笑为她的眼睛增添了光辉，因为在那段时间里，她以为他的感情和愿望仍然坚定不移；但她不会感到安心。
她专注地坐在工作上，努力保持镇定，不敢抬起眼睛，直到因焦虑的好奇心而将目光投向她姐姐的脸上，那时仆人正走向门口。简看起来比平常稍微苍白一些，但比伊丽莎白预期的要沉着。绅士们出现时，她的脸色有所上升；然而，她以相当从容的态度接待了他们，举止得体，既没有任何怨恨的迹象，也没有任何不必要的奉承。
伊丽莎白对两人尽可能保持礼貌，只说了很少的话，然后又坐下来继续她的工作，她投入的热情是平时很少有的。她只敢看达西一眼。他像往常一样显得严肃；她觉得，他的神情更像是在赫特福德郡时的样子，而不是她在彭伯利见过的模样。不过，也许在她母亲面前，他无法像在她的舅舅和舅妈面前那样表现自己。这是一个令人痛苦，但并非不可能的推测。
宾利她也曾一瞥，并在那短暂的时间里看到他显得既高兴又尴尬。班纳特太太以一种礼貌的态度接待了他，这种礼貌让她的两个女儿感到羞愧，尤其是当与她对他朋友所表现出的冷淡且拘谨的礼仪和举止相比时。
尤其是伊丽莎白，她知道母亲将自己最宠爱的女儿从无法挽回的耻辱中保护出来，都要归功于后者，因此如此不当的区别对待让她感到极其受伤和痛苦。

达西在询问她加德纳先生和夫人的情况后——一个她无法不感到困惑就回答的问题——几乎没有说什么。他并没有坐在她身边：也许这就是他沉默的原因；但在德比郡并非如此。在那里，当他无法与她交谈时，他会与她的朋友们交谈。但现在过了好几分钟，仍未听到他的声音；偶尔，当她无法抗拒好奇心的冲动抬起眼睛看他的脸时，她发现他看着简的次数和看她的次数一样多，而且经常只盯着地面看。比上次见面时更显出思虑更多、取悦之心较少的神态。她感到失望，并为自己的这种失望而生气。

title: Great Expectations · 选段 4
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: “Besides,” said Mr. Pumblechook, turning sharp on me, “think what you’ve got to be grateful for. If you’d been born a Squeaker—”
“Well, but I mean a four-footed Squeaker,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “If you had been born such, would you have been here now? Not you—”

“But I don’t mean in that form, sir,” returned Mr. Pumblechook, who had an objection to being interrupted; “I mean, enjoying himself with his elders and betters, and improving himself with their conversation, and rolling in the lap of luxury. Would he have been doing that? No, he wouldn’t. And what would have been your destination?” turning on me again. “You would have been disposed of for so many shillings according to the market price of the article, and Dunstable the butcher would have come up to you as you lay in your straw, and he would have whipped you under his left arm, and with his right he would have tucked up his frock to get a penknife from out of his waistcoat-pocket, and he would have shed your blood and had your life. No bringing up by hand then. Not a bit of it!”

“Trouble?” echoed my sister; “trouble?” and then entered on a fearful catalogue of all the illnesses I had been guilty of, and all the acts of sleeplessness I had committed, and all the high places I had tumbled from, and all the low places I had tumbled into, and all the injuries I had done myself, and all the times she had wished me in my grave, and I had contumaciously refused to go there.

I think the Romans must have aggravated one another very much, with their noses. Perhaps, they became the restless people they were, in consequence. Anyhow, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose so aggravated me, during the recital of my misdemeanours, that I should have liked to pull it until he howled. But, all I had endured up to this time was nothing in comparison with the awful feelings that took possession of me when the pause was broken which ensued upon my sister’s recital, and in which pause everybody had looked at me (as I felt painfully conscious) with indignation and abhorrence.
“Yet,” said Mr. Pumblechook, leading the company gently back to the theme from which they had strayed, “Pork—regarded as biled—is rich, too; ain’t it?”
O Heavens, it had come at last! He would find it was weak, he would say it was weak, and I was lost! I held tight to the leg of the table under the cloth, with both hands, and awaited my fate.

My sister went for the stone bottle, came back with the stone bottle, and poured his brandy out: no one else taking any. The wretched man trifled with his glass,—took it up, looked at it through the light, put it down,—prolonged my misery. All this time Mrs. Joe and Joe were briskly clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn’t keep my eyes off him. Always holding tight by the leg of the table with my hands and feet, I saw the miserable creature finger his glass playfully, take it up, smile, throw his head back, and drink the brandy off. Instantly afterwards, the company were seized with unspeakable consternation, owing to his springing to his feet, turning round several times in an appalling spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and rushing out at the door; he then became visible through the window, violently plunging and expectorating, making the most hideous faces, and apparently out of his mind.

I held on tight, while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him. I didn’t know how I had done it, but I had no doubt I had murdered him somehow. In my dreadful situation, it was a relief when he was brought back, and surveying the company all round as if they had disagreed with him, sank down into his chair with the one significant gasp, “Tar!”
paragraphsZh: “此外，”庞布尔乔克先生转向我，严厉地说，“想想你应该感激什么。如果你生来就是一个吱吱叫的——”
“嗯，但我是指一个四条腿的吱吱叫的，”庞布尔乔克先生说。“如果你生来是那样的，你现在会在这里吗？当然不会——”
“但我不是说那种形式，先生，”彭布尔丘克先生反对被打断;“我是说，和长辈及上级一起享受时光，通过他们的谈话提升自己，享受奢华的怀抱。他会那样做吗？不会。那你的目的地会是什么？”他又转向我。“你会被按商品市场价卖掉多少先令，屠夫邓斯特布尔会走到你躺在吸管里时，用左臂抽打你，右臂挽起裙子，从马甲口袋里掏出小刀，然后流你的血，夺走你的生命。那就不能用手抚养了。一点都不！”
“麻烦？”我妹妹回声般地说；“麻烦？”然后列出了我曾犯过的所有疾病，犯过的所有失眠行为，从所有高处摔下的经历，跌入的所有低谷，对自己造成的所有伤害，以及她曾希望我早早离世的所有时刻，而我固执地拒绝了去那里。
我想罗马人一定彼此非常惹恼对方，尤其是用他们的鼻子。也许，这就是他们最终变得不安分的原因。无论如何，沃普斯尔先生的罗马鼻在我叙述自己的过失时让我非常恼火，我真想一边拉着它一边让他尖叫。但在此之前我所忍受的一切，与我姐姐叙述完毕后随之而来的沉默所带来的可怕感受相比，根本算不了什么，在那短暂的沉默中，每个人都用愤怒和厌恶的目光看着我（正如我痛苦地意识到的那样）。
“不过，”庞布尔丘克先生温和地把大家的注意力拉回到偏离的主题上说，“猪肉——要是煮熟了——也很美味，不是吗？”
天啊，这一刻终于来了！他会发现它是淡的，他会说它是淡的，而我完了！我双手紧握桌子腿，藏在桌布下面，等待我的命运。
我的姐姐去拿石瓶，拿回来后倒出了他的白兰地：其他人都没有喝。那个可怜的人摆弄着他的酒杯——拿起来，通过光看了看，又放下——延长了我的痛苦。与此同时，乔夫人和乔正麻利地清理桌子，为派和布丁让路。
我无法将目光从他身上移开。我总是用手和脚紧紧抓住桌腿，我看到这个可怜的家伙顽皮地拨弄着他的酒杯，拿起来，微笑着，仰头，把白兰地喝光。随即，所有人都陷入难以形容的惊恐之中，因为他猛地站起身，转了好几圈，进行一种可怕的痉挛性咳嗽舞蹈，然后冲出门；随后他从窗户里可见，剧烈地扑腾和吐痰，做出最可怕的表情，显然已经失去了理智。
我紧紧抓住，而乔夫人和乔跑向他。我不知道我是怎么做到的，但我毫不怀疑自己以某种方式杀了他。在我可怕的处境中，当他被带回来的时候，我感到一丝宽慰，他环视着周围的众人，好像他们与他意见不合，然后带着那唯一重要的喘息声，坐回他的椅子上，说：“鞭打！”

title: Great Expectations · 选段 5
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: —still, in my desire to be wiser, I got this composition by heart with the utmost gravity; nor do I recollect that I questioned its merit, except that I thought (as I still do) the amount of Too rul somewhat in excess of the poetry. In my hunger for information, I made proposals to Mr. Wopsle to bestow some intellectual crumbs upon me, with which he kindly complied. As it turned out, however, that he only wanted me for a dramatic lay-figure, to be contradicted and embraced and wept over and bullied and clutched and stabbed and knocked about in a variety of ways, I soon declined that course of instruction; though not until Mr. Wopsle in his poetic fury had severely mauled me.

Whatever I acquired, I tried to impart to Joe. This statement sounds so well, that I cannot in my conscience let it pass unexplained. I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common, that he might be worthier of my society and less open to Estella’s reproach.

The old Battery out on the marshes was our place of study, and a broken slate and a short piece of slate-pencil were our educational implements: to which Joe always added a pipe of tobacco. I never knew Joe to remember anything from one Sunday to another, or to acquire, under my tuition, any piece of information whatever. Yet he would smoke his pipe at the Battery with a far more sagacious air than anywhere else,—even with a learned air,—as if he considered himself to be advancing immensely. Dear fellow, I hope he did.

It was pleasant and quiet, out there with the sails on the river passing beyond the earthwork, and sometimes, when the tide was low, looking as if they belonged to sunken ships that were still sailing on at the bottom of the water. Whenever I watched the vessels standing out to sea with their white sails spread, I somehow thought of Miss Havisham and Estella; and whenever the light struck aslant, afar off, upon a cloud or sail or green hillside or water-line, it was just the same.—Miss Havisham and Estella and the strange house and the strange life appeared to have something to do with everything that was picturesque.

One Sunday when Joe, greatly enjoying his pipe, had so plumed himself on being “most awful dull,” that I had given him up for the day, I lay on the earthwork for some time with my chin on my hand, descrying traces of Miss Havisham and Estella all over the prospect, in the sky and in the water, until at last I resolved to mention a thought concerning them that had been much in my head.
“There is some wisits p’r’aps,” said Joe, “as for ever remains open to the question, Pip. But in regard to wisiting Miss Havisham. She might think you wanted something,—expected something of her.”
Joe felt, as I did, that he had made a point there, and he pulled hard at his pipe to keep himself from weakening it by repetition.

“You see, Pip,” Joe pursued, as soon as he was past that danger, “Miss Havisham done the handsome thing by you. When Miss Havisham done the handsome thing by you, she called me back to say to me as that were all.”
I had thought of that too, and it was very far from comforting to me to find that he had thought of it; for it seemed to render it more probable.

But Joe had got the idea of a present in his head and must harp upon it. “Or even,” said he, “if you was helped to knocking her up a new chain for the front door,—or say a gross or two of shark-headed screws for general use,—or some light fancy article, such as a toasting-fork when she took her muffins,—or a gridiron when she took a sprat or such like—”
paragraphsZh: ——尽管如此，为了追求更大的智慧，我还是以极其严肃的态度将这篇文章背了下来；我也不记得曾质疑过它的价值，只是我曾认为（现在依然如此）其中批评的数量有些超过了诗的本身。出于对知识的渴望，我向沃普斯尔先生提出请求，希望他能施舍一些智力的“面包屑”给我，他也友善地答应了。然而，事实证明，他只想要我作为一个戏剧性的木偶，被反驳、被拥抱、被哭泣、被欺辱、被抓握、被刺伤和以各种方式被碰撞，我很快就放弃了这种教学方式；尽管在此之前，沃普斯尔先生在他的诗性狂热中已经严重地伤害了我。
无论我获得了什么，我都尝试传授给乔。这个说法听起来很不错，以至于我凭良心不能让它不加解释地过去。我想让乔少些无知和平庸，让他更配得上我的陪伴，也不那么容易受到埃斯特拉的责备。
沼泽地上的旧炮台是我们的学习之地，而一块破碎的石板和一小段石板笔是我们的教育工具：乔总是会加上一根烟斗。我从未见过乔能从一个星期天记住事情到下一个星期天，或者在我的教导下学到任何信息。然而，他在炮台上抽烟斗时，总显得比其他地方更有智慧气度——甚至带着学者的样子——仿佛觉得自己在取得巨大的进步。亲爱的伙伴，我希望他确实如此。
外面江上风帆飘荡，越过土堤，一切都显得宜人而宁静；有时潮水低落，看起来仿佛是沉没船只仍在水底航行。每当我注视那些扬起白帆驶向大海的船只时，不知为何就会想起哈维沙姆小姐和埃斯特拉；每当光线斜照在远处的云彩、帆、绿坡或水线时，情况也是一样。——哈维沙姆小姐、埃斯特拉、那个奇怪的房子以及奇异的生活似乎与一切风景如画的事物都有某种关联。
一个星期天，当乔悠然地享受着他的烟斗，自夸自己是“最无聊的”，以至于我那天已经不打算再理他时，我躺在土堤上，用手托着下巴，盯着四周的景象，试图在天上和水里看到哈维舍姆小姐和埃斯特拉的痕迹，直到我最后决定提起一个关于她们的念头，这个念头在我脑海中盘旋已久。
“也许有些拜访，”乔说，“总是留有疑问，皮普。不过说到去拜访哈维舍姆小姐，她可能会以为你想要什么——期待她做些什么。”
乔觉得自己点到了要害，就像我一样，他使劲吸了几口烟斗，以免通过重复而削弱他的观点。
“你看，皮普，”乔一旦渡过那个危险就继续说，“哈维香小姐对你做了件好事。当哈维香小姐对你做了件好事时，她叫我回来告诉我，就当那已足够了。”
我也曾想过这件事，而发现他也想到了这一点，对我来说一点都不安慰；因为这似乎使它更有可能是真的。
但是乔脑子里已经有了送礼物的念头，必须不停地提起它。“或者，”他说，“如果有人帮你去给她的前门做一条新链子，——或者说帮她弄一两打鲨鱼头螺丝用作日常用途，——或者一些轻便的小玩意儿，比如她吃松饼时用的烤叉，——或者她吃小鲱鱼时用的烤架什么的——”

title: Great Expectations · 选段 6
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: I thought Mr. Jaggers glanced at Joe, as if he considered him a fool for his disinterestedness. But I was too much bewildered between breathless curiosity and surprise, to be sure of it.
“Very well,” said Mr. Jaggers. “Recollect the admission you have made, and don’t try to go from it presently.”

“Bear in mind then, that Brag is a good dog, but Holdfast is a better. Bear that in mind, will you?” repeated Mr. Jaggers, shutting his eyes and nodding his head at Joe, as if he were forgiving him something. “Now, I return to this young fellow. And the communication I have got to make is, that he has great expectations.”

“I am instructed to communicate to him,” said Mr. Jaggers, throwing his finger at me sideways, “that he will come into a handsome property. Further, that it is the desire of the present possessor of that property, that he be immediately removed from his present sphere of life and from this place, and be brought up as a gentleman,—in a word, as a young fellow of great expectations.”
My dream was out; my wild fancy was surpassed by sober reality; Miss Havisham was going to make my fortune on a grand scale.

“Now, Mr. Pip,” pursued the lawyer, “I address the rest of what I have to say, to you. You are to understand, first, that it is the request of the person from whom I take my instructions that you always bear the name of Pip. You will have no objection, I dare say, to your great expectations being encumbered with that easy condition. But if you have any objection, this is the time to mention it.”
My heart was beating so fast, and there was such a singing in my ears, that I could scarcely stammer I had no objection.

“I should think not! Now you are to understand, secondly, Mr. Pip, that the name of the person who is your liberal benefactor remains a profound secret, until the person chooses to reveal it. I am empowered to mention that it is the intention of the person to reveal it at first hand by word of mouth to yourself. When or where that intention may be carried out, I cannot say; no one can say. It may be years hence. Now, you are distinctly to understand that you are most positively prohibited from making any inquiry on this head, or any allusion or reference, however distant, to any individual whomsoever as the individual, in all the communications you may have with me. If you have a suspicion in your own breast, keep that suspicion in your own breast. It is not the least to the purpose what the reasons of this prohibition are; they may be the strongest and gravest reasons, or they may be mere whim. This is not for you to inquire into. The condition is laid down. Your acceptance of it, and your observance of it as binding, is the only remaining condition that I am charged with, by the person from whom I take my instructions, and for whom I am not otherwise responsible. That person is the person from whom you derive your expectations, and the secret is solely held by that person and by me. Again, not a very difficult condition with which to encumber such a rise in fortune; but if you have any objection to it, this is the time to mention it. Speak out.”

“I should think not! Now, Mr. Pip, I have done with stipulations.” Though he called me Mr. Pip, and began rather to make up to me, he still could not get rid of a certain air of bullying suspicion; and even now he occasionally shut his eyes and threw his finger at me while he spoke, as much as to express that he knew all kinds of things to my disparagement, if he only chose to mention them. “We come next, to mere details of arrangement. You must know that, although I have used the term ‘expectations’ more than once, you are not endowed with expectations only. There is already lodged in my hands a sum of money amply sufficient for your suitable education and maintenance. You will please consider me your guardian. Oh!” for I was going to thank him, “I tell you at once, I am paid for my services, or I shouldn’t render them. It is considered that you must be better educated, in accordance with your altered position, and that you will be alive to the importance and necessity of at once entering on that advantage.”
paragraphsZh: 我以为贾格斯先生看乔的时候，好像觉得他因为无私而是个傻瓜。但我在呼吸急促的好奇和惊讶之间太过迷惑，不能确定这一点。
“很好，”贾格斯先生说。“记住你已经承认的事情，现在不要试图否认。”
“那么记住，Brag 是条好狗，但 Holdfast 更好。记住这一点，好吗？”贾格斯先生重复说道，闭上眼睛，对乔点头，好像在原谅他什么。“现在，我回到这个年轻人身上。我必须传达的信息是，他有很大的期望。”
“我被指示要将这个消息传达给他，”贾格尔斯先生说着，侧着手指指向我，“他将继承一笔可观的财产。此外，目前财产的持有者希望他立即离开现有的生活环境和这个地方，接受绅士的培养——总之，成为一个大有前途的青年。”
我的梦想破灭了，我狂野的幻想被清醒的现实超过了；哈维舍姆小姐将以宏大的方式让我继承财富。
“现在，皮普先生，”律师继续说道，“我接下来说的其余部分，是对你说的。你首先要明白，我受命的当事人希望你一直保留皮普这个名字。我敢说，你对自己的巨大期望被附加上这个简单条件，是不会有异议的。但是，如果你有任何异议，现在就是提出的时候。”
我的心跳得非常快，耳朵里嗡嗡作响，以至于我几乎结结巴巴地说不出我没有异议。

“我想不可能！现在你必须明白，第二点，皮普先生，你那位慷慨资助者的名字仍然是一个深奥的秘密，直到那个人选择揭晓为止。我有权提到，这个人打算亲口当面告诉你。何时何地会实现这个意图，我无法说；没人能说。可能是多年之后。现在，你必须清楚地明白，在你与我所有的交流中，你被明确禁止就此事进行任何询问，或提及、暗示任何个人作为资助者，无论这种提及多么间接。如果你心中有怀疑，就把怀疑留在自己心里。”这个禁令的原因是什么，根本无关紧要；原因可能是最强有力、最严肃的，也可能只是一个简单的心血来潮。这不是你该去探究的。条件已经确定。你接受它，并视其为具有约束力地遵守，这是我根据我所接受指示的人所交付的唯一定的条件，而我对他人不承担其他责任。那个人就是你期望的来源，这个秘密仅由那个人和我保守。同样，这并不是一个很难的条件来阻碍如此的好运；但如果你有任何异议，现在就是提出的时候。请直言。」

“我想不可能吧！现在，皮普先生，我与附加条件已经说完了。”虽然他叫我皮普先生，并且开始有些讨好我，但他仍然摆脱不了那种欺压和怀疑的气息；即使现在，他说话时偶尔也会闭上眼睛，用手指指着我，似乎在表示，如果他愿意提的话，他知道各种能让我丢脸的事情。“接下来，我们要谈的只是安排的细节。你必须知道，虽然我不止一次使用了‘期望’这个词，但你不只是被赋予期望。我手上已经存有一笔资金，足以满足你适当的教育和生活开支。请把我视作你的监护人。哦！”因为我正打算感谢他，“我立刻告诉你，我的服务是有报酬的，否则我不会提供。这被认为你必须接受更好的教育，以符合你改变后的地位，并且你会意识到立刻开始利用这一优势的重要性和必要性。”

title: Great Expectations · 选段 7
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: “Gracious me, Flopson!” said Mrs. Pocket, looking off her book for a moment, “everybody’s tumbling!”
“Why, if it ain’t your footstool!” cried Flopson. “And if you keep it under your skirts like that, who’s to help tumbling? Here! Take the baby, Mum, and give me your book.”

Mrs. Pocket acted on the advice, and inexpertly danced the infant a little in her lap, while the other children played about it. This had lasted but a very short time, when Mrs. Pocket issued summary orders that they were all to be taken into the house for a nap. Thus I made the second discovery on that first occasion, that the nurture of the little Pockets consisted of alternately tumbling up and lying down.

Under these circumstances, when Flopson and Millers had got the children into the house, like a little flock of sheep, and Mr. Pocket came out of it to make my acquaintance, I was not much surprised to find that Mr. Pocket was a gentleman with a rather perplexed expression of face, and with his very grey hair disordered on his head, as if he didn’t quite see his way to putting anything straight.

Mr. Pocket said he was glad to see me, and he hoped I was not sorry to see him. “For, I really am not,” he added, with his son’s smile, “an alarming personage.” He was a young-looking man, in spite of his perplexities and his very grey hair, and his manner seemed quite natural. I use the word natural, in the sense of its being unaffected; there was something comic in his distraught way, as though it would have been downright ludicrous but for his own perception that it was very near being so. When he had talked with me a little, he said to Mrs. Pocket, with a rather anxious contraction of his eyebrows, which were black and handsome, “Belinda, I hope you have welcomed Mr. Pip?” And she looked up from her book, and said, “Yes.” She then smiled upon me in an absent state of mind, and asked me if I liked the taste of orange-flower water? As the question had no bearing, near or remote, on any foregone or subsequent transaction, I consider it to have been thrown out, like her previous approaches, in general conversational condescension.

I found out within a few hours, and may mention at once, that Mrs. Pocket was the only daughter of a certain quite accidental deceased Knight, who had invented for himself a conviction that his deceased father would have been made a Baronet but for somebody’s determined opposition arising out of entirely personal motives,—I forget whose, if I ever knew,—the Sovereign’s, the Prime Minister’s, the Lord Chancellor’s, the Archbishop of Canterbury’s, anybody’s,—and had tacked himself on to the nobles of the earth in right of this quite supposititious fact. I believe he had been knighted himself for storming the English grammar at the point of the pen, in a desperate address engrossed on vellum, on the occasion of the laying of the first stone of some building or other, and for handing some Royal Personage either the trowel or the mortar. Be that as it may, he had directed Mrs. Pocket to be brought up from her cradle as one who in the nature of things must marry a title, and who was to be guarded from the acquisition of plebeian domestic knowledge.

So successful a watch and ward had been established over the young lady by this judicious parent, that she had grown up highly ornamental, but perfectly helpless and useless. With her character thus happily formed, in the first bloom of her youth she had encountered Mr. Pocket: who was also in the first bloom of youth, and not quite decided whether to mount to the Woolsack, or to roof himself in with a mitre. As his doing the one or the other was a mere question of time, he and Mrs. Pocket had taken Time by the forelock (when, to judge from its length, it would seem to have wanted cutting), and had married without the knowledge of the judicious parent. The judicious parent, having nothing to bestow or withhold but his blessing, had handsomely settled that dower upon them after a short struggle, and had informed Mr. Pocket that his wife was “a treasure for a Prince.” Mr. Pocket had invested the Prince’s treasure in the ways of the world ever since, and it was supposed to have brought him in but indifferent interest. Still, Mrs. Pocket was in general the object of a queer sort of respectful pity, because she had not married a title; while Mr. Pocket was the object of a queer sort of forgiving reproach, because he had never got one.
paragraphsZh: “天哪，Flopson！”Pocket太太抬起头看了一会书，说道，“大家都在翻滚呢！”
“哎呀，不就是你的脚凳吗！”Flopson喊道。“如果你一直把它放在裙子下面，还能帮谁翻滚呢？来吧！把孩子交给我，妈，把你的书给我。”
Pocket太太照着建议去做，笨拙地在膝上晃了一下婴儿，其他孩子则在旁边玩耍。这持续时间很短，Pocket太太很快就下令，他们都要被叫进屋里午睡。于是我在第一次经历时就有了第二个发现：小Pocket们的养育方式就是轮流翻滚然后躺下。
在这种情况下，当弗洛普森和米勒斯把孩子们带进屋子里，就像一小群绵羊一样，而波克特先生从屋里出来与我相识时，我并不太惊讶地发现，波克特先生是一个面带相当困惑表情的绅士，头上的灰发凌乱，好像他并不太明白该如何把事情理顺。

波克特先生说他很高兴见到我，并希望我见到他不会感到遗憾。“因为，我真的没有，”他带着儿子的微笑补充道，“是一个令人害怕的人物。”尽管他有困惑和非常灰白的头发，他看起来仍像一个年轻人，而且他的举止似乎非常自然。我使用“自然”这个词，是指毫不做作；他那焦虑的样子带着几分滑稽，如果不是他自己意识到那几乎滑稽，这种搞笑的感觉就更明显了。当他和我说了一会儿话，他带着略显焦虑的眉毛皱起（眉毛乌黑而漂亮），对波琳达夫人说：“贝琳达，我希望你已经欢迎了皮普先生？”她从书中抬起头说道：“是的。”然后她心不在焉地朝我微笑，并问我是否喜欢橙花水的味道？由于这个问题与任何已发生或将要发生的事务无关，无论是近还是远，我认为它像她先前的接近一样，只是出于一般谈话中的居高临下的态度随意提出的。

我在几个小时内就发现了，并可能立刻提到，波克特太太是某位意外去世的骑士的唯一女儿，这位骑士为自己创造了一个信念——如果不是因为某人的完全出于个人动机的坚决反对，他去世的父亲本可以被封为准男爵——我忘记了是谁，如果我曾知道的话——是君主的、首相的、大法官的、坎特伯雷大主教的，还是其他人的——然后他便依据这个完全虚构的事实，把自己附加到世上的贵族之列。我相信他自己也曾因挥笔冲击英国语法而被封为骑士，这是在某个建筑奠基仪式上，用羊皮纸写下的一篇拼命的演讲，同时还可能为王室人物递上了泥刀或砂浆。不管怎样，他已经指示把波克特太太从摇篮中带上来，仿佛她天生就该嫁入贵族，而要防止她获得平民的家庭知识。

这位明智的父母对这位年轻女士建立了如此成功的看护，以至于她长大后极具装饰性，却完全无助且无用。凭借她这样美好形成的性格，在青春的最初花季，她遇到了Pocket先生：他也是青春的最初花季，还未完全决定是要登上法官之座，还是戴上主教的帽子。因为他选择哪条路只是时间问题，他和Pocket太太抓住了时间的前额（从长度上判断，它似乎需要修剪），在明智的父母不知情的情况下结了婚。这位明智的父母既没有可以给予或拒绝的东西，除了他的祝福，于是经过一场短暂的斗争后，他大方地为他们安排了这份嫁妆，并告知Pocket先生。波克特先生认为他的妻子是“王子的珍宝”。自那时起，波克特先生就把王子的财宝投资于世俗之道，本应为他带来可观的利息。然而，波克特夫人总体上是那种奇怪的、带有尊敬的同情的对象，因为她没有嫁一个有头衔的人；而波克特先生则是那种奇怪的、带有宽容责备的对象，因为他从未得到过头衔。

title: Great Expectations · 选段 8
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: As we were going back together to London by the midday coach, and as I breakfasted under such terrors of Pumblechook that I could scarcely hold my cup, this gave me an opportunity of saying that I wanted a walk, and that I would go on along the London road while Mr. Jaggers was occupied, if he would let the coachman know that I would get into my place when overtaken. I was thus enabled to fly from the Blue Boar immediately after breakfast. By then making a loop of about a couple of miles into the open country at the back of Pumblechook’s premises, I got round into the High Street again, a little beyond that pitfall, and felt myself in comparative security.

It was interesting to be in the quiet old town once more, and it was not disagreeable to be here and there suddenly recognised and stared after. One or two of the tradespeople even darted out of their shops and went a little way down the street before me, that they might turn, as if they had forgotten something, and pass me face to face,—on which occasions I don’t know whether they or I made the worse pretence; they of not doing it, or I of not seeing it. Still my position was a distinguished one, and I was not at all dissatisfied with it, until Fate threw me in the way of that unlimited miscreant, Trabb’s boy.

Casting my eyes along the street at a certain point of my progress, I beheld Trabb’s boy approaching, lashing himself with an empty blue bag. Deeming that a serene and unconscious contemplation of him would best beseem me, and would be most likely to quell his evil mind, I advanced with that expression of countenance, and was rather congratulating myself on my success, when suddenly the knees of Trabb’s boy smote together, his hair uprose, his cap fell off, he trembled violently in every limb, staggered out into the road, and crying to the populace, “Hold me! I’m so frightened!” feigned to be in a paroxysm of terror and contrition, occasioned by the dignity of my appearance. As I passed him, his teeth loudly chattered in his head, and with every mark of extreme humiliation, he prostrated himself in the dust.

This was a hard thing to bear, but this was nothing. I had not advanced another two hundred yards when, to my inexpressible terror, amazement, and indignation, I again beheld Trabb’s boy approaching. He was coming round a narrow corner. His blue bag was slung over his shoulder, honest industry beamed in his eyes, a determination to proceed to Trabb’s with cheerful briskness was indicated in his gait. With a shock he became aware of me, and was severely visited as before; but this time his motion was rotatory, and he staggered round and round me with knees more afflicted, and with uplifted hands as if beseeching for mercy. His sufferings were hailed with the greatest joy by a knot of spectators, and I felt utterly confounded.

I had not got as much further down the street as the post-office, when I again beheld Trabb’s boy shooting round by a back way. This time, he was entirely changed. He wore the blue bag in the manner of my great-coat, and was strutting along the pavement towards me on the opposite side of the street, attended by a company of delighted young friends to whom he from time to time exclaimed, with a wave of his hand, “Don’t know yah!” Words cannot state the amount of aggravation and injury wreaked upon me by Trabb’s boy, when passing abreast of me, he pulled up his shirt-collar, twined his side-hair, stuck an arm akimbo, and smirked extravagantly by, wriggling his elbows and body, and drawling to his attendants, “Don’t know yah, don’t know yah, ’pon my soul don’t know yah!” The disgrace attendant on his immediately afterwards taking to crowing and pursuing me across the bridge with crows, as from an exceedingly dejected fowl who had known me when I was a blacksmith, culminated the disgrace with which I left the town, and was, so to speak, ejected by it into the open country.
paragraphsZh: 当我们一起坐中午的长途汽车回伦敦时，我在彭布尔丘克的恐吓下吃早饭，几乎拿不稳杯子，这给了我一个机会说我想去散步，如果他愿意让车夫知道我会在赶上汽车时回到座位上，我会沿着伦敦路走一会儿。这样我在早餐后就能立即从蓝公牛酒店溜走。然后，我绕开彭布尔丘克宅邸后方的开阔地大约走了两英里，重新回到高街，稍微越过那片陷阱，我觉得自己比较安全了。
再次置身于宁静的老城是件有趣的事，而偶尔被人认出并盯着看也并不令人不悦。有一两位商人甚至从店里冲出来，朝街上走了一小段，好像是要转身回去，仿佛他们忘了什么，然后与我面对面经过——在这种情况下，我不知道是他们假装没看到的更糟，还是我假装没看到的更糟。不过，我的地位还是很显眼的，我对这一点毫不不满，直到命运让我遇上了那个极其卑劣的家伙——特拉布的小子。

当我沿着街道走到某一点时，我看到特拉布的男孩走近，用一个空蓝色袋子抽打自己。我认为，以平静且无意识地注视他最适合我，也最有可能平息他邪恶的心思，于是我带着那种表情走上前去，并因自己取得的成功而略感自我欣慰，然而突然间，特拉布的男孩膝盖撞到一起，头发竖起，帽子掉了，他全身剧烈颤抖，踉跄着走到路中间，并对众人喊道：“抓住我！我好害怕！”佯装因为我的庄重外表而陷入一阵恐惧和懊悔。在我经过他时，他的牙齿在头里咯咯作响，并以极度羞辱的姿态，匍匐在尘土中。

这是件难以忍受的事，但这算不了什么。我又前进了不到两百码，出乎我难以形容的恐惧、惊讶和愤慨，我再次看到特拉布的男孩走来了。他正绕过一个狭窄的转角。他的蓝色书包背在肩上，眼中闪烁着诚实的勤奋，他步态轻快，显然决心愉快地前往特拉布家。忽然，他察觉到我，像以前一样受到了严厉的惩罚；但这一次他的动作是旋转的，他围着我踉踉跄跄地转圈，膝盖更加受罪，双手举起，仿佛在乞求宽恕。他的痛苦引来一群观众的极大欢喜，而我感到完全困惑。

我还没走到邮局那条街的尽头，就又看见特拉布的孩子从后面的小路跑出来。这一次，他完全变了样。他穿着蓝色手提包，就像穿着我的大衣一样，昂首阔步地走在人行道上，朝我所在的街对面走来，身边还跟着一群兴奋的小朋友，他不时地挥挥手，对他们喊道：“不认识你！” 当特拉布的孩子从我身边走过，拉高衬衫领子、拧弄鬓角、叉着腰、夸张地扭动胳膊和身体，然后对小伙伴们慢吞吞地说：“不认识你，不认识你，老天啊，我真不认识你！”时，他给我带来的恼怒和伤害是无法用语言表达的。在他紧接着开始叫嚣并带着乌鸦追我穿过桥时所带来的耻辱，就像一只极度沮丧的鸟，它曾经认识我，当我还是一个铁匠时，这种耻辱达到了顶点，我离开小镇时的耻辱就是如此，可以说，是它把我赶向了开阔的乡间。

title: Great Expectations · 选段 9
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: Next day the clothes I had ordered all came home, and he put them on. Whatever he put on, became him less (it dismally seemed to me) than what he had worn before. To my thinking, there was something in him that made it hopeless to attempt to disguise him. The more I dressed him and the better I dressed him, the more he looked like the slouching fugitive on the marshes. This effect on my anxious fancy was partly referable, no doubt, to his old face and manner growing more familiar to me; but I believe too that he dragged one of his legs as if there were still a weight of iron on it, and that from head to foot there was Convict in the very grain of the man.

The influences of his solitary hut-life were upon him besides, and gave him a savage air that no dress could tame; added to these were the influences of his subsequent branded life among men, and, crowning all, his consciousness that he was dodging and hiding now. In all his ways of sitting and standing, and eating and drinking,—of brooding about in a high-shouldered reluctant style,—of taking out his great horn-handled jackknife and wiping it on his legs and cutting his food,—of lifting light glasses and cups to his lips, as if they were clumsy pannikins,—of chopping a wedge off his bread, and soaking up with it the last fragments of gravy round and round his plate, as if to make the most of an allowance, and then drying his finger-ends on it, and then swallowing it,—in these ways and a thousand other small nameless instances arising every minute in the day, there was Prisoner, Felon, Bondsman, plain as plain could be.

It had been his own idea to wear that touch of powder, and I had conceded the powder after overcoming the shorts. But I can compare the effect of it, when on, to nothing but the probable effect of rouge upon the dead; so awful was the manner in which everything in him that it was most desirable to repress, started through that thin layer of pretence, and seemed to come blazing out at the crown of his head. It was abandoned as soon as tried, and he wore his grizzled hair cut short.

Words cannot tell what a sense I had, at the same time, of the dreadful mystery that he was to me. When he fell asleep of an evening, with his knotted hands clenching the sides of the easy-chair, and his bald head tattooed with deep wrinkles falling forward on his breast, I would sit and look at him, wondering what he had done, and loading him with all the crimes in the Calendar, until the impulse was powerful on me to start up and fly from him. Every hour so increased my abhorrence of him, that I even think I might have yielded to this impulse in the first agonies of being so haunted, notwithstanding all he had done for me and the risk he ran, but for the knowledge that Herbert must soon come back. Once, I actually did start out of bed in the night, and begin to dress myself in my worst clothes, hurriedly intending to leave him there with everything else I possessed, and enlist for India as a private soldier.

I doubt if a ghost could have been more terrible to me, up in those lonely rooms in the long evenings and long nights, with the wind and the rain always rushing by. A ghost could not have been taken and hanged on my account, and the consideration that he could be, and the dread that he would be, were no small addition to my horrors. When he was not asleep, or playing a complicated kind of Patience with a ragged pack of cards of his own,—a game that I never saw before or since, and in which he recorded his winnings by sticking his jackknife into the table,—when he was not engaged in either of these pursuits, he would ask me to read to him,—“Foreign language, dear boy!” While I complied, he, not comprehending a single word, would stand before the fire surveying me with the air of an Exhibitor, and I would see him, between the fingers of the hand with which I shaded my face, appealing in dumb show to the furniture to take notice of my proficiency. The imaginary student pursued by the misshapen creature he had impiously made, was not more wretched than I, pursued by the creature who had made me, and recoiling from him with a stronger repulsion, the more he admired me and the fonder he was of me.
paragraphsZh: 第二天，我订购的衣服全部送到了家里，他把它们穿上。不管他穿上什么，对于他来说都显得不如之前穿的（在我看来悲惨得多）。在我看来，他身上有某种东西，使得试图掩饰他显得毫无希望。不管我怎么给他打扮，打扮得再好，他看起来就越像沼泽地上那个懒散的逃犯。这种在我焦虑的想象中的效果，毫无疑问，部分是由于我对他那张老面孔和举止越来越熟悉；但我也相信，他走路拖着一条腿，就像上面还压着沉重的铁块，从头到脚，这个人的每一根血肉里都是罪犯的本质。

他孤独的茅屋生活对他产生了影响，给了他一种任何衣着也无法驯服的野性气息；除此之外，还有他后来在人群中受标记生活的影响，更重要的是，他意识到自己现在正在躲避和隐藏。无论他坐姿、站姿，吃喝方式——用高肩膀、勉强的姿态沉思——拿出他那把大号角柄小刀，擦在腿上再切食物——将轻薄的玻璃杯和茶杯举到唇边，仿佛它们是笨拙的小杯——切下一块面包，用它吸干盘子里最后的肉汁，好像要充分利用每一份食物，然后用面包擦干手指，再吞下去——在这些行为以及一天中每分钟都会出现的千百个小而无名的细节里，囚犯、罪犯、奴隶，明白得不能再明白了，清晰可见。
这是他自己提出要抹一点粉的主意，而我在克服了阻力后也同意了抹粉。但我只能把它起作用时的效果比作胭脂作用于死者的可能效果；因为他身上那些最想压抑的东西，透过那层薄薄的伪装，似乎都以可怕的方式爆发出来，从他的头顶迸发出来。尝试过后就被放弃了，他把灰白的头发剪短了。

言语无法表达我同时对他感到的那种强烈的恐惧与神秘感。当他在晚上入睡时，双手紧握扶手，光秃的头上布满深深的皱纹垂落在胸前，我会坐在那里注视他，想着他做过什么，把日历上的所有罪行都加在他身上，直到那种强烈的冲动使我想要站起来逃离他。每一刻都加深了我对他的厌恶，以至于我甚至认为在被如此困扰的最初痛苦中，我可能会屈从于这种冲动，尽管他为我所做的一切和他所冒的风险，但我知道赫伯特很快就会回来。有一次，我真的在夜里从床上起来，开始穿上我最差的衣服，急忙打算把我拥有的一切都留给他，然后去应征到印度当一名列兵。

我怀疑即使是鬼魂，也无法比那孤寂房间里的漫长傍晚和漫长夜晚里伴随着风雨呼啸而过的情景给我带来更多的恐惧。为了我而捉住并绞死一个鬼魂是不可能的，而他可能会被绞死的想法，以及他真的会被绞死的恐惧，都大大增加了我的恐怖。当他不睡觉，或者用他那副破旧的牌玩一种复杂的耐心纸牌游戏时——这是我以前和以后从未见过的游戏，他用小刀在桌子上标记赢得的牌数——当他既不做这两件事时，他会让我给他读书——“外文，亲爱的孩子！”当我顺从时，他一句话也不懂，却会站在火炉前，用一个表演者的神态打量我，而我会透过用来遮住脸的手指之间看到他，用哑剧的方式向家具示意，让它们注意到我的熟练。那个被他亵渎地创造出来的畸形生物追逐的假想学生，并不比我更可怜——我被创造我的生物追逐着，对他产生的反感却更强烈，并且这种反感随着他对我的赞赏和喜爱而愈发加深。

title: Great Expectations · 选段 10
author: Charles Dickens
paragraphs: There was something so natural and winning in Clara’s resigned way of looking at these stores in detail, as Herbert pointed them out; and something so confiding, loving, and innocent in her modest manner of yielding herself to Herbert’s embracing arm; and something so gentle in her, so much needing protection on Mill Pond Bank, by Chinks’s Basin, and the Old Green Copper Rope-walk, with Old Barley growling in the beam,—that I would not have undone the engagement between her and Herbert for all the money in the pocket-book I had never opened.

I was looking at her with pleasure and admiration, when suddenly the growl swelled into a roar again, and a frightful bumping noise was heard above, as if a giant with a wooden leg were trying to bore it through the ceiling to come at us. Upon this Clara said to Herbert, “Papa wants me, darling!” and ran away.
“There is an unconscionable old shark for you!” said Herbert. “What do you suppose he wants now, Handel?”

“That’s it!” cried Herbert, as if I had made a guess of extraordinary merit. “He keeps his grog ready mixed in a little tub on the table. Wait a moment, and you’ll hear Clara lift him up to take some. There he goes!” Another roar, with a prolonged shake at the end. “Now,” said Herbert, as it was succeeded by silence, “he’s drinking. Now,” said Herbert, as the growl resounded in the beam once more, “he’s down again on his back!”

Clara returned soon afterwards, and Herbert accompanied me upstairs to see our charge. As we passed Mr. Barley’s door, he was heard hoarsely muttering within, in a strain that rose and fell like wind, the following Refrain, in which I substitute good wishes for something quite the reverse:—

“Ahoy! Bless your eyes, here’s old Bill Barley. Here’s old Bill Barley, bless your eyes. Here’s old Bill Barley on the flat of his back, by the Lord. Lying on the flat of his back like a drifting old dead flounder, here’s your old Bill Barley, bless your eyes. Ahoy! Bless you.”

In this strain of consolation, Herbert informed me the invisible Barley would commune with himself by the day and night together; Often, while it was light, having, at the same time, one eye at a telescope which was fitted on his bed for the convenience of sweeping the river.

In his two cabin rooms at the top of the house, which were fresh and airy, and in which Mr. Barley was less audible than below, I found Provis comfortably settled. He expressed no alarm, and seemed to feel none that was worth mentioning; but it struck me that he was softened,—indefinably, for I could not have said how, and could never afterwards recall how when I tried, but certainly.

The opportunity that the day’s rest had given me for reflection had resulted in my fully determining to say nothing to him respecting Compeyson. For anything I knew, his animosity towards the man might otherwise lead to his seeking him out and rushing on his own destruction. Therefore, when Herbert and I sat down with him by his fire, I asked him first of all whether he relied on Wemmick’s judgment and sources of information?

This I did accurately, with the reservation just mentioned; and I told him how Wemmick had heard, in Newgate prison (whether from officers or prisoners I could not say), that he was under some suspicion, and that my chambers had been watched; how Wemmick had recommended his keeping close for a time, and my keeping away from him; and what Wemmick had said about getting him abroad. I added, that of course, when the time came, I should go with him, or should follow close upon him, as might be safest in Wemmick’s judgment. What was to follow that I did not touch upon; neither, indeed, was I at all clear or comfortable about it in my own mind, now that I saw him in that softer condition, and in declared peril for my sake. As to altering my way of living by enlarging my expenses, I put it to him whether in our present unsettled and difficult circumstances, it would not be simply ridiculous, if it were no worse?
paragraphsZh: 克拉拉以一种顺从的方式仔细观察这些商店时，赫伯特一边指出，她身上有一种如此自然和迷人的特质；她以谦逊的方式把自己交付给赫伯特的怀抱，显得如此信任、充满爱意和天真；她又是如此温柔，在米尔池岸边、在支流盆地旁、在老绿铜绳道上，如此需要保护，老巴利在横梁上咆哮——以至于我不会为了我从未打开过的钱包里的所有钱而取消她和赫伯特之间的订婚。
我正带着喜悦和钦佩看着她，突然下面的咆哮声再次变成了怒吼，上面传来可怕的撞击声，仿佛一个木腿巨人正试图把天花板打穿来找我们。对此，克拉拉对赫伯特说：“爸爸要我了，亲爱的！”然后跑开了。
“这就是个无良的老家伙！”赫伯特说。“你猜他现在想干什么，汉德尔？”
“就是这样！”赫伯特喊道，好像我提出了一个非凡的猜测。“他把朗姆酒提前调好，放在桌子上的一个小桶里。等一下，你就会听到克拉拉把他抱起来喝一些。看，他开始了！”又是一声吼叫，尾音拉得很长。“现在，”赫伯特说，当吼声戛然而止，周围陷入寂静，“他在喝酒。现在，”赫伯特说，当咆哮声再次在房梁中回响，“他又仰面倒下了！”
克拉拉不久后就回来了，赫伯特陪我上楼去看我们的照顾对象。当我们经过巴利先生的门时，听到他在里面嘶哑地咕哝着，声调起伏如风，我在下面的副歌中用美好的祝愿代替了完全相反的东西：——
“嘿！祝你的眼睛幸福，这是老比尔·巴利。这是老比尔·巴利，祝你的眼睛幸福。这是老比尔·巴利仰躺着，天哪。像一条漂浮的老死比目鱼一样仰躺着，这是你的老比尔·巴利，祝你的眼睛幸福。嘿！保佑你。”
在这种安慰之中，赫伯特告诉我，那看不见的巴利会在白天和黑夜与他交流；经常在白天，一边用安装在他床上的望远镜扫视河流，同时用一只眼睛观察它。
在他位于房顶的两间小舱房里，那儿清新通风，且比楼下巴利先生所在的地方要安静，我发现普洛维斯安顿得很舒适。他没有表现出任何惊恐，似乎也没有感到值得一提的害怕；但我注意到，他的态度有些柔和——具体如何说不清楚，我当时无法描述，后来即便努力回想也想不起，但确实如此。
白天休息给了我思考的机会，结果我完全下定决心对他关于康佩森的事情一言不提。因为据我所知，他对那人的敌意可能会促使他去寻找他，从而自取灭亡。因此，当赫伯特和我坐在他的火旁时，我首先问他是否依赖温米克的判断和信息来源？

我准确地做了这一点，只是在之前提到的保留下；我还告诉他，韦米克在新门监狱听说（我无法说是从官员还是囚犯那里听到的）他受到一些怀疑，而且我的书房也有人监视；韦米克建议他暂时保持低调，而我则离他远一些；以及韦米克关于帮他出国所说的事情。我补充说，当然，当时机成熟时，我会和他一起走，或尽可能紧随其后，因为这样在韦米克看来最安全。至于随后会发生什么，我没有触及；事实上，现在看到他处于那种柔弱状态，又明确因我而处于危险之中，我自己心里也一点都不清楚，也不舒服。至于通过增加开支来改变我的生活方式，我问他，在我们目前这个不稳定且困难的情况下，如果这样做不会更糟，会不会简直是荒谬的？

title: The Federalist Papers · 选段 4
author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, John Jay
source: Project Gutenberg · Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, John Jay
paragraphs: This is an idea not superficial or futile, but solid and weighty. It deserves the most serious and mature consideration of every prudent and honest man of whatever party. If such men will make a firm and solemn pause, and meditate dispassionately on the importance of this interesting idea; if they will contemplate it in all its attitudes, and trace it to all its consequences, they will not hesitate to part with trivial objections to a Constitution, the rejection of which would in all probability put a final period to the Union. The airy phantoms that flit before the distempered imaginations of some of its adversaries would quickly give place to the more substantial forms of dangers, real, certain, and formidable.

1. This objection will be fully examined in its proper place, and it will be shown that the only natural precaution which could have been taken on this subject has been taken; and a much better one than is to be found in any constitution that has been heretofore framed in America, most of which contain no guard at all on this subject.

A FIRM Union will be of the utmost moment to the peace and liberty of the States, as a barrier against domestic faction and insurrection. It is impossible to read the history of the petty republics of Greece and Italy without feeling sensations of horror and disgust at the distractions with which they were continually agitated, and at the rapid succession of revolutions by which they were kept in a state of perpetual vibration between the extremes of tyranny and anarchy. If they exhibit occasional calms, these only serve as short-lived contrast to the furious storms that are to succeed. If now and then intervals of felicity open to view, we behold them with a mixture of regret, arising from the reflection that the pleasing scenes before us are soon to be overwhelmed by the tempestuous waves of sedition and party rage. If momentary rays of glory break forth from the gloom, while they dazzle us with a transient and fleeting brilliancy, they at the same time admonish us to lament that the vices of government should pervert the direction and tarnish the lustre of those bright talents and exalted endowments for which the favored soils that produced them have been so justly celebrated.

From the disorders that disfigure the annals of those republics the advocates of despotism have drawn arguments, not only against the forms of republican government, but against the very principles of civil liberty. They have decried all free government as inconsistent with the order of society, and have indulged themselves in malicious exultation over its friends and partisans. Happily for mankind, stupendous fabrics reared on the basis of liberty, which have flourished for ages, have, in a few glorious instances, refuted their gloomy sophisms. And, I trust, America will be the broad and solid foundation of other edifices, not less magnificent, which will be equally permanent monuments of their errors.

But it is not to be denied that the portraits they have sketched of republican government were too just copies of the originals from which they were taken. If it had been found impracticable to have devised models of a more perfect structure, the enlightened friends to liberty would have been obliged to abandon the cause of that species of government as indefensible. The science of politics, however, like most other sciences, has received great improvement. The efficacy of various principles is now well understood, which were either not known at all, or imperfectly known to the ancients. The regular distribution of power into distinct departments; the introduction of legislative balances and checks; the institution of courts composed of judges holding their offices during good behavior; the representation of the people in the legislature by deputies of their own election: these are wholly new discoveries, or have made their principal progress towards perfection in modern times. They are means, and powerful means, by which the excellences of republican government may be retained and its imperfections lessened or avoided. To this catalogue of circumstances that tend to the amelioration of popular systems of civil government, I shall venture, however novel it may appear to some, to add one more, on a principle which has been made the foundation of an objection to the new Constitution; I mean the ENLARGEMENT of the ORBIT within which such systems are to revolve, either in respect to the dimensions of a single State or to the consolidation of several smaller States into one great Confederacy. The latter is that which immediately concerns the object under consideration. It will, however, be of use to examine the principle in its application to a single State, which shall be attended to in another place.
paragraphsZh: 这是一个非肤浅或徒劳的想法，而是坚实而分量的。无论哪个党派，每一位谨慎诚实的人都值得认真而成熟地思考。如果这些人能坚定而庄重地停下来，冷静地思考这个有趣思想的重要性;如果他们能以各种态度审视它，追溯其所有后果，他们就不会犹豫放弃对宪法的琐碎反对，而拒绝宪法很可能将为联邦带来最后的阶段。那些在某些对手混乱想象中飘荡的幻影，很快就会被更实质、确定且可怕的危险所取代。
1. 这个反对意见将在适当的地方被全面审查，并且将显示在这个问题上唯一可以采取的自然预防措施已经被采取；而且采用的措施比迄今为止在美国制定的任何宪法中所能找到的要好得多，这些宪法大多数在这个问题上根本没有任何防护措施。

一个坚强的联邦对各州的和平与自由将具有至关重要的意义，它是抵御国内派系和叛乱的屏障。无法阅读希腊和意大利小共和国的历史而不感到恐惧和厌恶，因为它们不断受到各种纷扰的困扰，以及快速接连的革命使它们在暴政与无政府状态的极端之间持续振荡。如果它们偶尔显现平静，那也只是即将到来的狂风暴雨的短暂对比。如果偶尔出现幸福的间隙，我们看到它们时心中会夹杂着遗憾，因为意识到眼前的美好景象很快就会被动乱的浪潮和党派的愤怒所吞没。如果短暂的荣耀之光从阴暗中迸发出来，虽然它们以瞬息且转瞬即逝的辉煌使我们目眩，但它们同时告诫我们，应当哀叹政府的恶行扭曲了那些明亮天赋和崇高才能的方向，并玷污了它们的光辉，而这些才能和天赋正是孕育它们的宝地应当受到如此公正赞誉的原因。

从那些共和国家年鉴中所显示的弊病中，专制的拥护者提出了论据，不仅反对共和政府的形式，而且反对公民自由的基本原则。他们谴责所有自由政府与社会秩序不符，并在其朋友和支持者的不幸上幸灾乐祸。对人类而言，幸运的是，那些以自由为基础建立的宏伟体系，经过几个世纪的繁荣发展，在少数辉煌的例子中，已经驳斥了他们阴暗的诡辩。我相信，美洲将成为其他同样宏伟的建筑的宽广而坚固的基础，这些建筑同样将成为他们错误的永久纪念。

但是，不能否认的是，他们所描绘的共和政府的画像，过于忠实地复制了所借鉴的原型。如果人们发现设计出更完美结构的模型是不切实际的，那么开明的自由拥护者将不得不放弃这种类型的政府，因为它不可辩护。然而，政治学这门学科，像大多数其他科学一样，已经取得了很大进步。各种原则的效力如今已被充分理解，而这些原则在古人时要么根本未知，要么了解得不完全。权力分配到不同部门的常规；引入立法上的制衡；设立由司法官员组成、秉持良好行为任职的法院；人民在立法机构中通过自己选举的代表进行代表：这些都是完全新的发现，或是在近代才取得主要进展的完善方式。它们是手段，而且是强有力的手段，通过这些方式可以保持共和政府的优点，并减少或避免其缺点。对于有助于改善民众民事政府体系的这些情况的目录，我将冒昧地（尽管这对某些人可能显得新奇）再添加一条，依据的是一个已被用于对新宪法提出反对意见的原则；我的意思是扩大这些体系运行的轨道，无论是就单个州的规模而言，还是就将几个较小的州合并为一个大联邦而言。后者是直接涉及所讨论目标的。不过，将这一原则应用于单个州的情况也将是有用的，这将在其他地方讨论。

title: The Federalist Papers · 选段 5
author: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, John Jay
source: Project Gutenberg · Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, John Jay
paragraphs: To this great national object, a NAVY, union will contribute in various ways. Every institution will grow and flourish in proportion to the quantity and extent of the means concentred towards its formation and support. A navy of the United States, as it would embrace the resources of all, is an object far less remote than a navy of any single State or partial confederacy, which would only embrace the resources of a single part. It happens, indeed, that different portions of confederated America possess each some peculiar advantage for this essential establishment. The more southern States furnish in greater abundance certain kinds of naval stores--tar, pitch, and turpentine. Their wood for the construction of ships is also of a more solid and lasting texture.
